<meta>This page transitions from the flyleaf into the main thematic notes of the manuscript. The writer begins to defend the terminology used by the 13th-century philosopher Ramon Llull by grounding his "unusual" language in the authority of the Bible.</meta>

I say

Note that Ramon <note>original: "Raymundus." This refers to Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher and theologian.</note> is the author of the doctrine of correlatives <note>original: "doctrine correlativorum." A central Lullian concept where every divine attribute (like Goodness) is understood through an active, passive, and connecting principle (e.g., the Goodener, the Goodened, and the act of Goodening).</note> which are never found among others. Page 3.

Note that propositions composed of principles, even if they seem unusual and outside the common way of speaking to some, are not <unclear>absurd</unclear> but are more in harmony and conformity with the language of Holy Scripture. For in many places in Holy Scripture such a way of speaking is found, as seen in Exodus, chapter 15.

For he has been gloriously magnified; the horse and the rider he has thrown into the sea. <note>Exodus 15:1. The author uses this to show the "magnified" form of the attribute of Greatness.</note>

<margin>cb. t.</margin> Where Greatness <note>original: "magnitudo"</note> is seen combined with glory and <unclear>majesty</unclear> and power.

Your right hand, O Lord, is magnified in strength <margin>cet d.</margin> and has struck the enemy; where greatness, power, and <term>unparity</term> <note>original: "unparitay." In Lullian thought, this likely refers to the "imparity" or the unique, non-equal distinctions between the various divine attributes within God's unity.</note> are revealed.

In the multitude of your glory you have cast down your adversaries. <margin>cb. d.</margin> where greatness, glory, and <insert>+</insert> <unclear>infinity</unclear> are revealed.

<summary>The author defends the unique philosophical language of Ramon Llull (specifically his "doctrine of correlatives") by demonstrating that similar structures and combinations of divine attributes appear in the Biblical Song of Moses in Exodus.</summary>

<keywords>Ramon Llull, doctrine of correlatives, Exodus 15, divine attributes, Greatness, Power, philosophy and scripture, unparity</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page serves as the title page for the work, following the blank flyleaf noted on the previous page.</meta>

**Of the enlightened professor of Sacred Scripture** <note>original: *sacre pagine*, a traditional term for a doctor of theology or professor of the Bible</note>, **the most distinguished master Ramon Llull. The Great, General, and Ultimate Art**: the achiever and **key-bearer** <note>original: *clauigera*; the book is presented as a "key" to unlock all other branches of knowledge</note> of whichever of Llull’s own arts and sciences, providing an easier entrance to them. Never before has it been **more suitably committed to the art of printing**; and refined by Master Bernard de Lavinheta, **a most faithful interpreter of that art**. Together with **figures** <note>technical diagrams used in Llull's logical system</note> properly **inserted** in their place, which are **explanatory** of the whole work. Moreover, with titles and annotations added to each **part, chapter, and rubric; with an added alphabetical index** or inventory embracing the **more choice maxims**, referring back to the page numbers.

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page follows the title page, providing introductory verses and epigrams that praise Ramon Llull and his "Great Art." The previous page introduced the book as a "key" to all sciences; this page elevates Llull’s divinely inspired wisdom above classical philosophy.</meta>

## By Laurentius Theobaldus of Le Mans regarding the doc-
## trines of this art devised by Ramon Llull—a man skilled in
## no language or art except by divine inspiration: 
## an epigram addressed to the reader.

What harvest does this little book hold for you, O refined reader,
Though the honor of the agate <note>The agate was often associated with protection and value in the Renaissance; here it suggests that even a small or rare thing can be precious.</note> be slender and rare.
It explains here what the chorus of doctors—the very pattern of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom.</note>—
Did not reveal in the bright schools of Athens.
What neither our ancient age nor our own era knew better:
Llull gave this ethereal art from heaven.
Whatever Aristotle held, whatever famous
Greece weighed, whatever King Croesus <note>Known for his legendary wealth; here used to suggest the "wealth" of worldly knowledge.</note> or the Sorbonne <note>The famous theological college of the University of Paris.</note> possesses.
With an easy genius he penetrated to the heavenly axes <note>The poles of the celestial spheres or the heavens themselves.</note>
And through pure virtue completed this great work.
If rash Icarus had skimmed the lowest seas
With his wings, he would have fallen then into the icy waters.
And because he desired to see the starry seats,
He was cast down when the sun's help was withdrawn.
Llull turned his flights from the middle to the depths,
And yet the sea does not hold the man, for his heights are secure.
Among the heaps of books, O refined reader (for he holds the
Trophies), be wise and choose this work.

### A chained poem <note>original: *concathenatum Carmen*; a poetic form where the end of one phrase or line is repeated at the start of the next.</note> concerning the work.

The work touches upon mystical things / but the work which touches upon mystical things
Lays down a great burden / but the burden which it lays down:
Seeks out wide baths <note>A metaphor for spiritual or intellectual cleansing and purification.</note>: or the work which touches upon mystical things.

-> The author to Choerilus <note>original: αὐτ. προς Χαιριλ.; Choerilus was an ancient Greek poet often used as a symbol for a poet of varying quality.</note> <-

You strike the myriad forms, O Muse of many shapes:
Choerilus does not easily sow simple things among the wise. <note>original: μυριδια τας τυππεις αυθις πολυειδια μουσα: / ουκ ευσπειρει απλους Χαιριλος αμφι σοφων. This Greek couplet suggests that the wisdom contained herein is complex and multi-faceted, not meant for the simple-minded.</note>

<summary>This page features a series of introductory poems (epigrams) by Laurentius Theobaldus of Le Mans praising Ramon Llull’s "Great Art" as a divinely inspired system that surpasses classical Greek philosophy and contemporary academic knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>Ramon Llull, Laurentius Theobaldus Cenomanus, epigram, divine inspiration, Aristotle, Sorbonne, Greek philosophy, Icarus metaphor, chained poem</keywords>

**THIS GREAT ART**, general and final, was begun by the Blessed Raymond at Lyon upon the Rhône <note>original: "Lugduni super Rhodanum"—The city of Lyon, France, situated on the Rhône river.</note> in the month of November, in the year of the Lord 1305. And it was finished by him in the city of Pisa, in the monastery of Saint Dominic, to the praise and honor of God, in the month of March, in the year of the Lord 1308 of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. May it be commended to Him and to the Blessed Virgin Mary, His mother. **AMEN.**

# TO THE BLESSED RAYMOND
## LULL. A SHORT PRAYER. <note>original: *Oratiuncula*—A small prayer or brief oratorical address.</note>

> To you, Raymond, bearing the palm of martyrdom, <note>Raymond Llull (c. 1232–1316) was a philosopher and missionary who, according to tradition, was martyred in North Africa.</note>
> I fly for refuge; shatter the dog-like teeth <note>A common medieval metaphor for the "barking" of critics, detractors, or heretics.</note> aimed at you;

> of doctrine; may it be revealed, for it has lain hidden too much, concealed from the world.

<meta>This page transitions from the general front matter and prayers found on the previous page to the actual text of the *Ars Magna Generalis et Ultima*. It establishes the philosophical necessity of a "general science" and introduces the symbolic alphabet that forms the foundation of Llull’s combinatory logic.</meta>

->Prologue.<-

# The Ultimate General Great Art of the Illuminated Doctor, Master Raymond Lull.

**S**ince we have produced many general arts, we wish to explain them more clearly through this one which we call the "ultimate," because we do not intend to create another after this. Indeed, we compile it from the others and explicitly add some new elements.

<margin>The human intellect consists more in opinion than in science.</margin>
¶ Because the human intellect is established far more in opinion than in science <note>In this context, "science" (*scientia*) refers to certain, demonstrable knowledge, whereas "opinion" refers to probable but uncertain belief.</note>; and since every science has its own specific principles which differ from the principles of other sciences; therefore, the intellect requires and desires a single general science for all sciences. This science should have its own general principles in which the principles of other particular sciences are implied and contained, just as the particular is contained within the universal. The reason for this is so that other principles may be subordinated, ordered, and regulated by these [general] principles, so that the intellect may find rest in those sciences through true understanding and be removed and distanced from erroneous opinions.

<margin>This science is a prerequisite for the others.</margin>
¶ Through this science, other sciences can be easily acquired. For the particular principles of those sciences shine through and appear in the general principles of this art, provided that the particular principles are applied to the principles of this art, just as a part is applied to its whole.

<margin>General principles of this art.</margin>
¶ The principles for this art are these: Goodness. Greatness. Eternity or duration. Power. Wisdom. Will. Virtue. Truth. Glory. Difference. Concordance. Contrariety. Beginning. Middle. End. Superiority. Equality. And Inferiority. And they are called "general" because all the "goodnesses" of other sciences are applicable to one general Goodness. And I say the same for all "greatnesses" in relation to one general Greatness. And so it must be said for the others in their own way.

---

<margin>How this science is called "general."</margin>
¶ Furthermore, this science can be called general because it has general questions applicable to all other arguments, whatever they may be. For all [arguments] are implied in these questions. And they are these, namely: Whether it is. What it is. From what it is. Why it is. How much it is. Of what kind it is. When it is. Where it is. In what way it is. And with what it is. And there are ten, as they appear here numbered.

<margin>Note on the nature of this Art.</margin>
¶ Likewise, this art is general by reason of the mixing of principles and rules which it possesses, as will be shown below. For just as a proposition taken in a common sense is general to all propositions, so in their own way these composite principles, taken in common, are general to all particular composite principles. ¶ But so that doubt may be removed: I say that all other principles are particular with respect to these principles of this art. Just as "Great Goodness," which is composite, is common to the goodness of Peter and William, and of a horse, and so on for others.

<margin>On the division of this art.</margin>
### ¶ On the division of this art.
¶ This art is divided into 14 parts: namely, the Alphabet. The Figures. The Definitions. The Rules. The Table. The Clearing <note>original: *Evacuationem*—In Lullian logic, this refers to the systematic exhaustion of all possible combinations within a figure.</note> of the third figure. The Multiplication of the fourth figure. The Mixing. The Nine Subjects. The Application. The Questions. The Habits. and the Method of Teaching.

<margin>First principal part of this art.</margin>
## ¶ The first principal part: on the Alphabet.

<margin>The alphabet of this art is this.</margin>
**T**he Alphabet for this art is this:
<margin>Explanation of the alphabet.</margin>
¶ **B**: signifies Goodness. Difference. "Whether?" God. Justice. And Avarice.
¶ **C**: signifies Greatness. Concordance. "What?" Angel. Prudence. And Gluttony.
¶ **D**: signifies Eternity or duration. Contrariety. "From what?" Heaven. Fortitude. And Lust.
¶ **E**: signifies Power. Beginning. "Why?" Man. Temperance. And Pride.
¶ **F**: signifies Wisdom. Middle. "How much?" Imagination. Faith. And Sloth.
¶ **G**: signifies Will. End. "Of what kind?" The Sensitive power <note>The "sensitive" refers to the animal soul or the faculty of perception.</note>. Hope. And Envy.
¶ **H**: signifies Virtue. Superiority. "When?" The Vegetative power <note>The "vegetative" refers to the level of living things that grow but do not feel, like plants.</note>. Charity. And Anger.
¶ **I**: signifies Truth. Equality. "Where?" The Elemental power <note>The "elemental" refers to the basic physical building blocks of matter (earth, air, fire, water).</note>. Patience. And Falsehood.

B

<summary>This page introduces the "Ars Magna," explaining the need for a universal science based on general principles and defining the symbolic alphabet (letters B through I) used to represent various philosophical and theological concepts.</summary>
<keywords>Ramon Llull, Ars Magna, General Principles, Lullian Alphabet, Scholastic Logic, Combinatory Logic, Divine Attributes</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the general introduction. Having argued for the necessity of a "general science" to unify all knowledge, the author now begins the second part of the work, which introduces the symbolic alphabet and the geometric "Figures" that allow the practitioner to calculate truths.</meta>

<header>Second Part</header>

<margin>
Note.

Why the alphabet was established.
</margin>
**A** signifies: glory; minority <note>In Llull's system, "minority" is one of the relative principles used to compare the scale or importance of subjects.</note>; how and with whom; the instrumental; piety; and inconstancy. This alphabet, indeed, must be known by heart; for if not, the practitioner <term>artista: a student or master of the Lullian "Art"</term> will be unable to use this art or put it into practice.

The alphabet in this art exists so that through it the principles and questions of this art may be signified, along with those things contained within them, and so that the subject of inquiry may be brought forward, in order that the understanding may be true and certain, and not doubtful.

## The second principal part of this work: which is concerning the figures; and first concerning the first figure, signified by A.

# THE FIRST FIGURE

<note>A circular diagram known as the 'First Figure' of the Lullian Art. It features a central letter 'A'—representing God or the Unity of the system—surrounded by three rings of text and a nine-pointed star connecting all segments. This star illustrates that every divine attribute is interconnected and convertible with every other.</note>

**Outer Ring (Letters):**
B | C | D | E | F | G | H | I | K

**Middle Ring (Principles):**
GOODNESS | GREATNESS | DURATION | POWER | WISDOM | WILL | VIRTUE | TRUTH | GLORY

**Inner Ring (Attributes):**
GOOD | GREAT | ENDURING | POWERFUL | WISE | WILLING | VIRTUOUS | TRUE | GLORIOUS

<summary>This page introduces the symbolic alphabet of the Lullian Art and presents the 'First Figure' (Figure A), which maps nine divine attributes (Dignities) to specific letters to enable logical combinations.</summary>
<keywords>Ramon Llull, First Figure, Lullian Art, Divine Dignities, alphabet, Goodness, Greatness, Duration, Power, Wisdom, Will, Virtue, Truth, Glory</keywords>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page follows the introduction to the Lullian alphabet. Having established the letters used to represent fundamental concepts, the author now introduces the geometric "Figures"—the core mechanical components of Ramon Llull’s "Art"—which allow these concepts to be combined and analyzed. This page specifically focuses on the First Figure (A) and the beginning of the Second Figure (T).</meta>

# On the Figures.

<margin>Four figures.</margin>
<margin>Concerning the first figure / which is circular.</margin>
**T**here are four figures: as shown on the present page. ¶ The first figure is designated by the letter **A**: and it is circular, divided into nine chambers <note>In Llull's diagrams, "chambers" refers to the segments or compartments within the circular figure.</note>. In the first chamber, indeed, stands **B**: in the second, **C**: and so on for the others. It is called "circular" because the subject is changed into the predicate and vice versa: as when it is said: "great goodness / good greatness" or "eternal greatness / great eternity." Concerning God: "God is good," and so on for the others in their own way.

<margin>What the circulation of the first figure is useful for.</margin>
¶ Through such circulation, the practitioner <term>artista: a student or master of the Lullian "Art"</term> will be able to recognize those things which are convertible <note>In logic, two terms are "convertible" if they can be swapped without changing the truth of the statement (e.g., in Llull's system, "God" and "Goodness" are interchangeable).</note> and those which are not: just as "God is good" and similar statements can be converted. However, "God" and "angel" are not convertible; nor are "goodness" and "angel"; nor are "his goodness" and "his greatness"; and so it goes for other terms. ¶ In this figure, all things are included, such as when it is said: "God is good, great, eternal," and so on for the rest. "An angel is good, great, durable," and so on. "Avarice is not good, but evil," and so on in its own way. ¶ In this figure, the proper and appropriated attributes <term>passiones: properties or characteristics of a subject</term> existing between the subject and the predicate are recognized. "Properly," <margin>proper attribute</margin> such as when God is good, great, and similar. And an angel, who has innate goodness, greatness, and the like. "Appropriately," <margin>appropriated attribute</margin> such as an evil angel, who has appropriated malice; and this is meant in a moral sense. And so it is with fire: which has a "good" and "great" dryness by means of the earth. And a human, morally: having "good" and "great" prudence, justice, and so forth for the rest. ¶ Indeed, the practitioner <margin>note: the practitioner must be skilled</margin> of this art must become accustomed to and visualize this figure, and apply it to the proposition at hand, according to what we have said about it, so that the intellect may be able to attain truths through it: and this truly and realistically.
¶ Here ends the explanation of the first figure.

# SECOND FIGURE

<margin>Absolute corruption <note>original: "Corruptio absoluta." In this context, "corruption" refers to the natural breakdown or decay of physical things.</note></margin>
<margin>Concerning joined composites <note>original: "unitis compositis." This refers to how different elements are unified into a single compound thing.</note></margin>

->**T**<-

<note>This page displays the "Second Figure" (Figure T) from the Lullian Art, representing the relations between things. It consists of a nine-pointed star (representing nine relative principles) enclosed within concentric circles containing ontological categories. This figure is used to compare terms—for instance, asking if two things are different, equal, or in opposition.</note>

**Outer Circle Segments:**
<note>These segments define the "scope" or levels at which the relationships in the star can be applied.</note>

- **B**: Between the sensible & the sensible; between the sensible & the intellectual; between the intellectual & the intellectual. <note>In Llull's philosophy, "sensible" refers to physical things we can perceive with our senses, while "intellectual" refers to abstract things known by the mind, like angels or concepts.</note>
- **E**: Cause. Quantity. Time.
- **H**: Between substance & substance; between substance & accident; between accident & accident. <term>substance and accident: "Substance" is the essence of a thing (like a tree), while an "accident" is a non-essential quality (like being green or tall).</term>
- **C**: Between the sensible & the sensible; between the sensible & the intellectual; between the intellectual & the intellectual.
- **F**: Of conjunction. Of measurement. Of extremity.
- **I**: Between substance & substance; between substance & accident; between accident & accident.
- **D**: Between the sensible & the senses; between the sensible & the intellectual; between the intellectual & the intellectual.
- **G**: Of perfection. Of termination <note>The "end" or completion of a thing.</note>. Of privation <note>The absence or lack of a quality.</note>.

**Inner Star Points (Clockwise from top):**

- Difference <gloss>differentia</gloss>
- Beginning <gloss>principium</gloss>
- Greatness <gloss>maioritas</gloss> <note>Also translated as "superiority."</note>
- Agreement <gloss>concordantia</gloss>
- Middle <gloss>medium</gloss>
- Equality <gloss>equalitas</gloss>
- Opposition <gloss>contrarietas</gloss>
- End <gloss>finis</gloss>
- Smallness <gloss>minoritas</gloss> <note>Also translated as "inferiority."</note>

folio iii.

# CONCERNING THE FIGURES

<margin>**The second triangular figure.**</margin>
**T**he second figure consists of three triangles: namely, those of **difference**, **concordance**, and **contrariety**, as they appear within it. $\P$ Above the angle of difference are written: the sensible and the sensible; the sensible and the intellectual; and the intellectual and the intellectual. The same applies to the angles of concordance and contrariety. This is to signify the difference that exists between one sensible thing and another—for example, between one body and another. It also signifies the difference between the sensible and the intellectual—such as between the body and the soul—and between the intellectual and the intellectual—such as between God and an angel. The same logic follows for concordance and contrariety. $\P$ Above the angle of the **beginning** <note>original: "principii"</note> are written: cause, quantity, and time. By "cause," the substantial principles are signified, which are the efficient, formal, material, and final causes. By "quantity" and "time," the accidental principles are signified, such as the nine categories <term>nine categories: refers to Aristotle's 'predicaments,' the basic ways in which things can be described, such as quality, relation, or place</term>. $\P$ Above the angle of the **middle** are written: junction, measurement, and extremity, to signify the three species of the "middle." For instance, the middle of junction is like a nail that joins two posts together. The middle of measurement is like a center point that exists equally in the middle of a circle. The middle of the extremities is like a line in the middle between two points <unclear>points</unclear>.

<margin>**Three species of the end.**</margin>
$\P$ Above the angle of the **end** <note>original: "finis"</note> are written: termination, privation, and final cause, to denote that there are three species of an end. For there is an end of termination, like the boundary of a kingdom or a field. Likewise, there is an end of privation, such as death, which finishes life. And there is a causal end, such as God, who is the end and cause of all things. $\P$ Above the angle of **majority**—and the same for the angles of **equality** and **minority**—is written: "between substance and substance." This is to signify that one substance is greater than another, such as the substance of a human, which is greater in goodness or virtue than the substance of a stone. $\P$ Likewise, "between substance and accident," to signify that a substance is greater than an accident, such as the substance of a human being greater than his size <note>original: "quantitas"</note> and similar qualities. $\P$ And "between accident and accident," to denote that one accident is greater than another, such as understanding being greater than sensing. The same can be said in its own way regarding minority, since these terms are relative to one another. And between substance and substance there is equality, as with a human and a stone, which are equal in the general category of substance. Between accident and accident there is equality, such as understanding and loving, which are equal in the category of accidents. And between substance and accident there is equality, such as quantity and its subject, which are equal through extension and surface area.

<margin>**The green angle.**</margin>
$\P$ The green angle, which consists of difference, concordance, and contrariety, is general to all things. For whatever exists is either in a state of difference, concordance, or contrariety. Within the triangle itself, everything is implicit. However, **difference** is more general than concordance or contrariety. For more things can be different than can be concordant or contrary. For example, Peter and Martin are different; they agree in species <note>original: "specie conveniunt," meaning they are both human</note>; but they are contrary in their characters, for one is just while the other is unjust. And so it goes for others in their own way.

<margin><insert>M. 1</insert></margin>
$\P$ Difference is the cause of plurality, just as concordance is the cause of unity. For just as difference distinguishes between one thing and another, so concordance composes many things into one. Contrariety, however, corrupts and dissolves. Therefore, just as the green triangle exists naturally in a subject, so the intellect is morally discursive: distinguishing, concording, descending, and ascending through the three species of difference, concordance, and contrariety mentioned above. And so, the intellect with "difference" is simply general to its object. The same applies to concordance and contrariety. But when it constrains itself through the scale established in the three species, it is neither entirely general nor entirely special. For example, when it says: "difference exists between the sensible and the sensible," and so on; but when it descends to individuals, it is, in a moral sense, entirely particular.

<margin>**The red triangle.**</margin>
$\P$ The red triangle, which consists of the **beginning**, **middle**, and **end**, is general to all things, because it contains all things within itself; whatever exists is either in the beginning, the middle, or the end. Outside of these three terms, no being can exist. The "beginning" is a being to which all other beings are subordinate. Yet a universal beginning can by no means exist without nature or morality, having within itself that which begins, that which is begun, and the act of beginning <note>original: "principiante, principiatum & principiare." This is a core Lullian concept: every attribute has an active, passive, and verbal form.</note>.

<margin><insert>triangular principles</insert></margin>
For just as the nature of heat cannot exist without a heater, a thing to be heated, and the act of heating, so the nature of a "beginning" cannot exist without the nature of the three things predicted above. Thus, the artist <note>The practitioner of the Lullian Art.</note> must recognize these three in the universal beginning, because they belong to its essence causally through the proper qualities of the subject. They do not exist merely occasionally, for they are acquired in a moral sense. Causal principles speak of necessity, while occasional principles speak of contingency and "well-being." $\P$ And so the artist must ascend and descend from the universal to the particular and vice-versa. $\P$ The "middle" is as universal as the "beginning." For just as an agent with a principle...

B iii

Llull explains how the mind uses these categories to compare sensible physical objects and intellectual concepts like the soul or God.</summary>

->Second Part<-

...begins with the beginning. Thus, it mediates with the middle. And also through the middle <note>referring to the "middle of junction" mentioned on the previous page</note>: it joins distinct beings into one composite or mixture. But through the middle of measurement: it measures acts / just as the intellect [measures] its own understanding, existing in the middle between the one who understands and that which is understood : and sight [measures] its own seeing. The generator [measures] its own generating / and the judge his own judging : and so on for other similar things.

¶ Through the middle of extremities: there are essences and continuations / just as goodness, which is a simple essence existing as the middle between greatness and duration / having within itself "good-ing" <note>original: "bonificare." Llull creates verbs from nouns to describe the active expression of an essence</note> / existing in the middle between the "good-er" <note>the active principle</note> and the "good-able" <note>the passive principle</note> / which join together in the act of "good-ing": and all three are one undivided goodness: though morally, not at all. These three species of the "middle" are indeed the ladder through which the intellect descends and ascends by investigating the middles of beings. And in a similar way, it follows concerning the "end" <note>original: "fine"</note> / with which the efficient cause brings beings to rest at the ultimate goal. But in the "privative end," it does not rest at all / because it is privative <note>referring to the end of a thing's existence or its lack; a "negative" end</note>: and in the "terminative end" / one being is indeed separated from another: one rest from another. Such an investigation is very useful and clear for the intellect to reach the beings of things. 

<margin>The yellow triangle</margin>¶ By the yellow triangle is understood a universal majority <term>majority: in Llull’s logic, this refers to the state of being greater or more universal</term> to which all other majorities are subordinate. For with this majority / the agent "makes-greater" <note>original: "maiorificat"</note> just as it "begins" with the beginning. And this same logic applies to equality and also minority in its own way. 

¶ Just as goodnesses and other substantial things are placed in the category of majority / so goodnesses and other accidental things <term>accidental: qualities that are not essential to a thing's nature, like color or position</term> are reduced to the genus of minority. And in innate substantial goodness, the "good-er," the "good-ed," and the act of "good-ing" are equal by essence. And so it can be said of the intellect and the will / "fire-ness" <note>original: "igneitate"</note> and similar things in their own way. And thus concerning the equality of causal and moral accidents. Indeed, through those three aforementioned species, the intellect shall ascend and descend / so that it may reach the realities of things / as they pertain to the genus of majority, equality, and minority / and also to the substantial and accidental genus. ¶ And this ascent and descent is highly methodical <note>original: "artificialis," meaning "according to the rules of the Art"</note> for acquiring the sciences.

<margin>Epilogue</margin>¶ We have spoken of the second figure, which is the instrument of the intellect with which it acts upon the first figure / because through "difference" it distinguishes between goodness and greatness and such things: and with "concordance" it finds harmony. And thus for others in its own way. Furthermore, it distinguishes with "difference" within the essence of goodness: through the "good-er" / the "good-ed" / and the act of "good-ing." And with "concordance" it indeed agrees that they are the same by essence naturally: but morally not so / because the difference is not innate but acquired, since they are principles by occasion.

<margin>
An explanation of the third figure, divided into thirty-six chambers.
</margin>

<margin>
The purpose of the figure.
</margin>

**T**he third figure is composed of the first and second <note>The "First Figure" represents the nine attributes of God/Principles (B-K), and the "Second Figure" represents the nine relations (Difference, Concordance, etc.).</note>, and it contains thirty-six chambers <note>original: "cameras." These are the cells or compartments where two concepts meet to form a logical proposition.</note> within itself as is apparent. In each chamber there are two letters: in the first, **b.c.**; in the second, **b.d.**; and so on for the others. It is composed of two figures because its **b** is equivalent to the **b** found in the first figure <note>Goodness</note> and the **b** found in the second <note>Difference</note>. The same applies to **c**, which is equivalent to the **c** in the first <note>Greatness</note> and the **c** in the second <note>Concordance</note>, and likewise for the rest. ¶ The purpose for which this figure is placed in this Art is to show how, with one principle, a person may apply or associate another principle—just as **c** and **d** are applied to **b**, all the way through to **k**. Thus, through **c** and **d**, one gains knowledge of **b**, according to whatever knowledge one desires concerning **b**. And just as we speak of **b**, it is to be understood similarly for **c**: one looks at **c** with **b**, and afterwards with **d**, and so on until the chamber of **c. k.** The same follows for the other chambers in order, ending with the chamber of **i. k.** This may be done at will, according to how much a person wishes to multiply arguments toward the same conclusion, by observing the meanings of the chambers and applying them to the subject at hand.

¶ This figure teaches how to descend from the universal to the particular <note>In medieval logic, "descending" means moving from broad, abstract concepts to specific, concrete examples.</note> step-by-step in four ways. First: by speaking through the chamber of **b.c.**, saying "Goodness has great difference and concordance." Second: since the intellect considers the angles of "difference," it descends from the universal to the particular by understanding that difference and concordance exist between one sensory thing and another sensory thing <note>original: "sensuale & sensuale." This refers to physical objects perceived by the senses.</note>, as was said in the second figure. Third: it descends further when it considers that difference and concordance are good in fire and air through their concordance in heat <note>Llull uses the four elements—fire, air, water, earth—as specific examples of how abstract principles like "Concordance" manifest in nature.</note>. In the fourth way, it descends by understanding that good difference and concordance exist between the "bonifier" <note>the one who does good</note> and the "bonified" <note>original: "bonificatum," that which is made good</note>, etc., which are the true essence of Goodness. And just as we have spoken regarding **b.c.**, so it can be said for the other chambers of this figure.

B iij <note>This is a printer's signature mark used for binding the book.</note>

->On Definitions.<-
Folio 5.

<margin>On the fourth figure having three circles.</margin>
# The Fourth Figure:
has three circles, as appears within it, and it encompasses the first figure, the second, and the third. Within it are gathered those principles from which the table is composed. For instance, a chamber of B, C, and D makes a column in the table composed of B, C, and D. And a chamber of B, C, and E makes a column composed of B, C, and E. <note>The Fourth Figure is a volvelle—a paper instrument with rotating disks. By spinning the circles, the practitioner can align the letters B through K to create three-letter combinations, which are then used to look up specific "columns" of logic in the combinatorial table.</note>

<margin>Why figure B is placed in this art.</margin>
The intention behind why this figure is placed in this art is so that the table may be formed from it in order, and so that a person may know how to find many reasons and many conclusions by applying the aforementioned reasons to a single conclusion. This is done by looking at the meanings of the letters and applying them to the proposition in such a way that neither an inconsistency nor an impossibility follows from those meanings.
<margin><gloss>fitting</gloss> <gloss>impossible</gloss></margin>

<margin>To what the middle circle is useful.</margin>
**The middle circle:** teaches how to find the "middle" of a conclusion, just as C is [a middle], and so for the others. For example, it is the middle through which B and D participate in magnitude. <note>In Lullian logic, the "middle" is the term that connects the subject and the predicate.</note> And thus D, existing between B and E, does not permit the participation of goodness and power through its specific property; therefore, a concordant or copulative middle causes an affirmative conclusion, while a contrary or disjunctive middle causes a negative one.

### The end of the second principal part of this work.

## On Definitions: and this is the third principal part.

<margin>The third principal part of this work: which is on definitions.</margin>
# This third part:
is about the definitions of the Principles, such as the definition of goodness, which is this: **Goodness** <note>original: "Bonitas"</note> is the being by reason of which the good acts well. And **Greatness** <note>original: "Magnitudo"</note> is the being by reason of which goodness, duration, and the rest are great. And this phrase "and the rest" signifies the other principles, though not simply; for example, to say "in God there is goodness, greatness, etc." does not imply that in God there is "majority," "minority," or "contrariety." <note>Llull is distinguishing between the Absolute Principles (like Goodness) which apply to God, and the Relative Principles (like Minority) which only apply to created things.</note>

**Duration:** is that by reason of which goodness, greatness, etc., endure.
**Power:** is that by reason of which goodness, greatness, and the like can exist and act.
**Wisdom:** is the property by reason of which the wise one understands.
**Will:** is that through which goodness, greatness, and similar things are desirable, and through which the good, great, etc., subject <note>original: "suppositum"</note> is willing.
**Virtue:** is the origin of the union of goodness, greatness, and similar kinds.
**Truth:** is that which is true regarding goodness, greatness, and the like.
**Glory:** is the very delight in which goodness, greatness, and the others find rest.

**Difference:** is that through which goodness, greatness, and the like are clear and unconfused reasons; and also [through which] the "bonifier," the "bonifiable," and "bonifying" are unconfused. <note>Llull uses these active/passive/verbal forms (bonificans, bonificabile, bonificare) to show how an attribute like Goodness functions within itself.</note>
**Concordance:** is that by reason of which goodness, greatness, and the rest agree in one or in many.
**Contrariety:** is the mutual resistance of certain things due to diverse ends.
**Principle:** <note>original: "Principium," meaning both "beginning" and "foundational rule."</note> is that which relates to all things by reason of some priority.
**Middle:** is the subject through which the end flows into the principle, and the principle flows back into the end, partaking of the nature of both.
**End:** is that in which the principle finishes.
**Majority:** is the image of immensity, greatness, eternity, and the rest.
**Equality:** is the subject in which the end of concordance, goodness, greatness, and the others find rest.
**Minority:** is a being close to nothingness.

<margin>Note the principles</margin>
Regarding the nature of the principles, some are substantial and some are accidental. Contrariety, however, is always accidental. But the principles that are substantial require substantial definitions, and those that are accidental require accidental ones. Just as "to bonify" <note>to act as goodness</note> is appropriate to goodness that is substantial, so too does an accidental definition fit accidental goodness, with which an agent "bonifies" the "bonifiable" accidentally.

<margin>Definition can be made in many ways</margin>
It should be known that a definition can be made in many ways, but all are reduced to two modes. And each mode has four species. The first mode is when it is made through the efficient cause, power, matter, and end. Through the efficient cause, as when it is said: it is appropriate for God to create and to save. Through power, as when it is said: power is the being through which matter has its own passion. Through matter, as when it is said: matter is the being from which an agent acts. Through the end, which is the definition as has already been stated.

The second mode is as we shall state in Rule C. Regarding these two modes, the aforementioned definitions can be applied, such as a form which is defined by its act: as when "elementary power" <note>original: "proyelementatiua"</note> is the being to which it is specifically appropriate to "elementize"; and for the vegetative to vegetate; for the sensitive to feel; for the imaginative to imagine; and for the rational to reason. And so it is for goodness, to which it is specifically appropriate to "bonify," and for greatness to "magnify," and so with the others. And the same can be said of the efficient cause. Just as with a human, to whom it is specifically appropriate to "humanize" <note>original: "hominificare"</note>; for a lion to "lionize"; for fire to heat; and so with the others.

And such a mode of defining is very easy and useful. Furthermore, the definitions made through Rule C are very easy, useful, and clear. Such as a definition that is interchangeable with its defined term: like "goodness is the being to which it is specifically appropriate to bonify." And it is the being that specifically has within itself an innate "bonifier," "bonified," and "bonifying." Likewise, it is the being in a subject with which the "bonifier" bonifies the subject. Furthermore, goodness is a being having action in a subject. And...

# Part Four.

<margin>composition</margin>
Just as we spoke of goodness, so it can be said of the other principles. Through the two aforementioned modes, the practitioner can indeed define everything. However, beyond the Art, there is another mode that is confused and wordy: namely, when definitions are made at one's pleasure or by chance, without considering the proper and appropriate definitions existing between the subject and the predicate. An example is when it is said: "God is an infinite and eternal being" <note>original: "deus est ens infinitum z eternū"</note> and "Man is a rational animal." And again: "He is an animal to whom alone it belongs to ride or to write," and so on in its own way. 

Furthermore, definitions are made through **composition**, namely when one principle is defined with another. For instance, when it is said: "Great goodness is a being by reason of which that which is good and great acts in a good and great way." And if "eternity" is added, this means that "great goodness is eternal." That goodness itself is defined thus: "Great and eternal goodness is a being by reason of which that which is good, great, and eternal acts in a good, great, and eternal way." In such a manner, the 
<margin>demonstration</margin>
practitioner can make **demonstrations** through principles—true and even necessary principles—through which things cannot be otherwise. 

Furthermore, just as goodness is a being by reason of which a good thing acts well, so it can be said of magnitude. **Magnitude** is a being by reason of which a great thing acts greatly; and **eternity** produces the eternal. And so it goes for the others. 

Moreover, to explain the definitions of the principles, the practitioner can explain and declare them according to their nature. For goodness 
<margin>nature of things</margin>
would not have a nature without an innate <term>bonifier</term> <note>Llull uses unique active, passive, and verbal forms for each principle to show they are dynamic. A "bonifier" (bonificans) is the active force of goodness.</note>, a <term>bonified</term> <note>The object or recipient of goodness (bonificatum).</note>, and the act of <term>bonifying</term> <note>The action itself (bonificare).</note>. Nor would magnitude exist without a magnifier, a magnified, and magnifying; nor eternity without an eternizer, an eternized, and eternizing; and so on for the others. 

And if the principles did not have a nature, goodness would not be a being by reason of which a good thing acts well naturally. Nor would duration be a being by reason of which goodness, magnitude, and the rest endure. Therefore, if these definitions were destroyed, the principles themselves would be nothing; nor would the whole universe exist, which is false, because we have experience of the universe that it is. 

Likewise, through this principle of **wisdom**, it must be understood that it is understood by the intellect; and in every other being, because of rational substance, an instinct is understood through wisdom, and a desire is understood through the **will**. 

Furthermore, perhaps someone possessing <margin>slanderous</margin> "canine teeth" <note>A metaphor for a biting or cynical critic.</note> and a "serpentine tongue" will one day scorn and slander our principles and their definitions. However, the Art requires that one principle assist another. For example, if it were said: granted that magnitude is the being by reason of which goodness is great, and that all goodnesses are equally great, then one must deny the principles of **majority**, **minority**, and **contrariety**, which do not permit all goodnesses to be equally great.

->The end of the third principal part of this work.<-

***

# The fourth principal part, which is about the rules.

<margin>The Rubric of the fourth part of this work, which is about the rules.</margin>

The **rules** are ten: namely, **Whether**, **What**, and the rest, as is already signified in the alphabet. These rules are ten general questions through which all that exists is constituted. Through them, the thing being questioned is brought to light, colored, and signified to the intellect according to the essence and nature of the rule, as is evident in grammar. For just as all declinable noun-words are included in the five declensions and can be declined through them, so in their own way all other questions (which can be made) are included in these ten of this Art because of the aforementioned rules. They are reduced to them and are regulated by them by reason of the universality they possess. And just as these questions are general, so are their species. For just as goodness is entirely general with its general parts—the bonifier, the bonified, and bonifying—without which it cannot be entirely general, so it is with the ten questions of this Art, which are general along with their species.

## Concerning Rule B.

<margin>Question 1. Concerning Rule B.</margin>
<margin>This rule has three species.</margin>

The rule of **B** is **Whether** <note>In Llull's alphabet, B represents the question "Utrum" (Whether).</note>. It concerns **possibility**: whether this thing being questioned is or is not. Such possibility causes faith, or belief, or supposition, which supposes that either side is possible—namely the affirmative or the negative. This rule of B has three species: **doubt**, **affirmation**, and **negation**. 

Through the first species, one must suppose whether a thing is or is not, so that the intellect is not stubborn or bound, but rather investigative, so that it can pass through to reach either the affirmative or the negative as being true. This must be done with this condition: that it always concedes that which is more "recollectable," intelligible, and lovable to be true in its conclusion, aiding itself with the principles and their definitions and with the other rules. 

For example: if it is asked *whether the intellect exists*. It seems that it does, because "to be" is more recollectable, intelligible, and lovable than "not to be." And this is according to the aforementioned investigation of the principles. For when it is said that "that which is more recollectable and lovable is to be chosen," it must be understood that it is chosen with greater intelligibility and not with less. For when the affirmative or negative is chosen with less...

And in this step consists the entire power of this rule.

## Concerning Rule C.

<margin>Question 2: Concerning Rule C, which has four species.</margin>
<margin>First species.</margin>
**R**ule C concerns **quiddity** <term>quiddity: from the Latin "quid," meaning the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term>, because it is the subject and source of the definitions of beings, just as was figured in the definitions of the principles. This rule has four species. The first species concerns definition, and a definition is that which can be swapped with the thing defined, as when it is said: "the intellect is the being of its own essence." Again, it is that being to which "to understand" properly belongs, and so on for others in their own way. <margin>Second species.</margin> ¶ The second species occurs when one asks about that which a thing has in itself essentially and naturally, without which the thing itself cannot exist. For example, when one asks what the intellect has in itself essentially and naturally, without which it cannot be. And the answer must be that it has an innate **intellective power** <note>original: "intellectivū"</note>, an **intelligible object** <note>original: "intelligibile"</note>, and an **act of understanding** <note>original: "intelligere"</note>. <note>Llull believed every active essence has three parts: the doer, the object of the deed, and the act itself.</note> Therefore, the intellect, by its intellective power, is the agent and the understander; and with its own proper and innate intelligible object, it is the "possible intellect" in which it understands foreign intelligible things which are not of its own essence; and its "understanding" is an innate and intrinsic act. All three of these are one intellect and one essence, undivided. Within that intrinsic act of understanding of the intellect itself, foreign understanding is "imprinted," just as a foreign intelligible object is imprinted within the intrinsic intelligible object. And this is indeed necessary so that passion corresponds with passion, and act with act, and that they relate to each other appropriately. However, I say this when the intellect is practical; but when it is theoretical, it is not so. Rather, the intellect itself is simply what it is, like a whole that exists through its parts which are co-essential to it. ¶ Through what has been said regarding the intellect, one understands the way in which the intellect is both one and particular—and universal insofar as it can understand this or that. And thus it is with its intelligible object, which is universal for receiving this or that intelligible object successively. And so too for the intrinsic act, namely understanding, with foreign acts occurring successively. That what has been said about the intellect is true is sufficiently probable through the definitions of the principles and Rule B. For if it were not true, the intellect would not have imaginative goodness, nor duration, etc., nor would it have a nature by which it is both universal and particular; nor would Rule B be entirely true, which is impossible.

<margin>Third species.</margin>
¶ The third species is when one asks: "What is a thing in another?" And the answer must be given according to the category of quality. For example, the intellect is active through its intellective power when it reaches an object, and it is passive when it receives "species" <note>Species: the mental images or forms of external objects</note>. It is "great" when it has a great and difficult object. It is "true" when it understands truly, and "false" when it understands falsely. It is bound and necessitated by memory when it believes; but it is in liberty and at rest when it understands truthfully. <margin>Fourth species.</margin> ¶ The fourth species is when one asks what a thing *has* in another. For instance, when it is asked: "What does the intellect have in its object?" And the answer must be that it has action and passion, as was shown in the third species. It has action in grammar, logic, and geometry; it has passion in the political sciences; and it has goodness and moral virtues, and blame through sin; and so it goes for other qualities. <margin><note>Handwritten marginal notes</note></margin> ¶ We have spoken of Rule C and its species. And just as we have given examples through the intellect, so in its own way can examples be given for physical subjects. For example, in fire, to which it properly belongs to "ignite" substantially and to "heat" accidentally; fire has an **igniter** <note>original: "ignificativū"</note>, a **thing ignitable** <note>original: "ignificabile"</note>, and the **act of igniting** <note>original: "ignificare"</note>. And in a lamp and in a wick there is fire, having action in the elements according to time. This is the same as the vegetative power in a living body, the sensitive power in a feeling body, and the imaginative power in an imagining body. In celestial things, however, it is not so. For a star does not produce another star, nor an angel another angel, because they lack substantial generation, since they are incorruptible and indivisible substances. Concerning God, His definition and nature are understood in another way, according to Divine Goodness and Eternity.

## Concerning Rule D.

<margin>Question 3: Concerning Rule D, which has three species.</margin>
<margin>First species.</margin>
**T**he third question concerns **materiality** <term>materiality: from "materia," here asking about the origin or "stuff" of a thing</term> and has three species. The first is: "Of what is the thing?" as when one asks: "Of what is the intellect made, absolutely?" And the answer must be that the intellect is made of itself; that is, it was not made from anything else, but was created insofar as it is a thing that once was not. <margin>Second species.</margin> ¶ The second species is when one asks: "Of what is something made or constituted?" as in asking: "Of what is the intellect composed?" And the answer must be that it is composed of its co-essential principles, namely: its intellective power, its intelligible object, and its act of understanding. Similarly, a man is constituted of his body and his soul. And a nail is made of iron, and so for similar things.

<margin>Third species.</margin>
¶ The third species is when one asks to whom a thing belongs, or whose it is: such as asking: "Whose is the intellect?" or "Whose is the kingdom?" And the answer must be that the intellect belongs to the man, and the kingdom belongs to the king. Through this rule, one asks "of what" a thing is. ¶ Rule D has been explained and applied to the intellect; thus it can be applied to other subjects in its own way: as is evident regarding the whole universe, which is "of itself" according to the first species, and not from any other pre-existing principle. And through the second species, it is seen that it is constituted of form and substantial matter. From...

# Fourth Part

<margin>in part... 2</margin>
In what way do particular forms descend? From what matter do particular matters [descend]? Indeed, the universe belongs to God, because it is His creature. And this can be understood regarding universal and substantial **goodness** and **greatness**, etc., which are primitive <note>In Llull's system, "primitive" refers to the most basic, uncomposed principles from which all other things are derived.</note> in terms of their genus. Through the second species of this rule: goodness is composed of the **bonificative**, the **bonificable**, and **to bonify** <note>original: "bonificatiuo/bonificabili z bonificare." These are Llull's invented terms for the active power of goodness, the capacity to receive goodness, and the act of being good.</note>; and greatness is composed of the **magnificative**, the **magnificable**, and **to magnify** as universals; and it is the same for the others in their own way, because they are parts of it. And this same thing can be said for all particular goodnesses, greatnesses, and so on for the rest. These goodnesses descend from the aforementioned [universal] goodness, and greatnesses from the aforementioned greatness, and so on for others; similarly for the **elements** <term>elements: the four basic building blocks of the physical world—fire, air, earth, and water</term> and **elemented things** <term>elemented things: complex physical objects made from a mixture of the four elements</term> in their own way. However, it is not the same for a human being according to the second species, for a human is composed of soul and body, which differ in genus and nature, just as corporeal and incorporeal substance [differ]. And it is the same for **substance** and **accident** <note>A substance is a thing that exists in itself (like a tree), while an accident is a quality that only exists in something else (like the greenness of the tree).</note>: just as **quantity** is not of the essence of a substance but is its "habit" <note>An external or accompanying state.</note> by reason of which it is "how much" [quantified]. And so it is for **quality**, by reason of which it is "of what kind" [qualified]. And so it is for other accidents. Truthfully, however, substance and accident are composed in a body, for without this composition a body cannot exist.

Through the third species of this rule: accidents are in a substance; they do not exist through themselves but through the substance. The reason for this is that one and the same accident is not made of "this and that" [diverse parts]. But a substance is indeed so: since it is constituted of "this matter" and "that form," by reason of which it exists through itself. And an accident is its likeness, figure, and instrument. ¶ Furthermore, an accident such as **quantity** is of itself according to the first species when it is primitive (insofar as it is general); all other quantities are from it and descend from it. It is indeed undivided insofar as it is primitive, but it is divided into many particular qualities, just as general **quality** is divided into many particular qualities. This division is "by accident," namely through substantial division, which is indeed divided by fragmentation and the generation of species, differences, and number. ¶ Furthermore, there are other accidents from which the sciences are made, which appears in **logic**, which deals with **second intentions** <term>second intentions: logical concepts that refer to other concepts (like "genus" or "species") rather than to real-world objects</term> joined to the first. And so it is with mechanical accidents, such as the shape of a chest, which is the shape of the wood. And the shape of a tower, from the shapes of the stones. And so on for others in their own way. ¶ Through this rule, the practitioner in this Art investigates "primitivities" and "simplicities" via the first species. Through the second, he investigates composition. Through the third, he investigates dominance and possession. This rule is indeed general to all things. ¶ We have spoken concerning **Rule D** <note>Rule D in Llull's system asks "How?" (Quomodo) and "With what?" (Cum quo).</note>, and that which is true is evident through itself, and through all the definitions of the principles and through Rules B and C. It is indeed quite probable: because if substantial goodness (and likewise for the intellect and such things) were not according to the second species of this rule, it would lack that species, and thus it would not have that from which it exists; whence it would follow that it would not exist through itself, but would be like an accident which lacks the second species of Rule D. Nor would goodness itself be a "reason" substantially, nor would a good thing produce a good thing substantially from the essence of goodness; and thus a certain goodness would not be a substance but an accident. And thus the definition of greatness, duration, and the others would be destroyed. And so for the rest. Furthermore, all things would be accidents, which is impossible and against Rules B and C. And in this passage, the doctrine is given for the way in which the practitioner of this Art proves one truth with another, by applying the definitions of the principles and Rules B and C, which was said for this purpose regarding Rule D.

### The Fourth Question, which is "Why?"

<margin>Question 4, which is about "Why," contains two species.</margin>
<margin>existence</margin>
The fourth question is "Why?", which has two species: one is by **existence**, the other is by **agency**. Just as by existence, one asks "Why is there an intellect?"; the answer must be according to the existence of the intellect: it is because of its own proper **intellective power**, **intelligible object**, and **act of understanding** <note>original: "intellectiuo/ intelligibili z itelligere." Again, the Lullian ternary: the power, the object, and the action.</note>; just as the whole which exists is what it is through its co-essential parts of which it is made. And [by agency] the intellect understands so that it may move itself toward its end, which end is that it may understand God and the truths of other beings. And so that a person may possess the habit of science through this rule, one asks: Why are there things? That the intellect exists through a "formal why," as was said above, seems to be true through the definition of goodness, greatness, and the rest, and through Rule B and through the second species of Rule C, without which the intellect would have neither the nature of existing nor of acting. ¶ Furthermore, just as was said regarding the intellect, so it can be said regarding **substance**, which exists through its **causes** and its **occasions**. Through its causes, such as through form, matter, efficient, and final [causes]. Through occasion, such as through definition, habituation, and contingency. And so for the other accidents. Through "Why" itself, there are indeed genera, species, individuals, the liberal arts, trades, virtues, and vices.

<margin>Question 5. Concerning Rule E.</margin>

<margin>Simplicity over essence, one through difference... in goodness and greatness</margin>
**T**he fifth question asks about **quantity**, which has two species: namely, the simple and the composite. For example, if it is asked: how great is the intellect? And one must answer according to the simplicity of its essence: that the intellect is as great as the being <note>original: "esse," referring to the fundamental existence of a thing.</note> of its essence. But according to composition, the answer should be: it is as great as it is through its existence and agency, or through its own **intellectivating**, **intellectible**, and **to understand** <note>original: "intellectiuū intelligibile z intelligere." These are Llullian technical terms for the active, passive, and verbal components of any faculty.</note> of which it consists. Through this rule, the measurements of beings and their number are sought. That what has been said about the intellect is true seems probable enough through the definition of **goodness**, **greatness**, and the rest; and through the second species of Rule C and D. Because goodness, insofar as it is a simple essence and form, has a quantity that is continuous and distinct from other essences by reason of its genus and nature.

<margin>6.1 - Difference over essence by reason of its natural genus: but insofar as it is the principle for producing good/merit.</margin>
But insofar as it is the principle <note>original: "ratio"</note> for producing good, it has a discrete nature through the **bonificative**, the **bonificable**, and **to bonify**. And from this indeed flow external and discrete quantities through the composition it has in an individuated subject, in which goodness has continuous and discrete quantity. And just as has been said of goodness, so it can be said of other superior forms which cause the lower continuous and discrete quantities. For example, in a stone, which is endowed with one continuous quantity, while also having discrete quantities by reason of the essences of the **elements** <term>elements: the four basic qualities (fire, air, earth, water) believed to compose all matter</term> from which it is composed. And likewise for a plant through its "elementative" and "vegetative" powers; and for a man through the "elementative," "vegetative," "sensitive," "imaginative," and "reasoning" powers from which he is composed. And likewise for a tower or a ship constructed by art. However, these are not as continuous as a natural subject, but are more discrete than a natural subject by reason of their integral parts.

[...things]. And this is the indicator if it is asked: What kind of thing is fire through its own proper quality, which is its heat? And the answer should be that it is hot and heating; and through its dryness, which is a quality appropriated to it through the earth, it is "dryable." But in the air, it is "drying" through dryness. And so for others; through this rule, one asks about proper and appropriated quality. Proper qualities are superior causes, and appropriated ones are inferior. For example, the heat of fire is a superior quality, and its dryness is inferior. And so it is for natural goodness, which is superior, while moral goodness is inferior. Through this rule, the artist inquires into those things which are superior and inferior between the subject and the predicate. Proper qualities, I say, are proper passions <note>In medieval logic, a "passion" (passio) is a property or attribute that naturally follows from the essence of a thing.</note>; and appropriated qualities are similarly appropriated passions.

# On the sixth rule. F.

<margin>Question 6. Concerning Rule F.</margin>
<margin>proper, appropriated</margin>
**T**he sixth question asks about **quality**, which has two species: namely, the proper and the appropriated. Just as it is asked through the first species: What kind of thing is the intellect? And the answer should be: the intellect is such as its own proper **intellectivity**, and its **intelligibility**, and its own proper **to understand**. And if it is asked through the second species: The answer should be that the intellect is such as its habit, or its quality is its intelligibility appropriated through action placed in its own proper intelligibility, through which it reaches other intelligible beings.

# On the seventh rule. H.

<margin>Question 7. Concerning Rule H.</margin>
<margin>The essence of time is difficult to understand</margin>
**T**he seventh rule asks about **time**: and it has as many species as the second, third, and nineteenth rules. And we do this because the essence of time is very difficult to understand. And first, we will apply Rule H to Rule C through the first species of Rule C. For example, when it is asked: when is the intellect? And the answer should be: it is then, when its being is. And through the second species, the answer should be: it is then, when it has its own essential parts.

<margin>time or 6</margin> <margin>when it is in others... to be held</margin>
Likewise, the answer should be through the third species: when the intellect is in another; and it is then in another when it acts within it, just as the practical intellect acts in a subject. The fourth species is: when it is asked, when does the intellect have something in another? To which it should be answered: then, when it understands the likeness of that thing. And as we have said of the intellect through Rule C, so it is. Through the first species of Rule D, the answer should be: that time is a primitive essence, because it is not produced from another essence, nor generated, just as **prime matter** <term>prime matter: the most basic, formless substrate of all physical things</term> is not derived from other matter, and just as the first form is not from another form. And thus time, insofar as it is primitive, is the first form from which its particular forms are caused, such as days, hours, and the rest. Through the second species of Rule D, by means of motion containing within itself the "to move," the "mover," and the "moved" or "mobile," it comes from the **temporificative**, the **temporificable**, and **to temporify** <note>These are Llull's terms for the active, passive, and functional aspects of time's creation.</note>. However, I do not say that time and motion are identical in essence, but they are two habits from which the subject is characterized and affected. Through the third [species]...

# Fourth part.

<margin>Modal rule.</margin>
Under the species of Rule D, we say that **time** is subject to the agent in things to be done through acting: because substance naturally or morally clothes itself in time. ¶ By the **modal rule**, it is to be understood that time consists of the **mover**, the **moving**, and the **mobile** (or motion): and this is habitual, just as a part is substantially within a part. And the likeness of time consists—just as a figure consists of the **past**, **present**, and **future**—in the same way that within the habit of heat there is a figure, a **heat-giver**, a **heat-able** thing, and the act of **heating**. And in motion, there is the **to move**, the **mover**, and the **mobile** (or that which is moved). ¶ Through
<margin>Second instrumental species.</margin>
the second instrumental species of Rule K, **time** is the instrument of substance along with motion, so that substance may be able to act: in the subject, however, it is "able to be done" <note>original: "agibilis"</note>, and its "ability to be done" is a figure through time and through motion. And in this step, it appears in what way the intellect reaches the essence of time truly and realistically. And that this is true is indeed provable through the definitions of the principles and Rules B, C, D, E, F, and G. Nevertheless, it is necessary that the intellect be very high and clear, and also removed from confusion and doubt, by reason of the preparation of the matter both subjectively and objectively.

## Concerning the eighth question, which is about place: marked by the letter J.

<margin>Question 8, which is about place: marked by J. It has ten species.</margin>
<margin><gloss><unclear>signification in the letter ... and through ...</unclear></gloss></margin>
**T**he eighth question asks about **place**: just as one might ask, where is the intellect? And this rule or question has fifteen species: which pertain to the second, third, ninth, and tenth rules. And first, concerning the first species of Rule C: just as the intellect is in its "where" <note>original: "in ubi"</note> essentially and naturally: namely, in its own being or essence: just as a man is a man in his humanity and his own being. And also the intellect is in itself according to the second species: like its parts are in its whole. ¶ Through the third species, the intellect is in the soul or in the man, or in the place in which the man is. ¶ Through the fourth species, the intellect is in that power through which it possesses the habit of knowing, and it is also in that subject in which it performs a practical act. And so on for similar cases. ¶ Through this rule, it is asked where things are in a place, and where things are simply without a place: just as the intellect, which is in a place according to the third and fourth species, is not in a place according to the first and second. ¶ Since we have led the intellect through the concept of place, we have therefore in some way known place through the mediation of Rule C: namely, that **place** is a being to which it properly belongs to locate, having within itself the **place-giver**, the **place-able**, and the act of **placing** <note>original: "collocatiuuū / collocabile z collocare." Llull treats "Place" as an active faculty that performs the function of "placing" things.</note>. And it is a habit in a located subject, in which subject it has its being: just as heat is in fire, and action is in the agent,

<margin><gloss>place.</gloss></margin>
and things of this sort. ¶ Likewise, place is known through the first species of Rule D, because just as the intellect is primary (not having anything pre-existing from which it is materially derived), so place is primary insofar as it is general, being one part of the universe. In itself, according to the first species, it is neither sensible nor imaginable, but only intelligible. Nevertheless, through the second species of Rule D, its figure is visible and imaginable—I do not say according to its essence. Through the third species of Rule D, place belongs to the occupant possessing the place: just as a heated thing possesses heat by being habituated with heat. ¶ Through these three species, the essence of place is reached through understanding alone. Thus, a **particular place** in a sustained subject is diffused and derived from the **universal place** sustained in a universal subject. This universal place indeed locates all things that are located. Just as all hot things are hot through universal heat. And thus all moved things are moved in a universal manner. ¶ Through the rule of modality, place is known. For through this, a part is in a part, just as fire is in air and vice versa, as is evident in a compound body; and form is in matter and vice versa. And all parts are in the whole, and vice versa: and the whole transmits its likeness or its figure outside itself: just as one place is in another by accident, and all particular places are in the universal place. And the figure of place appears in the **container**, the **containing**, and the **contained**. ¶ Furthermore, place is known with the second species of Rule K. For place is an instrument of substance, with which instrument it locates part in part. Just as one is habituated in a habit: namely, the good in goodness, the white in whiteness, the great in greatness, and such. <margin>How he may know place by definition.</margin> And the figure of this instrument appears through sense and imagination in placing flour in water, and water in flour, and things of this sort. ¶ We have spoken of place through the discourse we made concerning it, through the mediation of Rules C, D, and K; we have notice and knowledge of it: and the definitions of the principles and Rules B, C, D, E, F, G, and H bear witness to this.

## Concerning the modal rule: marked by the letter K.

<margin>Question 9, concerning the modal rule: signified by K.</margin>
**O**ne question is concerning **mode**: namely, to ask "how" <note>original: "quomodo"</note> things are. And it has four species. ¶ The first question is like asking how a thing is in itself: just as the intellect is a being through itself, since the intellect has a mode of being through itself, and is removed from every other essence. <margin>Second species.</margin> ¶ The second species is when it is asked how...

It introduces the Modal Rule (Rule K) to explain "how" things exist in themselves or in relation to others.</summary>
