# Concerning the rules.

...the intellect is in another, and that other is in itself: And it must be answered that the intellect has a way of being in the will, and the will in it, insofar as with it and memory, the rational soul can be constituted. <margin>Third species.</margin> ¶ The third species is when it is asked how the intellect is in its parts and its parts in it. And it must be answered that the intellect is in its parts and its parts in it through that nature by which it can exist from its own **intellective**, **intelligible**, and **to understand** <note>These are Llull's "correlatives": the active power, the object/passive capacity, and the act itself.</note>, and through which way these three can be its parts. <margin>Fourth species.</margin> ¶ The fourth species is when it is asked how the intellect transmits its likeness outside itself: And it must be answered that the intellect can transmit its likeness outside itself through the **habit of science** <note>Knowledge or learned skill.</note>: by understanding many things which it makes "intelligible" within its own intelligible capacity. ¶ Through this rule, one asks about the modes according to which certain things have a way of being through themselves, or one in another as was said above. ¶ Furthermore, it must be understood that **difference** causes differences, and thus it is "modal" for distinguishing things. And **concordance** accords several things into one composite; thus it is "modal" by joining. And thus follows the mode through which a part is in a part and the whole is in its parts. Just as in a **denarius** <note>A silver coin; here used to illustrate how different essences can intermingle while remaining distinct.</note> in which gold is in silver and silver in gold, each remaining in its own essence and its own being. Such "modality" is a general being under which are all particular modalities, and its subject and likeness. Just as **figure** is the likeness of substance, and **color** is the likeness of the colored thing, and so forth. And natural modality is the likeness of natural modality. ¶ And that what has been said about modality is true seems probable by reason of the definitions of the principles and through these rules—namely B, C, D, E, F, G, H, and I. And this is clear to the artist of this Art who observes well.

### Concerning Rule K: which is about instrumentality.

<margin>Tenth question concerning instrumentality.</margin> The tenth rule is about **instrumentality**: this is to ask *with what* things are, or *with what* they act: And it has four species similar to those of the rule of modality. <margin>First species.</margin> ¶ The first species is like asking *with what* the intellect is a part of the soul: And it must be answered that the intellect is a part of the soul with **difference**, **concordance**, and **power**, and so with the other principles except for **contrariety** <note>Llull teaches that the powers of the soul must exist in harmony, not opposition.</note>. <margin>Second species.</margin> ¶ The second species is *with what* the intellect understands things other than itself: And it must be answered that the one understanding understands by **acquiring** and by **mixing** one species <note>The mental image or form of a thing.</note> with another, and placing them in its own intelligible capacity, just like an eye that reaches its own likeness in a mirror. <margin>Third species.</margin> ¶ The third species is when it is asked *with what* the intellect is **universal** and **particular**: And it must be answered that it is universal insofar as it has one active, intellective, formal power with which it reaches many things in one universal intelligible object—which is the essence of the intellect itself—with which and in which (namely, the universal intelligible) many species are intelligible, just as in one mirror many images are visible. And it is particular when it descends by practicing, namely, by understanding some specific species which it acquired and saved in memory. <margin>Fourth species.</margin> ¶ The fourth species is when it is asked *with what* the intellect transmits its likeness outside itself: And it must be answered: with its own **intellective**, **intelligible**, and **to understand** with which it makes species to be understood, and through memory to be recallable, and through the will to be choosable for loving or hating. <margin>Division of instruments.</margin> ¶ Through this rule, one asks about the instruments of things, whether spiritual or corporeal. ¶ Furthermore, one kind of instrument is **substantial**: such as the male and female who have a substantial instrument with which they generate offspring. <margin>substantial <gloss>substantial</gloss></margin> Another is **accidental**, such as fire which, with its heat, heats that which can be heated. <margin>accidental <gloss>accidental</gloss></margin> And as a man who, with **justice**, makes himself just. <margin><gloss>general</gloss></margin> Another is **universal**: such as the intellect which, with its intelligible capacity, makes this or that "foreign" intelligible thing. <margin><gloss>particular</gloss></margin> And as the male who, with one and the same rod <note>Likely referring to the reproductive organ or a symbolic staff of generation.</note>, generates many sons; and fire with its heat heats many heatable things. And as the smith who, with one and the same hammer, makes many nails. Indeed, **particular** instruments are this and that and the rest, with which a builder constructs a house. And as two propositions from which a conclusion is made. And so of others in their own way. <margin>intrinsic instrument <gloss>intrinsic</gloss></margin> Another is an **intrinsic** instrument: such as the "intelligible" which is of the essence of the intellect. <margin>extrinsic <gloss>extrinsic</gloss></margin> Another is **extrinsic**, which is "foreign," with which a teacher generates science. And as the hammer with which the smith fashions a nail. That what we have said about instrumentality is true, all the definitions of the principles of this Art and all the rules attest and prove. And similarly what has been said of the ten rules: which rules are **vessels** for all things that can be understood and are proportionate to the human intellect.

->End of the fourth part.<-

**B**: Goodness
**D**: Duration / Eternity

**G**: Will
**H**: Virtue
**I**: Truth

# Fifth part.

<note>This table is a logic grid from the "Art" of Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316). Each letter serves as a variable for a divine attribute: **b** (Goodness), **c** (Greatness), **d** (Duration/Eternity), **e** (Power), **f** (Wisdom), **g** (Will), **i** (Truth), and **k** (Glory). The letter **t** represents the "Triangle" of relations—a set of logical tools used to compare and connect these attributes. Practitioners of this system would read these combinations to systematically contemplate the unity and interaction of these universal principles.</note>

<note>The following tables represent the combinatorial "logic machine" of Ramon Llull. In this system, letters are used as variables for universal principles. 
**B**: Goodness | **C**: Greatness | **E**: Power | **F**: Wisdom | **G**: Will | **I**: Truth | **K**: Glory. 
The letter **T** represents the "Triangle" of relations (Concordance, Difference, and Contrariety). The letter **S** in these tables typically refers to the "Soul" or the "Subject" being acted upon or considered within these relations. By permuting these letters, Llull believed one could calculate all possible truths regarding the divine attributes.</note>

<note>This table is a logical grid used by Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316) for his "Great Art." Each four-letter cell is a formula representing a relationship between universal principles, known as Dignities.
**B**: Goodness | **C**: Greatness | **D**: Duration (Eternity) | **E**: Power | **F**: Wisdom | **G**: Will | **I**: Truth | **K**: Glory | **S**: Subject (the Soul or the individual) | **T**: Relation (the "Triangle" of Concordance, Difference, or Contrariety).
For example, "d e f t" explores the relationship between Duration, Power, and Wisdom.</note>

# Fifth part.

<note>The "Fifth Part" refers to a specific stage in the combinatorial process of the Lullian Art. Here, the letters function as algebraic symbols for philosophical concepts: **B**: Goodness, **D**: Duration/Eternity, **F**: Wisdom, **G**: Will, **I**: Truth, **K**: Glory, **S**: Subject/Soul, **T**: Relation/Triangle. The addition of **l** and **z** often indicates specific subdivisions or "species" of these general principles in later Lullian commentaries.</note>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion of the combinations of divine attributes. Having established the primary figures of the Art, Llull now introduces the "Table," a comprehensive tool that maps every possible logical relationship among the principles, moving from abstract definitions to a practical method for answering complex philosophical and theological questions.</meta>

Fifth Part.

# ¶ Rubric concerning the Table.

**T**his table is composed of eighty-four columns, as has been said. It is the subject or instrument in which the solutions to questions are investigated, by applying them to the matter at hand—either affirming or denying, harmonizing principles and rules, and avoiding any contradiction between them. The letter **t** in the table signifies that the letters placed before it are <term>principles</term> <note>These are the Absolute Principles from the "First Figure," such as Goodness, Greatness, and Eternity.</note> from the first figure, and the letters after it are from the second figure <note>The Relative Principles, such as Difference, Concordance, and Contrariety.</note>. For example, in the "chamber" **b.c.t.b.**, the **b** preceding the **t** signifies <term>Goodness</term>, and the **c** signifies <term>Greatness</term>. The **b** after the **t** signifies <term>Difference</term>; and so it follows for the others. The investigation performed in the table exists at a higher level of signifying truths than that which is performed using the figures alone. ¶ The table of the fourth figure is derived by revolving the second and third circles, as appears in the table itself, up to eighty-four columns. In this revolution consists the "binding" of the columns: **b.c.d.** turns into the column **b.c.f.**, and so on successively from column to column until the last, which is **h.i.k.**, as is seen in the table. Thus, in every column, all other columns are implied; by reason of this implication, every column provides aid to every other. ¶ To the solution of any single question, all the meanings of all the abstract and "hand-guided" <note>original: "manuductuarum." These are simplified or practical examples used to lead the student's mind to a conclusion.</note> questions related to that question can be applied. In this step, the great universality of this table of this Art becomes apparent. ¶ Furthermore, in every column, there are twenty questions arranged on the surface. We shall give an example of this in the first column, which is **b.c.d.**, by predicating first of Goodness, then of Greatness, and finally of Eternity, as follows:

¶ The first is: whether <term>Goodness</term> is so great that it is eternal?
¶ The second: whether there is any goodness so great that it contains within itself things that are different yet coessential to it?
¶ The third: whether goodness is so great that it contains within itself things that are concordant and coessential to it?
¶ The fourth: whether a goodness containing within itself contrary things is great?
¶ The fifth: whether eternal goodness is different?
¶ The sixth: whether eternal goodness is concordant?
¶ The seventh: whether eternal goodness has contrariety within itself?
¶ The eighth: whether goodness contains within itself difference and concordance?
¶ The ninth: whether goodness contains within itself difference and contrariety?
¶ The tenth: whether goodness contains within itself concordance and contrariety?
¶ The eleventh: what is the great difference of eternity?
¶ The twelfth: what is great and eternal concordance?
¶ The thirteenth: what is great and eternal contrariety?
¶ The fourteenth: what is great difference and concordance?
¶ The fifteenth: what is great difference and contrariety?
¶ The sixteenth: what is great concordance and contrariety?
¶ The seventeenth: from what does the difference of the concordance of eternity arise? <note>original: "de quo est." Literally "from what it is," a standard scholastic way of asking about the origin or essence of a property.</note>
¶ The eighteenth: from what does the difference of eternity arise?
¶ The nineteenth: from what does the concordance of contrariety and eternity arise?
¶ The twentieth: from what does the difference of concordance and contrariety arise?

¶ We have produced twenty questions through column **b.c.d.**, which contains twenty "chambers" within it. The first chamber is **b.c.d.**, the second is **b.c.t.b.**, and so on until the twentieth, which is **t.b.c.d.** From each chamber, we have extracted one question, as shown above. And just as we made twenty questions in the first column, so twenty others can be made in the second, and twenty more in the third, and so on in order until the final column, which is **h.i.k.** ¶ Through these questions and solutions, the <term>intellect</term> is elevated to such a high degree of universality that it is rendered immeasurable and inestimable. This is by reason of the generality of the predicate and the subject. In this step, it is clear in what way this Art is highly general and useful. ¶ To provide the doctrine and method for solving the aforementioned questions, we wish to solve them by applying the meanings of the letters to the purpose in such a way that the definitions of the principles and the types of rules are not destroyed.

<margin>To the first question.</margin>
¶ And first: to the first question it must be answered, when it is asked whether goodness is so great as to be eternal, I say that it is. And this is indeed manifest through the definitions of <term>Goodness</term>, <term>Greatness</term>, and <term>Eternity</term>. For if goodness is the being by reason of which that which is good performs good acts, and greatness magnifies that goodness and eternity, and the definition of eternity makes that goodness and greatness endure, then it is necessary that the act of goodness be infinite and eternal, and consequently the essence of goodness must be so as well. And thus it is concluded that goodness is great and eternal. For without greatness and eternity, it could not have an infinite and eternal act—namely, the act of "bonifying" <note>original: "bonificare." Llull's invented verb for the active work of Goodness.</note>. And this can be affirmed through <term>Rule B</term> <note>Rule B is the first rule of the Art, which asks "Whether?" (Utrum), and focuses on the existence and possibility of the subject.</note> and through the second species.

<summary>This page introduces the "Table" of 84 columns, a combinatorial tool used to generate and solve complex philosophical questions by linking absolute principles with relative properties. Llull demonstrates this by listing twenty systematic questions derived from the first column (b.c.d.) and providing a logical proof for why Goodness must be both Great and Eternal.</summary>

<page-num>folio 15.</page-num>
<header>Concerning the Table.</header>

# Concerning the Table.

Through the first species of **Rule D** <note>In Llull's Art, "Rule D" typically asks "Why?" and concerns the cause or essence of a thing.</note>, the affirmation must be held: because eternity is the primitive essence beyond which there is no other prior principle <note>original: "priacct̄s," likely a contraction for "principium."</note>, and its primitivity is good and great; and thus it follows of necessity that there is some greatness and eternal goodness. ¶ Furthermore, through the third species of **Rule D**, it is signified that there is no contrariety which has dominion in eternity, but rather the opposite: such dominion would only exist if eternity did not have primitive and great goodness. Therefore, goodness is so great that it is eternal.

<margin>To the second question.</margin>
¶ Regarding the second [question], when it is asked: whether there is any goodness so great that it is differentiated? **Solution.** I say that there is. This is indeed manifest through their definitions. For if <term>Goodness</term> <note>The attribute of being good.</note> is the being by reason of which a good agent acts good, and <term>Greatness</term> is the being by reason of which goodness and difference are great, it is indeed necessary that within goodness there are different things <term>coessential</term> <note>Sharing the same fundamental essence or being.</note> to it: namely, the <term>Good-maker</term> <note>original: "bonificans"; the active principle or agent of good.</note>, the <term>Good-made</term> <note>original: "bonificatum"; the object or result of the good action.</note>, and the <term>act of Good-making</term> <note>original: "bonificare"; the verb or activity connecting the agent and object.</note>. For this belongs to the nature of goodness, greatness, and difference: that within the essence of goodness there are things that are really and simply distinct. And yet that goodness itself is essentially undivided, great, and unconfused. ¶ Likewise, the question must be held in the affirmative by **Rule B** <note>Rule B asks "What is it?" and deals with definitions.</note>, as is evident in itself, and also by **Rule C**. For through the first species, goodness itself is defined and converted essentially and concretely with its concrete parts. And through the second species, <term>Difference</term> is placed with Greatness: so that goodness has within itself the Good-maker, the act of Good-making, and the Good-made, which indeed it could not have as a nature without distinction; nor could goodness be the reason for a good [being] that would produce good from itself. And thus goodness itself would be an empty nature of greatness if difference were lacking. ¶ Furthermore, regarding the same, greatness and difference are naturally in goodness, as is clear through the third species of **Rule C**. And goodness is also naturally in them. And through the fourth species, greatness and difference have their acts in goodness, and similarly goodness in them, by reason of the fourth species of **Rule C**.

<margin>To the third question.</margin>
¶ Regarding the third question, when it is asked: whether goodness is so great that it contains within itself things that are concordant and coessential to itself? To which it must be answered that it is so, as is clear through their definitions: for if goodness does not contain things that are concordant and coessential or natural to it, then great goodness would not differ from <term>contrariety</term> <note>The state of conflict or opposition.</note>, nor would it be great without such <term>concordance</term> <note>The state of harmony or agreement.</note>, which is impossible; which impossibility is necessitated by the definitions of goodness, greatness, and eternity.

---

¶ Furthermore, the first species of **Rule C** agrees with this by affirming it, which establishes the conversion by defining goodness and its concordant things: namely, the Good-maker, the Good-made, and the act of Good-making; and the <term>Concorder</term>, the <term>Concorded</term>, and the <term>act of Concording</term>. With these, supreme goodness and concordance are converted with supreme greatness. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species, it is shown that goodness has within itself good, concordant things without which great goodness could not exist. And also the third species of **Rule C** establishes that greatness and concordance are in goodness with their acts: namely, with <term>Greatening</term> and <term>Concording</term>. And goodness is in them with the act of doing good. And the fourth species says that every reason has its act and its essence in the other. And in this step appears the height of the intellect which truly and realistically attains this; to which height it could not ascend except by the help of God.

<margin><insert>A-cur1</insert></margin>
¶ Regarding the fourth question, when it is asked whether goodness containing within itself things that are contrary and coessential to itself is great: It must be answered that it is not: because it lacks concordance, which is indeed more absolute than contrariety. The reason for this is that concordance with goodness establishes being by generating. And contrariety with malice establishes the privation of goodness by corrupting: and this is what the definitions of goodness, greatness, and contrariety intend. That what we have said is true is required by **Rule B** itself, and also the first species of **Rule C**. For if great goodness contained within itself contrary things, it would indeed be a great evil for it; and greatness and smallness would be converted into that same goodness, which is impossible. And also through the second species of **Rule C**, which places in goodness the Good-maker, the Good-made, and the act of Good-making with greatness: therefore, regarding this question, the negative must be held. Likewise, the third species says that contrariety could not be in a good subject with greatness. And the same judgment applies to the fourth species, which says that contrariety could not have its act in great goodness.

<margin>To the fourth question.</margin>
<margin>with reason</margin>
¶ To the fourth question <note>The author repeats the numbering or addresses a sub-point of the fourth inquiry.</note>, when it is said: is eternal goodness differentiated? It must be answered that it is: because unless eternal goodness were differentiated, it could not act an eternal good from eternity; for the reason that difference would not govern the agent in its active number, nor the thing to be acted upon in its passive number. And I say that same thing about the act: if difference were lacking, it would cause their confusion; and eternity would not have the nature of <term>eternizing</term>, nor goodness the nature of <term>good-making</term>; and thus all these definitions would be—

<summary>This page uses the logical rules of Llull's Art to argue that Goodness must contain internal distinctions (the Good-maker, the Good-made, and the Act of Good-making) to be active and perfect. It further proves that Great Goodness must possess internal harmony (Concordance) and cannot contain conflict (Contrariety), as that would result in corruption or evil.</summary>
<keywords>Scholasticism, Ramon Llull, Divine Attributes, Goodness, Greatness, Eternity, Difference, Concordance, Contrariety, Logic, Theology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the logical demonstration of how divine attributes (like Goodness and Eternity) interact. Llull uses his signature "ternary" logic, where every attribute consists of an active agent (ending in -ans), a passive object (ending in -atum), and the act itself (ending in -are). This page specifically moves through Questions 6 to 9, applying Rules B, C, and D from his system to prove the internal consistency of these attributes and to argue against the eternity of the world.</meta>

->### Fifth part.<-

...constructed, which is impossible. ¶ Furthermore, **Rule B** <note>Rule B usually asks "Whether a thing exists?"</note> agrees to this same point, supporting itself with the aforementioned definitions. Also, by the first species of **Rule D** <note>Rule D asks "Why?" or "From what?"</note>, it is indeed affirmable. For the rule itself says that eternal goodness is just as primitive through acting as it is through existing; for if the difference between the agent and the actable object is removed, the act is removed, and consequently the agents themselves are removed. And idleness and the deprivation of the nature of eternal goodness are generated, which is impossible. Still, the second species of **Rule D** seems to affirm this same thing: for without the difference of the <term>good-maker</term> <note>original: "bonificantis"</note>, the <term>good-makable</term> <note>original: "bonificabilis"</note>, and the act of <term>good-making</term> <note>original: "bonificare"</note>, it would have no source from which to exist; nor could eternity govern it, which would be an evil for it against the eternal good, which is impossible. ¶ Furthermore, through the third species of **Rule D**, it is clear that if the negative of the question were held, it would follow that some being would be eternal while having eternal malice: which would prevent the eternal reason of goodness from being the reason for the eternal good, which would produce an eternal good lacking difference: which is false and also impossible and against **Rule B**. Therefore, etc.

<margin>To the 6th question.</margin>
¶ To the sixth [question]: whether eternal goodness is concordant? The answer is affirmative through their definitions: because eternity says that goodness and <term>concordance</term> <note>The state of being in agreement or harmony.</note> endure. And concordance says: that goodness and eternity agree in one and in many; and eternal goodness is the reason from the eternally concordant thing, by which the good produces good. This, however, could not be unless eternal goodness were concordant through the **good-maker**, the **eternalizer**, and the **concorder**; and the **good-made**, the **eternalized**, and the **concorded**; and through **good-making**, **eternalizing**, and **concording**. ¶ Furthermore, what we have said is sufficiently probable; and also through **Rule C** <note>Rule C asks "What is it?" and defines the nature or composition of a subject.</note>, the affirmation must be held: for goodness is that form which properly contains in itself difference and concordance, along with the good-maker, the good-made, and good-making, which are well-ordered by difference and concordance; with which order the <term>differer</term> and the <term>concorder</term> are agents; the <term>differentiable</term> and the <term>concordable</term> are the <term>patients</term> <note>In medieval logic, the "patient" is the recipient of an action.</note>; and through the fourth species, they have the acts of differentiating and concording; and goodness has the act of good-making.

<margin>To the 7th question.</margin>
¶ To the seventh: when it is asked whether eternal goodness contains <term>contrariety</term> <note>The opposition between two things, like hot and cold.</note> within itself? The answer is yes, assuming the world is eternal: which is clear through the definition of contrariety; since from eternity and in eternity the world is good and evil through eternal goodness and eternal malice, generation, corruption, and privation. And eternal goodness could not be a good reason that produces an eternal good without contrariety and malice. And eternity is the cause why good and evil endure from eternity; and **Rule B** cannot agree to this, nor the first species of **Rule D**, for from eternity good and evil would be privative while concording. And by the second species, the whole universe would be composed of good and evil; and the First Cause, namely God, would be forced into causing the world from eternity only with malice and with goodness: which is impossible. By reason of this impossibility, the negative of this question must be held; and in this step it appears that it is impossible for the world to be from eternity.

<margin>To the 8th question.</margin>
¶ To the eighth: when it is asked whether goodness contains difference and concordance within itself? The answer is yes. This is clear through their definitions. For if goodness did not have differing and concordant things, it could not be the reason for the good by which it produces good, and concordance could not exist without the difference of things. And if difference were removed, there would be confusion and hiddenness between the good-maker/good-made and between the concorder and the concorded. Rather, I say there would be an implied contradiction, which is impossible. ¶ Also, the first species of **Rule C** says: that eternity is a being to which <term>eternalizing</term> <note>The act of making something eternal or the internal activity of eternity itself.</note> properly belongs. Moreover, this property cannot exist without the concordance of the **eternalizer**, the **eternalized**, and the act of **eternalizing**, which concordance is naturally necessary, as was indicated through the second species of the same rule. And through the third species, it is to be seen that the eternalizer in the eternalizable is the agent; and the eternalized or the eternalizable is the patient; and the eternalizer has the act, namely, eternalizing, as was indicated through the fourth species of **Rule C**.

<margin>To the 9th question.</margin>
¶ To the ninth question: when it is asked whether goodness contains difference and contrariety within itself? The answer is yes in certain subjects: just as in a <term>composite of elements</term> <note>original: "elementato"; a physical body made of the four elements.</note> in which the elements differ and are contrary, such as fire and water through hot and cold, and such as air and earth through moist and dry. And this is good, because without such contrariety a composite of elements could not exist. ¶ Furthermore, **Rule B** agrees with what we have said. Also, through the first species of **Rule D**, the negative of the question must be held: that is, that in the essence of goodness, the good-maker, the good-made, and good-making cannot be contrary; because if so, through the second species of the same rule [the] good...

<margin>To the tenth question.</margin>
¶ To the tenth, when it is asked whether goodness contains within itself concord and contrariety? In such a composite, air and fire agree through heat; air and water through moisture; water and earth through cold; and earth and fire through dryness. Yet fire and air are contrary through the dry and the moist; air and water are contrary through cold and heat; water and earth are contrary through moisture and dryness; and earth and fire [are contrary] in motion through lightness and heaviness. And what we have said is manifest through the definitions of concord, goodness, and contrariety. For the <term>elementing principle</term> <note>original: "elementans"</note> could not be the reason in a subject that produced a good composite of elements; and furthermore, the definitions of concord and contrariety would be distinct.

And by the third species of the same rule, it is concordant in the air; and air is concordable in the fire regarding the genus of heat; but regarding the genus of moisture and dryness they are contrary: because fire, by reason of dryness, is contrary to air, and air to fire through moisture.

And let eternity be a being by reason of which greatness and difference endure. And difference is a being by reason of which one is the **eternizer**, another is the **eternized**, and the third is the **act of eternizing**.

And similarly the third species of **Rule C**: so that the **eternizer** is in eternity, greatness, and difference; the agent and producer having the produced object itself in eternity, greatness, and difference of nature. And the second species of **Rule D** <note>Rule D: "Why?" or "From what source?"</note> posits this same thing: so that eternity may have that from which it exists. And likewise for the third species of **Rule C**: so that the **eternizer** is in greatness and eternity and concord, magnifying and eternizing. Through the fourth species of **Rule C**: so that it may have a nature of eternizing the eternized, magnifying the magnified, and concording the concorded. And to this, the third species of **Rule D** agrees.

Nor indeed would eternity have a nature with which it could endure; and to have concord without them [is impossible]. Nor without concord could it stand apart from contrariety.

# Fifth part.

The eternity of the world posits an eternal evil that is not at rest; however, the eternity of God posits an eternal good that is at rest. The eternity of God posits that eternal evil is durable <note>That is, evil can persist as a consequence of the soul's duration, but it is not a primary eternal principle.</note>, whereas the eternity of the world posits that good is durable according to the definition of eternity. The second species of **Rule D** <note>Rule D asks "Why?" or "Wherefore?"</note> posits that eternal good and eternal evil are joined in a composite. Furthermore, the definition of **Greatness** <note>original: "magnitudo"; one of Llull's "Dignities" or divine attributes.</note> posits a great conjunction, and the third species of Rule D posits subjection on both sides. The second species of **Rule E** <note>Rule E asks "How much?" or "Of what duration?"</note> posits the contrary, the conserved, and the act of contrasting. Indeed, eternity is deviating when applied to both the eternity of God and the eternity of the world, for it would have dominion in both, producing an eternal contrary that is unquieted—which is impossible. By reason of this impossibility, the world cannot be eternal.

<margin>To the 14th question.</margin>
¶ To the 14th, through **Rule B** <note>Rule B asks "What is it?"</note>: what is great difference and concordance? It must be said that in the essence of **Greatness** there is a <term>Magnifier</term>, a <term>Distinguisher</term>, and a <term>Concorder</term> <note>original: "magnificans, distinguens, concordans"</note> which are one person, the same in number; and that the <term>Magnified</term>, <term>Differentiated</term>, and <term>Concorded</term> aspect be another person; and the act of <term>Magnifying</term>, <term>Differentiating</term>, and <term>Concording</term> be another person. All these three "persons" <note>Llull uses "persona" here to describe the structural correlatives of an essence: the agent, the patient, and the action itself.</note> are the same through essence, nature, greatness, difference, and concordance. This is to be seen through their definitions and through the first and second species of **Rules C and D**, and through the third species of **Rule C**, so that greatness, difference, and concordance are agents in act and are concording, separated from emptiness and idleness. Through the fourth species of Rule C, one has its act in another; without these acts, their definitions would not be true, which is impossible, as Rule B testifies.

<margin>To the 15th question.</margin>
¶ To the 15th, it is asked: what is great difference and contrariety? It must be answered that it is that causing cause of one contrary in another: as in an element in which fire and water are mixed; similarly air and earth; and between innate natural good and moral evil—namely sin and the like. This is evident through the definitions of greatness, difference, and contrariety. Difference declares and distinguishes these contraries. Contrariety in a subject deprives it of concordance and generates contrary appetites and ends. This is signified through Rule B, the first and second species of Rules C and D, and the third species of Rule C. Similarly, it is quite plain that one contrary is the agent and patient in the other. Through the fourth species of Rule C, one has an action in the other; through the third species of Rule D, it has subjection. In this passage, the great pains of Hell are figured. Through the fourth species of Rule C, one has an act in the other, without which acts their definitions would not be true—which is impossible, as Rule B testifies.

<margin>To the 16th question.</margin>
¶ To the 16th question, when it is asked: what is great concordance and contrariety? It must be said that it is that being which posits in the same subject things that are concording and contrariety, by generating and corrupting within an element. For example, fire and earth have concordance through generation with air, which is hot and dry, receiving dryness from the earth and giving heat to the air. Through the third species of Rule D, it is indeed the dominant existence over dryness and moisture, in which it posits great contrariety by corrupting. Just as we have said of fire, so it can be said of the other elements according to their qualities; thus it is to be seen through the first and second species of Rules C and D, and through the definitions of greatness, concordance, and contrariety. This is how elements enter into a mixture and compose a <term>composite body</term> <note>original: "elementatum"</note>. Through the third species of Rules C and D, one element is the agent and patient in another. Through the fourth species of Rule C, one element has action and passion in another, and also motion, by generating and corrupting.

<margin>To the 17th question.</margin>
¶ To the 17th question, when it is asked: of what is the difference of the concordance of eternity? It must be answered that it is of nature and relation. For Difference posits things that are distinct and naturally related through a <term>Distinguisher</term>, a <term>Distinguished</term>, and the act of <term>Distinguishing</term> in eternal concordance. According to its definition, this concordance posits a <term>Concorder</term>, a <term>Concorded</term>, and the act of <term>Concording</term>, within one essence and nature. In this, Eternity posits an <term>Eternalizer</term>, an <term>Eternalized</term>, and the act of <term>Eternalizing</term> by reason of its definition. This is manifest through Rule B and the first and second species of Rules C and D. The third species of Rule C posits action and passion without matter. The fourth species of the same rule posits natural eternal acts. To this, the third species of Rule D cannot contradict, because it is separate from the primitive acts that are differing and concording.

<margin>To the 18th question.</margin>
¶ To the 18th question, when it is asked: of what is the difference of eternity and contrariety? It must be said that it is of God and the world, assuming for the sake of argument that the world were eternal. This is clear through their definitions. For eternity posits innate good, eternal good, and moral evil, and difference distinguishes them. And contrariety posits eternal ends...

It must be answered that it concerns two eternities: namely, the eternity of God and the eternity of the world, assuming that the world were eternal; they certainly accord and discord in infinite duration. For God has infinite substance and the world a finite one; and the eternity of God is simply good, while the eternity of the world is both good and evil morally. And the definition of concordance destroys <insert>this view</insert>. And the definition of contrariety is of eternal necessity. And the definition of eternity is destroyed, because it does not proceed from the duration of greatness, goodness, and virtue to the duration of greatness, malice, and vices. And it is composed of primitive contraries eternally outside their own genus. And thus in its own contraries, concordance has a name through an implied contradiction; whence there is eternal concordance and eternal contrariety through the third species of Rule D, both subject and not subject, which is impossible.

¶ To the twentieth question, when it is asked: of what are difference, concordance, and contrariety? It must be answered that they are of themselves, because they are the <term>most general genera</term> <note>original: "genera generalissima"; in medieval logic, these are the highest categories of being that cannot be defined by a broader class.</note>, as is clear through their definitions. And Rule B testifies to this, as do the first and second species of Rule C and D. However, I do not say that contrariety falls within, or exists in, the second species of Rule C or D, because it is an <term>accident</term> <note>A property that is not essential to the nature of a thing.</note>; and an accident does not have matter from which it is simply made. For if it had matter, it would already be a substance composed of form and matter, which is impossible. And this is clear through the third species of Rule D.

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
¶ We have spoken of the first column, and we have given the doctrine concerning it, showing in what manner questions are extracted from it, and their solutions through definitions and rules. And just as we have done regarding this column, so can it be done with the other columns in their own way. And the questions we have made from it are general, and they can be applied to particular questions by descending through the steps of the <term>green triangle</term> <note>A mnemonic and logical figure in Llull's system representing the "Scale of Being" or the relationship between different levels of reality.</note>, through which the intellect is discursive, creating different sciences. And of this we give an example in the same column for solving questions through twenty different reasons by reason of the stated <term>chambers</term> <note>original: "camerarum"; these are the boxes in Llull's combinatory tables where two or more principles/letters meet.</note> from which they are extracted.

## Whether the world is eternal.

**The solution** to this question will be clear through the first column of the table; and it can be done through the other columns, because the columns are linked together. And first through the first chamber of the column, and then through the second, and so on in order until the last chamber, multiplying twenty reasons for the same question, holding the negative side of the question through the definitions and rules implied in that column.

<margin>On the doctrine of this art.</margin>
¶ The doctrine of this art is that the <term>explicit terms</term> <note>The specific words used in the phrasing of a question.</note> which are in the question should be taken up; as when it is said: "whether the world is eternal." In this question is "eternity," which is an explicit term since it is in the first figure. And through eternity, **D** is required <note>In the Lullian Alphabet, "D" often represents Eternity.</note>, and through D, the terms signified by D itself are acquired. And the scale which is in the angle of D—namely, the contrariety which is between the sensual and the sensual; and between the sensual and the intellectual; and between the intellectual and the intellectual.

¶ Likewise, through the word "whether" <note>original: "utrum"</note>, **B** is acquired <note>B represents the rule "Whether?" or "What?"</note>, and through B, those things which exist under it are acquired, as is clear in the Alphabet. And since we wish to apply **C** in the question, with it being implied in the question, whatever C contains is acquired. ¶ And thus the doctrine is given for applying the first column to solving the aforesaid question, for finding the explicit and implied terms, applying them to the purpose: namely, to the solution of the question in such a way that the definitions of the principles and rules remain unharmed, aiding oneself with the species of the other rules, to give the doctrine of how a person can help themselves with others. And first, through the first chamber, thus:

[**W**]hen it is asked whether the world is eternal: we say through [the rules of] B, C, and D that it is not. For if it were eternal, its reason <note>original: "ratio"; here meaning its defining principle or essential nature</note> would be from eternity producing eternal good: and greatness would magnify **that, that** <note>preserving the ditography "illam illam" from the original text</note> good reason from eternity and in eternity, as is clear through its definition: and eternity, from eternity and in eternity, would cause that production to endure: and thus no evil would be in the world, for the reason that good and evil are contraries: but evil is in the world, as is clear through experience. It is concluded, therefore, that the world is not eternal. ¶ Furthermore, Rule B <note>Rule B usually asks "What?" to define a subject's essence.</note> posits that the negative [position] of the question must be held according to the definitions mentioned above, and according to what we propose to say through Rule C and D, speaking thus: if the world is eternal, its eternity is causing as much duration of malice as duration of good. This is clear through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "Of what?" (matter or origin).</note> and through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Why?" (causality).</note>: evil would be as primary as good. For no day would be the first nor the last. And through the fourth species of Rule C, it would have rest in things that can be generated and corrupted: in things generated by reason of good, and in things corrupted by reason of evil. And through the second species of Rule D, divine eternity and its goodness would necessitate evil and rest, by causing the eternity of the world. And since all these things are impossi- <note>The argument continues in the next column.</note> ble, it is concluded therefore that the negative [position] of the question must be held.

...with eternal greatness. Because if it is goodness, it is also the reason that would produce good and evil. And greatness would magnify good and evil infinitely with eternal contrariety. And eternity would cause that great contrariety—both good and evil—to endure, which is impossible. ¶ Rule B <note>In Llull’s system, Rule B ("What is it?") defines the essence of a thing.</note> says that the world is not eternal through what has been said regarding the definitions. And the first type <note>original: "species"</note> of Rule C and D <note>Rules C ("Of what?") and D ("Why?")</note> posits primary contrarieties that are good, great, and eternal; and the second types of C and D posit a composition of goodness and malice, of greatness and smallness, of eternity and time, and of contrariety and concordance—which is impossible. ¶ To the same point: the third type of Rule C posits that contrariety is good and great in eternity, and consequently goodness and malice are good and great in eternity, which is impossible. ¶ To the same point through the fourth type of Rule C: and also the third type of Rule D has dominion in eternity; and goodness and greatness have eternal possessions over eternal contrariety, which is impossible. It is concluded therefore through the aforesaid that the world is not eternal.

## Regarding Chamber B.D.T.B.

<margin>Question 5 regarding chamber B.D.T.B.</margin>
**P**osing that the world is eternal, the <term>difference</term> <note>Llull uses "Difference" as a relative principle to distinguish between things.</note> that exists between one sensible thing and another sensible thing, etc., posits that there are three eternal differences, good and eternal, in which goodness is the reason producing an unconfused and eternal good—which is false and unthinkable. The difference existing between the sensible and the intellectual—specifically in <term>Socrates</term> <note>original: "Forte," a standard medieval abbreviation for "Socrates" (Sortes) used in logical examples.</note> and Plato—was not produced from eternity and in eternity, for the reason that it [the difference] is not [eternal]. And in a similar way, it can be said of dead beasts, elemental things, and vegetative things. But posing that the world is not eternal: the difference that existed between the sensible and the intellectual, and thus regarding other deceased men, can indeed be brought back into eternity through the <term>resurrection</term> with a good and blessed <note>original: "euterno," likely a portmanteau of "eu" (good/well) and "aeterno" (eternal).</note> state given by God through merit. ¶ Item: Rule B affirms this same thing, as does the first type of Rule C; for God is a being who remunerates <note>gives reward or status</note> in eternity. Furthermore, the first type of Rule D says that the eternity of God is simply primary over an eternity that differs from all time. And goodness indeed posits such a good difference. ¶ The second type of Rule C posits that in the eternity of the world, it is not innate to "eternalize" <note>original: "eternare," the act of making something endure forever.</note>; because if it were, it would multiply the "eternalized" thing infinitely in extension, which is impossible. ¶ To the same point: the second type of Rule D posits that if the world is eternal—which involves difference—even so, with eternity containing within itself the *eternalizer*, the *eternalized*, and the *act of eternalizing* (from which the eternity of the world consists), this is impossible. ¶ To the same point, it can be said through the second type of Rule C and the third of Rule D that the difference in the eternity of God and the world is good. This is false, because it subjects the eternity of God [to the world] in such a way that it takes away its eternal singularity. ¶ Furthermore, the fourth type of Rule C posits that if the world is eternal, it has too much <term>limit-ness</term> <note>original: "limitudine," likely referring to the boundaries or limitations of the created world.</note> with God through infinite duration: which is an eternal and confused evil; etc.

## Regarding Chamber B.D.T.C.

<margin>Question 6 regarding chamber B.D.T.C.</margin>
**P**osing that the world is eternal, the eternity of God and the eternity of the world would concord well together, which is impossible. Since the eternity of the world would contain within itself eternal malice through corruption and sin; and this appears sufficiently through Rule B with the definition of goodness, eternity, and <term>concordance</term>. ¶ Furthermore, the first type of Rule C posits that if the world is eternal, it follows that its eternity is a being beyond which there is no other preceding it by duration; which is [claimed] regarding the eternity of God; as is clear through the third type of Rule D, which indeed posits a subjection that cannot lead into non-existence that which is similar to it in duration. And this is also affirmed by the first type of Rule D, which says that the world always was, is, and will be. ¶ Item: the second types of Rule C and D posit this: for the substance of the world is of eternity, the "eternalizable," and the act of eternalizing. And thus it is impossible to reduce it to non-existence. ¶ To the same point: the third type of Rule C posits that goodness and eternity are subjected in eternal contrariety. And the fourth type of the same rule says that it has a "passion" <note>In scholastic terms, a "passion" is an attribute or a thing acted upon.</note> with malice. Therefore, etc.

# Fifth Part.

...with eternal things. And through the second type <note>original: "speciem"</note> of Rule C <note>In Llull's system, Rule C asks "From what?" and concerns the origin and composition of things.</note>, the world would have eternally innate contrariety, the thing being contraried, and the act of contrariety. And through the fourth type of Rule C, eternal goodness would have action upon eternal malice and vice versa, which is highly impossible, since Rule B <note>Rule B asks "What is it?" and defines the essence of a thing.</note> can in no way consent to this. ¶ It concludes, therefore, that it is impossible for the world to be from eternity.

## Regarding Chamber B.T.B.L.

<margin>Question 8 regarding chamber B.T.B.L.</margin>
**I**f the world is not eternal, the <term>goodness</term> and <term>difference</term> existing between the sensual and the intellectual <note>Llull distinguishes between things perceived by the senses ("sensuale") and things understood by the mind ("intellectuale").</note>, etc., can have <term>concordance</term> in eternal duration <note>original: "euo" (aevum), referring to a state of everlasting time or the age of the angels.</note>. But if it is from eternity, they can in no way have this, since there never would have been a first man nor will there be a last. And thus the world is a confused subject in which moral goodness would not have concordance from eternity; nor would concordance within it have its own concordance from eternity; nor would concordance within it have its own definition. This is evident through everlasting corruption, privation, and fault, which is against the first rule. And through the first type of Rule C, the world is a subject in which goodness has neither concordance nor rest. And through the first type of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Why?" and concerns the cause of a thing.</note>, goodness, difference, and concordance are primary and innate forms separated from perfection; and the world is confused through the second type of Rule D. And through the second type of Rule C, it has an innate "confusing" agent, a "confusable" object, and the act of "confusing." Furthermore, through the third type of Rule D, there is some ruling being that renders the world confused. Moreover, through the third type of Rule C, the first cause of the world would be evil, since that cause holds dominion in the world. And this is by reason of the fourth type of Rule C, which is impossible; therefore it is concluded that the world is not eternal.

## Regarding Chamber B.T.B.D.

<margin>Question 9 regarding chamber B.T.B.D.</margin>
**I**f the world is eternal, its <term>contrariety</term> <note>The principle of opposition or conflict between things.</note> is innate and eternal and sustained in goodness and malice, contrary to the clear "difference"; and this would be through the eternal and universal <term>ladder</term> <note>The "scala" or ladder of being, representing the hierarchy of creation from the lowest material things to the highest spiritual ones.</note> existing between one sensual thing and another sensual thing, etc. Such a ladder could in no way sustain contrariety. ¶ Furthermore, the first rule agrees in every way and affirms that the negative side of the question must be held. To the same point, the first type of Rule C posits that if the world is eternal, then contrariety is an impediment to every good divided between one sensual thing and another, etc. And eternal goodness is indeed the being that perfects the ladder existing between one sensual thing and another, etc. And the difference existing between the sensual and the sensual is the being that distinguishes between good and evil. And again, through the second type of Rule D: the world is composed of primary contrarieties that are both good and differing. This is indeed false and manifest through the first type of Rule D. Furthermore, through the second type of Rule C, the third type of the same rule, and the third type of Rule D, it is clear that the world is subject to its own innate parts. Moreover, through the third type of Rule C, it is corruptible in its innate parts, while the world itself—by reason of the fourth type—would have an eternal state <note>original: "habitum"</note>. And since all these things are impossible: therefore, etc.

## Regarding Chamber B.T.L.D.

<margin>Question 10 regarding chamber B.T.L.D.</margin>
**I**f the world is eternal, its goodness (which would be eternal and innate) is through the ladder of the sensual and the sensual, etc.; that ladder itself would be habituated with eternal concordance and contrariety, which is impossible because it is against the definitions of the aforementioned reasons. ¶ Furthermore, Rule B testifies to the same in the negative. Moreover, the first type of Rule C says that the world is a substance composed of eternal contraries while itself being corruptible, even though it is eternal; this is highly impossible and dissonant to reason. Likewise, the first type of Rule D posits a primary corruption by reason of the primary contrariety existing between goodness and malice. Concordance, however, primarily posits the opposite; and the second types of Rules C and D posit that the world is a mixture of contraries, one placed within the other. ¶ Furthermore, the third type of Rule C says that the world is corruptible in its contrariety, and incorruptible in its concordance, and good in its goodness, and evil in its malice. ¶ Further, Rule D posits that the world is subject to its own imperfection by some being existing outside its essence. And it is also so far separated from God that God is not good, but is an evil God; which is the most impossible thing of all. Wherefore, etc.

And it must be answered: that the essence which places a distinct eternity between one sensual thing and another through an <term>eternizer</term> <note>original: "eternantem"</note>, an <term>eternized</term> <note>original: "eternatum"</note>, and the act of <term>eternizing</term> <note>original: "eternare"</note> is impossible. Rule B regarding the aforementioned also bears witness in the negative. Furthermore, the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C usually asks "From what?" or "Of what?" dealing with the composition of a thing.</note> posits and agrees that the aforementioned definition is false and impossible. ¶ Moreover, the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D usually asks "Why?" or "How much?" dealing with quantity and action.</note> affirms that the primary things are corruptions and incorruptions: great by their magnitude, eternal by their eternity, and distinct or clear by their difference. ¶ Likewise, the second species of Rules C and D posit that the world is composed of these very things. ¶ Additionally, the third species of Rule C says that the world is incorruptible in the heavens and corruptible in <term>elementated things</term> <note>Physical objects composed of the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note>; yet for the world to have an incorruptible nature by reason of the fourth species of Rule C, and to be eternally incorruptible with a great difference, is a contradiction, and also goes against the third species of Rule D; therefore, etc.

## Regarding chamber C.D.T.C.

<margin>Question 12 regarding chamber C.D.T.C.</margin>

**S**i the world is eternal: it is asked, what is the great concordance of its eternity? And through the third species of Rule D, the magnitude of God is hindered in its effect of acting, while eternity is not at all. Whence there follows by accident a great and eternal contrariety between divine eternity and magnitude through the second species of Rules C and D; whence it follows that the magnitude of God is contrary in its eternity and vice versa. And it also appears that divine eternity would have a higher power and vigor than its magnitude, which is false and impossible; and this is proven by Rule B and the definitions of magnitude, goodness, and eternity. Therefore, etc.

Therefore, etc.

# On chamber C.T.C.D.
<note>In Llull's system, a "chamber" (camera) is a specific combination of logical principles used to test a proposition. Here, C stands for Greatness, T represents the Triangle of relations (Difference, Concordance, Contrariety), and D stands for Duration or Eternity.</note>

<margin>Question 16 regarding chamber C.T.C.D.</margin>
Postulating that the world is eternal, it is asked: what is the great distance existing between its great concordance and its contrariety? And it must be answered through the first species of rule C.D. <note>Rule C usually asks "What is it?" and Rule D "From what?" or "Why?"</note>, which is that form which causes a contradiction: as appears through the eternal scale existing between the sensual and the sensual <note>original: "sensuale & sensuale"; referring to the hierarchy of physical things perceived by the senses</note>, etc., because it joins itself in eternity, which is a simple principle / in which there are composites through the second species of rule C.D. And indeed, one principle is subjected to another / through the third species of rule D, and the second and third species of rule C posit a great and eternal distance: since concordance and contrariety are opposites in a subject / one having in the other a contrary nature through the fourth species of rule C. And since the eternity of the world posits for itself a coessential contradiction / which contradiction can by no means exist. It is concluded, therefore, that the world is not eternal.

# On chamber D.T.B.C.
<note>B represents Goodness.</note>

<margin>Question 17 regarding chamber D.T.B.C.</margin>
Postulating that the world is eternal: it is asked, from what is its eternity? It must be answered through the first species of C.D., which concerns the primitive infinite and finite differences / and concordances sustained in the scale of the sensual and the sensual, etc. Eternity, as far as its genus is concerned / is the infinite duration of dominion and concordance which are in the scale according to their genus: and they are finite in extension / quantity, as well as habit and situation: and in eternity they are eternal. Whence it follows through the second species of rule C.D. that the world is composed of infinite and finite parts / with eternity having dominion through the fourth species of rule C / and through all other innate parts which are finite. ¶ Furthermore, it holds subjugation through the third species of rule D, which is false and impossible / and it is also proven through rule B <note>Rule B asks "Whether a thing is?"</note> and through the definitions of the aforementioned principles. Therefore, etc.

# On chamber D.T.B.D.

<margin>Question 18 regarding chamber D.T.B.D.</margin>
If the world is eternal: it is asked, from what are its innate and coessential contrarieties and differences / since they are its proper passions sustained in the scale of the sensual and the sensual, etc.? And it must be answered through the first species of rule C.D. that they are from primitive and eternal differences / and contrarieties which are composed through the second species of rule C.D., these themselves having dominion and subjugation through the fourth species of C / and through the third species of D. This is by one reason or principle existing in another eternal subject / just as one natural point exists in another point: from which a line is continuous and composed: which is false and impossible. And it is also manifest through rule B and through the definitions of the principles, therefore, etc.

# On chamber D.T.C.D.

<margin>Question 19 regarding chamber D.T.C.D.</margin>
Postulating that the world is eternal: it is asked, from what are its natural and coessential concordances and contrarieties designated through the scale of the sensual and the sensual, etc.? And similarly it is asked, from what are its moral concordances and contrarieties? And it must be answered through the first species of rule D that they are from themselves: and through the first species of rule C, eternity is a being composed of contraries <note>original: "ens ex contrarijs composituz"</note>: as is evident through the second species of rule C.D., it having in itself a <term>concordant</term>, a <term>contrariant</term>, and an <term>eternizer</term>: and a <term>concorded</term>, a <term>contraried</term>, and an <term>eternized</term>: and <term>to concord</term>, <term>to contrary</term>, and <term>to eternize</term> <note>These triadic terms (agent, patient, action) are central to Lullian logic, showing how a principle functions within itself.</note>: which is indeed to posit an opposite in the object. And the world is in its corruptible and incorruptible parts / as is manifest through the third species of rule C, it having through the fourth species of the same rule infinite revolutions in number / multiplying an infinite and eternal number / with the world existing in infinite rest and labor / which is false and impossible: and this is proven through rule B and the definitions of eternity, concordance, and contrariety. It is concluded, therefore, quite clearly, that the world is not eternal.

# On the evacuation of the third figure.

Through the first species of rules D and C, <note>In Llull's Art, Rule C asks "What is it?" and Rule D asks "From what?" or "Why?"</note> it is shown that the world is made of partitioned parts <note>original: "partibus punitiuis"; likely a transcription error for "partitiuis," referring to the world being composed of distinct, finite parts</note> ordered toward a certain eternal end through difference and concordance, and not from primitive parts ordered to an eternal end through difference and contrariety. And thus divine eternity is the cause of the world and not the cause <note>This refers to the distinction between God as the necessary cause and the world as a contingent effect</note>. And through the second species of rules C and D, the world is composite and not composite, possessing through the fourth species parts that are innate and not innate. And through the third species of rule C, it is in an end and not in an end. And through the third species of rule D, the world is subject to God and not subject; necessitated and not necessitated; and removed from contingency and joined with contingency: and thus it is and is not. <p> And since all these things are contradictory, false, and impossible—which is evident through the rule and the definitions of the aforementioned principles—it has therefore been demonstrated quite clearly that the world is not eternal. <p> We have proven the world to be "new" <note>meaning "created in time" or having a beginning</note>; by which proof it is necessary that God exists, since the world cannot cause itself or bring itself from non-being into being: because if it did, it would already exist <margin>Corollary.</margin> before it existed, which is a contradiction. <p> We find, therefore, that God exists with His grace and blessing, in which discovery we rejoice greatly, because we shall have being after death by reason of His great goodness, justice, and charity.
<margin>Conclusion.</margin> <p> Thus the doctrine of the practice of this art has been given; namely, the way in which the intellect descends to particulars by multiplying twenty reasons for one and the same conclusion, mixing the principles and the species of the rules; by which mixtures and discoveries the solutions to questions are made. And this has been exemplified through the first column; and similarly, it can be exemplified through the second and third <margin>General subject of this art.</margin> columns, etc., in order. <p> And in this step it appears in what way the intellect possesses a general subject: namely, the table of this art for finding "middle terms" <note>In logic, the term that connects the subjects and predicates of a syllogism</note> regarding whatever matter they may be, provided that it is known what is meant by the name; from which and with which middle terms the conclusion is made, which middle terms are the subject of this art.

<p> The end of the preceding principal part of this work.

# The sixth principal part: On the evacuation of the third figure.

<margin>Rubric of the sixth part.</margin> **T**he third figure is divided into thirty-six chambers, as is evident within it: and in each chamber are implicated twelve propositions and twenty-four questions, and <margin>What it means to "evacuate."</margin> the solutions to them. <p> And we call it "to evacuate" <term>evacuation</term> <note>Llull's technical term for systematically extracting every possible logical combination or argument from one of his figures</note> when we extract the propositions, questions, and their solutions: and from implication we lead the doctrine itself to explication, providing the craftsmanship and practice of this art. For just as we solve questions here with the principles, definitions, and species of the rules, so can the artist of this art solve "foreign" <note>external or unfamiliar</note> questions with them, provided only that the artist knows what is meant by the name.

### On chamber B. C. of the third figure

<margin>The first chamber, which is B.C.</margin> **I**n this chamber, we first make propositions by changing the subject into the predicate; then we shall make questions, and just as we will exemplify the twelve propositions of chamber B.C., so it can be exemplified for the other chambers contained in this third figure. And afterward, we will make solutions by proving them through three propositions in each chamber. And just as we will give an example of those, so it can be given for other propositions contained in those same chambers. <p> Regarding the first, therefore, it must be said thus. <p> Wherefore it should be known that in the third figure the intellect "evacuates" the chambers because it abstracts from them as much as it can, receiving from each chamber those things which the letters signify, and applies those signified things to the purpose. And thus the intellect itself makes itself applicative, investigative, and inventive. And of this we shall give an example from one chamber containing the twelve aforementioned propositions. And just as follows for that one, so it follows for the others. And this is how: <p> From chamber B.C., the intellect draws twelve propositions, saying thus: Goodness is great; goodness is differing; goodness is concordant. Greatness is good; greatness is differing; greatness is concordant. Difference is good; difference is great; difference is concordant. Concordance is good; concordance is great; concordance is differing. <p> Having made these twelve propositions by changing the subject into the predicate and vice versa, this chamber is evacuated.

<summary>Llull concludes his argument that the world must have a beginning (is "new") and moves into the practical application of his "Third Figure," explaining how to systematically extract logical propositions from combinations of principles like Goodness and Greatness.</summary>

# Part Six.

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's logic regarding propositions.</note> ...by these very propositions. Then, let the intellect empty <note>In this context, "empty" or "exhaust" (evacuare) refers to the systematic process of examining every possible logical combination within a specific part of the Art.</note> the compartment with twelve means, because it consists between the subject and the predicate with which they agree in genus or species. And with those means, the intellect will make itself argumentative and decisive. And these aforementioned means are extracted from the twelve aforementioned propositions: as when it is said, "everything that is magnified by greatness is great; but goodness is that which is magnified by greatness; therefore, goodness is the state of being great," and so on for the others.

Once this emptying is done, the intellect should empty the compartment itself with twenty-four questions, because in every proposition there are two implied questions. And it is done like this:

Goodness is great. **Whether** goodness is great? **What** is great goodness?
Goodness is different. **Whether** goodness is different? **What** is different goodness?
Goodness is concordant. **Whether** goodness is concordant? **What** is concordant goodness?
Greatness is good. **Whether** greatness is good? **What** is good greatness?
Greatness is different. **Whether** greatness is different? **What** is different greatness?
Greatness is concordant. **Whether** greatness is concordant? **What** is concordant greatness?
Difference is good. **Whether** difference is good? **What** is good difference?
Difference is magna. **Whether** difference is great? **What** is great difference?
Difference is concordant. **Whether** difference is concordant? **What** is concordant difference?
Concordance is good. **Whether** concordance is good? **What** is good concordance?
Concordance is great. **Whether** concordance is great? **What** is great concordance?
Concordance is different. **Whether** concordance is different? **What** is different concordance?

Once this emptying of questions is done, the intellect should then empty the compartment with the definitions of goodness and greatness, and with the three species <note>The "species" of the rules are specific ways of applying a general question (like "What?") to a subject.</note> of difference and concordance, as is evident in the second figure. Next, it should empty the compartment with the three species of Rule B and with the four species of Rule C. Once this emptying is completed, the intellect should afterward solve the aforementioned questions in that emptying, following the conditions of the compartment, by affirming or denying. And thus, the intellect expels doubts from the compartment and rests in it, calmed; it also recognizes itself to be very general and skilled, and habituated in great knowledge.

Now, however, we will provide the solutions by proving them through three propositions, following the previously mentioned order. And it is like this:

**Goodness is great.** Whether goodness is great? And the answer is "yes." This is evident through the definition of greatness and through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "What is it?" The first species defines the essence of the subject.</note>, which says that greatness is the being by reason of which goodness is great. And through the second species of Rule C, it is seen that goodness is great because it possesses co-essential <term>correlatives</term> <note>Llull's theory of "correlatives" suggests that every principle consists of an active, a passive, and a verbal power—here, the "bonifier," the "bonifiable," and "to bonify."</note>: the bonifier <note>original: "bonificativum"</note>, the bonifiable <note>original: "bonificabile"</note>, and the act of bonifying <note>original: "bonificare"</note>, with which it has a great nature and rest. As is evident through the fourth species of Rule C, and through the third species of the same rule, it exists in difference and concordance with their definitions, by distinguishing and according—and this within its own genus and its own essence, from which "great goodness" arises morally. It is proven, therefore, that goodness is great. And Rule B <note>Rule B asks "Whether?"</note> testifies to this.

It is asked: **What is great goodness?** And the answer is given through the first species of Rule C: that great goodness is that essence which, through the second species of Rule C, contains within itself the distinct and concordant "bonifier," "bonified," and "bonifying." These are indeed of its own essence and nature, with which it has—through the fourth species—its own actions, passions, and acts. With these, through the third species, it is moved morally; thus, in what way is it a great reason for the good, that it should produce from itself a great good? Without all these things, goodness cannot be intensely and naturally great, nor can it be of the genus of substance.

It is asked: **Whether goodness is different?** And the response is "yes," as is evident in the angle of the second figure, and also through the "difference of goodness." For goodness would not be the reason for the good—that it might produce the good—unless it were difference, or unless it had the nature of difference; nor could difference cause all natural things with their own and natural passions. And Rule B proves this, as does Rule C. And this is by the first species: since unless goodness were different, this definition could not be made of it: "Goodness is the being to which bonifying properly belongs." And by the second species: goodness is naturally relative. And by the third: goodness is a "habit" <note>An internal state or disposition.</note>: one between this sensual thing and that sensual thing, and another habit between this sensual thing and that intellectual thing, etc. Furthermore, through the fourth species of the same rule: goodness has one nature in this stone and another in that plant, etc.

It is asked: **What is different goodness?** and it must be answered through the first species that goodness is that reason with which the bonifier is distinguished from...
