# On the Emptying of the Third Figure.

...by itself <note>This continues the definition of "Different Goodness" from the previous page.</note> into the <term>made-good<gloss>original: bonificatum; the passive or receiving aspect of goodness</gloss></term> and the <term>act of making good<gloss>original: bonificare; the verb-action that connects the giver and receiver</gloss></term>. Furthermore, through the second species <note>Llull uses "species" here to mean categories or specific applications of a logical rule.</note>, different goodness is that being which has in itself coessential and natural relations, with the entire essence of goodness existing in each related part with simplicity. Further, through the third species, different goodness is diffusive <note>spreading or communicative</note> in several habits differing by species. For one is in gold; another is in a ruby, and so on. To the same point through the fourth species, different goodness has one habit in one subject and another in another, as has been proven through <term>Rule B and C<gloss>Rule B asks "Whether a thing is?" and Rule C asks "What a thing is?"</term>.

**Goodness is concordant.** Is goodness concordant? And it must be answered that it is, through the first species. For unless it were concordant, there would be no reason for a good thing to produce a good thing in its own species. And through the second species, unless goodness were concordant, its own relative parts would lack agreement, which would be an evil for it and would be against their own nature and their own genus. To the same point, through the third species, by reason of the concordance of goodness, there is between a sensual thing and another sensual thing a good, concordant, and diffusive habit. To the same point, through the fourth species, goodness with its own concordance has a diffusive nature between one sensual thing and another, etc. And this has been demonstrated through the definition of goodness and concordance, and through Rule B.

It is asked: **What is concordant goodness?** And it must be answered through the first species of Rule C that concordant goodness is 그 essence in which the <term>good-maker<gloss>original: bonificans; the active principle or "doer" of good</gloss></term>, the made-good, and the act of making good properly agree. And this is provable through the second species. To the same point through the third: concordant goodness is that form by which one human and another human are the same in species. To the same point through the fourth species: concordant goodness is 그 nature with which one good human has a good concordance with another, whether naturally or morally.

...second species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Of what is a thing made?" or "From what does it originate?"</note>. For if goodness were [made] of the good-maker, the made-good, and the act of making good, it would indeed be impossible for it to have the nature of lasting by itself. And through the third species of Rule D, goodness is indeed durable substantially as to itself, and the good accidents flowing from it also last; and this occurs both naturally and morally.

It is asked: **Of what is enduring goodness?** And it must be answered through the first species that it is of itself, because it has the primitive relative parts from which it is constituted, which is evident through the second species of Rule D. To the same point: goodness is subject to its own whole in which it exists. And this has been proven through Rule B.

**Goodness is different.** Concerning this <term>compartment<gloss>original: camera; a cell in the Lullian grid where two principles intersect</gloss></term>, it has already been spoken of above in compartment B.C.

**Of what is enduring goodness?** And it must be answered through the species of Rule D, as was indicated above.

**Goodness is contrary.** Is goodness opposing? <note>original: contrarians</note> And it must be answered that it is, as is evident through the "ladder" of the sensual and sensuality. And to this the definitions of goodness, difference, and contrariety testify, and also through Rule B.

To the same point: **Of what is opposing goodness?** And it must be answered that it is of several good habits, such as heat, cold, moisture and dryness, heaviness and lightness, generation and corruption, and the like. And this is true through the first species. But through the second species of Rule D, the goodness of contrariety is by accident <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that isn't essential to a thing's nature, like being hot or cold.</note>, as in an element in which the elements oppose each other through contrary qualities. But through the third species, it is seen that contrariety, which is an accident, is subject to substantial goodness just as an instrument is subject to an efficient cause.

# On Compartment B.D.

<margin>Second compartment B.D.</margin>

**B**onitas <note>Goodness</note> is enduring. **Is goodness enduring?** And it must be answered that it is, by the definition of duration; and the same by its own definition, and through the angles designated as B.C. in the Second Figure. And Rule B proves this, and similarly Rule D through all its definitions, such as through the first by which it is primitive: as when it is said, goodness has related and coessential things to itself with which it lasts in its own nature; and the second species of Rule D proves this.

# On Compartment B.E.

<margin>Third compartment B.E.</margin>

**B**onitas <note>Goodness</note> is powerful. **Is goodness powerful?** And it must be answered through the definitions of goodness and power that it is, because power is the being by reason of which goodness can exist and act. And unless goodness were powerful, there could be no reason why a good thing would produce a good thing. And also Rule B affirms that goodness is powerful.

**Why is goodness powerful?** And it must be answered through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?"</note> because it is of the coessential [parts]: the good-maker, the made-good, and the act of making good. And thus goodness as the agent and the power...

# Sixth Part

It <note>Goodness</note> makes good those <term>foreign things capable of being made good<gloss>original: bonificabilia peregrina; external objects or beings that receive goodness from an outside source</gloss></term> within its own <term>intrinsic capacity to be made good<gloss>original: bonificabili intrinseco; the internal potential within a being to receive or contain goodness</gloss></term>. Indeed, these foreign things are not of the same genus or nature as the intrinsic capacity of that goodness itself. Through the second species, however, goodness is powerful so that other essences may be shaped by it. This was observed through Rule B <note>Rule B is the first of Llull's logical rules, asking the question "Whether a thing is?"</note>. ¶ Regarding the question "Is goodness different?", this has already been answered in the <term>chamber<gloss>original: camera; a specific intersection or combination of two principles in Llull's logical diagrams</gloss></term> of B. C. <note>The combination of Goodness and Greatness.</note> ¶ Goodness acts as a principle: is goodness a principle? It must be answered that it is, according to its own definition: because it is the "reason for a good thing that it should produce a good thing." This is proven by the definitions of "principle" and "difference" through the <term>ladder of the sensual and the sensual<gloss>original: scalam de sensuali et sensuali; a logical method of rising from physical perceptions to intellectual truths</gloss></term> etc., in which goodness is the general principle from which descends the "good difference" existing between this plant and that one. The same applies to the good principle, whether causal or accidental. This is affirmed by Rule B and the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "How much?" or "Of what kind?"</note>, because goodness exists through its own <term>made-good<gloss>bonificatum</gloss></term>, its <term>capacity to be made good<gloss>bonificabile</gloss></term>, and its <term>act of making good<gloss>bonificare</gloss></term>. And through the second species, goodness exists so that other principles under it may be "good things" having good qualities through that goodness itself.

## On Chamber B. F.
<note>This section explores the intersection of Goodness (B) and Wisdom (F).</note>

<margin>Fourth chamber B. F.</margin>
**B**oodness is knowable. Is goodness knowable? It must be answered that it is: which is evident through Rule B and through the ladder of difference existing between the sensual and the sensual etc. It is also evident through the three species of the <term>middle<gloss>original: medij; the intermediary stage of an action</gloss></term> led into the essence of goodness, by which the intellect recognizes the distinct natural origins from which goodness possesses continuous quantity. The definition of the "middle" proves this. ¶ Is goodness different? It must be answered that it is, as was proven in chamber B. C. ¶ Is goodness capable of having a middle? It must be answered that it is: because "difference" declares that in goodness there is the "act of making good" <note>original: bonificare</note> existing as the middle between the "maker of good" <note>original: bonificantem</note> and the "thing being made good" <note>original: bonificabile</note>. For otherwise, goodness could not be the reason for a good thing to produce a good thing, nor would it have natural motion, nor even real relations. This is sufficiently probable through Rule B. ¶ To what extent is goodness knowable? It must be answered: as much as a natural or moral "middle" can enter into goodness itself through the ladder existing between the sensual and the sensual, along with the definitions of goodness, difference, wisdom, and the middle. Rule B testifies to this. ¶ To what extent is goodness differentiable? It must be answered: as much as it is diffused through the chambers of the Third Figure by reason of the mixing of the principles habituated to goodness. ¶ To what extent is goodness capable of having a middle? It must be answered: as much as the "middle" can enter it regarding the definition of the middle, goodness, wisdom, and difference, as was proven through Rule B and through the first and second species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks "Whose is it?" or "Why?"</note>. This is because goodness, regarding its essence, has continuous quantity, and regarding its relations, it has discrete quantities caused by difference.

## On Chamber B. G.
<note>This section explores Goodness (B) in relation to Greatness or the End (G).</note>

<margin>Fifth chamber B. G.</margin>
<margin><insert>This chamber is very useful.</insert></margin>
**B**oodness is lovable. Is goodness lovable? It must be answered that it is, as is evident through the definitions of goodness and the <term>end<gloss>original: finis; the purpose or ultimate goal</gloss></term>, Rule B, and the ladder of the sensual and the sensual etc. ¶ Is goodness differentiable? It must be answered as was said above. ¶ Is goodness finishable <note>meaning: can it reach its purposeful conclusion?</note>? It must be answered that it is. For if it were not finishable, it would no longer be the reason for a good thing to produce a good thing; nor would there be a clear reason through "difference" having natural and intrinsic reasons, and extrinsic moral reasons; and its boundaries would be malice and privation <note>the total absence of a quality</note>, which is false and impossible. Rule B affirms this along with the definitions of goodness, difference, and the end, and likewise the ladder of the sensual and the sensual etc. ¶ What kind of goodness is lovable, differentiable, and finishable? It must be answered that substantial goodness is lovable through its own innate and related <term>passions<gloss>attributes or things that happen to a substance</gloss></term>, declared through difference, and quieted <note>satisfied or brought to rest</note> through the end. And there is another moral or accidental goodness, such as the goodness of the will, of magnitude, etc. And likewise the goodness of justice, wisdom, etc. ¶ What kind of difference of goodness is lovable? It must be answered that it is that which places intrinsic relations and passions within goodness. And on the outside, it places moral relations. This has been proven through the ladder of the sensual and the sensual. ¶ What kind of end is lovable? It must be answered that it is the "highest end" which is the First Cause <note>God</note> and the proper end of natural and also moral goodness. And so concerning the end of "difference," without which—and without the ladder of the sensual and the sensual etc.—the universe could not truly exist; it would be privation and despair, by reason of which privation the world would indeed have no being. ### On the evacuation of the third figure.

The destruction of the whole follows the destruction of the parts. And this is signified through Rule B <note>Rule B is the first of Llull's nine rules, asking "Whether a thing exists?" or "Whether it is?"</note> and also through Rule G <note>Rule G asks "How much?" or "Of what quantity?"</note>.

->**Concerning the Chamber of B. H.**<-

<margin>The sixth chamber: B. H.</margin>
**G**oodness is virtuous. Whether goodness is virtuous? And the answer is yes: which is evident through the definition of goodness, of virtue, and of greatness, and through the <term>ladder of difference<gloss>original: scalam differentie; a logical tool for distinguishing between levels of being</gloss></term> existing between one sensual thing and another, etc. And similarly through the ladder of greatness existing between one substance and another, etc. And this is affirmable through the second species of Rule B. ¶ Whether goodness is different? And the answer should be as before. ¶ Goodness is greater. Whether goodness is greater? And the answer is yes: for goodness is "more good" through its substance than through its <term>accidents<gloss>original: accidens; a non-essential quality, like a color or a temporary state, as opposed to the core essence</gloss></term>, and through its substantial relations rather than its minor and accidental ones. And goodness is greater in one subject than in another, just as in the ladder of the more-sensual and the sensual, and in the ladder of greatness existing between one substance and another, etc. ¶ In what way is goodness virtuous? And the answer is that it is virtuous when it is in its very being; but it is *morally* virtuous when it is <term>habituated<gloss>original: habituata; possessing a "habit" or steady disposition of the soul</gloss></term> by the habits of justice and prudence, etc. And this is demonstrated through the definitions of goodness, virtue, greatness, and difference, and through Rule B. ¶ When is goodness differentiable? The answer is: when it is in its own being. And this is through the principle of "difference" which establishes real relations without which goodness cannot have its own nature. And it is also differentiable when it is moral. For one habit exists through justice, and another truly through prudence, etc. This is proven through the definitions of the aforementioned principles. ¶ When is goodness greater? And the answer is: when it exists substantially rather than morally. It is also greater when it is habituated by a moral virtue existing in practice, rather than when it is not in practice. Furthermore, it is greater when it acts with charity and when it acts with justice. And the same judgment applies to "substantial acting" and "accidental acting." And this is indeed provable through Rule B.

->**Concerning the Chamber of B. J.**<-

**G**oodness is true. Whether goodness is true? And it must be answered through Rule B that it is so. And similarly through the definitions of goodness, virtue, difference, and equality. For if goodness were not true, then goodness would not be the "reason for a good thing to produce a good thing"; nor could truth place this within what is true. For neither could difference enter between the <term>bonifier, the bonifiable, and the act of bonifying<gloss>original: bonificans, bonificabile, and bonificare; Llull's "concrete" triad of the actor, the object, and the action</gloss></term> in a truthful way; nor would equality have a subject in which to rest, as it exists between the concrete forms of goodness. Thus, the ladder of the sensual and the sensual, etc., and similarly the ladder of substance and substance, etc., would be destroyed. And the world can by no means exist without these ladders, which is impossible. Therefore, goodness is a true essence and exists through itself. ¶ Goodness is different. Whether goodness is different? The answer is as was said before. ¶ Goodness is equal. Whether goodness is equal? The answer is yes. This is evident through Rule B and through the definitions of the aforementioned principles. For goodness is the "reason for a good thing to produce a good thing"; and truth places this within what is true along with difference and equality, so that goodness may exist equally diffused between the true bonifier, the bonified, and the act of bonifying. This is designated through the ladders of the sensual and the sensual, etc., and of substance and substance, etc., in the Second Figure. ¶ Where is true goodness? And the answer is through the first species of Rule C and D <note>Rules C and D ask "Of what?" and "Why?"</note> that it is in itself, since it is a primitive essence according to its genus. And also through the second species of Rule C and D, it is in its own good and true "concrete forms." And it is in truth, difference, and equality, like a habit in one who is habituated. And it is also in the ladder of the sensual and the sensual, etc., and in the ladder of the substantial and the substantial, etc. And Rules B, I, and K affirm this.

<meta>This page continues the "Evacuation of the Third Figure," a logical process where the author, Ramon Llull, explores the combinations of primary principles. ...to be given, as is clear in the **ladder of the sensory** <note>original: "scala sensuali"; refers to the hierarchy of things perceivable by the senses.</note> and the sensory, etc., and in the **ladder of the substantial** and the substantial, etc. Goodness is indeed lesser in a stone than in a plant; and in a plant it is lesser than in a brute animal; and in a color lesser than in the act of seeing; and in seeing lesser than in understanding, and so with the others. And this is affirmable through **rule B. K.** <note>Llull’s logical rules are lettered. Rule B asks "Whether a thing exists?" and K represents "Glory." This rule explores the existence of Glory within the principle of Goodness.</note>

¶ **How is glorious goodness?**
And the answer is that glorious goodness has its mode through **difference** <note>Difference is one of Llull's "Relative Principles," used here to distinguish the unique essence of a thing from others.</note>, which posits that it is one substantial essence distinct from all others; and that it has different substantial things which are of its own genus and nature, with which it has an intrinsic nature set in rest. And this is indeed glorious for it, as it exists in glory and glory exists in that very goodness. It also has moral modes in causing distinct moral habits, both good and glorious. And to this the rules of **B. K.** bear witness.

¶ **With what is goodness different?**
The answer is that it is different through itself, and with the **difference** that posits that the essence itself is distinct from all other essences that are not of its species and nature. And there is another mode by which goodness is different: namely, with its **coessential and substantial relatives** <note>Llull views every principle as a triad: an active force (e.g., the Bonifier), a passive object (the Bonified), and the act itself (Bonifying).</note> with which it causes accidental goodnesses. And this is signified in the ladder of the sensory and the sensory, etc., and in the ladder of the substantial and the substantial, etc.

# On the Chamber of L. D.

<margin>
The ninth chamber, which is C. D.
</margin>

**G**reatness is eternal. **What is eternal greatness?**
The answer is through the definition of **greatness**, **eternity**, **concordance**, and **contrariety** <note>These are primary principles in Llull's Great Art. He seeks to show they are logically compatible and co-exist within the divine or universal structure.</note>, by saying thus: Eternal magnification is a being having in itself—according to the first and second species of **Rule C. D.**—concrete things that are great, infinite, and eternal, as well as primitive. And through the third species of **Rule C. D.**, the said concrete things exist with an infinite magnitude of concordance and even contrariety, and are separated from all subjection, with each concrete thing existing within another concrete thing.

¶ Indeed, the whole essence of eternity exists in each of the aforesaid concrete things. And similarly, the whole being of concordance; and each has its own distinct number from the other within the other, these three concrete things existing as one essence and not as several.

¶ **What is great concordance?**
Great concordance is that essence which stands through the second species of **Rule C. D.**, and through the third species of **Rule C.**; the whole essence of concordance is in another, and every concrete part of concordance is the whole essence of concordance. It is also the mistress of all other accidental or "foreign" concordances <note>Llull distinguishes between internal concordance (the harmony within a single substance) and accidental concordance (the relationship between two different things).</note>.

¶ **What is great contrariety?**
The answer is that it is that form which causes corruptions in "elevated" things, and causes habits of privation: namely, injury, lust, and so forth.

¶ **It is asked:** of what are eternal greatness, concordant greatness, and contrary greatness composed? And the answer is found in what was said above, as is clear to one who looks closely.

¶ And we proceed in this manner for the sake of relief, and so that boredom is not produced in the mind of the student due to repetition.

# On the Chamber of L. E.

<margin>
The tenth chamber, which is C. E.
</margin>

**W**hat is **great power**?
The answer is that it is a being in which greatness and power are **interchangeable** <note>original: "convertuntur"; a logical term meaning the terms are co-extensive and can be swapped in a proposition without changing its truth.</note>. And this is signified through the first species of **Rule C.** And through the second species of **Rule C.**, it is great power because it has formal and coessential concrete things: namely, the **magnifier**, the **power-maker**, the **magnified**, the **empowered**, and the acts of **magnifying** and **empowering**. This is signified through the second species of Rule C, and also through the first species of **Rule E**. Through the third species of Rule C., it exists in other essences so that they may be able to exist and act through it. Through the fourth species, however, it has actions and passions of acting and suffering in an appropriate subject.

¶ Furthermore, through the second species of **Rule E.**, there is great power so that all things other than itself are magnificently possible; and this is proved through the definition of greatness and power.

¶ **Greatness is concordant. What is great concordance?**
The answer is through that which was said in chamber **C. D.**

¶ **Greatness is a great principle. What is a great principle?**
To which it must be said that it is a being in which greatness and **principle** are interchangeable, without any matter or accident. And this is signified through the second species of **Rule C.** and through the first of **Rule E.** But the **magnifying beginner** <note>original: "magnificans principians"</note> exists so that there may be a **magnified result** <note>original: "magnificatum principiatum"</note>, and so that from both may proceed **magnifying** and **beginning**, along with the definition of greatness, power, concordance, and principle.

### On the chamber of C. F.

<margin>The eleventh chamber, which is about C. F.</margin>

**G**reat intellect exists. What is great intellect? The answer is that it is a being in which greatness and intellect are convertible <note>In Llull’s logic, "convertible" means terms are interchangeable or essentially one; where there is true Greatness, there is true Intellect.</note>. And this is signified through the first species of the rule. Furthermore, greatness of intellect is that which has its co-essential and relative concrete parts: namely, the **knower**, the **known**, and the **act of knowing** <note>original: "intelligentem/ intelligibile/ et intelligere." This triad represents the internal activity of the intellect.</note>; with which it has a distributive nature; and that its essence is continuous and indivisible. And this is signified through the second species of Rule C. ¶ Furthermore, the greatness of the intellect is such that all intelligible things are within its essence; and this is signified through the third species of Rule C, so that the intellect itself may be magnificently practical. Moreover, through the fourth species, intellect is such that it has a general relation to all things, like an intellect that understands "this" and "that"; and that it has an object of understanding in which it understands this and that; and with these, it is practical and particular and successive, both through the **ladder of the defensive and the sensory** <note>original: "scalam defensualium et sensualium"; the "ladders" are Llull's way of describing the ascent from physical sensations to abstract reasoning.</note> etc., and through the ladder of the medium of conjunction etc. ¶ What is great concordance? The answer is through that which was said in the chamber of C. D. <note>Chamber C. D. refers to the combination of Greatness and Eternity/Duration.</note> ¶ Greatness is mediating. What is a great medium? To which the answer must be through the **ladder of the medium** and through the **ladder of concordance**; and through the first and second species of Rule C. F. For without these, a great medium could not exist at all; and also without such a medium, greatness would be empty and idle; and similarly, without such greatness, the medium could not be great. And that what has been said is true is indeed proven through the definitions of the principles and the species of the rules; and also through the aforementioned ladders, in which the intellect is successive in ascending and descending, acquiring and habituating sciences. ¶ **Question.** How great is the greatness of the intellect? And how great is its concordance, and likewise for its medium? And it must be said that it is as great as it has been signified to be. However, through what has been said of its greatness and concordance and medium in the paragraphs placed in the chamber of C. F., we leave the aforementioned things to a person who speculates well and knows this Art. And we do this for the sake of brevity.

### On the chamber of C. G.

**G**reat will, what is it? This is the internal structure of the Will.</note> formally; in which beloved, it is formally active with the act of loving. And through the fourth species, it has all lovable things within itself. G. ¶ What kind of will is great, and what kind of concordance, and what kind of end? To this question, the answer must be through what was said above. For the solutions are implied in what was said above; and they can be technically explained for the purpose at hand.

# Sixth part

...as was said previously. ¶**Greatness is greater**; but what is "greater greatness"? The answer is that it is that substance which is furthest removed from smallness, minority, and accident. Furthermore, through the second species of Rule C <note>Rule C usually asks "Of what is it composed?" The second species focuses on the internal, co-essential relations of a principle.</note>, it is a being having within itself the **magnifier**, the **magnified**, and the **act of magnifying** <note>original: "magnificantem / magnificatum z magnificare." These represent Llull's functional triad: the doer, the receiver, and the action itself.</note>. ## On the chamber of C. I.

**G**reatness is true. What is "true greatness"? The answer is that it is that substance which is most distant from falsehood and from accident, having within itself—through the second species of Rule C—**truer versions** of the **magnified**, the **magnifiable**, and the **act of magnifying** <note>original: "veros / magnificatum / magnificabile / magnificare."</note>; existing both outside of place and within place infinitely, and without contradiction. 
¶Furthermore, through the third species, it is the cause that brings about true greatnesses existing in a place—rather than false ones—whether they be substantial or accidental. ¶Moreover, through the fourth species, it possesses great and true actions in every new subject. And this is proven through the definitions of the principles of the chamber of C. I. <note>The combination of Greatness and Truth</note>, as well as through the rules. ¶What is "great concordance"? The answer is as before: but if it is asked "what is greater concordance?", the answer is that it is the "greater substance" having within itself substantial and greater relations, removed from all accidents. ¶"Great equality" exists. What is "great equality"? The answer is that it is the substance having within itself its own relatives, segregated from all "greater-ness" and "lesser-ness." Furthermore, through the second species, it is the cause of all related "greater-ness" and "lesser-ness," existing itself in a place (though not confined by it) and infinite outside of place. Furthermore, through the fourth species, it possesses whatever it wills in that place. And this is probable through the rule and through the definitions of the principles of chamber C. I. ¶Where are "great virtue," "great concordance," and "great equality"? The answer is that they are within themselves through the second species of Rule C. And through the third species, they are in other subjects caused by them. And thus for the first and fourth species in their own way. And this same thing is to be understood through the species of Rule I <note>Rule I asks "How?" (Quomodo?)</note> in its own way.

## On the chamber of C. K.

**G**reat glory; it is asked, what is it? The answer is that it is that substance which is most distant from depravity and punishment: it is a being having within itself, through the second species of Rule C, **glorious versions** of the **magnifier**, the **magnified**, and the **act of magnifying**. Through the third species, it is the cause in all external substances and accidents. And through the fourth species, it possesses great glory in that which is greatly glorified, and vice versa. And thus it is for the "act of magnifying" and the "act of glorifying." And this can be affirmed through the rules of C. K. and the definitions of the principles of the chamber of C. K. <note>The combination of Greatness and Glory</note>. ¶What is "great concordance"? The answer is as before. But if it is asked: "what is the great concordance of glory?", the answer is given through all four species of Rule C, since it is that which is signified through them. And to this, the definitions of greatness, concordance, and glory bear witness. ¶What is "great minority" <note>smallness or less-than-ness</note>? The answer is that it is an accident closer to "non-being" than to substance. Likewise, it is a being that does not have co-essential relatives within itself through the second species of Rule C. But, through accident, there are some substantial greatnesses there: as is evident in the "sensual scale" <note>the hierarchy of things perceived by the senses</note> joined to the "scale of substance" <note>the hierarchy of essential being</note>, and so on. And this is proven through the rules of C. K. and through the definition of "minority." ¶How does "great glory" exist? And likewise for "great concordance": the answer is through the third species of Rule C, with those relations existing one within the other by magnifying, glorifying, and according, segregated from all "minority." ¶With what does "great glory" exist? And likewise for "great greatness" and "concordance": the answer is that it exists with the **magnifier**, **glorifier**, and **accorder**; the **magnified**, **glorified**, and **accorded**; and the **act of magnifying**, **glorifying**, and **according**. It also exists with the conversion of identity of essence, substance, and nature—these three relations being distinct from one another by their own number through the second species of Rule C. ¶Furthermore, "great glory" (and likewise "great concordance") exists with the "sensual scale" and so on, and similarly with the "substantial scale" and so on. But this latter is not as "great" as the first, because the first is the cause, while the others are secondary.

# On the evacuation of the third figure.

<margin>The sixteenth chamber, which is D.E.</margin>
# On the evacuation of the third figure.

**P**owerful duration <note>original: "Duratio potens." This refers to the combination of Duration (D) and Power (E).</note> through the first species of rule D <note>In Llull's system, Rule D asks "What is it?" (Quid?). The first species asks about the thing in itself.</note>, what is it? The answer is: it is of itself, since it is primitive <note>A "primitive" principle is a fundamental building block that cannot be broken down further.</note> as to its essence and power, which gives it the ability to exist and to act. And through the second species of rule D, it is asked: of what consists powerful duration? The answer is: it is of its own relations <note>original: "relationis," likely referring to the internal structure of the principle.</note> and of the relatives of power. And through the third species of the same rule, it is asked: whose is powerful duration? It must be said that it is of substantial duration and power, since it is a habit <note>term: habit <gloss>a stable disposition or quality held by a substance.</gloss></note> with which substantial duration and power can endure. ¶ Of what consists the duration of contrariety? The answer is that it is of the primitive qualities, truths, and vices that endure because they are able to endure. ¶ Of what consists the duration of principles? It must be said: it is of primitive durations and primitive principles, with duration communicating its essence to the principle, and the principle communicating its essence to duration. ¶ Why does power endure? The answer is that it endures because it is of the powerful, the enduring, the durable, and that which is possible to endure, and the power in the composite subject in which they exist. ¶ Why does the contrariety of power endure? It must be said it is because it is habituated by contrary relatives, and of duration and power in the composite subject in which they are. ¶ Why do the principles of power endure? It must be said they endure by reason of the substantial relatives habituated in the genus of duration and power.

## On the chamber of D.F.

<margin>The seventeenth chamber, which is D.F.</margin>
**K**nowable duration <note>original: "Duratio scibilis." This combines Duration (D) and Knowledge/Intellect (F).</note>, of what does it consist? The answer is that it is of the intellectual endurer, the durable, the intelligible, to endure, and to understand <note>These are the "correlatives" of the principles: the actor, the object, and the act itself.</note>. ¶ Of what consists the duration of contrariety? It must be said that it consists of enduring, joining, and measuring, by reason of continuous duration. ¶ How great is duration? The answer is: it is as great as its essence and its concrete parts. ¶ How great is the duration of a property? The answer is: it is as great as the properties or moralities in the subject in which they exist. ¶ How great is the duration of the mean <note>original: "duratio media," referring to the principle of the Middle/Bridge.</note>? It must be said: it is as great as the act of enduring and mediating existing between the mediating duration, the durable, and the mediable.

## On the chamber of D.G.

<margin>The eighteenth chamber, which is D.G.</margin>
**L**ovable duration <note>original: "Duratio amabilis," combining Duration (D) and Will/Love (G).</note>, of what? The answer is that it is of foreign species <note>original: "specieb⁹ peregrinis," perhaps referring to external ideas or forms introduced to the mind.</note> led into the durable and the lovable, and of those things themselves. ¶ Of what consists the duration of contrariety? The answer is the same as before. ¶ Of what consists the duration of the end <note>original: "finis," meaning purpose or goal.</note>? The answer is: it is of the quietener, or the act of quieting, and enduring beyond which appetite does not extend. ¶ What is the quality of the duration of the will? The answer is: it is such as it is through substantial correlatives, which are indeed of the genus of the duration of the will from which its own passions arise. Appropriately, these passions are those with which the subject is habituated and situated. ¶ Of what quality are contrary durations? It must be said: they are such as those which endure in the subject through contrariety. What quality are durable ends? The answer is: they are such as the appetite is habituated to through them, to the extent that it does not seek to have rest outside of them.

## On the chamber of D.H.

<margin>The nineteenth chamber, which is D.H.</margin>
**V**irtuous duration <note>original: "Duratio virtuosa," combining Duration (D) and Virtue (H). Note: The woodcut initial in the source is a 'Q', but the text begins "Duratio".</note>, of what is it? The answer is: it is of itself and of virtue, whether substantially or accidentally. ¶ Of what is the duration of contrariety? The answer is the same as before. ¶ Of what is the duration of majority <note>original: "maioritatis," the principle of Being Greater.</note>? The answer is: it is of the greater endurer, the durable, and the act of enduring; and the magnifier, the magnifiable, and the act of magnifying. ¶ When is virtuous duration? It must be said: it is then when it is in the species of D and H realistically. ¶ When is the duration of contrariety? The answer is: it is then when there is generation and corruption, or contrary qualities, or contrary morals in the subject in which they are. ¶ When is the duration of majority? The answer is: it is then when powers or substances have their acts.

It must be said: it is the same as before. ¶ Of what is the duration of equality? It must be said: it is of the endurer, the co-equaler, and the durable, the co-equalable, and the act of enduring, the act of co-equaling... <note>The sentence continues onto the next page.</note>

...Where is the duration of truth? It must be answered that it is in all species <note>original: "speciebus"</note>. Where is the duration of contrariety? ## Concerning the chamber D.K.

<margin>The twenty-first chamber, D.K.</margin>

**D**uration is gloriable <note>D represents Duration and K represents Glory/Praise. This section explores how things endure in a state of glory.</note>. ¶ From what does the duration of glory consist? It must be said that it is with the relatives of division in a subject habituated toward corruption.

## Concerning the chamber E.G.

<margin>The twenty-third chamber, E.G.</margin>

**P**ower is lovable <note>E represents Power and G represents Will or Love.</note>. Why is it lovable? It must be said that one is proper, such as its own possibility; another is appropriated, such as its own lovability. ¶ What kind of principle is it? It must be answered that one is a qualitative principle substantially, and the other accidentally; and the substantial is habituated by the accidental. ¶ What kind of end <note>original: "finis"</note> is it? It must be answered that one end is perfecting, another is terminating, and another is privative, as is evident in the scale of the second figure.

## Concerning the chamber E.H.

<margin>The twenty-fourth chamber, E.H.</margin>

It must be said that it exists at that time when it is the cause so that other principles may exist and act. ¶ When does a principle exist? It must be said that it is when its "primitivity" <note>its fundamental, first state</note> exists, and when it has its correlatives, etc. ¶ When does majority exist? It must be said that it is when powers have greater acts or effects.

## Concerning chamber E.I.

**P**ower <note>Represented by the letter E in Llull's Alphabet.</note> is true <note>Represented by the letter I.</note>. Why is it true? <margin>The twenty-sixth chamber, which is E.K.</margin>

## Concerning chamber E.K.

**P**ower is glorious <note>K represents Glory or Praise.</note>. It is asked: why is it glorious? It must be answered: because it has its substantial correlatives in which glory is impressed and habituated. ¶ Why is power a principle? It must be answered as before. ¶ Why is power minor <note>original: "minor"; K also represents Minority in certain contexts of the Art.</note>? It must be said that it is because its correlatives are situated in minority and are habituated by it, by reason of which it causes divisions, and the "lesser" which belongs to the genus of minority, just as the "greater" belongs to the genus of majority. ¶ How does power exist? It must be answered that it exists through the mode of modality <note>The 'how' or manner of being.</note>, when it is habituated by modality. ¶ How does a principle exist? It must be answered that it exists through the mode it has in its correlatives from which it is constituted; it possesses this mode since it is habituated with the power by which it can act as a principle. And so it is with glory, with which it has the mode of glorying, when in its intrinsic capacity to be a principle, it originates "foreign" beings <note>original: "entia peregrina"; things outside its own essential nature.</note> which are not of its own genus. ¶ How does minority exist? It must be answered that its mode is to participate with division, emptiness <note>original: "inanitione"</note>, corruption, and annihilation. ¶ With what is power glorious? It must be said that it is glorious with glory, just as glory is powerful with power. ¶ With what is a principle? It must be said that it is with its correlatives and with power, without which it cannot be. ¶ With what is minority? It must be said that it is with division and corruption and emptiness.

<margin>The twenty-seventh chamber, which is F.G.</margin>

## Concerning chamber F.G.

**W**isdom <note>F represents Knowledge/Wisdom.</note> is lovable <note>G represents the Will or the Lovable.</note>. It is asked: how much is it lovable? It must be answered that it is as lovable as the will is knowable, because it has equal correlatives. ¶ The middle <note>The connection or path between beginning and end.</note> is lovable. It is asked: how much is it lovable? It must be said that it is as lovable as there is loving in the will through joining and measuring. ¶ Is the end <note>The purpose or completion of a thing.</note> so much knowable? It must be answered that it is as knowable as knowledge is able to find rest in the end. ¶ It is asked: what kind of knowability is the proper passion <note>original: "passio"; in this context, a property or attribute received by a subject.</note> of the intellect? It must be said that it is that through which the intellect has an intrinsic passion in which "intelligibilities" or "foreign species" are generated, these being placed in the genus of intelligibility according to the second species of G <note>referring to the second rule of the Will.</note>. ¶ What is the proper middle? It must be answered that it is a mediatable thing in which there are foreign or appropriate mediations. ¶ It is asked: what is the proper end of the intellect? It must be said that it is the thing understood, quieted <note>brought to a state of rest or completion.</note> in its own proper intelligibility.

<margin>The twenty-eighth chamber, which is F.H.</margin>

## Concerning chamber F.H.

**T**he intellect is virtuous <note>H represents Virtue.</note>. It is asked: how much is it virtuous? It must be said that it is as much as it is habituated with virtue. ¶ The middle of the intellect is just as virtuous: it must be said that it is as much as its "ladder of the middle" <note>The logical or ontological steps used to reach a conclusion.</note> is habituated. ¶ How great is the "majority" <note>original: "maioritas"; Greatness.</note> of the intellect? It must be answered that it is as great as the intellect surpasses in reaching objects with a greater understanding. ¶ When is the intellect virtuous? It must be answered: it is then, when it is habituated with natural and moral virtue. ¶ When is virtue mediated? It must be answered: it is then, when virtue enters the middle, and by reason of this entrance, virtue consists in the middle. ¶ When is greatness understood? It must be said: it is then, when the intellect reaches the essence and the act of virtue.

<margin>The twenty-ninth chamber, which is F.I.</margin>

## Concerning chamber F.I.

**T**he intellect is true <note>I represents Truth.</note>. It is asked: how much is it true? It must be said: as much as exists between the intellect and the act of understanding. ¶ How great is the equality of the intellect?

## Concerning chamber F. K. <note>The OCR reads "F.R.," but the text discusses "Glory," which is represented by the letter K in Llull's system.</note>

**T**he intellect is glorious. How much is it glorious? It must be said: as much as it measures glory in the act of understanding. ¶ How great is the minority <note>or "smallness"</note> of the intellect? It must be said: it is as great as the intellect is habituated in it. ¶ How does the intellect understand? It must be said: it is by way of the sensitive and imaginative [faculties] with which it is joined; it has this manner by imposing foreign species <note>term: species <gloss>Mental images or representations of external objects gathered by the senses.</gloss></note> into its own proper intelligible <note>the realm of things that can be understood</note>. ¶ How does the intellect measure its own understanding? And it must be answered that it measures it by having a manner of acting and of being acted upon <note>original: "agendi & patiendi"</note> in reaching objects. ¶ How does the intellect have a "lesser understanding"? And it must be answered: it is by way of believing, because believing is not of its own kind <note>Llull argues that intellectual "knowing" is a higher, more certain category than "believing."</note>. Likewise, it has lesser understanding when it is habituated in a lesser modality. ¶ With what does the intellect understand? It must be said: with the act of understanding and with the species of the sensitive and imaginative faculties, those species being impressed upon its own proper intelligible. ¶ With what does the intellect join the species of the sensitive and imaginative? It must be said: with its own understanding. ¶ With what does the intellect have lesser understanding? It must be said: with the proximity and nearness of ignorance, and with the idleness of the intellect, the will, and the memory.

## Concerning chamber G. H.

It must be answered: it is that which has a greater act of loving, a greater lover, and a greater lovable object, and also that which has a greater habit of virtue, goodness, etc. ¶ When does the Will have greater virtue?

# Concerning the multiplication of the fourth figure.

...then it is when it causes greater virtues.
¶ **Virtue**, when is it equal? It must be said that it is then when it causes virtuous understanding, remembering, and loving. ¶ **Virtue**, where is it true? It should be answered that it is in truth, outside of which it cannot be true. ¶ **Virtue**, where is it greater? It must be said that it is both in substance and in accident <note>In the medieval philosophy Llull uses, a "substance" is a thing that exists in itself (like a person), while an "accident" is a quality that exists only within a substance (like a person's height or hair color).</note>. ¶ **Virtue**, where is it equal? It must be said that it is in its substantial correlatives <note>term: correlatives <gloss>In Llull's system, every principle like Virtue or Truth is composed of three parts: the actor (e.g., the Virtuous), the object (the thing made Virtuous), and the act itself (the making Virtuous). These three must be in balance.</gloss></note> which are habituated <note>In medieval thought, a "habit" is a stable disposition or quality that allows a faculty to act easily and naturally.</note> concerning equality.

## Concerning chamber B.K. <note>In Llull's standard alphabet, B represents Goodness and K represents Glory. However, the text here discusses Virtue (usually H). The "B.K." likely refers to a specific cell in a logic table.</note>

**Virtue** is glorious. It asks: when is it glorious? It must be said that it is then when glory is impressed upon its correlatives. ¶ **Glory**, when is it greater? It must be said that it is then when it has a greater "to glory" <note>original: *gloriari*, the active verbal process of being glorious or rejoicing</note>. ¶ **Virtue**, when is it equal? It must be said that it is then when it causes equal understanding, remembering, and loving. ¶ **Glory**, how is it virtuous? It must be said it is by the way it has in causing a lesser act. ¶ **Virtue**, with what is it glorious? It must be answered: with the greater act of glory. ¶ **Minority** <note>or "Smallness"</note>, with what is it glorious? It must be said that it is with the lesser act appropriated to it, habituated from glory.

## Concerning chamber I.K.

<margin>The thirty-sixth chamber, which is I.K.</margin>
**Truth** is glorious. It asks: where is it glorious? And it must be answered that it is in its correlatives placed or situated in glory. ¶ **Truth**, where is it equal? It must be answered: in its substantial correlatives, outside of which it can least of all have equality. ¶ **Truth**, where is it lesser? It must be answered: it is in a lesser habit and act. ¶ **Truth**, how is it glorious? And it must be answered: by the way it has in causing a true and glorious act. ¶ **Truth**, how is it equal? It must be answered: by the way it has in its substantially equal correlatives. ¶ **Will** <note>original: *Voluntas*</note>, how is it lesser? It must be answered: it is by the way it has in causing a lesser act. ¶ **Truth**, with what is it glorious? It must be said: with the rest <note>or "peace/quietude"</note> which it has in glory and in its correlatives. ¶ **Truth**, with what is it equal? And it must be answered: with the equality of its correlatives and its habits. ¶ **Truth**, with what is it lesser? It must be said: it is with an accident, just as it is greater with substance.

<margin>Conclusion.</margin>
¶ **We have spoken** about the evacuation <note>In this context, "evacuation" means the exhaustive process of working through every possible logical combination in a figure until it is "emptied."</note> of the third figure; and just as we have exhausted it with the propositions and questions noted within it, so the artist of this Art can exhaust the chambers through all the propositions and questions applied in the chambers of which I have not spoken for the sake of the lengthiness which we wish to avoid. For any chamber has 12 propositions and 24 questions. ¶ Furthermore, we have said that every chamber is general to particular questions: namely to a question made concerning God, concerning an angel, etc. ¶ Furthermore, we say that whoever well knows the doctrine we have given in this third figure would know how to practice throughout the whole Art generally.

The fourth way is concerning the knowledge of fallacies. ¶ The fifth way is how other sciences are easily learned and in a truer way through this science. And first, we must speak of the first way.

# The Seventh Part

With the chambers having been made: namely **b.c.e.** and **b.c.f.** up to chamber **b.i.k.**, <note>In Llull’s system, letters represent principles: B is Goodness, C is Greatness, D is Duration, E is Power, F is Wisdom, G is Will, H is Virtue, I is Truth, and K is Glory.</note> twenty arguments can therefore be produced in any chamber. And thus, by turning the circles so many times, there are eighty-four columns in the table. ¶ But regarding this matter, it has been discussed in the table of the fourth figure. ¶ Further, multiplication occurs from chamber to chamber, just as chambers **c.d.e.** and **c.d.f.** and **d.e.f.** and **d.e.g.** behave like chamber **c.d.e.**, and so on for the others in their own way up to chamber **h.i.k.** And so it is for the multiplications through the revolutions of the circles. And this multiplication exists because one principle is habituated <note>In medieval philosophy, "habituated" means a principle has been integrated or disposed to act in conjunction with another.</note> and multiplied with another principle and with its own proper passions and appropriations. ¶ Further, there is a fourth multiplication. For the fourth figure contains within itself the third figure, just as chamber **b.c.d.** contains chamber **b.c.** and chamber **c.d.** in the third figure. Likewise, chamber **c.d.e.** contains chamber **c.d.** and chamber **d.e.** in the third figure, and so for others in their own way. In these four ways does the multiplication consist.

## On the discovery of middle terms.

<margin>
First response.

On the discovery of middle terms.
</margin>

**I**n chamber **b.c.d.**, and similarly for others in their own way, **c.** consists in the middle circle, because it exists between **b.** and **d.** And because **c.** is joined with **b.** and with **d.** through certain positions: namely, habits and situations existing between the subject and the predicate. And when the artist <note>The "artist" refers to the practitioner or student of Llull’s "Great Art" (Ars Magna).</note> wants a middle term, <note>term: middle term <gloss>In a syllogism, the middle term is the concept that connects the subject and the predicate of a conclusion (e.g., in "All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal," the middle term is "man").</gloss></note> he should always investigate in the middle of the circle. For just as it belongs to "animal" to stand in a measured and conjunctive way between "substance" and "man" when it is concluded that man is a substance; so the letter which is in the middle circle ought to stand between the letter existing in the upper circle and the letter existing in the lower circle, as when one argues thus: Every **c.** is **b.** and every **d.** is **c.**, therefore every **d.** is **b.** ¶ And just as it is necessary through certain conjectures and passions that an animal be a substance and a man be an animal: so the artist of this art ought to conjecture through those things which **b.** and **c.** signify, namely their subalternate principles. Just as **b.** sounds or signifies **Goodness**, **Difference**, and **Whether** <note>These represent the first principle, the first relative principle, and the first "Rule" or question in Llull's system.</note>. And **c.** signifies **Greatness**, **Concordance**, and **What**. And **d.** signifies **Duration**, **Contrariety**, and **Of what**. And in this sounding or signifying consist the definitions of the principles and the types of rules with which the artist must conjecture the middle term with the upper letter and the lower letter in his own way. ¶ And in this step, the intellect forms knowledge of the universal affirmative, the universal negative, the particular affirmative, and the particular negative; and of instances, demonstration, and <term>manuduction</term> <gloss>A "leading by the hand"; a pedagogical method of guiding someone step-by-step to a logical conclusion.</gloss>; and also of the possible and impossible. ¶ In these five ways the intellect habituates itself. And this is done in this way: when it is said "every **c.** is **d.**" and "every **b.** is **c.**", let it be granted by distinguishing: such as greatness which is good through goodness, and goodness which is great through greatness. And goodness which has great <term>correlatives</term> <gloss>The triad of the actor, the object, and the act (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and loving) which Llull believes exists within every principle.</gloss> signified through the second type of **c.**, and greatness which has good correlatives through goodness signified through the second type of **c.**, and so on for greatness and duration in their own way. ¶ Further, when it is said "every **c.** is **b.**" and "every **d.** is **c.**", the universal affirmative and universal negative arise; and this is by reason of the **Difference** subalternated in **b.**, and in **d.** **Contrariety** is subalternated. And just as when it is said: "no stone is an animal, every man is an animal, therefore no man is a stone." For the reason for this is that a stone does not have sense, etc. ¶ "Every animal is a substance, some man is an animal, therefore some man is a substance." And thus: every **c.** is **b.**, some **d.** is **c.**, therefore some **d.** is **b.** The reason for this is that the contrariety which is subalternated in **d.** cannot be the concordance which is subalternated in **c.**, nor could great malice be great goodness. Because if so, one would be placing the opposite in the object, which is impossible and against the correlatives of the second type of Rule **c.** And when it is said "no animal is a stone, some man is an animal, therefore some man is not a stone." Just as when it is said: no **c.** is **b.**, some **d.** is **c.**, therefore some **d.** is not **b.**, and the reason for this is in its own way according to what was said in the third syllogism, in which a particular affirmative is concluded. ¶ Through what has been said in the four ways of syllogizing, the intellect knows necessary instances, by denying that every **c.** is not **d.**, nor is every **d.**, **c.** And it also knows possibilities and impossibilities, such as created goodness which cannot be created greatness by reason of **Difference**, which posits that every principle exists through itself; but it posits as possible that goodness be habituated regarding greatness. ¶ Further, it knows demonstrations through the first type of Rule **g.** and manuduction through the second type of Rule **g.**, and this is represented in all the chambers of the third figure in which...

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of Ramon Llull’s "Art," moving from the combinatorial mechanics of the Fourth Figure to the logical application of "finding the middle term." It connects the abstract principles (like Goodness and Difference) to the concrete construction of syllogisms and formal proofs.</meta>

<page-num>folio 27.</page-num>
<header>On the multiplication of the fourth figure.</header>

# On the multiplication of the fourth figure.

...is **g.** ¶ Furthermore, he finds the middle term by **contracting**; <note>In medieval logic, "contraction" refers to narrowing a general concept (like "Animal") to a more specific one (like "Human").</note> namely, when a principle that is entirely general is contracted to a principle that is neither entirely general nor entirely specific. For example, **Difference**, which is a most general or entirely general principle, is contracted to the differences between one sensitive being and another, which are neither most general nor most specific. And when they are contracted to the most specific or entirely specific—such as to this animal, or to this plant, or to this stone—an individual is constituted from those very differences, both substantially and also accidentally through its own proper quantity, quality, and so on. Even when that individual is placed in its own proper species, then those differences are the **middle term** existing between the most general principle and the most specific. And just as has been said of **Difference**, so it can be said of **Goodness**, etc. For Goodness is an entirely general or most general principle. And when it is contracted to Greatness, etc., then it is not the most general principle nor the most specific. But when **Great Goodness** is contracted to this concrete thing constituted from that same great goodness—with respect to its form and its matter, and also with respect to its quantity and quality, etc.—so that it is placed in its own proper species and individuated under it: then Great Goodness (which is neither most general nor most specific) is the middle term existing between the **abstract** and the **concrete**, tasting of the nature of the extremes. Through this nature, the artist can find a middle term existing naturally between the **major and minor proposition**; and through such a middle term, demonstrations are made from first and true necessary principles, against which no objection can be found. ¶ Furthermore, he finds the middle term through its own **letter** and through its own **circle**: namely through **f.**, which signifies the middle, and through the middle circle. For example, placing **f.** under **b.** and above **c.** (which is below), considering that through **b.** it has goodness and difference, and through **c.** greatness and concordance. And so they consist between **b.** and **c.**, by reason of which **c.** passes to **b.** through the middle; as when it is said: "Every **f.** is **b.**; every **c.** is **f.**; therefore every **c.** is **b.**" But this is only with respect to the middle genus. And just as we have spoken in chamber **b.f.c.**, so it can be said in chamber **c.f.d.**, and in chamber **d.f.e.**, and so on. ¶ Through what has been said regarding the middle term, the artist can have very general material for finding many middle terms. And this is clear with the definitions of the principles and with the species of the rules.

<margin>
The method of proving.
</margin>
<margin>
<note>Handwritten note: "analytics"</note>
</margin>

**P**roof is general, and its species are: through **demonstration on account of why** <note>original: "propter quid"; a demonstration that explains the cause of a thing.</note>; and through **demonstration of equivalence** <note>original: "equiparātie"; a Lullian term for a proof where the terms are equal in power or definition.</note>; and through **demonstration that** <note>original: "quod" or "quia"; a demonstration that proves a fact exists without explaining the cause.</note>—which are divided. And through this syllogism we propose to give an example: ¶ *Every animal is a substance; every human is an animal; therefore every human is a substance.* And first we will prove the major premise; then the minor. ¶ And first, through demonstration **on account of why**: an animal is constituted from the sensitive and the sensible, because it is composed of elements, vegetated, sensing, and imagining. ¶ And thus it follows that it is a **substance**, because it is composed of substantial parts. And since substance is higher and animal is lower, the animal indeed has higher causes: namely, the **form** and **matter** from which it is constituted; and its parts are lower, because they are caused by the form and matter which are general principles. ¶ And thus it is truly concluded **on account of why** an animal is a substance. ¶ Through demonstration **of equivalence**, it is proved thus: General form and general matter are equally primitive causes. And this is clear through the first species of Rule **D**. And because an animal is caused from its own proper form and matter—moving through the elemental, the vegetative, etc.—these are equal principles of the animal itself. By reason of this, it follows that an animal is a substance constituted from its own proper form and matter, which descend equally from equal, most general principles (that is, from the first form and the first matter). And this is clear through the second species of Rule **D**, and through the first of **E**, and through Rule **B**. ¶ Through demonstration **that**, it is proved thus: an animal exists; and because it exists, its causes indeed exist: namely, the form and matter from which it is; without which it cannot be. And because form and matter constitute substance, it truly follows that an animal is a substance. ¶ Now we intend to prove the **minor premise** <note>"Every human is an animal."</note> through the same three species. And first, **on account of why**: when the **embryo** is constituted in the womb from the elemental, the vegetative, etc., and is itself shaped and formed with human members; and when the **rational soul** (which is a substance) is introduced into that embryo: then from itself and its lower parts, it constitutes a human. And thus the animal which is an embryo is transmuted into a human through the human species in which it is placed with all its co-essential parts. ¶ And thus it follows that the soul is the cause why a human is a substance; and this is clear through the first species of Rule **C**. ¶ Through **equivalence**, I prove it thus: The rational soul has...

**D**iversity of the middle term <term>middle term|The term that connects the two premises of a syllogism to reach a conclusion.</term> is the genus of fallacies; and because **f** signifies the middle term. **f**, which is in the middle circle, is the instrument for finding and for knowing fallacies, by placing and revolving it under the letters which are in the upper circle, and placing it over the letters in the lower one, thus composing "chambers" <term>chambers|The cells or specific combinations formed by the intersection of principles in Llull’s revolving wheels.</term>: such as placing **f** under **b** and over **c**, observing how **b** and **c** relate to each other in fallacies with **f**, and vice-versa. ## On the fallacy of equivocation.

<margin>What the fallacy of equivocation is</margin>
<margin>X</margin>
**E**quivocation is the different meaning of one and the same name, which arises from the fact that one name signifies several different things. And a paralogism <note>A piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning.</note> is formed thus: Every dog is able to bark; the celestial constellation is a dog; therefore the celestial constellation is able to bark. <note>original: "Omnis canis est latrabilis/celeste sydus est canis: ergo celeste sydus est latrabile." A classic medieval example of equivocation on the word "canis" (dog/the Dog Star).</note> And we assign this chamber **b.f.c.**: through **b** we understand the difference between an animate body and an inanimate body. Through **f** we understand that an animate and inanimate body are not joined by reason of the same species. Through **c** we understand that an animate body has sensitive correlates, and an inanimate one does not have sensitive correlates. And thus the artist knows in what way the error occurs by reducing it to the impossible: by reason of which knowledge the intellect knows that the logic cannot stand before natural reality; and especially by this art, reducing it to the impossible—such as a star, which is a being in which it is impossible for it to be of the genus and nature of "barkability." ¶ Furthermore, through chamber **d.f.e.** and so on for the others, one knows in what the paralogism errs. Since this "dog" which is of the elemental, vegetative, and sensitive nature can bark according to the second species of rule **d**; but the star, if it does not have such correlative principles, cannot bark: because it is not constituted from those same principles. And this is evident through the second species of rule **d**, and through the first of **c**, and also through the scale of the middle term.

## On amphibology.

<margin>What amphibology is.</margin>
**A**mphibology <term>amphibology|A fallacy resulting from ambiguous sentence structure rather than a single ambiguous word.</term> is a deception arising from the fact that one and the same sentence signifies several things: and the paralogism is formed thus. Whatever is Aristotle's is possessed by Aristotle. But this book is Aristotle's: therefore it is possessed by Aristotle. ¶ For this fallacy we assign this chamber **d. f. h.** Through **d** let us know that its third species signifies that this book is not possessed by Aristotle, since it is not possessed except by a human joined with the elemental, vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rational powers: as is clear through the second species of rule **d**. But **f** signifies the middle measure of reason, of conjunction, and of continuation in the subject in which it is. **h**, however, signifies that the book which is in this "now" <note>In the present moment.</note> is not possessed by Aristotle, for the reason that he is dead. And this same thing can be known through chamber **b. f. g.**, etc. Since **b** places a difference between a man now dead and one living. And **f** places a conjunction between the sensual and the intellectual in a dead man. Not **g**, which places "appropriation" <note>The relationship of a quality to its subject, or in this case, authorship.</note>: namely, that Aristotle made such a book as this, but it is not properly possessed by Aristotle, because he is dead.

## On the fallacy of division.

## On the fallacy of the figure of speech.

<margin>What is the fallacy of division?</margin>
The <term>fallacy of division</term> <note>A logical error where one assumes that what is true of the whole must also be true of the individual parts.</note> is a deception arising from the potential multiplicity of a statement when the parts of the statement can be divided from one another. A <term>paralogism</term> <note>A piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning.</note> is formed thus: Every animal is either rational or irrational; but not every animal is rational; therefore, every animal is irrational. ¶ To this deception, we apply this camera **c.f.g.** By **c**, we recognize that when one word is in one subject, with the agreement of the subject's correlates—through the second and third species of rule **c**—one meaning follows. But when it is placed in the contrary without reference to the subject, it varies the meaning by dividing it: as is clear through the scale **b.c.** in the second figure. By **f**, it is recognized that the beings "rational" and "irrational" are not joined; nor do they measure themselves in the same species through a continuous middle ground. By **g**, we recognize that the ability to laugh is proper to a rational being, but not to an irrational one. Through camera **e.f.i.** etc., let the deception be known. By **e** and **f**, as was said above. By **i**, we recognize that truth is not established in a "true" where diverse things are the same; nor does equality establish that they are equal in species, nor in the same place as each other.

<margin>What is the fallacy of the figure of speech?</margin>
The <term>fallacy of the figure of speech</term> <note>A fallacy where a word's grammatical form suggests a meaning or category it does not actually belong to.</note> is a deception arising from the fact that one word is similar to another word. A paralogism is formed thus: Whatever you saw yesterday, you see today; but yesterday you saw [a] white [thing]; therefore today you see white. ¶ To this paralogism we apply camera **b.f.g.** By **b**, we understand the difference between "what" <note>original: "quid"; referring to the substance or essence.</note> and "what kind" <note>original: "quale"; referring to an accidental quality like color.</note>. By **f**, that they do not join each other, nor measure themselves to the same object in one [way], since they are different. By **g**, we understand that properly "what" requires its own meaning, and "what kind" likewise; but in the appropriation in which the principle does not rest, the deception consists. Through camera **d.f.h.**, the deception is recognized. By **d**, the contrary ends are known, because whatever changes, changes into a "what kind." And by **f**, the deprivation of continuity between the past "now" and the present "now" is recognized. By **h**, through the fourth species of rule **c** and the first of **d**, it is known that one has a meaning through "what" and the other through "what kind"; because "what" speaks of substance, while "what kind" speaks of <term>accident</term> <note>In logic, an "accident" is a property that does not change the essence of a thing, such as its color or size.</note>.

# Seventh part

<margin>
On the fallacy of the accident.
</margin>

**T**he fallacy of the accident is a deception arising from the fact that something is simply inherent in both of those things which are, in some accidental way, one and the same. And the <term>paralogism</term> <note>A piece of false reasoning or an illogical argument.</note> is formed thus: I know Coriscus; but Coriscus is the one approaching; therefore, I know the one approaching. <term>To this deception, we assign "camera" b.f.c.</term> <note>Llull uses "cameras" (letter combinations) to categorize logical relationships. "b.f.c." helps the student distinguish between the person's identity and their current action.</note> Through **b**, we understand the difference between one perceptible thing and another perceptible thing, for Coriscus is one thing and "the one approaching" is another. Through **f**, let it be known that "the one approaching" and Coriscus do not exist in a continuous middle of extremes. Through **c**, we understand that Coriscus can be in one seat while another person is the one entering. <term>Furthermore, through camera g.f.h.</term>, the deception is recognized. Through **g**, we understand that Coriscus has his own proper number, and another approaching man similarly has a name that is assigned to him along with the deception. Through **f**, it is known that Coriscus is not joined with any approaching man in one and the same measure. Through **h**, it is known that Coriscus, while sitting, is not at that same time the one who is approaching.

## On the fallacy of the qualified and the absolute.

<margin>
On the fallacy of the qualified and the absolute.
</margin>

**T**he fallacy of the qualified and the absolute <note>original: "secundum quid et simpliciter." This fallacy occurs when someone takes a statement that is true only in a specific, limited sense (qualified) and treats it as if it were true in a general, universal sense (absolute).</note> is a deception arising from the fact that we take a statement made in a qualified sense as if it were stated absolutely. And the paralogism is formed thus: Every man in whom whiteness exists is white; Socrates is white as far as his teeth are concerned; therefore, Socrates is white. <term>To this deception, we apply camera c.f.i.</term> Through the fourth species of rule **c**, we understand that an <term>Ethiopian</term> <note>In medieval logic, the "Ethiopian" was a standard example used to discuss parts and wholes: he is white "in part" (his teeth) but black "simply" (his skin).</note> has whiteness in his teeth, eyes, and nails, but blackness in his body. Through **f**, we understand that this whiteness is not continued throughout the whole body. Through **i**, we understand that he is white in one place and black in another. <term>Furthermore, through camera g.f.k.</term>, through **g** we understand that he is properly white in his teeth, and is "appropriately" white when it is falsely concluded that he is white [simply]. Through **f**, it is recognized that the Ethiopian is a subject in which there are several discrete quantities: such as the quantity of a tooth and the quantity of a foot—the tooth being characterized by whiteness and the foot by blackness. Through **k**, we understand that the Ethiopian is colored only with whiteness in the tooth and blackness in the body.

## On the fallacy of the ignorance of the refutation.

<margin>
On the fallacy of the ignorance of the refutation.
What a refutation is.
</margin>

**T**he fallacy of the ignorance of the refutation <note>original: "ignorantiam elenchi." This involves proving a conclusion that may be true, but does not actually address or contradict the opponent's original point.</note> is a deception arising from the fact that those things which are necessary for the definition of a refutation are not observed, especially regarding the nature of the contradiction. <term>A refutation, moreover, is a syllogism</term> of contradiction which is sometimes one syllogism and sometimes two. It is one when a syllogism concludes the contradiction of some previously given proposition; for example, if some animal were given that is incorruptible, and one proceeds thus: Every composite of contraries is corruptible; every animal is such a composite; therefore, every animal is corruptible. This is the contradictory conclusion of the first proposition given. For two syllogisms constitute a refutation when a contradiction is concluded from two syllogisms: just as in the aforementioned syllogism, another such syllogism may be set against it: No blessed thing is corruptible; some animal is blessed; therefore, some animal is not corruptible. <term>Regarding the reasoning</term> of the refutation, therefore, it consists of the syllogism and the contradiction. Whatever, therefore, is against the definition of a syllogism and a contradiction is also against the definition of a refutation. And the paralogism is formed thus: Two are double compared to one; two are not double compared to three; therefore, two are double and not double. This is not valid because the omission of the requirement of "being the same" <note>Meaning, "double" must be relative to the same thing for a contradiction to exist.</note> means there is no contradiction; and this was declared through the second species of rule **c**. <term>To this deception, we apply b.f.c.</term> Through **b**, we understand that two differs from one and vice versa. Through **f**, we understand that two is more than one in discrete quantity. Through **c**, we understand that two agrees in being an even number, and three agrees in being an odd number. <term>Furthermore, through camera d.f.e.</term>, through **d** we understand that an even number—namely two—is constituted of two units according to the second species of rule **d**. One is the principle of number according to the first species of rule **d**. Through **f**, we know that two and one are not measured equally in number through the first species of rule **e**, because two is a double, and one is not a double.
