And the paralogism is formed thus: A rational animal runs; therefore, a man runs. <note>Since "rational animal" is the definition of "man," the argument assumes what it is trying to prove.</note> <term>To this deception, we apply camera e.f.h.</term> Through **e**, we understand that the principle is not proved in the major proposition, but is only supposed. Through **f**, we understand that the major proposition...

## On the fallacy of the consequent.

<margin>On the fallacy of the consequent.</margin>
**F**allacy of the consequent <note>original: "fallacia consequentis"</note> is a deception arising from the fact that the consequence is thought to be entirely the same as the <term>antecedent</term> <note>The first part of a logical statement, upon which the second part (the consequent) depends.</note>. It forms a <term>paralogism</term> <note>A piece of false reasoning.</note> thus: If it is a donkey, it is an animal; but you are an animal; therefore you are a donkey. This is not valid, for the consequence first posited is not reversible <note>That is, while all donkeys are animals, not all animals are donkeys.</note>. To this deception we apply **camera b. f. d.** Through **b**, we understand that a donkey and a rational animal differ in species, because the difference that exists between one sensory thing and another is not the same as that between a sensory thing and an intellectual thing. Through **f**, we understand that the sensory and the intellectual are joined in a man, but not in a donkey. Through **d**, we understand that in a man, the sensory and the intellectual are joined together in the constitution of the man himself; but in a donkey, they are not. Through **camera d. f. e.**: Through **d**, we understand that a subject consisting of the sensory and the sensory is not interchangeable with a subject consisting of the sensory and the intellectual. Through **f**, we understand that a man and a donkey do not fall under one continuous middle of extremes. Through **e**, we understand that a man exists in order to understand; but a donkey does not.

## On the fallacy of non-cause as cause.

<margin>On the fallacy of non-cause as cause.</margin>
**F**allacy according to "non-cause as cause" <note>original: "non causam ut causa"</note> occurs when, among the premises from which a conclusion follows, some proposition is placed that contributes nothing to the conclusion, and thus is not the cause. However, "cause" here refers to that which is a cause for the inference, according to which the premises are said to be the causes of the conclusion. A paralogism is formed thus: Soul and life are the same. And death and life are contraries. Generation and corruption are contraries; but death is corruption; therefore life is generation, and to live is to be generated—which is impossible. To this deception we apply **b. f. c.** Through **b**, we understand the difference between the soul and life; for life is a higher category, as is evident in brute animals through the continuous <term>vegetative soul</term> <note>The level of soul responsible for growth and nutrition, found in plants and animals.</note> and <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>The level of soul responsible for perception and movement, found in animals.</note>; and through the <term>reasoning soul</term> <note>The highest level of soul, unique to humans, capable of logic.</note> continued from the sensory and the intellectual, we understand the difference. Through **f**, we understand the life of the rational soul as not being continuous with the life of a brute animal. Through **c**, we understand that in the rational soul, life is a continuous magnitude of intellect, will, and memory. In brute animals and in plants, this is not the case at all. Furthermore, we recognize the deception through **camera d. f. e.** Through **d**, we know that life in plants or in brute animals belongs to corruptible <term>correlatives</term>; but in the rational soul, not at all, since it is not made of contraries. Through **f**, we know that a cause and a non-cause are not joined in the subject. Through **e**, it is known that the soul lives by resting in its end, namely in God; but death does not.

## On the fallacy of many questions.

<margin>On the fallacy according to many questions.</margin>
**E**llacy <note>The original text uses a decorative 'E' here, though the word is 'Fallacia' (Fallacy).</note> according to "many questions" <note>original: "plures interrogationes"</note> is a deception arising from the fact that a single response is given to a question that is actually multiple, because the question is proposed in a single way. A paralogism is formed thus: "Do you think that a man and a donkey are a rational animal?" And if "yes" is said, it proceeds thus: "A man and a donkey are not a rational animal; therefore a man is not a rational animal." To this deception we shall apply this **camera b. f. c.** Through **b**, we understand that the difference existing between one sensory thing and another differs from the difference existing between a sensory thing and an intellectual thing; by reason of which a man and a donkey cannot be the same. Through **f**, we understand that a man and a donkey are not under one continuous middle of extremes. Through **c**, we understand that a man and a donkey do not agree in the same species nor in the same number. Likewise, through **camera d. f. g.**, the deception is recognized. Through **d**, we understand that a man is constituted of three souls: namely, the vegetative, sensitive, and reasoning souls. A donkey, however, is not; but of the vegetative and sensitive only. Through **f**, we understand that a man can have knowledge as a habit; but a donkey cannot. Through **g**, we understand that "risibility" <note>The capacity to laugh; a classic logical example of a property unique to humans.</note> is a proper attribute of man, and also "intelligibility" is essential to him; but these do not apply to a donkey.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of logical fallacies, specifically how Ramon Llull’s "General Art" and its combinatorial "cameras" (logical chambers) can be used to identify errors and bridge the gap between formal logic and the "truth of things" in fields like theology and natural philosophy.</meta>

# Part Eight

<margin>On the fallacy of contradiction.</margin>
**T**he fallacy of contradiction <note>original: "fallacia contradictionis"</note> is a deception: and it depends on the eight propositions mentioned above which clearly conclude a contradiction, which we have composed in the *New Logic* found by way of a general art. A <term>paralogism</term> <note>An argument that is formally false or fallacious.</note> is formed thus:
> No stone is visible; a certain stone is visible; therefore, a certain stone is both visible and not visible.

¶ To this paralogism, we apply this **camera b.f.c.** <note>Llull uses "cameras"—diagrammatic chambers or cells represented by letters—to map the relationships between concepts like Goodness, Greatness, etc.</note> Through **b**, we understand that there is a difference between a visible and an invisible stone, because an invisible stone is not visible in itself, as it is not possessed of a sensitive <term>habit</term> <note>A "habit" (habitus) in medieval philosophy refers to a stable quality or state of being.</note>. However, a stone becomes visible by accident, because the sense of sight "habituates" itself to the stone’s color and position. Through **f**, we understand that when the stone is invisible, it is not joined with the species of visibility, but when it is visible, it is so joined. Through **c**, we understand that sight is not an agent acting upon an invisible stone according to the fourth species of that same rule; nor does it have a <term>passion</term> <note>A "passion" in this context is the state of being acted upon by an external force or object.</note> under the power of vision. But regarding a visible stone, the exact opposite can be said.

¶ Furthermore, through **camera g.f.h.**, the deception is recognized. Through **g**, we know that visibility is not a "proper passion" <note>An essential property belonging only to a specific species.</note> of man; rather, through an accident, the sight appropriates visibility to him, because color, shape, and position are its objects. Through **f**, we understand that a stone does not possess sensitivity. Through **h**, we understand that a stone is sometimes visible and sometimes not visible.

¶ We have spoken of fallacies applied to the rules so that the deceptions of fallacies may be recognized. And through what we have said, the intellect recognizes that a logician, when dealing with fallacies, does not dare to stand against a naturalist <note>A "naturalist" or "natural philosopher" studied the physical world, as opposed to the formal rules of language and logic.</note>. Suppose it were as you, the logician, say: this impossibility and that, and so forth, would follow in the nature of things—as is evident in the nature of definitions, principles, and rules. And at this step, the intellect recognizes that in a dispute, one logician might not reach a rest or conclusion with another logician, because they do not descend to the truth of the thing; instead, they stand only upon names and the similarities of things through the definition of contrariety. But if a logician disputes with a naturalist, the truth of the thing is quickly sought, and they quickly find rest in the end. This is because the logician can by no means deny experiences which they reach through the sensitive, imaginative, and reasoning faculties, as was said above.

### § On the Method of Teaching.

<margin>On the method of teaching and briefly mastering all sciences.</margin>
**T**hrough the fourth figure <note>A reference to the fourth combinatorial figure of Llull's Art, often used to find "middle terms" for arguments.</note>, more truly than through the others, a method is given by which other sciences can be easily and briefly acquired, such as theology, philosophy, etc. This is done by finding a "middle term" that is neither the most general nor the most specific. The reason for this is that this science possesses the most general principles and also the most general rules. Other sciences, however, have subordinate principles; thus, their middle term is imperfect without this science. Because of this, men learn with difficulty over a long period. And when they doubt, they do not have the most general principles to which they may recur artistically <note>That is, according to the "Art" (the systematic method) of Llull.</note>, as the artist of this Art does.

¶ Furthermore, other sciences will be taught using this part by placing a **camera** in which **f** serves as the middle term for the authoritative texts <note>original: "auctoritatibus"</note> of other sciences. This is done by explaining the authorities within the camera, according to the way in which **f** could enter those same authorities, explaining and reducing them to a <term>syllogism</term> <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> according to the doctrine stated above. We shall give an example of this. Thus, one reads in theology:
> God is pure act <note>original: "deus ē purus actus." A central concept in Scholasticism meaning God is fully realized activity with no unfulfilled potential.</note>.

<margin>In theology.</margin>
¶ This authority is provable through these two cameras: namely **b.f.c.** and through **camera d.f.e.** And this is done in this way: through **b**, we will have goodness and difference. Through **c**, that goodness is a great reason having in itself great, good, and distinct correlatives. Through **d**, [these are] eternal and primitive. Through **e**, they are quieted by reason of the end; and through the second species of rule **d** and the first of **e**, they are necessary. And through **f**, they are joined and well-measured, infinitely eternal, and separated from every accident.

¶ And thus, having made this explanation, it is seen and clear:
> that God is pure act in existing and in acting.

<margin>In philosophy.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, one reads in philosophy:
> that nothing comes from nothing <note>original: "q de nihilo nihil fit." The ancient Greek and medieval axiom "Ex nihilo nihil fit."</note>.

¶ To explain and clarify this authority, we assign **camera d.f.e.** Through **d**, we explain that "nothing" is not a principle; for if it were, "nothing" would already be "something." Likewise, through **d**, "nothing" is not the matter for anything. For if something could be made from it, it would already be "this something." The same is understood concerning the third species of **d**: for if "nothing" were subject to anything, it would indeed be something. **F** also sounds or signifies that from "nothing," nothing may be made. Nor can "nothing" have a middle term; for if it had a middle, it would already be something. Through **e**, it is understood that "nothing" cannot be a material, formal, efficient, or final cause; nor can it be possessed of any power; for if it were the opposite, it would follow that it was something.

¶ And thus, the aforementioned authority has been clarified and explained through the aforementioned camera. However, I do not say that the world is eternal <note>A crucial disclaimer: many medieval philosophers following Aristotle argued the world was eternal, but Christian doctrine required a beginning in time (Creation). Llull is clarifying that his logic does not lead to the heretical view of an eternal world.</note>.

<summary>This page explains how Llull's logical "Art" can resolve contradictions and provide a superior method for teaching sciences like theology and philosophy. It demonstrates this by applying his symbolic "cameras" to explain complex axioms such as "God is pure act" and "Nothing comes from nothing."</summary>

# On the mixture of principles and rules.

Indeed, it is new and has a beginning, as was proven above. But that authority which says **the world was created from nothing** <note>original: "mundus creatus est ex nihilo"</note> can be explained through the aforementioned **chamber $\Delta$** <note>Llull uses "chambers"—symbolic cells in his combinatorial diagrams—to organize logical relations.</note>. For it posits that God is primary through eternity, power, and intellectivity. And through the third species of Rule **D** <note>Rule D in Llull's system usually asks "Why?"</note>, His power is not subject to anything; thus He can understand and produce the world, which was not in act nor in potency in nothingness. It follows, therefore, that the world exists in act through creation, with God measuring His own infinite power, intellectivity, primitivity, and so on.

¶ Furthermore, one reads that **being and one are interchangeable** <note>original: "ens & vnu convertūtur"</note>, as are truth and one, and goodness and truth. These authorities can be explained through **chamber b.f.c.**, and likewise for other chambers such as **chamber b.f.g.** Since through **B**, we have differences such as between the sensual and the sensual. For in a stone, "one" is a certain being; in a plant, "one" is another being; and in a sensing creature, it is another, and so on; and likewise for the "one" and the "true," and the "good" and the "true."

¶ These goodnesses, unities, and truths are not strictly interchangeable; because if they were, difference would be destroyed, and consequently the <term>medium</term> <note>In Llull's system, the "medium" is the principle that links an agent to its object or a beginning to its end.</note> would be destroyed as well. The same applies to <term>concordance</term> <note>The principle of harmony or agreement between different things.</note>, which is impossible. For there is one measurement in a stone, one continuous medium, and one quantity in a stone, but another in a plant, and so on. And thus, regarding the literal text, the authorities cannot stand as written, because the "chamber" cannot enter the authorities according to the literal exposition of the letters, but enters with an allegorical sense, and this is done with **Rule G**.

¶ Since <term>correlatives</term> <note>Pairs of terms that imply one another, like "father" and "son," or in Llull's logic, "bonifier" and "bonified."</note> regarding unity are not properly the same as they are regarding being, goodness, and truth—though they are "appropriated" as such—it is because every principle communicates itself to another. In this way, the principles remain differentiable, concordable, and able to be mediated, according to their respective reasons. Each principle has its own proper rest through its own proper essence and act, and no inconsistency follows. To this, **Rule B** <note>Rule B usually asks "What?" or defines the essence of a thing.</note> consents along with all the other rules.

¶ Just as we have given examples concerning theology and philosophy, explaining and declaring them with the "chambers," so can it be done for other sciences: namely, for medicine, law, and morals, etc.

¶ Since if an authority contains within itself the truth of a chamber of the <term>fourth figure</term> <note>The Fourth Figure is Llull’s most complex combinatorial tool, often a set of three concentric circles used to generate logical propositions.</note>, those chambers can enter the authority with their definitions and species, by affirming or denying. And thus it is not impossible for an authority to be true. For no authority established from first, true, and necessary principles contradicts reason. And this rule is infallible and necessary.

<margin>General rule.</margin>

¶ End of the seventh principal part.

# Part Eight: On the mixture of principles and rules.

<margin>Heading of the Eighth Part.</margin>

**P**art this <note>The decorative woodcut 'P' marks the start of a major new section.</note> is divided into two parts: namely, the mixture of principles where one is deduced with another, and the second part is concerning principles deduced through the rules.

¶ In this part, the doctrine is given on how one principle may be known through other principles, by deducing it through those principles and through all species of the rules. Therefore, when there is a doubt concerning any principle, one should recur to this part, where the truth about it can be found with the aforesaid principles and the species of rules. For example, if one asks whether any **goodness** is a substantial **being**.

¶ Again, whether any moral goodness is a <term>habit</term> <note>A stable quality or disposition of the soul.</note> and a real being. At that time, one should recur to the chapter on goodness deduced through other principles and through the rules; and one should hold that which will seem most rational according to **Rule B**, with the other rules and the definitions of the principles mixed into it.

<margin>The center and subject of this art.</margin>

¶ And this mixture is the center and subject of this art.

¶ It is true that in the **Third Figure**, a mixture of rules and principles was made. But in this part, we shall declare them in order, with one principle deduced through all principles and through all rules by continuous deduction, so that the intellect may be singularly discursive through every principle.

¶ And first, we shall speak of the first part.

### On goodness deduced through the principles.

<margin>On goodness deduced through the principles.</margin>

**B**oodness <note>The decorative woodcut 'B' begins the specific analysis of the principle of Goodness.</note> is, in itself, the reason for the "good" to act or produce good. And because it is great through **Greatness** <note>Magnitudo: one of Llull's Nine Divine Dignities or Principles.</note>, it is a "doubled reason" for the good to produce a great good.

¶ Goodness through **Duration** is durable; and thus it is the reason for the good to produce a durable good. And because it is great through Greatness—as was said—it is a "tripled reason," so that the good acts as a good that is both great and durable. Goodness through **Power** is able to exist and to act; and thus goodness—through what it has in itself, and through what it has from Power, and through what it has from Greatness, and through what it has from Duration—is a "quadrupled reason" for the good to produce and act as a good that is great, durable, and powerful. And so it goes with the other principles, with which they can be mixed in many ways by following the method we have handed down.

It argues that all true authorities must align with rational principles and demonstrates how to multiply the definitions of a principle to reach a deeper understanding of its nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition into the Eighth Part of Ramon Llull’s "General Art." Following the previous discussion on how logical "chambers" (combinations of principles) explain theological truths like creation from nothing, the text now begins a systematic demonstration of how each "Dignity" or divine principle (like Goodness or Greatness) interacts with every other principle to define the nature of reality.</meta>

->### Eighth part.<-

However, we exclude contrariety and smallness, with which it <note>Referring to the principle being discussed, likely unity or goodness.</note> cannot have a multitude. And because we wish to avoid prolixity, we do not want to give examples of what is quintupled or sextupled, etc.; rather, we will exemplify and show how it is combined through all principles.

¶ Goodness through wisdom is knowable. And thus there is a reason for a scientific good <note>original: "bono scientifico," referring to a good that is also an object of knowledge</note> to perform a known or scientific good. 

¶ Goodness through the will is lovable; therefore, there is a reason for a good through love to perform a lovable or loved good. 

¶ Through virtue, goodness is virtuous. And thus there is a reason for a virtuous good to perform a virtuous good. 

¶ Goodness through truth is true; and thus, rightly and truly, there is a reason for a good to perform a true good. 

¶ Goodness through glory is glorious; and thus there is a reason for a good to perform a glorious good. 

¶ Goodness through difference is clear and not confused. And thus, rightly, distinctly, and clearly, there is a reason for a good to perform a good clearly distinct from itself. 

¶ Goodness through concordance is concordable; and thus, rightly and concordantly, there is a reason for a good to perform a concordant good that has been agreed upon. 

¶ Goodness is against malice, which is its contrary. And thus concordance is against contrariety, because they are opposites; and so goodness, rightly and concordantly, is against malice and contrariety. 

¶ Goodness through a principle has the nature of a principle; and thus it is the reason for a good and a beginning thing to produce a good that is begun. 

¶ Goodness has the nature of a middle through the "medium" <note>In Llull's system, the "Middle" is the link between a beginning and an end.</note>; and thus, rightly and mediately, there is a reason for a good to perform a good by means of a middle. 

¶ Goodness through the end has the nature of an end; and thus, rightly and finally—or perfectly—there is a reason for a good to perform a good that is perfect and at rest. 

¶ Goodness through greatness has the nature of greatness <note>original: "maioritatis," literally majority or superiority</note>; and thus, rightly and magnificently, there is a reason for a good to perform a magnified good. 

¶ Goodness through equality is of the nature of equality; and therefore, rightly and equally, there is a reason for a good to produce a good made equal from several things. 

¶ Goodness that is smaller has the nature of smallness <note>original: "minoritatis"</note> through the principle of smallness; and therefore, there is a reason, rightly and in a lessening way, for a smaller good to perform a lessened good; and this is said respectively or comparatively. 

¶ This concludes the discussion of goodness derived linearly through all the principles. And because we have spoken of it generally, the Artist <note>Llull refers to the student or practitioner of his logical system as the "Artist."</note> can find many things at will in the line of goodness.

# On greatness derived through the principles.

<margin>Derivation of greatness through the principles.</margin>
**G**reatness is good through goodness, and goodness is great through greatness. And so from these follows the concrete <note>In this context, a "concrete" is the substantive manifestation of an abstract quality, like "a great good" vs "greatness."</note> thing, which is a great good.

<margin>2</margin>
¶ Greatness is enduring through duration, and duration is great through greatness: and from these follows the concrete "great and enduring."

<margin>3</margin>
¶ Greatness through power is able to exist and act, and power through greatness is great. And so greatness with power is the reason why there is a great concrete thing having great power of existing and acting.

<margin>4</margin>
¶ Greatness is knowable through wisdom, and wisdom through greatness is great: and these two cause a great and scientific concrete thing having great knowledge.

<margin>5</margin>
¶ Greatness is lovable through the will, and the will is great through greatness: and thus they cause a great loved concrete thing, in which it has its support.

<margin>6</margin>
¶ Greatness through virtue is virtuous, and virtue through greatness is great: and from these is caused a great virtuous concrete thing, in which they have their support. And the concrete thing itself is the "being," and the qualities themselves are the "essences." And in this step, it appears how several essences compose one being with themselves.

<margin>7</margin>
¶ Greatness through truth is true, and truth through greatness is great: and from them follows a great true concrete thing, in which they have their support.

<margin>8</margin>
<note>Likely intended as 8, but printed as 7</note>
¶ Greatness through glory is glorious, and through greatness, glory is great. And from them follows the subject, in which they have magnificence and delight.

<margin>9</margin>
¶ Greatness through difference is distinct, by reason of which distinction in the essence of greatness there are distinguished: the magnifier, the magnifiable, and the act of magnifying <note>This is Llull's "Ternary" logic: every principle has an active agent, a passive recipient, and the verb connecting them.</note>. And the difference is great through greatness, and therefore in the same subject they participate through magnifying and distinguishing.

<margin>10</margin>
¶ Greatness through concordance is concorded, and concordance is magnified through greatness: and therefore in the same subject they participate through magnifying and concording.

<margin>11</margin>
¶ Greatness is able to be opposed through contrariety, insofar as it is through transmutation; but naturally it is not against itself. And contrariety is great through greatness: just as fire and water, which through greatness have great contrariety, by heating and by cooling.

<margin>12</margin>
¶ Greatness through the nature of a principle has in itself principles co-essential to itself: namely, the magnifier, the magnifiable, and the act of magnifying. And the principle is magnified through greatness, having in itself naturally a great magnifying power.

->## On the mixture of principles and rules.<-

<margin>13</margin> That which can be a principle and the act of being a principle. ¶ **Greatness** <note>In Llull's system, Greatness is the principle by which all other virtues are expanded to their maximum capacity.</note> through the *middle* <note>The "middle" is a logical principle used to link a beginning to an end.</note> possesses the character of mediating; and the middle through greatness possesses the character of magnifying (provided, however, that they exist in the same subject). ¶ **Greatness** <margin>14</margin> is the reason why the *end* is great; and the end is the reason why greatness is at <margin>15</margin> rest / and this occurs within the same subject. ¶ **Greatness** through *majority* <note>The principle of being "greater" or "superior."</note> is greater: and majority is great through greatness: and it is necessary that in any subject each has its own act: namely, greatness / magnifying / and majority / making greater. ¶ **Greatness** by reason of *equality* holds things co-equally within itself / namely: the <term>magnifier</term>, the <term>magnified</term>, and <term>magnifying</term> <note>original: "magnificativum / magnificabile / magnificare." Llull uses these triadic structures (active, passive, and the act itself) to describe the internal workings of every principle.</note> are equally of greatness: and equality, by reason of greatness, holds within itself great things that are co-essential to it, namely: the great / the <term>equalizer</term> / the <term>equalized</term> and the act of <term>equalizing</term>. <margin>17</margin> ¶ **Greatness**, in relation to that which is "greater," is separated from *smallness* <note>original: "minoritate." Smallness or minority is seen as a lack of being.</note>: because greatness could not be what it is if it were joined with smallness. The reason for this is that smallness and minority are interchangeable: namely, regarding the subject in which they exist: just as **sin** is not a "thing" <note>This reflects the medieval philosophical idea that evil or sin is not a positive substance, but a "privation" or a lack of the good.</note>: and likewise an **accident** <note>A quality (like color or size) that cannot exist on its own but must exist within a substance or subject.</note> cannot exist by itself.

# On duration deduced through the principles.

<margin>On duration deduced through the principles.</margin>
**D**uration <note>Duratio: The principle of permanence or existence through time.</note> is good through **goodness** / and goodness lasts through duration. And therefore, duration directly causes duration: but goodness does so indirectly: that is, by <term>accident</term>. And this is the reason for a good thing: that it may perform a lasting good. ¶ **Duration** is the reason why **greatness** lasts / and it is great through greatness: and therefore in the subject in which they exist / they participate through *lasting* and *magnifying*: provided however that there is no obstacle present to hinder their acts. ¶ **Duration** is the reason why **power** lasts: and power is the reason why duration can exist and act. And thus in the subject in which they exist / they participate through *lasting* and *being able*. ¶ **Wisdom** lasts through the reason of duration: and duration is knowable through wisdom. And so in the subject in which they exist / they participate through *lasting* and *knowing*. ¶ **Duration** is lovable through the **will**: and the will is durable through duration. And therefore in the subject in which they exist / they agree through *lasting* and *loving*. ¶ **Duration** is virtuous through **virtue**: and virtue is durable through duration. And therefore in the subject in which they exist / duration is distant from vice through virtue: just as it is distant from <term>privation</term> <note>The total absence of a quality that should be present.</note> through duration. ¶ By the nature of **duration**, its act is to *last*. By the nature of **truth**, its act is to *verify*: and truth lasts through duration: and duration through truth is true. ¶ **Glory** lasts through the reason of duration: and duration is glorious through the reason of glory. And therefore duration is distant from punishment through glory: and glory is distant from privation through duration. ¶ **Duration** is clear and unconfused through **difference**: and difference lasts through duration: and thus duration, through difference, possesses the <term>durative</term>, the <term>durable</term>, and the act of <term>during</term> differently and distinctly. And difference, through duration, possesses the durative, the durable, and the act of during permanently and lastingly. ¶ Through the reason of **concordance**, duration possesses within itself concordant things: and by the reason of duration, concordance possesses within itself lasting and permanent things. ¶ **Duration** contradicts its *contrary* and destroys it as much as it can: and **contrariety** destroys duration as much as it can. And the reason for this is / because contrariety agrees with *non-being*: while duration speaks of *being*. ¶ **Duration** through the **beginning** possesses the character of a beginning: so that all things that last / last under the character of duration. And therefore the beginning lasts through the reason of duration. ¶ **Duration** by reason of the **middle** possesses a middle, namely the act of lasting existing in the middle between the <term>durative</term> <note>That which causes duration.</note> and the <term>durable</term> <note>That which is able to last.</note>. And the middle, by reason of duration, lasts in the subject in which it is. ¶ **Duration** by reason of the **end** is perfect and at rest: and the end lasts by the reason of duration in the subject in which it is. ¶ **Duration** by reason of **majority** is "majorified" <note>Made greater or expanded.</note> in a certain subject: and majority, by the reason of duration, is sustained lastingly in the subject. ¶ **Duration** by reason of **equality** possesses the character of "co-equating." For it holds the <term>durative</term>, the <term>durable</term>, and the act of <term>during</term> as co-essential to itself. And equality, by reason of duration, lasts in the subject in which it is. ¶ **Duration**, in the subject in which it is, by reason of **minority**, is "about nothing": and minority, by reason of duration, lasts and is effective concerning "being."

# On power deduced through the principles.

<margin>On power deduced through the principles.</margin>
**P**ower is good through **goodness**. And goodness, through **power**, can exist and act. And therefore, they mutually move the subject in which they exist—according to the nature they possess—to act and exist well and powerfully. ¶ **Power** is great through **greatness**: and greatness can exist and act according to power. And therefore, in the subject in which they exist / that which one lacks / the other supplies according to its own nature. But sometimes there is something already present that hinders this, which is a principle of another...

<meta>This page continues Ramon Llull’s systematic investigation of the "Dignities" (divine attributes). While the previous page focused on the interaction of "Greatness" with other principles, this page moves into the "Eighth Part" of his treatise, exploring how "Power" (Potestas) and "Wisdom" (Sapientia) are defined and modified by their relationship with other fundamental concepts like Duration, Truth, and Equality.</meta>

-># Eighth part<-

**Power** is durable through *duration*. And duration is able to exist and act through power: and if duration is eternity, then existing and acting are necessary, because in eternity there is no newness. ¶ **Power** is knowable through *wisdom*. And wisdom is able to exist and act through power: and if they are <term>convertible</term> <note>In Lullian logic, "convertible" means two attributes are essentially identical and interchangeable, a state that exists perfectly only in God.</note>, existing, understanding, and acting are by necessity, since they cannot be otherwise; but this is understood regarding God alone. ¶ **Power** is lovable through *will*, and the will is able to exist and act through power: and if they are convertible, the subject in which they exist is able by necessity to exist, act, and love. ¶ **Power** is virtuous through *virtue*: and virtue is able to exist and act through power: and thus the subject in which they exist can be powerfully and virtuously by existing and acting. ¶ **Power** is true through *truth*: and truth is able to exist and act through power. And if they are not convertible in the subject in which they exist: the lack of conversion implies that the subject in which they reside can be a liar and idle. ¶ **Power** is delightful through *glory*: and similarly, glory is able to exist and act through power. And if they are convertible in the subject in which they exist: then necessary power is far removed from pain, and glory is far from impotence. ¶ **Power** is an unconfused and clear reason through *difference*: and difference is able to exist and act through power. And if they are convertible in the subject in which they exist: it follows by necessity that the subject is actually in a state of being able to distinguish itself well. ¶ **Power** is "concordable" through *concordance*: and concordance is able to exist and act through power. And if they are not convertible, the lack of conversion implies that it is impossible for power and harmony to exist together in the subject. ¶ **Power** cannot be against itself through *contrariety*: nor can contrariety be impotent through power. And because they are not convertible, the lack of conversion implies that some power is separate from contrariety. ¶ **Power** possesses the nature of beginning things through the *principle*: and the principle possesses the nature of <term>empowering</term> <note>original: "possificandi." A term coined by Llull to describe the act of making something capable or powerful.</note> through power: and if they are convertible, "being able" and "beginning" are separate from contingency and newness. ¶ **Power** possesses the nature of mediating through the *middle*: and through this nature, "being able" exists in the middle of the <term>powerful</term> and the <term>empowered</term> <note>Llull often splits a concept into the actor, the acted-upon, and the act itself.</note>. And the middle is able to exist and act through power: and therefore the middle places the influences from the end and the reflections from the principle, and understands their nature. ¶ **Power** is able to be at rest through the *end*: and the end is able to exist and act through power. And if they are convertible, it is impossible for rest not to exist in the subject in which they reside. ¶ **Power** possesses the nature of magnifying through *majority*: and majority possesses the nature of empowering through power. And because they are not convertible, the lack of conversion makes them limited in the subject in which they exist. And in this step, it appears how things capable of growth grow up to a limit determined by nature: and in old age, they have an inclination toward corruption. ¶ **Power** possesses the nature of co-equating between the powerful, the empowered, and the act of power through *equality*. And equality possesses the nature of empowering through power: and if they are convertible, it is impossible for the "ability" and the "co-equating" to be otherwise. ¶ **Power** through *minority* is concerned with non-being: and minority through power is concerned with being. And therefore power and minority are not convertible. For if they were convertible, being and non-being would be interchangeable: which is impossible.

### On wisdom deduced through the principles.

<margin>On wisdom deduced through the principles.</margin>

**Wisdom** is good through *goodness*, and goodness is knowable through wisdom. And if they are convertible in the subject in which they exist: they are the reasons for acting well and understanding well: and they cannot be otherwise. ¶ **Wisdom** is great through *greatness*: and greatness is knowable through wisdom. And if they are convertible, the subject in which they exist consists through "infinition" <note>The act of making infinite.</note> and understanding, and they cannot be otherwise. ¶ **Wisdom** is durable through *duration*: and duration is knowable through wisdom: and if that duration is eternity, "knowing" and "eternalizing" in the subject in which they reside are by necessity: and their opposite is impossible. ¶ **Wisdom** is powerful through *power*, and power is knowable through wisdom: and if they are convertible, there is just as much "being able" as there is "understanding," and in them "more or less" is impossible. ¶ **Wisdom** is lovable through *will*, and will is wise through wisdom: and if they are convertible, there is just as much "loving" as "understanding" in the subject. ¶ **Wisdom** is virtuous through *virtue*: and virtue is knowable through wisdom. And if they are not convertible in the subject in which they exist, ignorance is possible, and even vice. ¶ **Wisdom** is true through *truth*: and truth is knowable through wisdom. And if they are not convertible, truth is merely "believable" <note>Meaning it is a matter of faith (credibilis) rather than direct intellectual knowledge.</note>: and understanding can be a lie. ¶ **Wisdom** is delightful through *glory*, and glory is knowable through wisdom: and because they are not convertible, knowing can exist with suffering, and delight can exist with ignorance. ¶ **Wisdom** is clear through *difference*, by reason of which it possesses an understanding, intelligibly...

Llull explains how these attributes interact to create necessity, morality, and the natural limits of growth and decay.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Ramon Llull’s exploration of the "Dignities" (divine attributes) and their interactions. Having previously discussed Greatness and Power, the text now examines Wisdom (Sapientia) and Will (Voluntas), showing how they function through his logical principles of Difference, Concordance, and Contrariety.</meta>

folio 32.
->On the mixture of principles and rules.<-

# On the mixture of principles and rules.

...to understand them as distinct from one another; for without distinction, they would be confused. And through **wisdom**, difference is intelligible: which nevertheless would not be intelligible without the <term>differentiator, the differentiable, and the act of differentiating</term> <note>Llull typically breaks every attribute into a triad: the active agent, the passive object, and the verb representing the action. Here, he applies this to the concept of Difference.</note>. ¶ **Wisdom**, through *concordance*, possesses concordant things: namely, the understander, the thing understood, and the act of understanding; which accord in one essence that is made of them. And they accord in existing as many, because one is not the other. And this concordance itself is intelligible through wisdom. ¶ Through *contrariety*, there is **ignorance**: the enemy of wisdom, because it hinders its understanding; but the wisdom that is <term>converted</term> <note>In Llull's system, "conversion" refers to the state in God where attributes are essentially identical. If wisdom and concordance are convertible, they are perfectly unified.</note> with concordance does not fear contrariety, because contrariety cannot hinder its understanding. ¶ **Wisdom**, through the *principle*, is the principle of understanding. And the principle, through wisdom, is intelligible. And if they are converted in the subject in which they exist, they are so by necessity, and they cannot be otherwise. ¶ Understanding, through the nature of the *middle*, consists in the middle between the one understanding and the thing understood. And the middle is intelligible through wisdom. **Wisdom**, through the *end*, is restful; and the end, through wisdom, is knowable. And in the subject in which they exist, if they are not converted, there can be understanding without rest, and rest without understanding. ¶ **Wisdom**, by reason of *majority*, can receive in itself a greater understanding; but because it is not converted with majority <note>This refers to created beings; only in God are wisdom and "greatestness" perfectly identical and infinite.</note>, it cannot increase infinitely, but only finitely, beyond which limit it cannot extend itself. ¶ **Wisdom**, by reason of *equality*, has in itself essential and equal ratios: namely the innate, the understander, the thing understood, and the act of understanding; and equality through wisdom is intelligible, which intelligibility is drawn out through the <term>equalizer, the equalizable, and the act of equaling</term> objectively. ¶ **Wisdom** (or the intellect), is not converted with *minority*: for if it were converted, it would always have less understanding, and it would be more fitting for it to be ignorant than to understand, which is impossible.

## On the Will as derived through the principles.

<margin>On the Will derived through the principles.</margin>

**W**ill, through *goodness*, is good. And goodness, through the **will**, is lovable: and if they were converted, the subject in which they existed would always be acting well and loving, and could not be otherwise. ¶ **Will**, through *greatness*, is great: and greatness, through the **will**, is lovable: and therefore the lovability of the will is great, and the lovability of greatness is also great. And if they were converted, there would be <term>lovingness and lovability</term> in infinity regarding the magnifiable, the magnifier, the act of magnifying, and the act of loving. ¶ **Will**, through *duration*, is durable. And duration, through the **will**, is lovable: and if duration (which is eternity) and will were converted, then by necessity the act of eternizing and the act of loving would exist from eternity and into eternity. ¶ **Will**, through *power*, is able to exist and act. And power, through the **will**, is lovable. And in a subject in which they are not converted, the **will** can be powerless, and power can be unloved. ¶ **Will**, through *wisdom*, is knowable: and wisdom, through the **will**, is lovable. And if this exists with greatness and eternity, it follows that understanding and loving exist by necessity. ¶ **Will**, through *virtue*, is virtuous, and virtue, through the **will**, is lovable; but if they are not converted, virtue can be hateful and the will can be vicious. ¶ **Will**, through *truth*, is true. But where **will** and truth are not converted, truth can be hateful and the will can be false. ¶ **Will**, through *glory*, is delightful: and thus glory, through the **will**, is lovable: and thus the **will**, through glory, is far from pain; and glory, through the **will**, is far from hatred. ¶ **Will**, through *difference*, contains in itself a distinction between the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving: and these are clear and not confused within it. And difference, through the **will**, is lovable. ¶ **Will**, through *concordance*, has in itself concordant things: namely the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving: and concordance, through the **will**, is lovable. And because it is lovable with goodness, greatness, duration, power, etc., there are within it the lovable, the concorder, the concordable, and the act of concording. ¶ **Will**, with *contrariety*, hates vice and sin: and if **will** and contrariety were converted, the **will** could never love virtues through concordance. ¶ **Will**, through the *principle*, is the principle of loving. The reason for this is: because all lovable things are lovable by reason of the **will**. It follows that the principle, in regard to the reason of the **will**, is lovable. And in this step, it appears how one being causes something from itself so that it might receive some utility from it. ¶ **Will**, by reason of the *middle*, has in itself a middle: namely, the act of loving: and the middle, by reason of the **will**, is lovable. ¶ **Will**, by reason of the *end*, is perfected in rest when it sees itself possessing in itself a good, great, durable, and powerful rest in loving, without which the end cannot be sufficient for it. ¶ **Will**, with *majority*, is in a greater act of loving: and so that it might have a greater act, majority is lovable. ¶ **Will**, according to the reason of *equality*, has a nature for equaling through the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving. And equality, through the **will**, is lovable.

It defines the "triadic" nature of these attributes (e.g., lover, beloved, and loving) and distinguishes their perfect unity in God from their limited expression in created beings.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical demonstration of Ramon Llull’s "General Art." Following the previous page’s discussion on Wisdom and Will, Llull now moves to Part Eight of this section, applying his combinatorial logic to the concepts of Virtue (Virtus) and Truth (Veritas).</meta>

->Part Eight.<-

The will, when combined with **minority** <note>In Llull's system, "minority" refers to the principle of limitation, contraction, or the less-than-perfect state of created things compared to God.</note>, is focused on nothingness, and with nothingness it exists outside of emptiness or idleness. If will and minority were convertible <note>original: "conuerterentur"; in Lullian logic, "convertibility" means two terms are essentially identical. If Will and Minority were identical, the will would essentially be a drive toward nothingness.</note>, non-being would be more desirable than being, which is impossible.

### On Virtue derived through the principles.

<margin>On Virtue derived through the principles.</margin>

**V**irtue is good through **goodness**, and goodness is virtuous through **virtue**. Thus virtue, by means of goodness, is the reason for a good agent to act well; by itself, this acting is virtuous. ¶ Virtue is great through **greatness**, and greatness is virtuous through virtue. This would not be the case if it did not possess the <term>virtuizer, the virtuizable, and the act of virtuizing</term> <note>original: "virtuisicantem / virtuisicabilem et virtuisicare." Llull creates these three-part structures for every attribute: an active part, a passive part, and the action itself, showing they are one in essence.</note> which are of its essence and identical with itself. ¶ Virtue lasts through **duration**. If it is numerically identical with duration, then the virtuizer, the virtuizable, and the act of virtuizing always endure in their essence. ¶ Virtue is powerful through **power**; thus it can prevail against vice and sin. But it cannot do so when a person does not wish to act from that power. The reason for this is that such a person is both vicious and idle. ¶ Virtue is knowable through **wisdom**, and wisdom has the capacity to know what is virtuous through virtue—assuming, however, that the act of the **will** passes through, which causes the one who loves <note>Llull argues that knowledge (Wisdom) and love (Will) must work together for virtue to be realized in a person.</note>. ¶ And in this step it appears how one virtue is a helper to another. ¶ Virtue is lovable through the will, and the will is virtuous through virtue; thus they come together through the act of loving and the act of virtuizing. ¶ Virtue is true through **truth**, and truth is virtuous through virtue. If they were identical in the subject in which they exist, there would never be falsity or sin in that subject. ¶ Virtue is delightful through **glory** <note>Llull often uses "Gloria" to mean the delight or "rest" found in achieving a goal.</note>, and that delight is virtuous through virtue. ¶ And in this step it appears how a virtuous person, in the act of delighting, desires glory. ¶ Virtue, through the principle of **difference**, is clear and not confused, because difference creates a distinction between the virtuizer, the virtuizable, and the act of virtuizing; yet they are identical in essence. And it has the power so that difference may have the virtue to perform this task. ¶ Virtue, through **concordance**, possesses within itself essential concordant things from which there is one essence. And virtue ordains that concordance be virtuous for this purpose. ¶ Virtue is against its **contrary**, namely vice and sin; it stands against them with goodness, greatness, and so on. ¶ **Contrariety** stands against virtue with the deprivation of its habit <note>A "habit" (habitus) is a settled disposition or character trait.</note>, and with the deprivation of the habits of will, greatness, etc. Virtue, through **priority**, is primary, because whatever is primary is primary through priority, and whatever is virtuous is virtuous through virtue; therefore the **principle** is virtuous through virtue. ¶ Virtue, through the **middle**, is capable of mediation, and the middle is virtuous through virtue. ¶ Virtue, through the **end**, is perfected and at rest. Thus the just, with virtue, strive toward rest. ¶ Virtue, through **majority**, has a greater nature, and majority through virtue has a virtuous essence. ¶ Virtue, through **equality**, has the nature of equalizing justice with providence, and so on. And thus regarding understanding and loving, which are sometimes equally virtuous. ¶ Virtue, by reason of **minority**, is sometimes lesser, just as it is sometimes greater. And so, when it is lesser, it accords with non-being, just as when it is greater, it accords with being.

### On Truth derived through the principles.

<margin>On Truth derived through the principles.</margin>

**V**erity (Truth) is good through **goodness**, and goodness is true through **truth**. If they are converted, the good and the true are always the same. But when they are not converted in a particular subject, someone may desire to have the good in a false way—neither truly nor virtuously. In this step, it appears that in man, goodness and truth are not always converted. ¶ Truth is great through **greatness**; it would not be great unless it possessed the <term>verifier, the verifiable, and the act of verifying</term> <note>original: "verificantem / verificabilem / verificare." Again, Llull applies his triadic logic to show that Truth is an active, self-consistent force.</note> essentially within itself. ¶ Truth endures through **duration**, because the verifier, the verifiable, and the act of verifying endure within it. Similarly, when acting morally within, combined with that which is outside—as in the physical senses where the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>A medieval biological concept referring to the essential, life-sustaining fluids of an organism.</note> acts with the nutritional—truth is powerful through **power**. If it is identical with power, no falsehood can prevail against it. ¶ Truth is knowable through **wisdom**. And wisdom desires truth so that it may truly relate itself to the thing known. ¶ Truth is lovable through the **will**, so that the will may truly possess its beloved. ¶ Truth is virtuous through **virtue**, and virtue is true through **truth**; therefore they participate through the act of verifying against the act of falsifying and sinning. ¶ Truth is delightful through **glory**, and glory is true through **truth**.

->Folio 32.<-
->On the mixing of principles and rules.<-

# On the mixing of principles and rules.

And thus the just truly and gloriously tend toward eternal glory. ¶ Truth, by means of **difference**, is clear and set apart from confusion. And difference establishes that in truth there is one who is the <term>verifier</term>, another who is the <term>verified</term>, and another which is the <term>act of verifying</term> <note>original: "vnus sit verificans / alius verificatus / et alius verificare." These represent the active, passive, and verbal/active components of a single essence in Llull's logic.</note>; and truth establishes this within that which is true. ¶ Truth, by means of **concordance**, contains within itself coessential things that agree—namely, the <term>verifying, the verifiable, and the act of verifying</term>—which agree in essence; and they agree in that they are several; and truth establishes that concordance truly possesses what it has. ¶ Truth is against **falsehood**; and it stands against it with its verifying, verifiable, and the act of verifying. And therefore, it is simply set apart from it. ¶ Truth, by means of **principle**, has the nature of being a principle, just as a principle, through the nature of truth, has the nature of verifying. And therefore, truth is a principle, because whatever is true under the reason of truth is true. ¶ Truth, by means of the **middle**, performs the act of verifying in the middle between the verifier and the verifiable; and truth establishes this within that which is true. ¶ Truth, by means of the **end**, is at rest; and the end, through truth, is true; and in a subject in which they are the same, truth is never found with labor, nor the end in error. ¶ One truth is greater than another; and one **majority** is truer than another. And this is because they are not convertible <note>original: "non conuertuntur." In this context, it means that "truth" and "majority" are not always exactly the same thing or interchangeable.</note>. ¶ Truth, by reason of **equality**, has within itself equally the verifier, the verifiable, and the act of verifying; and equality, through truth, truly possesses that which it has. ¶ One truth is smaller than another; and that which is **minor** participates in non-being, because it has less of "being" <note>original: "minus habet de esse." In Scholastic thought, truth and being are connected; therefore, a lesser truth has a diminished state of existence.</note>; and truth establishes this in that which is true, and minority also establishes this in its own kind.

# On Glory derived through the principles

<margin>On glory derived through the principles.</margin>

**G**lory, through **goodness**, is good. And thus, by reason of the goodness which it possesses, it is the reason for a good agent to act for a good end and through itself; and that this acting is glorious. ¶ Glory, through **greatness**, is great; and it is not great without its own <term>glorifier, the glorified, and the act of glorying</term>; and if its greatness is infinite, then in its act of glorying, it is "to infinitize." ¶ Glory, through **duration**, lasts; and if it is eternity, its lasting is through "eternizing," in which there can be no innovation or change. ¶ Glory, through **power**, is powerful in acting and existing; and if it is the same as power, it is impossible for it to be in a state of failure or idleness. ¶ Glory, through **wisdom**, is stable; and wisdom, through glory, is delightful; and thus they come together through the acts of delighting and knowing. ¶ Glory, through the **will**, is lovable, and the will, through glory, is delightful; and thus the will, by delighting, desires the beloved; and if, in a subject in which they exist, the will and glory are not the same, the will sometimes possesses sadness, because it does not possess the beloved. ¶ Glory, through **virtue**, is virtuous; and virtue, through glory, is glorious; and thus a virtuous person, by taking delight, acquires virtues. ¶ Glory, through **truth**, is true; and truth, through glory, is glorious; and thus a true person in their truth and glory is in delight and rest. ¶ Glory, with **difference**, is clear and set apart from confusion. For difference establishes that one is the glorifier, another the glorified; and likewise for the act of glorying; and glory in this establishes delight. ¶ Glory, through **concordance**, has things that agree, both in one and in many—namely, the <term>glorifying, the glorifiable, and the act of glorying</term>. ¶ Glory, with the act of glorying, stands apart from the pain of its contrary, without which it could not perfectly stand apart. ¶ Glory, through **principle**, has the nature of a principle. And in a subject in which the glorifier and the originator are the same, they originate from themselves that which is glorified and united; and similarly they glorify and originate the act of glorying and the act of originating, by "breathing" and loving, as appears in divine matters <note>This is a reference to the Christian Trinity, where the Holy Spirit is described as "breathing" (spiration) and the bond of love between Father and Son.</note>. ¶ Glory, through the **middle**, is inflowing and outflowing; and the middle, through glory, is in delight and glorification. ¶ Glory, through the **end**, is at rest; and the end, through glory, is in glorification. And therefore, a glorifier without the glorified and the act of glorying cannot be at rest. ¶ The greater glory is, the more it is in delight; and the greater **majority** is, the more it is the image of delight. ¶ Glory, without an **equality** essential to itself, cannot exist through itself in delight, because it would fail in having equally the glorifier, the glorifiable, and the act of glorying. ¶ Glory, with **minority**, is near pain and non-being; therefore, with majority, it stands far from pain and non-being.

# On Difference derived through the principles.

<margin>On difference derived through the principles.</margin>

**D**ifference is good through **goodness**; and goodness is distinct through **difference**. And therefore, difference and goodness are the reasons in a subject in which they exist for it to act well and distinctly, or to produce a distinct good. ¶ Difference is great through **greatness**, because it causes the distinction between genus and genus, and species and species, and individual and individual; and indivi...

<meta>This page continues the logical exploration of the fundamental "principles" of Ramon Llull’s Art. Having previously discussed Truth and Virtue, the text now focuses on the principle of Difference (Differentia) and how it combines with other principles like Duration, Power, and Wisdom. It transitions at the end to the principle of Concordance.</meta>

->Eighth part<-

...dual way, an individual and its own act. And thus **difference** is so great that it contains within itself the principles; and **magnitude**, indeed, is distinct through difference because it [difference] places magnitude in its own proper number or genus; and within magnitude, it places the distinction between the <term>magnifier</term>, the <term>magnifiable</term>, and the <term>act of magnifying</term> <note>original: "magnificatiuum / magnificabile et magnificare." Llull uses these three-part structures (the active agent, the passive object, and the verb) to describe the internal workings of any fundamental quality.</note>, which are of the essence and nature of magnitude.

¶ **Difference** lasts through **duration**, and duration through difference has within itself distinct things which are of its essence, namely: the <term>endurer</term>, the <term>endurable</term>, and the <term>act of enduring</term>. And difference lasts through duration: a distinction that is converted with eternity, from eternity into eternity, it lasts by distinguishing between the <term>eternizer</term>, the <term>eternizable</term>, and the <term>act of eternizing</term>; and this is signified by the most blessed Trinity. 

¶ **Difference** is an innate power absolutely: and it is powerful through **power**, because it causes in power the distinction between the <term>powerful</term>, the <term>possible</term> <note>original: "positum" (that which is placed or possible)</note>, and the <term>act of being able</term>. And power can do this with difference. 

¶ **Difference** is knowable through **wisdom**. And wisdom, by the nature of difference, can understand the distinction between the <term>intellector</term>, the <term>intelligible</term>, and the <term>act of understanding</term>, so that they may be intelligible things; for without difference, they could not be objects or be understood. 

¶ **Difference** through the **will** is desirable: so that the will can have in itself the nature of loving; and that there may exist a clear reason between the <term>lover</term>, the <term>lovable</term>, and the <term>act of loving</term>, without which distinction reason would be confused and powerless to love. 

¶ **Difference** through **truth** is virtuous: and **virtue** through difference has within itself distinct things in which it has agency and existence: and virtue through difference is separated from vice. Indeed, without difference itself, all things would be numerically the same. 

¶ **Difference** through **truth** is true, and truth through difference establishes true things, just as it is true that there is a distinction between the <term>verifier</term>, the <term>verifiable</term>, and the <term>act of verifying</term>; and between the <term>understander</term>, the <term>understandable</term>, and the <term>act of understanding</term>. 

¶ **Difference** through **glory** is delightful: and glory through difference can have delight through the <term>glorifier</term>, the <term>glorifiable</term>, and the <term>act of glorifying</term>, which could not exist in glory without distinction. 

¶ **Difference** through **concordance** has within itself concordant things which it receives into itself by distinguishing between the <term>concordant</term>, the <term>concordable</term>, and the <term>act of concording</term>. And difference does this with its own <term>differentiator</term>, <term>differentiable</term>, and the <term>act of differentiating</term>; and together difference and concordance in the subject in which they are, place that subject as one in common, which has in itself several concordant and different things, from which it is constituted as a single substance, one man, etc. 

¶ **Difference** and innate **contrariety** differ. And this is because sometimes difference agrees with innate concordance by distinguishing, concording, and generating. And sometimes difference with contrariety acts against concordance by distinguishing, opposing <note>original: "contrariando"</note>, and concording; and this is so that the corruption of one becomes the generation of another, and vice versa. And this happens in a similar way in moral matters, as we shall signify. 

¶ **Difference** through **principle** has the reason of priority, so that it is a general principle for all differences: and this with its own proper <term>differentiator</term>, <term>differentiable</term>, and the <term>act of differentiating</term>; without which it could not be in that height, nor have the reason of a principle. 

¶ **Difference** through the **middle** has the nature of a middle: and in itself has a middle, namely <term>to differ</term>, with which it is distinguished from another—namely, the very <term>differing</term>—and it exists between the differentiator and the differentiable. 

¶ **Difference** through the **end** is at rest: and its rest is to distinguish between one thing and another so that it may have subjects in which it is, and can have agency. 

¶ **Difference** by reason of **majority** is greater in one subject than in another. Since in substantial essences <note>e.g., the soul or an angel</note> it is greater than in accidental ones <note>e.g., color or height</note>. Whence difference has a greater action in distinguishing substantial goodness from accidental magnitude, and it has a greater action in distinguishing several things within the same essence that constitute the essence itself [rather than] in distinguishing essence from essence: as was signified in the intellect, in which the <term>understander</term>, the <term>understandable</term>, and the <term>act of understanding</term> differ through difference; which are innately and equally parts of the intellect. Nevertheless, between essence and essence it places itself more extensively. 

¶ **Difference** through **equality** has within itself equal things: just as equality through difference has within itself distinct things. And therefore in the subject in which they are, they communicate with each other through <term>differing</term> and <term>co-equaling</term>. 

¶ **Difference** through **minority** is smaller, if through majority it is greater: and because minority is a small subject or a small "something," difference cannot enter it with its magnitude, nor can it differ much through it: and according to how much the "small" enters, it distinguishes the "small."

It establishes Difference as the mechanism that prevents all things from being identical and allows for generation and corruption.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical exposition of the fundamental "principles" of Ramon Llull’s Art. Having concluded the section on Difference, the text now applies the same systematic analysis to Concordance (Concordantia) and begins the analysis of Contrariety (Contrarietas).</meta>

folio 34.

->On the mixture of principles and rules.<-

# On the mixture of principles and rules.

<margin>The deduction of concordance through the principles.</margin>
**C**oncordance is good through goodness, and goodness is concordant through concordance: and thus, within the subject in which they exist, they participate by making things good and by bringing them into agreement. ¶ Concordance is great through magnitude: and it would not be great if it lacked the <term>concordant</term>, the <term>concordable</term>, and the <term>act of concording</term> <note>original: "concordatiuo / concordabili ⁊ concordare." Llull breaks every quality into three parts: the active agent, the passive object, and the verb or action itself.</note>: which belong to its very essence. Indeed, contrariety would be greater if it could block this; however, concordance is greater than contrariety, because contrariety is not a substantial principle <note>In Llull's philosophy, "being" (like goodness or concordance) is more real and powerful than "non-being" (like evil or discord), which he views as a lack or a destruction of substance.</note>, as is proven in the *Ars Maior* <note>The "Great Art," Llull's primary work on his logical system.</note>. ¶ Concordance is durable through duration, while the concordant, the concordable, and the act of concording—from which it is made—endure within it. ¶ Concordance can exist and act through power, and power possesses things in agreement through concordance: and therefore, as much as concordance and power join together in the subject in which they exist, they distance themselves from contrariety. ¶ Concordance is knowable through wisdom or the intellect: and when the intellect makes concordance its object by understanding its essence and its essential components (the concordant, the concordable, and the act of concording), it reaches and perceives it more than if it only considered the essence alone; and concordance communicates itself more to the intellect through the act of agreeing. ¶ Concordance is lovable through the will: because concordance places its own act within the will, so that the <term>lover</term>, the <term>lovable</term>, and the <term>act of loving</term> <note>original: "amā/amabile ⁊ amare"</note> meet in an identity of essence. ¶ Concordance accords virtue with virtue in the subject in which they exist: and it does this within its own essence and the essence of virtue, for it could not do this externally, because its action would have no subject in which to be sustained. ¶ Concordance is true through truth, and truth is concordant through concordance: and therefore, in the subject in which they exist, they stand apart from contrariety and falsehood through the acts of concording and verifying. ¶ Concordance is delightful through glory, and glory is concordable through concordance: and therefore one reason seeks the other. ¶ Concordance cannot exist without difference: but difference can exist without concordance, insofar as it joins with contrariety. And in this step it appears that difference is a more general principle than concordance. ¶ Concordance and contrariety are opposites: because what concordance builds, contrariety destroys, and vice versa; but concordance is a higher principle than contrariety, because it aligns with "being" through agreement, while contrariety aligns with "non-being" through conflict. ¶ Concordance, by the nature of being a principle, is general to all things capable of agreement: because the principle establishes that concordance has one active principle, another passive, and another neutral; with these, it contains within itself all lesser concordances held beneath it. ¶ Concordance through the <term>middle</term> <note>The "Middle" is one of Llull's logical rules, often used to bridge two concepts.</note> is inward-flowing and outward-flowing through the concordant and the concordable, and vice versa: and the "act of concording" is the middle ground between them. ¶ Concordance rests through the act of concording, the concordant, and the concordable: outside of which it could not find rest, nor could the "end" be a state of rest without concordance. ¶ Concordance is sometimes greater and sometimes lesser. The reason for this is that in one subject, greater things agree than in another—as in a human more than in a rose, and in a rose more than in a stone. ¶ Concordance meets with equality, so that it may have within itself the concordant, the concordable, and the act of concording in equal measure as co-essentials, without which equality could not be the subject in which the end of concordance might rest. ¶ Some concordance is lesser than another: and it is lesser because it cannot exist alongside magnitude and majority. And therefore, concordance paired with minority is close to nothingness; that is, close to the contrariety which is its opposite.

## On contrariety deduced through the principles.

<margin>The deduction of contrariety through the principles.</margin>
**C**ontrariety is sometimes good through goodness, and sometimes bad through malice. Through goodness: such as a person who uses virtue to contradict vice, or like the opposition of the elements <note>Earth, air, fire, and water.</note>, without which there would be no generation <note>The creation of new life/matter.</note>. It is bad through malice: such as an unjust person who uses vice to contradict virtue, or like sickness which is against health, and death against life. ¶ Contrariety is great through magnitude, for there is great contrariety between God and a sinner, between water and fire, between good and evil, and between truth and falsehood, and things of this sort. ¶ Contrariety lasts through duration, but not through itself: because it is an <term>accident</term> <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a quality that isn't essential to a thing's nature (e.g., the color of a shirt), as opposed to its "substance."</note> which does not exist by itself; rather, it lasts as an accident since it is a state of deprivation inclining "being" toward "non-being." And yet it lasts because the beings themselves are distinct, such as the just and the unjust, sight and blindness, understanding and ignorance, heating and cooling, joy and sorrow, and so with others. ¶ Contrariety can exist and act through power, because one contrariety is innate...

<summary>This page defines Concordance and Contrariety within Llull's logical system, explaining how Concordance builds "being" through internal agreement while Contrariety tends toward "non-being" or destruction. It highlights that even negative qualities like Contrariety can serve a "good" purpose when resisting vice or balancing nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the systematic analysis of the "Principles" of the Art.
