Eighth part.

and another is moral <note>original: "moralis." Here used to distinguish human behavior and ethics from "natural" physical properties.</note> innate, just as through heat and cold. Moral: just as it is possible to sin; however, contrariety in sinning does not of itself have the power of opposing, but it is a habit acquired by man, with which man sins. ¶ Contrariety is knowable by reason of objective wisdom: not that contrariety causes one to know; rather, it is against knowing through ignorance. ¶ Contrariety in one way is desirable, in another way not desirable: such as the contrariety of the elements <note>The four elements (earth, air, fire, water) were thought to exist in a state of balanced opposition.</note>, and the contrariety through which virtue is against vice. Undesirable contrariety: such as the contrariety through which death is against life, and vice against virtue. ¶ Contrariety between vice and virtue sets itself and communicates itself, so that a man through it may be against vice, or a man, if he wishes, may be against virtue through vice: not that it forces the man to act concerning it, because he has free will to act with it, either well or poorly. ¶ Some contrariety is true, others false. True, such as justice against injustice. False, such as injury which is truly a habit against the habit of justice. ¶ Some contrariety is through pleasure, another through sadness. Through pleasure: such as a man who, in committing a vice, rejoices against virtue. Through sadness: such as one who has pain for things committed. ¶ Contrariety has three different modes as was said in its chapter in the first part of the first distinction. ¶ Contrariety with its modes is against concordance, and vice-versa: as appears in the chapter on concordance, and in the chapter on contrariety, in the first part of the first distinction. ¶ Contrariety by reason of its principle is naturally innate, so that it contains all natural contrarieties in itself; however, moral contrariety is a habit acquired by man, as was said above. ¶ Contrariety is capable of being mediated <note>original: "mediabilis." Llull means that a middle ground or a reconciling factor can be found between two opposing things.</note>, and this in two ways: namely naturally and morally. Naturally, as heating which contradicts cooling, and vice-versa. Morally, as acting well: that is, one man who acts well and another who acts poorly are in a way opposed through contrarieties. ¶ Contrariety of itself is never at rest: because if it were, its rest would be perfect, and thus contrariety with perfection would agree with non-being; and being with non-being, which is impossible. ¶ Of contrarieties, one is greater, the other lesser. Greater, such as vice against virtue. Lesser, such as heating against cooling. ¶ Contrariety in one way agrees with equality, in another way not: as is clear in the four elements. Absolutely it does not agree with equality: as in virtue and sin, which have no agreement. ¶ Contrariety always agrees with minority by reason of its kind. The reason for this is: because it inclines being toward non-being. ¶ And therefore he who pricks more, pricks through it, is more pricked <note>original: "pungit... punct." Likely referring to the "sting" of sin or the pangs of conscience.</note>, and placed in danger and tribulation, and far from patience. And from such contrariety, may almighty God deign to deliver us.

## On the Principle deduced through the principles.

<margin>The deduction of the principle through the principles.</margin>
**P**rinciple is good through goodness, and goodness through the reason of principle acquires the name of principle. Since that which is "bonifiable" or "bonifying" <note>original: "bonificabile vl' bonificatiuū." Terms used to describe something capable of being made good or something that makes other things good.</note> exists through the reason of goodness. And therefore to principle <note>original: "principiare." Llull uses this as a verb meaning "to act as a principle" or "to originate."</note> good is good. And goodness is the reason and the principle for a good man to do good. And if a good man does not do good: he does evil, because it is against his reason, and against the reason of a good principle. ¶ Principle is great through magnitude. Since whatever is "principlable" or "principled" <term>principiatum</term> <note>The "principled" is the effect or result produced by a "principle."</note> is under the reason of principle. And because so many and such great things are great, being both "principlable" and "principled": therefore principle is great. However, it is not great if it does not "principle" something great, provided it can "principle" something great. And if magnitude and principle are converted <note>In logic, "converted" means they are co-extensive or identical in scope.</note> in the subject in which they are: it is necessary that in that subject they exist infinitely and "principle." ¶ And in this step it appears that of necessity, in the being of God, it is to produce through "infinitizing" and "principling." <note>Llull is arguing that God, as an infinite Principle, must eternally and infinitely be active within Himself.</note> ¶ Principle is durable through duration: and if duration is eternity, and principle is the same as eternity, it is necessary that there be "principling" and "eternizing" in the subject in which principle and eternity are the same. ¶ Principle is powerful through power: and if power and principle are the same, it follows that absolutely and without any hindrance, principle can "principle" as much as is its essence, and as much as is the essence of power. ¶ Principle is knowable through wisdom: and if wisdom is infinite and eternal, and is the same as the principle, then with that principle it is knowable "infinitizing" and "eternizing" and "knowing": and this by necessity. ¶ Principle through the will is lovable: and thus it is the same with magnitude and eternity, and with the will in the principle itself it is lovable to principle, to magnify, to eternize, and to love: and it cannot be otherwise. ¶ Principle through virtue is virtuous: and through prin[ciple]...

<meta>This page continues the systematic analysis of the "Principles" of the Art, specifically looking at how the "Beginning" or "Principle" (Principium) and the "Middle" or "Mean" (Medium) interact with other concepts like Goodness, Truth, and Power. <page-num>Folio 35.</page-num>
<header>On the mixing of principles and rules.</header>

# On the mixing of principles and rules.

The power of the parts is that of the principle: and if in the subject in which they exist, "acting as a principle" and "acting as a virtue" are hindered, then the principle and the power are not the same. ¶ A principle is true through truth: and if it is identical with truth, and eternity with truth, it is necessary that in that principle there exist the acts of beginning, verifying <note>original: "verificare"; the act of making or being true.</note>, and eternizing. ¶ Through glory, a principle is gloriable and delightful: and if it were converted with glory, then "to be glorified" and "to act as a principle" are of necessity converted. ¶ A principle is clear and unconfused through difference: and if the principle is the intellect, then "to act as a principle" and "to understand" are converted: and difference posits that one is the "understander," another the "understandable"; one the "beginner," and another the "principled." <note>This refers to the Lullian "Correlatives," where every essence has an active agent, a passive object, and the act itself.</note> Otherwise, the principle and the intellect could not be distinguished from confusion. ¶ Through concordance, the principle has the nature of concording, which it could not have without concordance: and the "beginning-agent," the "begin-able," and the "act of beginning" would be of the essence of the principle. ¶ Contrariety is against the principle when it hinders its act, <term>namely</term> "acting as a principle": but in a subject in which the principle is identical with power, contrariety cannot hinder the principle from acting as a principle. Since it has nothing with which it might have power that would be of the genus of power. ¶ The principle goes to the end through the medium, without which medium it could not go to the end: and when the medium is hindered, the power of the principle and the end fails: and the appetite suffers, and sadness and labor follow: but when goodness, magnitude, and duration flow in, the power is multiplied and the hindrance is destroyed. ¶ The principle finds rest through the end, and it could not rest through the end without the act of beginning: but when the "beginner" in the "principled" thing (which is of its essence) believes it can find rest through an act of beginning which is merely accidental, it cannot: and in this step it appears that God alone is the Principle and the Rest. ¶ One principle is greater and another lesser. It is greater when it is in act rather than mere potentiality, in which no principle can be greater than a principle existing in act. Since a principle which is in potentiality is focused on nothing compared to that which is in act. ¶ And in this step it appears that God, who is the greatest principle that can be, has the act within Himself: specifically, the "beginner" <note>original: "principiantem"</note>, the "begun" <note>original: "principiatum"</note>, and the "act of beginning" <note>original: "principiare"</note>; as is apparent in divine matters. <note>This is a philosophical defense of the Trinity: Father (beginner), Son (begun), and Holy Spirit (the act of beginning/love).</note> No principle can exist without a nature of equality within itself. The reason for this is: because it seeks to have equality in itself through the "beginner," the "begin-able," and the "act of beginning": but it rests in itself: therefore, etc. ¶ God is the principle, and is the highest and perfect principle. Whence it follows that this through which God is most distant from the "minority" <note>The state of being lesser or limited.</note> of a principle must be in Him: of necessity, therefore, in God there is the "act of beginning," the "beginner," and the "begin-able" or "begun." Therefore, etc.

## On the medium derived through the principles.

<margin>Derivation of the medium through the principles</margin>

**M**edium is good through goodness: because the principle could not come to the end without the medium, nor could the end be a place of rest; therefore goodness, through the act of "good-making" <note>original: "bonificare"</note> which is the medium, is the reason why the good acts as good. ¶ The medium is great through magnitude: and because there is a great distance between the principle and the end, the medium must be great: however, it is not "greatest" unless it is of the very essence of the principle and the end. ¶ The medium lasts through duration and the influence of the end from the resistance of the principle: and if the medium and duration are converted and exist, eternity lasts from the eternal, as does the influence and resistance, the "acting as a medium" and "eternizing." ¶ Through power, the medium can exist and act: and power, by reason of the medium, possesses its "being able." ¶ The medium is knowable through wisdom, and is not knowable without the principle in the end. ¶ The medium is lovable through the will, without which it could not have "loving," nor the "lover" and the "beloved," nor would the principle find rest in the end. And if the medium and the will are converted, then "acting as a medium" and "loving" are converted. ¶ The medium is virtuous through virtue, and virtue passes through the medium from the principle to the end: and virtue consists in a suspended medium. <note>Refers to the Aristotelian idea that virtue is the "mean" (medium) between two extremes.</note> ¶ The medium is true through truth: and truth, by reason of the medium, has in itself "verifying," which is its medium. ¶ Without glory, the medium could not have glory, nor could the "glorifier" have delight in glory. ¶ The medium is clear and unconfused through difference: just as in the essence of the intellect there is "understanding": because one is the "understander" and the other the "understandable": and "understanding" is their act: but if there were no difference between the understander and the understandable, the medium would be confused and not clear: without the concord of the understander and the understandable, "understanding" could not be the medium: because it would not have the necessary components to act. ¶ Sometimes the medium is a hindrance through contrariety: the reason for this is: because the influence of the end and the resistance of the principle fail in the subject in which they are: because the subject is imperfect: but when it is perfected, contrariety is removed from the subject, and the medium...

<meta>This page continues the systematic analysis of the Lullian "Principles." While the previous page focused on the "Principle" (Beginning), this section explores the "Means" (Medium), the "End" (Goal/Finis), and "Greatness" (Maioritas). <header>The Eighth Part</header>

...is perfected. ¶ The **Means** <note>original: "Medium"; in this system, the bridge connecting a beginning to its goal.</note> belongs to the nature of the principle, without which it could not exist; and when it is not perfected, it does not belong to the nature of the end. But when it is perfected, it belongs to the nature of the end. ¶ The means rests in the end: because through the means itself the principle passes to the end; and in the passage of the principle to the end, the means passes also, because it cannot pass without the means. And in this step, it appears in what way elements and other mixable things enter into a mixture. ¶ One means is greater, another is lesser. The greater is like a substantial means, which belongs to a substantial principle and end, with which it is one substance, one essence, and one nature. The lesser is an accidental means, such as running or eating, etc., which are not of the essence of the runner and the runnable, or the eater and the edible. ¶ The means through equality stands equally between the principle and the end: and this occurs perfectly when it is of their essence and is formally separated from all matter. Since matter cannot be in the means, because form "says more" <note>has a higher ontological status</note> than matter; yet according to the way of speaking and the proposition, it is said that the act is caused equally by them. ¶ No means existing between matter and form is far from <term>minority</term> <note>original: "minoritate"; a state of being lesser, limited, or closer to non-existence.</note>. The reason for this is that matter implies "less" and form implies "more": and therefore it follows that a means existing between a disparate "former" and "formed" is distant in every way and simply from minority.

## On the End deduced through the principles.

<margin>On the End deduced through the principles.</margin>
**T**he **End** <note>original: "Finis"; the final cause, goal, or completion of a thing.</note> is good through goodness, so that rest may be good, and goodness may rest; and thus goodness, by resting, is the reason for a good thing to do good. But when a good thing does not do good, goodness and the good thing do not rest, because the good thing remains idle against the purpose of goodness. ¶ The end is great through greatness, so that essence and greatness may rest within the end itself. ¶ However, the end is not "greatly great" if the "rester," the "rest-able," and the "act of resting" <note>These are the Lullian "correlatives": the active agent, the passive object, and the verbal action (quiescens, quiescibilis, quiescere).</note> are not of its essence. ¶ The end endures through duration: and if it is converted with duration, it rests through itself. And if it seeks a foreign end with which to rest, it is not the highest end. ¶ The end can exist and act through power: and power can rest through the end. And if they are converted, it can rest as much through acting as through existing. Just as in the Godhead, in which He rests as much in acting as in existing, and so on for others. ¶ The end is intelligible through wisdom: and it is intelligible in so far as it rests, just as it exists; and if not, it is not the highest end, but an inferior one having a desire for the higher. ¶ And in this step, it appears that all created beings desire the highest end, or ought to desire it. ¶ The end is lovable through the will: and because it is great, it is greatly desirable. And because it is good, it is well desirable; and because the will is great, it should love and desire it greatly. And if it does not do this from its own greatness, it is idle and does injury to nature, by reason of which it is in labor without rest. ¶ The end is virtuous through virtue: and thus with virtue there is rest. ¶ The end with truth is true: and thus rest is truly acquired, and not truly labor and sadness. ¶ Beyond glory, the end cannot be rest, nor glory outside the end; and it consists in delight. ¶ The end with "difference" is an unconfused being. And this is because it has the nature of the "perfecter," the "perfectible," and "to perfect," which are of its essence, without which it would be confused; and it would also be the end of another, and not of itself, which is impossible. ¶ The end through concordance has things that are concording: and concordance through the end has things that are resting. ¶ With contrariety, the end cannot be rest. The reason for this is that the end and concordance are friends, while contrariety and concordance are enemies. ¶ The end is that in which the principle rests: and when it is converted, the end with the principle is "principle-ing" <note>original: "principians"; the act of functioning as a source or beginning.</note>; and when they are not converted, it is possible that the principle does not rest in it. ¶ The end without a means cannot be the subject of the principle so that it may rest in it, since the end and the principle without a means are disparate. ¶ In a greater end there is greater rest: and greater rest is when the "rester," the "rest-able," and "to rest" are the same by essence. ¶ An end without the equality of the "rester," the "rest-able," and "to rest" cannot be the subject in which concordance rests: since when equality is lacking, rest is lacking. ¶ No end with minority is rest: because minority is near to nothingness; and nothingness procures labor and sadness insofar as it is a <term>privative habit</term> <note>A state defined by the absence of a quality that should be present.</note> of perfection.

Therefore, when it produces a greater good according to the logic of goodness and greatness, substance or a greater good produces substantially, and...

<meta>This page continues the "Eighth Part" of the treatise, specifically the section titled "On the mixing of principles and rules." Having previously discussed the "Means" (Medium), the text now shifts to an exhaustive analysis of "Greatness" (Maioritas) and begins the section on "Equality" (Equalitas).</meta>

# On the mixing of principles and rules.

...it places the produced thing itself into the substantial species of goodness and greatness. ¶ **Greatness** <note>original: "Maioritas"; in this system, it refers to the ontological "size" or importance of a being's essence.</note> is great, and some magnitude is greater; from which it follows that it is a substance. For if it were not greater, then substance could not be "more great" than an accident. ¶ Greatness lasts through duration, and duration is greater through substance. For if not, an accident would last by itself and not through a substance; and it would be possible for something to be greater through <term>minority</term> <note>the state of being lesser or more limited</note> rather than through greatness, which is impossible.

¶ Greatness is able to exist and act through power, and power can be greater through greatness; from which it follows that greatness and power can be substantial parts in the **subject** <note>original: "supposito"; the underlying individual or being</note> in which they are found. ¶ Greatness is knowable through wisdom, and thus it is a substantial object. If greatness were not knowable in itself but only by accident, it would be impossible. Greatness is lovable through the will, so that the will, through greatness, can have a greater object.

¶ Greatness is the image of the immensity of virtue <note>original: "virtutis"; here meaning power or excellence</note>. From this it follows that some greatness is a subject; for if not, it could not be the image of the immensity of virtue, because an accident could not suffice for this. Let "minority" be judged as one thing, and substance as "greatness." ¶ Greatness is true through truth, and truth is greater through truth. From this it follows that some truth is substantial; for if not, it could not be greater than an accident, nor could greatness be true through substantial truth.

¶ Greatness is delightful through glory, and glory has a greater delight through greatness; therefore, it is necessary to grant some substantial greatness, so that there may be a greater glory through substance than through an accident. ¶ Greatness is unconfused through **difference** <note>original: "differentia"; a Lullian principle used to distinguish essence from accident</note>, which distinguishes between substantial and accidental greatness; without this distinction, greatness would be confused. ¶ Greatness without **concordance** <note>original: "concordantia"; the principle of affinity or harmony</note> could not be an image of immensity, virtue, magnitude, etc. This concordance establishes that some greatness is a subject in existing and acting.

¶ Greatness overcomes lesser contrariety <note>opposition or conflict</note> with greater concordance; for truth's greatness, when paired with greater contrariety, could not overcome a greater concordance. The reason for this is that greatness belongs to its own genus. ¶ And at this step, it becomes clear in what way sinners sin: they possess guilt because virtues are "greater" in a positive sense, while vices are "lesser" in a **privative** <note>referring to the lack or removal of a good</note> sense.

¶ Greatness, by the nature of a principle, is a principle; and a principle, through greatness, has the nature of a substance. If not, it could not be "more" to this effect. For a principle to be so much "greater" that it can do no more, it must have within itself co-essential parts from which it is made. If it were not so, it could be greater potentially and not actually, and a greater greatness could exist in potentiality than in actuality, which is impossible.

¶ Greatness without a **means** <note>original: "medio"; the bridge between a start and a finish</note> co-essential to itself—namely, <term>to make greater</term> <note>original: "maiorificare"</note>—could not exist in its own genus; nor could the means be a substantial being without greatness. ¶ Greatness causes a greater rest <note>original: "quietem"; the state of reaching the end or purpose</note>; from which it follows that some end is substantial by reason of simple greatness. For **God** <note>original: "des"; shorthand for Deus</note> is not an end in respect to "minority," but in respect to being "greatness." The reason for this is so that God might be separated from pride, envy, and such things.

¶ Greatness without equality could not be an image of immensity, goodness, magnitude, and so on, because it would have nothing with which to relate. Therefore, it has things equal to itself and co-essential: namely, <term>that which makes greater</term> <note>original: "maiorificans"</note>, <term>that which can be made greater</term> <note>original: "maiorificabile"</note>, and <term>to make greater</term> <note>original: "maiorificare"</note>.

¶ Greatness and "minority" are opposed in the subject in which they exist respectively, just as substance and accident are; however, not naturally, because substance and accident agree in constituting a single term, such as a body. Therefore, greatness of itself agrees with *being*, and "minority" with *non-being*. Yet some greatness agrees with non-being, because it causes sin or corruption <note>for example, a "greater" sin leads to a greater lack of being</note>.

## On equality deduced through the principles.

<margin>On equality deduced through the principles.</margin>

**G**ood quality is the reason for a good thing so that it may act equally well. And this definition is the fountain from which natural and moral justice arises. ¶ Equality is great through magnitude; and magnitude, by reason of equality, has things equal to itself and co-essential within it. Indeed, equality could not be great through magnitude without a "co-equalizing nature" consisting of <term>the equalizer</term> <note>original: "coequantem"</note>, <term>the equalized</term> <note>original: "coequabilem"</note>, and <term>to equalize</term> <note>original: "coequare"</note>, which are co-essential and natural to it.

¶ Equality lasts through duration, because that which is "durative" is sufficient for that which is "durable" in the equalizer, since it makes "the equalized" and "to equalize" last. And if equality and eternity were the same in lower things as in the eternal, and from eternity, then "to equalize" and <term>to make eternal</term> <note>original: "eternare"</note> would endure in them without the corruption of one and the generation of another; which is impossible...

It then introduces "Equality" (Equalitas) as the foundation of natural justice and explains its internal trinitarian structure of equalizer, equalized, and equalizing.</summary>

# Eighth part.

...ble. And thus it is clear that the world is new <note>original: "novus"; in this context, it means the world is not eternal but was created at a specific point in time.</note> because within it, equality and eternity are not interchangeable. ¶ **Equality** is powerful through power; power, through equality, has within itself things co-equal to it and co-essential <note>Sharing the same essence or fundamental nature.</note>. And thus, in the subject in which they exist, they cause "to co-equalize" and "to be able." And if they were the same in lower things <note>Meaning created, earthly things as opposed to divine things.</note>, they would necessarily be "to co-equalize" and "to be able" to such an extent that they would eliminate all inequalities from the world; and all things would be equal and equally powerful, which is impossible. In this step, it appears how one impossibility leads to another.

¶ **Equality** is knowable through wisdom; and because wisdom is great through greatness, and equality similarly so, it follows of necessity that equality is in act through its co-essentials: the <term>equalizer</term>, the <term>equalized</term>, and the <term>act of equating</term> <note>original: "coequante, coequabile, z coequare"; these are Lullian technical terms for the active, passive, and verbal components of a single principle.</note>. And if equality is the same as the intellect, it follows that within it there are always "to co-equalize" and "to understand."

¶ **Equality** is lovable through the will: the reason for this is so that the will can possess things through the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving. And because the will and equality are great through greatness, powerful through power, and resting through the end, they are necessarily in act.

¶ **Equality** is virtuous through virtue: and virtue, through equality, has equal things within itself. And so in this step, it appears that the virtues are co-equalizable, and that this co-equating is virtuous.

¶ **Equality** is true through truth: because it could not receive the quality of truth without its own nature, it must impress its own quality and nature upon truth; so that truth, by the logic of equality, has within itself things co-equal and co-essential.

¶ **Equality** is delightful through glory, and glory is co-equalizable through equality. Therefore, in glory, the one who glories delights in co-equating for himself that which is glorified and that which is capable of glory.

¶ **Equality** through difference is a logic that is distinct, demonstrative, and clear. The reason for this is: because difference establishes that one is the equalizer, another is the equalized, and another is the act of equating. But if difference were removed from equality, equality would be emptied of clarity and would be overshadowed and filled with darkness.

¶ **Equality** through concordance has concordant things; and concordance through equality has co-equating things. And if they are interchangeable, they are always permanent through the act of co-equating and the act of concording. And contrariety and equality cannot act as principles together.

¶ **Equality** and contrariety are not friends, because equality and concordance are friends; and in this step, it appears that justice arises from equality and concordance, and injury <note>original: "iniuria"; injustice or harm.</note> from contrariety and inequality.

¶ **Equality** is a principle by the logic of a principle; and a principle, by the logic of equality, has within itself things equal to itself and co-essential. And if they are interchangeable, they are always permanent through the act of beginning <note>original: "principiare"</note> and the act of equating.

¶ **Equality** through the mean <note>original: "medium"; the middle ground or mediating principle.</note> has a mediating nature; and the mean, through equality, is co-equating; and thus they agree with each other through equating and mediating.

¶ **Equality** is the subject in which the end of concordance rests; and in that very rest is greatness, so that rest may not exist without the greatness of equality, being entirely separated from <term>minority</term> <note>the state of being lesser or more limited</note>, which is not of the nature of rest.

¶ **Equality** is greater through greatness, and equality, as to its essence and nature, requires things equal to itself and co-essential, so that it may be entirely separated from minority, its enemy. ¶ And in this step, it appears how greatness outside the soul is a real and natural being.

¶ **Equality** and minority are enemies. The reason for this is: because where there is equality, there cannot be minority; for if it were there, it would destroy equality. Nevertheless, insofar as some equality is less than another along with minority, it has some commonality through which it coincides with non-being <note>original: "non esse"; the state of not existing or nothingness.</note>.

## On minority deduced through the principles.

<margin>
On minority
deduced
through the
principles.
</margin>

**M**Inority through goodness is not concerned with nothingness, because goodness is always concerned with something; but goodness through minority is concerned with nothingness. And therefore, every good man who does not attain the good is idle: regarding goodness, he is lesser and concerned with nothingness; but this happens by accident.

¶ **Minority** is not of the nature of greatness in respect to "majority" <note>Greatness or being more.</note>, which is its contrary; yet it is great insofar as it is a substance. Things and substances and substantial beings differ specifically through majority and minority.

¶ **Minority** lasts through duration in its own kind, which would be impossible if it were of eternity, which is not of the kind of minority. And in this step, it appears that the world is not eternal. Because if it were so, it would be of the kind of eternity: which eternity would be lesser than the eternity of God; just as the goodness of the world is lesser than the goodness of God.

¶ **Minority** through power can be that which it is, but not beyond that which it is. And thus it is regarding its ability to act.

¶ **Minority** is knowable by reason of wisdom; and wisdom, by reason of minority, is lesser; I say "lesser" when it is in potentiality...

...active or idle: because being in potentiality and idleness go together with minority <note>The state of being lesser, smaller, or inferior in degree.</note>. But actuality and agents go with greatness.

¶ **Minority** through the will is lovable; not so that the will directs minority toward itself, but so that it loves minority in some object so that it may love greatness. For example, in water, the will loves the heat which causes a "minority" <note>A reduction or lessening of the water's natural coldness.</note> in the water, so that a man may be warmed and bathed by that water.

¶ **Minority** through virtue is virtuous: for virtue restores that which the subject of minority possesses in small quantity; just as a mustard seed has great virtue through its sharp taste and multiplies into many seeds.

¶ **Minority** through truth is true: the reason for this is that truth truly establishes itself around "non-being"; and minority, by diminishing, establishes that one truth is less than another.

¶ **Glory** through minority is lesser: and thus glory through minority is not at rest. Instead, glory, by reason of its abundance, would multiply its delight in a subject where there is minority, were it not that minority hinders it. It hinders it because minority cannot, in itself, contain great delight.

¶ **Minority** through difference is a clear reason <note>original: "ratio inconfusa"; an unconfused or distinct logic.</note>: but according to its kind <note>original: "secundum genus"</note>, its charity is small.

¶ **Minority** participates with concordance, so that it may be constituted from many concordant things. But that concordance is small, because it cannot enter into minority along with greatness.

¶ **Minority** with contrariety is against greatness: and minority with contrariety is against minority. And in this step, it appears how easily minority can be defeated.

¶ **Minority** through principle belongs to the nature of a principle: and thus it is a principle under which all lesser agents of small value are placed.

¶ **Minority** through the "middle" is capable of being mediated: namely, it is the middle point between equality and greatness, through which things tend toward the "non-being" in which they are not, until they pass through that very minority and receive their nature, and come to nothing.

¶ **Minority** in itself is never at rest. The reason for this is because it exists around "non-being": but greatness knows it, because greatness exists around "being"—and greatness makes minority its handmaid.

¶ **Minority** and greatness cannot be the same thing: because greatness speaks of "being," and minority of "non-being." However, they agree well regarding a single end, just like a mistress and her handmaid.

¶ **Minority** and equality cannot be the same in species. The reason for this is that minority consists between equality and non-being: while equality consists between greatness and minority.

### Is goodness a general principle? And it must be answered that it is, as is clear through rule B <note>Rule B usually corresponds to the question "What is it?" or "Whether it is?"</note> and through the "ladders" of the second figure in which all good things are comprised. These ladders are general and good through goodness, which goodness they could not have if general goodness were lacking. 

¶ Through the first species of rule C <note>Rule C typically asks "What?" or defines the essence of a thing.</note>, it is asked: **What is general goodness?** And it must be answered that it is a being <note>original: "ens"</note> that contains within itself all spiritual goodnesses sustained in spiritual subjects.

¶ Through the second species of rule C, it is asked: **What does goodness have within itself that is co-essential to it?** And it must be answered that it has the "concrete relations" <note>The Lullian "triad" of the agent, the patient, and the action (e.g., the Bonifier, the Bonifiable, and the act of Bonifying).</note> which are co-essential to it, from which it is made and without which it could not be a general principle. This is provable through the first species of rule C and the second of rule D. 

¶ Through the third species of rule C, it is asked: **What is goodness in another?** To which it must be answered that it is a "habit" in a subject which is habituated with active or passive goodness; that which is through the active is "well-doing" <note>original: "bene agens"</note>, and through the passive is "well-suffering" <note>original: "bene patiens"; meaning to receive action in a good or proper way.</note>.

¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: **What does it have in another?** And it must be answered that it has existence in a subject without which it could not be; and it has within that subject action and passion by reason of its nature signified in the second species. ¶ It is asked...

### Eighth part.

Through the first species of Rule D <note>In this system, Rule D asks the question *De quo?*—"Of what?"</note> regarding **goodness**: it must be answered that it is of itself; so that it is general and has its nature designated through itself in the second species of Rule C, and in the first and second species of Rule D. And through the second species [of Rule D], regarding contracted <note>term: contracted; meaning limited or specific goodness rather than universal goodness</note> goodness: "of what is it?" And the answer is that it is of itself, insofar as it is an innate substance: as was signified through the second species of Rule C and the first species of Rule E. For otherwise, it would not have natural existence through itself, which is impossible. ¶ Furthermore, **goodness** existing as a natural or moral habit <note>term: habit; a settled disposition or quality of a person or thing</note> is a signifier of substantial goodness, derived and diffused, just like a likeness is a signifier of the thing it simulates. ¶ Again, through the third species of Rule D: "whose" is goodness? And it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it is, like the habit of the one who possesses the habit, and the quantity of the thing quantified, and such things. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks *Quare?*—"Why?"</note> it is asked: why is goodness? And the answer is that it is through itself, as was seen through the second species of Rule C and the first species. ¶ Further, through the second species of Rule E it is asked: why is goodness? The answer is that **goodness** exists so that other principles may be good through it; for if goodness were removed, no principle would be good, just as if heat were removed, no being would be heated. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks *Quantum?*—"How much?" or "How great?"</note> it is asked: how great is goodness? And the answer is that it is as great as its habit is; but in a subject, it is a part of that subject. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: how great is goodness? And the answer is that it is as great as its concrete correlatives <note>note: original: "correlativa"; in Llull’s logic, these are the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle, such as "the goodness-maker," "the thing made good," and "the act of making good."</note> and its co-essential parts, as has already been proved in the second species of Rule C.

<margin>g.</margin>
¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks *Quale?*—"Of what kind?"</note> it is asked: what kind of thing is goodness? And the answer is that it is a proper property <note>term: passio; a characteristic or attribute that necessarily follows from the essence of a thing</note> of the substantial or accidental subject in which it is; and with a proper property, the predicate is derived, without which the subject cannot exist, just as "animal" is a predicate of "man." ¶ Again, through the second species it is asked: what kind of thing is goodness? And it must be said that it is such as a good habit is in a subject that possesses that habit: like the sweetness of honey which is good, and the justice of a just man. ¶ Through all species of Rule H <note>Rule H asks *Quando?*—"When?"</note> it is asked: when is goodness? And the answer is that it is at that time when the good thing itself exists, time being present in good and continuous successive motion, according to the scale of the Second Figure <note>note: The "Second Figure" is a diagram in Llull's Art used to show the relationships between different principles.</note>; indeed, in this response all the species of Rule H are implied as they relate to time. But we leave the specific applications to the person who is well-versed and observant of this Art. And we do this for the sake of brevity. At this stage, the intellect is heavily burdened. Truly, the more it is burdened, the more elevated and general it becomes. ¶ It is asked through all species of Rule I <note>Rule I asks *Ubi?*—"Where?"</note>: where is goodness? And the answer is as was previously said of time; namely, it is in itself: as is manifest through the second species of Rule C and through the first and second species of rules D and E, and through the principles of the First Figure which concern goodness as a habit and as a position. ¶ Through the first species of Rule K <note>Rule K asks *Quomodo?*—"How?" and *Cum quo?*—"With what?"</note> it is asked: how is goodness? And the answer is that goodness is a part of the subject in which it exists, as is clear through the scale of "difference" <note>note: "Difference" is one of the principles used to distinguish between things.</note> and through the second species of Rule C and the first of Rule G. ¶ Further, through the second species of Rule K it is asked: how is goodness in another principle? And the answer is through the second species of Rule C. And this is clear in the first part regarding the mixing of principles, and in the first scale of the Third Figure through chamber B-C and chamber B-K <note>note: Chambers (camerae) refer to specific combinations of letters/principles in the combinatorial grids used by the author.</note>. ¶ Furthermore, it is asked through the third species of K: how is goodness in the whole, and the whole in it? And it must be said that it is in the whole just as a habit is in the one who possesses it, as was signified through the scale mentioned above. ¶ Through the fourth species of K it is asked: how does goodness transmit its likeness outward? And the answer is through the manner it has in the second species of Rule C, in which the "good-making" agent generates foreign or accidental goodnesses within its "good-makeable" object, which are held as habits; just as sweetness is in honey (which is good) and justice is in the just man. ¶ It is asked through all species of Rule K: with what is goodness? To which it must be answered that it is with itself and with other principles, and also with its correlatives without which it could not exist, as is clear in the second species of Rule C; with these it generates and impresses foreign goodnesses; and it is with the first and second species of Rule D. And similarly with the scale of the Third Figure determined by B-C and B-K, in which scale it diffuses itself, giving its likenesses to them.

# On the mixing of principles and rules.

...[Greatness is] that with which a great thing causes "to make great." And this has been seen through Rule B <note>Rule B in Llull’s Art usually corresponds to the principle of "Difference," but here it acts as a confirming axiom.</note>.
¶ Through the second species [of Rule C] <note>Rule C asks *Quid?*—"What?"</note>, it is asked: what does **greatness** have in itself? And it must be answered that in physical things it has the <term>greatener</term> <note>original: *magnificamentum*; the active power of greatness</note>, the <term>greatened</term> <note>original: *magnificatum*; the capacity to be made great</note>, and the act of <term>greatening</term> <note>original: *magnificare*; the actualizing process</note>, which are co-essential to it. With these, it causes substantial extensions in a subject, from which quantities are caused; with these, it measures itself and other principles in the physical subject in which it exists. In a spiritual great thing, however, it causes great acts: namely, great understanding, remembering, and loving, practiced by those possessed of spiritual greatness, while that greatness itself exists in the spiritual principle. And this is the same for a spiritual great thing in its "making good," "lasting," "judging," etc., as is proven through Rule B.
¶ Furthermore, through the third species: what is greatness in another? And it must be said that it is the "form-ing" form of a great formed thing and a great material thing, as was signified through the first species of D. 
¶ Further, through the fourth species, it is asked: what does greatness have in another? It must be answered that it has great action and passion <note>term: passion; the state of being acted upon by an external force</note> in the great subject in which it is, with which it is natural. And this was signified through the first rule of D.
¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks *De quo?*—"Of what?"</note>, it is asked: of what is greatness? It must be answered that it is of itself, so that it may be primary in the act of greatening; for if it did not "greaten," it would not have that of which it consists, nor consequently the "greatened" thing which it would be, which is impossible. This, moreover, is evident through Rule B.
¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what is greatness? And it must be answered that it is of its natural <term>correlatives</term> <note>term: correlatives; the internal active, passive, and verbal components of a principle (e.g., greatener, greatened, greatening)</note> signified in the second species of C.
¶ Further, through the third species, it is asked: whose is it? And it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it is, because the subject acts with it in itself, naturally or morally. And this was signified through Rule B.
¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks *Quare?*—"Why?"</note>, it is asked: why is greatness? And it must be answered through the second species of Rule C, because it consists of the greatener, the greatenable, and the act of greatening, by reason of which greatness has the nature of being what it is.
¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why is greatness? And it must be answered: so that other principles may be great through it. And this is signified in the <term>figure</term> <note>The "Figure" refers to the circular diagrams Llull used to show the relationships between concepts.</note> through all the other chambers in which "C" <note>In Llull's notation, "C" represents Greatness.</note> is present.
¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks *Quantum?*—"How much?"</note>, it is asked: how much is greatness? And it must be answered that it is as great as its essence is continuous in the subject, designated through the scale of the <term>Third Figure</term> by B-C and C-D, all the way to the chamber C-K.
¶ Through the second species, it is asked: how much is greatness? And it must be answered that it is as great as it can hold of its correlatives signified through the second species of C. And likewise regarding the relationships of greatness flowed from it in the first and second figure, substantialized, related, and numbered.

<margin>g.</margin>
¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks *Quale?*—"Of what kind?"</note>, it is asked: what kind of thing is greatness? And it must be answered that it is such as it is through the first species of Rule C, and through the first and second of D, E, and F. And Rule B testifies to this.
¶ Again, through the second species, it is asked: what kind of thing is greatness? And it must be answered that it is such as its diffused and discursive habits are in the Third Figure, through the scale B-C and C-D, up to C-K.
¶ Through the first species of H <note>Rule H asks *Quando?*—"When?"</note>, it is asked: when is greatness? And it must be answered that it is then, when its subject in which it is sustained and joined exists. And this is provable through the scales of the Third Figure constituted by B-C and C-D up to C-K; in which scale all fifteen species of Rule H are implicated when greatness, having been moved, consists in time, and time in it. But to explain this would be very lengthy; rather, it belongs to the <term>artist</term> <note>The "artist" here refers to a practitioner or student of Llull's "Art" (Ars Magna).</note> who knows this Art.
¶ Through all species of Rule I <note>Rule I asks *Ubi?*—"Where?"</note>, it is asked: where is greatness? And it must be answered that it is with all species of "I" in the chambers designated in the Third Figure. And through the Art, it is applicable to the proposed human intuition, and to the one who knows this Art.
¶ It is asked through the species of the first Rule K <note>Rule K asks *Quomodo?*—"How?"</note>: how is greatness? And it must be answered that it is through that mode which it has in Rule C, D, E, F, G, H, and I, as was signified in the scale of the Third Figure.
¶ Through the second Rule K, it is asked through all species: with what is it? And it must be answered that it is with its correlatives signified in the second species of C. And it is with the first and second species of Rule D, E, F, G, H, and I, and with the first modal species, without which it cannot be what it is.
¶ Furthermore, it is with other principles, without which it could not be that which now has the nature it possesses in itself and in others. And what has been said is known through itself and is also proven through Rule B.
¶ We have spoken of **greatness** as discussed through the rules, by reason of which it has been shown in what way the human intellect has a very general subject for attaining many and great operations caused by greatness and led into the subject in which they are. And therefore, since this is so, what wonder is it if through this general Art the human intellect is made very general for causing great and many sciences, easily discovered?

Part Eight
<header>Part Eight</header>

# Part Eight

<margin>
On eternity deduced through the rules.
</margin>

**I**t is asked: is there eternity? And it is answered that there is: because if not, the world would have originated itself and made itself anew, and would have been before it was: and thus a contradiction would follow, which is impossible. And this has been proven through Rule B <note>Rule B in Llull’s system typically addresses the question *An est?* (Is it?), establishing the existence of a subject.</note>. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks *Quid est?* (What is it?). Llull divides these questions into "species" or sub-questions.</note>, it is asked: what is eternity? It must be answered that it is a being which is <term>converted</term> <note>In Llullian logic, "conversion" means terms are co-extensive or interchangeable in their scope; here, eternity is equal to infinite goodness, power, etc.</note> with its infinite goodness, greatness, power, and virtue. And this is probable through the first and second species of D, E, and F. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what does eternity have in itself? And it must be answered that it has its substantial and primitive <term>correlatives</term> <note>The internal structure of any Llullian principle: an active power, a passive capacity, and the action itself.</note>: as is proven through the first and second species of Rule D and E. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: what is eternity in another? It must be answered that it is a being existing before time: and this is probable through its definition stated above and through the first species of Rule D. ¶ And through the fourth species it is asked: what does eternity have in another? And it must be answered that it has the power of annihilating whatever exists, because its power is infinite. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks *De quo?* (Of what/From what?).</note>, it is asked: of what is eternity? And it must be answered that it is of itself, because it is primitive and singular: and this is clear through Rule B. ¶ And through the second species it is asked: of what is eternity? And it must be answered that it is of the <term>eternizer</term> <note>original: *eternante*; the active principle of eternity</note>, the <term>eternizable</term> <note>original: *eternabili*; the capacity to be eternal</note>, and <term>to eternize</term> <note>original: *eternare*; the act of eternalizing</note>, without which it could not be what it is: and without these it would indeed be empty and idle: and even its being could happen to be in nature <note>i.e., it would be a mere accident rather than an essential substance</note>: and this is manifest through the second species of Rule C and through the first of D and E. ¶ Further, through the third species it is asked: whose is eternity? And it must be answered that it is no one's: since an infinite being can by no means exist under another. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks *Quare?* (Why?).</note>, it is asked: why is eternity? <unclear>and it is answered that it is</unclear> from infinite primitive substantials, and co-essential to itself. ¶ <margin>g</margin> and from the eternizer, the eternizable, and to eternize, without which it could not be what it is: nor could it exist through itself: and this is probable quite evidently through all species of Rule C and B. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: why is eternity? It must be answered: so that its goodness, greatness, and power may be primitive and the initiators before all things. And this is manifest through Rule B and similarly through the first species of D. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks *Quantum?* (How much?).</note>, it is asked: how great is eternity? and it must be answered that it is as great as can exist outside of time, otherwise it would not be infinitely primitive and continuous and singular without time. And this is probable through Rule B and through the first species of C. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: how great is eternity <term>discretely</term> <note>discrete quantity refers to things that can be counted or separated into parts, as opposed to continuous quantity</note>? and it must be answered that it is as great as was shown through the second species of Rule C, D, and E. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks *Quale?* (What kind?).</note>, it is asked: what kind of quality does eternity have? To which it must be said that it is such as its definition and meaning deduced through the second species of Rule C and through all species of D, E, and F. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what kind is eternity? And it must be answered that it is the cause of new time, thus existing and preceding outside time and motion, just as its substance is <term>intense</term> and <term>extended</term> outside the quantity of the world. And this is affirmable through all species of Rule C, D, E, and F and also through Rule B. ¶ Through all species of Rule H <note>Rule H asks *Quando?* (When?).</note>, it is asked: when is eternity, or when was it, and when will it be? To which it must be said through the species of Rule C, D, and K: namely, that it was before time had been: so that it preceded time in its eternal duration: just as its infinite greatness precedes the finite quantity of the world. ¶ Furthermore, eternity is the *now* in which it was from eternity, and in which it will now be in eternity: and this without motion and succession: and in such a *now* time can by no means exist: nor can it ever be of the genus of eternity. ¶ Furthermore. Eternity will be then when time will not be in an eternal subject. The reason for this is so that the immobility of eternity might thus measure and encompass the mobility of the world: just as in the immense and infinite substance of God [it encompasses] the finite quantity of the world: and to this all rules with their species bear witness. ¶ Through Rule I <note>Rule I asks *Ubi?* (Where?).</note>, it is asked: where is eternity? and it must be answered through rules C, D, and K and through other rules: namely, that it is as much outside the <term>heavens</term> <note>original: *celum*; referring to the physical spheres of the universe</note> with its immense infinity, as it is outside time and motion with its infinity and immobility: and as it is with its infinite goodness outside finite goodness. Nevertheless, divine eternity is in the world and in all its parts, not that it is placed there, because it is infinite and invisible: as is clear through the second species of Rule C and D, and has also been proven through Rule B. ¶ Through the rule of <term>modality</term> <note>Rule K asks *Quomodo?* (How?).</note>, it is asked: how is eternity? And it must be answered that the mode is designated in the second species of Rule C, D, and E, without which eternity would not have a mode of existing and acting in its nature: which all the rules assert. ¶ Through the rule of <term>instrumentality</term> <note>Also part of Rule K: *Cum quo?* (With what?).</note>, it is asked: with what is eternity? And it must be answered that it is with its co-essential relatives designated in Rule C, D, and E. And thus with its infinite singular goodness, greatness, power, etc. just as with

# On power deduced through the rules.

<margin>On power deduced through the rules.</margin>
**I**t is asked whether there is any infinite power: And it must be answered that there is. And this is attested to by the chapter on eternity. ¶ For if there were no infinite power, then eternity, which is infinite, would not have that by which it could be infinite: and this has been proven through Rule B <note>Rule B in Llull’s logic asks "An est?" (Is it?), establishing existence.</note>. Likewise, through the third species of Rule D: unless there were infinite power, it would follow that power would hinder the finite from existing. From which it would follow that power was a <term>privative habit</term> <note>A "privative habit" is a quality defined by the absence of something else; the author argues power is a positive, substantial force, not just an absence.</note> subordinate to a finite and positive habit, which is impossible. ¶ It is asked through the first species of Rule C: what is infinite power? And it must be answered that it is a being to whom "to be infinitely able" properly belongs. And this has been seen through the first species of Rule D. And Rule B also testifies to this. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what does infinite power have in itself? And it must be said that it has natural and essential relations with which it can well be that which it is. And this is demonstrable through Rule B and through the second and third [species] of Rule D and E. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: What is power in another? And it must be said that it is a being causing actions and <term>passions</term> <note>original: "passiones." In scholastic philosophy, a "passion" is the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note> in a subject, by reason of which the subject can have actions and passions: and this can be affirmed through Rule B. ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked: what does power have in another? And it must be said that it has actions just as a cause has effects, and it has passions in the subject in which it exists, the power itself being <term>habituated</term> <note>Endowed with the quality or state of.</note> with goodness and greatness [etc.]. And this was seen through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D it is asked: from what is power? It must be said that it is from itself, because it is a general principle. And this is provable through Rule B. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: from what is power? It must be said that it is from the <term>power-er</term>, the <term>power-able</term>, and <term>to power</term> <note>original: "possificate, possificabile, & possificare." These are Llull’s technical terms for the active component, the passive component, and the act of the principle of Power.</note>. And this is provable through the second species of C and E. ¶ Further, through the third species it is asked: whose is power? To which it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it is: which indeed acts upon the patient with its power. And this is self-evident. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E it is asked: why is there power? It must be said that it is because it is from the power-er, the power-able, and to power: but <term>accidentally</term> <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has but which is not essential to its nature, like the color of a stone.</note> it is a habit in the subject in which it is: just as whiteness exists because its subject is white. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: why is there power? It must be said so that other principles may have existence and agency through it. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F it is asked: how great is power? It must be said that it is as great as its nature can enter: and this is manifest through the second species of C: so that from them there may be one continuous existence. And to this Rule B and the first and second species of Rule D testify. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: how great is power? It must be said that it is as great as its <term>concrete relates</term> <note>The specific, manifested forms of the principle’s internal relations.</note> are, as seen through the second species of Rule C, the first of G, and through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G it is asked: what kind is power? It must be said that it is such as is the proper passion of the subject: just as the infinity and eternity of God, without which God could not be that which he is. ¶ Likewise, through the second species it is asked: what kind is power? It must be said that it is such as is the habit in the subject, like goodness or greatness, which can be what they are through power. And a judge can be [a judge] through power. And this is manifest through Rule B. ¶ It is asked through all species of Rule H: when is power? And it must be said through the first species of the rule that it is then when its definition is. And through the second of the same, it is then when it has correlatives co-essential to itself. ¶ Further, through the third it is then when it is a habit in the subject. ¶ Further, through the fourth of the same, it is then when it has actions and passions in a subject. ¶ And through the first species of Rule D it is then when time can exist through power and through motion, and motion in time. ¶ Further, through the second of D, it is then when it is from its correlatives. ¶ Further, through the third of D, it is then when it is the instrument of the subject in which it is. ¶ And through the first species of the <term>Modal Rule</term> <note>One of the rules in Llull's system concerning the "mode" or way in which something exists.</note> it is then when it has its mode through itself. And through the second species it is then when it is a habit in a subject. ¶ And through the third species it is then when one correlative is in another: and all are one essence and the essence is in them. ¶ And through the fourth species it is then when other principles are habituated by it, and from the likenesses of that power. ¶ Through the rule of <term>instrumentality</term>, power is further then when it is with its correlatives. ¶ And through the second species it is then when one principle is with another. ¶ And through the third it is then when several essences can be in one common [thing]: and one in another and the common in them. ¶ Furthermore

Eighth part.

...through the fourth species <note>The "fourth species" of Rule C in Llull’s system typically asks what a thing has in another, or its external effects.</note>, it is then when it causes its likenesses in a passing subject along with its intrinsic <term>coessential relatives</term> <note>Llull uses "coessential relatives" or "correlatives" to describe the internal structure of a principle: for Power, these would be the Empowerer, the Empowered, and the act of Powering.</note>. And thus it has been shown how power exists in time, and time and motion exist within power itself. But in this discourse, the intellect is greatly burdened, yet it is also exalted. And all these rules prove this; without them, the intellect could not reach such heights.

¶ Through all species of Rule I <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi).</note>, it is asked: where is power? It must be said that it is in "where" through the same manner as was said above concerning time. For it is in its own definition, and it is in its correlatives, in which everything possible is "possibilized" <note>Original: *possibile est possibile*. In Llull's Latin, this suggests the active making-possible of things.</note>; and outside of them, no being is possible except in them, because no impossible thing can exist. Again, it is in the subject in which it exists as a habit, and in the subject in which it performs its actions and passions. And it is in place fundamentally; and it is in those things of which it consists, and it is in the subject to which it belongs. And it is in the <term>modality</term> in which it has its mode of existing and acting, and of generating its own likenesses. And it is in the subject which acts and suffers along with that power. And this has been demonstrated through all the aforementioned species, and it is provable through Rule B.

¶ Through the rule of modality <note>Rule K asks "How?" (Quomodo).</note>, it is asked: how is power? and it must be answered that the mode of power is according to how it has its mode of being and acting in the subject in which it is, and the subject is in it, having actions and passions through power. And this is sustained through a continuous line in the species of the rules. But to explain this would be prolix; nevertheless, the explanation itself is possible and easy for those who hold to the method of this Art.

¶ It is asked "with what" power exists through the rule of instrumentality: and it must be said that it is with its coessential relatives, and it is with all species of the rules, without which it cannot exist, nor can they exist without power. ¶ And this is sufficiently explainable to those accustomed to this Art. ¶ And let these things suffice concerning power.

# On wisdom deduced through the rules.

<margin>Deduction of wisdom through the rules.</margin>
**I**t is asked whether any wisdom is a <term>habit</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, a "habit" (*habitus*) is not a routine behavior, but a stable quality or disposition of the mind that allows it to perform an action easily.</note>: and it must be said that it is. For if there were no wisdom that was a habit, the intellect would no longer have anything with which to objectify real and necessary truths; and thus it would be naked and powerless, which is impossible. And this is provable through Rule B.

¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "What is it?"</note>, it is asked: what is wisdom existing as a habit? and it must be answered that it is an instrument with which the intellect acts properly and well, because it is so well-habituated to it; just as fire is habituated to heat, a cloaked man to a cloak, and a just man to justice.

¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does wisdom have in itself coessentially? and it must be answered that it has its own correlatives without which it cannot exist.

¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is it in another? and it must be said that it is a habit existing in another.

¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does wisdom have in another? and it must be said that wisdom existing as a substance has its habit in the subject, with which subject it understands well.

¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo) or the origin/matter of a thing.</note>, it is asked: of what is wisdom? it must be said that it is of itself as a fundamental and general principle for all knowable things.

¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what things is it composed? and it must be said that it is of its essential relatives: that which is a substance, and that which is an accident or habit, does not have "things of which it is made," since it is a simple form. And this is manifest through Rule B, the second species of Rule C, and the fourth species of Rule K.

¶ Further, through the third species, it is asked: to whom does wisdom belong? to which it must be said that it belongs to the subject in which it is, just as a cloak belongs to the cloaked man, and so forth.

¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare).</note>, it is asked: why is there wisdom? and it must be said that wisdom existing in a subject is because it consists of the "intellective," the "intelligible," and the "act of understanding." And if it is an accident, it is because the intellect is habituated by it, just as a logician is habituated by logic, and the like.

¶ Furthermore, through the second species, it is asked: why is there wisdom? and it must be answered: so that the wise person may hold knowledge well and prudently. And this is proven through Rule B.

¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum).</note>, it is asked: how great is wisdom? and it must be answered that it is as great as the habit existing in the subject in which it resides.

¶ Further, through the second species, it is asked: how great is wisdom? and it must be answered that it is as great as its concrete parts are habituated by that wisdom itself, just as there is the "heater," the "heatable," and the "act of heating," which indeed exist as habituated by heat.

¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks "What kind?" (Quale).</note>, it is asked: what kind of thing is wisdom? and it must be said that it is such as its innate concrete relatives are, being habituated by it and designated by the second species of Rule C.

¶ Furthermore, through the second species, it is asked: what kind of thing is wisdom? it must be said that it is such as can habituate its concrete relatives: namely, well, magnificently, etc., as is manifest through Rule B, and also through the third species of Rule C, and the fourth species of Rule K.

¶ Through all species of Rule H <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando).</note>, it is asked: when is wisdom? and it must be said...

And through the rules C, D, and K, this is probable. ¶ Through all species of Rule I <note>Rule I in Llull's system asks "Where?" (Ubi).</note>, it is asked: where is wisdom? It must be said that it exists with its own correlative foundations, so that they may be habituated by it. And it exists with the act of goodness, because it is good. And it exists with the act of virtue, for it is virtuous. And it exists with the act of glory, for it is indeed delightful.

## On the Will, deduced through the rules.

<margin>On the Will, deduced through the rules.</margin>

<insert>**Q**</insert>ueritur <note>The large decorative 'Q' begins the Latin word *Quaeritur*, meaning "It is asked."</note>—it is asked: whether the will is immortal? And it must be answered that it is so, regarding its essence: because it is not constituted of contrary, composed relatives, as is clear through the second species of Rules C, D, and E. Nevertheless, it is "mortal" when it is habituated in sin, because it has deviated from the second species of Rule E; and Rule B testifies to this. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C, it is asked: what is the will? And it must be answered that it is a being to which it belongs to will and not to will <note>original: "velle z nolle"</note>; so that through the second species of Rule E, it could be at rest. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does the will have in itself naturally? And it must be answered that it has the **lover**, the **beloved**, and the **loving** <note>original: "amantem/amatu z amare"</note> constituted from its own relation; and this is so substantially. With these, it habituates itself with a good habit or a bad one, and with a great habit or a small one, and this is so morally. And this has been proven through Rule B.

Through the third species, it is asked: what is the will in another? And it must be answered that it is in the subject in which there is a power habituated with virtues or with vices through its own willing or unwilling. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does it have in another? To which it must be answered that it has actions and passions by making things its object. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "From what?" (De quo).</note>, it is asked: from what is the will? And it must be answered that it belongs to man, since he himself moves it freely to its act: namely, to willing or unwilling. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare).</note>, it is asked: why does the will exist? And it must be answered: because it is constituted of its natural correlatives. Morally, however, it exists because in the subject in which it is, it is habituated by its own habit—just as a "cloaked man" is habituated by his "cloak." ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why is there a will? It must be answered: so that beings may be lovable or loved; for without the will itself, they could not be delighted in, as far as the "category of the will" is concerned. And this has been proven through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks "Of what kind?" (Quale).</note>, it is asked: what kind is the will properly? And it must be answered that it is a proper substantial "passion" <note>Here, "passion" refers to a property or a way of being affected, not necessarily an emotion.</note> in the subject in which it exists: just like a man, who cannot exist without his will. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what kind is the will by appropriation? And it must be answered that it is good through a good habit, or evil through an evil habit, with which the will clothes itself to will well or poorly. And this is clear through Rule B. ¶ Through all species of Rule H <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando).</note>, it is asked...
