### Eighth Part

When does the **will** exist? And it must be answered that it exists then both subjectively and objectively, since it is led through all the <term>species</term> <note>In Llull's system, "species" refers to the specific sub-questions or categories within a general logical rule.</note> of rules C, D, and K. However, this does not need to be explained further; for it is clear enough to an intellect that is well-observing and practiced in this art. And this is proven through rules B, E, F, and G. ¶ Through all the species of Rule I <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi).</note>, it is asked: where is the will? And it must be answered through all the species of that rule that it is in the subject, in which it exists both subjectively and objectively. And this is clear enough to one who looks closely at rules E, F, G, and H. ¶ Through all the species of the rule of <term>modality</term> <note>The Rule of Modality asks "How?" (Quomodo).</note>, it is asked: how is the will subjective and objective? And it must be answered that it exists through that mode by which it has been discussed through all the other rules; and their species have been clearly seen. To recount this, however, would be very lengthy; therefore, we leave it to the practitioners of this art. ¶ Through all the species of <term>instrumentality</term> <note>The Rule of Instrumentality asks "With what?" (Cum quo).</note>, it is asked: with what does the will exist? And we leave this answer to the reader of this art, because the answer can be found through the chapter on wisdom in the final paragraph. ¶ But here it is asked: with what does the will <term>objectify</term> <note>To "objectify" (obiectat) here means the act of the will directing itself toward an object of desire or choice.</note> its object? And it must be answered: with its **freedom**, which is indeed an innate habit within it. Furthermore, it objectifies with its <term>relatives</term> <note>original: "relatiuis." In Llull’s philosophy, these are the internal components of a principle—for the Will, these are the Willer, the Willed, and the Act of Willing.</note>; because the "willer," joined with the sensory and imaginative powers, extracts and brings forth "foreign species" <note>Images or sensory data coming from the outside world rather than the internal soul.</note> from things that can be sensed and imagined. At its own pleasure, the will impresses these images upon itself; once impressed, things that are "will-able" are generated and arise through desire, and things that are "hateful" arise through anger. This occurs in the intrinsic act of willing, from which arises an "accidental" foreign willing or refusing. And in this step, it appears that **refusal** <note>original: "nolle." The act of "not-willing" or rejecting.</note> is not part of the essence of the will, because it is caused by irascibility. This irascibility is the opposite of "will-ability." And in this step, the understanding is very profound.

## On virtue deduced through the rules.

<margin>On virtue deduced through the rules.</margin>
**Q**ueritur <note>Latin for "It is asked," a standard opening for a scholastic argument.</note> whether **virtue** is a common habit of the principles, so that these principles may have virtuous acts? And it must be answered that, as is clear through the second species of Rule E, a principle could not be the subject of "rest" <note>In Llull's physics/metaphysics, "rest" (quies) is the fulfillment or perfection of a thing's purpose.</note> unless virtue were a common habit of the principles. And this is probable through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "What?" (Quid).</note>, it is asked: what is virtue?

And it must be answered that it is the <term>habit</term> <note>A "habit" (habitus) is a stable disposition or quality that allows a person or a power to act easily and well.</note> from which the principles hold virtuous dispositions; and this is signified through Rule B. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does virtue have in itself <term>coessentially</term>? <note>Existing together in the same essence.</note> And it must be answered that it has its own **correlatives** <note>The internal triad of any principle; for Virtue, these would be the "Virtuer," the "Virtued," and the "Act of Virtuing."</note> from which it is made and with which it is a fountain for causing virtuous acts. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is virtue in another? And it must be answered that it is a habit in a subject, so that the subject may have a virtuous act; just as "heat" is in a fire so that it may have the act of heating. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does virtue have in another? And it must be answered that it has its act in a subject that has been habituated with accidental virtue. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo).</note>, it is asked: of what is virtue made? It must be said that it is of itself; otherwise it would not be a general principle, which is impossible. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what is virtue made? It must be answered that **substantial virtue** is made from its own substantial correlatives, signified through the second species of Rule C. For otherwise it could not have a foundation for existing by itself, nor even a nature, which is impossible. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to what does virtue belong? And it must be answered that virtue existing as a habit belongs to the substantial virtue which is the substance. And this is proven through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare).</note>, it is asked: why does virtue exist? And it must be answered that it is because it is constituted from its substantial relatives. Moreover, **accidental virtue** is an accidental being, because it is caused through substantial virtue. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species, it is asked: why does virtue exist? It must be answered: so that other principles may be able to rest virtuously with that same end. And this is manifest through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quanta).</note>, it is asked: how great is virtue? And it must be answered that natural virtue is as great as its extension throughout the whole universe. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species, it is asked: how great is virtue? And it must be answered that it is as great as its correlatives existing in different ways in subjects that differ by species. And this is signified through Rule B, and also through the first species of Rule D and the second species of Rule C. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks "Of what sort?" (Qualis).</note>, it is asked: what sort of thing is virtue? And it must be answered that virtue is a <term>proper passion</term> <note>A "proper passion" is a characteristic that necessarily belongs to a specific subject (like the ability to laugh belongs to humans).</note> in a subject. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what sort of thing is virtue? And it must be answered that accidental virtue is an appropriated being with which the subject is habituated. Thus the just...

In this line, one virtue attracts species with another so that it may be a participant with the other. ## On truth deduced through the rules.

<margin>On truth deduced through the rules.</margin>

**Q**uery: whether created truth <term>converts</term> with its own truth? It must be answered that it does not; because if it were so, it would be too similar to the truth of God, which indeed converts with His unity. And furthermore, it would convert with goodness, magnitude, duration, etc., by reason of which it would extend itself outside of time and place, which is impossible. And this is clear through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "What?" (Quid).</note>, it is asked: what is truth? And it must be answered that it is an incorruptible being. For if it were corruptible, a contradiction would be implied: namely, that it would be and would not be, which contradiction is impossible. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does truth have in itself essentially and naturally? And it must be answered that it has its correlatives without which it cannot exist; in which it is, and with which all things are verifiable; and outside its essence, no being can be true: as was seen through the first species of D. ¶ Furthermore, through the third species, it is asked: what such thing does truth have? And it must be answered that it has the <term>habit</term> <note>In this context, a "habit" is a stable disposition or quality that enables the subject to perform its function—here, the function of making things true.</note> with which it verifies the subject in which it is. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo).</note>, it is asked: of what is truth? And it must be answered that it is of itself: so that falsehood, which is its contrary, may not lie before it, and so that it might be able to rest in its own essence: and this was seen through the second species of Rule C. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what things is it? And it must be answered that it is of its correlatives: otherwise there would be no foundation for its "habit" with which it passes to verify other principles. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to whom does truth existing as a habit belong? And it must be answered that it belongs to its substantial foundation in which it is sustained: and this is clear through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare).</note>, it is asked: why is truth? To which it must be answered: because it is from its substantial correlatives. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why is truth? And it must be answered: so that other principles may be verifiable through truth itself. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum).</note>, it is asked: how great is truth? And it must be answered that it is as great as the other principles which are verified through truth itself. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: how great is truth? To which it must be answered that it is so great only because it is habituated by its own proper habit with which it causes foreign acts. And this was made clear through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks "What kind?" (Quale).</note>, it is asked: what kind of thing is truth? And it must be answered that proper truth is the proper habit of the subject in which it is, with which it verifies other principles. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species, it is asked: what kind of thing is truth? And it must be answered that it is an appropriated habit with which the intellect truly understands and reaches the real principles themselves: which indeed are truly intelligible, recollectable, and lovable, and truly exist: and so it is for sensible and imaginable things: and so for moral things: and to this, Rule B bears witness. ¶ Through all the species of Rule H, it is asked: when is truth? And it must be answered that it is then, when time is sustained and runs through those species: the reason for which is: for without truth itself, time and its species could indeed in no way truly exist. ¶ Through all the species of Rule I, it is asked: where is truth? And it must be answered that it is outside of falsehood: and it exists through all the species of F itself.

In God, indeed, there is infinite and eternal truth through existing and acting; and this is made clear through Rule B <note>Rule B is the first of Llull's nine "Rules," used here to affirm the existence and necessity of a principle.</note>. ¶ Through all the species of modality <note>Rule K asks "How?" For it cannot exist with malice and vices, since they are privative habits <note>A "privative habit" is a philosophical term for the absence of a good that should be present, such as blindness being the "privation" of sight.</note> with which falsehood exists; and in that falsehood, no likeness of truth can exist: because if it were feigned, it would be composed of contraries and would imply a contradiction, which is impossible.

## On glory deduced through the rules.

<margin>Deduction of glory through the rules.</margin>
**T**hrough Rule B, it is asked: whether glory is a general and real principle? And it must be answered: yes; because if not, the universe would be emptied in the second species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare).</note> and all principles would be without delight and rest; which is impossible. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "What?" (Quid).</note>, it is asked: what is glory? And it must be answered: it is the essence beyond which no delight can exist. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what does glory have in itself co-essentially and naturally? And it must be answered that it has its correlatives, namely: the glorifier, the glorifiable, and the act of glorifying. With which and in which all things are glorifiable and delightful; and this was signified through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo).</note>. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: what is glory in another? To which it must be answered that glory existing as a habit is instrumental in substantial glory: with which substantial glory places other principles in the appetite for delight and rest. ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked: what does glory have in another? And it must be answered: it has, in the subject in which it exists, actions and passions, both in delighting and in resting. And in this step it appears in what way the "form" delights itself in acting, and the "matter" in suffering <note>In medieval philosophy, "passion" or "suffering" refers to the state of being the recipient of an action.</note>. And this is clear through the male and the female, and through the second species of Rule C. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D, it is asked: what is glory of? And it must be answered: it is of itself, so that it may be a primitive principle in which there are delightful things; otherwise appetite and delight would be outside the essence of glory, which is impossible. And this is made clear through Rule B. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: what is glory of? And it must be answered: it is of its correlatives; otherwise glory existing as a habit would not have that in which it was sustained. ¶ Further, through the third species it is asked: whose is glory? It must be answered: glory existing as a habit belongs to glory existing substantially. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E, it is asked: why is glory? It must be answered: glory is constituted of its relatives. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: why is glory? It must be answered: glory existing as a habit, together with substantial glory, places other principles in delight and rest. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum).</note>, it is asked: how great is glory? And it must be answered: it is as great <unclear>as it</unclear> is in its being, like an abstract thing in its concrete form. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: how great is glory? And it answers: it is as great as its correlatives and its habit, with which it multiplies "rested" species, just as the intellect with its habit places understood species. And in this step it appears how one principle helps itself with another to multiply species. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks "What kind?" (Quale).</note>, it is asked: what kind is glory properly? And it must be answered: properly, glory is the proper "passion" <note>Here, "passion" refers to a characteristic or property that naturally arises from an essence.</note> of the subject in which it is. <margin>Rule G</margin> ¶ And further, through the second species it is asked: what kind is glory? To which it must be said: appropriated glory is such as the principles are habited and rested by it. ¶ Through all the species of Rule H <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando).</note>, it is asked: when is glory? And it must be answered: it is then, when time has run through all the species of Rule H from one "now" into another successively: just as a glorifier who in one "now" delights in one species, and in another "now" in another: and this in his own intrinsic glorifiable, in multiplying a "foreign" act of glorifying <note>Llull uses "peregrinum" (foreign/extrinsic) to refer to actions or properties that relate to things outside the essence.</note>, with which

[The Art] places its innate "glorifying" <note>original: "gloriari"; here used as the active function of the principle of Glory.</note> in practice; and this is present through all habitable species. ¶ Through all the species of the rule, it is asked: **where is glory?** To which it must be responded: it is in its correlatives <note>In Llull’s system, "correlatives" are the three components of any principle: the active (e.g., the glorifier), the passive (the glorified), and the act itself (glorifying).</note> and in its own primitive self. ### On Difference deduced through the rules.

<margin>On Difference deduced through the rules.</margin>

**W**hether Difference <note>Difference is one of the "Absolute Principles" in Llull's Art, allowing for variety and distinction in the world.</note> is a general, real principle? And we say that it is: as is evident through Rule B. Because if it were not, the world would not naturally consist of its parts, which are naturally primitive through **Difference**, and concordant through **Concordance**, and opposing through primitive **Contrariety**. These could not exist without primitive Difference, without which the world would be emptied of primitive concordances and contrarieties; and this is also seen in the second species of Rule E, and in natural desire and rest; for [without difference] all things would want to be numerically the same. Therefore, it is concluded that the affirmative side of the question must be held. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C, it is asked: **what is Difference?** It must be responded: it is the cause of multiple beings through its act, namely, "to differ." And this is proven through Rule B and through the "ladder of difference" placed in the Second Figure or in the third "chamber" <note>term: chamber (camera) — a cell or compartment in Llull’s combinatory diagrams where two or more principles meet.</note> from B-C even unto chamber B-K, in which Difference is discussed and diffused, causing plurality. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **what does it have in itself naturally and essentially?** And it must be responded: it has its correlatives, namely: the **Differentiator**, the **Differentiated**, and **to Differ** <note>original: "differens, differentiatum, et differentiare."</note>, without which it cannot exist. With these, it contains within itself all its species that differ among themselves. ¶ Further, through the third species, it is asked: **what does Difference have in another?** And it must be said: it is a being having "foreign" differences <note>A "foreign" or "accidental" difference is one that comes from outside a thing's core essence.</note> within its essential "differentiable" part, with which it causes plurality from that habituated difference. ¶ Further, through the fourth species, it is asked: **what does Difference have in another?** And it must be said: it has plurality thus habituated from itself, just as coals are habituated by heat; and this is demonstrated through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D, it is asked: **from what is Difference primitively?** And it is to be responded: it is from itself. Because if not, all things would desire to be one and the same in number, which is impossible. For I do not desire to be you, nor a stone, etc., nor vice versa. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species, it is asked: **from what things is Difference [made]?** And it is to be responded: it is from the Differentiator, the Differentiated, and the act of Differing. These are indeed consubstantial to it, with which it makes all things differ according to its own habit. Without this, things would not be self-existing, nor would they have a foundation, nor could substance and accident differ. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **whose is Difference?** And we say that Difference, existing as a habit, belongs to "substantial difference"; and all these things are provable through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E, it is asked: **why is Difference [there] formally?** And it must be responded: because it is from its own co-essential relative parts. ¶ Further, through the second species, it is asked: **why is Difference [there] finally [in terms of purpose]?** And it is to be responded: so that there may be multiple things, which cannot exist without it. If the aforementioned Difference were removed from the world, the world itself would be emptied and annulled, because it would neither be, nor would it possess anything. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F, it is asked: **how great is Difference?** And it must be said: there are two most general differences: one is **substantial**, causing substantial differences that differ substantially because Difference diffuses itself in them by reason of "mixture." ¶ There is also another **habitual** difference, with which substantial difference makes the principles differ from one another. ¶ Further, through the second species: **how great is Difference?** To which it must be said: it is as great as "Quantity" extends itself in its correlatives. For just as Difference habituates Quantity by containing it within its genus, so Quantity measures Difference by containing it within its genus. And this can be seen through Rule B...

Through the first species of Rule G <note>original: "regule g."; Rule G asks "Of what kind?" (Qualitas).</note> it is asked: **what kind of thing is difference?** The answer is that difference is a proper part of the world, without which the world cannot exist. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: **what kind is difference by appropriation?** And we say that it is an "appropriated passion" <note>term: passion (passio) — in medieval logic, a property or attribute that naturally belongs to a subject.</note> of the world, with which substantial difference "habituates" <note>term: habituates (habituando) — the process by which a principle "clothes" or imparts its character to another.</note> other principles that are not of its own kind. And this is made manifest through Rule B. ¶ Through all the species of Rule H <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando).</note> it is asked: **when is difference?** And it must be said that difference existed then, when the world was created and begun, because it is a primitive principle. Just as the world was created with its parts—namely time, place, motion, and so on—so was it created with its own difference, as has already been said. ¶ Furthermore, difference is now, and it will be in another "now" in eternity, without which it cannot exist. ¶ And let this suffice regarding difference in relation to time, which is evident through Rule B and through all species of Rule H. ¶ Through all the species of Rule I <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi).</note> it is asked: **where is difference?** And it must be said that it is in all these species, and this is clear in itself. ¶ Furthermore, difference is in "place," because place differs from quantity, time, and so on. And difference is in place because without it, difference could not be a proper "passion" of the world. ¶ Through the rule of modality <note>Rule K, which asks "How?" (Quomodo).</note> it is asked: **how is difference?** And it must be responded that it exists through that "mode" <note>term: mode (modus) — the specific way or manner in which a principle operates.</note> which it has in its correlatives <note>The "correlatives" are the three internal components of any principle: the active agent, the passive object, and the act itself (e.g., the differer, the differed-upon, and the act of differing).</note> and also through that mode which it has in habituating other principles with itself. For just as a man has a mode of writing by moving the hand, and with the hand moving the pen, and with the pen moving the ink, and with the movement of the ink moving and shaping the letters; so difference has its mode through its "modality," by differentiating one thing from another substantially. And this is demonstrable through all species of the rules. ¶ Through the rule of instrumentality <note>Rule K also asks "With what?" (Cum quo).</note> it is asked: **with what is difference?** And it must be responded that it is with its relatives, with its habit with which it habituates other principles by diversifying them; and also with goodness, greatness, and so on; and with motion, quantity, quality, and so on. Without these principles, difference cannot exist, and through difference itself, these principles are what they are. For if difference were taken away, the principles would certainly not be what they are.

A deduction of Concordance through the rules.

### On concordance deduced through the rules.

**P**er Rule B <note>Rule B is the rule of affirmation and definition.</note> it is asked: **is concordance substantial?** And it must be answered that it is; so that substance can be a whole composed of its substantial parts, with the substance existing as "one" under the reason of unity, and existing as "multiple" under the reason of plurality—and this is by reason of substantial concordance. For if concordance were not substantial (or a substance), then the entire essence of "form" and the entire essence of "matter" would not be concording to constitute a third substantial thing. And thus that third substantial thing would be the emptying out of all mixing and composition, which is impossible. It is concluded, therefore, that concordance is a substantial part in the subject in which it exists; and this is evident through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "What?" (Quid).</note> it is asked: **what is concordance?** And it must be answered that it is 그 essence to which "to concord" <note>original: "concordare"; the act of bringing into agreement or harmony.</note> properly belongs, and outside of which essence there is no being that concords or is "concordable." ¶ Furthermore, through the second species it is asked: **what does it have essentially and naturally in itself?** And it must be said that it has its correlatives: namely, the concorder, the concorded, and the act of concording. ¶ Furthermore, through the third species it is asked: **what is it in another?** And it must be answered that it is "concording" even in contrariety—just as fire in water is heating, even though it is its contrary. And it is in distinct difference; and it is simply sustained in its correlatives; and also in property; and in Rule D materially, and in Rule E formally. And in Rule F quantitatively, and in Rule G qualitatively, and in Rule H temporally, and in Rule I locally, and in Rule K modally and instrumentally. ¶ And through the fourth species it is asked: **what does it have in another?** It must be answered that it has existence, agency, and nature in its correlatives; and in Rule D materially, and so on for the others in their own way, as was said above in the third species. And this is demonstrable through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo).</note> it is asked: **from what is concordance?** And it must be answered that it is from itself, because it is primitive. Otherwise it would be from some being underlying it that was not of its own kind and nature, which is impossible. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: **from what things is concordance?** And it must be said that it is from its correlatives, so that it can exist substantially from them. ¶ And through the third species it is asked: **whose is concordance?** And it must be answered that existing concordance is the "habit" of substantial concordance, just as a cloak belongs to the one cloaked, and so on. And this is demonstrable through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare).</note> it is asked: **why is concordance formal?** And it must be said: because of its correlatives. In this step it is explained that "substance" is why things are "substantial." Likewise it is asked: **why is there concordance?** And it must be said that concordance, which is a habit, exists because substantial concordance habituates itself with that very habit, just as the cloaked person is habituated by the cloak. In this step, the intellect knows "because of what it is," "that it is," and "why it is"; and from these it produces knowledge. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: con-

...concordance, **why is it as an end?** <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare). In medieval thought, the "end" or "final cause" is the purpose for which a thing exists.</note> And it must be answered: so that other principles might be able to find rest within that concordance itself; and this has been shown through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum).</note> it is asked: **how great is concordance?** And it must be said that it is great in two ways. In the first way, it is as great as its own substance. In the second way, it is as great as its own "habit" <note>term: habit (habitus) — a condition or "clothing" of a substance; here, how a principle manifests in a subject.</note>: just as a cloaked man <note>original: "cappatus"</note> is as great as his own substance is, and yet he is also as great as the "cloaked-ness" itself is.

¶ Furthermore, through the second species <note>of Rule F, concerning discrete quantity.</note> it is asked: **how great is it discretely?** And it must be answered: it is as great as its own correlatives <note>term: correlatives (correlativa) — in Lullian logic, the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle (e.g., concordant, concordable, and to concord).</note> are, and this is made manifest through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks "Of what kind?" (Qualitas).</note> it is asked: **what kind of thing is concordance?** And it must be said: it is such as is the proper "passion" <note>term: passion (passio) — a property or attribute that naturally belongs to a subject.</note> of the subject in which it exists. And in this step, the intellect recognizes a great and necessary bond existing between the subject and the predicate. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: **what kind is it by appropriation?** And it must be said that it is such as it is through its own goodness, greatness, and so on. And this is clear and manifest in itself.

¶ Through all the species of Rule H <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando).</note> it is asked: **when is concordance?** And it must be answered: it is then, when it has pervaded all the species of Rule H, and thus concordance is in time itself; just as time is sustained and pervaded by concordance in the act of "concordating." And this is evident in itself to the practitioner of this Art who observes closely. ¶ Through all the species of Rule I <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi).</note> it is asked: **where is concordance?** And it must be answered: it is in all the species of Rule I; it is there where it can be defined, and it is in its correlatives; it is there where it contradicts contrariety, and it is there where it performs its act. Furthermore, it is there where it is primitive, and it is there where it is constituted. Moreover, it is there where it is subjective, modal, and instrumental.

¶ Through the Rule of Modality <note>The Rule of Modality asks "In what way?" (Quomodo).</note> it is asked: **in what mode is concordance?** And it must be said that it is through that mode by which it has pervaded the subjects in which it exists: namely, in all the species. Just as a crystal <note>original: "cristallus"</note> placed upon a green subject receives a green color from it, and upon a red subject a red color, so concordance placed in "Goodness" receives one mode, and in "Greatness" another mode, and so on. And the same can be said concerning the species of the rules; and this is plain in itself.

¶ Through the Rule of Instrumentality <note>The Rule of Instrumentality asks "With what?" (Cum quo).</note> it is asked: **with what is concordance?** And it must be answered: it is with its correlatives from which it is made, and it is with all the species of the rules; it is with good goodness, and with great greatness, and so on. And this is demonstrable. ¶ We have spoken of concordance; and according to what has been said of it, a man can use concordance to speak against contrariety, which is a vice; and this rule is very general and moral against sins.

## On contrariety deduced through the rules.

<margin>The deduction of contrariety through the rules.</margin>
**I**t is asked through Rule B <note>Rule B asks "Whether?" (Utrum).</note>: **Whether contrariety is a substantial principle?** And it must be answered that it is not; rather, it is an accidental one, as was said at the beginning of the chapter on concordance. For if it were substantial, it would hinder concordance, which would then not be the primary thing in the joining of form and matter of that substance; and in the second species of Rule E, no principle could be lacking, which is impossible, as is plain through the second species of Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "What?" (Quid).</note> it is asked: **what is contrariety?** To which it must be answered: it is that essence outside of which no being can be "contrary." ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **what does contrariety have in itself essentially?** And it must be answered that it has its own accidental correlatives: namely, the contrariating, the to-contrariate, and the contrariable <note>original: "contrariantē / cōtrariare et cōtrariabile"</note>, without which it cannot exist; just as a "habit" assists differently in its subjects. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: **what is contrariety in another?** And it must be said: it is the "contrariating" force within concordance, by hindering it from concordating with the "contrariating" force; just as concordance in youth is the "concordating" force by hindering the "contrariating" force of old age. <note>original: "s̄cietati" (senectuti)</note> ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked: **what does it have in another?** And it must be answered: it has the nature of corruption, just as concordance has the nature of generation. And this is evident through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo).</note> it is asked: **of what is contrariety?** And it must be said: it is of itself, because it is primitive; for unless it were primitive, it would indeed be derivative of a concordance lying before it, which is impossible. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **of what things is contrariety?** And it must be answered: it is of the opposition and collision of qualities, such as heat and cold, dryness and moisture, lightness and weight, brightness and darkness, health and sickness, death and life, justice and injury, affirmation and negation, generation and corruption, and the like. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: **whose is contrariety?** And it must be answered: it is the property of the subject in which it exists. And this is manifest through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare).</note> it is asked: **why is contrariety?** And it must be said: it is because the subject is "habituated" by it; just as heat exists because a subject is hot, and thus it is habituated by heat; and deafness exists because some man is deaf; and injury exists because someone is injurious, and the like. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F it is asked: **how great is contrariety?** And we say that it is as great as the subject habituated by it. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: **how great is contrariety?** And it must be said that it is as great as the subjects that are discretely habituated by it: such as fire and...

-> # Part Eight <-

...ignited and to ignite belong to the habituated thing <note>This continues the analogy of a "habit" or "clothing"—just as a cloaked man is "habituated" by his cloak, a subject is "ignited" by the quality of fire.</note> itself: and this is to be seen through Rule B <note>Rule B: The rule of definitions and truth.</note>. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks "Of what kind?" (Qualitas).</note> it is asked: **what kind of thing is contrariety?** And it must be answered that it is a "proper passion" <note>term: proper passion (propria passio) — an essential attribute or property that naturally belongs to a subject.</note> of the subject, such as the contrariety of the world which is innate to it. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **what kind of knowledge is it appropriately?** It must be said that it is an "appropriated passion" in the subject in which it exists: just as a sinner habituates himself in sin against virtue; and thus also deafness, sadness, and the like. And this is manifest through Rule B. ¶ Through all species of Rule H <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando).</note> it is asked: **when is contrariety?** And it must be said that it exists when the subject is habituated by it. Furthermore, it exists when its subject is practical in both mode and instrument. And this is evident in itself. ¶ Through all species of Rule I <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi).</note> it is asked: **where is contrariety?** And it must be said that it is in the species where it performs its act, such as in the generation and corruption of things made of elements <note>original: "elementatis" — physical things composed of the four elements.</note>. It is between willing and not-willing; it is between good and evil; and it is in all privative habits <note>A "privative habit" is a condition defined by the absence of something, like blindness being the absence of sight.</note>. And this is clear in itself. ¶ Through the Modal Rule <note>Rule: "How?" (Quomodo).</note> it is asked: **how is contrariety?** And it must be answered that contrariety has a mode of imposing one contrary upon another, so that it may expel "concordance" (agreement) from the subject in which it exists. It has a privative mode by depriving the ability to agree through the act of opposing, and it has a mode of hindering the final purpose. It also has a mode of multiplying by persevering, and so forth. And this is provable in itself. ¶ Through the Instrumental Rule <note>Rule: "With what?" (Cum quo).</note> it is asked: **with what is contrariety?** And it must be said that it is with mixed contrarieties in the subject in which they exist, and it is with privative habits. For just as concordance is the cause of "being" along with its substantial correlatives <note>term: correlatives (correlativa) — the internal structure of a Lullian principle: the doer, the thing done, and the act of doing.</note>, so contrariety is the cause of "non-being" along with its accidental correlatives. And just as concordance with generation produces being, so contrariety with the deviation of the end causes non-being and the like.

## On the Principle deduced through the rules.

<margin>Deduction of the principle through the rules.</margin>

**P**er Rule B <note>A large decorative initial 'P' marks the start of this section.</note> it is asked: **whether the Principle is substantial?** And it must be answered: yes. Because if it were not, substance would not belong to the category of "principle," but it would be a primitive accident; and thus substance would not exist through itself, but by accident, which is against the species of Rule D and E, and Rule B. Therefore, etc. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "What?" (Quid).</note> it is asked: **what is a principle?** And it must be said that it is a being outside of which no being can begin <note>original: "principiare" — to act as a principle or to originate.</note>. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **what does it have essentially within itself?** And it must be answered that it has its own substantial correlatives <note>The triad of the Originator, the Originatable, and the act of Originating.</note>, in which all foreign principles are "un-originatable." ¶ Furthermore, through the third species it is asked: **what is it in another?** And it must be answered: the principle which is the "agent" is acting within the "thing being originated," and the "thing being originated" is the patient within the "originator," and both are joined in the act of originating. And the principle which is a "habit" exists in the substantial principle that is habituated by it, and in the "thing being originated" there is motion. ¶ Likewise, through the fourth species it is asked: **what does it have in another?** And it must be answered: a principle existing formally has its action in matter, and matter receives "passion" (the effect) from it; it has mobility from the agent, and in the end, it has rest. And this is manifest through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo).</note> it is asked: **of what is the principle made?** And it must be said that it is of itself, so that it can be "primitive" <note>That is, the first or most basic thing.</note>; otherwise it would not be a general principle. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **of what things is it composed?** And it must be said that it is of efficient cause, form, matter, and end. An accidental human principle consists of a substantial likeness, and together they compose a corporal principle through quantity (how much), quality (what kind), and so on. ¶ Furthermore, through the third species it is asked: **to whom does it belong?** It must be answered that a principle existing as a "habit" belongs to a principle existing "substantially," just as a cloak belongs to the cloaked man. And all these things are necessary, as is to be seen through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare).</note> it is asked: **why is there a principle?** And it must be said: in two ways. In the first way, it is because it is established from the "originator," the "thing being originated," and the "act of originating." In the second way, there is an accidental principle because the substantial principle is habituated by it. And in this step, the intellect creates "science" (knowledge); for it also recognizes demonstrations of the "reason why" <note>original: "propter quid" — a logical term for a demonstration that explains the cause of a fact, not just the fact itself.</note> and that which they join together. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species it is asked: **why is it so finally (at its end)?** And it must be said: so that other principles may be subordinated under it, which is the most general. And this is plain in itself. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum).</note> it is asked: **how great is a principle?** And it must be answered that it is as great as its essence, as is manifest through the middle of its extremities. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species it is asked: **how great is it discretely?** And it must be answered that it is as great as its correlatives are: through "difference," it is different; and through "concordance," it is concordant. Yet they are the same in essence. And this is proven through Rule B. And we have experience of this in man, in whom the "elemental" <note>The physical/chemical nature.</note> is one principle, the "vegetative" <note>The biological/growth nature.</note> another, the "sensitive" <note>The animal/sensory nature.</note> another, the "imaginative" another, and the "rational" another. Yet all five under the number five are one man. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks "Of what kind?" (Quale).</note> it is asked: **what kind of thing is a principle?** And it must be said that a "proper" principle is the most general kind which we investigate; however, an "appropriated" principle is a foreign principle that is acquired and subordinated, as... <note>The text cuts off here, to be continued on the next page with the word "figuratum."</note>

It follows the previous discussion on "Contrariety" and transitions into how the "Middle" connects the "Beginning" (Principle) and the "End."</meta>

-> # On the Mixing of Principles and Rules <-

Through all species of **Rule H** <note>Rule H asks "When?" (the category of Time).</note> it is asked: **when is the principle?** And it must be answered that it exists when its <term>correlatives</term> <note>Lullian technical term: the internal structure of a thing consisting of an agent (e.g., Bonifier), a patient (Bonifiable), and the act itself (Bonifying).</note> exist, with which it is most general. It existed when the <term>subaltern</term> <note>Intermediate or subordinate principles that fall under a more general category.</note> principles existed, such as the categories <note>original: "praedicamenta"</note> of Quantity, Quality, etc. It also exists when there is a "course" under which moving things, mobile things, and the act of moving are habituated <note>or "clothed/disposed."</note>; and these are passing from one "now" into another successively through one place, and from one "now" to another "now" through another place, generating a motion converted with that course. This is clear through all species of Rule H. 

¶ Through all species of **Rule I** <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (the category of Place).</note> it is asked: **where is the principle?** And it must be answered that it is in its correlatives, because it exists within them. It is also in all subaltern principles, just as a cause is in its effect. It is in motion because it is habituated by it; and it is in "site" or position when it is situated within it. This is both modal and instrumental, and is provable through Rule B <note>Rule B: The rule of definitions used to prove truths.</note>. 

¶ Through the **Rule of Modality** <note>Asking "How?" (Quomodo).</note> it is asked: **how is the principle?** It must be answered that it is a causal principle by way of the correlatives from which it is composed. The "habitual" principle exists in the manner that a causal principle has in habituating other "foreign" <note>original: "peregrina"—principles that are not intrinsic to the subject but are added to it.</note> principles with its own habit, so that they may become principles by multiplying their likenesses within them; and this is through itself. 

¶ Through all species of the **Rule of Instrumentality** <note>Asking "With what?" (Cum quo).</note> it is asked: **with what is the principle?** It must be answered that it is with its correlatives from which it is made. It is with its own nature, without which it cannot exist. General principles are with the most general substantial principle in which they are situated, as is manifest through the second species of Rule C.

---

¶ Through the **second species** <note>Referring to species of Rule C (What?).</note> it is asked: **what does the Middle have within itself essentially?** It must be said that it has its correlatives: namely, to join together, and to apply and continue one extremity with another extremity; as is shown in the "angle" in the Second Figure <note>A reference to Lull’s diagram of the "Middle," which connects the "Beginning" and the "End" like the vertex of a triangle.</note>. 

¶ Through the **third species** it is asked: **what is the Middle in another?** It must be answered that it is the "pointing" <note>original: "punctio"—the act of connecting or puncturing into.</note> in form and matter, such as "to ignite" in wood; it is "to heat" in heat, and "to vegetate" in a plant, and "to sense" in the sense-faculty, and "to imagine" in the imaginative faculty, and "to reason" in the reasoning faculty, and "to move" in motion, and "to generate" in generation, and the like. 

¶ Through the **fourth species** it is asked: **what does it have in another?** It must be answered that it has the "habit" from which it is habituated, and with which it causes secondary acts that are not of its own genus; all these things are manifest through Rule C. 

¶ Through the **first species of Rule D** <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo) regarding origin.</note> it is asked: **from what is the Middle primarily?** It must be answered: from itself, so that it may be a general principle in its own right. 

¶ Through the **second species** it is asked: **from what things is it composed?** It must be answered: from the essence of form and matter in which it exists, and from motion and the like. 

¶ Further, through the **third species** it is asked: **to what does the Middle belong?** It must be answered: to the whole subject in which it exists; this is evident in itself and is proven by Rule B. 

¶ Through the **first species of Rule E** <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare).</note> it is asked: **why is the Middle so formally?** To which we say: because it is constituted of its correlatives, as is manifest through the second species of Rule C. 

¶ Again, through the **second species** it is asked: **why is the Middle so finally?** <note>Regarding the "final cause" or purpose.</note> And we say: so that subjects may be full and continuous, and so that the categories <note>original: "predicamenta"</note> may have their secondary acts, just as substance "substantiates," quantity "quantifies," and thus the agent acts, and the mover moves; and so with the others in their own way, just as a liner "lines," etc. Without these acts, the powers <note>original: "potentie"—potentialities or faculties.</note> could not exist in reality; this is clear in itself and through Rule B. 

¶ Through the **first species of Rule F** <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum).</note> it is asked: **how great is the Middle?** It must be said that it is as great as the "continuing" power is in the subject in which it exists: such as the "joining" in a junction, the "generating" in generation, the "running" in a race, and the "composing" in a composition. In the third mode, it is like **Man**, who is the "third middle" constituted of soul and body, and such like. 

¶ Through the **second species** it is asked: **how much is the Middle?** And it must be answered that it is as much as each part of the whole middle is; such as in an "elemented" thing <note>A physical object made of the four elements.</note>, the acts of "igniting," "air-ifying," "aquifying," and "earthing," from which one common elemental act is made; and so of others in their own way. This is clear. 

¶ Through the **first species of Rule G** <note>Rule G asks "What kind?" (Quale).</note> it is asked: **what kind of thing is the Middle?** It must be answered that it is of such a kind as is the "proper passion" <note>An essential characteristic that always follows the nature of a thing.</note> of the subject in which it is; such as "igniting" in fire, and "running" in a race, and the like.

## On the Middle derived through the rules.

<margin>On the Middle derived through the rules.</margin>
**Is there a single most general Middle in the substance of the world?** And it must be answered that there is; otherwise, there would be no subaltern middles, and thus the world would be emptied of any middle that continues, measures, or joins. Existence would have no "concordance," nor would the "Principle" (Beginning) have a subject through which it could pass to the "End" where it would come to rest; and thus there would be no motion, and many other inconveniences would follow, which is impossible, as is evident through Rule B. 

¶ Through the **first species of Rule C** <note>Rule C asks "What?" (Quid).</note> it is asked: **what is the Middle?** And it must be said that it is the subject in which the Beginning and the End meet one another and join themselves together, so that the Beginning may be able to rest in the End. The most general Middle is the cause of all corporal <note>Physical or bodily.</note> middles.

Eighth part

Furthermore, regarding the second species <note>The "species" of a Rule refer to specific sub-questions or applications of that rule in Llull's logic.</note>, it is asked: **what sort of thing is the middle?** And it must be answered that it is like a nail joining two posts at an appropriate middle point; and similarly, like heating in hot water, and such things; and this is self-evident. ¶ Through all species of **Rule H** <note>Rule H asks "When?"</note>, it is asked: **when is the middle?** And it must be answered that it exists when its subjects exist—such as joining, measuring, continuing, moderating, and craftsmanship; and this has been seen through Rule B. ¶ Through all species of **Rule I** <note>Rule I asks "Where?"</note>, it is asked: **where is the middle?** And it must be answered that it is in all subjects in which it exists: such as the "humanity" which is in the soul and body; as the "igniting" in fire; as "moving" in motion; as "modality" in a mode; and "instrumentality" in an instrument; and such things. This is indeed manifest to anyone well-observing this Art. ¶ Through the **Rule of Modality** <note>This asks "In what way?" or "How?"</note>, it is asked: **how is the middle?** And it must be answered that it exists through the mode which the form has in acting, and the matter in being acted upon <note>original: "patiendo," referring to the passive capacity of matter.</note>; as fire in heating; as a plant in vegetating; as a sense in sensing; as the imagination in imagining; and the reasoning power in reasoning. And these modal "middles" are the parts with which an agent possesses a mode in a modal, intermediary, or moral way. And this is self-evident. ¶ Through all species of **Instrumentality**, it is asked: **with what is the middle?** And it must be answered that it is with its <term>correlatives</term> <note>Lullian technical term: the internal structure of a principle consisting of an active part, a passive part, and the act itself.</note>; and it is with the extremities in the middle of which it exists; as "generating" exists with the "generator" and the "generatable." And "bonifying" <note>The act of making good.</note> with the "bonifier" and the "bonifiable," and such things. And "running" with the "runner" and the "runnable" <note>the path or capacity for running</note>. And this is clear through itself and through Rule B.

-> ## On the end deduced through the rules. <-

<margin>
On the end

**Q**UERIŤ <note>The large decorative initial 'Q' features a seated figure, likely a scholar or the author himself, signifying the start of a major new section.</note> It is asked through **Rule B** <note>Rule B asks "Whether a thing is?"</note> **whether there is an ultimate end?** And it must be answered that there is; otherwise, the "middle" would be determined by the part of the beginning, but not by the part of the end. And thus, there would be motion and process from the rear part toward infinity, and the beginning would never reach an end and rest; which is impossible, and contrary to the first species of Rule D and the second of Rule E. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule C** <note>Rule C asks "What is it?"</note>, it is asked: **what is the end?** And it must be answered that it is the principle outside of which there is no rest <note>original: "quies." In Llull’s physics, all things move toward an "end" to find their natural state of repose.</note>. ¶ Further, through the second species, it is asked: **what does it have essentially in itself?** And it must be answered that it has its correlatives: namely, the "quieter" <note>that which brings rest</note>, the "quieted" <note>that which receives rest</note>, and the "quieting" <note>the act of resting</note>, in which all other principles find their rest. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **what is the end in another?** And it must be answered that it is "good" in goodness, "great" in magnitude, "different" in difference from all other principles; and "concordant" in concordance with all other principles, with the exception of contrariety. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: **what does it have in another?** And it must be answered that it has "the good" in the <term>habits</term> <note>Habitus: a disposition or "clothing" of the soul or a substance.</note> of goodness, and also the "situating" of other principles; and in difference, it has an act differing from all acts of other principles; and this is self-evident through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule D** <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (origin or material).</note>, it is asked: **of what is the end?** And it must be answered that it is of itself: because if not, the beginning would not have a place in which it could rest; and its nature would be emptied of motion and appetite <note>The natural desire of a thing to reach its goal.</note>, which is impossible. ¶ Further, through the second species, it is asked: **of what is the end?** And it must be said that it is of its correlatives, as was said in the second species of Rule C. ¶ Furthermore, through the third species, it is asked: **whose is the end?** And it must be answered that the "created end" belongs to the "uncreated end" <note>i.e., the finite purpose of a creature points toward God, the ultimate end.</note>; and it also belongs to the subject in which it is, so that from it, the subject becomes "habituated": just as a man in a cloak <note>original: "cappatus"</note> is habituated by the cloak; and Rule B manifests and declares this. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule E** <note>Rule E asks "Why?"</note>, it is asked: **why is the end?** And it must be answered that it is because it is constituted from its correlatives. And this answer is according to the "wherefore" <note>original: "propter quid," a formal logical demonstration of the cause.</note>. But according to the "because" <note>original: "quia," a demonstration from the effect.</note>, it must be said that it is because its subject is habituated by it, just as the cloaked man is habituated by the cloak. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that a "demonstration of the wherefore" is more powerful than a "demonstration of the because." ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **why is the end?** And it must be answered: so that all other principles may be able to rest in the end itself. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule F** <note>Rule F asks "How much?"</note>, it is asked: **how great is the end?** And it must be answered that it is as great as its subject is habituated by it. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species, it is asked: **how great is the end?** And it must be answered that it is as great as its correlatives are regarding their "habituated quantity"; we say this, however, regarding the *created* end, but not the *uncreated* <note>God</note>, since the latter is infinite, by reason of which its correlatives cannot have a finite quantity. ¶ Furthermore, there is an "end of privation" from which all privative habits arise—such as deafness, malice, and injury, and such things. ¶ Likewise, there is another "end of termination" <note>The physical or logical boundary of a thing.</note> by which the ultimate end is different from all other principles: such as from goodness, magnitude, or being created; and thus of other principles in its own way. Otherwise, all principles would be numerically the same, and the world would be emptied of the "end of termination," and consequently of the nature of motion and appetite, which is impossible. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule G** <note>Rule G asks "What kind?"</note>, it is asked: **what kind of thing is the end?** And it must be answered that it is such as it can be through the proper <term>passion</term> <note>In logic, a "passion" is a characteristic property that flows from the essence of a thing.</note> of the subject. Such as the "will," which is of such a kind as it can be through "lovability," which is the proper passion of the will itself; and of possibility, power, and such things. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **what kind of thing is the end appropriately?** And...

And it is through the mode of concordance, which accords the end with all other principles, except however for contrariety. Again, it is through the mode of the middle, because it mediates the end itself through all other principles; and it is through the mode of appetite <note>In medieval philosophy, "appetite" (appetitus) refers to a natural inclination or desire for a goal.</note> which desires to rest in the end itself; and so of the others in their own way. ¶ Through all species of instrumentality, <note>The Rule of Instrumentality asks "With what?" And with appetite, it is desirable, and so forth.

## On majority deduced through the rules.

<margin>On majority deduced through the rules.</margin>

**I**t is asked whether majority is a primitive principle in regard to its own kind? And it must be answered that it is so, through the first species of Rule B; because if it were not, it would exist by accident <note>original: "per accidens" — an incidental property rather than an essential one.</note> and not by itself; and thus a substance existing as primitive and greater than an accident would not be existing by itself, but by accident, which is impossible. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C, <note>Rule C asks "What?" (Quid).</note> it is asked: **what is majority?** And it must be answered that it is a being existing by itself, outside of which it is impossible "to majorify." <note>original: "maiorificare" — Llull’s technical term for the act of making something greater or excelling.</note> ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **what does majority have in itself essentially and naturally?** And it must be answered that it has its correlatives from which it is composed. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **what is it in another?** And it must be answered that it is a "habit" under which subordinate majorities are situated. Such as the majority of substantial and accidental goodness. ¶ Again, it is a being distinct from all other principles in the subject in which it is; without which distinction all principles would be the same in number and outside of equality, minority, and relation; which is impossible, since the world cannot be emptied of the aforementioned things. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: **what does majority have in another?** and it must be answered that it has its act, namely "to majorify," with which it is seen to generate, grow, move, and the like. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D, <note>Rule D asks "From what?" (De quo), "Of what?" (Quid), and "Whose?" (Cuius).</note> it is asked: **from what is majority?** And it must be answered that it is from itself; because if not, it would either be from equality or minority, which belongs to the genus of relation. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **of what is it?** It must be answered that it is of its correlatives: namely, of the majorifier, the majorifiable, and the act of majorifying, in which its essence is sustained and founded. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **whose is it?** It must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it is, because the subject is "habituated" <note>Possessing a certain quality or habit.</note> by it. And all these things are clear and manifest. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E, <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare).</note> it is asked: **why is majority?** And it must be said that it is because in it are its concrete relatives naturally and essentially. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species, it is asked: **why is majority?** And it must be answered: so that other principles may be subordinated to its genus and be "indented" <note>original: "dentata" — likely meaning "fitted" or "interlocked" like the teeth of a gear.</note> with it. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F, <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum).</note> it is asked: **how great is majority?** And it must be said that it is as great as the containment in the subject in which it is. ¶ Further, through the second species, it is asked: **how great is it?** and it must be said that it is as great as the subordinate majorities subsisting in it; and this is signifiable through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G, <note>Rule G asks "What kind?" (Quale).</note> it is asked: **what kind is majority?** It must be answered that it is such as it can be through its own passion existing in the subject in which it is. ¶ Again, through the second species of the same rule, it is asked: **what kind is it?** and it must be said that it is such as it can be through an appropriated existence in the subject in which it is; just as one man is greater in quantity, and more intensely white through whiteness, and more just through justice than another man. ¶ Through all species of Rule H, it is asked: **when is majority?** and it must be answered that it is then when it is; and it is real in all its species of its rules in which it is situated; and this is evident to one looking closely. ¶ Through all species of Rule I...

# Eighth Part.

It is asked **where superiority is**: And it must be said that it is in a greater subject, <term>habit</term>, <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "habit" (habitus) is a stable disposition or quality, such as a skill or a virtue.</note> place, and the like; and this is clear through all the species of Rule I. <note>Rule I in Llull's system asks "Where?" (Ubi).</note> ¶ Through the rule of modality, <note>Asking "How?" (Quomodo).</note> it is asked **how superiority is**: And it must be answered that it is by way of the <term>difference</term> <note>Difference is one of Llull's principles used to distinguish between things.</note> that causes its <term>correlatives</term> <note>Llull’s "correlatives" are the three components of any principle: the active doer, the passive receiver, and the action itself (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and loving).</note> to be greater by being different. ¶ Likewise, it is by way of <term>concordance</term> which causes them to be greater by being in accord. And it is by way of Rule G, by reason of greater appropriations and the like; yet these superiorities exist under "Superiority" as a <term>genus</term> <note>A "genus" is a general category that contains specific sub-types (species).</note> to those aforementioned superiorities; just as particular whiteness exists under universal whiteness, and this is self-evident. ¶ Through all the species of instrumentality, it is asked **with what superiority is**: And it must be said that it is with its correlatives and with its greater habit with which subalternate superiorities are habited; or rather, the greater acts in which they shine back, or their likenesses.

## On equality deduced through the rules.

It is asked **whether there is a certain equality that is a most general principle**: And it must be answered that there is: as is evident through the subalternate and individuated equalities of plants, which are of the same species; and likewise it is manifest in fruits which are equally individuated: and this has been seen through Rule B. <note>Rule B asks "Whether?" (Utrum).</note> ¶ Through the first species of Rule C, <note>Rule C asks "What?" (Quid).</note> it is asked **what equality is**: And it must be said that it is a being to which "co-equaling" properly belongs. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked **what it has in itself essentially**: And it must be answered that it has its innate correlatives from which it is constituted: namely, from the co-equalizer, the co-equalized, and co-equaling. ¶ Again, through the third species it is asked **what it is in another**: and it must be said that it is active and passive: because it is equally constituted from <term>form and matter</term>. <note>The two basic components of all physical things in Aristotelian thought: "form" gives the essence, and "matter" provides the physical substance.</note> ¶ Likewise, through the fourth species, it is asked **what it has in another**: and it must be said that it has its habits with which individuals are equally habited: just as in an orchard the apples are equally of the same species: and so it is of the elemental, sensible, imaginable, rational, and mechanical things, of the liberal arts, and also of morals. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D, <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo).</note> it is asked **of what equality is**: And it must be answered that it is of itself: otherwise subalternate equalities would not have a genus without which they cannot exist. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked **of what things equality is**: and it must be said that it is of its essential correlatives, without which it can least of all be what it is: and if they were lacking, <term>accidental</term> <note>original: "peregrine" — literally "foreign" or "wandering," used in logic for qualities that are not essential to a thing's nature.</note> equalities would fail. ¶ Again, through the third species it is asked **whose equality is**: and it must be said that the equality of acts belongs to the equality of powers: just as the equality of understanding, remembering, and willing belongs to the equality of the intellect, memory, and will: and so too with sensible things. And this is self-evident. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E, <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare).</note> it is asked **why equality is**: And it must be answered that it is because it exists from its equal, substantial, true, and necessary relatives with which a demonstration "because of which" <note>original: "propter quid" — a logical proof that explains the cause of a thing's existence, not just that it exists.</note> is made: and also a demonstration through <term>equivalence</term>. ¶ Again, through the second species it is asked **why equality is**: and it must be answered that it is in the soul: so that God may be equally understood, remembered, and loved by it: and in sensible things it exists so that objects may be equally sensible and the like. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F, <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum).</note> it is asked **how great equality is**: And it must be said that continuous equality is as great as that which is sustained in its subjects. ¶ Again, through the second species it is asked **how great it is**: And it must be answered that it is as great as it is in its correlatives and in an unequal, accidental number: and this is clear in itself. ¶ <margin>g</margin> Through the first species of Rule G, <note>Rule G asks "Of what sort?" (Qualis).</note> it is asked **of what sort equality is properly**: and it must be said that it is such as it can be through the "proper passion" <note>A "passion" here means an attribute or property that naturally follows from a thing's essence.</note> of the subject in which it is. Just as the equality of substance, of form, and of matter. And just as there are innate equalities of sensual beings, etc. ¶ Likewise, through the second species it is asked **of what sort it is appropriately**: and it must be said that it is such as it can be through the appropriate passions of accidental subjects in which it is: such as two logicians in logic, and two judges in justice, and two cloaked men in cloaks: and the like. ¶ Through all species of Rule H, <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando).</note> it is asked **when equality is**: and it must be answered that it is then when it is truly in the species of Rule H, as in its <term>concretes</term>, etc. And just as in a race which consists equally between the runner and the race-track: and the present time between the past and the future: and so of others in their own way. ¶ Through all species of Rule I, <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi).</note> it is asked **where equality is**: and it must be answered that it is in itself: because it is in its correlatives: and in the subject in which it is equally deduced through action and passion: and it is in goodness, magnitude, etc., in which it is equally present, so that the principles may be equal. And it is in difference so that its correlatives may be equally differing: and it is in concordance so that its correlatives may likewise be equally concordant: and it is in modality so that it may be done modally: and it is in instrumentality so that the whole may be done instrumentally.
