# On the mixing of principles and rules.

This is manifest through rule B. <note>Rule B in Llull’s logic refers to the question "Whether?" (Utrum), used to establish the existence or possibility of a thing.</note> ¶ Through the rule of **modality**, it is asked **how equality is**: and we say that it exists according to the mode it has in its <term>correlatives</term>; <note>Llull’s "correlatives" are the three components of any principle: the active power, the passive capacity, and the action itself. For Equality, these would be: that which makes equal, that which is made equal, and the act of equaling.</note> and it exists by way of the justice of weight, measure, and proportion in the subject in which it resides—and this occurs both naturally and artificially. This is quite clear in itself. ¶ Through all the species of **instrumentality**, it is asked **with what equality is**: and the answer is that it is with its correlatives; it is with <term>difference</term> <note>original: "differentia"</note> by which the agent distinguishes; and it is with <term>concordance</term> <note>original: "concordantia"</note> with which the agent accords equally; and with its own proper property with which it causes proper <term>habits</term> <note>In this context, a "habit" (habitus) is a stable quality or disposition of a thing.</note> of this kind, as is evident in things composed of elements, in plants, etc. And this can be signified through rule B.

## On minority deduced through the rules.

<margin>On minority deduced through the rules.</margin>

**I**t is asked **whether minority exists as a substance in one way and as an accident in another**: <note>In Scholastic thought, a "substance" is something that exists by itself (like a tree), while an "accident" is a quality that exists in something else (like the greenness of the tree).</note> And it must be answered that it does. For if it were not so, the substantial relation existing between majority and minority would be destroyed, and all principles would be equal. Furthermore, the real relation of majority and minority would not exist between substance and accident, which is impossible. And rule B proves this. ¶ Through the first species of rule C, it is asked **what minority is**: And we say that it is a being to which it properly belongs to <term>minorify</term> <note>Llull uses the verb "minorificare" (to minorify) to describe the action of making something smaller or placing it in a lesser state.</note> and to distance itself from majority. ¶ And through the second species, it is asked **what it has in itself**: and it must be said that it has its innate correlatives, in which and with which all other principles are "minorifiable" by dividing and annihilating the subject in which it resides. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked **what it is in another**: And it must be said that it is a "consummating" being, such that it can exist near to nothingness. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked **what it has in another**: and it must be answered that it has a lesser essence, a lesser being, and a lesser nature, quantity, quality, etc. And this is clear in itself. ¶ Through the first species of rule D, it is asked **from what minority comes**: and it must be answered that it is from itself, so that it may be a general principle without which subordinate minorities of the <term>genus</term> of minority could not exist. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked **from what substantial minority comes**: And it must be said that it comes from its correlatives, without which it could not have nature or existence. However, accidental minority is from itself, insofar as it is a habit with which substantial minorities are "habited," and the minorities of the powers are of their own kind. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked **to whom minority belongs**: And it must be said that it belongs to the agent, insofar as from it and with it the agent causes minorities. And all these things are self-evident and also clear through rule B. ¶ Through the first species of rule E, it is asked **why minority is**: And it must be said that it is because of its correlatives, by reason of which it is a principle according to its kind. ¶ Further, through the second species, it is asked **why it is**: and it must be said that it is so that there may be lesser beings of their kind, without which there could be no motion, division, generation, corruption, or <term>privation</term>. <note>Privation is the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present.</note> And this is sufficiently graspable in itself. ¶ Through the first species of rule F, it is asked **how great minority is**: and it must be answered that it is as great as that which is outside the category of majority and equality. ¶ Further, through the second species, it is asked **how great minority is**: and it must be said that it is as great as its correlatives, its subordinate minorities, and its individuals which belong to its kind. ¶ Through the first species of rule G, it is asked **what kind minority is**: And it must be answered that it is of such a kind as can be through the proper "passion" <note>In philosophy, a "passion" is a property or attribute that a subject undergoes or possesses.</note> of the subject in which it is; just as one substance is lesser than another through its own proper passion, without which it cannot exist. ¶ Likewise, through the second species, it is asked **what kind it is**: and it must be said that it is of such a kind as is the lesser <term>predicament</term> <note>A "predicament" (praedicamentum) refers to one of Aristotle’s categories of being, such as Quantity or Quality.</note> appropriated to it, such as a smaller quantity, quality, etc. ¶ Through all species of rule H, it is asked **when minority is**: and it must be answered that it is then when it is really sustained through all the species of rule H which are of its kind, and it is also then when it is in practice through the act of "minorifying"; and all this is plain to one who looks closely. ¶ Through all species of rule I, it is asked **where minority is**: And it must be said that it is in itself, since it is in its correlatives with which it exists; and it is in a composite subject of lesser substance and accident—just as someone wearing a cloak is in a smaller cloak, and water is in a lesser heat, and a horse is in a lesser gallop, and the like; and a man in a lesser mode, and a craftsman in a lesser craft. ¶ Through the rule of **modality**, it is asked **how minority is**: and it must be said that it is by way of the mode it has in its correlatives, such that it is lesser in being and acting than some other principle—just as some man in moral matters has a mode of existing in lesser virtue, doing a small amount of good; and a horse in running sometimes has a "small run." And this is clear in itself. ¶ Through the rule of **instrumentality**, it is asked **with what minority is**...

## Ninth principal part: On the nine subjects named above in the alphabet.

<margin>
Ninth principal part: On the nine subjects named above in the alphabet.

Since everything that exists is implied in the nine subjects, and nothing exists outside of them, we wish to place them in this art, so that with them the art may be general, because they are general to all things. And therefore, by running through the aforesaid subjects using the principles and rules of this art, we will be able to have knowledge of these subjects. On the investigation of the divine dignities.
</margin>

First, I suppose that God exists, which we will prove in the second principal part of the aforementioned division. ¶ God is: and His being is good; but His being could not be good without **goodness**, just as a colored thing cannot be colored without color. And therefore His goodness exists, since His being is good; and this is necessary. ¶ God is: and His being is **great**. For if it were not great, it would no longer be worthy of being God; whence it follows that divine magnitude is a real thing. ¶ God exists and His being is **eternal**; for if anything were beginning, it would no longer be worthy of being God: and so eternity exists, without which an eternal being cannot exist. ¶ God is: and since He is, He can be: therefore **power** exists, without which God cannot be. ¶ God is: and He Himself knows Himself. Otherwise, His being would not be worthy of being God. There is therefore divine **wisdom**, without which God could not know Himself. ¶ God is: and He loves Himself, for otherwise He would not be worthy to be God. There is therefore divine **love**, without which God could not love Himself. ¶ God is: and His being is **virtuous**; <note>In this context, "virtuous" refers to the possession of "Virtue" (Virtus) as a power or strength of being, rather than just moral conduct.</note> otherwise God would be vicious, and thus not worthy of being God. There is therefore divine **virtue**, without which God cannot be virtuous. ¶ God is: and His being is **true**; for if not, He would be false, and consequently not worthy of being God. There is therefore divine **truth**, without which God could not be true. ¶ God is: and His being is **glorious**; because if not, He would no longer be worthy of being God. There is therefore divine **glory**, without which God cannot be glorious. ¶ We have proven that the divine dignities exist really, without which God could not be; therefore they are numerable, each existing in its own proper number. The reason for this is: for unless each existed in its own proper number, God would not exist. And so, for God to be, there must be in Him many real reasons or dignities. However, even if they do not differ in essence—for all are one and the same divine essence—one is the other essentially. Otherwise, goodness would be great by accident, <note>In medieval logic, an "accident" is a non-essential property. Llull argues God's attributes are essential, not accidental.</note> and vice versa. And the same can be said of the others. ¶ And in this step, the human intellect recognizes that God, insofar as He considers the unity of His essence, does not consider many reasons; but insofar as He considers that He cannot be without many reasons, He numbers them really: just as a human being who, insofar as he does not consider being one, does not consider many. But insofar as he considers that he cannot be without many, he understands and knows that there are many within himself. ¶ We have inquired into the divine dignities, and we found them coessential to God.

and substantial from eternity and in eternity. The reason why they exist consists in themselves and not outside of them. For otherwise, they would exist by accident, and similarly God would as well, which is impossible.

¶ And this stands against certain **Saracens** <note>A medieval term for Muslims; here referring to specific theological debates regarding the nature of divine attributes</note> who believe they have a high and subtle knowledge of God. They say that God is one and has no **dignities** <term>Dignities: The Lullian term for God's fundamental attributes, such as Goodness, Greatness, and Eternity.</term> in relation to Himself, but rather holds them only so that He may act through them upon creatures. For example, they say He is good so that He may produce a good creature, and great so that He may create a great creature, and He is eternal so that the creature may be durable, and so on.

¶ From this, it is clearly evident that in their words or sayings they imply a contradiction. For if it were as they say, then just as God is infinite in His **reasons** <note>Divine principles or logical grounds</note>, He would indeed create infinite and eternal creatures—which He does not do, nor do they themselves say He does. For they say the world is "new" <note>Created in time rather than eternal</note> and measured or limited.

¶ Furthermore, they imply a contradiction by saying God is the **First Cause**; for He would not be the First Cause if His reasons existed for the sake of the world. In that case, God and His dignities would exist so that the world might exist, which is a very absurd thing to say.

## On the intrinsic acts of the divine reasons.

<margin>On the intrinsic acts of the reasons.</margin>
¶ It is said that power is in vain if it is not brought into act. Furthermore, it is established that power is known through acts, and acts are known through their objects. Thus, it is signified that the divine dignities have acts, without which the dignities of God would be in vain throughout infinity and eternity; and God would not know His own dignities, nor would He "objectify" Himself <note>To be the object of His own thought or action</note>. From this it would follow that God would not be God through His dignities, which is false, as was proved above.

¶ Furthermore, if divine **Goodness** did not have an act—and likewise for the others—it would then have no nature; it would be idle and empty, and would not be directed toward any end. This is impossible and against "Rule E" <note>A rule in Llull's system concerning "Why?" or purpose</note> and also against the second species of "Rule C." Therefore, etc. The divine dignities therefore have intrinsic, co-essential, and natural acts.

¶ Furthermore, if the dignities did not have co-essential acts, each one would indeed be a **privative habit** <term>Privative habit: A state defined by the absence of a natural quality, such as blindness being the absence of sight.</term>. For just as blindness is a privative habit because it has no act (namely, seeing), so divine Goodness would be a privative habit if it did not have an intrinsic act co-essential to itself, which is <term>to make good (bonificare)</term>. Similarly, **Greatness** would be without <term>to make great (magnificare)</term>; **Eternity** without <term>to make eternal (eternare)</term>; **Power** without being able; **Wisdom** without knowing; **Will** without willing; **Virtue** without <term>to make virtuous (virtuificare)</term>; **Truth** without verifying; and **Glory** without glorifying. God would not be worthy to be God with habits that were privative and co-essential to Him, which is impossible.

¶ Therefore, the divine dignities have intrinsic, co-essential, and real acts. ¶ Furthermore, it is known: every perfect goodness has an act; and the same can be said of divine Greatness and Eternity, etc. Therefore, etc.

¶ Furthermore, no goodness is perfect without an act; and the same can be said of divine Greatness and Eternity. ¶ It is concluded, therefore, by affirming and denying, that the divine dignities have intrinsic and co-essential acts.

## On the infinity of the divine reasons.

<margin>On the infinity of the divine reasons.</margin>
¶ Divine Goodness is the reason for a good thing producing good; and it has already been proved that it has an act, namely, **to make good**. And so, if Greatness is the being by reason of which Goodness is great, then Goodness is the reason for a good thing producing a *great* good. And because Eternity is the reason through which Goodness and Greatness endure, Goodness is therefore the reason for producing a great and eternal good. But Goodness could not be such a reason unless it were itself infinite and immense; therefore, Goodness is necessarily infinite.

¶ Divine Greatness exists, as has been proved, and it similarly has an act, namely, **to make great**. And because Eternity is the being by reason of which Greatness endures, and Power is that by reason of which Greatness is able to exist and act:

¶ There is therefore an infinite and immense subject through which "to make great" can spread itself from eternity and in eternity; and such a subject we call **infinite Greatness**.

¶ Eternity is a measure existing all at once and together, having nothing before it nor anything after it; and its subject is eternal from eternity. Thus, Eternity is an infinite reason; and this is indeed good and great, and through Power it is able to be so.

¶ Eternity exists, as has been proved, and it has an act, namely, **to make eternal**. And because Eternity can exist and act infinitely, it follows of necessity that **Power** is infinite, without which Power, Eternity could not have an act nor an infinite essence.

¶ The **Wisdom** of God (or Intellect) exists, as has already been proved above; and Eternity is the reason through which it endures, and through Power it is able to exist and act; and Greatness...

[It] is that through which He can diffuse Himself immensely; and through goodness, an infinite intellect is good; and through the will, He is lovable, because of which an infinite intellect is necessitated, such that it cannot be otherwise. ¶ The divine will exists, and likewise its act, as has already been proved above. And if it is infinite in eternity and from eternity, it is indeed infinitely intelligible; but if it were finite, it would be [merely] understood, and would not be infinitely intelligible, nor consequently would the divine intellect be lovable and loved from eternity and into eternity; and thus the definitions of goodness, greatness, etc., would fail, which is impossible. ¶ It is therefore proved that the divine will is infinite.

¶ Divine virtue <note>Original: *virtus*; in this context, it refers to both moral excellence and inherent power or efficacy.</note> exists, and its acts exist, as has been proved above. And therefore, if it is infinite, all is well; but if not, it would indeed be "vicious" through some defect impeding it from being infinite. And consequently, all other reasons that allow it to be limited—even if they themselves were infinite—would be affected; and because the finite cannot extend or diffuse itself as much as the infinite, it clearly appears that the other dignities <term>Dignities: Ramon Llull’s specific term for the fundamental attributes of God (Goodness, Greatness, etc.) that act as the building blocks of reality.</term> would be partly defective and partly not, which is highly impossible. ¶ Therefore, the divine virtue is infinite.

¶ Divine truth exists, and its acts exist, as was proved above. And since it is true that goodness, greatness, etc., are reasons that are infinite in reality, it is necessary that truth be infinite; otherwise, the infinity of the aforementioned reasons would not be true, because it would have nothing with which to be true. ¶ Divine glory exists, and its acts exist, as was proved above. But the essence of glory itself is either infinite, or finite, or partly finite and partly infinite. If it is absolutely infinite, all is well, because no inconsistency follows regarding itself or the other dignities. If, however, it is partly finite and partly infinite, a very great inconsistency follows. For all the other dignities would not have an infinite subject for glory and rest; and thus a finitude of glory would be a "privative habit" <note>A philosophical term meaning the absence of a quality that should be present, like blindness is the absence of sight.</note> through which the other dignities would suffer pain, which is quite impossible. ¶ It follows necessarily, therefore, that divine glory is infinite.

# On the infinity of the acts of the divine reasons.

**D**ivine goodness is the reason for a good [being] to produce good. And because greatness is the reason why goodness is great; furthermore, through eternity it is eternal; through power it can exist and act; through the intellect it is understood; through the will [it is] loved; through virtue [it is] virtuous; through truth [it is] true; and through glory it is glorious. ¶ It follows therefore of necessity that the act of goodness—that is, **to act as good** <note>Original: *bonificare*. Llull turned the nouns for God's attributes into active verbs to show that God is eternally active within Himself.</note>—is infinite in accordance with the infinity of goodness, and also in accordance with the infinity of all the other dignities or reasons.

¶ The greatness of God is infinite, and it has an act, as was proved above. And therefore its act—namely, **to act as great** <note>Original: *magnificare*.</note>—is either infinite or it is finite. If infinite, all is well; but if not, it is like a tree in which the "elemental" <note>The basic physical matter.</note> power is more extended than the "vegetative" <note>The life-force or power of growth.</note> power, because at the ends of the tree there are sometimes dry branches in which the vegetative power is not present, but only the elemental. And thus a finite act would suit an infinite greatness, rather than an infinite act; which is an evil against the good, and the small against the great. Consequently, **acting as great** and **acting as eternal** <note>Original: *magnificare* and *eternare*.</note> could not be converted <note>In logic, "convertible" terms are those that are co-extensive or identical in scope.</note> with one another, and all other acts of the divine reasons would fall short of the act of greatness, and similarly the act of greatness would fall short of them, by reason of which they would be small. ¶ From this it would follow that the infinity of the essence would fail in the finitude of its act by distancing itself from an infinite act, which is against its nature; and it would rest more in a small act than in a great one, which is dissonant with reason and contrary to the infinity of **acting as good** which we proved above. ¶ It is concluded, therefore, that the divine **acting as great** is infinite.

¶ **To act as eternal** exists, as was proved above; and similarly infinity and eternity. The act of eternity—that is, **acting as eternal**—is either infinite or it is finite. If it is infinite, all is well, for no inconsistency follows; but if it is finite, a great inconsistency follows: because **acting as eternal** would be terminated by time, and consequently eternity would be the subject of time from eternity and in eternity, which is quite impossible and contrary to the infinity of the divine dignities already proved above. ¶ It is concluded, therefore, that **acting as eternal** is an infinite act.

¶ **To act as power** <note>Original: *possificare*; the active exercise of divine Power.</note> is the act of power, as was proved above. But **acting as power** is either an infinite act or a finite one. If it is infinite, all is well; because just as a finite **acting as power** suits a finite power, so—and much better—does an infinite **acting as power** suit the infinite power proved above. And if [only] a created **acting as power** suited infinite power, then power would degenerate and depart from its nature, both in regard to God and also in regard to the creature. ¶ Furthermore, **acting as good**, **acting as great**, and **acting as eternal** could not be infinite acts, because no one gives what he does not have; because of which a contradiction follows, for **acting as good**, **acting as great**, and **acting as eternal**, which are infinite acts (as has been proved), could not be infinite; and because

# ## On God deduced through principles.

**I**n this chapter, we will discuss God through principles in two ways. ¶ The first will be intrinsic, regarding His own nature. ¶ The second will be extrinsic and voluntary, regarding His relationship toward His creatures. # ## On God deduced through goodness.

<margin>On God deduced through goodness.</margin>
**G**od is good, and He is His very own goodness; from which it follows that His goodness is the reason why He produces a **necessary good** <note>In Llull's theology, the "necessary good" refers to the internal activities of the Trinity (the processions), which must be infinite and eternal by nature.</note>. The reason for this is that goodness and God are interchangeable in the unity of nature. This is evident through the definition of goodness, just as in a plant, the "vegetative power" is the reason why it produces a necessary vegetative growth—provided the plant has the right conditions for growing. Just as God has His own conditions for producing an intrinsic **bonified** <note>Original: *bonificatum*; the result or object of the act of "bonifying" (making good).</note>; therefore, God produces an intrinsic bonified, and this He does with His infinite **bonifying** <note>Original: *bonificare*; the active verb of goodness.</note> through His entire infinite goodness. ¶ When God knows Himself to be good in producing the "bonified," He considers that it is indeed good to produce a **created good** <note>Unlike the "necessary good" of the Trinity, "created good" refers to the voluntary creation of the universe.</note>, so that His intrinsic bonifying may be understood, loved, remembered, and praised by that creature; and so that God may "bonify" those powers [of the creature] when they are correctly directed toward Him as their object. For this reason, He created the power of understanding, of willing, and of remembering in the angel and in the rational soul. Consequently, He gave them all the conditions pertaining to them, so that they might perfectly enjoy God and acquire good merit. And in this step, the human intellect recognizes the primary intention which God had for creating good creatures.

# ## On God discussed through greatness.

<margin>On God discussed through greatness.</margin>
**G**od is great, and He is His own infinite greatness, with which He has an infinite **magnifying** <note>Original: *magnificare*; the active expression of the attribute of greatness.</note>, without which He could not have infinite greatness, nor even an infinite act. And because greatness is that by reason of which goodness and eternity are great, therefore these dignities, with their acts, concur to produce an infinite **magnified** <note>Original: *magnificatum*; the result of the act of magnifying.</note>, and likewise a bonified, an eternized, etc., so that each dignity may have its own infinite act in the infinite "magnified." ¶ While God knows Himself to be thus great and also infinite, in both being and acting, He consequently knows Himself to be well-conditioned and disposed to produce a great creature. This is so much the case that He would produce an infinite creature if a creature were capable of receiving infinite greatness; He is like a fire which, if it had an infinite supply of wood, would magnify and multiply its flame even unto the sphere of the moon; and so God...

# On God deduced through power.

<margin>On God deduced through power.</margin>

**G**od is powerful: and He is His own very power. For God knows Himself internally with absolute and ordered power: but externally with ordered power only: because God does not produce creatures from His own nature: but He produces them effectively <note>That is, as an effect outside of Himself.</note>. Just as a real man who paints a man on a wall / who is not of his own nature. ¶ And thus the human intellect knows with what intention God created created powers: namely so that creatures with them might be able to understand / love / and remember / and praise God: and thus the human intellect knows that the infinite and internal **possified** / is the cause of all finite and external **possifiables** <note>Things capable of being brought into existence.</note>.

# On God deduced through wisdom.

<margin>On God deduced through wisdom.</margin>

# On God deduced through virtue.

<margin>On God deduced through virtue.</margin>
**G**od is virtuous: and He is His own virtue; and His acts <term>which</term> <note>original: "q" (que)</note> are coessential and natural to Him—and therefore just as He loves Himself as being necessitated to produce an infinite beloved—so He loves and knows Himself as being necessitated to know and produce an infinite virtuous one. And to this all the dignities concur with their acts: so that through infinite virtue they might be virtuous and infinite; and they cannot behave otherwise. God, thus loving and knowing Himself, intrinsically inclines Himself and passes over to loving and knowing Himself to be ordered and disposed to creating natural virtues: such as the figures and signs of infinite and eternal virtue, etc., with which created virtues the infinite and eternal virtue might be known, loved, remembered, and praised.

¶ Furthermore, He passes over to creating moral virtues, of which we shall speak below in the ninth subject, because they are the way to paradise; and so that God might reward **men** <note>original: "hoīes" (homines)</note> with them from His own virtuous glory. And while the intellect considers this, it wonders why **men** in this life are not more morally virtuous than they are vicious, since their virtues have their origin from the supreme virtue, but vices do not.

But then it knows that this is because men have **free will** <term>liberum arbitrium</term> to do good or evil. But they incline themselves more to the sensitive power <note>the physical senses and desires</note> and love it more than the rational power. ¶ Furthermore, the divine intellect asks why this is permitted to happen, since He Himself is virtuous and not vicious, and is spiritual and not sensual.

Then the intellect knows that the reason for this is so that the justice of God might have a subject in which it can act. Nevertheless, it must be known that **free will** relates to two different parts: namely, to the good created part with which it does good; and to the evil uncreated part with which it does evil and sin—which is the uncreated part, arising from the side of uncreated nothingness by accident. For insofar as man is brought forth from nothing, he has an inclination toward nothingness, which is against "being"; whence it is made manifest that free will partly agrees with "being" and partly with "non-being," or with nothing (which is the same thing); and this equally.

¶ But the intellect still asks: since God knows that man will sin, why did He create him? And it knows this because of this: <term>because</term> He created a good free will for him, with which he can remove himself from sin and hate it if he wishes; if, however, He had not created man, God would do injury to His justice, because He would not have a subject in which He could act.

# On God deduced through truth.

<margin>On God deduced through truth.</margin>
**G**od is **true** <note>original: "ver?" (verus)</note>: and He is His own truth: and thus He truly loves and knows Himself as necessitated to produce an infinite **verified object** <note>original: "verificatum." Just as Will has a "volitum," Truth has a "verificatum"—the internal object of God's truthful action.</note> through His whole infinite essence. And from that essence He produces it as His own infinite verified object, so that He might **have** <note>original: "hīe" (habere)</note> sufficiency from eternity and in eternity: so that other dignities might have true infinite acts through that verified object. Thus God, loving and knowing Himself as necessitated to produce an infinite true one: from there He loves and knows that it is indeed true to create created natural truth, and also moral truth: so that through them the infinite verified object might be understood, loved, remembered, and also praised.

¶ But here the intellect wonders, asking from where a lie arises. And afterwards it knows that it arises from nothingness, from which man is created; just as a falling stone, which by its weight tends toward the center that it desires.

**G**od is glorious: and He is His own glory: and thus He loves and knows Himself as producing an infinite glorified one produced from infinite glory. ¶ For it cannot be produced from any other essence. **For** <note>original: "em" (enim)</note> all other essences are finite **reason** <note>original: "rno" (ratio?)</note>...

## On God deduced through difference.

<margin>On God deduced through difference.</margin>
**R**ecalling the scale of **difference** placed in the **second figure** <note>The "Second Figure" in Llull's Art is a diagram of triangles representing relations like Difference, Concordance, and Contrariety.</note>, the human intellect denies that the difference which is in God is between the sensual and the sensual, nor between the sensual and the intellectual; rather, it is between intellectual and intellectual existence, being essentially the same. And this manifests what is said concerning the principles of the **first figure**. For without difference or distinction, the divine dignities or reasons could not have infinite acts. And this clearly appears in **Goodness**. For the <term>bonifying</term> <note>original: "bonificare." The active function of goodness.</note> of Goodness itself could in no way exist without the difference of the <term>bonifier</term> <note>original: "bonificans." The active principle of goodness within God.</note> and the <term>bonified</term> <note>original: "bonificatum." The object or result of the act of goodness.</note>. Indeed, acting cannot exist without the distinction of an agent and a thing able to be acted upon; thus, neither can "bonifying" exist without the aforementioned parts. Here, however, the intellect asks whether the aforementioned difference places many essences in God; it considers and knows that it does not, just as there are not many "goodnesses" in him. The reason for this is: because the **bonifier**, which is the whole of that goodness, produces from itself the whole **bonified**—infinite and eternal—and the "bonifying" and "eternalizing" are produced from the whole of both of them. And in this step, the intellect knows that difference is clear and unconfused in that infinite goodness, because it posits that the **bonifier** is one distinct from the **bonified** and the **bonifying**; and the **bonified** is another distinct from the **bonifier** and the **bonifying**; and similarly, that the **bonifying** is another distinct from the two mentioned above—each of these existing in its own number. Yet these exist as the same through essence; otherwise, difference would be confused in them, and consequently eternity would fail, and thus each of the three aforementioned would not preserve its own number, which is impossible. And furthermore, the divine intellect would fail; it would be ignorant of what kind the **bonifier** was, and what kind the **bonified** was, and what kind the **bonifying** was. And thus these two dignities would fail, and consequently all others with their acts, and thus they would be primitive acts, which is impossible. Nevertheless, concerning the aforementioned difference, it must be understood rightly that it is not "above" the aforementioned dignities, nor even above the aforementioned <term>correlatives</term> <note>Llull's technical term for the -ans, -atum, and -are triplets (e.g., Bonifier, Bonified, Bonifying).</note>—namely the bonifier, the bonified, and the bonifying—but it is essentially and equally the same reason with them in distinguishing: just as goodness is in bonifying, greatness is in magnifying, etc. While God knows the aforementioned difference to be in himself, with which his reasons are clear and able to have infinite acts, he knows that it is good to create differences with which many creatures might exist, by whom he might be understood, loved, remembered, and also praised. And in this step, the intellect knows what is the cause of the multitude of things differing in genus, species, and number. ¶ Still the intellect asks: whether between God and a creature there is a **real difference** or an **intentional** one made by the soul? And it knows that through the difference which God has in himself—natural and co-essential—and through that which creatures have—natural and co-essential—God and creatures differ **really**. ¶ For without such differences they would not differ really, but only through an intentional difference made by the soul, which is quite impossible. Whence it is therefore clear that they differ through real differences, not through intentional ones.

### On God deduced through the principle.

<margin>
On God deduced through the principle.
</margin>
**G**od is the **principle** <note>original: "principium." This term encompasses the concepts of "beginning," "origin," and "source."</note>; and he is also his own principle, as in his goodness in which God is the **originator** <note>original: "principiāns." The active force that begins an action.</note> of the **originated** <note>original: "principiati." The result or object of the action.</note>, namely, the **bonified**. And he is an originator who possesses something pleasing to himself, just as it is co-essential to his goodness **to bonify**, which in the nature of his goodness is not the originator, but is only originated by the originator and the originated; just as **to love** is originated from the **lover** and the **beloved**. ¶ While God considers that he is such a perfect principle, he moves toward creating the world from nothing in such a way that one individual generates another individual, just as one man generates another man and one plant generates another plant similar to itself. And this is done with a substantial and natural originating. ¶ Furthermore, he creates another principle, such as the **understander** who causes the **intellect** objectively. And the understander and the intellect cause **understanding** accidentally, so that the intellect may acquire knowledge; and the same can be said of the **will**, so that it may be clothed with the habit of love.

### On God deduced through contrariety.

<margin>
On God deduced through contrariety.
</margin>
**G**od is "contrary," but he is not **contrariety**; yet he is certainly "opposing." For he effectively gives penance to the sinner, yet he also causes contrarieties, as is shown in the **scale of contrariety** <note>A hierarchy of opposing forces, such as heat vs. cold or virtue vs. vice.</note>. ¶ God, indeed, is not contrariety itself. For his own concordance is infinite, having an infinite and eternal act. But at this step the intellect doubts: since God is infinite concordance, why then does he permit contrariety to exist? To this it is answered that "opposition" exists between God and the sinful man, so that the **justice** of God may draw out its own act upon the sinner. For just as a mirror is disposed to receive all figures impressed upon it, so God is disposed to the tormenting of sinners. ¶ Furthermore, unless God created natural contrarieties in the world, the world would not be such as it is. ¶ At this point the intellect also doubts: since in the divine will there is an infinite "willing," why then does God have a "not-willing" <note>original: "nolle." This refers to God's rejection or disapproval of certain things, like sin.</note>? To understand this, the intellect helps itself with the example given above: for just as a mirror receives the likeness of whiteness and blackness, so God loves the virtuous man by **willing**, but hates sinners by **not-willing**.

### On God through the "middle" by discourse.

<margin>
On God through the middle by discourse.
</margin>
**I**n God there is a **middle** <note>original: "medium." This refers to the connecting link or the process between a beginning and an end.</note>, such as "to bonify" in his goodness, and "to magnify" in his greatness, etc. And he is his own middle because he is infinite, by which God measures himself insofar as he is infinite through his intrinsic acting just as through his existing; in which "to mediate," the **mediator** and the **mediated** join together so that they are one continuous and absolute middle. ¶ While God thus knows himself to be the middle, he then moves to the causes created by him, as is clear in the definition of the middle, and also in the **scale of the middle** placed in the **second figure** <note>One of the primary diagrams in the Lullian Art used to show relationships between concepts.</note>: such as "acting," which is the middle existing between the **actor** and the **actable**; and such as "loving" between the **lover** and the **lovable** or the beloved.

### On God through the "end" by discourse.

<margin>
On God through the end by discourse.
</margin>
**G**od is his own **end** <note>original: "finis." Here meaning the ultimate purpose, goal, or perfection of a thing.</note>; and he is not a "privative" end <note>An end that marks a stopping point or a lack.</note>, but in that end there are many terms: just as in his goodness in which the **bonifying** is one term, the **bonified** is another term, and **to bonify** is another term; and all these three rest in one goodness. ¶ While God thus knows himself, he moves by reason of the "end" to create many ends in the world, such as the habit of goodness which is one end morally, by which the **bonifier** habits himself by producing the **bonified**, which is another end. And thus it is with **to bonify** in its own way. And all these three terms rest in that goodness which is their end. But when a man is deprived [of this] he moves toward sin, even when the habit of goodness is his term. And consequently, man deviates from his end, by reason of which he tends toward eternal labor <note>Meaning eternal suffering or the punishment of hell.</note>.

Ninth part

# On God through the discourse of majority,

<margin>On God through the discourse of majority.</margin>
**D**eus is greater than the world and even all things contained within it: for His reasons <note>original: "rationes." In this context, these are the divine dignities or attributes like Goodness and Greatness.</note> are infinite and possess infinite acts. And because of this, just as He is greater than the world with His goodness and greatness, so He exists before the world with His **majority** <note>original: "maioritas." This term refers to the state of being greater or superior in essence and power.</note>. Furthermore, just as God with His substance is greater than the world with its majority, so indeed God with His eternity is greater than the world, while the world exists only with its **novelty** <note>original: "nouitas." This refers to the world's status as a created thing with a beginning in time, as opposed to God’s eternal existence.</note>. Again, just as divine substance is greater than an accident, so the divine substance exists before the accidents of the world. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that it is impossible for the world to have existed from eternity. While God thus recognizes His own majority, He proceeds to create finite majorities through which His own majority—which is signified in the **ladder of the second figure** <note>A diagram in Llull’s Art that shows the hierarchy of being from God down to the elements.</note>—may be known and loved.

# On God through the discourse of equality,

<margin>On God through the discourse of equality.</margin>
**I**n God there is **equality**: so that it may appear in His co-essential goodness, and so forth. For since the **bonifying** <note>original: "bonificans." The active principle of doing good.</note> has two actions substantially: namely, that which is **bonified** <note>original: "bonificatum." The object receiving the goodness.</note> and the act of **bonifying** <note>original: "bonificare." The verb or middle act connecting the doer and the receiver.</note>. That which is bonified indeed has one "passion" <note>In medieval logic, a "passion" is the state of being acted upon.</note> from the bonifying agent and has one action: because it "bonifies" the act of bonifying; and this act of bonifying has the two aforementioned "passions." And since divine goodness is infinite and has an infinite act (as has already been proven above), therefore divine equality itself is infinite and separated from every **accident** <note>original: "accidente." A non-essential property that can change, unlike a substance.</note>. For in an infinite subject, no accident can exist. God, thus considering His own infinite equality, proceeds to create finite substantial equality and also accidental equality. He creates substantial equality so that the infinite equality may be known through likeness. Likewise, He creates accidental equality so that infinite equality may be known through unlikeness; for one opposite is known through the other.

# On God led through minority.

<margin>On God led through the discourse of minority.</margin>
**I**n God there is no **minority** <note>original: "minoritas." The state of being lesser or inferior.</note>: because He is infinite majority and eternal. For otherwise, one opposite would be the other opposite, which is impossible. And for this reason, it is fitting for God to **majorify** <note>To make something greater or to move it toward perfection.</note>, but not to **minorify** <note>To make something lesser or to diminish it.</note>. But because the world cannot exist at all without minorities, God disposed Himself to create minority in the world, so that through finite minorities, His own infinite majority might be known. For one opposite is better known through the other; whence the intellect knows that God is absolute majority by reason of His eternity, while the world is minority by reason of its smallness or novelty. God, knowing Himself thus disposed to create majority rather than minority, creates minorities for the sake of majorities, just as the body of a man exists for the sake of the rational soul. And all bodily things exist for the man’s body, and leaves and flowers exist for the sake of the fruit. And so it is with other **secondary intentions** <note>Goals that are means to an end.</note> in relation to **primary intentions** <note>The ultimate goal or purpose.</note>. We investigate God through the explained principles mentioned before, so that we can have knowledge of Him; and just as we gave an example through the aforementioned explained principles, so it can be given through the implicit principles, keeping to the same method we have held.

# On God led through rule B.

<margin>On God led through rule B.</margin>
**I**t is asked **whether God exists** <note>original: "vtruz deus sit." This is the classic question of existence, corresponding to "Rule B" in Llull's system.</note>. To prove that God exists, we wish to keep to the method of the Art: namely, to mix the principles with the rules to investigate and prove that God exists, making **Eternity** the subject and applying it to the other principles; and first through **Goodness**. Eternity exists. For if it did not exist, the world would have originated itself. And thus it would have existed before it existed, which is impossible; for no being can originate itself. Therefore, eternity has its own **concrete** <note>original: "procretum." In this logic, every abstract quality like "Eternity" must have a concrete subject that embodies it, i.e., "An Eternal Being."</note>, namely an eternal being; for no essence can exist without its concrete manifestation, and vice versa. It is infinite duration itself, and its infinity is good. Whence it follows that goodness is the reason for the eternal one to act well from eternity and in eternity through an infinite and good duration. That being is infinitely good, for whom goodness is the reason to act well infinitely and eternally: and such a being we call God. Therefore, it is clear through the aforesaid that God exists; and the human intellect, holding to the method of the General Art, cannot deny this. Eternity exists, as has already been proven above; and it is great through **Greatness** in such a...

so immense and infinite: just as his magnitude is infinite in duration or eternity. And such an eternal being, existing as the **subject** <note>In scholastic logic, the "subject" is the underlying reality that possesses certain qualities or attributes.</note> of the aforementioned eternity and magnitude, we call **God**, who exists necessarily by reason of the things mentioned; for an infinite and eternal being is necessary, as it cannot be otherwise. ¶ Eternity is (as was proven above), and because it is, it is an infinite power, without which infinity cannot exist; this power is the reason for eternity, so that it might exist and act infinitely; and such a subject of the aforementioned eternity we call **God**. ¶ Eternity is, and its being is infinite and intelligible; from which it follows that some eternal being is alive or possesses life, without which it could not be an eternal intelligible being; and such an infinite and eternal being we call **God**. ¶ Eternity is, and it is infinite duration; it is indeed lovable; from which it follows that the eternal being has life, without which it could not be loved from eternity and in eternity; and such a loved and eternal being we call **God**. ¶ Eternity is infinite, and thus it is **virtuous** <note>Possessing "virtue" here means having the inherent power or excellence to perform its proper function.</note>; for without infinite virtue it could not be virtuous at all. From which it follows that its virtue is infinite, so that vice is not found within it; from which it follows that its eternity has an act, namely **to eternize** <note>original: "eternare." This is a characteristic Lullian verb, turning an attribute into an active process.</note>, in which act all the principles of the **first figure** <note>The "First Figure" in the Lullian Art represents the circular diagram of divine attributes like Goodness, Greatness, and Eternity.</note> have eternal acts: just as goodness has **to bonify** <note>original: "bonificare," the active outpouring of goodness.</note>, eternity has **to eternize**, and power has **to power-ify** <note>original: "possificare," the active exercise of power.</note>, etc. Otherwise, virtue itself would be vicious and injurious, which is impossible; and such an eternal and virtuous being we call **God**. ¶ Eternity is, and because it is infinite, it is therefore an infinite and glorious being; there is therefore infinite glory, without which an eternal, infinite, and glorious being could not exist; in which being, **to glorify** and **to eternize** are infinite, without which the eternal being would have eternal pain, which is false and impossible. And such a being, in which there is glorifying and eternizing, we call **God**. ¶ Eternity is, and in it its **coessential reasons** <note>These are the divine attributes (Goodness, Greatness, etc.) which are distinct in their logical function but identical in their one essence.</note> are clear and not confused: namely its concrete form which is **the eternal**, and it is **good** through goodness, and **great** through greatness, and **powerful** through power, etc. This is not because they are different reasons in their existence, but in their acting: namely, in the eternal being itself, its goodness and greatness are the same by essence; thus eternity is not good and great by **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential quality (like the color of a shirt). Here, God is good by His very nature, not by an added quality.</note>, but through itself. By reason of action, however, they are clear: because eternity is the reason for the eternal one that it acts as eternal, and greatness that it acts as great, etc. And by reason of eternity, it is necessary that there be an **eternized product** <note>original: "eternatus productus." This refers to the internal processions within the Godhead, such as the relationship between the Father and the Son.</note>; from which it follows necessarily that in the essence of eternity there is a **good and great eternizing producer**, distinct from the **good and great eternized product**, and that they are distinct from the acts of **eternizing**, **bonifying**, and **magnifying** through an essential relation existing as one essence; otherwise the reasons would be confused. And such an eternal and absolute being we call **God**. ¶ Eternity is, and consequently an eternal being is; and in the eternal being itself, its coessential reasons accord in the one and in the many; namely, that just as eternity is infinite duration, so its goodness is infinite **bonification**, and its greatness is infinite **magnification**, and its power is infinite **power-ifying**, and its intellect is infinite **understanding**, and its will is infinite **willing**, etc. And all of these are one good, great being, etc. which being possesses through goodness an infinite bonifying, through greatness an infinite magnifying, etc., and such a being we name **God**. ¶ Eternity is, and consequently an eternal being is; and because eternity itself is infinite, etc., it follows that the eternal being is infinite, because the being itself is good. No finite being can contradict the eternal and infinite being when it acts as the eternal good and great, etc. Nor indeed could the eternal being itself be otherwise, since its coessential virtuous reasons are infinite and have infinite acts. And such a being we name **God**. ¶ Eternity is, and it is itself; but eternity is infinite duration; it cannot be infinite duration [in time]: the reason for this is that time cannot exist without motion; but eternity is without motion. From which it follows that eternity is the first and last principle existing before time absolutely; and such an eternal being, existing as the first and last principle, we say is **God**. ¶ Eternity is: and because it is an absolutely identical infinite essence, it follows that in it is **eternizing**, which is the **middle** between the **eternizer** and the **eternized**, without which eternity would be infinite as to its existence, but finite as to its acting—by reason of which its absolute infinity would be destroyed, which is impossible. And such an eternity, in which there is coessential eternizing, we say is **God**. ¶ Eternity is, and because it is infinite in existing and acting simultaneously: so that its **end** <note>The "end" or "purpose" (finis) here is equal to the "beginning" or "existence," implying a perfect, completed circle of being.</note> is equal to its existence; namely, that just as it is infinite as to its existence, so it relates to infinite acting, through the **eternizer**, the **eternized**, and **to eternize**. And such an eternity, which relates to the ultimate end, we say is **God**. ¶ Eternity is, and it is the greatest duration that can be, with the greatest goodness that can be, and with the greatest greatness that can be, which **minority** cannot contradict, as they are infinite reasons in existing and acting. And such a majority of duration is **God**. ¶ Eternity is, and consequently an eternal being is. In which eternal being, its coessential goodness, greatness, etc., are equal to eternity: so that its goodness, greatness, etc., are as infinite as to their **bonification** as eternity is as to its duration. And such an eternal being we say is **God**. ¶ Eternity is: and because

<page-num>The Ninth Part.</page-num>

...infinite duration is indeed infinitely distant from smallness <note>original: "minoritate"; here meaning the state of being less than or finite</note>, which is finite: and consequently from the finite, which is less than eternity. And the same can be said of any lesser agency or existence, whatever they may be. ¶ It has been proven that God exists according to his own nature through all principles: nevertheless, it can be proven through all principles by syllogism <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note>: no infinite being exists without infinite power; eternity is infinite; therefore, etc. And such a being is not the heavens <note>original: "celum"; referring here to the physical celestial spheres of the medieval cosmos</note>, nor anything contained beneath them: therefore, we say such a being is God. And the question asking "whether God exists" is resolved: because we have proven him to exist with the principles and **Rule B** <note>In Llull’s system, "Rule B" asks "Whether a thing is?" and investigates its existence.</note>. Regarding his existence and his intrinsic agency, knowledge can be had through the mediation of his grace: but I say this in terms of **apprehension** <note>An awareness or basic understanding of something.</note>: yet not with **comprehension** <note>A full, exhaustive understanding of a subject's nature.</note>: for God is infinite, but our intellect is finite.

## On God as
## deduced through Rule C.

<margin>On God as deduced through Rule C.</margin>
**P**hrough the first species of **Rule C** <note>Rule C in Llull’s "Art" asks "What is it?" and seeks definitions.</note>, it is asked: **What is God?** So that we may have a clearer knowledge of God, we wish to define him through his definitions. In these, the **subject** and **predicate** are convertible: because one cannot exist without the other, by reason of the natural union which the subject and the predicate possess: just as asking, "What is substance?" And the response is that it is a being subsisting through itself: and asking, "What is a being subsisting through itself?" It must be said that it is substance. ¶ God is the being in whom his **reasons** <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning his divine attributes like goodness or greatness</note> are convertible. Indeed, the being in whom his reasons are convertible is God. ¶ God is the being in whom the divine reasons have infinite acts: just as infinite **Goodness** has an infinite **act of making good** <note>original: "bonificare"</note>, and **Greatness** has an infinite **act of making great** <note>original: "magnificare"</note>, and so on. Moreover, the being in whom there is Goodness having an infinite act, etc., is God. ¶ God is the being for whom his coessential Goodness is the reason why he performs good that is infinite and eternal: indeed, the being for whom his coessential Goodness is the reason why he performs good that is infinite and eternal, is God. ¶ God is the being who cannot exist without infinite reasons: but the being who cannot exist without infinite reasons is God. ¶ God is the being who "makes good" <term>Good-maker (bonificans): Llull's term for the active principle of goodness</term> who cannot exist without the "thing made good" <term>Good-made (bonificatum): the passive principle of goodness</term> and the "act of making good" <term>To make good (bonificare): the verb or action connecting the two</term>; moreover, to be the infinite "thing made good" and the "act of making good"—which could not exist without the "Good-maker"—is God. ¶ God is a **substance** stripped of every **accident** <note>In scholastic philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential quality (like color or size). Llull argues God has no accidental properties; he is pure essence.</note>: indeed, a substance stripped of every accident is 

God. ¶ God is an absolute being not depending on anything else: an absolute being not depending on anything else is God. ¶ God is the being who does not need anything outside of himself: the being who does not need anything outside of himself is God. ¶ God is the being who cannot be otherwise than he is. Moreover, the being who cannot be otherwise than he is, is God. ¶ God is the being who possesses himself for his own purpose as much as he is himself: moreover, the being who possesses himself for his own purpose as much as he is himself, is God. ¶ God is the being who can do as much from himself as he himself is. Moreover, the being who can do as much of himself and in himself as he himself is, is God. ¶ God is the being above whom there is no **majority** <note>original: "maioritas"; greatness or superiority</note>, and the being above whom there is no majority is God. ¶ God is the being who knows himself as an agent as much as he himself is. The being who knows himself as an agent as much as he himself is, is God. ¶ God is the being for whom it is impossible not to be. The being for whom it is impossible not to be is God. ¶ We have defined God through twenty reasons in which the subject and the predicate are necessarily converted: as is evident through Rule B. ¶ And through such necessary definitions, the human intellect is greatly clarified for knowing the divine essence, and his intrinsic and natural acts. ¶ Concerning God, however, **accidental descriptions** can be made thus: God is the Creator, and the Governor, and the First Cause, and the First Mover, and the Savior, and such as these. Through such descriptions, however, the intellect is not as much clarified as through the substantial definitions mentioned above. ¶ Through the **second species of Rule C**, it is asked: **What does God have in himself coessentially and naturally?** To this it must be answered that he has coessential, natural, and substantial **relatives** <note>Llull’s "relatives" (correlatives) are the internal triplets of an attribute, like the Lover, the Beloved, and the Act of Loving.</note>. Just as through his Goodness he has the Good-maker, the Good-made, and the Act of making good. And through his Greatness he has the Great-maker, the Great-made, and the Act of making great. And through his Eternity he has the Eternal-maker, the Eternal-made, and the Act of making eternal, and so on. ¶ Without these correlatives, indeed, the aforesaid reasons could not exist in God; nor could our intellect have knowledge of his essence. For without them, the reasons or dignities of God would be empty, idle, and imperfect: and each would be a **privative habit** <note>A state defined only by the absence of something else, like darkness being the absence of light.</note>. And consequently, God would need to be "made worthy," since he himself would lack perfect reasons: because without such an intrinsic "having," the nature of the relation would be destroyed: and also the nature of the aforesaid reasons: which is impossible. ¶ Through the **third species of Rule C**, it is asked: **What is God in another?** To which it must be said that he is in his effect as the First Cause, the First Mover, Ruler, and Governor, acting in his effect according to his plea...

It introduces the "Llullian correlatives"—the active, passive, and verbal components of divine attributes—as the necessary internal structure of God's being.</summary>

...then [God's power is] absolute, without any resistance from its own effect. ¶ Externally, indeed, God possesses lordship and power according to his will, just as a cause is absolute in its effect. He also holds ultimate right over creatures, because he is their creator and governor. For this reason, God is prepared to judge sinners according to their works. For he created creatures for his own service, which is the ultimate end <note>The final purpose or goal.</note> of the creature.

### On God as deduced through Rule D.

<margin>On God as deduced through Rule D.</margin>
**P**hrough the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D in this system asks "De quo?" or "From what / of what" a thing is made or originates.</note>, it is asked: From what is God? And it must be answered that he is from himself. For thus, having infinite reasons <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning the divine attributes or principles like Goodness, Greatness, etc.</note> possessing infinite acts, he cannot be from any other pre-existing thing. Rather, he himself is pre-existent to all other beings that are distinct from him by essence: just as the divine goodness is the primary source of all other goodness. Just as an infinite being is the primary source of a finite being. And so it can be said of the divine magnitude and eternity, and so on. And in this step, the human intellect recognizes that God is **pure act** <term>actus purus: a philosophical term meaning a being with no unfulfilled potential, who is completely and eternally "in action."</term>.

¶ Through the second species of Rule D, it is asked: Of what is God? And to this it must be answered that he is of his aforementioned **correlatives** <note>In Llull’s logic, "correlatives" are the internal components of an attribute: the active power, the passive capacity, and the action itself.</note>: just as the divine goodness is of—is of its own *good-maker*, *good-made*, and *making-good* <note>original: "bonificante / bonificato & bonificare"; these represent the active, passive, and verbal aspects of the attribute of Goodness.</note>: and all these three are of goodness itself: just as a concrete thing is of its own essence: and as a man is of his humanity, and a lion of its lion-nature, and so on. And in this step, our intellect recognizes that in God no malice, smallness, or novelty can exist.

¶ Through the third [species of] Rule D, it is asked: Whose is God? And to this it must be answered that he is not subject to anyone: for he is infinite and eternal: nevertheless, in paradise he is the **subject** <note>In this context, the "object of focus" or the foundation of experience.</note> to all the saints who receive from him their presented glory.

### On God as deduced through Rule E.

<margin>On God as deduced through Rule E.</margin>
**P**hrough the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Quare?" or "Why?" something is, seeking its cause.</note>, it is asked: Why is God? And it is to be answered that he is formally through his correlatives, from which he is [constituted]. And consequently, through his co-essential reasons: and because in him the subject and the predicate are interchangeable <note>meaning God's "being" and "attributes" are the same thing</note>: as was proven above in his definition. Just as a substance exists through the fact that it is composed of its matter, form, and their union. And a man of his body, soul, and their union. And so it can be said of a **syllogism** <note>A logical argument</note> that its joining middle term is with its superior and inferior. ¶ Furthermore, God exists through this: because his infinite reasons are interchangeable according to the identity of his essence. For all are one singular divine essence: and further, because all his dignities <note>divine attributes</note> have infinite acts: and in his definition, the subject and predicate are essentially interchangeable: as was said above. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that God is immutable <note>unchanging</note>: and that his being cannot be otherwise than it is.

¶ Through the second species of Rule E, it is asked: Why is God? And it must be answered that he exists because of his own absolute **end** <note>purpose or goal</note>. For an infinite and eternal end cannot exist for the sake of a finite end. ¶ This is further demonstrated: namely, that God exists for the sake of an absolute end, and not for another. For each correlative of his dignities exists for the sake of the other correlative: because each exists so that the other may be: otherwise none could have infinite goodness, magnitude, etc. ¶ Furthermore, God exists so that his active powers may exist, and vice-versa. ¶ Moreover, in God his co-essential reasons exist so that he himself, with them, may have intrinsic and infinite acts: so that his agency is as infinite as his existence. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the error of those who say that God has reasons [attributes] so that he may act finitely with them externally, like an efficient cause in an external subject, by accident. Such an error is evident. For God, without co-essential natural reasons having intrinsic and infinite acts, would not be the highest and infinite being: because he would not be the highest good, great, or eternal through himself, but through another: indeed, a man, or a rose, or a lion would have more regard for an end than God, because they have their own natural ends toward which they hold themselves so that they may be what they are. And thus it is clear that the aforementioned error is revealed.

### On God as deduced through Rule F.

<margin>On God as deduced through Rule F.</margin>
**I**t is asked: How great is God? <note>Rule F asks "Quantum?" or "How much?"</note> To which it must be answered that "quantity" is spoken of in two ways: namely, **really** and **numerically**. Real quantity is like the quantity of a body; but numerical is as when one, two, etc., are counted. Real quantity indeed signifies...

It critiques the idea that God only acts on external things, asserting instead that His infinite attributes have eternal, internal actions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Ninth Part" of the treatise, specifically concluding the discussion on God's quantity (Rule F) before moving into Rule G (Quality) and Rule H (Time/Place). The author uses Ramon Llull’s logical system of "correlatives"—active, passive, and verbal principles—to argue for the necessity of the Trinity and the nature of divine attributes.</meta>

Ninth part

...continuous or discrete. God indeed does not have real quantity <note>Physical size or mass.</note> because he does not have a body; a corporeal being certainly has quantity, but God himself has a continuous essence and goodness, etc. For in an infinite subject, quantity can in no way exist, just as in eternity, time and motion cannot have being. Numerical quantity <note>Discrete quantity, or the ability to be counted.</note> can exist in God by reason of his correlatives: just as in the divine goodness, in which the "good-maker" <note>original: *bonificans*; representing the Father.</note> knows himself to be a distinct unit, and knows the "one-made-good" <note>original: *bonificatus*; representing the Son.</note> to be another distinct from him. And in turn, the good-maker and the one-made-good know the "act-of-making-good" <note>original: *bonificare*; representing the Holy Spirit.</note> to be another distinct from themselves; and thus numerical quantity follows in them: namely, one, two, and three. 

And in this step, the intellect would wonder whether three correlatives or more are sufficient in the divine goodness. But it remembered the divine unity and singularity through which God is one and singular—just as he is good through his goodness, and great through his greatness, etc. Therefore, one singular good-maker who is not "made-good" is sufficient; and one singular one-made-good who is also a "good-maker"; and another singular "act-of-making-good" who is not a "good-maker." If, however, there were a fourth number there, etc., it would result in the destruction of unity and singularity. A fourth number would either be a good-maker not made-good, or one-made-good and a good-maker, or the act-of-making-good and not a good-maker; and thus there would be a superfluity there, which would be an evil against the nature of infinite goodness, and a vice against the great and eternal power of divine goodness. It would even act against the glory of divine goodness and would be a bad and privative habit, like deafness, ignorance, or deprivation, which is impossible.

Further, the intellect considers numerical quantity, which is the principle of number: the second unity arises from the first, and the third unity arises from them both, like a conclusion from two premises; and thus a perfect number follows, because every number is included in them—namely, even and odd. Two indeed is an even number; three, however, is odd. Hence it is clearly evident that a fourth unity is superfluous, and likewise a fifth, etc. For already even and odd have been obtained; and also because a fourth unity is disconnected from the second unity, which is the middle term between the first unity and the third—just as in the "mode of the first figure" <note>A reference to Aristotelian logic, where the first figure is the most perfect form of a syllogism.</note> in which the middle term is the subject in which the predicate of the major premise and the subject of the minor premise are joined, so that the subject and the predicate in the conclusion may agree in nature, as is clear through this syllogism: *Every animal is a substance; every man is an animal; therefore every man is a substance.* 

From this, therefore, the intellect recognizes that in the divine goodness a threefold number is sufficient, and that neither a larger nor smaller number is necessary. Nevertheless, in species there are more individuals than three—such as one, two, three, and four men in the human species—and those must be counted by more units or numbers, as is self-evident.

## On God as deduced through Rule G.

<margin>On God as deduced through Rule G.</margin>
**P**hrough the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G in this system asks "Qualis?" or "What kind?".</note>, it is asked: what kind of being is God? And to this it must be answered that God is such as are his properties or reasons and their co-substantial acts: just as through his goodness he is good, and through greatness he is great, and through eternity he is eternal, and so with the others. Furthermore, since goodness is the reason for a good thing because it produces "good," and through greatness it is great, and through eternity it is eternal—and goodness itself is this way—therefore goodness is the reason for God being of a certain quality in properly producing an infinite and eternal good. Just as heat—and much better so—is the reason for fire being of a certain quality in heating that which is made-hot, good, great, and durable. And this is signified in the correlatives which exist through the second species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "Quid?" or "What?".</note>. For without such proper and co-substantial qualities, God could not have his own being, nor being through himself, nor consequently would he have intrinsic, infinite, and eternal acts. 

Furthermore, he could not appropriately produce anything outside himself in another subject; for a quality of being that is attributed to something must be caused by a quality belonging to the thing itself, just as air and water are heated by the proper heat of fire. Through the second species of Rule G, it is asked: what kind of God is he? And it must be said that God is such by description: for he is creator and governor and savior and the like; just as God disposes himself to be just and merciful, pious and kind, as an agent in his own effect which is distinct from him by essence and nature.

## On God as deduced through Rule H.

<margin>On God as deduced through Rule H.</margin>
**Q**uestion: is God in time? To this it is answered: not properly, but by accident <note>In philosophy, "by accident" means something that is true because of a relationship to something else, rather than by its own fundamental nature.</note>. For an eternal being having an eternal act cannot be in time.
