# On the Nine Subjects.

Just as an infinite being <note>original: *ens infinitum*</note> cannot exist within a finite quantity; and just as the number three cannot be contained within the number five; nor can an evil essence exist within a good essence; nor can seeing exist within hearing; nor hearing within seeing; nor understanding within ignorance, and so forth. All these things are manifest through rules C, D, and K <note>These letters refer to specific principles in the author's logical system: C (Magnitude), D (Eternity/Duration), and K (the question of "How" or "With what").</note> to a person looking closely, though we leave them for the reader to declare for the sake of avoiding wordiness.

## On God through the discourse of Rule I.

<margin>On God through the discourse of Rule I.</margin>
The question is asked: is God in a place? <note>In this system, Rule I represents the question "Where?" (*Ubi*).</note> It must be answered that God is not properly in a place, but rather "by accident" <note>In philosophy, "by accident" means something that is not part of a thing's essential nature; here, God is "in a place" only because the things he created occupy space, not because he himself is spatial.</note>. For just as eternity cannot exist within time, nor goodness within malice, nor can the intellect truly understand while in a state of ignorance; so indeed God, by reason of his infinity and immensity, cannot be located within any specific place. For infinity and immensity are that through which God encompasses and passes through every place. ¶ From this it is clearly evident that He is in every place, and yet exists outside of every place, immeasurably and infinitely stripped of all physical quantity and surface. This is proven by rules B, C, D, and K.

## On God through the discourse of the rule of modality.

<margin>On God through the discourse of the rule of modality.</margin>
Through Rule K, it is asked: *how* does God exist, and *how* does he act? <note>Rule K represents Modality—the "How" of a thing's being.</note> ¶ To the first part, it must be answered that God has a mode of being through the same "mode" held by his coessential and natural reasons <note>These "reasons" or "dignities" are God's attributes, like Goodness and Greatness.</note>. This is illustrated in the chapter on Place, where it is asked where God is, and how God produces within his correlatives <note>The "correlatives" are the active, passive, and verbal aspects of an attribute, such as the Good-maker, the One-made-good, and the Act-of-making-good mentioned on the previous page.</note>, as was said above. ¶ Furthermore, it is clearly apparent to anyone who knows this Art that God has a mode of acting within his relatives: just as his goodness is the reason for a "good-maker" to act "goodly," and his greatness for a "great-maker" to act "greatly," and his eternity for the reason of being eternal. Therefore, goodness is the reason for the good-maker to produce what is good, great, and eternal, and so on. This occurs intrinsically—that is, within his own essence and nature—without any "accident" or external addition. ¶ Moreover, God has a mode of acting extrinsically <note>Outside of himself, i.e., in the created world.</note> by reason of the conversion of his "dignities" <note>Divine attributes.</note>. For when God created the world, his intellect understood it, his will willed it, his power "possibilized" it <note>original: *possificavit*; made it possible or gave it the power to be.</note>, and his goodness "bonified" it <note>Made it good.</note>. For it was good to create the world; and this happened in an instant, without a sequence of his various reasons. God has this same mode in performing miracles, in judging, in sparing, in giving grace, and the like: because he wills to act upon an object, he performs the act itself; his power empowers it, and his truth makes it true. And toward such an action, the created subject is obedient. For a finite being cannot resist an infinite being.

## On God through the discourse of the rule of instrumentality.

<margin>On God through the rule of instrumentality.</margin>
The question is asked: *with what* does God exist and act? <note>Rule K also covers Instrumentality—the "With what" or the means of an action.</note> ¶ It must be answered that he exists *with* his correlative, coessential reasons, without which he cannot be what he is, nor would he be the highest being—just as a man cannot be a man without a soul, a body, and a head. For if God were the highest without his goodness, he would no longer have the nature by which he is set apart from malice; and thus he would no longer be the highest, but rather the lowest, which is impossible. And if he were the highest without immensity, he would no longer have that by which he is distinct from physical quantity. And if he were not eternal, he could not be separated from time. And if he were not powerful through himself, he would not exist through himself; and so on for the others. And since he exists through himself, as proven above, it is clear that he exists *with* his coessential reasons, without which he would not be the highest. ¶ Furthermore, God acts intrinsically *with* his reasons, as appears in his correlatives designated by the second species of Rule C. ¶ Again, he acts *with* the aforementioned reasons and relatives extrinsically and effectively, though not naturally <note>Meaning he acts by choice/will, not by a blind necessity of nature.</note>. For he inclines himself morally toward his effect: just as a just person inclines toward judging with justice, or a logician toward a syllogism with reason, and so on. ¶ We have spoken of God as deduced through Rule K; and through those things we have said of him explicitly, the practitioner of this Art can speak of God through implicit principles reduced to explicit ones, just as we have done. ¶ We have treated the first subject at great length because its matter is very vast. We will not speak of the other subjects in this way, because their matter is not so widespread. Since knowledge can be gained of those subjects through what we have said about the first subject; this is indeed signified in the Homeland <note>original: *patria*; a common theological term for Heaven or Paradise.</note>. For the saints, by beholding God as their object, know all things.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "Nine Subjects" of Ramon Llull’s philosophical system. Having discussed God on the previous page, the text now moves to the second subject: the Angel. It applies the "Principles" (the Dignities like Goodness, Magnitude, etc.) to explain the nature and function of angelic beings.</meta>

Ninth Part

# On the second subject, namely the angel: and first as deduced through the principles.

<margin>The deduction of the angel through the principles.</margin>

**T**he goodness <term>Bonitas: One of the nine "Dignities" or primary attributes in Llull’s system, representing the fundamental quality of being good.</term> of an angel is the reason why it acts for the good; in so far as such a reason is great, it is the reason why the angel performs a great good. And in so far as it is lasting, it is the reason why it performs a lasting good, and so forth. However, I do not say that an angel produces or generates another angel: for if it were so, it would exhaust itself by reason of its infinity, goodness, and indivisibility, which it possesses far removed from length and width <note>The author argues that angels are non-physical, lacking spatial dimensions like "length and width," and therefore do not reproduce like physical creatures.</note>. That which is said to be within the angel is the good act of understanding, loving, and recollecting the natural principles.

¶ Furthermore, an angel shares good words with another. But the intellect wonders why angels do not have tongues, or organs, or such things, since good speech can exist among them. This is true until the intellect remembers that their speech is nothing other than the good act of understanding, loving, and recollecting one another: for through their goodness, all of this is good.

¶ The magnitude <term>Magnitudo: The principle of greatness or scale; it ensures that the other attributes (like goodness) are not small or limited.</term> of an angel is the reason why its goodness and duration are great. Whence it follows that goodness is great through its correlatives <term>Correlatives: A central Llullian concept where every attribute has an active part, a passive part, and the action itself. For example, Goodness consists of the "Good-ifier," the "Good-ifiable," and the "Act of making good."</term>, without which it would not be great.

¶ But here the intellect wonders: what does the angel "make good" <note>original: *bonificat*</note>, since it does not produce or generate another angel? It wonders until it remembers the act of the other "good-ifying" principles within its own proper "good-ifiable" part: just as the intellect makes other intelligible or understood principles within its own proper "intelligible" <note>Llull is explaining that an angel's activity is internal and spiritual, directed at its own essence rather than external reproduction.</note>.

¶ The duration of an angel is the reason by which it lasts: and its principles and acts also last in an instant, without a succession of time. But the intellect wonders what the cause of its sustenance is, since it does not receive nourishment or growth from the outside. It wonders until it remembers the angelic nature: which is certainly not composed of contrary elements <note>In medieval science, physical bodies decay because they are made of "contraries" (like hot and cold) that struggle; angels, being pure spirit, have no such internal conflict.</note>. And if the sun, which is a corporeal being, lasts without nourishment, how much more so an angel, which is a spirit stripped of any surface <note>original: *a superficie denudatus*; meaning it has no physical exterior or dimensions.</note>.

¶ The power <term>Potestas: The principle that enables a being to exist and to act.</term> of an angel is the reason why it is able to exist and act. But the intellect wonders, since the angel has no organs to serve as its instruments for acting. At that time, it remembers the correlatives of its power, with which it acts as if by means of instruments of "possification" <note>original: *possificando*; a term coined by Llull to describe the act of making something possible or exercising power.</note>. For just as heat, which is an accident, is the instrument with which fire is able to act by heating, so and much more so can an angel exist and act through the correlatives of its power. For these correlatives are substantial to it. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that the consubstantial principles of the angels are to them as if they were instruments.

¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the reason why the angel is at a higher level than lower beings.

¶ The intellect of an angel is the reason by which it understands with its correlatives: for with its "intellective" part it is "understanding"—that is, it is active in understanding within its "intelligible" part, in which it understands other beings. What wonder if it does this? For fire, which does not have as high a virtue as an angel, heats other elements within its own "ignitable" <note>original: *ignibili*; the part of a substance capable of being transformed by fire.</note> part.

¶ Yet the intellect still wonders in what manner the intellect of an angel understands things, since it does not form "species" <note>In medieval psychology, "species" were the mental images or signals filtered from the physical world through the five senses.</note> through the senses or through the imagination.

¶ But it remembers that the angelic intellect is like an instrument for understanding; yet it is consubstantial to the angel, just as the other principles are consubstantial to it, like the will of a man is for willing. But it is much more so for the angel, because a man cannot will without a bodily organ; the angel, however, who is a higher creature than man, can understand without an organ joined to it.

¶ An angel certainly uses its will as an instrument—though in truth it is not an instrument—for the natural will is in the angel for the purpose of willing: so that with that will it may perform the act of loving <note>original: *diligibilitatez*; here meaning the "lovability" or the act of choosing to love.</note> assigned to it by the supreme order.

¶ But the intellect wonders: what is the cause by which the will of an angel can love those things which are neither in the senses nor in the imagination? But it remembers its own rudeness and coarseness <note>The human intellect is described as "coarse" because it is tied to the physical body.</note> which it possesses because it is joined with sense and imagination. The will of an angel, however, can relate to an object without sense or imagination much more than a plant can relate to an "appetite" without sense or imagination.

¶ An angel has virtue <term>Virtus: In this context, both moral virtue and the inherent power or strength of a being.</term> with which it naturally acts within its own principles, insofar as through that virtue they are virtuous, and they have virtuous acts—and through goodness, they are good, and through magnitude, they are great, etc.

¶ But the intellect wonders in what way an angel acquires accidental virtues, until it remembers that an angel possesses virtuous habits by directing itself toward objects through virtuous understanding and loving: and also by acting justly, prudently, and charitably while helping us against sins and evil angels, bringing us proclamations from the Supreme Principle <note>God.</note>, reporting our prayers to Him, and praying for us.

¶ An angel, through its virtue, is a true "understander," "lover," and "rememberer," just as a man is—though much better—who through his soul truly understands, loves, and remembers; and through imagination truly imagines; and through...

¶ But the intellect wonders about this until it remembers the <term>elementatum: A physical body composed of the four elements (fire, air, water, earth).</term> elemented body, in which many elements agree in one composite: through fire it is ignited and heated; through air it is made airy and moistened; through water it is made watery and cooled; and through earth it is made earthy and dried. ¶ An angel is not composed of contraries <note>In medieval science, the four elements were "contraries" (e.g., hot vs. cold). Since angels are purely spiritual, they lack these conflicting physical qualities.</note>: for it is outside the elements by nature, just as it is outside of points, numbers, shapes, and the like.

¶ The angel is the medium or subject in which its End flows into its principles, and the principles flow back to the End, with each principle measuring itself with another only as much as it itself is: so that from them there is one complete substance. ¶ But the intellect wonders, since an angel does not have "quantity" in the sense of a physical line, in what way it can have measurements, as if it could be composed of several principles; this continues until it remembers <term>quantitas spiritualis: Spiritual quantity; the idea that a soul or angel can be "larger" in power or grace without taking up physical space.</term> spiritual quantity, sustained in a subject outside of lines and points: without which one angel could not have a greater essence and act than another; nor could one angel receive from God greater glory than another.

¶ The End of angels consists of two modes: namely, naturally and supernaturally. The natural end is like being a good, great end, etc., so that it may naturally have good and great acts. The supernatural end is that which comes from the part of its supreme object <note>The "supreme object" is God.</note>, which is supremely intelligible, lovable, and honorable. And because God is understood, loved, and recollected through the angel—whereas God is not "made" good or great through the angel—the intellect, will, and memory in the essence of the angel are directed toward a higher end than its other principles.

¶ But the intellect wonders about this "majority" and "minority" <note>Meaning "superiority" and "inferiority" or "greater" and "lesser" degrees of power.</note> existing within it, since in its essence all its principles are equal; this continues until it remembers what was said about its object above. ¶ The superiority which an angel has regarding its species is greater than the superiority of a human regarding his species. And therefore, just as a magnet attracts iron through its species <note>The original Latin uses "adamas," which can mean diamond or magnet/lodestone; here the context of attracting iron clearly indicates a magnet.</note>, so an angel, through the superiority of its species, has knowledge of lower things without a physical organ, and even power over them without an organ. ¶ But the intellect wonders in what way this can be; this continues until it remembers that this mode is difficult for the human to know, but not for the angel to perform: for the angel has a greater superiority regarding its species than a man regarding his. ¶ In an angel there is an equality of intellect...

### On the angel, deduced through Rule B.

**T**hrough <term>Rule B: A logical tool in Llull’s system used to ask "Whether a thing exists" or "If it is possible."</term> Rule B, it is asked whether an angel exists, or if angels exist. And therefore divine wisdom is knowable; and just as it is knowable and lovable, it is knowable and lovable with the greatness of its own "knowability" <note>original: "scibilitas"</note> and lovability. Therefore, it is most knowable and most lovable <unclear>having been attained</unclear>; and consequently so is its effect, because the effect is lovable. Therefore, the angel is a great effect, the best and greatest that could exist in a creature. And if it were not an effect of divine goodness, it would be more knowable...

## On the angel as derived through rule D.

<margin>On the angel derived through rule D.</margin>
Through the first aspect of rule D <note>Rule D in this system usually asks "De quo?" or "From what?"—inquiring into the origin or material of a thing.</note> it is asked: from what is an angel made? And it must be answered that it is made of itself, because it is not derived from any other thing. The reason for this is so that its innate goodness, magnitude, and so on, may be its innate, primary, dissimilar, and incorruptible principles, so that its essence can be permanent and incorruptible; nevertheless, we say that it was created by God. ¶ Through the second aspect it is asked: from what is the angel made? And it must be answered that it is made of its innate principles, such as its true goodness, magnitude, and so on. This is because each principle exists within it in a threefold way: such as goodness through the **good-made**, the **good-makeable**, and the **act of making good**; and magnitude through the **great-made**, the **great-makeable**, and the **act of making great**, and so on. <note>These are technical terms from Lullian logic: the "agent" (the one doing), the "patient" (the one receiving), and the "act" itself. This creates a trinity within every attribute.</note> And because these principles differ essentially, the angel is composed of its goodness, magnitude, and so on. And from all its "active" principles <note>original: "tiuis"; referring to the suffixes of active principles like *bonificativus*.</note> one common **form** is constituted within it with which it is active; and from all its "passive" principles <note>original: "bilis"; referring to suffixes like *bonificabilis*.</note>, namely the good-makeable and the great-makeable, etc., one **matter** is constituted with which it is passive. And from all its acts—namely, the act of making good, making great, etc.—one common **act** is constituted with which it causes external actions. Thus, from all the three aforementioned things, its substance is composed, united, and substantially separated from all physical matter. ¶ Through the third aspect it is asked: to whom does the angel belong? And it must be answered that it belongs to God with blessing, glory, and glorification; but the evil angel belongs to God with contradiction, punishment, and pain.

## On the angel as derived through rule E.

<margin>On the angel derived through rule E.</margin>
Through the first aspect of rule E <note>Rule E usually asks "Quare?" or "Why?"—inquiring into the reason or formal cause of existence.</note> it is asked: why is there an angel? And it must be answered that it is constituted from its natural principles, as we said above in the second aspect of rule D. Since its principle is composed with another, it is necessary that a being exists that is necessarily composed. Just as it is said that once the soul is joined with the body, a human follows by necessity. And once the elemental power is placed with the vegetative power, a vegetative element follows by necessity. ¶ Through the second aspect it is asked: why is there an angel? And it must be answered with respect to its "end" <note>The "end" or *finis* refers to the final purpose of a thing's existence.</note> that an angel exists so that it may understand, love, and recall God, and do Him honor, and fill the universe; for if there were no angel in its place, the universe would be a vacuum, as was proven above.

## On the angel as derived through rule F.

<margin>On the angel derived through rule F.</margin>
Through rule F <note>Rule F asks "Quantum?" or "How much?"—inquiring into the quantity or magnitude of a thing.</note> it is asked: how great is an angel? It must be answered that it is as great as the "being" of its essence is; this "being" has **continuous quantity** insofar as it is one substance. And it has **discrete quantities** because it is composed of many principles; and that this is true was indicated in the second aspect of rule D, where it is asked "from what" an angel is made. ¶ Through rule G <note>Rule G asks "Quale?" or "Of what kind?"—inquiring into the qualities of a thing.</note> it is asked: what kind of being is an angel? It must be answered that an angel is of two kinds: namely, through innate and proper qualities, and through appropriated qualities that are not natural to it. We call its natural and substantial goodness, magnitude, and so on, from which it is constituted, its "proper" qualities. And we call its acquired goodness, magnitude, justice, and so on, "appropriated" qualities. And in the evil angel, we call its malice, envy, and so on, "appropriated" qualities. ¶ Through rule H...

### Part Nine

->**It asks**<- about the time of an angel. And we say that an angel is in time because it was begun in time, without which beginning it would not have existed. The reason for this is: that which currently exists but once did not cannot exist without time. Furthermore, an angel is in time with regard to its opposites: that is, without succession and without motion; but when it acts outside itself, it acts from one "now" <note>original: "nunc"; in medieval philosophy, a 'now' is a discrete, indivisible instant of time.</note> into another. For example, when it acts on Sunday, it is doing that which it was doing on Saturday. And it is in one time when it is in Rome during the day, and in another time when it is in Paris at night. However, when it departs from Rome and is in Paris, its departure is without motion and without succession. For just as it does not require eyes to see color, so it does not require motion or succession in its departure; it simply wills, and it is where it wills.

¶ Through Rule *i* <note>The "Rules" (identified by letters like i, k, d) are part of a logical machine or system used by the author to provide structured answers to any philosophical question.</note>, it is asked about the place of an angel. The answer is that an angel is in a place because it was created in a place; but it is not in a place as something occupying space. This is because space cannot be occupied without lines, angles, and shapes, from which every angel is separate <note>Meaning angels are incorporeal and do not have physical dimensions.</note>. It is in a place in the sense that it is in one place and not in another where it is not; and it is in that place where it acts, for it cannot act in a place without being present. The reason for this is that it acts with its own essence and not with a physical organ.

¶ Through the first species of Rule *k*, it is asked how an angel exists and how it acts. The answer is that an angel has a mode of being through the composition of its principles, as was illustrated in the second species of Rule *d* above. And it has a mode of acting with its principles, with which it causes external acts: just as with its goodness something is "bonified" <note>original: "bonificatum"; a technical term meaning to make something good or to imbue it with goodness.</note>, and with its power something is "possified" <term>possificatus: a Lullian term meaning 'made powerful' or 'brought into the realm of power'</term>, and so on for the others.

¶ Through the second species of Rule *k*, it is asked with whom an angel is and with whom it acts. The answer is that it is with its innate and natural principles joined together, as was shown in Rule *d*. And it acts with them: namely, it understands with its intellect, it loves with its will, and it remembers with its memory. If it is good, it "bonifies" with its goodness and exercises power with its power. But if it is evil, it "evil-ifies" <note>original: "malificat"; the author creates this verb to show how an evil nature corrupts the very functions of thinking and loving.</note> its understanding, its remembering, and its loving; and thus it acts with its principles both intrinsically and extrinsically by causing an external act through an internal one. It is like a human being who creates words in the mind which they then produce with the mouth.

# On the Heaven, deduced through principles.

<margin>On the heaven, deduced through principles.</margin>

**I**n this chapter we shall treat the heaven alongside its innate principles from which it is composed, and how it relates to the lower principles <note>The "lower principles" refer to the four elements and the earthly realm of change and decay.</note> as a cause relates to its effect. ¶ The heaven is good through its innate goodness and is great through its natural magnitude. Therefore, its goodness and its magnitude are the reasons why it acts well, greatly, and naturally upon these lower things by moving itself and others. 

And if it is said that it sometimes acts badly—as in the case of Saturn, which is considered "evil"—I respond that this happens "by accident" <note>In philosophy, 'by accident' means a secondary or unintended consequence, rather than a primary intent.</note>. This is because lower things do not receive the influence well due to the conflicts between the elements; for this reason, Saturn sometimes causes monstrosities in lower things through excessive coldness and dryness. 

¶ The heaven is great and durable. It is great in essence and in its power to act; and it is durable because it is incorruptible and immaterial. There is no being except God that can compel it or hinder its motion. ¶ The heaven is durable in itself because duration is its innate quality. ¶ The heaven is powerful in itself because its power is an innate quality; and just as its duration is great and good, so its power is good and great. In this passage, it appears that the heaven can move itself, so that its goodness, magnitude, and duration do not fail its power, nor its power fail them.

¶ Just as the heaven has a natural will co-essential to itself, so it has a natural instinct co-essential to itself with which it governs its order, its motion, and the acts of its principles. Without this instinct, it could not do these things. For example, a lion has one instinct in common with Saturn through heat, dryness, cold, "nocturnality," masculinity, longevity, malice, plurality, and "dyasobristic" nature <term>dyasobristatem: a specialized term referring to the specific astrological influence or 'flavor' of the planet Saturn</term>. It has another instinct with Jupiter through goodness, "stagnation," and "dyajovian" nature <term>dyaioueicatem: a term referring to the specific astrological influence of the planet Jupiter</term>, and so on for the others. 

¶ The heaven has instinct, as stated above, and it has "appetite" <note>original: "appetitum"; in this context, a natural inclination or cosmic desire for its own perfection.</note>. With its appetite, it moves itself and lower things so that they might have an inclination toward it. It has one appetite with one planet and another with another, as was exemplified above regarding instinct. ¶ The heaven has appetite and it has virtue (power). And just as its appetite is natural and co-essential to it, so is its virtue. And just as its appetite is good through its goodness and great through its magnitude, so is its virtue. And just as it has one appetite with the lion...

This "difference" itself is imperceptible to the senses because it is a general principle. ¶ The **Heaven** consists of many differences, just as a whole consists of its many parts. And "concordance" <note>original: "concordantia"</note> is a principle co-essential to it, with which it causes many concords. Thus, it is one substance having many things within itself through difference and concordance. ¶ The **Heaven** has concordance: as has been said: and it has a "foreign contrariety" <note>original: "contrarietate peregrinam"; meaning a contrariety that is not part of its essential nature</note> that is not co-essential to it, so that it does not become corruptible. Rather, it is an instrument by which it opposes lower things, such as through heat and cold, dryness and moisture, through day and night, and things of this sort. With these, it causes monstrosities, lightning, thunder, sicknesses, misfortunes, and the like. Contrariety is not a principle of the heaven co-essential to it, but concordance is its principle, as has been said. And thus, the heaven acts more upon lower things by concord than by contrariety, by reason of which there are more instances of health than sickness, more good fortune than misfortune, and more frequently a man is born with two eyes than with one; and so it is with other things. ¶ The **Heaven** has its innate principles: as has been said: with which it gives a beginning to lower things effectively, through the mediation of lower natural beings, such as the qualities of the heavens and their properties. And just as with the elements, so with metals, plants, and sentient beings. To this concurs the magnitude of the heaven, which magnifies the power of the heaven and its instinct, appetite, virtue, and such things. From this follows the influence from higher things to lower things, and the "reflux" <note>original: "refluentia"; a returning flow</note> from lower things back up to the moon, and this happens continuously. The reason for this is that the heaven is always in continuous motion. ¶ In the **Heaven** there is a "mean" <note>original: "medium"; the middle point or connecting link in a process</note> co-essential to it, with which it causes lower means; just as the celestial "good-making" <note>original: "bonificare"; a technical term in this system for the active principle of goodness</note> causes eternal good-making, and celestial moving causes earthly moving, and so with others. ¶ The **Heaven** has a mean: as said above: through which and with which its principles pass toward their ends, so that they may rest in it. This "rest" consists in moving itself and lower things. The reason for this is that it was created for this purpose. ¶ The **End** of the heaven is with "majority" <note>original: "maioritate"; the state of being greater or fulfilling a higher purpose</note>, so that it may serve man, and man may serve God. For its end cannot be at a higher level than this. That is, beneath that greater end is its own "greater end," which is to move, etc. Just as the greater end of the vegetative power is to grow, and the greater end of the sensitive power is to feel. ¶ We have spoken of the majority of the heaven; and its greatest equality <note>original: "equalitas"; the balance of its internal principles</note> is the equality of its co-essential principles. The equalities of the heaven participate in "minority" <note>original: "minoritate"; the state of being lesser</note> with respect to the soul, because the heaven does not possess intellect, memory, and will, nor can it receive merit.

<insert>Decorative initial Q</insert> **It is asked**, whether the heaven exists from eternity. And it must be answered that it does not, as is indicated by Rule B <note>Rule B in this system usually asks "Whether a thing exists?" or "What is it?" and refers back to the primary principle of Goodness</note>. But for the greater evidence of this science, or art and teaching, we intend in this chapter to explain what pertains to the heaven. Through what we shall say about the heaven, we will give the student <note>original: "artiste"; literally a practitioner of the Art</note> the doctrine by which he will know how to act. And because we wish to avoid prolixity, we will apply Rule B only to the other letters placed in the alphabet of this Art up to R. And just as we apply B to the other letters, so can the other letters be applied to one another in turn. ¶ If the heaven were from eternity, it would not have been created from nothing, because it would have always been; nor would it have been made from something, because beyond the heaven there is no matter from which it could be made, nor within it, because its magnitude contains all things. And thus, divine goodness would not be the reason for God to act as a "good heaven," nor by the goodness of the heaven, because it would be eternal. And the same applies to the magnitude of God, which would not cause the magnitude of the heaven. Whence it follows that the world is not an effect as to its goodness and magnitude...

### Part Nine.

Therefore, there is a difference between God's goodness and the heaven's goodness, or a concordance; the same applies to magnitude, which requires a concordance according to justice between the cause and the effect. Therefore, if concordance is deprived, contrariety and injury arise, and greed is caused. God's goodness would not be a reason for Him to perform a great good effect if God did not consent to the reason of His own goodness. Since all these things are impossible, it follows that the heaven is created and new <note>The term "new" (novum) in medieval philosophy refers to something that has a beginning in time, rather than existing from eternity.</note>.

¶ **B.d.** If the heaven is eternal, then there are multiple eternities: namely, the eternity of God and the eternity of the heaven. Moreover, within the eternity of the heaven, infinite other eternities are implied, such as its innate goodness, its duration, and so on; the same would apply to its stars and their revolutions. Thus, injury and gluttony would have existed as early as justice and malice, and contrariety would be as old as goodness and concordance among men. This is because there would never have been a first man, nor a second, nor will there ever be a last. In this scenario, divine goodness fails, and there is no reason for God that divine goodness should precede malice, or that God's eternity should precede the heaven's eternity. It also follows that there would be no "other life" <note>the afterlife</note>, because all the matter contained within the heaven would not be sufficient for the resurrection of dead men—a point they <note>likely referring to the philosophers who argue for an eternal world</note> intend to prove. Thus God's justice would be defective and hindered from rewarding the just and punishing the unjust eternally; injury and malice would be the causes of this. God's strength would be weakened, and lust would be eternal. Since all these things would be impossible, it follows that the heaven is new and had a beginning.

¶ **B.e.** If the heaven is eternal through itself, it can be eternal; for an eternal being was never in potentiality to exist, nor is it in potentiality not to exist. Thus God's power would not be the cause of the heaven's power, nor God's goodness the cause of the heaven's goodness. Furthermore, God's power could not deprive the heaven of its power, because the heaven would govern itself through itself. Thus pride would be eternal, and consequently, sin. ¶ Whence it follows that the heaven would contain its own end within itself, and God would not be its end. For when the cause is removed, the effect is removed. Since all these things are evil, injurious, and full of pride—and it has been shown through Rule B that they are impossible—the negative side of the question <note>that the heaven is NOT eternal</note> must be held.

¶ **B.f.** If the heaven is eternal, then time is eternal. Thus God's eternity would not precede time, which is against justice and faith. Sloth <note>original: "acidia," or acedia, the "noonday devil" of spiritual apathy</note> would be eternal, and eternal injury would follow. This would be known by divine wisdom; and God's goodness is the reason for God to act for the good by destroying the aforementioned evils; yet [in an eternal world] God does not consent to this. Thus His own wisdom would know Him to be injurious, lazy, and evil. Since all these are impossible, therefore, etc.

¶ **B.g.** If the heaven is eternal, there is either one general eternal will for all the wills of men, from which all other particular wills are materially generated; or God creates the particular wills of men. If there is one general will, that general will is divisible, and particular wills are eternally corruptible parts of the general. Thus injury is done to those particular wills that love God. God's justice would not have an eternal judgment over them, nor over the wills that hate God and hope, and love envy. These things are impossible and against God's justice and goodness, even assuming that particular wills are not destroyed; for a general will could not suffice as the "matter" for this. Therefore, it is impossible for there to be a general eternal will. And if wills are created by God while the heaven is eternal, then creation has no end in which to rest, because there was never a first will, nor a second, nor will there be a last. This leads to the same inconvenience we stated in paragraph **B.d.**; therefore, etc.

¶ **B.h.** If the heaven is eternal, virtues and vices have existed from eternity, and in quantity, the vices are greater than the virtues. Divine goodness and charity are the reason for God that virtues should be greater than vices; yet [if the world were eternal] God would not consent to this. Thus He would be injurious and acting against His own charity and justice, which is impossible; therefore the opposite <note>that the world is not eternal</note> is necessary.

¶ **B.i.** If the heaven is eternal, its eternity is equal in duration to the eternity of God. Truth would be a lie, and patience and impatience <note>original: "patientia in patientia," likely a scribal error or contraction for "patience and impatience"</note> would be equally eternal. Since all these are against divine goodness, justice, and truth, it follows that the heaven is new; and it is just that divine goodness and truth should precede the duration of the heaven through their eternity, just as they precede the heaven’s limited and finite goodness and truth by their own immensity and infinity.

¶ **B.k.** If the heaven is eternal, the liberal and mechanical arts have existed from eternity. Thus there was no rest in this life. Piety and inconstancy would not be eternal, and consequently, neither would the hammer and the tongs <note>A common Llullian argument: if the world were eternal, even common tools like the "martellus et forpices" would have to be eternal or part of an infinite series, which was considered absurd.</note>. One eternity does not create another, nor does it rest in another. It would be a "minority" regarding nothing, and would never pass into nothing. Since all these things are evil and injurious, and against divine goodness and justice, it follows by necessity that the heaven...

The author argues that an eternal world would compromise God's justice, make the resurrection of the dead impossible, and imply that evil is as eternal as God.</summary>

## On the heaven, deduced through rule C. <note>In the Lullian system, "Rule C" asks the question "What is it?" (Quid est?).</note>

**P**rough the first species of rule C, it is asked: what is the heaven? And it must be answered that it is the **first movable thing** <term>primum mobile: the outermost sphere in medieval cosmology which moves all other spheres</term>; and it is a body having the greatest magnitude and the greatest motion. Beyond it, there is nothing movable. It is a body that moves by itself, because no mobility is greater than its own; and therefore, motion begins from it (speaking naturally) and remains from it. It is the fountain from which motion is at times derived, like streams from a spring. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does the heaven have in itself that is coessential and natural to it? And it must be answered that it has its own motivity, mobility, and the act of moving. Through its motivity it has its **form**; through its mobility it has its **matter**; and through moving, it has the **act** with which it creates external acts. It also has its innate goodness, magnitude, etc., and also the stars, planets, and signs <note>The zodiac signs</note>, and likewise for its other coessential parts. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is the heaven in another thing? And it must be answered that the heaven is in the elements as an agent, moving and influencing them, while having no "passion" <note>In this sense, "passion" means being acted upon or suffering change from an external source.</note> within itself from them. This is by reason of its great activity and motivity; also, in itself, it receives neither increase nor diminution. And the intellect marvels at this: how the heaven can be in such great motivity without any alteration or mutation of its substance. But the strong mind can consider the infinite divine power, which can create such an effect according to His pleasure. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does the heaven have in another thing? And it must be answered that the heaven naturally has dominion over the elements and "elemented" things <note>Things composed of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water), such as plants, animals, and humans.</note>. With this dominion, it causes natural movements in the lower regions: the four seasons, days, hours, thunder, lightning, wind, rain, snow, monthly cycles <note>original: "menstruositates," referring to lunar or periodic cycles in nature</note>, infirmities, and the like. It does this because lower things receive their movements and influences from the heaven, which acts as the efficient cause. ¶ Through the first species of rule D <note>Rule D asks: "Of what is it made?" (De quo?)</note>, it is asked: of what is the heaven made? It must be answered that it is of itself, because it is not made of any pre-existing matter from which it was derived. And because it is primarily of itself due to its "primitivity," it is incorruptible; and through itself, it is permanent in its motivity. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what is the heaven composed? And it must be answered that it is of its coessential parts: such as its innate goodness, magnitude, etc.

And this is signified by the second species of rule D. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to whom does the heaven belong? It must be answered that it belongs to God, just as an effect belongs to its cause; and because it is possessed by God, it causes effects in lower things as God wills. ¶ Through the first species of rule E <note>Rule E asks: "Why is it?" (Quare?)</note>, it is asked: why is there a heaven? And it must be answered that the heaven exists because it is constituted of its coessential parts, such as its innate goodness, magnitude, etc., excluding **contrariety** <note>The quality of having opposites (like hot and cold), which causes decay. Since heaven has no contrariety, it does not decay.</note>, which is not coessential to it; for if it were, it would be corruptible. It also exists because its celestial matter and form are joined within it, by which it is necessitated, just as a man exists when the soul and body are joined within him. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why is there a heaven? And it must be answered by reason of its **end** (purpose): that the heaven exists so that, as a "caused creator," it may cause the lower movements with which man is disposed to exist and to serve God. ¶ Through the first species of rule F <note>Rule F asks: "How much?" (Quantum?)</note>, it is asked: concerning the quantity of the heaven? And it must be answered that the heaven has quantity that is both continuous and discrete. It is continuous in a circular fashion, as it is shaped; it is discrete, as seen through the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note>, which is concave, and likewise for the sphere of Saturn, etc. ¶ Through rule G <note>Rule G asks: "What kind?" (Quale?)</note>, it is asked: what kind of thing is the heaven? And it must be answered that it is "of a kind" through its own appropriated primary qualities, such as its innate goodness, magnitude, its motion, and its figures; and likewise for its quantity. These are appropriated as heat and dryness, coldness and moisture, masculinity and femininity, and the like. And it is said that its appropriated qualities are in it because it acts with them upon lower things; just as the sun is said to be "hot and dry" because it heats and dries things out. ¶ Through rule H <note>Rule H asks: "When?" (Quando?)</note>, it is asked: concerning the time of the heaven? And it must be answered that the essence of the eighth sphere is in that "now" in which it was created; like a circle which exists without succession in regards to its essence. But by reason of its motion, it causes time in lower things: as in Saturn, which moves successively from one "now" to another "now." And there is "one day" from the eighth sphere down to the sphere of fire; but from the sphere of fire down to the earth, there are many days and many nights, by reason of the presence and absence of the sun. Thus, the sun is the reason why there are many days, nights, hours, and so forth. ¶ Through rule I <note>Rule I asks: "Where?" (Ubi?)</note>, it is asked: concerning the place of the heaven? And it must be answered that the eighth sphere is in that place in which it was created in regards to its essence; and so for Saturn, etc. But by reason of motion and many circles...

# Ninth part.

...positions <note>The text begins mid-word: likely "positions" or "operations"</note> from the eighth sphere down to the sphere of fire <term>sphere of fire: in medieval cosmology, the region between the moon and the upper atmosphere</term>, with respect to their alignment, occurs in several places. For example, Saturn is at one time joined with Aries, and at another time with Taurus. It is the same with the Sun, which is in one place of the heaven at one time, and in another place at another; in one place it causes day by its presence, and in another it causes night. 

¶ Through the first species of Rule R <note>In the Lullian system, "Rule R" typically investigates "How?" or "Modality."</note>, it is asked: how is the heaven? And the answer is that the heaven is modal <note>Meaning it possesses specific modes of being</note> through the particular modalities that belong to its essence, which are its innate parts: such as **goodness**, **magnitude**, etc. And likewise regarding its habit, position, and such things. 

¶ Through the second species of Rule R, it is asked: with what is the heaven? The answer is that it is with its natural parts with which it is composed: such as its **goodness**, **magnitude**, etc., with which it causes circular motions, as well as mobile goodnesses, magnitudes, and so forth.

### On the fourth subject, which is about man, through the principles of discourse.

**I**n man, his goodness exists as the reason why he should act for a specific good. Indeed, whatever a man does by virtue of his species, he does either naturally or morally. In man, spiritual and corporal goodness are joined by reason of his soul and body. Therefore, by this duality of reasons, he has a nature or reason for acting well: intellectually—by objecting, understanding, loving, and remembering; and corporally—such as by generating a human being, and by sensing and imagining. From both of these come forth good operations, as appears in the **liberal arts** <term>liberal arts: the traditional academic curriculum of the Middle Ages, including grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy</term> and the **mechanical arts** <term>mechanical arts: practical crafts like architecture, agriculture, or metalworking</term>. 

¶ In man, his **magnitude** <note>Meaning his greatness or extent</note> is twofold, just like his goodness. Therefore, when a man performs a good act, he performs it with magnitude as a "great" act, just as with goodness he performs it as a "good" act. 

¶ In man there is **duration**; and this is the reason for his goodness and magnitude, and likewise for other things that endure. This is twofold, as was said above: natural, and also moral or by choice. 

¶ In man, his **power** is twofold, as was said of goodness. It is that by which he is able to exist and to act. From this, it is clear that he can exist and act through his species. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes in what way it possesses a specific liberty for acting. 

¶ In man, his **intellect** is a specific thing with which he specially understands. It is not that his intellect descends from another intellect by way of generation, nor is it essentially the same as another intellect. Otherwise, it would have been "begotten," and also after the death of the man it would be annihilated or corrupted. It would also be situated in time, place, quantity, surface, division, succession, and motion; it would have shape, points, and lines—which is impossible. ¶ For all these things belong to the nature of "corporality," or the body. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that those who thought and affirmed that there was only **one single intellect** for all men spoke wrongly and falsely <note>This is a critique of "Monopsychism" or Averroism, the controversial theory that all humans share a single collective intellect.</note>. 

¶ Furthermore, our intellect recognizes through what has been said that the natural instinct of the human body is joined with the human intellect, as was said regarding goodness. ¶ The intellect has a mode through which it creates an "intelligible species" <term>intelligible species: a mental representation or concept</term> through the senses and the imagination within its own proper understanding, from which intelligible species it creates knowledge. 

¶ In man, his **will** is a specific power for him, with which he performs specific acts of loving. This will does not descend from some other general will; for otherwise, its essence would be subject to being generated or corrupted (just as was said of the intellect), and its liberty would be destroyed because it would be forced to will by its general principle. It would be like a body that has appetites by necessity through that which is superior to it—as when it hungers for food, drink, or sex, or craves heat when it feels great cold, and so on. ¶ Furthermore, if everyone had one single will, all men would be directed toward the same object at the same time, and also, when a man died, the rational soul would die. In that case, there would be no other life, nor would the justice and mercy of God have a subject in which to act—which is impossible and a great absurdity of differences. 

¶ Furthermore, the appetite of the body and the will are joined, as was said of goodness; by reason of this, the will creates species through the sensitive and imaginative faculties by the act of willing, just as the intellect does by the act of understanding; and the same can be said in its own way of the **memory**, which is a part of the soul. 

¶ In man, corporal and spiritual **virtue** <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to both moral character and "power" or "strength."</note> are joined; and because spiritual virtue is superior, it therefore forms and perfects the lower virtue. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the way in which moral virtues arise from spiritual and corporal virtue, as if from form and matter; we shall speak of these virtues in the ninth subject. 

¶ In man there is spiritual and corporal **truth**; and because spiritual truth is superior, it therefore perfects the lower truth. From this, the intellect recognizes that...

# On the nine subjects.

Just as the sense of nature perceives through sight and hearing, and so on with the other senses, so the soul truly reaches the essences of things by understanding, loving, and remembering. For otherwise, the lower part [the senses] would act more effectively with its own power than the higher part [the soul] would with its own, which is absurd to the reasoning of the intellect. And in this realization, the intellect rejoices greatly. ¶ In man, natural, spiritual, and corporal glory are joined: that is, natural pleasures are joined both spiritually and corporally. From this it follows that the soul has pleasure in acting within the body, and the body under the soul in experiencing that action, and the whole man with both of them together. ¶ And here the intellect recognizes in what manner a man experiences pleasure in his movements. ¶ In man, spiritual and corporal differences are joined: by reason of which the intellect understands in one way through sight, and in another through hearing, and so on with the others. Similarly, the body experiences in one way under the intellect, in another under the will, and in another under the memory. And through these aforementioned things, the intellect recognizes the manner in which it creates knowledge through discourse, the will creates love through loving, and the memory creates recollection through remembering.

¶ In man, the soul and body agree with one another by composing him, while the soul remains in its own essence and the body likewise in its own. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the way the soul and body agree by focusing on the same object: the body through seeing, hearing, and such things; the soul through understanding, loving, and remembering. ¶ The body of man is composed of the four elements. The soul, however, is not made of contraries, because it is incorruptible. And because the soul and body are joined in man, man therefore experiences "direct" and natural contrarieties <note>Physical struggles like heat vs. cold or health vs. sickness.</note> on the part of the body, but on the part of the soul, he experiences "oblique" and accidental contrarieties. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that every sin is an accident <note>In scholastic philosophy, an "accident" is something that is not part of the core essence. This means Llull believes sin is a deviation, not a fundamental part of the soul's nature.</note>. ¶ Since the soul and body are joined in man, man is an efficient cause, moving form into matter for the sake of an end: specifically, he moves the soul within the body. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which man is an efficient, material, formal, and final principle <note>These are the four Aristotelian causes: the actor, the stuff, the shape, and the purpose.</note>. ¶ In man, the soul and body are joined, in which act the "conjunction" signifies that there is a medium <note>A middle ground or bridge.</note> influenced by both the soul and the body. And this medium is the conatural and substantial act of understanding, willing, remembering, "elementating" <term>elementating: the process of physical composition involving the four elements</term>, vegetating, sensing, and imagining. Without these, man would not be substantially joined.

And man lives only as long as this material conjunction lasts in him; for when it is dissolved, man dies immediately. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which the soul and body are joined and how they measure their acts by dispensing and proportioning them, with the soul flowing in its power and the body flowing back its own, with man existing as the middle ground brought into the "third number" <note>The "third number" likely refers to the human person as the result of the union (1. Soul + 2. Body = 3. Man).</note>. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which there is radical and nutrimental moisture in man. Radical moisture <term>Radical moisture: A vital fluid medieval thinkers believed we are born with; it acts like the oil in a lamp, sustaining the flame of life.</term> is derived from primitive principles, points, and lines with which the soul is joined. And nutrimental moisture is its instrument, just like a weaver’s shuttle in a loom, in which points and lines are introduced through the movement of the "elementative," "vegetative," "sensitive," and "imaginative" powers, by flowing in and flowing back. And the radical moisture lives and increases itself from that which comes from outside, thus converting it into its own species through the vegetative power. ¶ Just as the vegetative power transforms <term>transubstantiates: Llull uses this word to describe how food is fundamentally changed into the substance of the person</term> food into flesh, nerves, and bones, and drink into blood; and it transforms food and drink into marrow, and also into bile <note>original: "colera"</note>, phlegm, and melancholy <note>original: "melancolia"</note>, and brain; and it changes them into the water of the eyes [tears], into spit, and even into sweat. ¶ In man, the spiritual end and the corporal end are joined naturally: by reason of which man conducts himself toward the aforementioned ends—toward the spiritual end with the soul, and toward the corporal end with the body. And indeed, from the soul and body, moral ends arise or emerge, with which the soul and body find the pleasures in which they rest. ¶ In man, the soul is the greater substantial image. But the body is the lesser image than the image of the soul. ¶ Furthermore, in the body, the imagination is a greater "sensitive image" because it presents objects and also moves the sensitive power itself secondarily; and the sensitive power is a greater image than the vegetative power, for it is grafted and founded upon it. And in turn, the vegetative power is greater than the elementative power, for the vegetative is founded upon the elementative. And so, in this step, the intellect recognizes that just as the substantial powers are greater and lesser, so too are the accidental powers in man. The soul and body are not equal; for the soul possesses superior principles, while the body possesses inferior ones. Nevertheless, they are joined: the soul is indeed entirely in the body, and vice-versa, so that man is equally joined and composed. Because man is brought forth from nothing in respect to creation, he is therefore placed in a state of minority <note>In Llull's hierarchy, being created from nothing means man is "lesser" (in minority) compared to God, yet he is the peak of the physical world.</note>.

### On man, derived through rules.

<margin>
Derivation of all through rules.
</margin>

**T**hrough rule B <note>In the "Ars Magna" of Ramon Llull, "Rule B" usually refers to the question "Whether?" (Utrum), used here to investigate the nature of human knowledge.</note> it is asked: whether man is more knowable through affirmation than through negation. And the answer is that, just as it appears, to predicate the predicate of the subject by affirming it is to define the subject of which the predicate is predicated—a nature existing between the subject and the predicate—as when it is said: "man is a rational animal" <note>original: "homo est animal rationale"</note>. When, however, the predicate is predicated of man negatively, no certainty or knowledge of man is obtained: as when it is said, "man is not a stone," or "man is not a plant." For a true affirmation places those things which are in the subject; a true negation, however, always removes them from the subject. A false negation likewise has a mode of removal from the subject. ¶ Furthermore, since affirmation precedes negation, just as an antecedent precedes its consequent, it is clear that man is more knowable through affirmation than through negation. To know that man exists while being ignorant of what man is, is to neglect the very being of man. ¶ And therefore, so that we may know what man is and have a great knowledge of him, we shall define him through thirty definitions taken in a broad sense, even though he can be defined by a single definition taken in a strict sense. But we define man in this way so that we may know him more clearly in our intellect. And these definitions will be abstracted from the twenty-eight principles of this Art and from the ten predicaments <note>The "Ten Predicaments" are Aristotle's categories, such as Substance, Quality, and Quantity.</note>, by predicating of the substance such a predicate that it agrees with the subject in nature. ¶ And first, through the first type of rule C <note>Rule C typically refers to the question "What?" (Quid).</note>, it is asked: what is man? And the answer is that he is an animal of whom more goodnesses of different species are predicated than of any other animal. ¶ Man is an animal in which one part is incorruptible <note>referring to the immortal soul</note>. ¶ Man is an animal in which there are more powers than in any other animal. ¶ Man is an animal that, with its own organ, creates intelligible species <note>mental concepts or images</note>. ¶ Man is an animal that uses virtues or vices. ¶ Man is an animal that truly uses the liberal and mechanical arts. ¶ Man is an animal in which there are more delights than in any other animal. ¶ Man is an animal in which there are more differences than in another. ¶ Man is an animal in which there are more concordances than in another. ¶ Man is an animal in which there are more contrarieties than in another. ¶ Man is an animal in which nature uses its principle more than in another. ¶ Man is an animal through whom all corporal things serve God. ¶ Man is an animal that relates to a greater end than any other animal. ¶ Man is an animal having a greater species than another animal. ¶ Man is an animal having more equalities than another animal. ¶ Man is an animal that can diminish itself more <note>original: "minorificare", referring to the ability to humble oneself or descend into lower states of behavior</note> than another animal. ¶ Man is a substance that is composed of more things than any other. ¶ Man is a substance in which there are more quantities of different species than in another. ¶ Man is a substance subsisting in corporal and spiritual qualities. ¶ Man is a substance subsisting in more relations than another. ¶ Man is a substance subsisting in corporal and spiritual actions. ¶ Man is a substance subsisting in corporal and spiritual passions. ¶ Man is a substance habituated by virtues or vices. ¶ Man is a substance existing in an upright posture while walking or sitting. ¶ Man is a substance having some part in itself without succession and time <note>referring to the timeless nature of the soul</note>. ¶ Man is a substance in which soul and body are placed toward one another. ¶ Man is a being multiplying the human species. ¶ Through the second type of rule C, it is asked: what does man have in himself that is co-essential? And the answer is that man has substance and accident, without which he cannot exist. Furthermore, he has within himself the correlatives of his own principles, and he has within himself habits which he has acquired accidentally. ¶ Through the third type, it is asked: what is man in another? And it should be said that man is in the man-making seeds; the woman, however, is in the seed of the nurse <note>This likely refers to the womb or the nurturing environment of the embryo</note> moving him and multiplying him from that which comes to him from the outside through nourishment. ¶ I saw a certain egg placed under a hen, and the shell of that egg was missing in one part of it, to the size of a penny; and in the middle of the internal membrane, there was one drop of blood the size of a millet grain, from which drop proceeded red and slender lines in the manner of hairs; and they were situated in the manner of a spider's web.

...and that drop moved itself and also that web, just as a spider does existing in the middle of its web. Furthermore, man is habituated in habit and situated in position.

Through the **fourth species** <note>The species of the Rules refer to different ways of applying a logical question. Rule D usually asks "What?" (Quid)</note> it is asked: what does man have in relation to another? And the answer is that he has knowledge in his habit <note>original: "habitu"; referring here to an acquired disposition or state of mind</note>, shape in his position, motion in time, and placement in space.

Through the **first species of Rule D** it is asked: from what is man made? And the answer is that he comes from his first parents as far as the body is concerned; but as for the soul, not at all, just as his intellect does not descend from another intellect, as has already been proven above.

Through the **second species** it is asked: of what is man composed? And the answer is that he is composed of his soul and his body; and his soul is from its spiritual principles, and his body is from its corporeal principles.

Through the **third species** it is asked: to whom does man belong? And the answer is that he belongs to God; and one man belongs to another as a servant to his master; and a sinful man belongs to the world, the flesh, and the devil.

Through the **first species of Rule E** <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare)</note> it is asked: why is man? And it is answered that he exists because he is joined from his soul and body; for that very conjunction necessitates his existence.

Through the **second species** it is asked: for what purpose is man? And it is answered that he exists to understand, remember, and love God; and to receive eternal blessedness from Him. Furthermore, so that he may be the medium through which all created corporeal things serving man may serve God. Also, so that man may multiply his species.

Through the **first species of Rule F** <note>Rule F asks "How great?" (Quantum)</note> it is asked: how great is man? To this it must be said that man is as great as his continuous substance <note>original: "substantia continua"</note>, through the amount of continuous quantity he possesses.

Through the **second species** it is asked: how great is man? And to this it is answered that he is as great as he is through his discrete parts <note>referring to things that can be counted, like limbs or thoughts, rather than measured as a whole</note>. Furthermore, it is asked how great he is as good or evil, etc., and the answer is that he is as great as the habit of his goodness or malice.

Through the **first species of Rule G** <note>Rule G asks "What kind?" (Quale)</note> it is asked: what kind of being is man? And the answer is that he is such as his proper qualities are, without which he cannot exist: such as his capacity for laughter, his shape, and similar things.

Through the **second species** it is asked: what sort of man is he? And to this it must be answered that he is good, or great-souled, and so on.

Through **Rule H** <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando)</note> it is asked: when is man? And the answer is that he is at that time when God creates the rational soul in the body, which leads the body into the human species. Furthermore, he is when he is in the present "now," but not in the past and future; and with such a present "now" derived through rules C, D, and K, man is knowable or to be known. And we leave this discourse to the person who perceives subtly, for the sake of brevity.

Through **Rule I** <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi)</note> it is asked: where is man? And the answer is that he is in his humanity. For he can in no way be outside of it. Furthermore, man is in the place where he is contained and situated, and this is signified through rules C, D, and K.

Through **Rule K** <note>Rule K asks "How?" (Quomodo) and "With what?" (Cum quo)</note> it is asked concerning man: how he is, and how he transmits his likeness outside of himself.

To the first, it is answered that he is by that mode through which his parts have a mode of joining and placing him.

To the second, it is said that he has a way of transmitting his likeness outside by generating <note>biological reproduction</note> and by abstracting letters and figures from the mind, with the movement of hand and pen and the like.

Through the **second species of Rule K** it is asked: with what is man? And it is said that he is with his first parents and with his <term>co-essential principles</term> <note>original: "coessentialib⁹ principijs"; in Lullian thought, these are the active and passive components that make up a thing's essence</note>, and also with the accidents without which he cannot be; and he is just with his justice, and is writing with his hand, and similar things.

Furthermore, it is asked whether the human intellect consists of memory and will, with which it is universal and particular? And it is said that it is universal with the universal principles of the soul, such as with spiritual goodness, greatness, and so on. Furthermore, it is universal through its natural correlatives designated through the second species of Rule K. But it is particular with the particularity of objects, and then it is practical, making one intelligible species and then another successively.

Nor would an animal know how to return to the spring; and so of other things. ¶ Imagination has greatness with which it magnifies its other principles. And this appears in this: because it imagines at will. ¶ Imagination is durable: for its objects endure while...

<meta>This page continues the systematic analysis of human and animal faculties using the "Rules" of the Art. While the previous page focused on the definition of man as a composite of soul and body, this section transitions into a specific investigation of the "imagination"—the faculty that bridges the gap between physical senses and the abstract intellect.</meta>

### Ninth Part

They present objects from the imagination. For just as spiritual objects endure in the rational animal <note>original: "animali rationali"; a standard philosophical term for a human being</note> through memory outside of the imagination, so sensory objects endure through the imagination outside of the sense in brute animals. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that just as the rational soul perfects the lower powers, so the imaginative power in brute animals perfects the lower powers.

**Imagination** has power in the sensitive faculty; indeed, the power of imagination descends to the lower power so that it can act with it upon itself, just as <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The "innate" fluid believed by medieval doctors to be the fuel of life, distinct from the moisture gained from food.</note> descends to nutritional moisture so that it can live with it.

**Imagination** has a natural instinct, as is evident in brute animals, which through imagination possess the industry to live and to evade evil, as a goat evades a wolf.

**Imagination** has an appetite with which it desires the thing imagined. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that imagination has an instrument so that it might exercise its act and be able to reach the object.

**Imagination** has a virtue <note>original: "virtutem"; here meaning an inherent power or capacity</note> with which it attracts <term>species</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, "species" are the mental "images" or "likenesses" of objects that travel from the object to the mind.</note> from sensory things, placing them in its "imaginable" <note>the internal space or faculty where images are stored</note>, in which it characterizes and imagines them.

**Truth** is the instrument of imagination, so that with it, it can truly reach the object; however, it sometimes fails, like an agent who fails in the task because the instrument is lacking, or because he does not know how to work with it.

**Imagination** causes pleasure or sadness in the subject in which it exists.

**Imagination** has a "difference" <note>In this logical system, "difference" is the quality that allows a faculty to distinguish between different things or perform different acts.</note>, with which and through which it acts in various ways upon the object, like a mirror which, through its difference, receives diverse images.

**Imagination** accords the object with the subject in which it is; like a mother who imagines her son, rejoicing with the image or likeness of the son acquired through her imagination.

**Imagination**, through contrariety, contradicts or resists the subject in which it is by presenting a hateful or undesirable object, such as a mother imagining her dead son with sadness.

**Imagination** is an efficient principle, transmitting nothing outside itself and making matter from sensitive things by abstracting from them the sensory species along with its form—namely, with its "imaginative" which is its form—so that by reason of this, it may rest in the objects.

**Imagination** is a medium in man, existing between the sensitive power and the intellective power, so that the intellect can acquire sensory and imaginable species within the imagination.

And in this step, the intellect recognizes that the species it acquires from sensory things, which it then draws or abstracts from the imagination, exist outside of or without the sense.

**Imagination**, however, is not a medium in the brute animal; rather, it is its supreme extremity or form, with which its life is habituated and completed, just as the rational soul is in the human body.

**Imagination** has a nature with which it fails in its end, which is the imagined object; otherwise, its imagining would not be its own proper act.

**Imagination** has "greatness" <note>original: "maioritatem"; a technical term in the Llullist Art referring to the principle of Magnitude</note>: for its substantial goodness is greater than its accidental goodness, and its intrinsic act is greater than its extrinsic act.

Furthermore, it has greatness in presenting a lion with respect to a goat; and it has greatness in presenting a tall man, or one taller than him, or the greatest of them.

**Imagination** has "equality" in its correlatives <note>A Llullist term for the internal relationships of a power (e.g., the power of imagining, the thing being imagined, and the act of imagining itself).</note>, designated by the second species of Rule C; for unless they were equal by essence, they could not relate equally to the object, which is impossible.

**Imagination**, by reason of "smallness" <note>original: "minoritatis"; the logical opposite of "greatness"</note>, tends toward that smallness when it presents the smallest object.
