# Of the nine subjects.

intrinsically. ¶ **Imagination** is active through the **imaginative power** existing under the mode of form, moved by the animal so that the object may be moved within the intrinsic "imaginable" <note>original: "imaginabili"; the internal space or capacity where images are formed</note> of the imagination itself. ¶ **Imagination** is passive in its "imaginable" just as in matter, so that within the imaginable itself there may be a characterized and imagined object. ¶ The **imaginative faculty** is an animal <term>habitus</term> <note>A stable disposition or internal quality that allows a faculty to function effectively.</note> with which it creates <term>species</term> <note>Mental images or likenesses of external objects.</note> of things that can be imagined. ¶ **Imagination** is a power assisting in the middle of a certain membrane of the animal's skull, in which the imaginations of objects appear to its imaginative faculty, just as images appear to the eyes in a mirror. ¶ **Imagination** is a power existing in time through the subject in which it resides, without which it can neither exist nor utilize an object. ¶ **Imagination** is a power existing in place for the sake of imagining an object in that place. ¶ We have defined imagination through the ten <term>predicaments</term> <note>The ten categories of Aristotle (Substance, Quantity, Quality, etc.) used to describe all things.</note>: and just as we defined it through those, so other bodily powers can be defined through the same in their own way. ¶ Through the second species of **Rule C**, it is asked: what does imagination have in itself? And it must be answered that it has its own **correlatives** <note>In this philosophical system, correlatives are the internal components of any essence: the "doer," the "receiver," and the "act."</note> without which it cannot exist: namely, the **imaginative** [agent], the **imaginable** [patient], and the **act of imagining**. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is imagination in another? To which it must be said that in man it is a disposition with which the **intellect** disposes itself toward perceiving lower things; and the **sense** disposes itself toward sensing along with imagination itself; and in a brute animal, imagination itself is the form and perfection of that animal. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does it have in another? And it must be responded that it has its object in the subject in which it resides: and it has its intention in things perceived by the senses, so that it may abstract species from them with its own light: namely, with its imaginative power. For the **imaginative power** is the investigator of species, and also their creator and clarifier within its own "imaginable" which is co-essential to it: just like a crystal which, with its transparency, colors itself with the color over which it is placed: and also like a mirror that shapes itself according to the things presented to it for reflection. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule D**, it is asked: of what is imagination? And it must be answered that it is of itself, because it is a specified species. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: from what is imagination? And it must be answered that it is from its own matter and form, so that with them it may be active and passive within the subject in which it resides. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to what is imagination subject? And it must be said: to man, and also to the soul of that man. In a brute, however, it is subject to the animal as a part

is subject to its whole. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule E**, it is asked: why is imagination? And it must be answered that it is constituted from its parts: namely, the **imaginative**, the **imaginable**, and the **act of imagining**. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why is it? And it must be said: so that an animal can perceive its object by imagining in the absence of the sense; and the sense itself, with the imagination, disposes and proportions itself to sense sensible things when the sense is present: just like a carpenter who imagines the figure of an **archetype** <note>The original mental plan or model before it is physically built.</note> so that he may lead it from potentiality into act. And like a bird disposing itself to fly when it is necessary. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule F**, it is asked: how great is imagination? And it must be answered that it is as great as its essence extended in its correlatives; or as great as its habit of the subject in which it is: just like a cloak <note>original: "cappa"</note> which is as large as the habit of the one wearing the cloak. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: how great is imagination? And it must be said that it is as great as its discrete correlatives are. But here the intellect wonders what the cause is why imagination increases or decreases its act: as when a man imagines a small stone, and then imagines that same stone to be as large as a mountain. Then he reflects upon himself, considering that in brute animals, imagination imagines an object in the same way that the sense feels or apprehends that object, and not otherwise—just like a goat that imagines a wolf as its sense feels or apprehends it. It cannot imagine the wolf to be as large as a mountain; because if it could so increase its imagining, it would then be creating **knowledge** <note>original: "scientiam"</note>, which is impossible for a brute. But because human imagination is subject to the **intellect**, and the intellect is a higher power than it, the intellect therefore uses imagination over the sense, to the extent that it makes it imagine a wolf as large as a mountain. And by this step, the intellect recognizes the way in which **geometry** measures the heavens and their heights. And also the way in which **arithmetic** counts infinite units along with geometry, by dividing one part into two, and thereafter into infinite parts. And it also recognizes the way in which a **logician** uses <term>secondary intentions</term> <note>Concepts that refer to other concepts (like "category" or "species") rather than to physical things.</note> joined to primary ones. ¶ Furthermore, it recognizes that something exists in the intellect that was never in the senses: for a wolf as large as a mountain was never in the senses. And when the intellect has recognized all these things, it then understands that, without a doubt, it is entirely another essence, remote from the others.

Ninth part

# Ninth part

...from bodily essences and from their conditions. And in this the intellect greatly rejoices because it understands itself to be immortal and incorruptible. ¶ Through the first species of **rule g** <note>In Llull's system, Rule G asks "Whose is it?" or "To what does it belong?"</note>, it is asked: To whom does imagination belong as a property? And what is proper to imagination itself? ¶ To the first, it must be answered that imagination is a property of the animal to which it belongs. ¶ To the second, it must be said that what is proper to imagination itself is to represent the likeness of a sense-perception in the absence of the sense itself; but at this the intellect marvels: since the imagination possesses neither hearing, nor eyes, etc., how can it reach the likenesses of the senses which it remembers? Just as a magnet <note>original: "adamantis"</note> attracts iron through its own form <note>original: "speciem"; in this context, "species" refers to an active power or formal influence rather than a biological category</note>, and rhubarb attracts bile similarly through its own: thus the animal attracts species or likenesses through its own form, mediated by the imagination, in the absence of the sense. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what is the appropriate quality of imagination itself? And it must be said that it is the likeness of the sensed thing, abstracted from it and brought into the imagination: such as the color of a colored thing, and the quantity of a quantified thing, and the sound of a bell, and the coldness of water, etc., with which the imagination represents the object by imagining. ¶ Through all species of **rule h** <note>Rule H typically asks "When?" or deals with time and duration.</note>, it is asked: when is imagination? And it must be said that it exists in that time in which the animal exists: for where an animal is, it cannot exist without imagination, just as it cannot exist without the sensitive faculty <note>The power of the senses</note>. However, we leave the manner in which imagination moves through the species of rule h to the one who observes them well, for the sake of brevity. ¶ Through **rule i** <note>Rule I typically asks "Where?" or deals with location.</note>, it is asked: where does imagination imagine its object? To which it must be answered: in its own essence, namely in its own intrinsic and substantial **imaginable** <note>original: "imaginabili"; the internal "space" or capacity where images are formed</note>, outside of which and without which no imaginable thing can be imagined; for just as a hot thing cannot be hot except in heat, so an imagined object cannot be imagined except in the aforementioned intrinsic and substantial imaginable of the imagination itself, which is the universal subject for all imaginable things. ¶ As for the discourse of imagination led through all species of i, we do not treat it here, but leave that discourse to the one observing well, as was said above regarding rule h. ¶ Through the first **rule K** <note>Rule K asks "How?" or "By what means?"</note>, it is asked: how does imagination present its object? But the intellect is at first hindered from answering, because that manner is not sensible until it remembers the four species of rule K, with which it intends the solution of the said question. For in the animal, the sensitive faculty and the imagination are parts joined together, having one composite organ, one existing within the other; by reason of which the imagination abstracts likenesses from sensed things by means of the sensitive faculty, with which it represents its object: just as fire mixed with water attracts likenesses from it with which it heats flesh, as appears through intercourse <note>original: "coitum"</note> when the imagination imagines the manner by which intercourse occurs. ¶ Through the second **rule K**, it is asked: with what does the imagination imagine its object? And it must be answered: with the organ in which it resides: namely with that internal membrane <note>original: "pellicula"</note> existing in the head of which we spoke above; and it reaches the object with the <term>complexion</term> <note>The physical balance of bodily humors (blood, phlegm, etc.) which was thought to determine health and temperament.</note> of the said membrane, namely with melancholy <note>The humor associated with the element of Earth, characterized as cold and dry, and believed to be responsible for retaining memories.</note>. For the back part of this membrane is thickened by reason of coldness, which causes a contraction like the lead that closes the parts existing behind a mirror, so that the transparency <note>original: "dyaphaneitas"</note> does not pass through to that side. The aforementioned membrane on the front side, namely towards the forehead, is porous by reason of dryness, which is a property of earth; this is indeed abstractive and evacuating, in which forehead man finds species through the intellect. Brute animals, however, [do so] with instinct, when the species are presented with the intellect or instinct to the surface of the aforementioned membrane. Namely, this intellect and instinct are presentations of species to the said surface through their own form, just as a magnet attracts iron through its own form; and then the aforementioned membrane colors and paints and clothes itself with images through its own form, just as a mirror does through its own. ¶ Furthermore, imagination reaches the object with the disposition of the sensitive faculty, and also with its own: and with the proportion of both: and with appetite and representation: and with the discovery of species and with the descent of the imagination itself to the sensed thing by means of the sensitive faculty. And thereafter with the approach returning from the sensed thing to the imagination itself by means of the sensitive faculty; and also with the nourishment of the species: and so with other things that could be said, with which the imagination reaches its object. And in this step, the intellect knows that just as it is where it occupies itself and is burdened by its object, so also is the imagination by its own, in its own way.

folio 61.

# On the nine subjects.

<margin>
On the sixth subject, which is about the sensitive faculty, derived through the principles.
</margin>

**[T]he sensitive faculty** is the power with which an animal feels; it is also the perceived thing in which the sensitive faculty of the animal is the "common sense" <note>The "common sense" (sensus communis) was a theoretical internal faculty that unified the inputs from the five individual senses into a single coherent perception.</note> and possesses the particular senses. ¶ **The sensitive faculty** is a good power because, with its goodness, it causes "good sensing"; and when magnitude is added, it causes "great sensing." ¶ **The sensitive faculty** is a great power because it causes "great sensing," as is evident in sexual intercourse, or in the touch of hot iron, or in the touch of boiling water. ¶ **The sensitive faculty** lasts for the duration of the subject in which it exists, along with its innate goodness, magnitude, etc. ¶ **The sensitive faculty**, through its own power, is able to exist and to act. And in this step, the intellect understands that an animal feels through its own "species" <note>original: "speciem"; in medieval philosophy, this refers to the formal likeness or "mental image" of an object that allows it to be perceived.</note>, just as a magnet attracts through its own. ¶ **The sensitive faculty** has an innate instinct, as is evident in a human being who feels fear toward a snake they see, and similarly a goat toward a wolf; and just as a puppy, though not yet seeing, has an instinct, appetite, and touch, and thus finds the teat and imagines it. In this step, the intellect understands which principles dispose the imagination toward imagining. ¶ **The sensitive faculty** causes in the animal an appetite for sensing, so that, by means of the animal in which it resides, it can exercise its act. ¶ **The sensitive faculty** has the virtue of sensing, as is evident in its particular parts; for just as sight cannot see without illuminated air, neither can it see unless it is habituated by an innate virtue and situated within it. ¶ **The sensitive faculty** truly senses through truth, just as a hand touching hot iron truly feels the heat. And in this step, the intellect understands that it truly understands its own object. For otherwise, the sensitive power (which is lower) would be superior to the intellect through its act, and the intellect (which is the superior power) would be lower than the sensitive faculty—which is impossible. The intellect greatly rejoices at the realization of this impossibility. ¶ **The animal**, through the sensitive faculty, has the pleasure <note>original: "delectationem"</note> of sensing, as is evident when it sees a beautiful figure or when it hears a beautiful song, and the like. ¶ **The sensitive faculty**, through the principle of "Difference," possesses particular senses by means of organs through which objects differ: such as color, which is the object of sight; sound, for hearing; and so forth. But the intellect marvels whether the judgment of the object is made by the common sense or the particular sense, until it remembers the water of a spring having many streams: it is essentially one within itself and in its streams, but it has one flow and one shape in one stream, and another in another stream. Similarly, the common sense has one location <note>original: "situm"</note> and one form in one organ, and another in another organ. ¶ **In** the sensitive faculty consists an innate concordance <note>original: "concordātia"</note>, through which the power, the object, and the act—though they are many—agree as one: namely, in the sensitive faculty, which is their essence. This is evident through its "relatives" <note>In Llull's system, "relatives" (relativa) are the active, passive, and verbal components of a concept, e.g., the sensor, the sensed, and the sensing.</note> signified by the second species of Rule C, etc. And in this step, the intellect understands the way in which the sense perceives the perceived thing with a "foreign habit" <note>original: "habitu peregrino"; an acquired quality or external impression rather than an innate one.</note> by which the perceived thing is habituated: such as by seeing the colored thing or smelling the scented thing. ¶ **In** the sensitive faculty, there is contrariety by accident, such as bitterness in taste, or roughness in touch, and the like. ¶ **But** the intellect marvels at what causes contrariety in the sense, until it remembers that the sensitive faculty is composed of the four elements; these indeed cause contrary qualities of habit, position, action, and passion in a composite being. Thus, any plant acts through its own species: such as an apple through sweetness, and wormwood through bitterness. ¶ **Likewise**, the intellect considers that the weakness of a sense causes "monstrosities" <note>meaning distortions or abnormalities in perception</note>, such as a sick man who finds bitterness in sweet food by accident. ¶ **The sensitive faculty**, being situated in its principle, is an "efficient cause" in that it causes the desire for food through flavor, and the pleasure and sweetness of sexual intercourse. The sensitive faculty itself is the "form" in the animal which moves it within "matter," so that the matter may be disposed to receive "passions" <note>receptions of sensory input</note>, so that the "end" or goal may follow: namely, the perceived object, such as the colored thing, the scented thing, and the like. ¶ **The animal**, through the sensitive faculty, is a perceiver <note>original: "sensatum"; here used in the sense of a sensing subject or the thing that has been made sensitive.</note>, just as a thing is colored by color and scented by scent. ¶ **The common sense** is the middle; however, the particular senses are the extremities, just as the circumference of a center is the extremity of that center, and the position of the thing positioned, and the habit of the thing habituated. And in this step, the intellect understands that the common sense is the cause of perceived things insofar as they are perceived, with the common sense itself using its particular senses as instruments. For example, an apple is perceived by the common sense using taste, smell, sight, touch, and "speech" <note>original: "affatu"</note>—by which the apple is named—and hearing, by which it is heard. ¶ **Likewise**, the sensitive faculty exists between the vegetative and the imaginative faculties, like a line between two points. ¶ **The imaginative faculty** is indeed founded in the sensitive, and the sensitive in the vegetative, so that the imaginative faculty can imagine the conditions of the vegetative faculty by means of the sensitive faculty. This is evident through the definition of "the middle" and through its scale designated in the "Second Figure" <note>One of the symbolic diagrams in Llull's Art.</note>. ¶ **In** the sensitive faculty consists an innate "end" <note>goal or purpose</note>, toward which end it moves itself.

Ninth part.

...to the sensed object with its instinct and appetite, and so regarding other innate principles. Just as a human who, with their feet and sight, moves toward the place in which they desire to rest: and in this step, the intellect understands that the sensitive faculty acts with its innate principles. 

¶ One sensitive faculty is greater than another sensitive faculty, but this is accidental <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without changing the essence of a thing (like being tall or short), whereas "essential" properties define what a thing is.</note>. For just as some water from a spring is greater in coldness, flavor, and healthfulness by reason of a better quality of its location: so one sensitive faculty is greater than another by reason of a better quality of its location regarding the species of the subject in which it exists. For example, an eagle possesses a greater sensitive faculty through sight than another animal; and a vulture through smell; and a dog through hearing; but a human through taste and touch. 

¶ In the sensitive faculty, quality consists between power, object, and act; and this is intrinsic regarding its <term>correlatives</term> <note>Lullian "correlatives" are triads of related concepts: the agent (the sensitiuū/senser), the patient (the sensibile/sensed), and the action (the sentire/sensing).</note>: namely, the senser, the sensed, and the sensing. However, I do not mean this regarding an external object, such as the sensed flavor of an apple and the flavor caused by the act of sensing. 

¶ One sensitive faculty is smaller than another sensitive faculty according to the subject in which it is. For a person who does not live by prey does not feel as much through taste as a bird that lives by prey; and so it can be said of others in their own way, as was signified in the chapter on majority.

### On the sensitive faculty, derived through the rules.

<margin>The sensitive faculty derived through the rules.</margin>
**I**t is asked: is the sensitive faculty from the one who generates or the one who creates? <note>This asks whether the ability to feel is inherited from parents (generated) or a direct act of God (created).</note> And it must be answered that it is from the one who generates: as is clear in the fact that an animal without a sensitive faculty cannot feel the corruptible conditions that it ought to feel—both in the imagination and not just in itself—because it is not naturally inserted and founded in the vegetative faculty <note>The vegetative faculty refers to basic life functions like growth and nutrition.</note>. ¶ Furthermore, [if it were not generated,] Martin would not be the son of John according to the species, which is impossible.

<margin>A notable question.</margin>
¶ But the intellect wonders: when a person dies, where does the sensitive faculty go, and where is it? And it must be said that it goes to its universal principles in which it remains and stays in its own number miraculously—provided, however, that there is a resurrection of human beings, so that the justice and mercy of God may have a subject upon which they can act. 

¶ It is asked through the first type of Rule C: what is the sensitive faculty? And to this it must be answered that its definition has already been given above. 

¶ Through the second type, it is asked: what does the sensitive faculty have in itself? It must be answered that it has its correlatives from which the common sense <note>The "common sense" (sensus communis) was a theoretical faculty that unified the inputs from the five individual senses into a single coherent perception.</note> is constituted. 

¶ Through the third type, it is asked: what is it in another? And it must be said that it is a being causing sensed beings with which it feels; like sight, which senses the colored thing impressed <note>original: "inctūm/ictum"; referring to the visual image "striking" the eye.</note> upon it by what is seen; and like smell, which causes the scent impressed upon it by what is smelled. 

¶ Through the fourth type, it is asked: what does the sensitive faculty have in another? And it must be said that it has an object: like sight has the colored and the shaped; and smell has the scented; and it has knowledge of the object itself, because it makes a judgment about it. 

¶ Through the first type of Rule D, it is asked: from what is the sensitive faculty? And it must be answered that it is from its principles: namely, from the first parents from whom it was derived and generated; for otherwise one animal would not be the child of another, which is impossible. 

¶ Through the second type, it is asked: of what is the sensitive faculty made? And it must be answered that it is made of its matter and form: because it is passive through its matter and active through its form. 

¶ Through the third type, it is asked: whose is the sensitive faculty? And it must be answered that it belongs to the animal in which it is, just as an instrument belongs to the agent who uses it. For the animal feels, lives, and generates another animal with it. 

¶ Through the first type of Rule E, it is asked: why is there a sensitive faculty? And it must be answered that it is joined and constituted from its matter and form. 

¶ Through the second type, it is asked: why is there a sensitive faculty? And it must be answered that it is so that its instinct and appetite can have natural acts, so that the animal can have the industriousness to live. Furthermore, it is so that the imaginative faculty can draw species <note>original: "species"; images or formal likenesses of objects.</note> from it and imagine the sensed object and perform its own act. 

¶ Through the first type of Rule F, it is asked: how great is the sensitive faculty? And it must be answered that it is as great as its subject is sensed by it. 

¶ But the intellect wonders in what way it can be continuous in the subject in which it is, and in which there are hair, nails, and bones that do not feel; until it remembers its <term>discrete quantity</term> <note>Discrete quantity refers to things that are distinct or separated (like numbers or separate parts), as opposed to continuous quantity (like a line).</note> signified by the second species. 

¶ Furthermore, the intellect wonders—since the sensitive faculty is not made of points, nor lines, nor does it have a shape—in what way it has quantity? Until it remembers a crystal placed over something colored: the crystal colors itself from that object. In this same way, the sensitive faculty is quantified and habituated by the quantity of the subject in which it exists. For point-based and line-based quantity multiply their species in the sensitive faculty, just as color in the crystal multiplies its color in the aforementioned crystal. 

¶ And in this step, the intellect understands in what manner one habit is placed upon another. ¶ Through the first...

->On the nine subjects.<-

# On the nine subjects.

Regarding the **first species of rule G** <note>In Llull's system, "Rule G" usually asks "Why?" or looks for the specific qualities that define a subject.</note>, it is asked: what are the appropriate sensitive qualities? And it must be answered that it is the "sensed" insofar as it is acquired from another and is placed within the sensing faculty itself; just like a colored stone, which is sensed through sight; or like a scented apple, which is sensed through smell; and so on for the others. And in this step, the intellect understands that just as the imaginative faculty <note>The power to form mental images.</note> multiplies its own forms, so does the sensitive faculty multiply its own. ¶ Through **rule B** <note>Rule B usually asks "What?" or "How?" regarding the nature of a thing.</note>, it is asked: in what way does the sensitive faculty consist in time and motion, since it is neither made of points nor lines? And it must be answered that it exists through the subject in which it is located. And this is approved by rules B, C, D, and R, as is apparent to one looking closely; and let this declaration suffice for the sake of brevity. ¶ Through **rule I** <note>Rule I asks "Where?"</note>, it is asked: where does the sensitive faculty feel? And it must be answered that it feels in the "intrinsic sensible," which belongs to the essence of the sensing faculty. For outside of such a sensible thing, no object is sensed. But in this step, the intellect wonders how a stone is sensed—and so on for others—since it is not placed within the essence of the sensing faculty or the sense itself, nor does it even participate with the eyes through physical contact. For if it did, sight would touch the substance itself and hearing would touch the bell; and even further, a brute animal would touch the substance, and thus would possess "science" <note>Scientific or certain knowledge (Latin: "scientia"), which medieval philosophers believed was reserved for rational humans, not animals.</note>, which is impossible. But it remembers the rose multiplying its scent in the air, which participates with the rose itself through contact. Similarly, sight multiplies its <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; in medieval optics, these are the "forms" or "likenesses" of objects that travel through the air to the eye.</note> in the air, which participates with the sight and the colored and sensed object; and let this suffice regarding the species of rule I for the sake of brevity. ¶ Through the **first species of rule R** <note>Rule R asks "How?"</note>, it is asked: how does the sensitive faculty feel? But the intellect is hindered at first from answering the aforementioned question, because that "mode" of feeling is not itself sensible <note>Meaning the act of sensing cannot itself be seen or touched.</note>; and he who wished to explain it according to the senses was hindered. But he shall descend to the imagination, in which that mode is imaginable, and to the memory, in which rule R is memorable; and then the intellect answers the aforementioned question: namely, that the sensitive faculty or sense has its mode of sensing through the mixing of its instinct, appetite, and power; and so on with the other principles with which it draws and collects the "similitude" <note>A likeness or image.</note> of the elements by which it senses the objects themselves. Just as from a colored thing it draws and collects its likeness, in which likeness the sense—namely, sight—places its own likeness. And with these likenesses, it gives substance to the colored thing. ¶ Through the **second rule R**, it is asked: with what does the sensitive faculty or sense feel? And it must be answered that it is with its "species," just as the <term>adamant</term> <note>original: "adamas"; here referring to a magnet or loadstone which draws iron to itself by an unseen power.</note> attracts iron with its species. And it also feels with its natural instruments: namely, hearing, sight, etc. It further feels with acquired species with which it senses foreign objects; and also with its instinct, appetite, power, and possibility, with which it moves its organs to feel.

## On the seventh subject, namely on the vegetative faculty, deduced through the principles.

<margin>
On the
seventh
subject,
namely
on the
vegetative
faculty,
deduced
through
the
principles.
</margin>

**T**he vegetative faculty is good: as is evident in plants, which through goodness are good for themselves and for other things that live off them; which indeed could not live without them, nor could they have such a "being" as they have.
¶ The vegetative faculty is great: for it encompasses and comprehends every growing and planted thing within the vegetative faculty itself. And here the intellect asks: is the vegetative faculty that is in animals the same as that which is in plants? To which it must be answered that it is one and the same vegetative faculty in "genus," but there are many differing in "species" in various subjects by reason of those subjects themselves, but not by reason of itself. For anyone who said that by reason of itself the vegetative faculty were many, would indeed be saying that one was many, and many were one, which is impossible. Therefore it is clear that it is one and the same in genus, but many differing in species in different subjects. ¶ The vegetative faculty lasts through its specific duration; but the intellect asks: from what does it endure, since its subject in which it exists is corruptible? But it remembers the "elemented" <note>Things composed of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note> from which it lasts, just as the flame of fire in a lamp lasts from the oil. ¶ The vegetative faculty is powerful through its specific power, in which all the vegetable powers of plants and animals are planted and rooted. ¶ The vegetative faculty has an instinct with which every growing thing applies itself to its operation, specifying and habituating itself according to its specific habit, position, quantity, quality, and the like. ¶ The vegetative faculty has an appetite: namely, that that which is elemented may be "vegetated"; just as sight has an appetite for that which is colored so that it may be sensed through it; that appetite is general to all appetites which are in the vegetative genus. ¶ The vegetative faculty is of a virtue <note>In this context, "virtue" means an inherent power or efficacy.</note> that is habituated, constituted, qualified, and positioned, as is evident in a plant. For that which comes to it through the earth, water, air, and fire in which it is planted, it transforms through its species; and it does this same thing through food and drink. Furthermore, the vegetative faculty has a power in plants of which physicians have experience.

### Ninth part.

¶ The vegetative faculty, by reason of truth, truly "vegetates" <note>In this context, to "vegetate" means to perform the biological functions of life: growing, feeding, and reproducing.</note> and possesses true conditions—namely true substance, quality, and so on—without which it would not be planted in its own truth. ¶ The vegetative faculty takes delight in preserving its own being and in multiplying its species, as is apparent in plants that reproduce; in doing so, they are able to avoid "non-being" <note>Death or the extinction of the species.</note>. ¶ The vegetative faculty is rooted and planted in "difference" <note>One of Llull's "Principles." Difference allows for the variety of species within a single genus.</note>, so that there may be many species within its genus. But the intellect asks: what is the cause why the color green is more general among plants than any other color? It then remembers earth and water, which together compose the color green, and in which the plant is most strongly rooted and nourished. ¶ Still the intellect wonders: why does a line <note>Likely referring to a geometric or formal progression.</note> not generate the hard surface of its fruit in the same way, as a nut does? And why does the rose have a red color, and the lily white? But it remembers "magnitude" <note>Another Lullian Principle, referring to the scale or greatness of a thing's essence.</note>, by reason of which the difference is great. ¶ The vegetative faculty possesses "concordance" <note>The Lullian Principle of harmony or agreement between things.</note> so that its species may agree with one another in certain things: just as pepper and garlic agree in "heat" <note>In medieval medicine, foods were classified by qualities: hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note>, while lettuce and pumpkin <note>original: "cucurbita"</note> agree in "cold"; and many things agree in the same color, position, and the like. This same thing can be said, in its own way, regarding the vegetative faculty in animals: for the vegetative faculty always follows the greater "complexion" <note>The specific balance of elements (fire, air, water, earth) in a body.</note> of the subject in which it resides. "Contrariety" <note>The Lullian Principle of opposition.</note> is the subject in which the vegetative faculty is planted, such that contrariety is the cause of corruption <note>Decay or death.</note>, just as concordance is the cause of generation. But the intellect asks: what is the cause why realgar <note>original: "realgal"; red arsenic sulfide, a deadly poison.</note> kills an animal, while wheat gives it life? And why are garlic and pumpkins contrary? But it remembers "magnitude," in which the contrariety of vegetation is planted. ¶ The vegetative faculty is a principle; within it, the vegetating thing (the composite) transmits one species into another. The "form" within the vegetative faculty is another principle in which the composite transmutes a new form into its old form, and new matter into old matter; and this is for the sake of the "end" <note>Purpose or goal.</note>: namely, the vegetated thing in which the species is generated and multiplied. ¶ The vegetative faculty is a general "medium" <note>A middle ground or bridge.</note> existing between the "elemental faculty" <note>The power of the four elements (fire, air, water, earth) within a body.</note> and the "sensitive faculty": like a line between two points. The vegetative faculty is inserted and planted within the elemental faculty, while the sensitive faculty is planted within the vegetative. And because the sensitive faculty is the "end" (goal), it is situated above the vegetative and flows into it; and the vegetative flows back to the sensitive with its own specific principles. Because the vegetative is above the elemental, it flows into it, and the elemental flows back to the vegetative. In this step, the intellect understands how plants and animals live, are nourished, and grow through the vegetative faculty (and from it) and through the elemental faculty (and from it). This specific step is useful to the physician.

Still, the intellect recognizes that a tree is a medium and a subject (or an instrument) in which and with which the vegetative faculty performs its act. Similarly, its principles have their own acts: like water entering a vessel through one hole and exiting that same vessel through another; and this occurs by way of generation, corruption, and "privation" <note>The absence or loss of a quality.</note>. ¶ In the vegetative faculty, the "end" has its species in the "second figure" <note>A reference to Llull's logical diagrams used to find relationships between concepts.</note>, designated in the "angle of the end." ¶ The end of privation is the cause of corruption within the vegetative faculty; and the sensitive and elemental faculties are the "boundaries" <note>termini</note> where the vegetative faculty itself is limited. The "end of perfection" is the object and subject of the vegetative faculty itself. ¶ In the vegetation of plants, one plant is larger than another; similarly in the vegetation of animals, one animal is larger than another: for one lion is larger than another lion or another animal—as a goat is larger than a hare, and so forth. The reason for this is so that the vegetative faculty can be planted in "majority" <note>The Lullian Principle of being "greater."</note>. This pertains to the majority of the ten "predicaments" <note>Aristotle's categories of being.</note> and the principles of this Art. But the intellect wonders: what is the cause why a great tree is "in potential" <note>The capacity to become something that is not yet realized.</note> within one small seed? But it remembers the spark of fire coming out of a stone when a man strikes the stone with steel: that spark is potentially a great flame, relative to the fuel it encounters. ¶ Still the intellect wonders why larger fruits are found on the same tree even though they are of the same species; and the same can be asked of leaves. But it remembers the previously mentioned question of the spark, and immediately the question is solved. ¶ In the vegetative faculty there is "equality" <note>The Lullian Principle of things being equal.</note>, so that many plants can be equal in species; and similarly many other things, like this lion and that lion, which are equal in species. Similarly, pepper and garlic are equal in their degree of heat; and many apples in the same orchard are equal in smell, taste, color, and the like. This could not be unless the vegetative faculty were planted and rooted in equality. ¶ Regarding the "minority" <note>The Lullian Principle of being "less."</note> of the vegetative faculty, one can say the same as was said of its "majority," for they are related. The vegetative faculty is reducible through minority to "non-being," because it "is," and yet it did not exist before it was created.

<meta>This page continues the logical investigation of the "nine subjects" within Ramon Llull’s philosophical system. Having previously introduced the vegetative faculty, the author now applies a series of "Rules" (questions labeled B through H) to define its nature, its relationship to the physical elements, and its role in the growth and transformation of life.</meta>

folio 64.
On the nine subjects.

# On the nine subjects.

<margin>On the vegetative faculty, deduced through the rules.</margin>

**T**hrough **Rule B** <note>Rule B in Llull’s system usually asks "Whether?" a thing exists or has a certain property.</note> it is asked: whether the vegetative faculty is a power that can be sensed? And it must be answered that it is, in a certain way: namely, according to the conjunction or composition that the vegetative has with the sensitive faculty <note>The power of perception and feeling found in animals.</note> in the subject in which it exists. And in another way, it is sensed through the voice, such as through **speech** <note>original: "affatus." Llull considered "affatus" or speech to be a sixth sense that allows for the external expression of internal thoughts.</note> which names it, and through hearing, which hears its name. However, the other senses cannot perceive it. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that speech is a sense, since it perceives its object and gives something audible to the sense of hearing. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule C** <note>Rule C asks "What is it?"</note> it is asked: what is the vegetative faculty? And it must be answered that it is a power transforming one species into another: as in animals, in which it transforms food into flesh; and in plants, where it transforms the **elementative** <note>The "elementative" refers to the most basic layer of physical existence composed of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note> into itself. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what does the vegetative faculty have within itself? And it must be answered that it has its **correlatives** <note>In Lullian philosophy, every power consists of three parts: the active (the vegetating power), the passive (that which is vegetated), and the act itself (the vegetating). This is his theory of "Trinitarian" structures in nature.</note> from which it is composed, and with which it performs its operations—namely, the *vegetating power*, the *vegetable* (that which is vegetated), and the *act of vegetating*. For in its own "vegetable," it vegetates all foreign vegetable matter; just as the sensitive faculty, in its own "sensible," perceives all foreign sensible things; and just as a heating agent, in its own "heatable," heats all things that can be heated. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: what is the vegetative faculty in another thing? And it must be answered that it is the foundation within the sensitive faculty, whereas it is itself founded upon the elementative faculty. In the **Categories** <note>original: "predicamentis." These are the Aristotelian categories of being, such as Substance, Quantity, and Relation.</note> it is the same as what it is: namely, it is a substantial part of the very substance in which it exists. In terms of **quantity**, the vegetative exists "above" the quantity of the elementative; and the same can be said of its quantity and relation, and so on. In this step, the intellect recognizes that the vegetative is a higher power than the elementative; but the intellect doubts whether its "relation" is a mere accident, until it remembers its **substantial relation** <note>A relationship that is part of the thing's essential nature, rather than an external or temporary trait.</note> which possesses an accidental relation as its instrument and "habit" with which it acts in the subject where it is; just as a substance acts by means of its accidents. ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked: what does the vegetative faculty have in another thing? And it must be answered that it has its own substance within the substance of the elementative, and its own quantity within the quantity of the elementative, and so on for the other categories. In this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which the vegetative is situated and placed within the elementative. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule D** <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (the material or origin).</note> it is asked: of what is the vegetative faculty made? And it must be answered that it is made of its own specific principles with which it acts. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: of what is the vegetative faculty composed? And it must be said that it is composed of its correlatives. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: to whom does the vegetative faculty belong? And it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it is, like a part belongs to its whole, and like an instrument to its agent. For the vegetative is the part of the animal with which it acts and lives. And the same applies to the plant. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule E** <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (the cause).</note> it is asked: why does the vegetative faculty exist? And it must be answered: because it is constituted from its parts, namely its correlatives. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: why does the vegetative faculty exist? And it must be answered: so that there may be something "vegetated," and so that a living thing may be nourished and grow, and may transform one species into another during reproduction. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule F** <note>Rule F asks "How much?" or "Of what quantity?"</note> it is asked: whether the vegetative faculty has **continuous quantity** <note>Quantity that is unbroken, like a line or a body.</note> in the subject in which it exists? And it must be answered that it does, so that it may be in continuous motion. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: whether the vegetative faculty has **discrete quantity** <note>Quantity made of distinct parts, like numbers.</note>? And it must be answered that it does, so that it may be in successive motion. But the intellect wonders how it can have both continuous and discrete quantity in the same subject, until it remembers that in respect to its essence, it exists in continuous quantity, but in respect to its correlatives (its parts), it has discrete quantity. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule G** <note>Rule G asks "Of what quality?" or "What property?"</note> it is asked: what property is its own? And it must be said that it has that general quality from which particular qualities descend—just as the heat of pepper and others descend from general heat, and the coldness of lettuce and gourd descend from general coldness. From this general quality of **elemented things** <note>original: "elementati." Things composed of the four elements.</note>, the specific property of the vegetative itself is derived; just as the quantity of the vegetative is derived from the general quantity of the elements. Let us say that the general quantity or property of the vegetative is the transformation of one substance into another. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what is the "appropriate" quality of the vegetative? And it must be answered that the act of vegetating is produced in the vegetative faculty effectively by the **motion of the heavens** <note>In medieval science, the movement of the stars and planets was believed to drive biological processes on Earth.</note>, just as the "seeing" of a stone is by accident. ¶ Through **Rule H** <note>Rule H asks "When?" or "In what time?"</note> it is asked: in what manner does the vegetative exist in time? But here the intellect is hindered in its answering until it remembers the elementative faculty, from which the vegetative is flowed [influenced], with which it exists in time and motion, just as through it, it exists in quantity, quality, and so on. The reason for this is that the essence of the elementative is point-like and linear, but the essence of the vegetative is not at all so; and this is through the rule... <unclear>con...</unclear>

<meta>This page continues Ramon Llull’s systematic analysis of the powers of the soul and nature. Ninth Part

**Rule R** <note>Rule R in Llull's system often refers to "Relation" or the relationship between principles.</note> has been signified: to those who look closely. ¶ Through **Rule I** <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi?).</note> it is asked: where does the vegetative faculty vegetate that which is vegetated? To which it must be answered: in its own intrinsic and substantial **vegetable** <note>In Llull’s Latin, the "vegetable" refers to the specific physical subject or body capable of growth.</note> outside of which and without which it cannot vegetate; just as a heating power cannot heat outside of its own heatable subject. The place of the vegetative faculty is indeed knowable through Rules C and D. And the vegetative faculty itself reaches substance because it participates with it through contact. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule K** <note>Rule K asks "How?" (Quomodo?).</note> it is asked: how does the vegetative faculty vegetate that which is vegetated? And it must be said that it vegetates in that manner which it holds regarding its own **correlatives** <note>Llull’s "correlatives" are a trio of terms for every action: the active doer, the passive receiver, and the action itself. For growth, these are the "vegetant," the "vegetable," and "vegetating."</note>: for the "vegetant" power places form and matter into its intrinsic vegetable subject, which come to it from the **elementative** <note>The elementative is the level of existence governed by the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note> faculty. And in that same vegetable, it changes its substance into another; the vegetative faculty strips the form and matter from the elementative level coming from it. And from those, the vegetative faculty itself clothes a new vegetated thing. ¶ But many modes concur in this manner, namely: the mode of proportion; the motion of generation, of corruption, of privation, and of augmentation; and the like, by placing part into part, and parts into the whole, and vice versa; and with the whole transmitting its likeness to that which is assimilated to it. ¶ Through the second species of **Rule K** <note>The second part of Rule K asks "With what?" (Cum quo?).</note> it is asked: with what does the vegetative faculty vegetate? And it must be answered that it vegetates it with its own proper correlatives: namely, with the vegetant, the vegetable, and the act of vegetating, which are co-essential to it. For the vegetant, in its own intrinsic vegetable, vegetates all foreign "vegetables" by means of the act of vegetating. Furthermore, it vegetates with the principles of this Art, namely with goodness and magnitude. ¶ And let these things which have been said of the vegetative faculty suffice; although many things could be said of it, nevertheless, whatever can be said of it is implied in the aforementioned things.

### On the eighth subject: namely, on the elementative faculty, deduced through the principles.

**E**lementative power is the power with which the elements enter into composition and exist beneath the elements. ¶ The elementative is a **good** power: for without it, bodily things would be idle and wandering from their end for which they exist; and the world would have no perfection. And therefore, insofar as it is good, it is the reason for goods so that it may act for the good. ¶ The elementative is a **great** power: because through its magnitude it encompasses many things, and its magnitude greatly magnifies its goodness and duration, and so forth. ¶ The elementative **endures** for so long that when one element is corrupted, it immediately and continually generates another, with none of its species differing, nor their conditions; because no element is corruptible as far as its essence is concerned. ¶ The elementative is **powerful** through its own species existing according to what it is, and by acting according to what it acts; which power indeed does not fail it in anything. ¶ For the elementative is able to "element" those things which are elemented <note>To "element" is the act of the elementative power composing things out of the four elements.</note> just as the vegetative is able to "vegetate" the vegetated, and the sensitive to "sense" the sensed, and the imaginative to "imagine" the imagined. ¶ The elementative has a **general instinct**, from which descends the instinct of species, and from those, the instincts of individuals and elemented things descend. And of this we have experience in the four seasons of the year: namely in spring, summer, autumn, and winter; in which the elementative has diverse operations. And also in the four regions: namely in the east, the west, the south, and the north. And this same thing can be said of the life of plants and animals. Furthermore, it has an instinct for receiving the virtue of the planets and of the **eighth sphere** <note>The "eighth sphere" in medieval astronomy refers to the firmament of the fixed stars, which was believed to influence the world below.</note>. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the cause of why any element acts through its own species. ¶ The elementative has an **appetite** to "element" the elemented things, by reason of which appetite the elements enter into mixture and composition—one element having an appetite for the upward direction, and another for the downward—so that it can exist beneath the elemented things. And in this step, the intellect recognizes what is the cause of the motion of elements in generating, corrupting, and depriving. ¶ The elementative has a **general virtue** from which descend the special virtues of the elements; which virtues are indeed the foundations for the vegetative and sensitive virtues. Nevertheless, its virtue is sometimes defective through **monstrosities** <note>Historical term for biological deformities or birth defects.</note> caused by the contrarieties of the elements. ¶ The elementative has **true conditions**, so that one species does not transmute itself into another species. And in this step, the **Alchemists** grieve and have cause for weeping <note>Llull frequently argued against alchemy, believing that the essential nature of elements (like turning lead into gold) could not be changed because species are fixed by God.</note>. ¶ The elementative has a **natural delight** in elementing in this way, just as the vegetative has in vegetating, and the sensitive in sensing: by reason of which the elementative magnifies and multiplies its acts as much as it can, so that its elemented things can exist in great delight. And in this step, let the intellect recognize what is the cause of intense heat, flavor, color, and the like. ¶ The elementative, through its **difference**, has diverse subjects in which it is diffused: such as in the four masses which are the objects of the senses: such as this flame, this air, this...

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of the vegetative faculty to the eighth subject of Ramon Llull’s system: the "elementative" faculty. This faculty describes the power of the four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—as they combine to form physical bodies.</meta>

<page-num>64</page-num>
->On the nine subjects. Folio 64.<-

# On the nine subjects.

water and this earth which we use. ¶ Likewise, the **elementative** <note>original: "elementatiua"; This is the natural power that governs how the four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—mix and interact.</note> power is present in metals, plants, and animals; however, in those things, it is not an object of the senses. Instead, it is perceived only by the imagination and the intellect. And at this stage, the intellect recognizes the cause of the error made by those philosophers who say that the elements are not actually present in composite things, but only exist within them in potential and virtue. <note>Llull is arguing against the idea that elements "disappear" when they mix; he believes they remain present and active.</note>

¶ By reason of its harmony, end, magnitude, goodness, power, instinct, appetite, and virtue, the **elementative** power is restrained and contracted within the things it creates (the "elemented" things). This happens so that a **temperament** <note>A balanced mixture of qualities.</note> may be created between contrary qualities: water stinging fire with its coldness, and fire stinging water with its heat; and air stinging earth with its moisture, and earth stinging air with its dryness. This allows the elementative power to generate a physical body by the process of "elementing," just as the digestive power produces what is digested, or as a blacksmith softens iron with heat to make a nail. At this stage, the intellect recognizes that harmony is the cause of generation in physical things.

¶ The elementative faculty is structured and situated by contrary qualities: namely heat, cold, moisture and dryness, lightness and heaviness, and rarity and density. Thus, this contrariety is the cause of **corruption** <note>In this context, "corruption" means the breaking down or decaying of physical things.</note> in physical things.

¶ In the elementative faculty there are four principles: the "elementing" agent is one efficient principle, which sends form into matter so that the goal may follow—namely, the physical, elemented thing.

¶ Furthermore, the principles of this Art concur in this: namely goodness, magnitude, etc., and also the movement of the heavens, which causes the movement of the elementative power in lower things.

¶ Moreover, within the elementative faculty itself, the ten categories (predicaments) are diffused, as are the rules of this Art. The principles are intellectual—specifically in an objective sense—while the rules are comparative in a subjective sense. At this stage, the intellect recognizes that the principles present the physical object, and the rules support it.

¶ The elementative faculty is a medium existing between the simple elements and the physical things they form, just as the particular senses exist between the common sense and the things perceived. And at this stage, the intellect recognizes the movement of the elementative power—from where the "influx" (flowing in) comes, from where the "reflux" (flowing out) comes, and in which subjects this discourse takes place.

¶ The goal of the elementative faculty is to possess and generate a physical body in which it may rest, beyond which the elementative faculty has no further desire. For if it desired something else beyond its physical product, its product would not be its proper goal. Thus, it finds more rest in that which does not depart from its nature than in that which does. A blacksmith would find more rest in a finished nail than in a son he fathered, or a lion would find more rest in hunting than in fathering its own kind—which is impossible. Therefore, it is clear that the goal of the elementative faculty is to possess and generate an elemented body, so that it may rest within it. At this stage, the intellect recognizes that the elementative faculty rests in the physical body just as the vegetative faculty rests in the plant, the sensitive in the sensed, the imaginative in the imagined, and the intellect in the understood.

¶ The elementative faculty is greater in a subject regarding one quality than another; for example, in pepper, it is greater regarding heat than regarding dryness. Furthermore, it is greater regarding dryness than moisture. Likewise, it is greater regarding moisture than coldness. At this stage, the intellect recognizes how the "majority" (greater strength) of the elementative faculty is ranked within the subject it inhabits. However, regarding youth and old age, it is not so: for the elementative power is greater in the middle than at the extremes—namely, in the middle of one's life rather than in youth or old age. It is like the sun, which is greater and hotter in its effect at noon than in the morning or evening.

¶ The elementative faculty is situated in equality. For the elements have equal essences and consistency, so that proportion can exist in physical things; thus this rose and that rose are equal in species, and so on for others in their own way. For otherwise, one element would destroy another element by its essence and nature, or one element would transform another into its own essence—as if a rose were to transform a lily or a violet into its own essence.

¶ The elementative faculty is situated in "minority" (smallness), because its first principles were brought forth and created from nothing. Likewise, the elementative power, according to how it exists in a smaller physical body, is situated and habituated by a smaller quantity, and so on.

### On the elementative faculty deduced through the rule.

<margin>On the elementative faculty deduced through the rule.</margin>
**I**t is asked whether the elementative faculty differs in essence from the elements. The answer is no. If they differed in essence, then the elements would have no subject in which they were composed, nor would the elementative faculty come from a generator, but rather from a creator. Furthermore, the qualities of the elements would change into a new subject; for example, the heat of fire that is in a stone would not be the same species as the heat of fire in the **sphere of fire** <note>In the medieval worldview, the "sphere of fire" was the region above the air and below the moon where the element of fire existed in its purest form.</note>—which is impossible. It is like humanity, which does not differ from the soul and body as they are joined...

Llull explains that this power works through a harmony of opposing qualities—like heat and cold—to reach a state of "rest" in the finished physical object.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the eighth subject, the elementative power (the force that combines the four elements), following the method of Ramon Llull. He uses a series of "rules" (questions labeled C through K) to explore the nature, location, and qualities of this power.</meta>

# Part Nine

...for [the elementative power] is from those, but not from one alone. ¶ Through the **first species of rule C** <note>In Llull's system, Rule C asks "What is it?" and the "species" are specific ways of answering that question.</note> it is asked: **what is the elementative?** And it must be answered that its definition has already been given above. ¶ Through the **second species** it is asked: **what does the elementative have in itself essentially and substantially?** And it must be said that it has its own **correlatives** <note>Llull's "correlatives" are the internal components of any essence: the active part, the passive part, and the act itself (e.g., the power to element, the thing being elemented, and the act of elementing).</note> from which it is made, and with which it acts in **elemented things** <note>original: "elementatis"; these are physical compounds like stones or animals made from the four elements.</note>: namely in a stone, a flame, a plant, and in animals. ¶ Through the **third species** it is asked: **what is it in another?** And it must be said that it is an instrument in the elements with which the elements themselves act upon elemented compounds. ¶ Furthermore, it exists within the **ten predicaments** <note>The ten categories of being defined by Aristotle (Substance, Quantity, Quality, etc.).</note> as that which it is; and it is the foundation within the **vegetative power** <note>The power of growth and nutrition.</note>. ¶ Furthermore, the elementative power is, in the potentiality of fire, an image of the infinity and eternity of God; for as much as it is fire, if it had infinite wood, it would burn infinitely and eternally. But because it does not have this, that power remains only as a disposition; it is finite because the matter is finite. ¶ Through the **fourth species** it is asked: **what does it have in another?** And it must be said that it has, in the subject in which it exists, its own matter, its form, its quantity, its quality, its motion, and such things; as is seen in a plant and in an animal. ¶ Through the **first species of rule D** <note>Rule D asks "From what?" or "Where does it come from?"</note> it is asked: **from what is the elementative?** And it must be said that it is from its own primitive principles placed within elementative things; and from those principles as if from universal matter and universal form, just like the elements. ¶ Through the **second species** it is asked: **from what is the elementative?** And it must be said that it is from its own specific form and matter, or it acts with them through its own species by "elementing" the elemented compounds. ¶ Through the **third species** it is asked: **to what does the elementative belong?** And it must be said: to the subject in which it is, just like a part belongs to its whole; as is evident in a plant which, by generating, "elements" another plant. ¶ Through the **first species of rule E** <note>Rule E asks "Why?"</note> it is asked: **why is there an elementative power?** To which it must be said that it is because it is composed of the elements. ¶ Through the **second species of rule E** it is asked: **why is there an elementative power?** To which it must be said: so that through it, elemented things may exist. Furthermore, so that the vegetative, sensitive, and imaginative powers may be founded, nourished, and generated by it. ¶ Through the **first species of rule F** <note>Rule F asks "How much?" or concerns quantity.</note> it is asked: **does the elementative power have continuous quantity?** And it must be answered that it does: so that its continuous quantity is a "genus" to the quantity of the individuals which are shaped and sustained within them. ¶ Through the **second species** it is asked: **does it have discrete quantities?** And it must be answered that it does:

as in elemented individuals having different quantities in number. Its quantity is **punctual** <note>Meaning "point-like" or concentrated.</note> because it is joined and constituted from the four elements. ¶ Through the **first species of G** <note>Rule G asks "Of what kind?" regarding quality.</note> it is asked: **what is its own proper quality?** And it must be answered: that which it has through its own elements, such as **choler** <note>One of the four "humors" or bodily fluids (yellow bile), associated with fire.</note> which is an elemented compound, to which heat is its own proper quality. ¶ Through the **second species of rule G** it is asked: **what is its appropriated quality?** And it must be said that dryness is its appropriated quality. For it receives dryness from the earth; and so it is with the other **complexions** <note>The specific balance of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in a body.</note>, besides heat, according to which it receives them from different sources. ¶ Through **rule H** <note>Rule H asks "When?" or concerns time.</note> it is asked: **in what manner does the elementative power exist in time?** And it must be answered that it exists in time with respect to the "now" in which it is. Furthermore, it exists in time by means of the motion in which it is, by increasing or altering the subject in which it is, and by moving from one place to another. And this is also covered by rules C, D, and K. <margin>v 61</margin> ¶ Through **rule I** <note>Rule I asks "Where?"</note> it is asked: **where is the elementative power?** And it must be answered: in elemented things. And this is **subjective** <note>Meaning it exists as part of the subject's own being.</note>, not **objective** like sight is in a colored thing. For unless the elementative power were in the elemented compound, the qualities would no longer be in the compound, or they would be without a subject—which is impossible. This is evident in a flame, in which there is heat, and in ice, in which there is cold, and such things. However, at this point the intellect **doubts** whether the dryness of the earth and the coldness of water are in the sphere of fire, since they belong to the lower elemented things, with moisture resisting and opposing the dryness of the earth, and the heat of fire opposing the coldness of water. Eventually, the intellect remembers that if all elements were not in the sphere of fire—nor in any sphere of any other element—their **general mixture** would be destroyed, and consequently their **particular mixtures** in elemented compounds would be destroyed. For the destruction of the universal leads to the destruction of the particular. Likewise, if the fire which is hot in its own sphere by its own nature were dry by its own nature, then the air which is moist by its own nature and hot through fire would be hot by its own nature. Furthermore, the water which is cold in its own sphere by its own nature and moist through the air would be moist by its own nature. Similarly, the earth which is dry in its own sphere by its own nature and cold through the water would be cold by its own nature. And thus there would be two qualities of any element in its genus: such as two "heats" in fire, and two "moistures," and two "coldnesses," and two...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "elementative power" (the force that blends the four elements). The author is refuting the idea that there could be multiple versions of the same elemental quality (like two types of dryness), arguing instead for a unified system of four elements that mix to create all physical things. He then transitions to the Ninth Subject of his system: Instrumentality and Morality.</meta>

<page-num>65</page-num>
->**On the nine subjects.**<-
k

...two drynesses, two fire-qualities, two air-qualities, two water-qualities, and two earth-qualities; and consequently there would be eight elements just as there are eight qualities mentioned above. This is an absurd thing to say, just as it is absurd to say there are two "whitenesses" in a single category, or two types of **vegetative power**, or two types of **sentient power**. ¶ Furthermore, natural appetite would be destroyed, because one fire would not seek out another fire; nor would fire seek the earth, since it would be dry in and of itself <note>In medieval science, elements "seek" each other to form compounds because they share certain qualities; if they were entirely self-sufficient, no movement or mixing would happen.</note>. The same can be said for the other elements in their own way. Thus, the specific "appropriated quality" <note>The primary quality of an element, such as heat for fire.</note> would be destroyed, as would the second species of **Rule G** <note>Rule G in Llull's system asks "Whose?" or "To what does it belong?".</note> which signifies that quality. ¶ Again, motion would be destroyed—both the appetite for moving upward and the appetite for moving downward. Consequently, Nature itself would be destroyed, because it would have no subject in which it could be sustained. The **elementative power** <note>term: elementative power; the hidden force that combines the four basic elements (fire, air, water, earth) into complex matter.</note> would also be destroyed, and by extension all **elemented things** <note>term: elemented things (Latin: elementata); physical objects like stones or trees made from the elements.</note>, **vegetative things** (plants), and **sentient things** (animals). Furthermore, every body existing **beneath the moon** <note>The sublunary sphere, where everything is made of the four elements and is subject to change and decay.</note> would be composed in a "vacuum of purpose," to such an extent that the "end" or goal of nature would simply be a state of deprivation, like blindness is to sight or deafness is to hearing.

And because all these things are highly impossible, it is clear through **Rule H** <note>Rule H asks "When?" or "Where?".</note> and through the definition of truth that all elemented things are mixed within their own spheres and masses. In complex elemented things, they are even more thoroughly mixed and composed: for instance, in plants they are composed with the **vegetative power**, and in animals with the **sentient** and **imaginative powers**; and this occurs by means of the elementative power being composed with them.

¶ But here the intellect wonders: how can earth, which is the lowest, ascend to the highest place, namely into the sphere of fire? For the air is in the middle, opposing the earth. And similarly, how can fire descend to us below, since water is its contrary? The intellect then remembers the "second concordance" shown in the **Second Figure** <note>The Second Figure is one of Llull’s diagrams showing how different principles (like Wisdom, Greatness, etc.) relate to one another.</note>. For fire descends by giving some of its heat to the air, and it comes down along with it; and the air, by giving its moisture to the water, agrees with it in descending. Thus, fire passes into the water through heated moisture. And water descends to the earth, giving it its cooled moisture <note>original: "frigiditate calefacta & humefacta"</note>. Conversely, earth ascends toward the fire by giving it its heated and moistened dryness. Since qualities do not abandon their own subject, as the qualities ascend and descend, the elements themselves ascend and descend. Thus follows **circular motion** and mixing.

¶ Through the first species of **Rule K** <note>Rule K asks "How?".</note>, it is asked: **how is the elementative power mixed and composed of the four elements?** But the intellect remembers the paragraph on "place" mentioned above, in which the solution to the question is implied and signified; and for the sake of brevity, this suffices to declare the aforementioned question. ¶ Through the second species of **Rule K**, it is asked: **with what does the elementative power "element" (create) elemented things?** It must be answered: with the instinct and appetite of the principles from which it is made, following the motion it has according to the nature of the definitions of those principles; and so it is with the rules in which its transition consists. The same can be said regarding the "impressions" <note>Influences or effects.</note> it has within the **ten predicaments** <note>The ten categories of Aristotle (Substance, Quality, Quantity, etc.).</note>, moved however by the general motion of the heavens. But to explain this would be long; the explanation is clear enough to anyone who knows this Art.

# On the ninth subject, which is on instrumentality.

<margin>On the ninth subject, which is on instrumentality.</margin>
**The ninth** subject concerns human skill or artifice (*artificio*), and it has three species. ¶ The first concerns **morals**. ¶ The second concerns the **liberal arts**. ¶ The third concerns the **mechanical arts**. We shall treat the first here, namely morals. We shall treat the second and third in the eleventh part of this book, specifically in the section on "application." ¶ It should be known that morality can be treated in two ways: according to the **virtues** and according to the **vices**. First, we shall treat **Justice**, which falls under the category of virtue.
