# Ninth Part

<margin>7</margin>
<margin>8</margin>
¶ ...acts: from which it is clear that **justice** arises from the reason of **goodness**. And in this step, the **intellect** recognizes that justice arises when its act begins / and that goodness is what disposes that justice / insofar as it is the reason for a good person to act well: since **greatness** is that by reason of which **duration** etc. are great: therefore greatness is the disposition of great justice, goodness, and duration: so that if a good person acts well in a great and lasting way etc., then at that time justice will be a great <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; in medieval philosophy, a "habit" is a stable disposition or character trait that makes an action easy and natural.</note> gathered from goodness, greatness, duration, etc. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that just as great justice is connected with the <term>principles</term> <note>Llull refers to his "Dignities"—fundamental attributes like Goodness, Greatness, and Power—as the building blocks of all reality.</note> and derived from them: just as goodness and greatness etc. endure through duration, so justice endures through it, provided however that no **injury** <note>original: "iniuria"; here meaning an act of injustice or harm that breaks the moral order.</note> intervenes. And in this step, the intellect recognizes how the habit of justice endures, even if a person is using another virtue, or even if he is sleeping. And in this step, the intellect is both moral and practical.

¶ Since **goodness** is the reason for a good person to act well / and **greatness** disposes that the good be great / and **duration** disposes that it be lasting: and **power** is the reason that the good can exist and act well / **justice** disposes that it be led forth through that acting. And when a good person acts well, then justice is born / and is led from potential into act.

<margin>10</margin>
¶ **Justice** is intelligible through the **intellect** / and lovable through the **will**. And therefore the intellect and the will themselves take it as their object; after justice is born, the acts of justice remain in potential. For justice itself is governed in duration, power, etc. ¶ Justice is disposed through goodness, greatness, etc.: and therefore it is lovable through the will. For everything good is lovable: and therefore when it is loved with the disposition of goodness, greatness, etc., then justice is led from potential into act. ¶ Justice is a **virtue**, which is indeed its own "genus": because many virtues stand under "virtue" as a category: and therefore just as virtue in general arises from goodness, greatness, etc., so justice arises in the same way that moral virtue arises. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the way in which a particular thing is ruled and directed by its universal. And in this step, **jurists** <note>Lawyers and legal scholars.</note> ought to greatly rejoice, because this step is an infallible general rule for all laws. ¶ Justice cannot exist without **truth**: and therefore when it is with truth, it follows that justice is knowable in the same way that truth is knowable in the discourse of principles and rules. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that justice is easy to know when the discourse of truth is placed in the mixture of principles and rules.

In **glory** <note>The state of heavenly blessedness.</note> goodness, greatness, etc., have delight and <term>rest</term> <note>original: "quies"; the state where a thing has reached its perfection or goal.</note>; but they could not have this without justice. And therefore when they are in delight, the **conscience** does not "bite" <note>An old metaphor for the "stings" of remorse.</note>: because justice is within that delight. From this it follows that the rest of the conscience signifies and declares the justice within that delight. ¶ Justice has two parts by reason of **difference**: namely, weight and proportion: in regard to weight, it is "intensive" <note>Focused on the strength or quality of the act.</note>: but in regard to proportion, it is "extensive" <note>Focused on the reach or quantity of the act.</note>: and therefore in legal cases, judgment is sometimes required intensively / and sometimes extensively / according to how the subject of the judgment is disposed and ordered to receive the judgment. ¶ Justice arises and lives through the **concordance** of principles: and therefore in recognizing the concordance of principles toward a single judgment, justice is recognized with its conditions. For once the cause is known, the effect is known. ¶ **Injury** is the enemy of justice: because injury is a "privative" habit <note>Medieval thinkers defined evil and injury as "privative"—not things in themselves, but the absence or "privation" of good.</note> / and because concordance is the friend of principles: therefore justice is a positive habit. For one contrary is known by the other. ¶ **Justice** speaks of or signifies "essence": but **law** <note>original: "ius"; often referring to the legal right or the body of law itself.</note> signifies the "being" of justice: and because essence is sustained in its being, therefore justice is sustained in law. From what has been said, it is clear that the **judge** is the "efficient cause" in the beginning of a release / which justice is the "formal principle" and law the "material principle": because it is formed through justice. **Judgment** is the "final principle": because in it there is rest. ¶ Justice is the **middle ground** between the **plaintiff** <note>original: "actorem"; the one bringing the lawsuit.</note> and the **defendant** <note>original: "reum"; the person being sued or accused.</note> / through which the judge gives to each his law. For just as justice cannot be a middle ground without judging / neither can it be so without "good-making," "great-making," etc., so that its judging is thus mixed with goodness, greatness, etc. ¶ The **end goal** of justice is the rest of the principles: because without justice they cannot rest. From which it follows that justice is the final subject in which the principles have peace between the plaintiff and the defendant by "rendering to each what is his own." <note>This is a classic definition of justice in Western law, famously found in Roman law (Justinian’s Code).</note> ¶ Justice is greater by substance and by accident. From which it follows that its "greater greatness" is substantial / and its "lesser greatness" is accidental. That greater greatness is with greater goodness, greatness, etc. and the lesser greatness is with lesser goodness and greatness etc. And therefore in legal cases, a judge ought to recognize which justice is greater or lesser, by recognizing substantial and accidental justice: and this knowledge is very necessary in cases: for justice sometimes stands for the plaintiff substantially / and for the defendant accidentally, and vice versa: as is clear through "being" and "well-being": for being in a case...

### Rules.

<margin>On justice deduced through the rules.</margin>
**P**er Rule B, <note>Llull's "Rules" are a set of investigative questions: B (Whether), C (What), D (Of what), E (Why), F (How much), G (What kind), H (When/How), I (Where).</note> it is asked: if justice is corrupted in a man, does that same specific justice return to him when the **injury** <note>original: "iniuria"; the lack of justice or a harmful act.</note> is "corrupted" (removed)? And it must be answered that it does not. For just as in nature, **matter** is disposed and proportioned successively, but the **form** is introduced into it in an instant; so a moral <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; a stable disposition of character. Llull argues that while you practice becoming just over time, the moment you truly possess the virtue is an instantaneous "perfection" of the soul.</note> is disposed and proportioned successively, but is perfected in an instant. And therefore, when a habit is corrupted, it is corrupted in an instant. ¶ Per the first species of Rule C, it is asked: what is justice? And it must be answered that it is that form which is properly suited to **judging**. ¶ Per the second species of Rule C, it is asked: what does justice have in itself, essentially and substantially? And it must be answered that it has its moral <term>correlatives</term>, <note>Llull’s "correlatives" are a triad of the active agent, the passive recipient, and the action itself. Here: the Justifier, the Justifiable, and the act of Justifying.</note> namely: the **justifier**, the **justifiable**, and **justifying**, with which it exists as a habit. But here the intellect doubts: does justice remain as a habit when a man is not using it—either while he sleeps or while he is practicing another virtue? And it must be answered that it is so: for justice is not corrupted unless an "injury" is introduced. ¶ Per the third species of Rule C, it is asked: what is justice in another? And it must be answered that in legal cases it is the **cause**, and in other virtues, it is their **connection**; such as humility and patience, which agree with one another justly. ¶ Per the fourth species of Rule C, it is asked: what does justice have in another? And it must be answered that it has objects in legal cases which are "justly objectified"; it also has the impressions of the principles, the rules, and the ten <term>categories</term>. <note>original: "predicamenta"; the ten categories of Aristotle (Substance, Quality, Quantity, etc.) which Llull incorporates into his system.</note> ¶ Per the first species of Rule D, it is asked: of what is justice? And it must be said that it concerns the disposition of the principles, the rules, and the ten categories, because it is contained under them. ¶ Per the second species, it is asked: of what is justice? And it must be said that it consists of its own specific matter and form, which descend through **difference** and **property** from general virtue; so that a just man, through justice, may act in judgment. ¶ Per the third species, it is asked: whose is justice? And it must be answered that it belongs to the **just man**, just as a cloak belongs to the one who is cloaked. ¶ Per the first species of Rule E, it is asked: why is there justice? And it must be answered that it is gathered from the tripartite principles, namely from the **justifier**, the **bonifier** <note>The "Bonifier" is the active principle of Goodness.</note> etc., and the **justifiable**, the **bonifiable**, and the acts of **justifying**, **bonifying**, and **magnifying**, etc. It is situated in the rules by its specific property, and is introduced through specific matter and form. For just as the same quality—namely the same meaning—is expressed through one specific form in a **rose** and through another in a **violet**; so the same virtue exists through a specific form and matter in **justice**, and through others in **prudence**. ¶ Per the second species, it is asked: why is there justice? And it must be answered: so that the principles from which it descends may have righteous acts in legal cases. Furthermore: so that the **city** may have **peace** and the **public good**. ¶ Per the first species of Rule F, it is asked: how large is justice? And it must be answered that it is a **continuous quantity**, insofar as it is a continuous habit; it is not, however, point-like nor linear, for it is not a condition of the body. It neither grows nor shrinks [physically], although its act may sometimes be large and sometimes small; just as the same **hammer** sometimes gives a great blow and sometimes a small one, according to the will of the agent using it as he pleases. ¶ Per the second species of Rule F, it is asked: what are its **discrete quantities**? And it must be answered that they are those which it has through difference. For justice has one quantity in the **judge**, another in the **plaintiff**, and another in the **defendant**; just as the same water takes one shape in a circular vessel and another in a triangular vessel. ¶ Per the first species of Rule G, it is asked: what kind of justice? And it must be said that it is such as it is through **goodness**, **greatness**, etc., without which it cannot exist. ¶ Per the second species of Rule G, it is asked: what kind is justice? And it must be said that it is such as it can be through the connection of other virtues, which have righteous acts through justice. ¶ Per Rule H, it is asked: in what manner does justice consist in time? Successively from one object to another, just as a ship in continuous motion...

Furthermore, it is with the agent who acquires it, and it is with **goodness**, because it is good; and so with the other things without which it cannot exist.

### On Prudence Deduced Through Principles.

<margin>Deduction of prudence through principles</margin>
**A** man subsisting by reason of **goodness**, when that goodness is the reason for a good man to act well, then at that time he is good by habituated prudence. When, however, he does not subsist by reason of goodness, then at that time he is imprudent. ¶ A man disposing his goodness with **greatness**, so that it may be a great reason for a good man to act with great goodness, is prudent. ¶ An ancient man <note>Likely referring to a man of experience or "long duration."</note> persevering in his prudence within causes—with that prudence, indeed, he submits new prudences. ¶ Prudence with **power** is able, and power with prudence is governed and acquired. ¶ Prudence is a habit of **knowledge** through understanding, and of **faith** through believing. ¶ Prudence is first and principally a habit through **love**; secondarily, however, through fear; for fear follows love. ¶ Prudence, when it is good, is then virtuous; when, however, it is bad, it is then vicious. ¶ Prudence with **truth** is true; but with falsehood, it is false. ¶ Prudence with small pain disposes great glory. ¶ Prudence disposes **differences**; but imprudence disposes confusions. ¶ Prudence connects virtue with virtue; but imprudence connects vice with vice. ¶ Prudence contradicts ignorance, which is its enemy; and imprudence contradicts the **intellect**, which is its enemy. ¶ Prudence conserves causes according to how they are arranged in the beginning. Imprudence, however, corrupts and destroys that arrangement. ¶ Prudence disposes the **middle** <note>The "middle" or "mean" is the virtuous balance between extremes.</note> existing proportionally between the beginning and the end. Imprudence, however, acts through the opposite. ¶ A prudent man rests with an end of perfection; but an imprudent man labors with an end of imperfection. ¶ Prudence with a majority of goodness and greatness is greater. Imprudence with a majority of malice is greater. ¶ Prudence with equal causes equalizes its acts; but imprudence with unequal causes wishes to make them equal. ¶ Prudence with the majority puts imprudence to flight. Imprudence, however, with the minority puts prudence to flight.

### On Prudence Deduced Through Rules.

<margin>Deduction of prudence through rules.</margin>
**I**t is asked whether prudence is simply of the genus of **science**? And it must be answered that it is not. For a man believing in true causes is prudent. <note>This distinguishes prudence (practical wisdom/belief) from "science" (demonstrable certain knowledge).</note> ¶ Through the first species of Rule C, <note>Rule C asks "Quid?" (What?).</note> it is asked: what is prudence? And it must be said that it is the habit with which a prudent person chooses a great good over a small one, and disposes themselves toward good contingencies, and turns away and separates themselves from evil ones. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does prudence have in itself that is coessential? <note>Coessential refers to the internal components that make up the essence of a thing.</note> To which it must be answered that it has its correlatives, without which a prudent person cannot act. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is prudence in another? And it must be answered that it is good in goodness; but it is evil in evil things; and it is strong in virtues; and it is weak in sins. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does prudence have in another? It must be said that in virtue it has merit; but in sin, it has guilt. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D, <note>Rule D asks "De quo?" (Of what?).</note> of what is prudence? And it must be answered that it is of the **phantasms** <note>original: "fantasmatib[us]"; mental images or impressions used by the intellect to form thoughts.</note> which the intellect acquires through diligence and experience so that it may flee labor and rest in the end. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what things [plural] is prudence? And it must be said that it is of its "finishable" things, <note>original: "finibilibus"; things that can be brought to a completion or end.</note> which alone are suitable to it. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: whose is prudence? And it must be said that it is of the subject in which it exists, "like a cloak of the cloaked." <note>A metaphor for how a quality fits or belongs to its owner.</note> ¶ Through the first species of Rule E, <note>Rule E asks "Quare?" (Why?).</note> it is asked: why is prudence? And it must be answered that it is...

# On Fortitude deduced through principles.

<margin>On Fortitude deduced through principles.</margin>

**F**ortitude is nourished, colored, and disposed, and proportioned and conditioned under the reason of goodness. ¶ Fortitude, when joined with the greatness of goodness, magnitude, duration, etc. (excepting contrariety and minority), is assailable and defensible. ¶ Fortitude, established <note>original: "antiquata"; literally "ancient," but in this context meaning a long-held or firm habit.</note> with the duration of goodness and magnitude, submits new fortitudes to itself. ¶ Fortitude, with the power of goodness, magnitude, etc., is capable of all things. ¶ Fortitude is stronger with understanding than with believing. ¶ Fortitude is stronger with love and with fear: without fortitude, no virtue is strong. ¶ Fortitude with truth causes boldness and victory. ¶ Fortitude with delight makes a man magnanimous. ¶ Fortitude with other virtues diversifies its own acts. ¶ Fortitude has greater concord with a greater virtue. ¶ Fortitude in sins is a <term>privative habit</term> <note>A "privative habit" refers to the absence of a proper quality where it ought to be; here, "strength" in a sin is not a true virtue but a lack of proper moral restraint.</note>. ¶ Fortitude has specific principles so that it can have specific acts. ¶ Fortitude is a medium existing between virtue and virtue. ¶ Fortitude with the ultimate end causes boldness and victory. ¶ Fortitude is greater through those things that are substantial than through those things that are accidental. ¶ Fortitude is stronger with equal causes than with unequal ones. ¶ Fortitude is lessened by a greater vice, and it is also assailable and conquerable by it.

# On Fortitude deduced through rules.

<margin>On Fortitude deduced through rules.</margin>

**W**hether fortitude is stronger through prosperities or through adversities? And it must be answered that it is so. For in prosperity it fights with sharpness and love. In adversity, however, it fights with patience and fear. ¶ It is asked through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E usually asks "Why," but the text here treats it as "What."</note>: what is fortitude? and it must be answered that it is a habit placing fortifiable things against vices. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what does fortitude have in itself that is co-essential to it? and it must be answered that it has its own correlatives <note>The Lullian "correlatives" (the doer, the thing done, and the doing) which make up the essence of any principle.</note> with which it is a habit. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: what is fortitude in another? to which it must be said that it is good in goodness and great in magnitude: for one virtue is, by accident, the habit of another virtue. ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked: what does it have in another? and it must be answered that it has a good act in goodness, and a great one in magnitude, etc., and a just one in justice; just as goodness is strong in fortitude. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (Matter/Origin).</note> it is asked: of what is fortitude? To which it must be answered that it is of the acts of the higher powers: namely, of understanding, loving, and remembering. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: of what is fortitude? To which it must be answered that it is of its own active and passive principles, so that it may have a specific act. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: to whom does fortitude belong? To which it must be said that it belongs to the subject in which it is, because that is its instrument. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Here Rule E is used for "Why."</note> it is asked: why is fortitude? and it must be answered that it is because it is an acquired habit. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: why is fortitude? Ninth part. <note>original: "Nona pars"</note>

# Ninth part.

it must be answered that it is itself, so that like other virtues, it can have victory against vices. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantity).</note> it is asked: how great is fortitude? To which it must be said that it is as great as the <term>acquired habit</term> <note>A "habit" in scholastic philosophy is a stable disposition or skill gained through repeated action.</note> itself is. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: how great is fortitude discretely? <note>Discrete quantity refers to things that can be counted, like individual acts, rather than continuous measurements.</note> To which it must be answered that it possesses a discrete quantity through which its act increases or decreases. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks "Of what quality?"</note> it is asked: what is the proper quality of fortitude? To which it must be answered that it is the quality of justice. (Time).</note> it is asked: when does fortitude consist in time? To which it must be answered that it does so through the manner signified by rules C, D, and K. (Place).</note> it is asked: where is fortitude? And it must be answered that it is in victory, just as an agent is in its effect, as is clear through the third species of rule C. (Association).</note> it is asked: with what does fortitude exist? To which it must be said that it exists with the principles and definitions of the other virtues and with the virtues themselves, and especially with power, will, hope, and charity, without which it cannot exist.

## Concerning Temperance deduced through the Principles.

<margin>Concerning temperance deduced through the principles.</margin>
<insert>T</insert> Temperance, subsisting by the reason of goodness, has a good act. ¶ Temperance with greatness is great, and has a great act. ¶ The more temperance lasts, the less labor it requires. ¶ Temperance without the power of the other virtues cannot have power. ¶ Temperance is knowable through its own act. ¶ Temperance is lovable in words, in expenses, and at the table. ¶ Temperance is that virtue which is most frequently necessary. ¶ Temperance causes its act along with truth. ¶ Temperance causes rest, health, and delight. ¶ Temperance always distinguishes between the greater and the lesser by choosing equality. <note>original: "equalitatez"; referring to the "Golden Mean" or the balanced middle path between extremes.</note> ¶ Temperance accords equal things to one end. ¶ Temperance most greatly contradicts <term>gluttony</term>. ¶ In the beginning, it is necessary that temperance be strong, so that it may follow the middle, and through the middle reach the end. ¶ Temperance is a moderate measure: decreasing more [of the excess] and increasing less [of the deficiency]. ¶ Temperance with the end rests in labor. ¶ Temperance with a greater virtue is greater. ¶ Temperance increases its act with equal things. ¶ Temperance labors with "minority" <note>Lullian term for a lack of intensity or presence of a principle.</note>, and with it, it is weak.

### On faith deduced through
### the principles.

<margin>On faith deduced through the principles.</margin>

**P**erceived through analogy, we must discuss this chapter so that we may see the manner in which **faith** is superior and the **intellect** is inferior. First, through **goodness**: because the intellect cannot take God as its object as much as He is able to be an object, therefore divine goodness is the reason why God proposes Himself to the human intellect by being an object and being believed. Indeed, this "understanding" is good; and at that time the intellect takes God as its object by **believing** Him to be the one, infinite, and eternal creator, savior, and such things. And the intellect does this above its own nature; and such an "objectifying" we call the holy, admirable, and good faith. ¶ God is a great object, and according to His greatness the intellect cannot grasp Him naturally; therefore God **magnifies** the intellect, so that it may act magnificently above its own nature by simply believing. And thus faith ascends above the intellect, just as **oil ascends above water**. For when the intellect reaches the fact that God is One through faith, it believes He is "One" more than it understands Him to be "One" through the act of understanding. For the intellect is higher through greatness when it believes without labor than when it understands with labor. ¶ Faith lasts through the duration given by God, whereas understanding lasts through acquired knowledge; hence it is clear that faith is superior, but intellect is inferior. And when a man habituated in faith sins through avarice or lust, etc., faith remains in the subject in part, though with a lack of form <note>In scholastic terms, "informis" (without form) faith is belief that remains even when the person is in a state of sin, though it lacks the "form" of charity.</note>. For the subject is not then disposed with justice, prudence, etc. ¶ Just like a donkey who is not fit to be dressed in silk. ¶ The **first cause** <note>God.</note> can do more than a secondary cause; and when the second cause acts with the first, then it can do things beyond itself. Therefore the intellect can, through the first cause, believe in it; but what it can do on its own is to understand God, yet with faith helping its understanding. As **Isaiah** said: "Unless you believe, you shall not understand" <note>original: "nisi credideritis, non intelligetis"; Isaiah 7:9. This was a central pillar of medieval epistemology, emphasizing that faith provides the foundation for rational inquiry.</note>. Just as some man who was not a philosopher, and later became a philosopher: while he was not a philosopher, he believed God existed; but when he became a philosopher, he understood God existed. And then the intellect ascended to that level of understanding in which it previously was by believing. Nevertheless, I do not say that faith is destroyed because of this, but rather that it ascends to a higher level of taking an object, believing more that God exists than understanding that He exists—just like oil in a vessel where it is above the water. And if one were to add more water to said vessel, the water would indeed ascend to that place where the oil was, and then the oil would ascend to a higher place where it was not before. ¶ God is intelligible by His very nature. And He causes the human intellect to understand much by nature, with God providing the habit of faith so that He, through faith, may help the intellect to understand. For the intellect can ascend more toward the "first intelligible"—namely toward God—with two habits than with only one; just as it can do more with prudence and fortitude than with prudence alone. When the intellect understands the first object, faith disposes the intellect for understanding, just as **charity** disposes the will for loving the first object. And just as the will could not love the first object without charity, so the intellect cannot understand the first object without faith. Hence it is clear that just as charity is not destroyed when the will loves the first object, so faith is not destroyed when the intellect understands the first object. ¶ Now, a power does not contradict its own general disposition; for through that disposition it ascends and is strengthened. ¶ Faith is...

->### Part Nine<-

...a virtue existing as a <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; a stable disposition of the soul acquired through grace or practice.</note> in the intellect; otherwise, faith could not be a virtue, nor could it be a habit in the same way that charity is—for charity could not be a habit unless the will were its subject. And therefore, just as charity makes the will ascend to love an object virtuously, so faith makes the intellect ascend to understand an object virtuously. ¶ Faith, joined with truth, is a habit of the intellect; and so, when it understands the **First Object** <note>original: "obiectum primum"; refers to God, the primary focus of the intellect in medieval theology.</note> with truth, it understands Him truly. For without truth, it cannot understand Him. And therefore, truth is a principle common to both faith and the intellect. Nevertheless, faith is higher in the act of believing, while the intellect is lower in the act of understanding. Therefore, when the intellect ascends to a higher degree of truth, faith likewise ascends to a higher degree within that same truth. For the habit is above, but the one possessing the habit is below—just like a cloaked man ascending a mountain, whose body is lower while his cloak is higher upon him. The intellect cannot understand God except with labor, just as a man ascending a mountain cannot reach the top without effort; but when the intellect ascends to God with faith, it does not labor, but rather delights in Him through believing. And because a power is higher when it acts without labor than when it acts with labor, the intellect is therefore "higher" when believing in divine glory than when merely understanding it. In believing, the intellect does not distinguish between what is conditional and what is necessary; instead, it believes broadly and without distinction. But when the intellect understands truly, it understands with necessity and without confusion. Therefore, the intellect is instantaneous in believing, but successive <note>original: "successivus"; meaning it proceeds step-by-step through a logical argument.</note> in understanding. Wherefore it is clear that the intellect is higher in believing than in understanding; the reason for this is that its act of believing is above its own nature, just as water is above its nature when it is being heated <note>Water is naturally cold in medieval physics; heat is an external quality that "elevates" it.</note>. ¶ Faith is a habit given by God, and thus it is governed by God just as it is created by God. From this it is clear that the intellect cannot govern such a habit, for it is above its own nature; nevertheless, the intellect disposes itself to submit to it by fearing to offend God, rather than by not believing in Him. And thus, a harmony arises between understanding and believing. Whatever Law exists through faith must be true. Just as a thing must be good through goodness, or great through greatness, and so on. And therefore, that Law must be true in which faith is higher in truth and more opposed to sins. In this step, the intellect recognizes which Law must be true: either that of the **Christians**, or the **Saracens** <note>original: "sarracenorum"; a medieval term for Muslims.</note>, or the **Jews**. ¶ In the beginning, faith disposes the intellect toward understanding, as is clear through Rule B <note>Rule B in Llull’s "Art" typically asks "What?" and defines the essence of the subject.</note>. And when the intellect is at a certain degree of understanding, faith disposes it

---

to that same degree in believing, so that it may then ascend to another degree of understanding; and so it goes from degree to degree, until the intellect ascends to the **First Object** and rests in Him through understanding—but most especially, while on this earthly journey, through believing. ¶ Faith is the medium by which the intellect acquires merit and the means of ascent to the First Object, which indeed flows faith into the intellect so that faith may be like a "foot" for the intellect to climb with. And the intellect has another foot by its own nature: namely, understanding. It is like a man ascending a ladder with two feet. On the first rung, the foot of faith is placed first. And on that same rung, the foot of the intellect is placed as it ascends step-by-step. And on the second rung, the foot of faith is placed first, and then the foot of the intellect follows, ascending step-by-step with faith taking priority and the intellect following after. It is similar to a formal debate, where a doubt is proposed first, followed by an affirmation or a negation. Believing is not the final goal of the intellect, but *understanding* is; nevertheless, faith is the instrument used to elevate its understanding through believing. And therefore, just as an instrument stands between the cause and the effect, so faith stands between the intellect and God—faith being flowed from God into the subject so that through it, the intellect may find rest in the First Object. ¶ That faith which is greater in goodness, greatness, etc., and also in hope, charity, etc., must be the true one; but a faith contrary to it would be lesser and false. Otherwise, positive principles would succumb to privative principles <note>In Llullian logic, a "positive" attribute like goodness is more real than a "privative" one like evil, which is just the absence of good.</note>, which is impossible. And in this step, the intellect recognizes which faith is greater and truer by identifying the one that possesses greater virtue and a greater object. ¶ That faith which believes there is the greatest equality among the "reasons" <note>original: "rationibus"; referring to the Divine Dignities or attributes like Goodness, Greatness, Eternity, etc.</note> of God must be true. But that which posits inequality among them must be false. For in God there is no "before" or "after," because divine goodness, greatness, etc., must have their equal correlates, just as the intellect and the will have equal powers. And in this step, the intellect recognizes which faith is true. ¶ With a "lesser" faith, the intellect cannot elevate its understanding, but it can with a "greater" faith. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that its "greater understanding" is not in conflict with its "greater believing," just as in climbing a ladder one foot is not against the other, nor in running is one foot against the other.

<page-num>folio 69.</page-num>
<header>On the nine subjects.</header>

<margin>On faith deduced through the rules.</margin>

# On the nine subjects.

**I**f it were proposed that the intellect could understand about God those things which it can believe through faith, faith would indeed be destroyed, and consequently, merit would be lost; as it is said: <note>original: "fides non habet meritum / cui humana ratio prebet experimentum"</note> "Faith has no merit to which human reason provides proof." <note>This is a famous quote from St. Gregory the Great, suggesting that if something can be proven by logic, it no longer requires the virtuous leap of faith.</note> To this, it must be answered that this is not the case. The reason for this is that faith indeed ascends above the intellect, as has already been shown; for the merit of faith stands first, while the merit of the intellect follows after. But if they were on the same level, what you say would indeed follow. ¶ Through the first type of **Rule C** <note>In this logical system, "Rule C" typically asks "What is it?" (Quid est?).</note>, it is asked: what is faith? To which it must be answered that it is a virtue given by God, so that through it we may believe that which we cannot understand through the intellect alone. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: what does faith have in itself co-essentially? And it must be answered that it has its own <term>correlatives</term> <note>original: "correlativos"; in the philosophy of Ramon Llull, these are the active, passive, and verbal components that make up a thing's essence.</note> with which it exists as a habit. ¶ Through the third type, it is asked: what is faith in another? To which it must be said that it is a <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; a stable quality or disposition of the soul.</note> existing in the intellect, standing above the habit which the intellect possesses through science; just as it appears to a taster tasting wine from a cask, by which he judges what kind of wine it is by the tasting. But because it is possible for the wine to be altered at another time, the intellect does not have certain knowledge through understanding, but through faith, it believes that it is such as it is. ¶ Furthermore, faith is good in goodness, and great in greatness, and so on. ¶ Through the fourth type, it is asked: what does faith have in another? And it must be answered that it has "understandability" in the intellect, and it has "lovability" in the will (for it is loved by the will), and "recallability" in the memory (because it is recalled by the memory). ¶ Through the first type of **Rule D** <note>Rule D typically asks "Of what?" (De quo?).</note>, it is asked: of what is faith? And it must be answered that it is of itself, because it is a created thing. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: of what is faith? And it must be answered that it is of its own active and passive relations, with which it is a special virtue. ¶ Through the third type, it is asked: to whom does faith belong? And it must be said that it belongs to the subject in which it exists, just as a cloak belongs to the cloaked man. ¶ Through the first type of **Rule E** <note>Rule E typically asks "Why?" (Quare?).</note>, it is asked: why is there faith? And it must be answered that it exists because it has its own cause. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: why is there faith? And it must be answered that it exists so that the intellect, through it, can believe that which it cannot understand by itself. Just as imagination exists so that a human may imagine that which he cannot perceive through the senses. ¶ Through the first type of **Rule F** <note>Rule F typically asks "How much?" (Quanta?).</note>, it is asked: how great is faith continuously? And it must be answered that it is as great as the extent to which a person can, with it, direct themselves toward objects. ¶ Furthermore, it is continuous because it is an indivisible habit. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: how great is faith discretely? To which it must be answered that it is as great as the number of its correlatives by which its act increases or decreases. ¶ Through the first type of **Rule G** <note>Rule G typically asks "What quality?" (Qualis?).</note>, it is asked: what is the proper quality of faith? And it must be answered: "belief" <note>original: "credulitas"; here meaning the capacity or act of believing.</note>. For this belongs to no other virtue. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of faith? And it must be answered: its goodness, its greatness, and so on. ¶ Through **Rule H** <note>Rule H typically asks "When?" (Quando?).</note>, it is asked concerning the time of faith. To which it must be answered through the third type of Rule C, that it exists in time because it is something new within it. And through the fourth type of C, it has corruption in time when a person does not believe those things about God which they used to believe; and it is "resurrected" in time when a person rises again by believing those things about God which they were meant to believe. ¶ Furthermore, it is in time because sometimes it has a great act, and sometimes a small one. ¶ Likewise, it is in time because sometimes it focuses on one object, and sometimes another. And the same can be said of Rule D and K in their own way. ¶ Through **Rule I** <note>Rule I typically asks "Where?" (Ubi?).</note>, it is asked: where is faith? To which it must be answered through the second type of Rule C, that it is in its correlatives; and through the third type of C, it must be answered that it is in the intellect, just as a habit is in its subject; and the same can be said of Rule D and K in their own way. ¶ Through the first type of **Rule K** <note>Rule K typically asks "How?" (Quomodo?) or "With what?" (Cum quo?).</note>, it is asked: in what manner does faith exist? To which it must be answered that it exists through that manner in which the First Object <note>God.</note> presents itself as an object to the intellect; and by believing, the intellect itself directs itself toward Him above its own power of understanding. ¶ Through the second type of Rule K, it is asked: with what does faith exist? And it must be answered that it exists with power, object, and act. Through the intellect, it exists with the power that uses faith effectively and morally; and it exists with the object—namely, with God—without whom it cannot be; and with the act—namely, with believing. But here the intellect itself doubts, asking: when it is not believing but understanding, where is the faith? To which it must be answered that faith is in the intellect itself, because it is its habit. And at that time, "believing" is in the intellect as a potential, but it is brought into act when the intellect believes.

## On hope deduced through the principles.

<margin>On hope deduced through the principles.</margin>

**H**ope is a habit of the memory, so that through the memory itself, by hoping, one may ascend to the First Object, just as the intellect does by believing. And first, we shall speak of goodness. ¶ Goodness belongs to the memory so that it may naturally recall God as much as it can; and when it can no longer do so naturally, hope assists it morally, with God presenting Himself...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the theological virtues, specifically moving from the nature of Faith to the nature of Hope. It explores how Hope interacts with the faculties of the soul—Memory, Will, and Intellect—using the logical framework established in the previous sections.</meta>

### Ninth part

**M**emory is moved by reason of its own goodness; and with memory thus having God as its object, it hopes beyond its own natural powers, just as the will, together with charity, ascends to God by loving. And this is a great good for the memory. 
¶ Memory is greater through two acts than through only one: namely, through hoping and <term>recollecting</term> <note>original: "recolere"; in this philosophical system, this refers to the specific action of the memory faculty.</note> together, rather than through recollecting alone. Therefore, the magnitude of God magnifies the memory of man when a man magnificently disposes himself to recollect God with the <term>habit</term> <note>A "habit" (habitus) is a stable disposition or quality that allows a person to perform an action easily and well.</note> of hope; so that when memory cannot fully recall Him, it may yet hope in Him. And this is the greatness of memory.
¶ Hope lasts in the subject along with the subject's disposition: namely, when one recollects God by reason of His goodness, magnitude, eternity, and so forth. But when the memory does not dispose itself toward recollecting, and sin becomes its habit, then hope has no subject in which it can remain, and thus it fails. 
¶ Memory, with its own power, is able to recollect; and likewise, with the power of God mediating through hope, it is able to hope in God. And so, speaking analogically, the "power" of hope is superior, while the "power" of memory is inferior; by reason of which the inferior power ascends to the object along with the superior power, just as the power of understanding ascends with the power of believing. 
¶ Now, a sinner who understands his great sins and the great justice of God at the hour of his death is close to despair through his understanding and recollecting. But hope, which is a habit of the memory, ascends to divine mercy when God presents Himself as an object to the sinner who possesses hope. Then the sinner draws himself away from despair; however, he could not do this unless hope were a habit of the memory. 
¶ When a man is in war or at sea in great peril, or has a great need for something to happen, his will is sometimes so weakened and broken by excessive fear that it cannot lift its love up to God; but the memory, by placing God as its object through hope, rouses the will to love Him with charity. And then the will is comforted and consoled by the memory. And the same can be said of the intellect, which finds no other remedy except to hope in God. 
¶ Memory with hope is as virtuous as the will with charity. And just as the will is virtuous without charity <note>The author likely means the natural capacity for virtue, as opposed to the supernatural virtue of charity.</note>, so is the memory without hope. Since memory and will are mutually helpful to one another, memory with hope aids the will, and the will with charity aids the memory, so that they may both be virtuous. Hope with truth is true, and with falsehood it is false. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that a sinner, when he can flee from sin and yet does not wish to, but instead intends to persist in it, believes he has hope but in fact does not. 
¶ For hope cannot share a subject with sin. 
¶ A sinner with hope feels delight; but without hope, he feels sadness and pain. For with hope he has love; but without hope he has hatred. 
¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that a sinner with hope ascends toward loving; without hope, he descends toward hating and despairing, turning "loving and hoping" into "hating and despairing." Who could estimate the sadness and pain that are in such a sinner? 
¶ There is a difference between recollecting and hoping, just as there is between understanding and believing. The reason for this is that hoping is superior, while recollecting is inferior. Recollecting is a natural act, but hoping is a supernatural act. Hoping and recollecting agree with each other. For recollecting prepares the way for hoping (assuming that the hoping is directed toward goodness, magnitude, etc.). And hoping causes the one who recollects to ascend by degrees, so that through the ascent of recollecting, hope itself can ascend. It is like a <term>cloak</term> <note>original: "cappa"; a common metaphor in this period where the property (the cloak) moves only because the subject (the cloaked person) moves.</note> that ascends a mountain through the ascent of the one wearing the cloak. 
¶ Legitimate hope and spurious hope are opposites, so much so that they cannot exist in the same subject. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction in the object. 
¶ Legitimate hope is that which exists with goodness and truth and such things, and it is set against malice and falsehood. Spurious hope, however, is that which exists with malice and falsehood and is set against goodness, truth, and so forth. And in this step, the memory grieves because it recollects so many sinners who are habituated in spurious and deformed hope. 
¶ In the beginning, the man hoping in God is the <term>efficient cause</term>; hope is the <term>form</term>. Those things which the man recollects are the <term>matter</term>, and the supreme object is the <term>end</term>, with recollecting serving as the basis for hoping. 
¶ Hope is the medium existing between the sinner and God, because it is the messenger of both: God flows hope into the sinner, and the sinner flows back his own good and great recollection to God. When a sinner or a man in need recollects God without hope, he finds no rest in his recollecting. The reason for this is that his recollecting is not at that level where rest is found. But when hope is joined to it, then recollecting ascends with hope to that level where rest is found. 
¶ That hope which is greater by reason of goodness and magnitude is a sign and light of true faith or law. For a lesser faith or law cannot support a greater hope. But a greater hope stands within a greater faith or law; otherwise, there would be a contradiction in the object. And in this step, the intellect recognizes which people stand in the true law. 
¶ Hoping and recollecting can exist together toward the supreme object at the same time, but not equally; for hoping is prior, and recollecting is posterior. Just as "willing" and "loving" can exist at the same time in one and the same subject. Loving, however, is prior (being the habit), while willing is posterior (being the action habituated by charity); just as at the height of a mountain, the cloak is above the one wearing the cloak. 
¶ Memory with smallness has recollection...

It distinguishes between legitimate hope and "spurious" hope based on their alignment with truth and goodness.</summary>

# On Hope derived through the rules
<margin>On hope derived through the rules</margin>

**Q**uestion: It is asked whether hope is a <term>habit</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, a "habit" (habitus) is a stable quality or disposition that allows a person to perform an action easily and well.</note> of the memory? And it must be answered that it is so, because in a time of necessity, the memory comforts and consoles the intellect and the will by hoping. And to <term>recollect</term> <note>original: "recolere"; the specific action of the memory faculty in this philosophical system.</note> thus ascends to the highest object through hoping, just as understanding ascends through believing, and willing through loving. 

Likewise, "to hope" does not belong to the category of certainty (which belongs to the category of knowledge), nor does it belong to the category of the will. For the will wants many things for which it does not hope; from which it follows that since hope is not of the category of the intellect, nor of the category of the will, it must be of the category of the memory. And since in the soul there are no powers except for those three mentioned above, hope further does not belong to the imaginative or sensitive faculties.

¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>The "Rules" refer to Ramon Llull’s system of logical inquiry, where Rule C asks "What is it?" (Quid), Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo), etc.</note>, it is asked: What is hope? And it must be answered that it is the virtue to which the act of hoping properly belongs. 

¶ Through the second species, it is asked: What does hope have in itself co-essentially? To which it must be said that it has its own special <term>correlatives</term> <note>In Llull's "Art," correlatives are the internal relational components of any principle: the agent (hoper), the patient (that which is hoped), and the act (hoping) itself.</note> with which it acts through its own species. 

¶ Through the third species, it is asked: What is hope in another? And it must be answered that it is a special virtue within other virtues, and also a messenger that consoles, comforts, and advises, and things of this sort. Furthermore, it is good within goodness, and great within greatness, etc. It is unimaginable in the imaginative faculty, insensible in the sensitive faculty, and indivisible in the subject. 

¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: What does hope have in another? And it must be said that it has "to hope" within "to recollect," just as charity has "to love" within "to will," and faith has "to believe" within "to understand." Furthermore, it has a good act in goodness, a great act in greatness, etc., and a just act in justice, etc.

¶ Through the first species of Rule D, it is asked: Of what is hope? And it must be answered that it is of itself, because it is a created habit. 

¶ Through the second species, it is asked: Of what is hope? To which it must be said that it is of its specific likenesses derived from the "relatives" of the memory, of which it is a habit. 

¶ Through the third species, it is asked: To whom does hope belong? And it must be answered that it belongs to the memory, just as an instrument belongs to the one who uses it.

¶ Through the first species of Rule E, it is asked: Why is there hope? To which it must be answered that it exists because its cause exists; just as an "artificial day" <note>A medieval term for the period from sunrise to sunset.</note> exists because the sun is above the earth. 

¶ Through the second species, it is asked: Why is there hope? And it must be answered that it exists so that the memory can lift its recollection in a time of necessity, by advising, helping, and comforting—advising the intellect in its understanding and the will in its willing, so that they may ascend to the highest object.

¶ Through the first species of Rule F, it is asked: How great is hope continuously? And it must be answered that it has a great and continuous quantity. For it has a great office in consoling, comforting, and elevating the other powers to the highest object; its own quantity is indivisible, since it is neither a point nor a line. 

¶ Through the second species of Rule F, it is asked: Concerning the "discrete" <note>Discrete quantity refers to things that can be counted or separated, as opposed to continuous quantity like a line.</note> quantity of hope? To which it must be answered that it has a discrete quantity with respect to its correlatives, from which it has differences, and with which its acts grow or decrease as it pleases.

¶ Through the first species of Rule G, it is asked: What is the proper quality of hope? And it must be answered that it is "to hope." For hoping belongs only to hope. 

¶ Through the second species, it is asked: What is the "appropriated" quality of hope? To which it must be said that it is goodness, greatness, and things of this sort.

¶ Through Rule H, it is asked: Concerning the time of hope? And it must be answered that it is in time; for it is a "new" habit <note>Meaning it is acquired or created in time, rather than being eternal like God.</note> and depends on past things. And it is in the present time because it exists; and furthermore, because it has its act and encompasses the future time, for it hopes for that. And this is signified by Rules C, D, and K. In this step, the intellect knows that hope is a very great habit in time.

¶ Through Rule I, it is asked: Where does hope have its act? And it must be answered that it has it in the "recollect-ability" <note>original: "recolibilitatem," referring to the memory's capacity for being recollected or activated.</note> of the memory, outside of which it cannot have it. For outside the "recollect-ability" of the memory, there is only oblivion, which is a privative habit. And this is signified through Rules C, D, and K.

¶ Through the first species of Rule K, it is asked: How does hope exist, and how is it destroyed? To which it must be said that it exists in the manner that the memory does, by disposing its act with the "Principles" <note>The "Principles" are Llull's fundamental concepts like Goodness, Greatness, etc.</note> and with other virtues; just as a person in a time of necessity, when they cannot help themselves with their own virtues, helps themselves with the goodness of God, etc., and similarly with the mercy and charity of God, and such. Its destruction, however, is when sin occurs in the subject in which it exists.

<summary>This page analyzes the theological virtue of Hope through the logical "Rules" of Ramon Llull's Art, defining Hope specifically as a faculty of the Memory rather than the Will. It explains how Hope functions as a "habit" that allows the soul to ascend to God, especially in times of spiritual necessity.</summary>

...which is evil and against the mercy and charity of God; by reason of which the sinner, deprived of hope, falls into despair. ¶ Through the second **rule, K**, <note>In Llull’s system, Rule K usually concerns "How" or "With what" a thing exists or acts.</note> it is asked: with whom is hope? To which it must be answered that it exists with the disposition of the subject in which it resides, and with the habits of the principles and virtues, and especially with the Supreme Agent <note>The "Supreme Agent" refers to God as the primary cause of all virtues.</note> who causes that very species, and through it, clothes and habituates the subject.

## On Charity derived through the principles.

<margin>
Charity
derived 
through

3.

**C**harity is a <term>habit</term> <note>A stable disposition or quality of the soul that makes acting rightly feel natural.</note> of the **will**; and charity, by reason of its **goodness**, elevates the will to love the divine goodness more than itself. ¶ Charity, by reason of its **greatness**, makes all goods common. ¶ Charity, with its **duration**, causes one to endure and to love with goodness, greatness, etc. ¶ The will, combined with the **power** of charity, overcomes all things. ¶ Charity, with great duration, disposes the **intellect** toward understanding the highest intelligible <note>That which is capable of being understood; here referring to the nature of God.</note>. Since God is supremely lovable, the will, through charity, elevates its "loving" to prize God more than itself. Since God is lovable <term>through Himself</term> <note>original: "per se amabilis"; meaning God's very nature is the cause of love, requiring no external reason.</note> and not "believable" or "hopeable" through Himself (insofar as He is of Himself), charity is therefore a higher virtue than the other virtues <note>Llull argues charity is superior because it unites the soul directly with God's essence (love), whereas faith and hope are means to an end.</note>. ¶ Charity lives with **truth**; it also overcomes things that are merely imaginable or sensible. ¶ Charity finds delight in all things. ¶ Charity does not distinguish between what is "mine" and what is "common." ¶ Charity leads all things back to a true good and a harmonious end. ¶ Charity finds no contrary. ¶ The will, through charity, is first in love, and through the act of willing, it follows afterward. ¶ Charity is the medium existing between the friend and his beloved. ¶ Charity rests in all things. That law in which charity is greater is also truer than any other law. ¶ Charity makes all goods equal. ¶ Charity, when combined with **smallness** <note>original: "minoritate"; the opposite of the Principle of Greatness.</note>, is weak.

## On Charity derived through the rules.

**Q**uestion: It is asked whether charity is a habit of the will? And it must be answered that it is so: so that the will, with charity, can love God more than itself. And first, as much as itself. ¶ Through the first species of **rule C**, <note>Rule C asks "What is it?" (Quid est?).</note> it is asked: what is charity? And it must be answered that charity is that virtue with which the will approaches the loving of God and one's neighbor <note>original: "primum"; in this context, the "first" neighbor or fellow man.</note> above its own natural power. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does charity have within itself that is <term>co-essential</term> <note>Llull's term for the internal relationships that make up an essence, such as a "lover," the "beloved," and the "act of loving."</note> to it? And it must be answered: its own specific relations with which it is a specific virtue. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is charity in another? To which it must be said that it is good within **goodness**, great within **greatness**, and the empress and governor in all the virtues. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does charity have in another? And it must be answered that it has whatever it wills in all things. ¶ Through the first species of **rule D**, <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo?).</note> it is asked: of what is charity? It must be said that it is of itself, because it is a created thing. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what is charity? To which it must be said that it is of the likenesses of the <term>correlatives</term> of the will, about which we have spoken in its own chapter. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: whose is charity? To which it must be answered that it belongs to the will, for it is the will's habit. ¶ Through the first species of **rule E**, <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare?).</note> it is asked: why is there charity? And it must be answered that it exists because it is an effect of God. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why is there charity? And it must be answered that it exists so that the will can love God above its own strengths, and also its friend and its enemy. And in this step, the intellect recognizes why charity is the highest virtue. ¶ Through the first species of **rule F**, <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum?) regarding quantity.</note> it is asked: concerning the **continuous quantity** of charity? To which it must be answered that it has a wonderful quantity, because the will, through it, loves God, and its friend, and its enemy. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: concerning the **discrete quantity** of charity? And it must be answered that it has a discrete quantity by reason of the difference of its correlatives, with which its act increases or decreases at will—while its continuous quantity remains without division, increase, or diminution. ¶ For charity is not a habit made of points or lines. ¶ Through the first species of **rule G**, <note>Rule G asks "Of what kind?" (Quale?) regarding quality.</note> it is asked: what is the proper quality of charity? And it must be answered that it is its own specific "loving." ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of charity? To which it must be answered: goodness, etc. For it is good, etc. For it is just, etc. ¶ Through **rule H**, <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando?).</note> it is asked: concerning the time of charity? To which it must be answered through the third species of rule C: that it exists in that time without succession, because it is a spiritual habit; but it exists in succession by means of the subject in which it is, and into which its acts flow and ebb, changing objects; and this is shown through rules C, D, and K. ¶ Through **rule I**, <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi?).</note> it is asked: where is charity? And it must be answered that it is in the subject **habituatively** <note>As a settled quality within the person.</note> and in the object **objectively** <note>As directed toward the thing being loved.</note>. And this is shown through rules C, D, and K. ¶ Through...

Through the first **rule K**, <note>In the Lullian system, Rule K typically addresses "How" (Modus) and "With what" (Instrument/Association).</note> it is asked: how is **charity**? And the answer is that it is in that manner by which a likeness is gathered from the **will**, derived through the principles, with the exception of contrariety and minority; <note>Lullian "principles" include Goodness, Greatness, Duration, etc. "Contrariety" and "Minority" are excluded here because Charity, in its perfect form, has no opposite or lesser state within its divine essence.</note> and it is also sustained in regular species, with God being its cause and the will being its object, along with a disposition free from sin. ¶ Through the second **rule K**, it is asked: with what is charity? To which it must be responded that it is with the Agent: namely with God, who is its cause; and with its will, which is its subject; and it is with the principles and rules in its own manner, and with other virtues without which it cannot exist.

**S**ince **patience** is a <term>habit</term> <note>A stable quality or disposition of the soul.</note> of the **will**, the will, with the **goodness** of its patience, overcomes its own malice. ¶ The will, with the **greatness** of patience, overcomes anger. ¶ Patience, with **duration**, endures against impatience. ¶ Through the **power** of charity and humility, the patient person overcomes all things. ¶ Patience arises, lives, and is nourished through the deliberation of the **intellect**. ¶ Patience with charity is of the genus of humility. ¶ Patience under charity is a greater virtue than under any other virtue. ¶ No anger can stand against true patience. ¶ Patience with <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passio"; here used in the philosophical sense of "undergoing" or "suffering" an action or hardship.</note> acquires joy and delight. ¶ Patience does not distinguish between the one who reviles and the one who is reviled. ¶ Patience is connected with charity, piety, and humility. ¶ Patience does not care for vengeance. ¶ Patience has suffering at the beginning, but action and victory at the end. ¶ Patience exists as a middle ground between labor and rest. ¶ A person habituated in patience is always at rest. ¶ Patience with greater labor is a greater virtue. ¶ Patience makes prosperity and adversity equal.

# On piety derived through the principles.

<margin>
On piety 
derived 
through 
principles.

**W**ill, with the goodness of **piety**, <note>original: "pietas." In medieval Latin, this term encompasses both religious "piety" and the "pity" or "compassion" one feels for others.</note> disposes itself to feel sorrow for the suffering of its neighbor. ¶ The greatness of piety moves the will to have great sorrow for the adversities of its friend and even its enemy. ¶ Piety lasts with charity, humility, patience, and gentleness. ¶ The will, with the power of piety, can cause sighs in the heart, and tears and weeping in the eyes, and sadness in the soul. ¶ The intellect understands that the signs of piety are charity, humility, patience, gentleness, sighs, and weeping. ¶ Piety is lovable, because with it the will destroys its own cruelty. ¶ Piety, with charity, humility, etc., shows itself to be a virtue. ¶ True piety is the true medicine of the will. The will, with piety, thinks that its own suffering and its own sadness are its glory and its delight. ¶ Piety, through the habit of charity, does not distinguish between one's own and the common. ¶ A pious man, through piety, reconciles and pacifies enemies. ¶ Piety, with charity and humility, patience and gentleness, contradicts impiety, which is its enemy. ¶ Piety is the formal and humble principle; sighs and weeping are its matter; touch is its end. <note>Llull is using Aristotelian categories here: the "form" or essence is the virtue itself, the "matter" is the physical expression (tears), and the "end" or goal is the physical act of comforting/touching the sufferer.</note> ¶ Piety consists in the midst of charity. ¶ Piety without action does not fail. And in this step the intellect knows that the will with piety delights itself; when the pious man grieves, laughs, and sighs. ¶ That law with which the greatest piety can be held must be the true one. ¶ The pious man equates his own sufferings with the sufferings of his neighbor. ¶ Piety with lesser signs shows itself to be lesser.

# On piety derived through the rules.

<margin>
On piety 
derived 
through 
the rules.
</margin>

**W**hether charity is a <term>habit</term> <note>A stable disposition of the soul.</note> of piety: and it must be answered that it is. The reason for this is that charity, by reason of the highest object [God], is prior; but piety, by reason of a lower object [one's neighbor], is later. ¶ Through the first species of **rule C**, it is asked: what is piety? To which it must be said that it is a virtue with which the will moves itself to have sorrow for the sufferings of its neighbor. ¶ Through the second species of **C**, it is asked: what does piety have in itself co-essentially? And it must be said that it has its own correlatives <note>A Lullian technical term for the internal components of an essence: the "Pity-er," the "Pity-ed," and the act of "Pity-ing."</note> with which it is a special virtue. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is piety in another? And it must be answered that it is the virtue signified in its signs: namely in charity, humility, patience, gentleness, sighs, weeping, and the like; just as wine is signaled to be sold by the branch of ivy existing before the tavern. <note>It was a common medieval custom to hang an ivy bush or branch over the door of a tavern to show wine was available inside.</note> ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does piety have in another? And it must be answered that it has its signs in a pious man, just as impiety has its signs in an impious man. ¶ Through the first species of **rule D**, it is asked: from what is piety? And it must be answered that it is from itself, because it is an acquired habit. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: from what is piety? And it must be answered that it is from that matter signified through its signs. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to whom does piety belong? And it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it is, like the instrument of an agent. ¶ Through the first species of **rule F**, it is asked: how great is piety continuously? And it must be answered that it is as great as is signified through its signs. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the discrete quantity of piety? And it must be answered that it has a discrete quantity with which it increases and decreases its act without increase and decrease of the continuous quantity of its essence. <note>In this logic, the "essence" of the virtue stays the same size, but the "quantity" of its outward expression or intensity can fluctuate.</note> ¶ Through the first species of **rule G**, it is asked: what is the proper quality of piety? And it must be answered: the compassion which it has for the suffering of its neighbor. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of piety? And it must be said: sadness. For sadness is a common form; and likewise of charity, humility: and so of its other signs. ¶ Through **rule H**, it is asked: regarding the time of piety. And it must be answered through the third rule C that it is in time when it is signified through its signs, and so of the others marked by C, D, K. ¶ Through **rule I**, it is asked: regarding the place of piety. And it must be answered that piety is in the pious man, and it is in all those signs with which it is marked. ¶ Through the first **rule R**, it is asked: how is piety? To which it must be said that it is through that manner which a pious man has to acquire it with charity, humility, patience, and gentleness, etc. ¶ Through the second **rule R**: with what is piety? To which it must be answered that it is with its signs, just as a blacksmith is with his tools: namely with the furnace, anvil, hammer, tongs, etc. ¶ We have spoken of the nine virtues; and just as we have spoken of them through principles and rules:

# On avarice derived through the principles

<margin>On avarice derived through the principles.</margin>
**A**varice, with its malice, destroys goodness, because it is not the reason for a good person to do good from good things.
¶ Avarice, with its greatness, magnifies malice, duration, and power through its act. As long as avarice lasts, so long lasts its insatiable act: and because of this, the avaricious man, by increasing riches, believes he is discerning <note>original: "descerre," likely a contraction for "discernere" (to discern). In this system, the sinner often falsely believes they are achieving a higher intellectual or moral state.</note>, but he cannot. ¶ The power of avarice is a privative habit <note>term: "privative habit" (habitus priuatiuus). In medieval philosophy, a privation is not just a "thing," but the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be there, like blindness is the privation of sight.</note> of the power of generosity: just as deafness is a privative habit of the power of hearing. Therefore, the avaricious man does not have a resting power. ¶ Just as faith elevates the intellect to believe truths beyond its own powers: so avarice elevates the intellect to believe falsehood beyond its own powers; and just as the avaricious man believes himself to be generous: so charity exalts the will to love beyond its powers. Thus avarice elevates the will to love future things: and it does not rest in those things which it already has. ¶ The avaricious man, the more he has, the more he believes himself to be virtuous. ¶ The avaricious man believes that which is true to be false: and vice versa, just like an unfaithful person. For falsehood and avarice agree: just as generosity and truth agree in their own way. ¶ The avaricious do not delight in what they have, for they still believe themselves to be in need; nor do they delight in those things they hope for, for they do not yet have them. ¶ The avaricious man does not distinguish between generosity and avarice, because he believes that which is avarice to be generosity. ¶ The avaricious man, by reason of avarice, cannot have concord with any virtuous man: for it contradicts all virtues. ¶ The more wealthy an avaricious man is, the more he contradicts his first principle <note>original: "primo suo." This refers to God as the First Principle of all Goodness.</note>: because he is contrary to the end of all good things. ¶ The avaricious man perverts positive principles into privative ones: and thus, the more he believes he is discerning, the more he labors: just as a man believing he sees better with blinded eyes than with seeing ones. ¶ The avaricious man joins and measures all things with his avarice. ¶ The avaricious man rests with the end of privation, just like a man suffering hunger, and it pleases him to suffer it. ¶ The avaricious man is more avaricious with greater riches: whence it is clear that the more he has, the more he desires to have. ¶ The avaricious man does not achieve equality <note>term: "equality" (coequat). One of Llull's principles; here it means a lack of balance or proportion.</note>: for avarice consists in extremes. ¶ Lesser avarice has lesser signs: just as greater avarice has greater signs.

# On avarice derived through the rules.

<margin>On avarice derived through the rules.</margin>
<margin>avars, luxury, anger</margin>
**W**hether avarice is a general sin objectively? And it must be answered that it is: because it targets and desires many and diverse objects.
¶ Through the first species of **rule C**, it is asked: what is avarice? And it must be answered that avarice is a sin which turns good things away from the end for which they were intended. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does avarice have in itself co-essentially? <note>term: "co-essentially" (coessentialiter). In Llull's logic, this refers to the internal relationships—the "doer," the "done," and the "doing"—within a concept.</note> And it must be answered that it has privative correlatives: just as generosity has its positive ones. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is avarice in another? And it must be answered that it is a privative habit in the avaricious man, with which he causes for himself poverty, and sadness, and labor: just as a man wearing a cloak that is too big causes for himself weariness and labor <note>original: "cappa cappati." A classic Lullian analogy where a "cloak" represents an accidental property or habit covering the subject.</note>. ¶ The avaricious man, habituated in a privative habit, has rest neither in his riches nor in other things: but rather labor and distress. ¶ Through the first species of **rule D**, it is asked: of what is avarice? And it must be answered that it is of itself: for it has no nature: nor is it a creature, because it is a sin: nor is it a virtue. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: from what is avarice? And it must be answered that it is from the moral defect of man: just as deafness is from a defect of nature: for just as deafness is a privative habit against the positive habit of hearing: so avarice is against the positive habit of generosity: and in this step, the intellect recognizes from what sin is made. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: whose is avarice? and it must be answered that it belongs to the avaricious man: just as the cloak belongs to the one cloaked. ¶ Through the first species of **rule E**, it is asked: why is there avarice? And it must be answered that it exists because man does not wish to have generosity: just as a man’s nakedness exists because the man is not clothed. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: for what purpose is avarice? And it must be answered: so that man may not have generosity, nor rest in his goods. ¶ Through the first species of **rule F**, it is asked concerning the continuous quantity <note>term: "continuous quantity" (quantitate continua). A philosophical term for things that form an unbroken whole, like a line, as opposed to discrete things like a pile of coins.</note> of avarice? And it is to be answered that it has continuous quantity: for it has a continuous habit: just like the cloak of the one cloaked. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked concerning the discrete quantity of avarice: to which it must be said that it has discrete quantity: so that it can increase and diminish its acts at will. ¶ Through the first species of **rule G**, it is asked: what is the proper quality of avarice? To which it must be said that it is insatiability: and in this step, the intellect recognizes that the more the avaricious man has, the more he desires to have. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of avarice? And it must be answered that it is poverty, labor, sadness...
