## On gluttony derived through the principles.

<margin>On gluttony derived through the principles.</margin>
**T**he gluttonous man, through excessive eating and drinking, does harm to himself; and yet he believes he is doing well. ¶ The gluttonous man, with his greatness, magnifies his own evil. ¶ The labors of the gluttonous man last longer than his delights. ¶ The glutton, with the power of gluttony, cannot stand against gluttony. ¶ Gluttony is a sin that disposes the intellect to believe that it is not a sin. ¶ Gluttony is a sin that disposes the will to desire excessive eating and drinking, just as faith disposes the intellect to believe. ¶ Gluttony is a sin that is simply against all virtues. ¶ Gluttony is a lying habit. For with it, a man deceives himself; and through it, he disposes himself toward infirmity and death. ¶ Gluttony causes delight in the sense of taste, but labors and pains in the sense of touch. ¶ The glutton confounds and darkens all powers, both higher and lower. ¶ The glutton accords excessive eating with excessive drinking. ¶ Gluttony contradicts courtesy <note>original: "curialitati," referring to the refined behavior or "courtliness" expected of a virtuous person.</note>, health, and riches. ¶ Gluttony gives joy in the beginning, but in the end, it gives sadness. ¶ Gluttony measures neither food nor drink. ¶ The glutton, because of gluttony, finds no rest.

## On gluttony derived through the rules.

<margin>On gluttony derived through the rules.</margin>
**W**hether gluttony is a greater habit of the **will** than of the **intellect**: And it must be answered that it is so. ¶ For the glutton desires food and drink with the will. # On the nine subjects. Folio 73.

...the gluttonous man: just as a cloak is defined by the cloaked person <note>original: "cappa per cappatum." This is a standard analogy in Lullian logic where a habit or quality (the cloak) is inextricably linked to the subject (the wearer).</note>. ¶ Through the second species <note>The "Rules" in this system are categories of questions. Rule E/F usually deals with "Why?" and "How much?"</note> it is asked: **why** is there gluttony? And it must be answered that it is so that a man through it might be mocked, lazy, poor, sick, and sometimes dead, and placed in hell. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F, it is asked: **how much** is gluttony? And it must be answered that it has such a great continuous quantity because it is indivisible, for the gluttonous man cannot be satisfied by it. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **how much** is gluttony discretely? To which it must be answered that it is as great as the number of times the gluttonous man employs it, by increasing or diminishing his acts according to his own pleasure. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G, it is asked: **what** is the proper quality of gluttony? And it must be answered that it is the insatiability of the soul through the sense of taste beyond its powers. And in this step the intellect recognizes the manner in which gluttony raises the appetite of the intellect above its own powers, just as fire raises water by heating it beyond its natural strength. ¶ Through the second species of Rule G, it is asked: **what** is the appropriated quality of gluttony? And to this it must be answered that it is uncourtliness, mockery, poverty, drunkenness, and things of this kind. And in this step the intellect recognizes that the first species belongs to the soul, but the second to the body, by reason of which gluttony is first effected in the soul and then in the body. ¶ Through Rule H <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando?)</note>, it is asked concerning the **time** of gluttony: And it must be answered that it is a new habit within that person. ¶ Furthermore, it exists in time because it uses **past** time; for the gluttonous man grieves that he did not drink and eat more. And similarly it uses the **present**, because through it he has his practice. And similarly it uses the **future** when he desires to eat and drink. ¶ Likewise, it uses time in hell, where he will suffer inestimable and eternal hunger and thirst. ¶ Through Rule I <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi?)</note>, it is asked **where** gluttony is: And it must be answered that it is a privative habit <term>privative habit: a state defined by the absence of a virtue (like temperance), rather than a positive existence</term> within its own correlatives <note>Correlatives are Lull's way of describing the relationship between the doer, the thing done, and the act itself.</note>, and in those things in which it exists. And this is signified through Rules C, D, and K. ¶ Through the first Rule K <note>Rule K asks "How?" (Quomodo?)</note>, it is asked **how** gluttony exists. And it must be answered that just as temperance exists in a positive mode, so gluttony exists in a privative mode. For the gluttonous man has neither mode nor measure in eating or in drinking. ¶ Through the second Rule K <note>Rule K also asks "With what?" (Cum quo?)</note>, it is asked **with what** gluttony exists: To which it must be said that it is with its cause, just as a cloak is with its cloaked wearer, because it is made or fashioned through him.

# Principles of Lust Deduced

<margin>
Principles of Lust deduced.
</margin>

Lust, by reason of the goodness of touch, works evil and blames the goodness of chastity. ¶ Lust, by reason of the great sweetness of touch, magnifies the greatness and the pain for the one who reasons. And in this step the intellect recognizes the manner in which conscience arises. ¶ Lust, by reason of the duration of bodily delights, causes lasting pains in hell. ¶ Lust submits spiritual power to corporal power. And in this step the intellect recognizes the manner in which the lustful man is bound. ¶ Lust perverts the intellect into believing that it is not a sin, just as avarice perverts it into believing that it is not a sin. And in this step the intellect recognizes what the obstinacy of the sinner is. ¶ Lust, by reason of the beauty of a woman's face, ensnares <note>original: "filocapit." A Lullian term meaning "to capture through love/lust."</note> the lustful man into loving the foulness and the interior stenches which the woman has within herself. And a man greatly ensnared by lust believes himself to be very virtuous. And the intellect marvels greatly at such a belief. ¶ Lust is a lying habit, because it begins with beauty and comes to rest in foulness. And that which is evil, it holds as good. ¶ The lustful man, through the delight he has in seeing, hearing, imagining, thinking, and touching, loses the glory of paradise on his journey and acquires eternal pains for all his powers in hell. ¶ The lustful man does not distinguish between the foulness and the beauty of a woman. For from these he makes one end, one resting place. ¶ The lustful man harmonizes beauty and foulness toward a single end. ¶ The lustful man contradicts chastity through lust, so that through chastity he might not have happiness. Nevertheless, he does not believe he is doing this. ¶ Lust begins with the senses, and multiplies its effect with the imagination, until it becomes a sin in the reasoning faculty. ¶ The end of lust flows into the senses, and the senses flow back to the end. And this happens by means of the imagination, until it is a sin in the perverted reasoning faculty. ¶ The lustful man first rests in beauties, then in foulness and stenches. ¶ Greater lust shows and demonstrates itself with greater signs. ¶ Man and woman sin equally through lust, but they do not love each other equally. ¶ Lust is lesser through the body but greater through the soul. For through the body it is "in the becoming," but through the soul it is "in the completed being."

# Part Nine

<margin>
On lust, deduced through the rules.
</margin>

**W**hether lust begins earlier through the imagination than through the senses? And it must be answered that yes, it does. For the imaginative power is closer to the reasoning power than the sensitive power is. ¶ Through the first species <note>In Lullian logic, the "Rules" are sets of questions (A-K) used to investigate a subject. Each rule has different "species" or ways of being applied.</note> of Rule C, it is asked: **what** is lust? And it must be answered that it is a sin to which it is uniquely proper to be lustful. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **what** does lust have in itself co-essentially? And it must be answered that it consists of its own correlatives <note>A Lullian term referring to the active, passive, and verbal components of a concept (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving).</note> with which it constitutes a specific sin. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: **what** is lust in another? And it must be answered that in the soul it is an "intended" sin, but in the body it is an "extended" one. In this step, the intellect recognizes how lust exists in the soul instantaneously <note>original: "sine successione." The soul experiences the intent all at once, whereas the body experiences the physical act over a span of time.</note>, but in the body it exists through a sequence of time. ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked: **what** does lust possess in another? And it must be answered that it possesses a kind of "height" through domination in the man in whom it resides, just as a cloak possesses a man by ornamenting him. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D, it is asked: **from what** does lust come? And it must be answered that it comes from itself: for it is a sin, and a sin does not come from anything else, because sin is essentially "nothing" <note>This follows the medieval philosophical idea that evil is not a positive creation but a "privation" or lack of good.</note>. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **from what** does lust come? And it must be answered that it comes from moral monstrosity, because it is a "privative habit" in moral matters, just as deafness is a lack of the natural sense of hearing. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: **to whom** does lust belong? And it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it exists, just as a cloak belongs to the cloaked man. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E, it is asked: **why** is there lust? And it must be answered that it is because an [evil] habit has been acquired. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **why** is there lust? And it must be answered that it exists so that chastity might not be; just as deafness exists so that hearing might not be, and as water is made hot so that it might not be cold. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F, it is asked: is this lust **continuous**? And it must be answered that it has a continuous quality because a habit [of the soul] is indivisible. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **how much** is lust discretely? To which it must be said that it is as great as the number of times lust can increase or diminish its own acts; and in this step, the intellect knows that within the same essence and habit, a "discrete quantity" consists of many individual acts that differ by number. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G, it is asked: **what** is the proper quality of lust? And it must be said that it is that through which it becomes a specific vice, just as heat is the proper quality of fire. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **what** is the appropriated quality of lust? And it must be answered that it is the "heating" with which the flesh of the lustful man grows. ¶ Through Rule H, it is asked regarding the **time** of lust? And it must be answered that lust exists at one time by "aptitude" <note>A potential or readiness for the sin.</note> by reason of the sensitive and imaginative powers, and at another time by the "completed act" by reason of the soul’s conception. And this is signified through Rules C, D, and K. ¶ Through Rule I, it is asked **where** is lust? And it must be answered that it is in the sensitive and imaginative powers as an instrument, but in the soul through its essence and habit. And this is signified through Rules C, D, and K. ¶ Through the first species of Rule K, it is asked **how** is lust? To which it must be said that it exists by way of seeing, hearing, touching, and imagining, and by way of the soul conceiving and commanding. ¶ Through the second species of Rule K, it is asked **with what** is lust? And it must be answered that it exists with perverse movements; just as hot water exists with its own perverse and contrary nature—namely, with heat—and as the intellect exists with ignorance, and hearing with deafness.

# On Pride, deduced through the Principles.

<margin>
On pride, deduced through the principles.
</margin>

**P**ride, by reason of its malice, makes the subject in which it resides descend; just as humility makes its subject ascend. ¶ The greatness of pride makes its subject small; just as humility magnifies its own. ¶ The duration of pride disposes the subject so that it may have eternal punishments in Gehenna <note>Hell.</note>. ¶ The power of pride cannot stand against the power of humility. ¶ That man is proud who believes he possesses his natural gifts and his riches from himself. ¶ A man who loves himself before God is proud. ¶ When a proud man is corrected, he believes himself to be virtuous and the one correcting him to be vicious. ¶ Pride is a lying habit; for it believes it is ascending when it is descending. And even when it believes it tells the truth, it tells a lie. A proud man does not rest with anyone, nor does anyone rest with him. ¶ The proud man does not distinguish between his own pride and another's humility. ¶ Pride has harmony with all other vices. ¶ Pride contradicts all virtues. ¶ Pride is a "principle" <note>In the Lullian system, a principle is a fundamental building block of reality or logic.</note> that makes that which is higher descend, and that which is lower ascend <note>Pride perverts the natural hierarchy of the universe.</note>. ¶ Pride blocks the "mean" <note>The middle point or path between a beginning and an end.</note> existing between the beginning and the end. For this reason, it descends and does not ascend. ¶ The proud man never finds rest. ¶ Greater pride possesses greater outward signs. ¶ The proud man finds no one as his equal, nor does he desire a companion. Lesser pride is through the body; greater pride, however, is through the soul.

# On the Nine Subjects.

<margin>On pride, deduced through the rules.</margin>

**W**hether pride exists primarily through the intellect or rather through the will? And it must be answered that it is through the intellect. For the intellect is the first to present an object <note>The "object" here refers to the thing being thought about or desired.</note>, while the will follows afterward in the act of choosing. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C in Llull's system asks "What?" (Quid?).</note>, it is asked: **what** is pride? To which it must be said that it is a sin that descends as much as it believes it is ascending. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **what** does pride have in itself co-essentially? And it must be answered that it has its own privative correlatives <note>In Lullian logic, "correlatives" are the active, passive, and verbal parts of a concept. "Privative" means they represent a lack or a void of a good quality.</note> which are opposite to the positive relatives of humility. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **what** is pride in another? To which it must be said that it is indicative in the intellect, elective in the will, and preservative in the memory; and it is the empress over all other sins. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: **what** does pride possess in another? And it must be answered that it possesses a descent in the subject in which it resides, just as the soul possesses motion in a running body. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo?).</note>, it is asked: **of what** is pride? And it must be answered that it is made of its own privative correlatives, which stand in contrast to the positive relatives of humility. Just as night is the absence of day, and deafness is the absence of hearing. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **of what** is pride? And it must be answered that it consists of its own specific correlatives from which a specific sin is formed. In this step, the intellect recognizes that the first species refers to the defect of its contrary, but the second refers only to itself. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **whose** is pride? To which it must be said that it belongs to its own subject, for it is the habit <note>In medieval philosophy, a "habit" (habitus) is a stable disposition of the soul or body.</note> of that subject. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare?).</note>, it is asked: **why** is there pride? And it must be answered: because humility has been made absent from the subject in which it should be; just as blindness exists in a subject because sight has been made absent from it. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **why** is there pride? And it must be answered that it exists so that humility cannot be there; just as the "end" <note>The "final cause" or purpose.</note> of fire exists in a choleric person so that the "end" of water cannot be in them. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum?), here regarding "continuous quantity" or duration.</note>, it is asked regarding the continuous quantity of pride? And it must be answered that pride possesses this, for it is an indivisible habit; indeed, when it is generated, it is generated in an instant. And when it is destroyed, it is destroyed in an instant. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked regarding the discrete quantity <note>Discrete quantity refers to things that can be counted as separate parts.</note> of pride? And it must be answered that it possesses this. For it is composed of several privative principles: namely, from privative goodness, privative humility, etc. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks "Which?" (Quale?).</note>, it is asked: **which** is the first species of pride? And it must be answered that it is an undue ascent. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **which** is the quality appropriate to pride? And it must be answered that it is a due and violent descent; the opposite may be said of humility. ¶ Through Rule H <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando?).</note>, it is asked regarding the **time** of pride? And it must be answered through the first species of Rule D: that it exists at the moment it begins to be; namely, when humility is destroyed in the subject and pride is introduced into it, as for example when it is said: "the generation of one is the corruption of the other" <note>original: "Generatio unius est corruptio alterius." A standard Aristotelian maxim: for a new thing to begin, the previous state must end.</note>. And this same thing is signified through Rule K. ¶ Through Rule I <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi?).</note>, it is asked: **where** is pride? And it must be answered that it is in the subject where humility once was or where it ought to be. And this is signified through Rules C, D, and K. ¶ Through the first Rule K <note>Rule K asks "How?" (Quomodo?) and "With what?" (Cum quo?).</note>, it is asked: **how** does pride exist? And it must be answered that it exists in a manner contrary to the manner of humility; just as loving is a manner of delight, but hating is a manner of suffering. ¶ Through the second Rule K, it is asked: **with what** does pride exist? And it must be answered that it exists with the privation of humility, of obedience, of justice, and such things; and also with all other things that are predicated of it.

<margin>Authority.</margin>

## On sloth, deduced through the principles.

<margin>On sloth, deduced through the principles.</margin>

**A** slothful <term>sloth: Latin 'accidia', a spiritual apathy or "noonday devil" that makes religious and moral duties feel burdensome.</term> man is swift and diligent when it comes to doing evil, but he is lazy when it comes to doing good. ¶ The slothful man is diligent in avoiding the common good. ¶ Sloth lasts alongside pride, laziness, anger, and the like. ¶ Sloth hinders those men who propose to do good and avoid evil, but are unable to; for their power is imprisoned by sloth. ¶ Sloth alters and infects the intellect, and yet it remains unknown by the intellect. ¶ Sloth makes the will lazy in loving the good, but diligent in loving evil. ¶ Sloth judges laziness to be a virtue, but judges diligence in the good to be a vice. ¶ Sloth is lazy regarding truths, but diligent regarding falsehoods. ¶ The slothful man does not take delight in positive habits, but in privative ones. ¶ Because of sloth and laziness, the slothful man does not distinguish with his intellect.

# Part Nine.

...in making knowledge, but it confounds it.
¶ The slothful man brings his higher and lower powers <note>In medieval psychology, "higher powers" usually refer to the intellect and will, while "lower powers" refer to the senses and physical appetites.</note> into agreement in all their capacities. For he is lazy in acquiring virtues. ¶ The slothful man contradicts the diligence of virtues with the busy-ness of vices. ¶ Sloth turns positive principles into privative ones <note>In this logical system, a "positive" principle is the presence of a good (like light), while a "privative" one is its absence (like darkness).</note>. Wherefore the slothful man murmurs and pretends to be a soothsayer; he gives advice when it is not necessary, he finds fault with good things, and he is an enemy of the end <note>The "end" (finis) refers to the ultimate purpose or goal of a human life—perfection in God.</note>. Furthermore, form binds and matter corrupts, so that the agent himself becomes habituated to laziness. ¶ Sloth hinders the middle way, so that the rightful beginning cannot find the end in which it should rest. ¶ The slothful man rests against the end, but labors at the finish. For sloth is the enemy of the end of perfection. ¶ Greater sloth is the fountain of all vices. ¶ The slothful man, with his sloth, is the fountain of all vices. ¶ The slothful man, with his sloth, makes the acts of vices equal, so that sloth is strong against the diligence of virtues. ¶ Lesser sloth concerns lesser diligence, greater sloth concerns greater diligence, or even wicked diligence.

## On sloth, deduced through the rules.

<margin>
On sloth
deduced
through the
rules.
</margin>

**I**t is asked whether sloth is a mortal sin? And it must be answered that it is: for it hinders all acts of the virtues. ¶ But here the intellect marvels: since sloth is a mortal sin, and is signaled and represented by many signs, why is it so little recognized by men, even though one remembers that the greater part of men are habituated to sloth? ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C in Llull's "Art" asks: "What is it?" (Quid?).</note>, it is asked: **what** is sloth? And it must be answered that sloth is a sin with which the slothful man grieves at the good of his neighbor, but rejoices in his neighbor's misfortunes. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **what** does sloth possess in itself co-essentially? And it must be answered that it possesses its own correlatives <note>In Llull's logic, "correlatives" are the active, passive, and verbal components of any essence.</note>, which are the privative correlatives of charity. For a charitable man rejoices in the good of his neighbor and grieves at his misfortunes. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **what** is sloth in another? And it must be answered that it is lazy in good things and malevolent; but in evil things, it is swift, diligent, and eager. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: **what** does sloth possess in another? To which it must be said that it has its own actions in all sins. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks: "Of what?" (De quo?).</note>, it is asked: **of what** is sloth? To which it must be said that it consists of the absence of charity in a subject where charity ought to be; just as a consequence does not exist when its antecedent is missing. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **of what** is sloth composed? To which it must be said that it is composed of its own specific privative correlatives, with which it is a specific sin. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **to whom** does sloth belong? And it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it exists, just as deafness belongs to the deaf man. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks: "Why?" (Quare?).</note>, it is asked: **why** is there sloth? And it must be answered that it exists because it is an acquired habit; just as day exists because the sun is shining its light upon the earth. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **why** is there sloth? And it must be answered: so that charity might not have a subject in which it can exist; for sloth is a privative habit against the positive habit of charity, hindering its end. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks: "How much?" (Quantum?).</note>, it is asked: concerning the **continuous quantity** of sloth? And it must be answered that it possesses this in all the vices caused by it. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: concerning the **discrete quantity** <note>In medieval logic, "continuous quantity" refers to things that are unbroken (like a line), while "discrete quantity" refers to things that can be counted (like numbers).</note> of sloth? And it must be answered that it possesses discrete quantities by reason of the different vices in which it performs different acts. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks: "What kind?" (Quale?).</note>, it is asked: what is the **proper quality** of sloth? To which it must be said that it is laziness (*pigricia*); for without it, sloth cannot act. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the **appropriated quality** of sloth? And it must be answered: malevolence and iniquity; for through these, the slothful man rejoices in evils and grieves at goods. ¶ Through Rule H <note>Rule H asks: "When?" (Quando?).</note>, it is asked: concerning the **time** of sloth? And it must be answered through Rule C that it is lazy in that time, so that the subject in which it exists does nothing useful while he has the time. ¶ Through Rule I <note>Rule I asks: "Where?" (Ubi?).</note>, it is asked: **where** is sloth? To which it must be said that it is in the laziness of the soul, the imagination, and the senses, which indeed neglect to do good but love to do evil. ¶ Through the first rule of K <note>Rule K asks: "How?" (Quomodo?) and "With what?" (Cum quo?).</note>, it is asked: **how** does sloth exist? And it must be answered that it exists in a manner contrary to the manner of charity. For just as charity has a way of being in loving the neighbor’s good and hating the neighbor’s evil, so sloth exists through the contrary manner. ¶ Through the second rule of K, it is asked: **with what** does sloth exist? To which it must be said that it exists with the privative habits of the virtues, namely with injustice, imprudence, etc. Furthermore, it exists with laziness, anger, and the like.

# Folio 75.

## On the nine subjects.

<margin>On envy deduced through principles.</margin>

**T**he envious person desires to possess the goods of another against reason, for which reason evil follows him in spiritual matters. And if the envious person truly recognized this often, he would no longer hold onto envy. ¶ The magnitude of envy exists alongside the magnitudes of other vices; therefore, it cannot be defeated by a single magnitude of virtue <note>The author argues that because envy connects to many other sins, one needs a whole "system" of virtues to overcome it, rather than just one good trait.</note>. ¶ Envy lasts as long as other vices endure; therefore, it cannot be defeated without the endurance of other virtues. ¶ The power of envy is rooted in the powers of other vices. And therefore, it cannot be defeated without the power of <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charitas"; in this context, the supreme virtue of selfless love for God and neighbor</note> acting within the powers of other virtues. ¶ The envious intellect is perverse and altered by envy. For it does not truly know itself; the cure for which consists in this: namely, that the person understands the envy itself. ¶ Envy turns the will away from the supreme good; nevertheless, it can be cured by frequently returning the will to the supreme object <note>Meaning God</note> by focusing upon it. ¶ The envious person does not possess virtues but vices; therefore, if he wishes to have virtues, let him exchange those things he has for those things he lacks. ¶ The envious person does not possess truth, but falsehood; therefore, he deceives himself. A cure can be applied: namely, that he does not deceive himself. ¶ When the envious person possesses the things he once envied, he still find no rest in them. For his own knowledge "bites" or stings him. ¶ Through envy, the envious person has as many diverse acts as there are other vices; nevertheless, he can be cured by frequently numbering or "counting" them <note>A practice of mindfulness or confession—identifying each specific envious thought to strip it of its power.</note>. ¶ Envy has no harmony with any virtue; the cure lies in recognizing this. Envy contradicts the virtues with <term>privative habits</term> <note>A "privative" habit is defined by the absence of a good, just as darkness is the absence of light.</note>; its cure is achieved through the opposition of positive habits. ¶ Envy begins with <term>sensibles</term> <note>Things perceived by the five senses.</note>, is arranged with <term>imaginables</term> <note>Things formed in the mind's eye.</note>, and is perfected with spiritual things, by destroying the imaginative and the sensible. ¶ Envy is the measure with which the envious person measures injury, imprudence, and the like. But the cure consists in the measure of justice, prudence, and the like. ¶ The envious person does not rest in the things he focuses on. For he desires them with great labor; however, a cure is given when that labor is avoided until they reach a state of rest. ¶ With greater envy, the envious person undergoes greater labors; nevertheless, with greater charity, he can be cured so that he may perform greater [virtuous] actions. ¶ Envy, through its own act, makes all the acts of others equal <note>Likely meaning that envy reduces everything a neighbor does to a single point of resentment.</note>. And the cure for this consists in the act of charity, through which all other acts of the virtues are made equal. ¶ The envious person believes that the things he possesses are smaller, and that the things he envies are larger; the cure consists in seeking what the true utility and the <term>end</term> <note>The "end" (finis) refers to the ultimate purpose or goal of a thing.</note> of that thing is.

***

### On envy deduced through rules.

<margin>On envy deduced through rules.</margin>

**I**s envy a more general sin, objectively speaking, than avarice? And the answer is yes. For the greedy person does not focus on as much as the envious person does. For the greedy person believes he can possess the thing he focuses on; however, the envious person focuses on many things that are impossible for him to have. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>In Llull's system, Rule C asks "What is it?" (Quid est?).</note>, it is asked: what is envy? To which it must be said that it is the sin with which the envious person desires to have the belongings of another without reason. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does envy have in itself <term>co-essentially</term>? <note>Inherent to its very being.</note> And the answer is that it has its own privative <term>correlatives</term> <note>Terms that exist in relation to each other, like "envier" and "envied."</note> with which it is what it is. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is envy in another? And the answer is that it is a habit in the envious person with which the envious one always labors with sadness and pain. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does it have in another? To which it must be said that it has height and "lying-before" in the envious person, just as a cloak is on a cloaked man. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "From what?" (De quo?) or "Of what?".</note>, it is asked: what is envy made of? To which it must be responded that it is made of its own privative and specific correlatives with which it is a specific sin; just as deafness is of its own parts, and hearing is of its own. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is envy about? To which it must be answered that it is about its own specific relatives, just as blindness is about its own. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: whose is envy? To which it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which the habit exists; just as malevolence belongs to the will, forgetting to the memory, and ignorance to the intellect. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare?).</note>, it is asked: why is there envy? And the answer is: because it is an effect caused by the envious person; just as deafness is an effect caused by a defect of hearing. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why is there envy? And it must be answered that it exists so that the subject in which the envy resides may suffer labor, and in hell, perpetual pain and sadness. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F deals with "How much?" (Quantum) or quantity.</note>, it is asked: concerning the continuity [or quantity] of envy? And the answer is that it possesses so much of it that with it, the envious person can measure avarice, luxury, gluttony, and the like. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: concerning the <term>discrete quantity</term> <note>In logic, quantity that can be counted in distinct units.</note> of envy? And...

...it must be answered that envy possesses that magnitude. For it can have many acts differing in number.

¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G in this logical system usually investigates "Quality."</note>, it is asked: what is the proper quality of envy? To which it must be said that it is a certain passion which the envious person has in desiring the things of others.

¶ Through the second species, it is asked what is the appropriated quality of envy. To which it must be said that it is injustice. For envy itself exists within injustice and imprudence. ¶ It is imprudence; and so on with the others.

¶ Through Rule H <note>Rule H concerns "Time."</note>, the time of envy is questioned. To which it must be said that it is in the person just like a new <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; in medieval philosophy, a "habit" is a stable disposition or ingrained character trait rather than just a repetitive action.</note> in a subject: because at one time it performs one act, and at another time another. Furthermore, because its subject is at one time in one place and at another time in another place, and so forth.

¶ Through Rule I <note>Rule I concerns "Place."</note>, it is asked where envy is. And it must be answered that it is in the soul from which it was crafted; and also in the imagination, for it was made through the mediation of the imagination. It is also in the sensible things by which it is signaled and figured.

¶ Through the first species of Rule K <note>Rule K concerns "Manner" (How) and "Instrument" (With what).</note>, it is asked: how does envy exist? To which it must be said that it exists by way of objecting to the goods of others against reason, along with the infected acts of the subject in whom it resides.

¶ Through the second species of Rule K, it is asked: with what does envy exist? And it must be answered that it exists with the privative habits from which it is formed: namely with malice, injustice, and similar things.

### On anger deduced through principles.

<margin>On anger deduced through principles.</margin>

**T**he Will moves itself with anger toward hating the good without <term>deliberation</term> <note>original: "deliberatione"; the process of rational thought and choice. Anger is seen as a failure of this process.</note>. And therefore the remedy consists in using deliberation. 

¶ Anger, with great fury, conquers all things; but the remedy is given through great abstinence and deliberation.

¶ Anger lasts as long as its act lasts. The remedy consists in focusing on a "foreign object" <note>Meaning a distraction or a different subject of thought to break the cycle of rage</note> and persevering in that.

¶ The power of anger is diminished by the power of patience, abstinence, and also deliberation.

¶ Anger confuses the intellect because it takes away the power of understanding from it; the remedy, however, is to restore its understanding to the intellect.

¶ Anger perverts the will into hating what it ought to love; its remedy is abstinence until the ability to love rises again.

¶ The will is in vice when it is with anger; its remedy is that it should be in virtue through abstinence.

¶ The intellect does not understand virtue when it is with anger; but the remedy consists in this: namely, that it may recognize virtue through patience.

¶ The angry man, when he suffers the force of hating, fails in loving and caring.

¶ The angry man does not distinguish between his own evil and the evil of another; the remedy consists in making that distinction.

¶ The angry man accords vice with vice; but a remedy can be given by according virtue with virtue.

¶ The angry man contradicts patience; the remedy for which consists in resisting him with patience.

¶ Anger begins with hearing, but it is destroyed with loving.

¶ Anger measures without measure; the remedy consists in measuring with measure.

¶ No man rests with anger; every man rests with patience.

¶ A greater anger without a greater patience is unassailable; but the reverse is not true: and in this step, the intellect recognizes that virtue is absolutely stronger than vice.

¶ Anger makes the acts of the intellect and the will equal in fury; the remedy for which can be given by making them equal with abstinence, patience, and <term>charity</term>.

¶ A lesser anger is conquered by a greater patience.

### On anger deduced through rules.

<margin>On anger deduced through rules.</margin>

**I**t is asked whether anger is generally a sin more than any other sin? And it must be answered that it is: for in its fury, the intellect has no deliberation.

¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C concerns "What."</note>, it is asked: what is anger? To which it must be said that it is a sin with which the will, without deliberation, hates the good and loves the evil.

¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does it have that is co-essential to itself? To which it must be answered that it has its <term>correlatives</term> <note>In this philosophical system, "correlatives" are the interconnected parts of a concept, such as the hater, the thing hated, and the act of hating.</note> confused by reason of its fury.

¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is anger in another? To which it must be said that in the will, it is a bond with which the will binds itself to hate without reason; the intellect to be ignorant; and the memory to forget.

¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does it have in another? To which it must be answered that it has "empire" in the will, because it commands it to hate the good and love the evil. Furthermore, it has dominion in the intellect and in the memory. For it commands the intellect to be ignorant and the memory to forget.

¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D concerns "From what" or "Of what."</note>, it is asked: from what is anger? And it must be answered that it is not "from" anything. For it is a sin; and sin is not made "from" anything, materially speaking <note>This follows the theological idea that evil is a privation or a lack of good, rather than a created substance with its own "matter."</note>.

¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what is anger? To which it must be answered that it is of its specific correlatives with which it exists in its own species.

¶ Through the third species, it is asked: whose is anger? To which it must be said that it belongs to the subject in whom it resides.

...it must be [judged] that it is such: because it exists in a subject in which charity, patience, and abstinence are absent. ¶ Through the second species [of Rule F], it is asked: why does anger exist? And to this it must be answered that it exists so that the virtues may not perform their own acts. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F in this system measures "Quantity." The first species usually refers to "continuous quantity."</note>, it is asked: how great is anger continuously? And it must be answered that it is as great as the degree to which it deprives acts of charity, patience, and abstinence; and also of justice, prudence, and the like. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: concerning the discrete quantity of anger? And to this it must be said that it possesses quantity insofar as its act increases or decreases. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G concerns "Quality."</note>, it is asked: what is the proper quality of anger? And it must be said that anger exists within that time. For it is a new <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; a settled disposition of character.</note>, and in that time it multiplies its act. ¶ Through Rule I <note>Rule I concerns "Place."</note>, it is asked: where is anger? And it must be answered that it is in the will by hating, and in injury by harming, and the like. It is also in movement: for the more it is moved, the more it multiplies its act. ¶ Through the first [species of] Rule K <note>Rule K concerns "Manner" (How) and "Instrument" (With what).</note>, it is asked: how does anger exist? To which it must be said that it exists by way of a perversion of the intellect, will, memory, and the imagination of anger; this perversion existing under the rationale of the cause of fury and without deliberation. ¶ Through the second [species of] Rule K, it is asked: with what does anger exist? And it must be answered that it exists with sensible and imaginable things; and also with a perverse soul, and with habits that deprive one of principles: namely with malice and the like.

<margin>Concerning falsehood deduced through the principles.</margin>
## Concerning falsehood deduced through the principles.

**A** false man, in deceiving another, deceives himself: the knowledge of which is gained through the definition of goodness. ¶ Falsehood is not recognized by its own magnitude; rather, it is recognized by the magnitude of <term>integrity</term> <note>original: "legalitas"; in this logical system, it refers to the principle of Lawfulness or moral Rectitude.</note>. ¶ Falsehood lasts as long as it is not recognized; for when it is recognized, it is destroyed. ¶ Falsehood does not have power against understanding, but against believing; indeed, prudence is its enemy. ¶ Falsehood, coupled with believing, deceives the understanding. ¶ Falsehood makes itself loved under the shadow of integrity; but the end <note>The "end" refers to the final result or purpose (teleology).</note> of integrity reveals and proves what it is. ¶ Falsehood, together with hypocrisy, feigns that it is the virtues; but prudence destroys it and manifests it for what it is. ¶ Falsehood does not act alongside the act of truth; wherefore it follows that it is recognized when the act of truth is present. ¶ Falsehood promises delights, but gives punishments: and through this, it is recognized. ¶ Falsehood does not distinguish, but confuses. Therefore, it is recognized by distinction. ¶ The false man brings sensible things and their signs into agreement so that he may deceive the imagination and the intellect; which, with its own concordance, shells the aforementioned falsehood like a nut. ¶ Falsehood contradicts the "end" with which falsehood is itself contradicted. ¶ Falsehood delights in the beginning, but in the end it grows sorrowful; by which reason it is acknowledged. ¶ Falsehood removes the "middle" <note>The "medium" or mean between the start and finish.</note> that is disposed between the beginning and the end. And therefore, it is recognized by this. ¶ The false man rests in the beginning, but labors in the end; by reason of which the falsehood itself is known. ¶ A greater falsehood is recognized by a greater degree of integrity. ¶ The false man equates like with like, by which reason the falsehood is known. ¶ Falsehood is recognized by a lesser virtue.

## Concerning falsehood deduced through the rules.

<margin>Concerning falsehood deduced through the rules.</margin>
**W**hether falsehood is as strong as integrity? And it must be answered that it is not: because integrity is a constructive <note>original: "politiuus"; relating to the building up or ordering of a state or soul.</note> habit, but falsehood is a privative <note>original: "puatiu’"; meaning it exists only as the absence or destruction of a good.</note> one. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "What is it?" (Quid est?).</note>, it is asked: what is falsehood? And it must be answered that it is a sin with which a man deceives and is deceived. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does falsehood have within itself that is co-essential to it? And it must be answered that it has its own correlatives from which its essence consists. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is falsehood in another? And it must be answered that in sensible things it is deceptive through contrary signs; and in the imagination it is deceptive through the ignorance of the intellect; and in the end, it is an enemy. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does falsehood have in another? To which it must be said that it has its own acts within privative principles, acting against the constructive principles. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo?).</note>, it is asked: of what is falsehood? And it must be answered that it is of itself. For sin is...

¶ Through the second species <note>The "species" are sub-questions or specific applications of a Rule.</note> [of Rule D], it is asked: from what does falsehood arise? To which it must be answered that it arises from its own specific privative principles <note>In this system, a "privative" principle is the absence or corruption of a good quality.</note> with which it constitutes a specific sin, just as deafness arises from its own [defects] which constitute a specific deformity. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to whom does falsehood belong? And it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it resides, just as a **habit** <term>habit: a settled or regular tendency or practice, especially one that is hard to give up.</term> belongs to a person. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Propter quid).</note>, it is asked: why does falsehood exist? And it must be answered that it exists because lawfulness is not present in its subject. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: for what purpose is there falsehood? And it must be answered that it exists so that a person may be deceived, just as an instrument exists so that an effect may be produced through it by someone. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum).</note>, it is asked: how great is continuous falsehood? And it must be answered that it is as great as the subject is capable of acting upon it. ¶ Through the second species of F, it is asked: how great is discrete falsehood? To which it must be said that it possesses a discrete quantity caused by privative principles. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks "Of what kind?" (Quale).</note>, it is asked: what is the proper quality of falsehood? To which it must be said that it is deception, for this is its specific act. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of falsehood? To which it must be said that it is lying, hypocrisy, and the like. ¶ Through Rule H <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando).</note>, it is asked concerning the time of falsehood: and it must be answered that it exists in time because it is a new habit, and it performs its acts within that time. ¶ Through Rule I <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi).</note>, it is asked: where is falsehood? And it must be answered that it exists in lying, hypocritical, and deceptive people. ¶ Through the first species of Rule K <note>Rule K asks "How?" (Quomodo) and "With what?" (Cum quo).</note>, it is asked: in what manner does falsehood exist? And it must be answered that it exists by way of a fiction <note>original: "figmenti"</note> for the purpose of deceiving and lying and the like. ¶ Through the second species of Rule K, it is asked: with what does falsehood exist? And it must be answered that it exists with dissimulation and deception and the like, as has been indicated by what has been said.

<margin>Concerning inconstancy deduced through principles.</margin>

## Concerning inconstancy deduced through principles.

**C**onstancy is a habit in which goodness is the reason why a good man acts well; and because inconstancy hinders this, it is therefore a sin. ¶ Inconstancy is overcome by the greatness of constancy. ¶ As long as inconstancy lasts, constancy is in a state of privation <note>Privation is the absence of a quality that should normally be present.</note>. ¶ The power of inconstancy has no strength against the power of constancy. ¶ An intellect joined with inconstancy does not possess strong understanding. ¶ Constancy joined with inconstancy is not lovable. ¶ Constancy joined with inconstancy is not a virtue. ¶ Constancy and inconstancy cannot exist together in truth. ¶ Inconstancy does not belong to the category of delight, but to the category of labor. ¶ Constancy opens and distinguishes differences; inconstancy, however, closes and obscures them. ¶ Constancy and inconstancy do not agree in genus or in species. ¶ It is in the nature of inconstancy that it must be resisted at the beginning. ¶ For afterwards, it is difficult to resist it. Since constancy is prior, all inconstancy is therefore posterior <note>In medieval logic, the "prior" thing is more fundamental or more "real" than the "posterior" thing.</note>. ¶ Constancy joins, but inconstancy disjoins. ¶ A constant man rests with constancy, but an inconstant man toils with inconstancy. ¶ Greater inconstancy cannot stand above greater constancy, nor can it hold a higher rank. ¶ Constancy and inconstancy are equally eligible by reason of free will, but they are not equally measurable. ¶ A lesser inconstancy is easily conquered by a greater constancy.

<margin>Concerning inconstancy deduced through the rules.</margin>

## Concerning inconstancy deduced through the rules.

**W**hether inconstancy is more a habit of the **will** <term>will: the faculty by which a person decides on and initiates action.</term> than of the **intellect** <term>intellect: the faculty of reasoning and understanding.</term>? And it must be answered that it is. For the will is more changeable than the intellect. The reason for this is: because the intellect is discursive <note>The intellect moves step-by-step through reasoning.</note>, while the will is suddenly changeable. Therefore, the intellect knows that the remedy against inconstancy is to remove the suddenness of the will by placing it into discourse <note>Rational deliberation.</note> alongside the intellect. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "What?" And it must be answered that it is a small stream deviated from the goal of constancy. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does inconstancy have within itself as coessential <note>Coessential: sharing the same essence or fundamental nature.</note>? To which it must be answered that it has its own correlatives <note>Llull’s "correlatives" are the active, passive, and verbal components of a concept (e.g., the deciever, the decieved, and the act of decieving).</note> with which it is what it is. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is inconstancy in another? And it must be answered that it is an empress in the will, disobedient in the intellect, shameful in the imagination, and unstable in sensible things. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does it have in another? And it must be answered that it has a lack of fortitude in the will, and deception in its promises. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D...

Regarding inconstancy, "of what" is it? To which it must be said that it is of itself: because it is a sin. ¶ Through the second species <note>The "species" are specific types of questions derived from a general Rule.</note> it is asked: from what does inconstancy arise? And it must be said that it arises from its own privative <term>privative: a term describing something defined by the absence of a quality, like darkness being the absence of light</term> and specific principles through which it is what it is. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: to whom does inconstancy belong? To which it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which its **habit** <term>habit: a settled or regular tendency or practice, especially one that is hard to give up</term> resides. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Propter quid).</note> it is asked: why is there inconstancy? And it must be answered that it exists because there is no constancy in the subject in which it resides; just as there is heat in warm water, for in that water there is no coldness. By this, the intellect knows in what manner natural habits are similar to moral habits. ¶ Through the second species of Rule E, it is asked: for what purpose is there inconstancy? To which it must be said that it exists so that constancy might not have being. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that sin is nothing: because it is against being. <note>This reflects a common medieval philosophical view that evil and sin have no independent existence but are merely the absence or "privation" of the good.</note> ¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum).</note> it is asked: how great is inconstancy? And it must be answered that it is as great as it is able to hinder constancy. ¶ Through the second species it is asked concerning the discrete quantity <note>Discrete quantity refers to things that can be counted or separated into units.</note> of inconstancy: to which it must be said that it possesses this because the will is frequently changeable in practice. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G asks "Of what quality?" (Quale).</note> it is asked: what is the proper quality of inconstancy? and it must be answered that it is the alteration of the will. ¶ Through the second species of Rule G, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of inconstancy? And to this it must be answered that it is the weakness of the heart's fortitude. ¶ Through Rule H <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando).</note> it is asked concerning the time of inconstancy: and it must be answered that it exists in that time in which the will is changeable and habituated by it. Furthermore, it exists in the time in which the will, through inconstancy, acts against constancy. ¶ Through Rule I <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi).</note> it is asked: where is inconstancy? and it must be answered that it is in the weakness of the will and also in the privation of perseverance and in its aforementioned locations. ¶ Through the first Rule K <note>Rule K asks "How?" (Quomodo).</note> it is asked: how does inconstancy exist? to which it must be answered that it exists through the contrary manner by which constancy exists: which indeed exists through the manner of discourse, deliberation, and choice with prudence, and especially with fortitude. ¶ Through the second Rule K <note>Rule K asks "With what?" (Cum quo).</note> it is asked: with what does inconstancy exist? and to this it must be answered that it exists with sudden alteration; and it is with its cause, of which it is the effect; and with the privation of constancy, just as a shadow exists with the privation of light. ¶ We have spoken of the nine subjects discussed or deduced through the principles and rules of this Art: and through those things we have said of them, the practitioner of this Art will be able to speak skillfully in a similar way regarding other foreign subjects attributed to them.

**A**pplication is divided into fifteen parts. ¶ The first part is through the implicit and the explicit. ¶ The second through the abstract and the concrete. ¶ The third through the First Figure. ¶ The fourth through the Second Figure. ¶ The fifth through the Third Figure. ¶ The sixth through the Fourth Figure. ¶ The seventh through definitions. ¶ The eighth through rules. ¶ The ninth through the Table. ¶ The tenth through the evacuation of the Third Figure. ¶ The eleventh through the multiplication of the Fourth Figure. ¶ The twelfth through the mixture of principles. ¶ The thirteenth through the nine subjects. ¶ The fourteenth through the hundred forms. ¶ The fifteenth through questions: and first we must speak of the first part.

## On application through the 
## implicit and the explicit.

<margin>The first section of the tenth principal part concerning application through the implicit and explicit.</margin>
**A**pplication which is done through the implicit and explicit should be done thus: namely, let the terms be taken which are in the question; as if one asks whether God exists. ¶ In this question, through "whether," 'B' is applied; and in 'B', Goodness and Difference are applied; <note>In the Art of Ramon Llull, letters like 'B' represent sets of concepts; 'B' typically signifies Goodness, Magnitude, Duration, Power, Wisdom, Will, Virtue, Truth, and Glory.</note> and thus the artist ought to help themselves with these terms, which are under 'B'. And if they wish to help themselves, let them apply those terms implied in the question itself which are made explicit in the Art: such as Magnitude, Eternity, etc. For if God is, He is through infinite Magnitude and Eternity. And if Magnitude and Eternity are not infinite, it follows that God is not: and thus one will have the "compartment" <note>original: "cameram"; a logical grouping or cell in Llull’s combinatorial diagrams.</note> B-C-D. ¶ Next, let the artist range through these terms to prove that God exists or to disprove it, just as three terms are ranged through principles and rules. If, however, there are two terms made explicit in the question—as if one asks: "Is God eternal?"—let them return to another term made explicit in that same question, namely to Power, etc. For if He is eternal, He is able to be eternal; and if He is not, He cannot be eternal. ¶ Furthermore, if there are three terms made explicit in the question, such as asking: "Whether it is good that God should be so infinite through His Magnitude as through His Eternity," one thus has the compartment B-C-D; and in B is implied...

<meta>This page continues the Tenth Part of the treatise, focusing on the practical application of the logical system. ...[applied to] goodness/difference/ and "whether": and in **c.** magnitude/concordance and "what is it": and in **d.** duration/contrariety/ and "of what." In these terms, the definitions and species of the **rules** <note>In Llull's system, Rules are categorized by letters (B-K) and address specific questions like "Whether," "What," or "How."</note> are implied. And thus, the entire **chamber** <term>chamber: a cell or intersection in a logical grid where two concepts meet</term> may be applied to the proposition: that is, to the conclusion. And just as we have given examples in the aforementioned things, so can it be exemplified in others. ¶ Furthermore, if it is asked whether God is more "in act" <term>in act: a state of actual existence or operation, as opposed to mere potential</term> through His understanding than through His eternity: let "greater" be applied to **majority**, and "lesser" to **minority**. For "lesser" belongs to the genus of minority, while "greater" belongs to the genus of majority. And if it is asked whether He is as powerful through His power as through His will: let [the intellect] return to **equality**, in which comparison is implied, just as "greater" is in majority and "lesser" is in minority. And if it is asked whether God is just: let it return to **virtue**, for "just" belongs to the genus of virtue; and let it return to **goodness**, since it is a good thing that God should be just: and so on for others in their own way.

## On application through the abstract and the concrete.

<margin>The second part of the tenth principal part, which concerns application through the abstract and the concrete.</margin>

This application is to be described in four ways. ¶ The **first mode** is when the terms placed in the question have a **substantial abstraction** <term>substantial: relating to the "substance" or essential nature of a thing</term>: such as an abstract and a concrete term; for example, "fire-ness" <note>original: "igneitas"</note> and "fire." Fire-ness is indeed a substantial essence, while fire is a concrete and substantial term. ¶ The **second** is when the abstract is **accidental** <term>accidental: a quality or "accident" that is not essential to a thing's nature, like color or posture</term> or an accident, and its concrete term is likewise: such as "this-ness" <note>original: "istitas," referring to the quality of being a specific individual thing</note> and "this"; I say "this" insofar as it is a **habit** <note>See previous page for the definition of habit.</note>, and thus it is accidental or an accident. ¶ The **third** is when the abstract is a substance and the concrete is an accident: such as "fire-ness" and "hot." I say "hot" insofar as it is a habit, because in that way it is an accident. ¶ The **fourth** is when the abstract is an accident and its concrete is a substance: such as "whiteness" and "white"; and I say "white" by reason of the body which is characterized by the habit of whiteness, and thus it is a substance and not an accident. All these four modes are implied in the terms of the question and vice versa; and thus they must be explained in the conclusion according to these four modes, so that the intellect is not deceived by a variation of the **middle term** <term>middle term: the term that connects the subject and predicate in a logical syllogism</term>.

## On application through the first figure.

<margin>The third part of the tenth principal part, which concerns application through the first figure.</margin>

According to what has been said, let this be done by affirming or denying: namely, **circularly** through the conversion of the subject and the predicate: such as "goodness is great; magnitude is good." And if they do not convert, such as "eternity [is] magnitude"; for some magnitude is not eternity and vice versa; nor is every goodness great, because some goodness is small: and so on for others in their own way.

## On application through the second figure.

<margin>The fourth part of the tenth principal part, which concerns application through the second figure.</margin>

Application through the **second figure** <note>The Second Figure in Llull's Art typically consists of three triangles representing different sets of relations: e.g., Difference/Concordance/Contrariety.</note> itself is done through the triangles themselves, and through the **ladders** <term>ladder: a hierarchical scale (scala) showing the descent from general to specific concepts</term> placed upon the angles. In these ladders are implied the most general principle, the most specific principle, and the **subalternate** <term>subalternate: an intermediate level in a hierarchy, between the most general and most specific</term> principle. A most general principle is, for example, "difference" having nothing above it. A most specific principle is, for example, the difference existing between this stone and this plant. A subalternate [principle] is, for instance, the difference existing between one sensible thing and another sensible thing, etc. ¶ And also in this ladder, the **ascent and descent** of the intellect is implied; and outside of these ladders, the ascent and descent of the intellect can in no way be implied. ¶ Nevertheless, we say that the terms of the second figure are explainable according to how they lie in the figure itself, according to what we say about it. ¶ Furthermore, we say that the second figure is applicable to the first, such as placing a **difference** between goodness and goodness, etc., and placing **concordance** between goodness and goodness, as is marked in the third figure.

## On application to the third figure.

<margin>The fifth part of the tenth principal part, which concerns application to the third figure.</margin>

Let the application of the question to the **third figure** <note>The Third Figure is a grid or table used to find "chambers" (combinations) of terms.</note> be done thus: namely, if the matter of the question concerns **b**, apply **c** to **b**; and if **c** is not sufficient for **b**, apply **d** to **b**. And so on in succession until the chamber **b.k.** And let [the intellect] look to the meanings of the chambers, affirming or denying, in such a way that the letter remains with its conditions and its meanings. ¶ However, if the matter of the question pertains to **c**, let the other letters be applied to **c**, just as we said concerning **b**. And this same thing can be said of **d**, **e**, etc., and such application is infallible and very general.

Having previously discussed the general rules and the first three figures, the author now moves to the Fourth Figure, the use of definitions, and the specific application of the "Rules" (B through K) to understand subjects like "Man" and "Nature."</meta>

<page-num>Folio 78.</page-num>

-># On Application<-

<margin>The sixth part of the tenth principal part, which concerns application to the fourth figure.</margin>
<margin>Note an application more general than the others.</margin>
**A**pplication of the **fourth figure** <note>The Fourth Figure in Ramon Llull's system often involves a set of concentric, rotating circles (volvelles) used to generate combinations of concepts represented by letters.</note> is done in this way: namely, if the subject matter of the inquiry fits the **chamber** <term>chamber: a cell or intersection in a logical grid where three concepts meet</term> **b.c.d**, let the terms be applied to that chamber. If the subject matter fits **b.c.e** with **e** and not with **d**, let the smaller circle be turned and let **e** be placed under **c**, and let the chamber **b.c.e** be formed. Then, let the meanings of the letters be taken up, by which the inquiry may be resolved. And just as we have spoken regarding these, so may it be said for others.
¶ This application is more general than that of the third figure, because the chamber consists of three letters; it is general to the extent that it contains within itself all the chambers of the **Table** <note>The "Table" refers to a large grid of possible combinations (typically 1,680) used in Lullian logic.</note>.

### On application through definitions.

<margin>The seventh part of the tenth principal part, which is on application through definitions.</margin>
**A**ccording to the method of this Art, the artist ought to define the terms that are in the inquiry, whether they are explicit or implicit. For instance, if one asks: "Is God infinite?" In that case, the person responding must define "God" and "infinity," saying: God is a being so perfect that He lacks nothing outside Himself; and infinity is a being to which belong infinite **correlatives** <term>correlatives: in Lullism, these are the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle (e.g., Loving, Loveable, and to Love)</term> without which it cannot possibly exist. 
¶ Furthermore, as it is said: "Goodness is a being by reason of which a good thing acts well," so it can be said that "magnitude is that by reason of which a great thing acts greatly," and so for others in their own way. 
¶ Furthermore, any term placed in an inquiry can indeed be defined in multiple ways by running through the species of the **Rules** <note>The Rules are a set of ten questions (B-K) such as "What?", "From what?", "Why?", etc.</note>. 
¶ First, through the species of **Rule C** <note>Rule C asks "What is it?" (Quid?).</note>: Man is a "rational animal" (according to the first species). According to the second species, man is an animal having his own proper correlatives: namely, **the man-maker, the man-makeable, and to man-ify** <note>original Latin: "hominificātem, hominificabile, et hominificare." These are Lullian technical terms for the active, passive, and functional essence of being human.</note>. 
¶ And through the third species: man is an animal acting in the mechanical arts, such as a writer writing, or a rider on a horse, and the like. 
¶ And through the fourth species of the same rule: man is a being having greater possession over beasts and plants. 
¶ Through the first species of **Rule D** <note>Rule D asks "Of what?" (De quo?).</note>: man is a primitive being in the nobility of "definedness." 
¶ Through the second species: man is a being constituted of soul and body. 
¶ Through the third species: man is a being to whom beasts and plants are subject, and the like. 
¶ Through the first species of **Rule E** <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare?).</note>: man is a substance by virtue of his humanity. 
¶ Through the second species: man is a being created to serve God along with vegetative and sensitive beings. 
¶ Through **Rule F** <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum?).</note>: man is a quantity-bearing and continuous being through his elemental, vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rational powers from which he is composed. And these five powers are his **discrete parts** <term>discrete parts: parts that are distinct from one another within a whole</term> because they are different from each other. 
¶ Through **Rule G** <note>Rule G asks "Of what kind?" (Quale?).</note>: man is a being to whom "to man-ify" properly belongs; he is a being capable of laughter, a being who writes and rides, and the like. 
¶ Through **Rule H** <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando?).</note>: man is a being who understands and reads within time, etc. 
¶ Through **Rule I** <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi?).</note>: man is a being digging in a vineyard, or in a church praying to God. 
¶ Through the **Rule of Modality** <note>Rule of "How?" (Quomodo?).</note>: man is a being having a mode of mechanical working and of generating another man. 
¶ Through the **Rule of Instrumentality** <note>Rule of "With what?" (Cum quo?).</note>: man is a substance generating another man with a woman; and with a hammer, he is a being driving a nail, and things of this sort. 
¶ And just as we gave an example regarding "man," so can examples be given for other things in their own way. 
¶ And in this passage, a teaching is given through which a person may know how to make definitions in different ways for one and the same thing; once the thing is known through these universal thoughts or definitions, it is no longer unknown as it was before. Therefore, the artist must define in such a way that the definitions remain uncorrupted.

### On application to the rules.

<margin>The eighth part of the tenth principal part, which concerns application to the rules.</margin>
**W**hen an inquiry is made regarding some doubt, the artist ought to apply that doubt to the rules successively. For just as a **crystal** placed against a red color takes that color upon itself, and if placed against green, takes that on as well, and so for others; so now, when an unknown thing is run through the rules and the species of the rules, then that unknown thing is "colored" or clarified by the species of the rules in which it has been placed both subjectively and objectively. Then the intellect, through the species of the rules, recognizes that which was previously unknown. We have already given an example of "man" defined through the rules, but for the sake of greater clarification, we wish to give an example of **Nature** as deduced through the rules. 
¶ Through the first species of **Rule C**, we say that nature is an essence sustained in its own natural concrete form and moved through a natural act in which the act is at rest. 
¶ Through the second species, it is an essence having co-natural correlatives: namely, **the nature-maker, the nature-able, and to nature** <note>original Latin: "naturatiuum, naturabile et naturare."</note>, without which it cannot exist. 
¶ Through the third species, nature is in the subject in which it is active and capable of suffering <term>suffering: in a philosophical sense, "to be acted upon" or "passive."</term> to "co-nature." 
¶ Through the fourth species, nature possesses in the subject in which it exists: action, passion, and act; and this through a natural agent and through natural form, matter, and...
