Tenth part.

...the end and with natural instruments.
¶ Through the first species of rule **d**, <note>Rule D in Llull’s system usually asks "What?" (Quid). Here it defines the essence of the subject.</note> nature is a primitive essence. ¶ Through the second species, it concerns its correlatives <term>correlatives: in Lullian thought, these are the active, passive, and verbal components of a concept (e.g., the power to heat, the thing being heated, and the act of heating)</term> by ascending to the essence; and its concrete form is derived from its properties by descending and contracting. ¶ Through the third species, nature is the subject in which it exists, because it acts upon itself naturally. ¶ Through the first species of rule **e**, <note>Rule E usually asks "From what?" (De quo).</note> nature exists: because it is a being containing within itself its own correlatives from which it is made. ¶ Through the second species, nature exists so that other beings may have existence and agency naturally. ¶ Through rule **f**, <note>Rule F usually asks "How much?" (Quantum).</note> nature is an essence possessing continuous quantity and the indivisible; and its concrete forms are discrete quantities relative to it. ¶ Through rule **g**, <note>Rule G usually asks "Of what kind?" (Quale).</note> nature has its own actions and passions: just as the nature of fire acts through heating; it possesses "appropriated" qualities, however, just as heated water has the power to heat, the capacity to be heated, and the act of heating. And in this step, the intellect understands that nature exists in time both continuously and successively: continuously indeed through continuous quantity; successively, however, through the discrete quantities in which nature exists within time. ¶ Through rule **i**, <note>Rule I usually asks "Where?" (Ubi).</note> nature is in a place: like a thing contained within a container, and an agent within that which can be acted upon. And it is in a subject in which it is sustained and moved. ¶ Through the rules of modality, nature has a mode of mixing, generating, and corrupting, and the like. ¶ Through the rules of instrumentality, nature exists with its instruments: just as a substance exists with its accidents, and a mechanic with his tools; and so with others. Thus indeed, nature, having been traversed through the species of the rules, is made known to the intellect, because these species signify both what nature is through its existence and its agency. And just as we have spoken regarding nature, so may it be said of other things, and even of concrete things according to what they are. ¶ Concerning a miracle, however, it cannot be said thus: since it is above nature. And so by traversing a miracle through the rules, the intellect understands the miracle through its contrary, because a miracle enters the species of the rules through a mode contrary to the way nature enters them. And in this step, the intellect knows how one contrary is understood through the other by using the rules.

## On application through the
## table.

<margin>
The ninth part of the tenth principal part.
On application through the table.
</margin>
**A**pplication of the table <note>The "Table" is a large grid in the Art that visualizes all possible combinations of the principles (represented by letters B through K).</note> occurs when the terms of questions are applied to the table itself. For if the terms of the question agree with the first column—namely **b.c.d.**, which is the first column—as if it were asked whether it would be a great good if the world were from eternity. Or if it is asked whether there is an infinite act: assuming that goodness is the reason for acting well, and that greatness is the reason for that act being great, and that eternity makes that act endure from eternity to eternity, then that same infinite act must endure. ¶ Furthermore, if the terms of the question fit the second column: such as if it is asked, why does the greatness of goodness or power exist? And the answer must be that it exists because of the correlatives of goodness, greatness, and power; and so for others in their own way. ¶ Moreover, any column is applicable to another: just as the second column is applicable with the first and with the third, because it contains **b.c.** from the first and similarly from the third; and so for the others, since they are chained together. And in this step, the intellect knows that all columns can be applied to the same conclusion. And thus it recognizes itself as very general through this application, which is itself very general. ¶ Also: when it is asked whether the world is eternal, then the second "chamber" <term>chamber: a specific cell or intersection in the Lullian Table where multiple principles meet</term> which is **b.c.t.b.** is applied to the upper chamber. And so for the chamber that is **b.c.t.c.**, and so for the others up to **t.b.c.d.** The reason for this is that "eternity" is the term explained in the question. ¶ Furthermore, if it is asked whether the power of the world is infinite: let the answer be applied to column **b.c.d.** just as the question about the eternity of the world was applied, and let the negative be maintained. For just as a great logical absurdity <note>original: "inconveniens"</note> would follow if the world were from eternity, so a great absurdity would follow if the world possessed infinite power. And just as we speak of the world, so can it be said of those things which it contains within itself. ¶ Moreover, if it is asked whether one angel produces another angel: let the answer be applied to **b.c.d.**, because between the essence of an angel and a man or a rose, there is a great difference. For the body of a man exists under the general matter of the elements, by reason of which one man can produce or generate another man, and one rose another. Concerning the angel, however, it is not so. For one angel does not have that from which he might produce another angel, since he is not derived from one and the same general angelic matter, as he is finite in his primitive state. ¶ Just as we gave an example through what we said about the table, so it can be said of many other things in their own way. ¶ The application that is made through the table requires that the species and rules of the chambers be preserved, and that those things which they signify be applied to the purpose: namely, to the conclusion, by affirming or denying appropriately <note>original: "convenienter"</note> or inappropriately, as is clear from the example mentioned above.

<margin>Tenth part of the tenth principal part concerning application through the evacuation of the third figure.</margin>

## On application through the evacuation of the third figure.

**T**he application that takes place via the third figure <note>The Third Figure in Llull's Art is a grid used to pair the nine primary principles (Goodness, Greatness, etc.) to see how they interact.</note> happens in this way: namely, that the terms which are explained in the question are applied to the evacuation <note>In this context, "evacuation" refers to the process of systematically exhausting all possible logical combinations within a specific "chamber" or cell of the diagram.</note> of the third figure, and specifically to that chamber with which the terms most agree. For example, if it is asked whether it is a "great good" that goodness and greatness have substantial correlatives, <term>correlatives: the active, passive, and act-based components of a principle, such as 'the power to love,' 'the lovable,' and 'the act of loving'</term> and whether those correlatives are in good and great concordance. Then, such a question should be applied to chamber **b.c.** <note>Chamber b.c. represents the intersection of Goodness (B) and Greatness (C).</note> ¶ And through what we have said in the chapter on evacuation regarding that chamber, the question will indeed be solved. The same applies to other questions, according to how their terms can enter a chamber, whether by affirming or denying, and whether fittingly or unfittingly. ¶ Furthermore, if a question is raised as to whether the contrariety of goodness can exist from eternity within eternity. This question should be applied to chamber **b.e.** <note>Goodness and Eternity.</note> and to chamber **c.d.** <note>Greatness and Duration/Eternity.</note> and to chamber **d.e.** <note>Power and Eternity.</note> According to what has been said regarding these chambers, the question will be solved. The same applies to other questions, based on how their terms enter the chambers: affirming or denying fittingly or unfittingly. ¶ Moreover, let a subalternate <note>A subordinate or less general question.</note> question be applied to a particular question, and vice versa. For instance, if it is asked: "Are there great correlatives in goodness?" Let this question be applied to this one: "Are there great correlatives in the goodness of Socrates <note>original: "Sortis," a standard scholastic shorthand for Socrates used as a placeholder for an individual person.</note> or of this rose?" Then let these questions be applied to chamber **b.c.** The answer will then be found already solved through what has been said. ¶ Furthermore, if it is asked what the correlatives of magnitude are made of, and what the correlatives of Socrates are made of? Let these questions be applied to chamber **c.d.** and let the subalternate question be applied to the particular question; at that time, the conclusion will be found declared and signified by what we have already said regarding that chamber. The same holds for other chambers. We shall provide an example of this in the treatise on questions.

<margin>Eleventh part of the tenth principal part concerning application through the multiplication of the fourth figure.</margin>

## On application through the multiplication of the fourth figure.

**W**e have said that the "multiplication" of the fourth figure <note>The Fourth Figure consists of three concentric circles that rotate to create triplets of principles, used primarily to build syllogisms.</note> consists of five modes: namely, in multiplication, in the finding of a middle term, in the proof of the major and minor premises, in solving fallacies, and in the instruction by which other arts can be easily learned. Therefore, if a practitioner of this art <note>original: "artista"</note> wishes to multiply many reasons for the same conclusion, to find many middle terms, to prove the major and minor premises, to solve fallacies, and to teach other sciences easily and briefly with this General Art: let them apply the method we held in the multiplication of the fourth figure. For that method is universal, and through that method, a particular method will be regulated and brought to light. For the particular shines back in the universal and vice versa; let these words suffice, for it has been sufficiently declared.

## On the application of the mixture of principles and rules.

<margin>Twelfth part of the tenth principal part, which concerns the application of the mixture of principles and rules, divided into two small parts.</margin>

**T**his Art is divided into two parts. ¶ In the first, we shall speak of explicit principles. ¶ In the second, of implicit principles, which we shall apply to the explicit principles in the places of the rules of this art. These principles shall be called the "hundred forms"; <note>The "One Hundred Forms" is a specific section of Llull's work defining a vast vocabulary of metaphysical and physical concepts.</note> we do this so that the art may be more material <note>Meaning "more concrete" or "more substantial" for the mind to work with.</note> to the intellect for finding many conclusions. We intend to say little about them, however, because we wish to avoid prolixity. But through what we say about them, the artist can recognize the process of any form through all the rules, just as we did in the deduction of the explicit principles, and also through the rules. And first, we shall speak of the first part thus.

## First part.

<margin>A question on the first part of this twelfth part.</margin>

**A** question contains within itself explained terms, such as if it is asked: "Is there a being that is good, great, and eternal?" Recourse should be had to the chapters on goodness, greatness, and eternity; and it should also be seen by what mode goodness is discoursed through the principles and rules—and likewise for the other principles. Then let the conclusion be drawn by affirming or denying, according to how the principles are such that the principles and rules remain unharmed. Then the intellect will find the truth concerning **b**, **g**, and **d**, etc. <note>In Llull’s notation, these letters refer to specific principles: B (Goodness), G (Truth), and D (Power).</note> This truth will be brought to light through that discourse. Just as we gave an example concerning goodness, greatness, and eternity, so it can be given for other principles. And let these things suffice for now for the first part.

# Ninth part.

...in making sciences, but it confuses them. 
¶ The slothful person brings their higher and lower powers <note>The "higher powers" refer to the rational soul (intellect and will), while the "lower powers" refer to the sensitive soul and physical appetites.</note> into agreement in all things. For since they are lazy, they are slow in acquiring virtues. ¶ The slothful person contradicts the diligence of virtues with the busy-ness of vices. ¶ Sloth perverts positive principles into privative <note>A 'privative' state is the absence of a quality that should be present, such as blindness being the privative state of sight.</note> ones. Therefore, the slothful person murmurs and pretends to be a prophet <note>original: "vaticinatorem"</note>; they give advice when it is not necessary, find fault with good things, and are an enemy of the end goal. Furthermore, sloth binds the form and corrupts the matter, so that the person acting out of laziness becomes habituated to it. ¶ Sloth blocks the middle path, so that a proper beginning does not find the end in which it should find rest. ¶ The slothful person rests in opposition to the end, but labors when at the end. For sloth is the enemy of the perfection of the end. ¶ Greater sloth is the fountain of all vices. ¶ The slothful person, through their sloth, is the fountain of all vices. ¶ The slothful person, through their sloth, equates the acts of vices so that sloth is strong against the diligence of virtues. ¶ Minor sloth concerns minor diligence, major diligence, or none at all.

## On sloth deduced through the rules.

<margin>On sloth deduced through the rules.</margin>
**I**t is asked <note>original: "Queritur"</note> whether sloth is a mortal sin? And the answer is yes; for it hinders all acts of virtue. ¶ But here the intellect wonders: since sloth is a mortal sin and is marked and figured by many signs, why is it so little known by men? It is because the greater part of men are habituated to sloth. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule C** <note>Rule C asks "What is it?" (Quid)</note>, it is asked: What is sloth? And the answer is that sloth is a sin through which the slothful person grieves at the good of their neighbor <note>original: "primi sui"</note>, but rejoices at their misfortunes. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: What does sloth possess within itself co-essentially? And the answer is that it has its own correlatives <term>correlatives: Lull's technical term for the active (the doer), passive (the receiver), and the act itself that exist within every principle</term> which are among the privative correlatives of charity. For a charitable person rejoices at the good of their neighbor and grieves at their misfortunes. ¶ Through the third species: What is sloth in another? And the answer is that it is lazy and malevolent regarding good things, but swift, diligent, and choosing regarding evil things. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: What does sloth have in another? To which it must be said that it has its own acts in all sins. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule D** <note>Rule D asks "From what?" or "Of what?" (De quo)</note>, it is asked: From what does sloth arise? To which it must be said that it arises from the absence of charity in a subject where charity used to be; just as a consequence does not exist when its antecedent is missing. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: Of what is sloth made? To which it must be said that it is made of its own specific privative correlatives, with which it is a specific sin. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: To whom does sloth belong? And the answer is that it belongs to the subject in which it exists, just as deafness belongs to the deaf person. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule E** <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare)</note>, it is asked: Why does sloth exist? And the answer is that it exists because it is an acquired habit; just as the day exists because the sun is shining over the earth. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: Why is there sloth? And the answer is: so that charity may not have a subject in which it can exist; for it is a privative habit against the positive habit of charity, hindering the end. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule F** <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum), referring to continuous and discrete quantity.</note>, it is asked: Regarding the continuous quantity of sloth? And the answer is that it has this in all the vices caused by it. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: Regarding the continuous quantity of sloth? And the answer is that it has this in all the vices caused by it. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: Regarding the discrete quantity of sloth? And the answer is that it has discrete quantities by reason of the different vices in which it has different acts. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule G** <note>Rule G asks "What kind?" or "Quality" (Quale)</note>, it is asked: What is the proper quality of sloth? To which it must be said that it is laziness <note>original: "pigricia"</note>, for without it, sloth cannot act. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: What is the appropriated quality of sloth? And the answer is: malevolence and iniquity; for through these, the slothful person rejoices in evils and grieves in goods. ¶ Through **Rule H** <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando)</note>, it is asked regarding the time of sloth? And the answer, according to Rule C, is that it is lazy in that time, so that the subject in which it exists does not do anything useful while they have the time. ¶ Through **Rule I** <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Ubi)</note>, it is asked: Where is sloth? To which it must be said that it is in the laziness of the soul, the imagination, and the senses; for these neglect to do good but love to do evil. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule K** <note>Rule K asks "How?" (Quomodo) and "With whom?" (Cum quo)</note>, it is asked: How does sloth exist? And the answer is that it exists in a manner contrary to the manner of charity. For just as charity has a way of being in loving the neighbor's good and hating their evil, sloth exists in the opposite way. ¶ Through the second species of Rule K, it is asked: With whom does sloth exist? To which it must be said that it exists with the privative habits of virtues—namely with injustice <note>original: "iniuria"</note>, imprudence, and so on. Furthermore, it is with laziness, anger, and the like.

# On the nine subjects.

<margin>On envy deduced through principles.</margin>

**T**he envious man desires to have the goods of others against reason: therefore evil follows him in spiritual matters. And if the envious man truly recognized this often: he would no longer have envy. ¶ The greatness of envy exists alongside the greatness of other vices: and therefore it cannot be conquered by a single greatness of virtue. ¶ Envy lasts as long as other vices last: therefore it cannot be conquered without the duration of other virtues. ¶ The power of envy is rooted in the powers of other vices. And therefore it cannot be conquered without the power of charity acting within the powers of other virtues. ¶ The envious intellect is perverted and altered through envy. For it does not recognize itself: the cure for which consists in this / namely that he himself understands it. ¶ Envy leads the will astray from the highest good: nevertheless it can be cured / by frequently bringing the will back to the highest object <note>In medieval theology, the "highest object" refers to God, the ultimate source of all good.</note> / by placing that object before it. ¶ The envious man does not have virtues but vices: therefore if he wishes to have virtues / let him change what he has into what he does not have. ¶ The envious man does not have truth: but falsehood: therefore he deceives himself. The cure for this can be applied / namely that he might not deceive himself. ¶ The envious man, even when he has the things he envied / still does not find rest in them. For his conscience gnaws at him. ¶ The envious man has as many different acts through envy / as there are other vices: nevertheless he can be cured by frequently counting them. ¶ Envy has no harmony with any virtue / and the cure lies in recognizing this. Envy contradicts virtues with privative habits <note>A 'privative habit' is the absence of a required good, like blindness is the absence of sight.</note>: the cure for which is achieved through the opposition of positive habits. ¶ Envy begins with things perceived by the senses: and is organized through things in the imagination: and is perfected in spiritual matters / by destroying what is imaginable and sensible. ¶ Envy is the measure with which the envious man measures injury / imprudence / and the like. But the cure consists in the measure of justice / prudence / and the like. ¶ The envious man does not rest in the things he focuses on. For he desires them with great effort: yet a cure is given / when that effort is avoided until he reaches rest. ¶ The envious man suffers greater labors with greater envy: nevertheless he can be cured with greater charity so that he may perform greater actions. ¶ Envy, through its own act, equates all the acts of others. And the cure for this consists in the act of charity, by which all other acts of virtues are made equal. ¶ The envious man believes that the things he possesses / are smaller: and that those things which he envies / are greater: but the cure consists in seeking what is the utility and the purpose of that thing.

### On envy deduced through the rules.

<margin>On envy deduced through the rules.</margin>

**W**hether envy is a more general sin objectively than avarice? <note>Avarice is greed for wealth; the text argues envy is broader because it covets things that cannot even be possessed.</note> And it must be answered that it is. For the greedy man does not focus his desire on as much as the envious man does. For the greedy man believes he can possess what he desires / but the envious man focuses on many things that are impossible to have. ¶ Through the first species of rule C <note>Rule C in this system asks "What is it?" (Quid est?).</note> it is asked, what is envy? To which it must be said that it is a sin with which the envious man desires to have the belongings of others without reason. ¶ Through the second species it is asked what envy has in itself essentially: and it must be answered that it has its own privative correlatives <note>In Lullian logic, 'correlatives' are the internal components of an essence (like the power to love and the object loved). Here, they are 'privative' because envy is a lack of good.</note> with which it is what it is. ¶ Through the third species it is asked / what is envy in another? And it must be answered that it is a habit in the envious person with which the envious person always labors with sadness and pain. ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked / what does it have in another? To which it must be said that it has height and precedence in the envious person: just as a cloak exists in a cloaked person. ¶ Through the first species of rule D <note>Rule D asks "From what?" (De quo?).</note> it is asked, envy is from what? To which it must be answered that it is from its own privative and specific correlatives with which it is a specific sin: just as deafness is from its own parts / and hearing from its own. ¶ Through the second species it is asked / envy is from what? To which it must be answered that it is from its own specific relatives: just as blindness is from its own. ¶ Through the third species it is asked envy whose is it? <note>Meaning "to what subject does it belong?"</note> To which it must be answered that it is of the subject in which it is a habit: just as ill-will belongs to the will and forgetfulness to the memory / and ignorance to the intellect. ¶ Through the first species of rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare?).</note> it is asked why envy is. And it must be answered that it is / because it is an effect caused by the envious person: just as deafness is an effect caused by a defect of hearing. ¶ Through the second species it is asked / why is envy? And it must be answered that it is so that the subject in which envy exists / may suffer labor: and in hell perpetual pain and sadness. ¶ Through the first species of rule F <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (De quanto?).</note> it is asked, concerning the continuous quantity of envy? And it must be answered that it has as much as the envious person can use to measure avarice / lust / gluttony and the like. ¶ Through the second species it is asked concerning the discrete quantity of envy? And the response is that it exists with the privative habits from which it is made: namely with malice, injury, and such things.

## On anger deduced through principles.

<margin>On anger deduced through principles.</margin>
The will moves itself with anger toward hating the good without deliberation. And therefore the remedy consists in deliberation. ¶ Anger with great fury conquers all things: but the remedy is given through great <term>abstinence<note>Here meaning emotional restraint or self-control.</note></term> and deliberation. ¶ For as long as anger lasts, so long does its act last. The remedy consists in presenting a foreign object and persevering in it. ¶ The power of anger is diminished by the power of patience, abstinence, and also deliberation. ¶ Anger confuses the intellect, because it takes away from it the power of understanding; the remedy, however, is to return its understanding to the intellect. ¶ Anger perverts the will into hating what it ought to love: its remedy is abstinence until it rises again through loving. ¶ The will with anger is in vice; its remedy, however, is that through abstinence it might be in virtue. ¶ The intellect with anger does not understand virtue: but the remedy consists in this, namely that through patience it might recognize it. ¶ A man angered with hating suffers it as a vice, but he recovers and is cured through loving. ¶ An angry man does not distinguish between his own evil and the evil of another: the remedy, however, consists in making a distinction. ¶ An angry man accords vice with vice: but a remedy can be given in according virtue with virtue. ¶ An angry man contradicts patience; the remedy of which consists in resisting it with patience. ¶ Anger begins with hearing and is destroyed by loving. ¶ Anger measures without measure: the remedy consists in measuring with measure. No man rests with anger; every man rests with patience. ¶ Greater anger without greater patience is unassailable; but not vice versa: and in this step the intellect recognizes that virtue is absolutely stronger than vice. Anger makes the acts of the intellect and will equal in fury; the remedy for these can be given in making them equal with abstinence, patience, and <term>charity<note>original: "charitate", the highest form of love.</note></term>. ¶ Lesser anger is overcome with greater patience.

## On anger deduced through rules.

<margin>On anger deduced through rules.</margin>
Whether anger is a more general sin than any other sin? And it must be answered that it is: for in its fury the intellect has no deliberation. ¶ Through the first species of rule **c**, it is asked: what is anger? To which it must be said that it is a sin with which the will, without deliberation, hates good and loves evil. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does it have co-essential to itself? To which it must be answered that it has its own <term>correlatives<note>Lullian technical term referring to the internal components of an essence (the power, the object, and the action).</note></term> confused by reason of its fury. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is anger in another? To which it must be said that it is a bond in the will with which the will binds itself to hating without reason; and the intellect to being ignorant; and the memory to forgetting. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does it have in another? To which it must be answered that it has command in the will, because it commands it to hate good and love evil. Furthermore, it has dominion in the intellect and in the memory. For it commands the intellect to be ignorant and the memory to forget. ¶ Through the first species of rule **d**, it is asked: from what is anger? And it must be answered that it is not from anything. For it is a sin; and a sin, materially speaking, is not made from anything. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what is anger made? To which it must be answered that it is made of its specific correlatives with which it exists in its species. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: whose is anger? To which it must be said that it belongs to the subject in which it is. ¶ Through the first species of rule **e**, it is asked: why is anger? And the response...

And the response is that it exists with sensible and imaginable things: and also with a perverse soul, and with habits that deprive one of principles: namely with malice and the like.

# On falsity deduced through principles.

<margin>
On falsity deduced through principles.
</margin>
**A** false man, in deceiving another, deceives himself: the knowledge of which is found through the definition of goodness. ¶ Falsity is not recognized by its own magnitude; rather, it is recognized by the magnitude of <term>legality<note>original: "legalitatis"; here meaning lawfulness, integrity, or moral rectitude.</note></term>. ¶ Falsity lasts as long as it is not recognized: for when it is recognized, it is destroyed. ¶ Falsity has no power against <term>understanding<note>original: "intelligere"</note></term>, but only against belief; indeed, prudence is its enemy. ¶ Falsity, when combined with belief, deceives the understanding. ¶ Falsity makes itself loved under the shadow of legality: but the end of legality reveals and proves what it is. ¶ Falsity, through hypocrisy, pretends to be virtue: but prudence destroys it and manifests it for what it truly is. ¶ Falsity does not act with the act of truth: whence it follows that it is known through the act of truth. ¶ Falsity promises pleasures, but it gives punishments: and through this it is known. ¶ Falsity does not distinguish, but confuses. Therefore, it is recognized by distinction. ¶ A false man brings sensible things and their signs into agreement so that he may deceive the imagination and the intellect; but the intellect, with its own concordance, lays bare the aforementioned falsity. ¶ Falsity contradicts the end, and by that very end, falsity is contradicted. ¶ Falsity delights in the beginning: but in the end it is sorrowful; by which reason it is recognized. ¶ Falsity removes the "middle" that is disposed between the beginning and the end. And therefore, it is known by this. ¶ A false man is at rest in the beginning: but in the end he labors, by reason of which falsity itself is known. ¶ Greater falsity is recognized by means of greater legality. ¶ A false man equates like with like, by which reason falsity is known. ¶ Falsity is recognized by its lack of virtue.

**I**t is asked whether falsity is as strong as legality? And it must be answered that it is not: because legality is a positive habit, but falsity is a <term>privative<note>original: "priuatiu[us]"; a condition defined by the absence of a good that should be present.</note></term> one. ¶ Through the first species of rule **c**, it is asked: what is falsity? And it must be answered that it is the sin with which a man is deceived and deceives. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does falsity have in itself that is <term>coessential<note>original: "coessentiale"; belonging to the same essence or nature.</note></term> to it? And it must be answered that it has its own <term>correlatives<note>original: "correlatiuos"; in Lullian logic, these are the active, passive, and verbal components of an essence (e.g., the deceiver, the deceived, and the deceiving).</note></term> of which its essence consists. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is falsity in another? To which it must be said that it has its own acts in privative principles, standing against positive principles. ¶ Through the first species of rule **d**, it is asked: from what does falsity come? And it must be answered that it is from itself. For sin is...

¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is falsity made of? To which it must be answered that it is made of its own specific <term>privative principles<note>original: "pricipiis specificis privatiuis"; principles defined by the absence or lack of a good quality, rather than the presence of a positive substance.</note></term> through which it is a special sin, just as deafness is made of those principles through which it is a special <term>monstrosity<note>original: "mōstruositas"; in medieval philosophy, a biological or moral deviation from the natural and intended order.</note></term>. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to whom does falsity belong? And it must be answered that it belongs to the <term>subject<note>original: "subiecti"; the individual person or mind in which the quality exists.</note></term> in which it resides, just like a <term>habit<note>original: "habitus"; a settled or regular tendency of character.</note></term>. ¶ Through the first species of rule **e**, it is asked: why is there falsity? And it must be answered that it is because there is no lawfulness within its subject. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: for what purpose is there falsity? And it must be answered that it exists so that a human may be deceived; it is like an instrument used so that an effect may be brought about by someone through its mediation. ¶ Through the first species of rule **f**, it is asked: how great is continuous falsity? And it must be answered that it is as great as the subject is capable of acting it out. ¶ Through the second species of **f**, it is asked: how great is <term>discrete falsity<note>original: "falsitas discretiua"; referring to falsity that can be measured in distinct, countable instances or units.</note></term>? To which it must be said that it has a discrete quantity caused by its privative principles. ¶ Through the first species of rule **g**, it is asked: what is the proper quality of falsity? To which it must be said that it is deception; for this is its specific act. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of falsity? To which it must be said that it is a lie, hypocrisy, and the like. ¶ Through rule **h**, it is asked concerning the time of falsity: and it must be answered that it exists in time because it is a new habit, and within that time it performs its acts. ¶ Through rule **i**, it is asked: where is falsity? And it must be answered that it is in lying humans, hypocrites, and deceivers. ¶ Through the first rule **k**, it is asked: how does falsity exist? And it must be answered that it exists by way of a fiction for the purpose of deceiving and lying, and the like. ¶ Through the second rule **k**, it is asked: with what does falsity exist? And it must be answered that it exists with dissimulation and deception and the like; as has been indicated by what was said.

# On inconstancy deduced through principles.

<margin>On inconstancy deduced through principles.</margin>
**C**onstancy is a habit in which goodness is the reason for a good person to act well; and because inconstancy hinders this, it is therefore a sin. ¶ Inconstancy is conquered by the magnitude of constancy. ¶ Inconstancy lasts as long as constancy is in <term>privation<note>original: "priuatiōe"; the state of being absent or lacking.</note></term>. ¶ The power of inconstancy has no power against the power of constancy. ¶ The intellect with inconstancy does not have strong understanding. ¶ Constancy with inconstancy is not lovable. ¶ Constancy with inconstancy is not a virtue. ¶ Constancy and inconstancy cannot exist together in truth. ¶ Inconstancy is not of the <term>genus<note>original: "genere"; a general category or class.</note></term> of pleasure, but of the genus of labor. ¶ Constancy opens and distinguishes differences; inconstancy, however, closes and obscures them. ¶ Constancy and inconstancy do not agree in genus nor in species. ¶ It is in the nature of inconstancy that it must be resisted in the beginning. For after a while, it is difficult to resist it. Since constancy comes first, therefore all inconstancy comes after. ¶ Constancy joins; but inconstancy disjoins. ¶ A constant person rests with constancy; the inconstant person, however, toils with inconstancy. ¶ A greater inconstancy cannot be over a greater constancy, nor can it hold a higher degree. ¶ Constancy and inconstancy, by reason of <term>free will<note>original: "liberi arbitrij"</note></term>, are equally choosable; but they are not equally measurable. ¶ A lesser inconstancy is easily conquered by a greater constancy.

---

# On inconstancy deduced through rules.

<margin>On inconstancy deduced through rules.</margin>
**W**hether inconstancy is more a habit of the will than of the intellect? And it must be answered that it is so. The will is indeed more changeable than the intellect. The reason for this is: because the intellect is discursive; the will, however, is suddenly changeable. Therefore the intellect knows that the remedy against inconstancy is to remove the suddenness of the will by placing it in discourse with the intellect. ¶ Through the first species of rule **e**, it is asked: what is inconstancy? And it must be answered that it is a stream diverted from the goal of constancy. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does inconstancy have within itself that is <term>co-essential<note>original: "coessentiale"; something that is part of the very essence or nature of the thing itself.</note></term>? To which it must be answered that it has its <term>correlatives<note>original: "correlatiuos"; related things that exist together or define one another.</note></term> with which it is what it is. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is inconstancy in another? And it must be answered that it is commanding in the will, disobedient in the intellect, bashful in the imagination, and fleeting in sensible things. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does it have in another? And it must be answered that it has a defect of <term>fortitude<note>original: "fortitudinis"; mental or moral strength.</note></term> in the will, and deception in its promise. ¶ Through the first species of rule **d**, it is asked:

What is inconstancy made of? Regarding this, it must be said that it is made of itself, for it is a sin. ¶ Through the second species <note>The "species" of rules refer to different ways of asking "What," "Why," "Where," etc.</note>, it is asked: what is inconstancy made of? And it must be said that it is made from its own <term>privative and specific principles<note>original: "principiis privativis & specificis"; in medieval logic, a privative principle defines a thing by what it lacks—in this case, inconstancy is defined by the absence of constancy.</note></term> with which it is what it is. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to whom does inconstancy belong? To which it must be answered that it belongs to the <term>subject<note>The person or mind.</note></term> in which its <term>habit<note>A settled disposition of character.</note></term> resides. ¶ Through the first species of rule **e**, it is asked: why is there inconstancy? And it must be answered that it is because in the subject in which it resides, constancy is not present; just like heat which is in hot water, for in that water there is no coldness. From this, the intellect recognizes in what way natural habits are similar to moral habits. ¶ Through the second species of rule **e**, it is asked: for what purpose is there inconstancy? To which it must be said that it exists so that constancy may not have being. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that sin is "nothing," because it is against "being" <note>A common medieval philosophical point: evil has no substance of its own; it is merely the absence or "privation" of good.</note>. ¶ Through the first species of rule **f**, it is asked: how great is inconstancy? And it must be answered that it is as great as the constancy it hinders. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked concerning the <term>discrete quantity<note>A mathematical/logical term for things that can be counted as distinct units, rather than measured as a continuous whole.</note></term> of inconstancy. To which it must be said that it possesses this because the will is frequently changeable in practice. ¶ Through the first species of rule **g**, it is asked: what is the proper quality of inconstancy? And it must be answered that it is the alteration of the will. ¶ Through the second species of rule **g**, it is asked: what is the <term>appropriated quality<note>A quality that is not essential to the thing's definition but is commonly associated with it.</note></term> of inconstancy? And to this it must be answered that it is the weakness of the heart’s fortitude. ¶ Through rule **h**, it is asked concerning the time of inconstancy; and it must be answered that it exists in that time in which the will is changeable and habituated by it. Furthermore, it exists in the time in which the will, through inconstancy, acts against constancy. ¶ Through rule **i**, it is asked: where is inconstancy? And it must be answered that it is in the weakness of the will and also in the privation of perseverance, and in its aforementioned locations. ¶ Through the first rule **k**, it is asked: by what means is there inconstancy? To which it must be answered that it exists through the opposite way by which constancy exists: for constancy exists through a way of discourse, deliberation, and choice with prudence, and especially with fortitude. ¶ Through the second rule **k**, it is asked: with what does inconstancy exist? And to this it must be answered that it exists with sudden alteration; and it exists with its cause, of which it is the effect; and with the privation of constancy, just like a shadow which exists with the privation of light.

## On application through the 
## implicit and explicit.

<margin>The first part of the tenth principal part: on application through the implicit and explicit.</margin>
**A**pplication that is done through the implicit and explicit should be done thus: namely, let the terms which are in the question be taken. For example, if it is asked: "Whether God exists?" ¶ In this question, through the word "whether," the letter **B** is applied <note>In Llull's system, letters like B, C, and D represent specific concepts. B usually stands for Goodness.</note>; and in **B**, Goodness and Difference are applied. Thus the artist must help themselves with these terms that fall under **B**. And if they wish to help themselves further, let them apply those terms implied in the question which are explicitly explained in the Art, such as Greatness, Eternity, etc. For if God exists, He exists through infinite Greatness and Eternity. And if infinite Greatness and Eternity did not exist, it follows that God would not exist; and thus one will have the "chamber" <note>original: "camerā"; a combination of terms in the Lullian combinatorial wheel.</note> **B.C.D.** ¶ Next, let him run through these terms to prove God exists or to disprove it, just as the three terms are run through the principles and rules. If, however, there are two explicit terms in the question—for example, if it is asked: "Whether God is eternal?"—let him recur to another term explained in the question itself: namely, to Power, etc. For if He is eternal, He is able <note>original: "potest"; a play on Power (Potentia).</note> to be eternal; and if He is not, He cannot <margin>through all power and</margin> be eternal. ¶ Furthermore, if there are three explicit terms in the question—such as asking: "Whether it is good that God is as infinite through His greatness as He is through His eternity?"—then one has the "chamber" **B.C.D.**, and in **B** is the implicit...

<meta>This page transitions from the specific analysis of "Inconstancy" to the "Tenth Part" of the treatise, which focuses on "Application." This section explains how the abstract rules and figures of the Lullian Art are applied to specific philosophical and theological questions.</meta>

-> # Tenth Part <-

...concerning goodness, difference, and "whether" <note>Lullian logic uses "whether" (utrum) as a primary mode of inquiry.</note>; and in **e**, greatness, concordance, and "what is"; and in **d**, duration, contrariety, and "from what." Within these terms are implied the definitions and species of the rules. And thus, the entire <term>chamber<note>original: "camera"; in the Lullian Art, a "chamber" refers to the intersection of two principles or letters in a combinatorial table.</note></term> may be applied to the proposition—that is, to the conclusions. Just as we have given examples in the preceding parts, so can it be exemplified in others. ¶ Furthermore, if it is asked whether God is more "in act" through His understanding than through His eternity: apply "greater" to greatness and "lesser" to smallness. For the "lesser" belongs to the genus of smallness, while the "greater" belongs to the genus of greatness. And if it is asked whether He is as powerful through His power as He is through His will: one should return to "equality," in which comparison is implied (just as "greater" is in greatness and "lesser" is in smallness). And if it is asked whether God is just: one should return to "virtue," for "just" belongs to the genus of virtue; and return to "goodness," since it is a good thing that God is just. The same method applies to other questions in their own way.

# On application through the abstract and the concrete.

<margin>The second part of the tenth principal part, which is on application through the abstract and the concrete.</margin>

**T**his application is to be explained in four ways. ¶ The first way is when the terms placed in the question have a <term>substantial abstraction<note>A concept that exists as a fundamental essence rather than a temporary quality.</note></term>, such as an abstract and concrete term—for example, "fireness" and "fire." "Fireness" <note>original: "igneitas"; a scholastic term for the essential quality that makes fire what it is.</note> is a substantial essence, while "fire" is a concrete and substantial term. ¶ The second way is when the abstract is accidental (or an <term>accident<note>A property that isn't essential to a thing's nature, like being "tall" or "hot."</note>) and its concrete form is similar, such as "habit-ness" and "habited"; in this case, I mean "habit" as it is an accidental property. ¶ The third way is when the abstract is a substance and the concrete is an accident, such as "fireness" and "hot." I say "hot" insofar as it is a <term>habit<note>A quality or state of being.</note></term>, because in that sense it is an accident. ¶ The fourth way is when the abstract is an accident and its concrete form is a substance, such as "whiteness" and "white"; and I mean "white" in the sense of a body that is characterized by whiteness, and thus it is a substance and not an accident. All these four modes are implied in the terms of the question and vice versa; and thus it must be explained in the conclusion according to these four modes, so that the intellect is not deceived by a change in the <term>middle term<note>A logical term used in a syllogism to connect the premises.</note></term>.

---

# On application through the first figure.

<margin>The third part of the tenth principal part, which is on application through the first figure.</margin>

**A**ccording to what has been said, let [the application] be done by affirming or denying: namely, in a circular fashion through the <term>conversion<note>Swapping the subject and the predicate of a sentence while maintaining its truth.</note></term> of the subject and predicate. For example: "great goodness" and "good greatness." However, some do not convert, such as "eternity" and "greatness"; for some greatness is not eternity, and vice versa. Nor is every goodness "great," because some goodness is "small," and so on in its own way.

---

# On application through the second figure.

<margin>The fourth part of the tenth principal part, which is on application through the second figure.</margin>

**A**pplication through the <term>second figure<note>In Llull's system, the Second Figure consists of three triangles representing relations: (1) Difference, Concordance, Contrariety; (2) Beginning, Middle, End; (3) Majority, Equality, Minority.</note></term> itself is done through the triangles and through the "ladders" placed upon the angles. In these ladders are implied the "most general principle," the "most specific principle," and the "subaltern principle." The "most general principle" is like a "difference" that has nothing above it. The "most specific principle" is like the "difference" existing between this stone and this plant. The <term>subaltern<note>An intermediate level between the most general and the most specific.</note></term>, however, is like the "difference" existing between one sensible thing and another sensible thing, etc. ¶ Furthermore, within this ladder is implied the "ascent" and "descent" of the intellect; and outside of these ladders, the ascent and descent of the intellect can in no way be involved. ¶ We say, however, that the terms of the second figure are explainable according to how they lie in the figure itself, according to what we say about it. ¶ Furthermore, we say that the second figure is applicable to the first—for instance, placing a difference between "goodness" and "goodness," etc., and placing concordance between "goodness" and "goodness," as is indicated in the third figure.

---

# On application to the third figure.

<margin>The fifth part of the tenth principal part, which is on application to the third figure.</margin>

**L**et the application of a question to the third figure be done thus: namely, if the matter of the question concerns **b** <note>In the Lullian Alphabet, 'b' usually represents Goodness.</note>, apply **c** to **b**. And if **c** is not sufficient for **b**, apply **d** to **b**. And so on, until the chamber **b. K.** is reached. And let [the intellect] look at the meanings of the chambers, affirming or denying, in such a way that the letter remains with its conditions and its meanings. However, if the matter of the question fits **c**, let the other letters be applied to **c**, just as we said concerning **b**. And this same thing can be said for **d**, **e**, etc. Such an application is infallible and very general.

---

# On application.

<margin>The sixth part of the tenth principal part, which is on application to the fourth figure.</margin>
**A**pplication by the art of the figure is done in this way: namely, if the subject matter of the question fits the <term>chamber<note>original: "camera"; in the Lullian Art, a chamber is the intersection of letters on his combinatorial wheels.</note></term> **b.c.d.**, let it be applied to that chamber. And if the matter fits **b.c.d.** along with **e**, then let the smaller circle be turned with **d**, and let **e** be placed under **c**, and let the chamber **b.c.e.** be formed. Then the meanings of the letters should be taken up to solve the question. Just as we have spoken regarding these, so may it be said regarding others.

<margin>Note an application more general than the others.</margin>
¶ This application is more general than that of the third figure, because a chamber consists of three letters; and it is general to such an extent that it contains within itself all the chambers of the table.

## On application through definitions.

<margin>The seventh part of the tenth principal part, which is on application through definitions.</margin>
**A**ccording to the second mode of this art, the artist must define the terms that are in the question, whether they are explicit or implicit. For example, if it is asked: *is God infinite?* Then the respondent must define "God" and "finiteness," saying thus: "God is a being so perfect that He needs nothing else outside Himself; and infinity is a being to which belong infinite <term>correlatives<note>original: "correlatiua"; in Lull's logic, these are the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving).</note></term> without which it could not possibly exist." ¶ Furthermore, just as it is said that "goodness" is the being by reason of which a good thing performs a good act, so it can be said that "greatness" is that by reason of which a great thing performs a great act; and so with others in their own way. ¶ Furthermore, a term placed in a question can indeed be defined in many ways by running through the <term>species of the rules<note>Lull's "rules" are a set of categorical questions (Whether? What? From what? etc.) designated by letters.</note></term>. ¶ And first, through the species of **rule c**, thus: "man is a rational animal"—and this is through the first species. Through the second species, "man is an animal having his own proper correlatives: namely, the humanizer, the humanizable, and the act of humanizing" <note>original: "hominificantem, hominificabile, et hominificare"; Lullian technical terms for the internal activity of being human.</note>. ¶ And through the third species, "man is an animal acting in the mechanical arts," such as one writing in a manuscript, or riding on a horse, and the like. ¶ And through the fourth species of the same rule, "man is a being having greater possession than the brutes and plants." ¶ Through the first species of **rule d**, "man is a primitive being in the nobility of sensitivity." ¶ Through the second species, "man is a being constituted of soul and body." ¶ Through the third species, "man is a being to whom the brutes, plants, and the like are subject." ¶ Through the first species of **rule e**, "man is a substance through his humanity." ¶ Through the second species, "man is a being created to serve God along with vegetative and sensitive things." ¶ Through **rule f**, "man is a quantitative and continuous being through his elemental, vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and reasoning powers, out of which he is composed." And these five powers are his distinct parts, because they are different. ¶ Through **rule g**, "man is a being to whom it properly belongs to humanize; he is a being capable of laughter, and a being that writes and rides, and the like." ¶ Through **rule h**, "man is a being understanding within time, laws, etc." ¶ Through **rule i**, "man is a being digging in a vineyard, or praying to God in a church." ¶ Through the **rule of modality**, "man is a being having a mode of performing mechanical tasks and generating another human." ¶ Through the **rule of instrumentality**, "man is a substance generating another human with a woman; or with a hammer, he is a being driving a nail, and the like." And just as we have given the example of man, so it can be given of other things in their own way. ¶ And in this step, a doctrine is given through which a person may know how to create various definitions of one and the same thing, so that the thing itself—which was previously unknown—becomes known through all these thoughts or definitions. And therefore, the artist must define in such a way that the definitions remain uncorrupted.

## On application to the rules.

<margin>The eighth part of the tenth principal part, which is on application to the rules.</margin>
**W**hen there is an inquiry about any doubt, the artist must apply that doubt to the rules successively. For just as a crystal placed in a red color takes that color upon itself, and if placed in green, it takes that upon itself, and so with others; so when an unknown thing is run through the rules and the species of the rules, then the unknown is "colored" or declared through the species of the rules in which it is placed both subjectively and objectively. And then the intellect recognizes through the species of the rules that which was previously unknown. And just as we gave the example of man defined through the rules, yet for the sake of greater clarification, we wish to exemplify the "nature" of a thing as it is deduced through the rules. ¶ Through the first species of **rule c**, we say that "nature" is an essence sustained in its natural concrete form and moved through a natural act, in which act it finds rest. ¶ Through the second species, it is an essence having co-natural correlatives: namely, the naturalizer, the naturalizable, and the act of naturalizing <note>original: "naturatiuum, naturabile, et naturare"</note>, without which it cannot exist. ¶ Through the third species, nature is in a subject in which it is active or passive in co-naturalizing. ¶ Through the fourth species, nature has in the subject in which it exists action, passion, and act; and this through a natural agent and through natural form, matter, and...

It demonstrates how an unknown subject becomes clear when filtered through various logical categories, using a famous metaphor of a crystal reflecting the colors around it.</summary>

# The Tenth Part.

end and with natural instruments.
¶ Through the first species of <term>Rule D<note>Rule D in Lull’s system typically asks "What?" (Quid?), leading to definitions of essence and its components.</note></term>, nature is the primitive essence. ¶ Through the second species, it consists of its <term>correlatives<note>original: "correlativis"; in Lullian philosophy, these are the active, passive, and verbal aspects of a principle—for example, the power to heat, the ability to be heated, and the act of heating.</note></term> ascending toward the essence; and its concrete form consists of those same things descending and contracting. ¶ Through the third species, nature belongs to the subject in which it exists, because it acts upon it naturally. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E, nature exists because it is a being containing within itself its own correlatives from which it is made. ¶ Through the second species, nature exists so that other beings may have their existence and agency naturally. ¶ Through Rule F, nature is an essence having continuous and indivisible quantity; and its concrete forms are discrete quantities to it. ¶ Through Rule G, nature has its own proper actions and passions, such as the nature of fire through heating; it has appropriated ones as well, just as heated water has the <term>power to heat, the ability to be heated, and the act of heating<note>original: "calefactiuum, calefactibile, et calefacere." This is a classic Lullian triad representing the internal structure of a natural property.</note></term>. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that nature exists in time continuously and successively: continuously indeed through continuous quantity, but successively through the discrete quantities in which nature exists in time. ¶ Through Rule I, nature is in a place, like the content in a container, and an agent in that which can be acted upon. It is also in a subject in which it is sustained and moved. ¶ Through the rule of Modality, nature has a mode of mixing, generating, and decaying, and the like. ¶ Through the rules of Instrumentality, nature is with its instruments, just as substance is with its accidents, and a mechanic is with his tools, and so on for others. In this way, when nature is discoursed through the species of the rules, it is indeed known by the intellect, because the species signify that which nature is through existence and agency. And just as we have spoken concerning nature, so can it be said of other things, and even of concrete things according to what they are.
¶ Concerning a **miracle**, however, it cannot be spoken of in this way, since it is above nature. And thus, by discoursing on a miracle through the rules, the intellect knows the miracle through its contrary; for a miracle enters the species of the rules through the contrary mode by which nature enters. And in this step, the intellect knows how one contrary may be known through the other by using the rules.

# On application through the table.

<margin>
The ninth part of the tenth principal part.
On application through the table.
</margin>

**T**he application of the <term>table<note>The "Table" is a central Lullian tool—a grid showing all possible combinations of the nine fundamental principles (represented by letters B through K).</note></term> occurs when the terms of questions are applied to the table itself. For if the terms of the question fit the first column—namely **b.c.d.**, which is the first column—as if it were asked whether it would be a "great good" if the world were from eternity. Or if it were asked whether there is an "infinite act," assuming that "goodness" is the reason for acting well, "greatness" is the reason for that act being great, and "eternity" makes that act last from eternity into eternity, then that same infinite act must endure. ¶ Furthermore, if the terms of the question match the second column: such as if it is asked, "Why is there greatness of goodness or power?" The answer must be that it is because of the correlatives of goodness, greatness, and power, and so on for others in their own way. ¶ Moreover, any column is applicable to another: just as the second column is applicable with the first and with the third, because it contains elements of the first (**b.c.**) and likewise of the third; and so with the others, since they are chained together. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that all columns can be applied to the same conclusion. Thus, it knows itself to be very general through this application, which is itself very general. ¶ Likewise, when it is asked whether the world is eternal, then the second <term>chamber<note>original: "camera"; a cell in the Lullian table representing a specific combination of principles.</note></term>—which is **b.c.t.b.**—is applied to the higher chamber. And so with the chamber which is **b.c.t.c.**, and so on for the others up to **t.b.c.d.** The reason for this is that "eternity" is the term explained in the question. ¶ Again, if it is asked whether the power of the world is infinite? Let the response be applied to the column **b.c.d.**, just as the question about the eternity of the world was applied, and let the negative side be held. For just as a great absurdity would follow if the world were from eternity, so a great absurdity would follow if the world had infinite power. And what has been said of the world can be said of those things which it contains within itself. ¶ Furthermore, if it is asked whether one angel produces another angel? Let the response be applied to **b.c.d.**, for there is a great difference between the essence of an angel and that of a human or a rose. For the body of a human exists under the general matter of the elements, by reason of which one human can produce or generate another human, and one rose another. But it is not so with an angel. For one angel does not have the material from which to produce another angel, since there is no derivation from one and the same general "angelic matter," as an angel is finite in its primitivity. ¶ Just as we have given an example through what we said regarding the table, so it can be said of many other things in their own way. ¶ Indeed, the application made through the table requires that the species and the rules of the chambers be preserved, and that those things which they signify be applied to the proposition—namely, to the conclusion—affirming or denying it appropriately or inappropriately, as is clear through the example mentioned above.

On application.

# On application through the evacuation of the third figure.

<margin>The tenth part of the tenth principal part, concerning application through the <term>evacuation<note>In Lullian logic, "evacuation" refers to the process of systematically exhausting all possible combinations of terms within a figure to find every potential relation or argument.</note></term> of the third figure.</margin>

**A**pplication that occurs through the <term>third figure<note>The Third Figure in Lull’s Art is typically a grid or table that pairs the nine Principles (Goodness, Greatness, etc.) with each other to form "cameras" or cells of inquiry.</note></term> is done in this way: namely, that the terms explained in a question are applied to the evacuation of the third figure, and specifically to that <term>camera<note>original: "camere"; literally "chamber" or "room," referring to the individual cells in Lull's logical tables where two principles intersect.</note></term> which the terms best fit. For example: if it is asked whether it is a "great good" that goodness and greatness have substantial correlatives, and whether those correlatives exist in a "good and great" concord. In this case, such a question should be applied to camera **B.C.** <note>Camera B.C. is the cell where Goodness (B) and Greatness (C) intersect.</note> ¶ And through the things we said regarding that camera in the chapter on evacuation, the question will indeed be solved. The same applies to other questions, according to how their terms can enter a camera, either by affirming or denying, and either fittingly or unsuitably. ¶ Furthermore, if a question is asked whether a contrariety of goodness could exist from eternity within <term>eternity<note>original: "eternitate." In Lull's system, Eternity/Duration is Principle D.</note></term>. Let that question be applied to camera **B.C.**, camera **C.D.**, and camera **D.E.** And according to what was said in those cameras, the question will indeed be solved. So it goes for other questions, according to how their terms can enter the cameras, affirming or denying fittingly or unsuitably. ¶ Furthermore, let a subalternate question be applied to a particular question, and vice versa. For example: if it is asked whether there are great correlatives in goodness. Let this question be applied to this more specific one: whether there are great correlatives in the goodness of <term>Socrates<note>original: "Sotis"; a standard medieval abbreviation for Socrates, used here as a placeholder for an individual person.</note></term> or of this rose. Then let these questions be applied to camera **B.C.** The response will then be found already solved by what has been said previously. ¶ Furthermore, if it is asked: what are the correlatives of greatness made of? and what are the correlatives of Socrates made of? Let these questions be applied to camera **C.D.**, and let the subalternate question be applied to the particular question; then, in time, the conclusion will be found declared and signified by what we have already said in that camera. The same applies to the other cameras. We shall give an example of this in the treatise on questions.

<margin>The eleventh part of the tenth principal part, concerning application through the multiplication of the fourth figure.</margin>

# On application through the multiplication of the fourth figure.

**W**e have said that the multiplication of the <term>fourth figure<note>The Fourth Figure consists of three concentric circles that rotate to create triplets of terms, used for constructing syllogisms and complex arguments.</note></term> consists of five modes: namely, in multiplication, in the discovery of the <term>middle term<note>original: "medij"; the central term that links the major and minor premises in a syllogism.</note></term>, in the proof of the major and minor propositions, in solving fallacies, and in the instruction by which other arts can be easily learned. Therefore, if an artist wishes to multiply many reasons for the same conclusion, find many middle terms, prove the major and minor propositions, solve fallacies, and easily and briefly teach other sciences with this general art: let him apply the method we held in the multiplication of the fourth figure. For that method is universal. Through that method, any particular method will be regulated and illuminated. For the particular shines within the universal, and vice versa; and let these things suffice, for it has been sufficiently declared.

# On the application of the mixture of principles and rules.

<margin>The twelfth part of the tenth principal part, which is about the application of the mixture of principles and rules into two distinct sub-parts.</margin>

**T**his Art is divided into two parts. ¶ In the first, we will speak of the explicit principles. ¶ In the second, of the implicit ones, which we will apply to the explicit principles in the places of the rules of this art. These principles shall be called "one hundred forms"; we do this so that the Art may be more concrete for the intellect to find many conclusions. We intend to say little about these because we wish to avoid prolixity. But through what we shall say of them, the artist can recognize the process of any form through all the rules, just as we did in the deduction of the explicit principles and through the rules. First, we shall speak of the first part thus:

## First part.

<margin>Question on the first part of this twelfth part.</margin>

**A** question contains within itself explained terms, such as if it is asked: "Is there a good, great, and eternal being?" One should recur to the chapters on Goodness, Greatness, and Eternity. One should also see the mode by which Goodness is discussed through the principles and rules, and so on for the other principles. Then, let a conclusion be reached by affirming or denying, provided that the principles and rules remain unharmed <note>The "rules" (questions like What? Why? How?) must be applied without contradicting the "principles" (the Divine Dignities like Goodness or Greatness).</note>. Then the intellect will find the truth regarding the matter sought. This truth will be illuminated through that discourse. Just as we gave an example using Goodness, Greatness, and Eternity, so it can be done for other principles. And let these things suffice regarding the first part.

<meta>This page continues the Tenth Principal Part concerning "Application." # Tenth part.

<margin>The tenth part of the tenth principal part, concerning the application of the nine subjects.</margin>

**W**e have spoken of the nine <term>subjects<note>The Nine Subjects are the levels of being in Lull’s system: God, Angel, Heaven, Man, Imaginative, Sensitive, Vegetative, Elementative, and Instrumentative.</note></term>: therefore, if a question concerns God, let it be applied to the first subject; and let the discourse proceed through it just as God is discursive in such a way that the affirmative or negative aligns with the text. ¶ If the question concerns an angel, let it be applied to the second subject in which the angel is the subject of discourse; and let that which agrees with the text be maintained regarding the question. And so it goes for the other subjects in their own manner.

## On the application to the hundred forms.

<margin>The fourteenth part of the tenth principal part, which is about the application to the hundred forms.</margin>

**W**e call these indeed the hundred <term>forms<note>The "Hundred Forms" is a specific Lullian list of philosophical and theological concepts (like Entity, Essence, Quantity, etc.) used to provide a comprehensive vocabulary for his logical system.</note></term>. For we consider them in the abstract: some will be most general, others will be subordinate; and to each form we assign its own <term>concrete<note>original: "concretum"; In Lullian logic, an "abstract" form is the quality itself (e.g., Goodness), while the "concrete" is the being that possesses it (e.g., a good thing or "bonificative").</note></term> form, so that each form may shine more clearly to the intellect—and especially regarding what it is, whether in the abstract or the concrete. For outside of these, no being can exist; and first, we must speak of the first part.

## On entity.

<margin>The first form, regarding entity.</margin>

**E**ntity <note>original: "entitas"; the state of being or existence.</note> in this Art is an <term>implied term<note>An "implied" or "implicit" term is one that is not one of the primary nine principles (like Goodness) but is understood to be contained within them or derived from them.</note></term>; and its definition can be made just as the definitions of the other explained principles of this Art are made. Therefore, let the artist apply it to the definitions of goodness, greatness, etc. For just as goodness is the cause why something good performs a good act, so entity is the cause why any being causes another being. And just as greatness is the cause why goodness is great, so entity is the cause why goodness is a being; and so it is for the others. Its concrete form is "being," and being is implied in the second species of **D** and in the first of **E**. And those things from which it is implied are in the second species of **C**. Therefore, whatever is asked about entity and being, let it be applied to the explained principles; and let such judgment be made regarding it according to the rules, just as was done for goodness, greatness, and so on.

## On essence.

<margin>The second form, regarding essence.</margin>

**S**ince entity and essence are convertible <note>In scholastic logic, "convertible" terms refer to the same reality but from different perspectives; wherever one is, the other must be.</note>, it follows that "to be" (*esse*) and "being" (*ens*) are convertible; and therefore, just as we spoke regarding entity and being, so we can speak regarding essence and "to be." ¶ If it is asked whether there is a difference between essence and "to be," then let one recur to the term <term>difference<note>original: "differentia"; one of the Nine Relational Principles in Lull's Art.</note></term>, which is an 

---

explained term; and let a judgment be made according to how difference is discoursed through all principles and through all rules; and then, without doubt, it will appear that the affirmative is to be held in the question. ¶ For "difference" is essence, and its <term>correlatives<note>Lull’s theory of "correlatives" suggests every essence has three internal components: an active power, a passive power, and the act itself (e.g., the power to love, the power to be loved, and the act of loving).</note></term> are in the nature of "height" when abstracting; and its concrete forms are in the nature of "infinity" when containing. Thus it is clear that difference exists between essence and "to be" (*esse*). And to this, Rule **B** <note>Rule B usually asks "What is it?"</note> consents.

## On unity.

<margin>The third form, regarding unity.</margin>

**U**nity is the form whose property is to unite. And it is indeed applicable to goodness, greatness, etc., since they are good, great, and so forth. Just as unity is good through goodness and great through greatness, so goodness is one through unity, and greatness is another unity—one creature through that same unity—and so it is for the others. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that "difference" distinguishes between goodness and greatness, so that there may be a principle of difference, so that every principle may have its own proper truth. And therefore, if there is an explained term in the question, let one recur to what was said in the discourse on goodness, greatness, and difference; and let the response be made according to what was said about them. ¶ The concrete form of unity is indeed implied in the concrete forms of goodness, greatness, etc. For a "good" thing is one, and a "great" thing is another one. That "one" itself has its correlatives from which it is composed. This is applicable to the second species of **D** and the first of **E**. And those correlatives themselves are applicable to the second species of Rule **C** and the first of **D**.

## On plurality.

<margin>The fourth form, regarding plurality.</margin>

**P**lurality is a form aggregated from many things differing in number, as is clear through the second species of Rule **C**, which is its source. It is indeed applicable to the explained principles, because it is good, great, and eternal. And just as it is good through goodness and great through greatness, etc., so goodness and greatness are many through plurality itself. And there are also many goodnesses differing in species. And the same for greatness, as is clear through the second species of Rule **C**, which is its source.
