# On application.

¶ The first causes of plurality indeed exist through difference, concordance, and equality; and so it is for other <term>correlatives<note>In the Lullian Art, "correlatives" refers to the internal triadic structure of any principle: an active power, a passive capacity, and the action linking them (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving).</note></term>. Plurality is applicable to the principles themselves and vice versa. Its <term>concrete<note>original: "concretum"; the specific thing or being that embodies an abstract quality.</note></term> form is applicable to the concrete forms of goodness, magnitude, etc. This is evident in an <term>element<note>In medieval science, the four elements (fire, air, water, earth) were the building blocks of all physical matter.</note></term> which is good and great; it is one thing constituted of many parts, so that plurality is sustained within it.

## On nature.

<margin>Fifth form: on nature.</margin>
**N**ature is the form whose proper function is <term>to nature<note>original: "naturare"; Lull uses this active verb to describe the inherent, dynamic activity of nature producing its effects.</note></term>. And because the principles are natural through nature, therefore nature is applicable to natural goodness and natural magnitude. In this way, nature can be known through the discourse of principles and <term>rules<note>The "Rules" (identified by letters B through K) are Lull's set of logical questions, such as "What?", "From what?", and "Why?"</note></term>; we have spoken of this more broadly above. ¶ Furthermore, nature is applicable to the natural correlatives of goodness, magnitude, etc., because those natural correlatives cannot exist without their concrete forms. ¶ The natural concrete is applicable to natural concrete things, as is evident through the second species of Rule D and the first species of Rule E. ¶ Furthermore, because goodness has one nature with magnitude, another with duration, etc., and vice versa, it is applicable to <term>mixture<note>original: "mixtio"; the Lullian concept of how different principles or elements combine and interpenetrate to form a specific being.</note></term>, where we have spoken of deduced goodness, magnitude, and duration.

## On genus.

<margin>Sixth form: on genus.</margin>
**G**enus is a being considered in a very broad and undifferentiated way, which is predicated of many things differing in species. We have said enough concerning genus in the *New Logic* which we have written. It is indeed applicable to the explained principles, because through it they are made general; just as a <term>genus<note>A general category or "family" in logic.</note></term> which is good through goodness, and great through magnitude, etc. It is also applicable to the explained correlatives, because those correlatives are general through it; and these correlatives are also known through the second species of Rule C. ¶ Furthermore, its concrete form is applicable to the second species of Rule D and the first of Rule E, by which we know that genus is a real being, existing by itself. For if it were not, the correlatives of the explained principles could not be general, nor consequently could the explained principles themselves be general.

## On species.

<margin>Seventh form: on species.</margin>
**S**pecies in this Art is an explained principle; and its definition is this: <term>Species<note>A specific category within a genus; for example, "Human" is a species within the genus "Animal."</note></term> is a being that is predicated of many things differing in number. Species is indeed applicable to the "places" in a mixture where we say "great goodness," etc. For goodness, which was most general, is no longer entirely general when we say "great goodness," because it has been contracted to a special magnitude; and so it is for the others. ¶ Furthermore, it is applicable to correlatives, because whichever of the explained principles possesses special correlatives, it possesses its own numerical difference through "difference." Thus species is applicable to <term>Difference<note>original: "differentia"; one of Lull's Nine Principles, used here to distinguish one thing from another.</note></term>, which is an explained principle in this Art; this difference distinguishes a genus into many species differing in number, just as "human" is one species and "lion" is another. ¶ Likewise, species is applicable to the <term>medium<note>The "Middle" or bridge between two extremes.</note></term>; for just as a medium consists between a beginning and an end, so species consists between a genus and an individual. In this step, the intellect recognizes that species is necessarily a real being; for just as a beginning and an end would not be at the extremities of a medium unless the medium were a real being, so consequently neither genus nor individual would be real beings. ¶ The concrete of a species is "the special," which is applicable to the second species of Rule D and the first of Rule E, by which it is knowable; it is, however, imperceptible to the senses but can be imagined. ¶ Furthermore, there are other species that are natural, such as "visibility" through the visual power and the like, which consist of sight and power, such as colors and shapes which are sensed in a subject through sight. ¶ Furthermore, there are other species which consist in the power of the soul through moral virtues: such as "justificabilities" through justice, "prudencabilities" through prudence, "credibilities" through faith, and "hopabilities" through hope. Such species are <term>phantasms<note>original: "fantasmata"; mental images or representations in the mind.</note></term>, like the imaginables of the imagination, the intelligibles of the intellect, the lovables of the will, and the memorables of the memory. Nevertheless, the species of the virtues are secondary.

## On individuality.

<margin>Octaua forma de indiuiduitate.</margin>
**I**ndividuality is definable through the first species of Rule C. For just as goodness is the reason for a good thing to act well, so individuality is the reason for an <term>individual<note>A single, unique member of a species.</note></term> to produce an individual. And just as individuality is good through goodness, etc., so goodness is individuated through individuality; and so it is with its concrete and relative forms, with which essences it is indivisible. These correlatives of goodness and correlatives of individuality are applicable so that the intellect may have knowledge of them...

Tenth Part

...indeed, <term>correlatives<note>original: "correlativa"; in Lull’s system, these are the three components of any principle: the active (producer), the passive (receiver), and the act itself.</note></term> can neither be sensed nor imagined, since they are situated and contained beyond physical shape in the <term>essence<note>The inner "being" or "what-ness" of a thing, distinct from its outward appearance.</note></term>. ¶ The <term>concrete<note>original: "concretum"; the specific, physical embodiment of an abstract quality.</note></term> of individuality is the individual. And this is demonstrable through the second species of Rule D and the first species of Rule E. In elemental things, however, it is sensible and imaginable, as is evident through this rose and this lion.

## On Property.

<margin>Fourth form: on property.</margin>
**P**roperty is an unfolded principle, as is clear through Rule G <note>Rule G asks "Which?" and "Of what?"—identifying the specific nature of a thing.</note>. But in other principles and rules, the principle is implied. And its definition is applicable to the first species of Rule C. ¶ For just as goodness is the reason why a good thing does good, so property is the reason why a proper thing acts in its own proper way. And just as goodness has its own correlatives through property, so property has its own good correlatives through goodness. Property is also applicable to "difference." For just as difference is the cause of differing, so property is the cause of <term>appropriating<note>original: "appropriandi"; the act of making something distinct or assigning it its specific characteristics.</note></term>; and so it goes for the others. ¶ Further: the concrete of property is the "proper," constituted from concrete correlatives; and this is signified through the second species of Rule D and the first species of Rule E, such as this man who is a proper animal, and this lion who is another proper animal, and this horse, and this rose which is another proper body. This applies likewise in moral matters, such as Socrates who has his own proper horse, and Plato similarly, as is clear through the third species of Rule D. And in this passage, the intellect recognizes from which principles the science of Law arises, and in which principles it consists, and which principles a jurist ought to use; it also recognizes that laws are applicable to the mixing of principles and rules.

## On Simplicity.

<margin>Tenth form: on simplicity.</margin>
**S**implicity is applicable to the principles of this Art, because through simplicity the principles are simple; just as simplicity is good through goodness, and great through magnitude. And just as the unfolded principles are discoursed upon in the mixing of principles and rules, so simplicity can be discoursed upon through all principles and rules. Indeed, its definition is through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C asks "What is it?"—defining the essence of a subject.</note>, for it is the form by which principles are simple. ¶ Simplicity, through the second species of Rule C, has its own simple correlatives: just as goodness has the simple <term>bonifying agent<note>original: "bonificativum"; the active power of goodness.</note></term>, the <term>bonifiable<note>original: "bonificabile"; the capacity to receive goodness.</note></term>, and the act of <term>bonifying<note>original: "bonificare"; the action of making good.</note></term>. Within simplicity and its correlatives, there exists one simple essence having simple and primitive principles through the first species of Rule D. Its concrete form, or its being, is "the simple." And this is signified through the second species of Rule D and the first species of Rule E.

## On Composition.

<margin>Eleventh form: on composition.</margin>
**C**omposition is a form aggregated from several essences. It is indeed applicable to the contraction and meeting of the unfolded principles, as is clear in the example of goodness being led into the principles; where it is said that "great goodness" is doubled, and "great and durable goodness" is tripled, and so on, by constituting a composite from several unfolded principles. And in this passage, the intellect recognizes where composition arises, and Rule K <note>Rule K asks "How?" or "By what means?"</note> agrees with this. ¶ Further, composition has its own composite correlatives, as is clear through the second species of Rule C. And so, in created things, the correlatives of goodness and magnitude, etc., compose the "great-ifiable" and the "good-ifiable"; and also the "to bonify" and "to magnify" are simply composed, etc., and they mutually constitute one essence, which essence we call "composition." Its being or its concrete form is "the composite," revealed to the enlightened intellect through the second species of Rule D and the first species of Rule E.

## On Form.

<margin>Twelfth form: on form.</margin>
**F**orm is applicable to the twelve principles; therefore, just as a principle is discoursed through the unfolded principles and rules, similarly form can be discoursed in its own way. We say this, however, regarding the composite form in created things, because the <term>bonifiable<note>original: "bonificabile"; here Llull equates the passive capacity of a principle with the concept of "matter" in the physical world.</note></term> is of the nature of matter; but in God, it is not. ¶ Form is that essence with which an agent acts naturally upon matter. That composite form itself has its own composite correlatives, as was said above. But a simple form in caused things does not have correlatives, because it is one simple part of a substance; namely, the "form-ifying" or the agent, considered according to the first species of Rule E. And the same can be said regarding accidental form. Such a form is indeed insensible and...

# On matter.

**M**atter is a simple, passive essence; it is applicable to the receiving of the principles once they are unfolded, such as to the "bonifiable" <note>That which is capable of receiving goodness.</note>, the "magnifiable," and so on. These are of the category of matter by reason of their passivity. ¶ Matter does not have its own <term>correlatives<note>original: "concreta" (here likely referring to the internal active/passive components); Lullian theory usually assigns three parts to a principle, but matter is uniquely passive.</note></term>, and this is through the second species of Rule C, because its simplicity requires that its "passion" (its capacity to be acted upon) be its one simple part of substance. Its primitive principle is designated by the first species of Rule D. ¶ The concrete, or the "materialized," is composed of several <term>passions<note>In scholastic philosophy, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note></term>, such as being "bonifiable" or "magnifiable." ¶ This materialized thing is declared through the second species of Rule D and the first of Rule E. This materialized thing is the fountain from which all particular matters are derived, just as the "formed" is that from which all particular forms descend when they are brought from <term>potentiality into act<note>The process by which a possibility becomes a reality.</note></term>.

# On substance.

**S**ubstance is applicable to the <term>contracted triangle<note>A specific Lullian diagram representing the relationships between different principles.</note></term>, insofar as it is said that "majority" <note>A state of being greater or more encompassing.</note> exists between substance and substance. Therefore, the discourse on substance is folded into the discourse on "majority" through all principles and rules. But its definition is applicable to the definition of goodness, and so on. For just as goodness is the reason why a good thing produces good, so substance, regarding its category, is the reason why it produces the "substantiated." ¶ Substance indeed has its own substantial <term>correlatives<note>The three-fold relationship of actor, receiver, and action.</note></term> through the second species of Rule C: namely, the "substantiated," the "substantiable," and "to substantiate." "Substantiative" applies to the "bonificative" <note>The power that makes things good.</note> or "magnificative"; the "substantiable" applies to the "bonifiable" and "magnifiable"; and "to substantiate" to "to make good" and "to make great." In this step, the intellect recognizes the way in which substance is composed of form and matter, and is marked out by them, and placed in the third number <note>Likely referring to the triad of form, matter, and the resulting substance.</note>. ¶ The concrete or "being" is substantial, as is designated to the intellect by the second species of Rule D and the first of Rule E, and also to the senses and imagination in things composed of the elements.

# On accident.

**A**ccident is folded into the <term>yellow triangle<note>One of the symbolic figures in Llull's Art, often associated with concepts like "Majority," "Equality," and "Minority."</note></term>, where it is said that "majority" exists between accident and accident. Therefore, its discourse is applicable through all principles and rules in the aforementioned triangle. ¶ Accident is a form that does not exist by itself; it does not exist for its own principal end, but rather for the end of the substance. However, accident does not have its own proper correlatives, but only "by accident" <note>Meaning it only possesses these properties because it is attached to a substance.</note>, because substance is given habit, quantity, and position by it. ¶ In the chapter on goodness, where it is said "goodness is great," etc., accident arises because there is a multiplication of the composite. "How much" arises through the accident of quantity. And because it is situated in a subject, "position" arises through accident; and so it is for relation, which is an accident, and for the other <term>predicaments<note>The ten categories of being defined by Aristotle (Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation, Place, Time, Position, State, Action, Passion).</note></term>, and also for motion and such things. ¶ The concrete accident is "accidental," which is applicable to the second species of Rule D and the first of Rule E—just as a chest, which is an accidental subject, is so because it has an accidental shape given by the craftsman. Likewise, a logician is a "master" only accidentally. And so it is for others in their own way.

# Tenth part.

...are measured through the difference that the difference itself makes, to the extent that they are neither more nor less. ¶ The "quantified" is its <term>concrete form<note>original: "concretum"; the specific instantiation of an abstract concept, like "a white thing" vs "whiteness."</note></term>, measured by quantity itself, just as a white object is colored by whiteness.

<margin>The seventeenth form: on quality.</margin>

### On quality.

**Q**uality is an <term>explicit term<note>original: "terminus explicatus"; a concept that is clearly defined and "unfolded" within the Lullian system.</note></term>, as is evident through Rule G, and its definition is applicable to the definition of goodness, etc. For just as goodness is an entity by reason of which a good thing does good, so quality is the form which establishes that the "bonifier" <note>the agent performing an act of goodness</note> has a certain quality while acting, and the "bonified" <note>the recipient of the act of goodness</note> has a certain quality while being acted upon. ¶ Quality itself is applicable to <term>substantial correlatives<note>original: "correlativa substantialia"; the interconnected parts of any being in Llull's logic, usually consisting of an agent, a recipient, and the act itself.</note></term> through the second species of Rule C, because the correlatives are shaped by quality. And quality itself is constituted from these same correlatives. Through the third species of Rule C, it establishes the "qualified" subject in which it exists; this qualified subject is its concrete form. ¶ Furthermore, quality is applicable to the second species of Rule D in the chapter on goodness, examined through the principles and rules, and likewise for greatness, etc. For goodness, which is a most general principle, does not have a specific quality until it is <term>contracted<note>original: "contracta"; narrowed down from a general concept to a specific instance or relationship.</note></term>. For example, when one asks: "What kind of quality does goodness have?" and one answers that it is great and enduring, etc., then quality arises as an <term>accident<note>original: "per accidens"; a property that is not part of the essential definition of a thing but belongs to it nonetheless.</note></term> through the contraction of the principles.

<margin>The eighteenth form: on relation.</margin>

### On relation.

**R**elation is an implicit term, and its definition is applicable to the definition of goodness, etc. For just as a good being creates a good thing through goodness, so a relative being creates a related thing through relation. For if there is a "relator," it follows there is a "related," and vice versa. If there is an antecedent, it follows there is a consequent, and vice versa. And if there is concordance, it follows that there is plurality, and so on for the others. The "related" is its concrete form, derived from relation itself and shaped by it, and so forth. ¶ Furthermore, relation existing as an accident is applicable to the contraction and mixing of the principles with the first species of Rule D and the second of Rule C. For if goodness is great, it follows that it has correlatives that are both good and great, without which goodness could in no way be great. And likewise for the others in their own way.

### On action.

<margin>The nineteenth form: on action.</margin>

**A**ction is a term implied within the correlatives, and it is applicable to those correlatives, namely to the "bonifier," the "magnifier," etc., and its definition is applicable to the definition of goodness, etc. For just as goodness is an entity by reason of which a good thing does good, so action is the reason in the agent why it acts upon the <term>patient<note>original: "passum"; the subject that receives the action.</note></term> in its concrete form; however, it is not a name applied in a <term>direct line<note>original: "per rectam lineam"; likely referring to the grammatical or logical derivation of the term within Llull's combinatorial diagrams.</note></term>. Indeed, the concrete itself is designated through the second species of Rule D. ¶ Furthermore, action is declared through the first species of Rule D in the correlatives through the second species of Rule C, and this is done through the definition of the <term>middle<note>original: "medium"; in Llull’s logic, the link between the beginning and the end of an action.</note></term>, and so on for the others in their own way.

<margin>The twentieth form: on passion.</margin>

### On passion.

**P**assion <note>original: "passio"; in this philosophical context, it refers to the capacity to be acted upon or the state of receiving an action, not an emotion.</note> is an implicit term. ¶ And it is applicable to the correlatives. ¶ Through the second species of Rule C, namely to the "bonifiable," the "magnifiable," etc. Therefore, just as those passive correlatives exist through the mixing of principles, so passion, which is a general principle, can be deduced through the mixing of principles and rules. ¶ Furthermore, the "patient" [the one being acted upon] is its concrete form, which is situated in passion and shaped by it. Indeed, passion arises in the contraction and mixing of principles, just as goodness is a passion insofar as it is shaped by greatness, and vice versa. And this is clear through the first species of Rule D, and Rule B agrees with this.

<margin>The twenty-first form: on habit.</margin>

### On habit.

**H**abit <note>original: "habitus"; here meaning a state of being, a disposition, or an outward condition (such as being "clothed" in a virtue), rather than a repetitive behavior.</note> is a principle, and it is implicit, but it is applicable to the explicit principles. For just as a good person does good by "habituating" <note>clothing or disposing</note> themselves in good moral virtue, so the one habituating disposes themselves in a moral habit by reason of habit itself; and likewise with goodness being "habituated" by greatness. ¶ The "habituated" is its concrete form. For just as a white thing is "habituated" by whiteness, and a cloaked man by a cloak, and fire by heat, and a just man by justice, so is the "habituated" by habit. ¶ Furthermore, through the first species of Rule D and in the mixing of principles and rules, the intellect recognizes from where habit arises and in which subjects it is spread. ## On position.

<margin>The twenty-second form: on position.</margin>
**P**osition is an <term>implicit term<note>original: "terminus implicatus"; a concept that is not self-evident but must be "unfolded" or derived through the logical rules of Llull's Art.</note></term>: but it is applicable to <term>correlatives<note>original: "correlativa"; the triad of agent, patient, and action (e.g., the Positioner, the Positioned, and the act of Positioning) that Llull believes exists within every essence.</note></term> through the second species of Rule C and D, and the first species of Rule E, and also to the definition of goodness, etc. Indeed, its own definition is applicable. For since goodness is the reason why a good thing performs a good act within the essence of goodness, it follows therefore that the correlatives of goodness are "positioned" <note>original: "assituata"; arranged or situated in relation to one another</note> and vice versa. And thus, position is an accident causing this "positioning" among the principles. ¶ Furthermore, through the first species of Rule D, specifically through the contraction and mixing of principles and rules, the intellect knows where position arises, and where it is led from potentiality into act: just as great goodness is positioned, and vice versa. And the correlatives of goodness are positioned within the correlatives of greatness; and Rule B pertains to this.

## On time.

<margin>The twenty-third form: on time.</margin>
**T**ime is a principle <term>explained<note>original: "explicatum"; a term already clearly defined in the foundational parts of Llull's system.</note></term> in the Art; but for the sake of explanation, we wish to show in what manner it is applicable to all principles and rules, just as its definition is applicable to the definition of a "principle." For time is that principle with which all created things were made "new" <note>meaning they had a beginning in time, unlike eternal things</note>. And its definition is also applicable to the tenth rule, because time is the instrument by which there are days and nights, and hours, and motion, and the like. ¶ Furthermore, time is applicable to correlatives through the second species of Rule C, when it is led from potentiality into act: as when an agent acts upon the "actable" <note>the thing being acted upon</note> with time, multiplying days, hours, nights, and so on for others. Its <term>concrete form<note>original: "concretum"; the actual thing that embodies the abstract quality.</note></term> is the "timed" or "temporalized."

## On place.

<margin>The twenty-fourth form: on place.</margin>
**P**lace is an explained principle derived through the principles and rules, and its definition is applicable to the definition of a principle. For place is the principle by which all beings are "containing" and "contained." It is indeed applicable to the tenth rule, because place is the instrument by which all mobile things are moved from a new place to a new place. ¶ Place itself is also applicable to the correlatives from which it emerges: when those substantial correlatives place "foreign" correlatives within themselves. Just as fire, through heat, "places" <note>collocat</note> heat within water that is being heated. And a generator, within its internal "generatable" <note>that which is capable of being produced</note>, generates the thing generated, and so forth. The "placed" is its concrete form.

## On motion.

<margin>The twenty-fifth form: on motion.</margin>
**M**otion is an implicit principle, and its definition is applicable to the definition of a principle, and also to Rule R, and so on for others. For motion is that principle by which all mobile things are mobile; and its correlatives emerge from substantial correlatives, just as an accident emerges from a substance. ¶ Motion is indeed the instrument with which a substance moves itself locally, augmentatively, and alteratively. Locally: such as the heavens, which move themselves circularly with their own "appetite" <note>in medieval physics, the "desire" of a celestial body to complete its perfect circular path</note>, which is a kind of motion. Augmentatively: such as a plant by growing and reproducing. Alteratively: such as wine that changes into vinegar, or water from coldness into heat, or a person from health into sickness, or justice into injury, and the like. Its concrete form is the "motive thing" <note>the thing that causes or undergoes motion</note>. The essence of motion is indeed insensible and unimaginable; but in the subject in which it exists, it is sensible and imaginable. For instance, sight reaches the mover and the moved when a hammer moves a nail. And touch reaches the "impulsed" motion. However, I do not say that it reaches the motion as to the essence of the motion itself, but only the figure; and so it is for others in their own way, just as sight reaches a falling stone, but it does not reach the essence of the motion, nor of the stone, but only the color and the figure.

## On immobility.

<margin>The twenty-sixth form: on immobility.</margin>
**I**mmobility is an implicit principle; but its definition is applicable to the definition of a principle. For just as a principle is the cause why beings are "principled" <note>brought into being by a principle</note>, so immobility is the principle by which immobile things are immobile or permanent. Immobility itself is applicable to its internal correlatives, from which it can by no means be separated. Just as form cannot be separated from action, nor matter from passion <note>the state of being acted upon</note>, nor the hot from heat, nor the good from goodness, nor a human from their species, etc. ¶ The concrete form of immobility is the "immobile." Its correlatives are the "immotive" <note>the active principle of unchangeability</note> and the "immobile" <note>the passive principle or state of being unchangeable</note>.

### On instinct.

<margin>27. The form of instinct.</margin>
**I**nstinct is an <term>implicit principle<note>original: "principium implicatum"; a foundational concept that contains other ideas within it, which must be "unfolded" through logical analysis.</note></term>; and it is applicable to wisdom, which is an <term>explicit principle<note>original: "principium explicatum"; a primary, self-evident quality such as Goodness or Wisdom.</note></term>. Consequently, it is applicable to the definition of wisdom along with the tenth rule. ¶ For just as wisdom is the being by reason of which a wise person understands, so natural instinct is the being by reason of which the subject in which nature exists acts naturally according to its entire species, as seen in a plant. For its instinct relates to the production of flowers, leaves, fruit, flavor, and the like. And so it is for the <term>lower animals<note>original: "brutis"; non-human animals guided by nature rather than reason.</note></term> which possess instinct and industry for living through the second species of Rule C. ¶ The <term>correlatives<note>original: "correlativa"; the Lullian triad of the agent, the patient, and the action (e.g., the instincting, the instincted, and the act of instincting).</note></term> of instinct are applicable to the correlatives of the explicit principles; and so for other species in their own way. Its concrete form is the "instinctive thing," as signified by the second species of Rule C and the first species of Rule E; and its purpose <note>original: "finis"</note> consists in the second species of Rule E.

### On natural appetite.

<margin>28. The form of natural appetite.</margin>
**A**ppetite of nature is an implicit principle: and its definition is applicable to the definitions of the will. For just as the will desires an object, and establishes it as something desired, and feels a longing for it, so appetite relates to its object so that it may <term>find rest<note>original: "desicat"; likely a contraction for "quiescat" (to rest) or "desiderat" (to desire). In Lullian physics, appetite seeks "rest" in its object.</note></term> within it. This is seen in the elements which have an appetite for <term>taking form<note>original: "elementandum"; the process of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) combining to create physical matter.</note></term>; and in the plant for growing; and for producing flowers, leaves, and fruit; and for multiplying its species into individuals. And the explicit principles concur in this: just as the animal goodness which is in the subject has an appetite so that it may have its act, namely, "to goodify" <note>original: "bonificare"; to perform the act of being good or making something good.</note>: and this is signified through the second species of Rule C. Appetite has its own correlatives applicable to the correlatives of the will. This appetite also has its <term>contraction<note>original: "contractum"; the specific application or narrowing of a general principle to a particular instance.</note></term>, as signified by the second species of D and the first species of E, with which it moves itself toward the second species of Rule C, so that it may find rest—just as a person moves themselves with their will toward their loves or toward the beloved, and so on.

### On attraction.

<margin>29. The form of attraction.</margin>
**A**ttraction is an implicit principle: and it is applicable to the definition of the <term>purpose<note>original: "finis"; the 'end' or goal towards which a thing is naturally directed.</note></term> and of goodness. For the purpose attracts the "purposed" thing to itself, just as the "goodifier" attracts the "goodified," and the will attracts the beloved, and the breath attracts what is breathed, and sight attracts the colored, and taste attracts the flavored, and so on. ¶ The correlatives of attraction are applicable to the correlatives of the explicit principles through the second species of Rule C. For the attractor attracts the attracted in the <term>passive state<note>original: "passione"; the condition of being acted upon.</note></term> of its essence: just as fire attracts air into its own heating, so that the air itself is heated: and breath attracts air, so that the air itself is breathed. And the power attracts the object, as the "objectified"; and so for others in their own way. Indeed, its concrete form is the "attracted thing": for it attracts natural species and operations to itself, so that it may be an agent: and so that through it the explicit principles may be able to have their acts, and find rest in the second species of Rule E, and so on: just as the magnet which, by its whole species, attracts iron: so that the dryness and coldness existing in the iron are <term>brought to rest<note>original: "desicant"; here meaning to settle or find fulfillment.</note></term> in the dryness and coldness of the magnet, which is a natural subject. At this step, the intellect understands the way in which those things which exist artificially are attracted by those things which exist naturally.

### On reception.

<margin>30. The form of reception.</margin>
**R**eception is an implicit principle: and its definition is applicable to the definition of the material principle, just as attraction is to the formal principle. And just as in the correlatives, the <gloss>active suffix</gloss> <note>original: "tiuus" (-tivum); the active component of a triad.</note> belongs to the genus of attraction, the <gloss>passive suffix</gloss> <note>original: "bilis" (-bile); the passive component of a triad.</note> belongs to the genus of reception. However, I do not say that reception has correlatives: because if it did, it would then follow that the active and the passive were numerically the same; and similarly form and matter, which is impossible. But I say that the receiver receives the "foreign receivable" in the passive state of its essence, just as sight receives color in its visible aspect, and the intellect receives foreign species in its intelligible aspect, and so on. ¶ And at this step, the intellect knows that the object does not move the power, but the power moves itself with the object. For otherwise the object...

...there would be an agent and a patient; and consequently potentiality and act would be confused. Both agent and patient would be the same in number in nature; and the same could be said of attraction and passion, which is impossible. Indeed, the <term>concrete form<note>original: "concretum"; in Llull’s logic, the "concrete" is the thing itself (e.g., "the good thing") while the "abstract" is the quality (e.g., "goodness").</note></term> of reception is "the received," which is applicable to the second species of Rule D and the first species of Rule E: specifically, that which is constituted from several parts in the subject in which it exists.

This concrete form is full; and this is manifest through the second species of Rule D and through the first, etc. And it is especially so when it is at rest through the second species of Rule E. ¶ Emptiness, however, is its opposite. Its definition is applicable to its contrary terms. And let these things suffice regarding evacuation, based on what was said before.

### On the phantasm.

<margin>31. The form of the phantasm.</margin>
**P**hantasm, or a "species," is applicable to the definition of species and of the will along with the fourth species of the instrumental [rule]: because these do not act except by means of phantasms. Indeed, a <term>phantasm<note>original: "fantasma"; a mental image or "species" derived from sensory perception that allows the mind to think about an object when it is no longer present.</note></term> is applicable to the first species of Rule D and to the definition of principles, and it works like this: A human seeing a horse does not imagine it [at that moment]; but when they close their eyes, or the horse is absent, then they imagine it. The phantasm is drawn out from the potentiality of the subject into act, and received in the imagination where the intellect collects it. The intellect then places it in its <term>intelligible<note>original: "intelligibili"; the object or form that the intellect can understand.</note></term> so that it may have knowledge, and also places it in the memory where it is preserved. Thereafter, it acquires another phantasm; and the same applies to the will through the <term>concupiscible and irascible<note>The "concupiscible" appetite seeks what is perceived as good/pleasurable, while the "irascible" appetite resists what is perceived as difficult or harmful.</note></term> powers. ¶ In this step, the intellect understands the way in which knowledge or a "mode" is generated; and to this all the explained principles and rules concur. For a general phantasm is very difficult to grasp because of the smallness of the being in which it resides. ¶ The concrete form of the phantasm is the "phantasied thing," constituted from several likenesses. In brute animals, however, it does not pass beyond the imagination. For if it did pass beyond, brutes would already possess <term>science<note>original: "sciam" (scientiam); formal, systematic knowledge or the ability to reason from principles.</note></term>. Instead, it remains in the imagination so that they may have the skill to live; and this is manifest through Rule B.

### On fullness.

<margin>32. The form of fullness.</margin>
**F**ullness is an <term>implicit principle<note>original: "principium implicatum"; a foundational concept that contains other ideas within it, which must be "unfolded" through logical analysis.</note></term>; and its definition is applicable to the definition of goodness, greatness, etc. For the fullness of goodness is the reason why it produces good. And the fullness of greatness is the reason why goodness is full of it, and vice versa. And thus it is signified in the mixture of principles and rules. ¶ Furthermore, the correlatives of fullness are applicable to the correlatives of goodness, which are full of the correlatives of fullness. Under this, the concrete form is "the full"; and this is manifest through the second species of Rule D and through the first, etc. And especially when it is at rest through the second species of Rule E.

### On diffusion.

<margin>33. The form of diffusion.</margin>
**D**iffusion is an implicit principle: and its definition is applicable to the definition of goodness, difference, etc. For goodness is the reason producing good: and it is <term>diffusive<note>original: "diffusiva"; the idea that "goodness" naturally tends to spread or share itself.</note></term>; it dilates itself in the subject in which it exists, contracting itself toward greatness, duration, and difference by distinguishing diffusion with its correlatives as signified through the second species. ¶ The concrete form of diffusion is "the diffused": it is habituated by diffusion and situated within it, etc., as is manifest through the second species of Rule D and the first species of Rule E. The opposite of diffusion is restriction, which is applicable to the definition of concordance; with this, indeed, the greedy person causes avarice.

### On digestion.

<margin>34. The form of digestion.</margin>
**D**igestion is an implicit principle. And its definition is applicable to the definition of virtue and majority. For innate virtue digests "foreign" virtues into its own species along with its majority: just as in a plant in which the elements are digested into its own species; and so in an animal through drink and food. ¶ The correlatives of digestion are applicable to the correlatives of virtue and majority. Its concrete form is "the digested," habituated by digestion.

### On expulsion.

<margin>35. The form of expulsion.</margin>
**E**xpulsion is an implicit principle: it is applicable to the definition of contrariety. For one contrary expels another contrary in the subject in which it exists. And this is evident in animals through feces, urine, and scabs. And in plants, it is evident through flowers, leaves, and fruit, which do not have permanence in the plant; and so also morally regarding a king expelled from his kingdom, and a sinner from the grace of God, and regarding the end why, etc. ¶ Furthermore, the correlatives of expulsion are applicable to the correlatives of con...

Its <term>concrete form<note>original: "concretum"; in Llull’s logic, the "concrete" is the thing itself (e.g., "the good thing") while the "abstract" is the quality (e.g., "goodness").</note></term>, however, is "that which has been expelled," which is habituated by the act of expulsion.

## On signification.

<margin>The thirty-sixth form, on signification.</margin>
**S**ignification is an implicit principle: its definition is applicable to all explicit principles and <term>rules<note>original: "reglas"; referring to the specific logical rules (labeled B through K) in Ramon Llull's "Art," which categorize different types of questions and relationships.</note></term>. For just as goodness is the reason that produces a good thing: goodness joined to magnitude signifies that a "great good thing" produces a "great goodness." And the same is said of the others. ¶ Indeed, the <term>correlatives<note>original: "correlativa"; in Lullian thought, every action has three parts: the active (e.g., "signifying"), the passive (e.g., "the signified"), and the verb connecting them (e.g., "signification").</note></term> of signification are applicable to the correlatives of goodness, magnitude, and so on. Together with these correlatives of signification, goodness indeed signifies that which it is, and those things which it contains within itself: its concrete form, however, is the "signified," which is habituated by that goodness. Hiding, however, is the opposite of signification, and its definition, etc., is applicable to the terms opposite to signification itself.

## On beauty.

<margin>The thirty-seventh form, on beauty.</margin>
**B**eauty is an implicit principle: and its definition is applicable to the definitions of the explicit principles. For goodness and magnitude, etc., are beauties, with the exception of contrariety and minority: nevertheless, a "proportioned minority" in the subject in which it exists is beautiful, as is evident in a small child. Indeed, the correlatives of beauty consist [of parts] according to the second species of <term>Rule C<note>Rule C in Llull's system asks "Of what?" (De quo?) and deals with the composition and origin of things.</note></term>, just as a beautiful cause naturally produces a beautiful effect. And just as the intellect in the imagination causes a beautiful figure with love, by reason of the end designated by the second species of Rule C; and also through <term>Rule G<note>Rule G asks "How?" (Quomodo?) and deals with the manner of being.</note></term>, by which beauty consists, and especially through its own quality and through its appropriated quality. And just as through "majority" beauty consists more than through "minority": as is evident in rhetoric, in which the rhetorician "colors" his words more toward a greater end than toward a lesser one.

## On novelty.

<margin>The thirty-eighth form, on novelty.</margin>
**N**ovelty is the first form whose subject is informed by new <term>habits<note>original: "habitibus"; here meaning states of being or characteristics that a subject possesses.</note></term>: just as the heaven is informed by place, time, and motion: and the same can be said of all individual things composed of the elements. And this is signified through the first species of Rule D, because novelty necessarily had to be thus: just as the first motion, time, and place were. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that outside of time, place, and motion, no novelty can exist, because it is necessary that they exist simultaneously and at once. And to this, rules B, H, and I agree.

## On the idea.

<margin>The thirty-ninth form, on the idea.</margin>
**I**dea in eternity is God: but in novelty, it is the creature—just like the shape of the ark which was "new" in the meditation of the carpenter: but once brought from potentiality into act, it was "old" <note>or "ancient," meaning established in reality.</note>. And this is manifested clearly enough in the divine correlatives signified by the second species of Rule C. ¶ For the Divine Thinker, in His own infinite and eternal "intelligible," attracts all novelties stripped bare of any created subject: these novelties are the "Divine Ideas": but through the third species of the same rule, they are creatures—new, finite, and limited.

## On mathematics.

<margin>40. The fortieth form, on mathematics.</margin>
**M**athematics is the form with which the human intellect strips a substance of the accidents that exist within them, so that it may create "genus" and "species" with which it may acquire and create science. This mathematical form is itself modeled and stripped bare by means of the "Idea" stripped from all creatures, so that the Idea may be known through the mathematical form. And this is clear through the first species of Rule D, the second species of Rule E, and the fourth species of Rule K. Such a form is indeed the "genus" in all forms that are brought from potentiality into act, as is evident in the ninth subject.

## On being existing in potentiality.

<margin>41. The forty-first form, on being existing in potentiality.</margin>
**B**eing existing in potentiality is a form existing in the subject in which it is, without motion, surface, quantity, quality, and the like; as is seen in fire, in which a tree exists in potentiality. And when that form is brought from potentiality into act, its accidents follow along in such a transition without its generation. And when the aforementioned form has arisen with the aforementioned accidents, it is already "habituated" with them: which accidents arise or have arisen from the accidents existing in act in the subject in which the aforementioned form was in potentiality. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes how one substance arises from another substance, and accidents from other accidents naturally. And to this, Rule D agrees, along with the definition of goodness and power.

...the beginning and the middle. Similarly, the second species of rule E and rule G, and the fourth species of rule K, agree with this.

### On pointness.

<margin>43. The form of pointness.</margin>
**P**ointness is the essence of a <term>natural point<note>original: "punctus naturalis"; in Llull’s philosophy, a natural point is a physical atom or the most basic building block of matter, rather than just a mathematical location.</note></term>, which is the smallest part of a body. A point is so small and indivisible that it cannot be reached by the senses or the imagination. ¶ And in this passage, the <term>intellect<note>The "Intellect" is often personified in these texts as a traveler or a student trying to grasp higher truths.</note></term> wonders how it can have knowledge of a natural point, since it is imperceptible and unimaginable; but it helps itself by using a "moral point" presented to the sight and imagination. Through this representation, it ascends to the knowledge of the natural point, about which it forms a science. And to this, rule B and the first species of rule D agree. And the same can be said of rules F and I.

### On the line.

<margin>44. The form of the line.</margin>
**A** natural line is a length constituted of many continuous points, the ends of which are two points; it is the second part of a body. It is called "second" because it is constituted of many points, as is indicated in rule K and rule F. A point signifies a <term>discrete quantity<note>original: "quantitatem discretam"; a quantity made of distinct, separate parts (like individual beads), as opposed to a "continuous quantity" (like flowing water).</note></term>, but length signifies a continuous one. ¶ And in this, it is clear why points signify a discrete quantity. For a line is divisible by points, whereas width arises and is caused by many continuous lines; and consequently, a surface arises from length and width existing together in the subject in which they are. Depth, however, arises from the "roundness" of points. For a point is naturally more round than it is long or wide, as is clear in the leafy branches of a tree. ¶ Furthermore, the reason for this is that the circle, by reason of the <term>heavens<note>original: "celi"; referring to the celestial spheres which were believed to be perfectly circular and the source of all natural motion.</note></term> whose constitution is the strongest figure, is more powerful in the motion of nature than any other figure. ¶ And in this passage, the intellect recognizes what the primary principles of the body are: namely the point, the line, length, width, surface, and depth.

### On the triangle.

<margin>45. The form of the triangle.</margin>
**A** triangle is a form having three angles held by three lines; this is clear in "elemented" things <note>Things composed of the four physical elements.</note> in which every elemented thing has its own triangle. For instance, fire has one acute angle through "hot and dry," another through "hot and moist," and another through "dry and cold." Such a triangle is attributed to fire; for fire, through "hot and dry," reigns over the other triangles. Similarly, air has another triangle through "moist and hot." Further, water through "cold and moist," and again, earth another through "dry and cold." ¶ And in this passage, the intellect recognizes the essences of which an elemented body is full, by reason of which the elements relate to one another in a composite through difference, concordance, and contrariety. ¶ But the intellect wonders how it can have knowledge of such triangles, since they have never been perceived by the senses. But it remembers the triangle of a plane figure which is sensible, with which it imagines and recognizes the natural triangle, mediated however by rule K and the second species of rules D and C.

### On the quadrangle.

<margin>45. The form of the quadrangle.</margin>
**A** natural quadrangle is a figure having four right angles; and in every angle of a triangle, two right angles are implied, because they are of the genus of the triangle. For every element has two qualities: namely one proper and another appropriated, as is clear in rule G. In the quadrangle, fire has one angle as a king, and air similarly another, etc. And it is clear because a quadrangle is divisible into four equal triangles with diagonal lines. ¶ And in this passage, the intellect recognizes the manner by which a quadrangle is multiplied by four triangles, and a triangle by three lines, and a line by continuous points.

### On the circle.

<margin>46. The form of the circle.</margin>
**A** circle is the final figure, and it is called "final" because it is more perfect than any other figure. For it contains within itself all other figures; it is constituted by them and descends from them, as is clear through the second species of rule D and the fourth species of K. For a circle is caused by the triangle, the quadrangle, etc., until the angles and the line are joined circularly, point by point, in the likeness of the heavens, which is the greatest figure; and rule B agrees with this.

### On the body.

<margin>47. The form of the body.</margin>
**C**orpus is a substance full of points, lines, and angles, situated with length, width, and depth, and habituated by surface. The body itself has co-essential parts: namely points and lines.

Furthermore, through the second species of Rule D, a body is made of its own co-essential parts. Through Rule F, it possesses both continuous and discrete quantity, and through Rule G, it is a common aggregation composed of substance and accidents. Through Rule H, it exists in time; through Rule I, it exists in place; and through Rule K, it is in motion. ¶ But the **intellect** wonders about the <term>eighth sphere<note>original: "octaua sphera"; in medieval cosmology, this is the sphere of the fixed stars, which was believed to be the outermost limit of the physical world.</note></term>, why it is not contained in any external place. It remains in doubt until it considers that every body is finite and shaped by its figure; otherwise, one would have to grant the existence of an infinite body, which is impossible.

# On figure.

<margin>49. The form of figure.</margin>
**F**igure is an <term>accident<note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has, but which is not essential to its nature—like a chair being blue.</note></term> constituted from position and state. Through the second species of Rule C, these are its parts; through the third species of the same rule, it is the "state" in a body; and through the fourth species, it possesses straight and curved lines. Indeed, figure joined with color is the object of sight; however, when it consists of lines and angles without color, it is the object of touch. Combined with all the aforementioned qualities, it is the object of the imagination. In this step, the intellect recognizes that the imagination is a more general power than sight. Furthermore, figure is not an object of the intellect without the aid of the imagination. And in this passage, the intellect recognizes that when a human being dies, the soul retains the <term>species<note>original: "species"; here meaning the mental images or forms of things perceived during life.</note></term> it acquired through the imagination, so that it may have a memory of this life and the body in which it once dwelt.

# On general rectitudes.

<margin>42. The form of general rectitudes.</margin>
**R**ectitudes <note>In this context, "rectitudes" refers to the six fundamental directions or dimensions of physical space.</note> are six in number, by which a body acts as a center through diametrical lines so that the body can be in motion: namely, upward and downward, forward and backward, to the right and to the left. These six rectitudes are co-essential to motion. ¶ But the intellect wonders why there are six, and no more or fewer. It then remembers that motion cannot be perfect without these; if there were more or fewer, it would indeed be imperfect. This is evident through the third and fourth species of Rule C. Through the second species of the same rule, it is indicated that the six aforementioned rectitudes are co-essential parts of the motion in which a body is positioned and disposed. But the intellect wonders why a spherical body does not possess such rectitudes—such as a person's head, an eye, an apple, or the like. But it remembers that the World is a spherical body, and this World does not rely on other rectitudes because it is the ultimate body which causes its likenesses in the aforementioned spherical bodies, so that the intellect may have knowledge of it; and Rules B and K agree with this.

# On monstrosity.

<margin>50. The form of monstrosity.</margin>
**M**onstrosity is a deviation of the motion of nature from its starting point to its intended end within a subject. This is caused by an excessive influence or a deficiency in the power of the bodies above <note>the stars and planets</note>, or the influences from the right, left, forward, or backward. Such motions cause <term>privative habits<note>A "privative habit" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like darkness being the absence of light.</note></term>, namely blindness, deafness, and the like. The reason for this is that it falls outside the second species of Rule C. In the third species, the motion itself is imperfect, and in the fourth species, it possesses those imperfections because the second species of Rule C is lacking.

# On derivation.

<margin>51. The form of derivation.</margin>
**D**erivation is the general subject through which a particular descends from a universal, just as a stream descends from a spring, a line from points, a triangle from lines, or a son from his parents through general instruments. It is also like a conclusion from its premises, and consequently an effect from its antecedent, or science from objects—mediated, however, by the intellect. ¶ And the intellect, considering derivation in this way, recognizes through the second species of Rule C that derivation contains within itself essential correlatives from which many particulars are derived: just as many sons come from the same parents, many elements from the four general elements, and many sciences are discovered by a single intellect. Indeed, the intellect contains within itself essential and general relatives with which it inquires and creates many sciences derived from the same form or species. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that its own relatives are higher, while the sciences are lower, and the species are in the middle, as if between a cause and an effect. In this step, it understands from what source and in what manner the sciences are derived.

# On shadow.

<margin>52. The form of shadow.</margin>
**V**mbra <note>Shadow</note> is a privative habit of light which cannot possess the rectitudes we spoke of above, because a body existing in the middle blocks the light. We have manifest experience of this through the shadow of a tree or a tower. But here the intellect asks...

[obje]ct/shadow of which there is color: and what is the meaning of shadow? And the **intellect** considers that air is <term>diaphanous<note>original: "dyafanus"; a term used in medieval science to describe materials that allow light to pass through, like air or glass.</note></term> because outside of a shadow it receives the color of the sun and fire, but with brightness. However, in the place where there is a shadow, the air receives the color of the earth—just as a **crystal**, when placed on a yellow base, takes on a yellowish quality, and when placed on a black base, takes on blackness. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that light is the color of the sun and fire; blackness is the color of the earth and the [interruption of] transparency of the air; and whiteness belongs to water, which causes whiteness. For crystal is nothing other than frozen water. ¶ Moreover, the **figure** of a shadow is the boundary where light and shadow end; the definition of a "medium" and the rules of measurement agree with this. ¶ But the intellect asks: what is the cause of the moon's shadow? It remains in doubt until it considers that the moon is a diaphanous body in which the shadow of the earth appears. Yet it wonders why this does not appear in the sun, which is also a diaphanous body. It remains in doubt until it remembers that the sun is colored by its own inherent light. The light of the moon, however, comes from the sun in the same way that the heat of the air comes from the heat of fire; the logical rules prove this.

# On the mirror.

<margin>Book 4. The form of the mirror.</margin>
A **mirror** is a diaphanous body disposed to receive all figures presented to it. But the intellect wonders: since glass is a diaphanous body, why does it not receive figures in the same way as a mirror, which is also made of glass? It remembers the chapter on shadows, which explains this doubt. For glass without **lead** is a diaphanous body that receives transparency on both sides, passing through the six straight lines we have already discussed. But it is not so in a mirror; for the lead resists some of those straight lines by reason of the thickness of its matter and its great compaction—for the parts of lead are very tightly packed together. Therefore, just as a tree causes a shadow because it stands in the midst of light, so the glass—existing between the lead, the air, and the colorless figure presented to it—generates within itself a shadow similar to the figure presented to it through similar qualities and colors. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the principles of the mirror's shadow.

# On color and the colored.

<margin>Book 4. The form of color and the colored.</margin>
**Color** is a quality that exists as the object of sight. In a "colored" thing, the figure of that thing is the container of the color. ¶ The **colored** thing is the substance in which the color is sustained. ¶ Color indeed has essential relationships; color is the state of these relationships. Through the rules of logic, color belongs to itself and to the colored thing. ¶ According to the rules, color is a "proper" quality in a real human or a real plant; but it is "appropriated" (or assigned) in a painted human or a painted plant, and so on. ¶ The <term>Unity<note>original: "Unitas"; abbreviated in the text as Utas. This refers to the philosophical concept of a thing being "one" or a single entity.</note></term> of color is not its own property, but is rather assigned to it; however, it truly belongs to the colored object. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the way one <term>accident<note>A property that is not essential to a thing's nature, such as its color or temperature.</note></term> is situated within another; just as this is said of color and the colored, so it can be said of heat and the hot.

# On proportion and the proportioned.

<margin>Book 5. The form of proportion and the proportioned.</margin>
**Substantial proportion** consists of parts of the same substance; this is evident in the concept of **infinity**, to which its own internal parts are proportioned, and without which infinity could not exist or act. Indeed, a finite thing is not proportioned to the infinite, except through the medium of infinity itself which proportions it. The same can be said of the **Eternalizer**, the **eternal**, and the **act of eternalizing** <note>These are Lullian terms for God, the creation, and the divine action.</note>, and so with other divine reasons. Similarly, one can speak of the essential relationships in created substances, such as in the **intellect**, in which the **one who understands**, the **thing understood**, and the **act of understanding** are relationships naturally proportioned to it. However, **knowledge** cannot be fully proportioned to the intellect; it can never satisfy it, just as wood cannot satisfy fire. For fire can burn more wood than the wood can provide to the fire. Nevertheless, **accidental proportion** can certainly exist between relationships, such as between that which is heated and the act of heating. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that no "accident" can be proportioned to a "substance" in terms of weight or magnitude. For substance is "more" and accident is "less"; this is clear through the definitions of majority and minority. However, according to the principle of **justice**, a proportion can be established between a substance and an accident, or between one accident and another. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the way the members of the soul...

## On disposition and the disposed.

<margin>that is, the form of disposition and the disposed.</margin>
**D**isposition in its substance is a form in which substantial <term>correlatives<note>In Llull’s philosophy, "correlatives" are the triads that make up a concept: the active agent, the passive recipient, and the action itself (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and loving).</note></term> are equally arranged through object, power, and act. This is seen in the infinite and eternal divine goodness, which is the arranged reason of the infinite and eternal good, so that it may produce an infinite and eternal good; this [product] is "disposed" toward the "bonifier" <note>original: "bonificanti"; a Lullian term for the active principle of goodness.</note>. And thus, "to bonify" can be said to be its "disposed state" through infinite and eternal goodness. 

However, there is another kind of disposition that happens by chance <note>original: "per accidens"; referring to external or non-essential circumstances.</note>, which is clear through the third species of Rule C <note>Rule C is one of Llull's logical tools used to investigate "Why" things exist.</note>. For example, God disposes himself to judge and proceed according to how a man disposes himself to receive judgment or mercy. I do not say this in terms of weight [of power], but in terms of justice. For God disposes himself more toward man by reason of His own goodness than man does toward Him—just as fire is more disposed to burn wood than the wood is disposed to satisfy the fire's burning. 

The same can be said of the human intellect. Indeed, the intellect is more disposed to understand an accidental object than the object is to be understood by it. For example, the "understandability" of a stone is not equal to the intellect; the intellect can understand higher things, such as a sensing being, or the heavens, or an angel, etc., which are higher forms of understandability than that of a stone. The same can be said of man: for a man can run more than he actually runs, since he does not always wish to run as much as he is able. The same can be said of other things in their own way.

## On creation and the created.

<margin>57. The form of creation and the created.</margin>
**C**reation exists in eternity as an <term>Idea<note>A divine archetype or blueprint existing in the mind of God before the world was made.</note></term> according to the second species of Rule C. Therefore, from eternity and in eternity, it is known through divine wisdom and loved through divine will. But in a created being, it is a <term>habit<note>A "habit" (habitus) here refers to a stable quality or condition of the soul.</note></term> and an action regarding the third and fourth species of the same rule. The creation that is an "Idea" possesses the "creation" that is a creature; with this, it has a "newly created thing," which is acted upon under that very action and conditioned under the new creation. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which the Idea passes into the "ideated" thing <note>The physical manifestation of the divine blueprint.</note>, multiplying its likeness according to the fourth species of Rule K <note>Rule K is a logical tool used to investigate "How" or "By what means" something happens.</note>.

## On predestination and the predestined.

<margin>58. The form of predestination and the predestined.</margin>
**P**redestination exists in the wisdom of God in eternity as an Idea; thus it is from eternity as it is in eternity. This is by reason of the correlatives of the second species of Rule C. For one who understands the eternal in his own proper eternal "understandable" understands all things: both past things and new things. Future and new things are from the "before" part <note>original: "a parte ante"; referring to eternity before time.</note>, that is, from eternity; but past and ancient things are from the "after" part, that is, in eternity. 

Therefore, a predestined person existing between these two aforementioned terms by chance is "clothed" in a new predestination—just as a man wearing a cloak is "clothed" in a new cloak. And so, predestination is one thing through the second species of Rule C, but another through the third species. For in respect to the second species, it is an Idea; but in respect to the third, it is a created "habit." A predestined person freely disposes himself toward this habit to do good, like a man who puts on a new cloak, or a judge who disposes himself to judge through the habit of justice. Otherwise, the predestination that is an Idea would not have a way of creating a "new" predestination viewed from eternity and in eternity—which is false, as is clear from Rule K. ¶ And in this step, the intellect rejoices because it has a great clarification regarding predestination; but it grieves because such a clarification is little known in the world. Indeed, the clouding of predestination leads many men into error and doubt.

## On mercy and the mercified.

<margin>59. The form of mercy and the mercified.</margin>
**M**ercy exists in eternity as an Idea according to the respect of Rule C. Regarding the third species, it is a "habit" existing in a newly predestined person who disposes himself to contrition, confession, and satisfaction for things committed, so that he may be clothed in mercy—just as the predestined is clothed in predestination through good works loved with his own free will. Otherwise, unless a sinner disposed himself to receive pardon, he could not be clothed in mercy; just as a man doing evil cannot have the habit of goodness. ¶ And in this step, let sinners rejoice as they act...

# On necessity and the necessitated.

<margin>60. The form of necessity and the necessitated.</margin>
**N**ecessity is a form that cannot be otherwise; this is evident through the second species of Rule C <note>Rule C in Llull’s Art asks "Why?"—the second species often deals with formal causes or the internal logic of a definition.</note>. And because nothing can exist without necessity, it follows that necessity is the antecedent and "the necessitated" <note>original: "necessitatus"; the object or state resulting from necessity.</note> is the consequence. An example of this is the divine goodness, which is infinite and eternal: it is the infinite reason for the good and the eternal, whereby it produces an eternal and infinite good. Therefore, the producer is "necessitated" by reason of goodness, and consequently, the product and the act of producing are necessitated. This is clear in the second species of Rule C. 

Furthermore, another kind of necessity and necessitated state follows: namely, if a man is good, he is necessitated toward the good. But if he is evil, he is necessitated toward evil. For the justice of God necessitates judgment in its judging just as the mercy of God necessitates pardon in its sparing. In this step, the intellect understands that when a sinner disposes himself to receive judgment by judging himself, he disposes himself to penance in order to receive pardon. Furthermore, the intellect understands the way in which the mercy and justice of God necessitate their own acts in a "new subject" <note>In Lullian logic, the "new subject" often refers to the specific instance or individual being discussed in a new context.</note>; the intellect is greatly rejoiced by the knowledge of this.

# On fortune and the fortunate.

<margin>61. The form of fortune and the fortunate.</margin>
**F**ortune is an act that falls outside the second species of Rule C alone. It is the habit through which a fortunate person disposes himself toward that good fortune or accident. For example, a traveler going on a pilgrimage who finds gold by chance: that very fortune exists through the second species of Rule D <note>Rule D usually asks "How much?" or "Of what kind?"</note>, and its existence in the subject in which it resides is through the fourth species of Rule C. It is that which exists through the third species of Rule D. It exists outside of "beginning, middle, and end," and outside of "concordance and contrariety" <note>These are Llull's "Principles"—the basic building blocks of his logic.</note>; however, it is not outside of "majority and minority." In this step, the intellect recognizes that fortune has very little "being" in itself, but in relation to the fortunate person, it has great being.

# On order and the ordered.

<margin>62. The form of order and the ordered.</margin>
**O**rder is the gathering of many principles so that one principle can coincide with another toward a single end. "The ordered" <note>original: "ordinatum"</note> is its concrete manifestation, and it is habituated by its own ordering. Order is first initiated through the second species of Rule C, so that it may be a habit in the subject in which it resides; it finds its rest through the fourth species of Rule C. Indeed, order has its own primitive principles, as is clear through the first species of Rule D and through the definition of a "principle." It is a consequence of the definition of "concordance," whose enemy is "contrariety," which fails in the manner designated by Rule K <note>Rule K is often used to identify the "middle" or the neutralization of opposites.</note>.

# On counsel and the consulted.

<margin>63. The form of counsel and the consulted.</margin>
**C**ounsel is a proposition that is in doubt, and "the consulted" <note>the result of the deliberation</note> is its end and point of rest. A counselor ought to look at that doubtful proposition through the second species of Rule C, running through Rule B <note>Rule B asks "What?" and deals with definitions.</note> and testing the way in which the "consulted" is shaped by the definitions of the principles. This is done through the "new subject" in the third species of Rule C, so that he may be habituated in the virtues in the fourth species of Rule C—a habit which should be removed from the vices of the "new subject" by means of Rules D, E, F, G, H, I, and K <note>Llull uses the letters of the alphabet to represent his different logical tools and divine attributes.</note>.

# On grace and the graced.

<margin>64. The form of grace and the graced.</margin>
**G**race is a primitive form, placed in "the graced" without the merit of the one receiving it. This is clear through the first species of Rule D, through the "majority" <note>superiority</note> of the one giving the grace, the "minority" <note>humility/lowliness</note> of the one receiving it, and also through the habit of charity. Furthermore, grace exists in the graced person through the definition of goodness and through the magnificence of a will that is habituated in liberality. Because of this, the intellect understands in this step how grace is diffusive within the subject in which it resides. When it is produced, it is not hindered by "superior principles" <note>divine or higher causes</note> but by "inferior ones"—specifically, when a person considers themselves worthy of receiving grace by reason of their own merit, rather than by reason of the generosity and kindness of the giver of grace.

# On perfection and the perfected.

<margin>65. The form of perfection and the perfected.</margin>
**P**erfection is a form at rest within a perfected subject, through which the perfected subject finds peace by habituating itself to that which is already habituated in the perfect subject, as is clear through the third species of Rule C. This kind of perfection is derived from the second species of Rule C through many streams—namely, through many principles and rules of this Art. Such perfection is primarily moral, as...
