...appears in the ninth subject. However, there is a natural perfection that is essentially and naturally most perfect, infinitely and eternally. Indeed, it is most perfect through its own and consubstantial <note>Consubstantial: sharing the same fundamental essence or substance.</note> relatives <note>In Llull's system, "relatives" (relativa) are the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle, such as the Greatener, the Greatened, and the act of Greatening.</note> designated by the second species of Rule C <note>Rule C usually asks "Why?" The "second species" of this rule typically investigates the formal cause or the internal essential reasons for a thing's existence.</note>. The "perfecter," by its consubstantial and natural perfection, produces the "perfected": and not from any other being. This perfected thing is coessential to the perfecter, and both together—namely, the perfecter and the perfected—fulfill the act of "perfecting," which is essential and substantial.

## On declaration and the declared.

<margin>The sixty-sixth form: on declaration and the declared.</margin>

**D**eclaration is a form in which the intellect, by making distinctions, exists by means of a definition of concordance that is entirely separated from a definition of contrariety. The "declared" is the subject in which declaration exists as a disposition <note>original: "habitus"; in scholastic philosophy, a stable quality or state of being.</note>, as is evident through the third species of Rule C. Its essence, however, consists in the second species of Rule C, in which the "understander" <note>original: "intelligens"; the active power of the mind.</note> declares that the "understood" <note>original: "intellectum"; the object being thought about.</note> is passive to itself, and this occurs through the act of understanding. In this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which a disposition arises from a substance as an accident <note>Accident: a quality that does not belong to the essence of a thing (like the color of a shirt) as opposed to its substance.</note>, so that declaration can be produced from knowledge—provided it is done through the principles and rules of this Art.

## On transubstantiation and the transubstantiated.

<margin>The sixty-seventh form: on transubstantiation and the transubstantiated.</margin>

**T**ransubstantiation is an act of nature in the "transubstantiated" thing when it is stripped of an old form. It puts on a new form so that its act can exist in liberty. For without such transubstantiation, nature would indeed be bound regarding its substantial act, and even regarding the act of its accidents; its state of deprivation would be immutable, and consequently, the definitions of its principles would be destroyed—which is impossible. The practitioner of this Art can have knowledge of this in a broad sense in the seventh subject, in which the vegetative power <note>The "vegetative" level of the soul or nature deals with growth, nutrition, and basic biological transformation.</note> is led through the principles and rules of this Art.

## On alteration and the altered.

<margin>The sixty-eighth form: on alteration and the altered.</margin>

**A**lteration is a form born in the "altered" thing, as is evident through the third species of Rule C. Such alteration arises from the alteration existing in the second species of Rule C, just as a stream flows from a spring. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the paths of natural and moral motion. In generation, it recognizes the natural path of motion itself; for in generation, form and matter are altered. For the "alterer," in its own "alterable" subject, alters the things that come to it, so that motion occurs in the process of becoming and in the completed state, by means of the definition of the "medium" <note>The "middle" or "medium" in Llull's Art often refers to the connecting link or process between a beginning and an end.</note>. Moral alteration, however, is when a person changes themselves from one disposition to another—such as from justice to injury, from anger to patience, from logic to medicine, from sadness to joy, and the like.

## On infinity and the infinite.

<margin>The sixty-ninth form: on infinity and the infinite.</margin>

**I**nfinity is a form having an actual infinite, removed from everything finite, which can in no way exist without an "infinited" <note>original: "infinitato"; that which is made infinite or the object of the infinite act.</note> subject. The reason for this is that its rest cannot exist in a finite subject. Infinity itself has its own correlates <note>Correlates: the triad of the active agent, the passive recipient, and the verb/action connecting them.</note> through the second species of Rule C, which it cannot have without infinite goodness, magnitude, eternity, and so on. For otherwise, it would imply a contradiction: namely, that it was both infinite and not infinite, and that it was both hindered and unhindered—which is impossible. Infinity itself is the cause of finitude or the finite, as is evident through the third species of Rule C, since infinity has an action in the "infinite" and in the finite being. Through the fourth species of Rule C, the finite is disposed toward "passion" <note>Passion: in this context, the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note> just as it is disposed toward "newness." For otherwise, it would have one infinite disposition and another finite one, which is impossible. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that just as finitude has coessential correlates—namely the "finisher," the "finished," and "to finish"—so, and much more excellently, does infinity have the "infinisher," the "infinited," and "to infinish" <note>original: "infiniente / infinitum & infinire"; Llull creates these terms to show that infinity is an active, dynamic process within God.</note>. Otherwise, the nature of finitude would possess more than the nature of infinity, which is impossible.

## On deception and the deceived.

<margin>The seventieth form: on deception and the deceived.</margin>

**D**eception is a positive disposition of the "deceiver" and a privative disposition <note>Privative disposition: a state defined by the absence of something that should be there (like blindness being the absence of sight).</note> of the "deceived." Therefore, through the second species of Rule C, the "understander" causes it in its own object of understanding by receiving it from the deceived. It provides a disposition to the object of understanding, and through the third species of Rule C, the deceiver is in the deceived, in whom it causes deception. The deceived person, however, does not deceive through their own second species of Rule C; rather, they are deceived in the third, and in the fourth they hold the disposition of deception, by which they deviate from the end <note>End: the "telos" or ultimate purpose of a person's existence.</note> for which they exist. And in this step, the intellect recognizes where sin arises and where it remains.

## On honor and the honored.

<margin>The 71st form: on honor and the honored.</margin>
**H**onor is an active disposition <note>original: "habitus"; in scholastic philosophy, a stable quality or state of being that allows one to act easily.</note> in the one who honors, but a passive one in the one who is honored. Therefore, the one honoring is more involved than the honored, because in the second species of Rule C <note>Rule C typically asks "Why?" The "second species" investigates formal or internal causes.</note> it causes the disposition of honor; in the third species it is the "honorer"; and in the fourth it possesses the disposition of honor. Meanwhile, the honored person receives it, and in the third species receives it, and in the fourth species of the same rule possesses the disposition of honor. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes in what way the same disposition is situated across many active subjects. ¶ Furthermore, it recognizes how the one who reproaches is more affected by the disposition of reproach than the one who is reproached. The intellect greatly rejoices in such knowledge discovered through this Art.

## On capacity and incapacity.

<margin>The 72nd form: on capacity and incapacity.</margin>
**C**apacity is the form by which a capable thing can contain and regard as much as can happen to it. Incapacity, however, is the opposite. ¶ Capacity indeed consists of the second species of Rule C, through which there is a positive disposition existing in the third and fourth species of the same rule. This is accompanied by the definitions of the principles <note>Llull's nine "Principles": Goodness, Greatness, Duration, Power, Wisdom, Will, Virtue, Truth, and Glory.</note> and the species of the rules. ¶ Incapacity, however, is not caused in the second species; for it is a privative <note>A "privative habit" is defined by the absence of a quality that should be present, like blindness is the privation of sight.</note> disposition and is removed from every benefit of the principles and rules. Nevertheless, incapacity is close to the definitions of contrariety and minority. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes what is the cause of a dull intellect, and of a crude or impious will.

## On existence and agency.

<margin>The 73rd form: on existence and agency.</margin>
**E**xistence is the form with which an existing thing exists as that which it is; and agency is the form moving the existing thing toward its proper end. This is evident through the second species of Rule C, Rule E <note>Rule E asks "How?" (Quomodo), dealing with the manner in which a thing exists or acts.</note>, and through the definitions of Goodness, Power, and the Medium <note>The "Medium" or "Middle" is one of Llull's "Principles of Relation," used to find the middle ground between extremes.</note>. And if the definitions are added, it follows more by necessity that existence is as great as agency. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that God is an "agent" <note>An "agent" here means an active doer or cause.</note> through the second species of Rule C, just as much as He exists through the first species of Rule E. Knowledge of these—namely existence and agency—can be held in the "First Subject" <note>Referring to the first subject of the Art, which is God.</note> in the chapter in which God is defined.

## On comprehension and apprehension.

<margin>The 74th form: on comprehension and apprehension.</margin>
**C**omprehension is the likeness of infinity; therefore, an agent comprehends with comprehension, and also apprehends with apprehension. But it comprehends by reason of the grace of infinity. Here the intellect wonders what the cause is why an agent with comprehension directs its object toward apprehension; but it remembers a man tasting a drop of wine, comprehending its quantity in his throat, and through that, apprehending the quantity of wine in the barrel. Just so, the intellect apprehends the essence of a sensed thing through the senses, but it does not "comprehend" <note>In this context, "apprehend" means to grasp or perceive partially, while "comprehend" means to fully encompass or understand something in its entirety.</note> the essence of the sensed thing when it is stripped of the senses. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes in what way it is both "comprehending" and "apprehending" through the discourse of the species of Rule E. Through the first species of Rule C it comprehends by defining, and through the second it apprehends; for it cannot comprehend itself, insofar as it is the "apprehender," yet by the first species of Rule C, it is the "comprehender." ¶ Furthermore, in the third species of Rule C it is the "comprehender," but in the fourth species of the same rule, it is disposed by both comprehension and apprehension. ¶ And in this step, the intellect is very high and subtle.

## On invention and the invented.

<margin>The 75th form: on invention and the invented.</margin>
**I**nvention <note>original: "inventio"; meaning discovery or the act of finding.</note> is the form through which the intellect finds the thing found. This is signified through the second species of Rule C: because the "finder," within its own proper discovery, finds "foreign" discoveries. Just as the intellect, within its own proper "intelligible" <note>The "intelligible" is that which can be understood by the mind, as opposed to the "sensible" which is perceived by the senses.</note>, makes the incoming species <note>The mental images or forms of external objects.</note> intelligible; and in the third species, the discovered thing is the cause in the act of finding; in the fourth species, however, the "found" is its own disposition. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes in what way it creates science <note>original: "scientia"; meaning organized knowledge or certain understanding.</note>, and what its subject is—namely this Art—because with the principles and rules, it finds the thing to be found.

## On likeness and the assimilated.

<margin>The 76th form: on likeness and the assimilated.</margin>
**L**ikeness is the form by which the "likener" makes its "assimilated" <note>The "assimilated" is the thing that is made to be like something else.</note> thing like itself. This likeness arises through the principles, such as Goodness, because every reason is good; and another likeness arises through the second species of Rule C, such as a likener who makes an assimilated thing like himself—namely, as a human father makes his son like himself...

# On the antecedent and the consequent.

<margin>The 77th form: on the antecedent and the consequent.</margin>
**T**he antecedent is the form causing the consequent. The consequent, however, is the subject with which the antecedent rests: the antecedent indeed consists through the principles and rules of this Art, and the consequent indeed arises from them. For if an agent acts with goodness and greatness, it follows that his act is good and great: and by consequence that it is <term>possificated</term> <note>original: "possificatus"; a term coined by Llull meaning "made possible" or "empowered with the potential to exist."</note>. And if goodness is great through greatness, it follows from this that greatness is good through goodness. ¶ Furthermore, if greatness is infinite duration through eternity, it follows that eternity is infinite immensity through greatness: and if power is infinite duration through eternity, it follows that eternity is infinite "possification" <note>the act of making something possible.</note> through power: and so of the others. ¶ Further, through the second species of Rule C <note>Rule C in Llull’s system typically asks "Of what?" or "What?" and investigates the internal components of a subject. The "second species" focuses on the formal causes.</note>, it is the antecedent to the third species of C, and it is the antecedent to the fourth species of Rule C, just as goodness with its "bonificative," "bonificable," and "to bonify" <note>original: "bonificatiuo/ bonificabili & bonificare"; these are Llull’s active, passive, and verbal forms of goodness.</note> is a disposition achieved in man. And if man is habituated in goodness, it follows that he has merit through his goodness. And so it is of other antecedents and consequents: just as if he is a man, it follows that he is an animal; and if two premises are present, it follows that the conclusion is in nature.

# On potency, object, and act.

<margin>The 78th form: on potency, object, and act.</margin>
**P**otency is the form with which the intellect reaches the object. The object, however, is the subject in which the intellect rests: but the act is the connection of potency and object. And all three consist through the second species of Rule C, just as in the correlatives of goodness in which the "bonificative" is the potency or form, and the active act is the "bonificative": and the object is the passive; while "to bonify" is the act emerging from both. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that those who say the object moves the potency assert what is false; and those who say the potency moves itself to the object with the object itself in the third species of C assert what is true. Potency is active and the object is in the same step: but in the fourth species, the potency has the action, and in the same species the object has the "passion" <note>In scholastic philosophy, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note>. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that that which moves naturally does not desire to be immobile, nor vice versa. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes who is capable of receiving the great clarification of philosophy.

# On generation and corruption.

<margin>The 79th form: on generation and corruption.</margin>
**G**eneration in created things is the form with which an agent causes new forms. But corruption is the form with which it deprives [removes] old forms. And <term>privation</term> <note>The absence or removal of a quality that should normally be present.</note> is the form existing in the middle of them. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the way in which these three forms consist in the subject in which they are: and the "generative" and "privative" are one form: and it is the same potency that generates new forms positively and corrupts old forms "privatively" with one and the same act constituted of generating and corrupting; yet the "generable" and the "corruptible" are not the same as it. For they have different ends from one another. For the "generable" concerns being, while the "corruptible" concerns non-being: although they are from one and the same agent and in the same subject: just as fire which is the agent, and from one and the same heat, has different acts: as appears in drying the rule <note>The Latin "regulam" here may be a transcription error for a material like "tegulun" (tile) or "regulam" (a straight piece of wood/metal); fire dries, dissolves, or softens depending on the object.</note>, and in dissolving, and in softening wax. Generation in the third species of Rule C is active. ¶ Corruption, however, in the same species is passive with the same natural motion. The reason for which is: that through the fourth species, the subject has action through generation and "passion" through corruption, in the subject habituated by both the privative and positive disposition. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes in what way generation, corruption, and privation are natural principles in <term>elemental compounds</term> <note>original: "elementatis"; things made of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note>. ¶ We have spoken of the 80 forms which are the explicit principles of this Art, to which the implicit principles can be applied: just as whatever is said of generation, corruption, and privation may be applied to the chapter on generation, corruption, and privation in such a way that those things said in the chapter itself are not harmed, for they are known through themselves. Now, however, we intend to apply this General Art to particular arts, so that it may be declared in what way this Art is general to all other arts, and so that those knowing this Art may more easily be able to learn and possess other arts: and first we shall speak of theology.

<header>On Application.</header>

<margin>The 80th form: Theology.</margin>

# On Application.

**T**heology is the science in which one speaks of God. And therefore, the first subject, designated by the letter **b** <note>In Llull’s "General Art," the letter **B** typically represents the principle of Goodness or the first subject, God.</note>, is the place in which one speaks of God <term>artistically</term> <note>original: "artificialiter"; in Llull’s context, this means "according to the rules of the Art," a systematic logical method, rather than "fake."</note>: because it proceeds through principles and rules. Therefore, those wishing to speak of God naturally or systematically should recur to the aforementioned subject and speak of God according to those things found within it. If, however, they wish to multiply the words that are within it, let them apply those words to the explained terms in the aforementioned subject in such a way that the explained terms remain intact, saying thus: *Whether it is possible for God not to exist.* And let him recur to those things said of God through **b. c.** etc. <note>These letters refer to the principles of the Art, such as Goodness (B) and Greatness (C).</note> And if he asks why God cannot "not exist," let him recur to the rule in which it is asked *why God is*. And if it is asked *whether God could be evil* or *whether there are multiple gods*, let him recur to the place in which it is said that goodness is the reason that produces an infinite and eternal good, and also to that place in which God is defined. ¶ Likewise, if it is asked which law is true—whether the law of Christians, or of Jews, or of <term>Saracens</term> <note>A medieval term for Muslims.</note>—let him recur to the subject in which one speaks of God and see in what way the law is implied within it. And if he wishes to preach about God, let him extract the material for his sermon from that subject, for to do otherwise is a great and very wide path to perdition; and so it is with other matters. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes in what way the first subject is a very great object for it, in which it takes much joy.

## On Philosophy.

<margin>The 81st form: On Philosophy.</margin>

**P**hilosophy is the subject in which the intellect contracts itself to all arts and sciences. Therefore, the philosopher can have a great subject of understanding through this Art. For he can philosophize through the subjects of <term>substance</term> designated by **c. d. e. f. g. h. i.** <note>These letters correspond to the "Nine Subjects" of the Art: God, Angel, Heaven, Man, Imaginative, Sensitive, Vegetative, Elementative, and Instrumentative.</note> and also through the <term>hundred forms</term> <note>Referring to Llull's "The Hundred Forms," a list of fundamental concepts used to categorize all knowledge.</note>. For the philosopher treats naturally of angels, of the heavens, of man, of the imaginative, sensitive, vegetative, and elemental powers. But he treats of miracles not at all, for they are above nature. Wherefore, if anyone asks a philosophical question, let him recur to the aforementioned subjects, applying the subject of his inquiry to them. Let him respond in such a way that the thing he seeks remains unharmed while holding to either an affirmative or negative question; for those things treated in the aforementioned subjects are clear and manifest to an intellect that understands subtly. If, however, the subject of inquiry is implicit or foreign, let it be applied to the aforementioned explained subjects, and let the inquiry be answered through them. This should be done in such a way that the explained and implied words agree reasonably in the proposed conclusion. In this step, the intellect knows that this Art is a marvelous and very general subject for the intellect of the philosopher.

## On Geometry.

<margin>The 82nd form: On Geometry.</margin>

**G**eometry is the art invented for measuring lines, angles, and figures. And because in this art one treats of <term>quantity</term> (designated by the letter **f**), and the process through **b. c. d. e. f. g. i.** and **r.** <note>Letters in the Lullian system representing principles like Goodness, Greatness, Power, etc.</note> is conducted by means of measurement (which is designated by **f** itself), therefore quantity itself is the subject of geometry. Just as superior measures cause inferior ones—for Goodness is one measure according to its own reason, and Greatness is another, and so on—this is signified by the scales of the <term>Second Figure</term> <note>One of the primary diagrams of the Art, used to show the relationships between different principles.</note> and by the species of rules. Therefore, Goodness, insofar as it is a measure, measures that which is good and great, so that the good and great agent may produce a good and great result. And this is signified in the place where we spoke of the point, line, triangle, quadrangle, circle, and figure. ¶ Furthermore, measures begin through the <term>correlatives</term> of the second species of Rule C <note>Rule C in Llull's system usually asks "What?" and its correlatives involve the agent, the patient, and the act.</note> and are derived into the third, in which are the "habituated" <term>measurer, the measured, and the act of measuring</term>. In the fourth species, however, the act of measuring has the condition of being figured, just as a colored thing possesses color. And this we shall signify through these two following figures.

## I suppose that this quadrangle is worth 
three <term>palms</term> <note>original: "palmos"; a traditional unit of length based on the width of the hand.</note>: and let it be divided into two equal parts by a diagonal line: and let one part be divided into two. And let the larger part be called **a.** with **b.** and the third **c.** Now it is asked: how does the intellect begin to find geometry? To which it must be answered: through the definition of the principle and through the rule of **f. h. i.** and **k.** and also through the subjects marked by **e. f. g.** <note>These letters refer to specific principles in Llull's "General Art," such as Wisdom (F), Virtue (H), Truth (I), and Glory (K).</note> For the intellect, through sight, reaches nine angles in this figure. **A** would have three; **b.** three; and **c.** three. 

But the intellect, together with the imagination, reaches twelve angles. For if **a.** is worth as much as **b.** and **c.** together, it has as many angles through the intellect with the imagination as **b.** and **c.** have through the senses. But **b.** and **c.** have six; therefore **a.** has six: three of which are in <term>act</term> <note>original: "actu"; meaning actually visible or present in reality.</note> according to sight; the other three, however, are in <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "potētia"; meaning they exist as a logical possibility or internal structure not immediately visible.</note> which the intellect, with the imagination, reaches outside of the senses. Because they were never in the senses, geometry creates knowledge from that quantity existing in potentiality; once that quantity is brought into the senses through similarity and through experience, such knowledge remains in the intellect and in the imagination outside of the senses. For this knowledge, the second species of rule **c.** is its subject, and the third and fourth are the experiences of said science.

¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the method by which geometry creates knowledge: namely, it measures the quantity which is in the senses with the quantity that is in its own potentiality. 

¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that this proposition is false: *nothing is in the intellect unless it was first in the senses.* <note>original: "nihil est in intellectu quin prius fuerit in sensu"; a fundamental tenet of Aristotelian philosophy which Llull argues against here.</note> For the line which is in the intellect was never in the senses; just as the three angles in potentiality which are in **a.** were never in the senses. 

¶ Furthermore, since the intellect cannot measure a circular line with a compass, how can it know how many palms a circular line would have if it were straightened out? Then the intellect ascends to higher measurements which are outside of the senses, of which we have already spoken. And after this manner, it descends to the measurements which are in the senses: and through the definition of the "middle," and through rule **f.**—namely, through <term>flow and ebb</term> <note>original: "fluxū et refluxum"; a logical metaphor for the movement of thought or process.</note>—and through discrete and continuous quantity, it measures the circular [line] outside of the senses, considering how many palms it can have. And first, it makes this figure in which there are three quadrangles and one circle, as is evident.

¶ I suppose that the smaller quadrangle is equivalent to four equal palms; and let the larger quadrangle be worth six palms. And so I say that whatever consists between four and six is equivalent to five palms. But the circle consists between the larger and smaller quadrangle, as is evident to the senses: because it is contained by the larger, and the circle itself contains the smaller collection of lines. Therefore, it is necessarily clear that if the circle were straightened out, it would be equivalent to five palms existing between six and four: just as in number, where the second unit exists equally between the first unit and the third. And this same thing can be said of three units existing equally in the number nine, which consist equally between three units placed before and after. 

¶ Furthermore, the intellect makes another demonstration: namely, it places one red quadrangle equally between the larger and smaller quadrangle, with which it <term>squares the circle</term> <note>original: "quadrat circulum"; a classic mathematical problem of constructing a square with the same area as a given circle.</note> according to the measure of the container and the contained. For if the circle contains the red quadrangle and vice versa, as is shown at their extremities, the line of the circle is worth as much as the line of the quadrangle. But the red quadrangle is equivalent to five palms, because it consists equally between the smaller and larger quadrangle. And this can be held through experience: if the red quadrangle were extended with a compass, then the circular line would be equivalent to whatever [the square is], if it were straightened out. 

¶ Again, through this demonstration, the red quadrangle and the circle are seen to be equivalent: if four times four are worth 16 houses. And similarly six...

<margin>89. The form of astronomy.</margin>
### On Astronomy.

Astronomy is the branch of knowledge with which astrologers recognize the virtues and movements that the heavens have effectively upon inferior <note>meaning earthly or terrestrial things.</note> things. In this art, the heavens are designated by the letter **b.** Therefore, if any doubt should arise concerning the heavens, one should return to the third subject and answer the doubt according to what is explained in the celestial subject; or in such a way that whatever is said of the heavens remains unharmed. 

For example, if it is asked: Is there any other heaven except for the heaven of this world? One should answer in the negative through the definition of **concordance** <note>original: "concordantie"; one of Llull's "Principles" where different things share a common nature.</note>. For if there were another heaven, they would both agree in their "bodiliness" and their shape without a common subject for both; this would imply a contradiction, which is impossible. For species cannot exist without a genus, nor can distance and proximity exist between them [without a shared space], as is apparent.

### The Third Figure follows.

¶ Through these two figures, one of which is called **a.** and the other called **b.**, things are indeed distant through their upper and lower parts, and not through their middle parts, as is clear through the three lines. For two are long and one is short. If one were to grant that a vacuum <note>original: "vacuitas"; the concept of a totally empty space, which many medieval philosophers argued could not exist.</note> was the subject of the long lines and the short line, then distance and proximity would be given in a vacuum subject, which is impossible. 

¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that another starry heaven is not capable of existing, so that the aforementioned inconvenience does not follow, nor is the definition of concordance destroyed. Nevertheless, I say that it is possible for a second heaven to exist because the power of God is infinite; and if it did exist, the distances and proximities would indeed exist in potentiality and in disposition, but they would not exist in actuality outside of the heavens, because a subject would be lacking—namely, a place—since a vacuum would exist between the heavens.

¶ But here the intellect wonders what the cause is: since the sun is not itself hot, what is the reason why it heats the air? But it considers that the sun causes heat through its presence just as it causes darkness through its absence, so that days and nights can exist.

<margin>89. The form of arithmetic.</margin>
### On Arithmetic.

Arithmetic is an art invented for the purpose of counting many units. The principles of arithmetic are the principles of this Art [of Llull]. For the primitive principles, insofar as they are primitive, are numerical. For instance, **Goodness** is one principle in its genus, and **Greatness** is another, and so on. And because the principles are mixed with one another, they compose a "numbered number" having two species: namely, an even number (like two principles) and an odd number (like three or five principles, etc.). and in these two species, every number is counted.

¶ There are other points of number considered through the "correlatives" of the second species of Rule C <note>In Llull's system, "correlatives" are sets of three related terms (agent, patient, and the act itself) that mirror the Trinity.</note>. For example, in the essence of **Goodness**, there is one correlative that is "the maker of good" <note>original: "bonificans".</note>, another that is "the thing made good" <note>original: "bonificatus".</note>, and another that is "the act of making good" <note>original: "bonificare".</note>. And in these three, the number is perfected as to the essence of Goodness. 

¶ Goodness in number signifies the first unity; and "that which is made good" signifies the second unity arising from the first. "To make good," however, is the third unity arising from the aforementioned. And because these three unities exist through even and odd numbers, therefore number is multiplied through the even and the odd. Just as three times three are nine unities; and through the composition of even and odd numbers, the fifth unity is found, because two and three are five unities. And thus...

And just as majority and minority are in the vowels, consequently equality is in **o** and **i**, for they cause no consonants. The intellect, thus considering **e** to be greater than **a** by reason of its matter, recognizes that it proceeds with the motion of the **earth**; **a**, however, proceeds with the motion of **water**. The reason for this is that earth has more matter than water. But **u** agrees with the motion of the **air**, which has less matter than water; **o**, however, agrees with the motion of the **heaven**, which is formed in the mouth through the voice in the likeness of a circular figure. But **i** agrees with **fire** by reason of its thinness and sharpness, because it has the least amount of matter.

## On Music.

<margin>85. The form of music.</margin>
**M**usic is an art invented for ordering many concordant voices into one song, just as many principles are ordered toward one end; and this definition is signified through the definition of **concordance** and the definition of a **principle**. ¶ Again, it is understood through its relation to the <term>correlatives</term> <note>In Llull's philosophy, "correlatives" are the active, passive, and verbal forms of a quality (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving).</note> of music: for just as a carpenter conceives the figure of a chest in his mind, and he himself leads it from potentiality into actuality, so indeed the musician conceives an ordered voice in the mind, and leads it into the **third species of Rule C**, in which music is a <term>habit</term> <note>A "habit" (habitus) here refers to a learned skill or internal disposition.</note> with which the musician is a practitioner. ¶ The musician is a practitioner through six degrees, ascending and descending, by saying: **ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la** <note>These are the six notes of the medieval hexachord, the precursor to our modern do-re-mi scale.</note>. But here the intellect wonders why there are six degrees, and neither more nor fewer. But it remembers the chapter on "rectitudes" <note>straightness or correct alignments</note> in the treatises above. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the way it ought to help itself with the **one hundred forms** treated above by applying them to the doubts being questioned. But the intellect still wonders about the five voices, why there are five and neither more nor fewer. But it remembers the four spheres of the elements and the **fifth essence** <note>The "quintessence" or ether, which makes up the heavens.</note> which are signified through the third and seventh subjects. And it remembers that they consist in motion, and that motion generates sound, and the musician extracts the voice from the sound. From this, the intellect recognizes that the original ordered voice is made of five simple voices from which consonant or composite letters are derived.

**R**hetoric is an art invented with which the rhetorician colors and adorns his words. And because this art is general, the rhetorician therefore has a general subject for ordering his words: namely, as when one says: **Goodness and Greatness**; and **Goodness is eternal**. And now it adorns them more when they are joined by saying: **Goodness is great and eternal**. And therefore the rhetorician adorns his words when he colors a beautiful subject with a beautiful predicate. Just as in **Figure A** <note>A specific circular diagram in Llull's Art representing the divine attributes.</note>, all principles are predicated of one and the same subject. ¶ There is another way of adorning or coloring: namely, to adorn a principle with its **correlatives**. For example, to adorn **Goodness** with the **Bonifier, the Bonified, and the act of Bonifying** <note>original: "bonificans, bonificatus, bonificare"; Llull's way of showing how a quality is dynamic and internal to a subject.</note>. ¶ Furthermore, to adorn any relative with other relatives by saying: **The Great and Eternal produces the Bonified, the Magnified, and the Eternized**. ¶ Moreover, there is another way of adorning: namely, to adorn a principle with its definition and with the definitions of other principles; as when he says: **Good, great, and eternal Goodness is the reason for a good thing producing that which is good, great, and eternal**. Just as the logician finds natural conjunctions between the subject and the predicate so that there may be a true conclusion in a **syllogism**, so the rhetorician inquires into the natural conjunctions between the subject and the predicate...

# On the Application

...spoken: so that a beautiful subject can be adorned by its essential predicate, by speaking thus: "The Lady Queen has a beautiful face, beautiful hair, beautiful hands," and such things.

¶ There is yet another way of adorning a subject through accidents <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that isn't essential to what a thing is—like a crown is accidental to a queen, but a face is essential to her body.</note>: as when it is said, "The Lady Queen has a beautiful crown," and "she speaks beautiful words," and "the Lady Queen is good." This is evident through the queen of **Rule G** <note>Rule G in Llull's Art usually relates to "How?" or "In what way?"</note>.

¶ Again, the rhetorician adorns with meaningful sound: as when one says "April" and "May," which are more beautiful words than when one says "October" and "November," because they signify flowers, leaves, the song of birds, the renewal of time, and of things being born. October and November do not. Likewise, one can speak of fountains, rivers, streams, meadows, trees, shadows, and such things: that they are beautiful words according to the senses and the imagination; and this is evident through **Rule E** <note>Rule E often concerns "Equality" or "Virtue" in Llull's system.</note>.

¶ Just as the rhetorician praises his friend with beautiful words applied to a good end, so he disparages and scorns an enemy with beautiful words that are removed and diverted from their proper end: as when one says to a dishonest monk, "If I had been a monk, I would have had beautiful and honest words." This is evident through the definition of the "end" of concordance and contrariety.

¶ Furthermore, the rhetorician adorns his words according to the duties of different people: as when a person speaks of <term>science</term> <note>meaning "knowledge" or "learning"</note>, of generosity, of chastity, and such things. Similarly, there is rhetoric in knighthood: when it is said, "The man speaks of daring, of prowess and nobility, of the horse, of the sword," etc. And of the art of trade, to speak of silver, of gold, of precious goods, and such things. And in agriculture, to speak of the field, the plow-iron, the garden, plants, and animals. For just as it is a beautiful word for a merchant to speak of gold, etc., so it is a beautiful word for a peasant to speak of the field or the iron, and such things.

¶ Furthermore, the rhetorician adorns with three degrees: namely the positive, the comparative, and the superlative. But he adorns more with the comparative than with the positive, and more with the superlative than with the comparative: as when he says, "The rose is beautiful"; but he adorns more when he says, "The rose is more beautiful than the violet." And yet more when it is said, "The rose is the most beautiful of all flowers." This is evident through the definition of **majority** and **minority**.

¶ Likewise, the rhetorician adorns when he colors a beautiful subject with a beautiful adjective, or "de-adorns" a beautiful subject with a beautiful adjective: as when it is said, "The queen is good," or "The queen is dishonest." For "dishonest" is a more beautiful word than "malice."

¶ The rhetorician colors matter with a beautiful form, and colors form with a beautiful matter: as when it is said, "The human body has a rational soul," and "The rational soul has a body well-disposed toward doing good with vigor," and such things. This is manifest through the ladder of the **Beginning** and its definition.

¶ Furthermore, the rhetorician adorns the "middle" with a beautiful "beginning," and adorns the "end" with a beautiful "middle," as in love, in which a good lover loves to love the good out of his own goodness; and the beloved is adorned and colored by his loving, just like a good person who is habituated with a good habit. This is evident through the definitions of **Beginning, Middle, and End**.

¶ Further still, the rhetorician can adorn his words more with substantial and necessary principles than with accidental or contingent ones, just as in deeds: that which *is* is more than that which *appears*. The reason for this is: because a necessary principle rests more in the end than an accidental or contingent one. This is evident through the triangle of **majority and minority**, and through the definition of **beginning and end**.

¶ Furthermore, the rhetorician adorns his words by explaining through the possible and the impossible, the easy and the difficult, the useful and the useless, the frequent and the rare, and such things; this is evident through **Rules B, C, D**, etc.

¶ Still further, the rhetorician adorns his words with beautiful proverbs applied to the purpose at hand, as is evident in the *New Rhetoric* which we have made <note>Llull is referring to his own book, "Rhetorica Nova" (1301).</note>.

## On Logic

<margin>84.</margin>
<margin><term>logic.</term></margin>

Logic is the art with which the logician finds the natural conjunction between the subject and the form of the predicate, which is the "middle" with which he knows how to make necessary conclusions. Logic, through the definition of the **middle**, finds the contiguous middle term; and through the concordances existing between the subject and the predicate; an example of this is given in the multiplication of the "Fourth Figure" <note>This refers to the mechanical logical device Llull invented, which used concentric circles to combine terms.</note>.

¶ Furthermore, the logician treats the five <term>predicables</term> <note>The five types of relationships a predicate can have with a subject: genus, species, difference, property, and accident.</note> and the ten <term>categories</term> <note>Aristotle's ten ways of describing any object (substance, quantity, quality, etc.).</note>; an example of this is in the *Treatise on a Hundred Forms*.

¶ Likewise, the logician treats the **syllogism**, figures, and fallacies; all of these have already been exemplified above in the multiplication of the Fourth Figure. Therefore, if any doubt arises concerning logic or some foreign question, let it be reduced to those things which are said about logic, by holding the affirmation or negation of the question in such a way that the things said about logic in this Art remain unharmed.

¶ Furthermore, the logician makes a predicate of a higher term for a lower term: just as "animal" is predicated of "man," and "body" of "animal," and "substance" of...

# Tenth part.

## On grammar.

...body. ¶ Likewise, he posits the multiplicity of **genus**: he posits the most general genus—such as the genus of **substance**—and the subaltern genus—such as **body** or **animal**. And similarly, he posits the multiplicity of **species**. For he posits the subaltern species, such as all those that exist between substance and man in a straight line. But **Man** is the most specific species <term>species specialissima: the lowest level of a classification that cannot be divided into further species, only individuals</term>; for beneath it, there is nothing. And all things are categorized through the triangle of majority, minority, and equality; and through the triangle of beginning, middle, and end. 

For example: **goodness**, which is the most general principle when it is not specified [contracted]; but when it is specified in the middle, it is a subaltern genus or principle—by saying, for instance: "goodness is great." For it stands between the most general and the most specific. But when it is specified to the most specific species or to an individual in respect to its end [purpose], then it is the most specific principle: as when it is said, "the goodness of a man" or "the goodness of Peter is great." 

Logic treats **difference** by differentiating, **concordance** by concording, and **contrariety** by contrariating; wherefore the intellect knows in what way logic is applicable or to be applied to **Figure A** and **Figure T** <note>Figure A and T are primary diagrams in Llull’s Art. Figure A represents the attributes of God (Goodness, Greatness, etc.), and Figure T represents relational principles (Beginning, Middle, End, etc.).</note>. The intellect also knows in what way the logician cannot stand before an "Artist" [a practitioner] of this Art. For the logician, wishing to destroy the principles of this Art—which are stable and immutable—is confounded by seeking from the practitioner exactly what he intends to conclude; and once the conclusion is understood, he is pinned down by the stability and immutability of the principles, species, and rules, and immediately he will not know how he might escape. 

¶ Likewise, the logician treats **definition** considered only through the first species of **Rule C** <note>Rule C in this system asks "What is it?" and is used to define the nature of things.</note>; the general Practitioner of this Art, however, treats it through all species of Rule C. The logician treats **secondary intentions** <note>Secondary intentions are logical concepts about concepts, like "genus" or "species," rather than things themselves.</note> joined to primary ones; but the general Practitioner treats primary things through the second species of Rule C, and secondary things through the first and fourth species, just like the logician. 

¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that logic is an unstable or fleeting science, whereas this General Art is permanent and stable. Likewise, the logician forms a conclusion with two premises; but the general Practitioner of this Art does so with a mixture of principles and rules. 

¶ Furthermore, the logician cannot find the **true law** with logic alone; but the general Practitioner finds it with this Art. For that law is true which the principles and rules of this Art can enter. 

¶ Moreover, logic is a difficult art to learn; but this Art is very easy by reason of the mixing and concatenation of principles and rules. Therefore, a Practitioner can learn more of this Art in one month than a logician can learn of logic in one year.

<margin>88. The form of grammar.</margin>

**G**rammar is the art for finding the way of speaking correctly and writing correctly through the definition of **difference**. 
¶ Grammar is divided into nine modes: 
¶ The first mode is about grammar itself and the number of the **eight parts of speech**. 
¶ The second is about **case**. 
¶ The third is about **conjugation**. 
¶ The fourth is about **declension**. 
¶ The fifth is about **gender**. 
¶ The sixth is about **government** <note>In grammar, "government" refers to how one word requires another to be in a specific form, like a verb requiring a specific noun case.</note>. 
¶ The seventh is about **construction**. 
¶ The eighth is about **orthography** [correct spelling]. 
¶ The ninth is about **figure**. 

¶ Grammar is applicable or to be applied to this Art. For just as grammar teaches the way of speaking correctly and writing correctly, so this Art teaches how to find other arts. Therefore, we apply grammar to this Art, so that it may be more certain and clarified in our intellect. 

¶ There are eight parts of speech, namely: **Noun**, **Pronoun**, **Participle**, **Verb**, **Conjunction**, **Preposition**, **Adverb**, and **Interjection**. 
¶ The **Noun** is applicable to the principles of this Art, such as to Goodness, Greatness, etc. For these are nouns. The **Pronoun** is likewise applicable or to be applied to them, for the pronoun stands in place of a proper noun. The principles of this Art are indeed nouns, as was stated above; and they have a "property" [a specific appropriateness], because they are proper nouns by reason of the universality they possess. For they can be applied to every faculty [of knowledge]. However, the principles of another faculty or science cannot be applied to other sciences; for they do not have a property so general as the principles of this Art have. 

¶ The **Verb** is to be applied to the second species of Rule C, namely: **to make good** [bonificare], **to make great** [magnificare], etc. <note>original: "bonificare, magnificare"</note>. For they signify action, just as the verb does. 
¶ The **Participle** is applicable in the same species of Rule C, as is evident through the meanings of "that which makes good" [bonificans] and "that which is made good" [bonificatum], "that which makes great," etc. 
¶ The **Conjunction** is implied in the same species of Rule C, specifically in "to make good" [bonificare]. For "to make good" joins the **maker-of-good** and the **thing-made-good** into being one perfect concrete thing, just as a conjunction joins different words into being one perfect sentence. 
¶ Furthermore, the **Adverb** is implied in the same species: as when it is said, "the maker-of-good makes his thing-made-good **goodly** [bene]." For every agent intends to lead forth its own effect from itself well; therefore the adverb is implied in it. 
¶ The **Preposition** is applicable to the fourth species of Rule C, or to the rule of instrumentality. For the grammarian [treats] of grammar itself...

<header>On application</header>

# On application

Grammar makes the instrument with which it reduces the **case** to the **act**. ¶ **Interjection** <note>In traditional grammar, a part of speech expressing emotion</note> is to be applied to the definition of the **will**; for through the will, sadness or joy is most clearly indicated.
¶ We must speak regarding the **case** [grammatical case].
¶ The **nominative case** is implied in the second species of Rule C, namely in the "bonifier" <term>bonificans: in Llull’s system, the active principle or "doer" of goodness</term>. For the bonifier of itself does not descend from any other in the act; and the nominative is the principle of the other cases descending from it. 
¶ Similarly, the **genitive** is implied in the second species of Rule C, namely in the "bonified" and "to bonify." For the bonified <note>the object of goodness</note> and the act of bonifying descend from the bonifier, just as the genitive case descends from its nominative. And it can also be applied to the third species of Rule D, for that signifies **possession**, just like the genitive. 
¶ Furthermore, the **dative** is implied in the second species of Rule C, in the "bonified" and "to bonify." For the bonifier gives being to it; and both the bonifier and the bonified give being to the act of bonifying. 
¶ Furthermore, the **accusative** is implied in the same rule, namely in the third species. For in it, the act of the agent is terminated, as if in the **patient** <term>patient: the person or thing that receives or undergoes the action of the verb</term>. For the accusative is that case in which the agent's act ends, as if in its object or patient. 
¶ Moreover, the **vocative** is implied in the fourth species of the same rule. For in it, the vocative has its "called" person objectively. It can also be applied in Rule B, as is clear to one observing the nature of said rule. 
¶ The **ablative** is implied in the second species of Rule C, namely in the **essence** of the bonifier, the bonified, and the act of bonifying. For the essence itself is the principle and cause of these three correlates <note>correlatives: Llull's term for the triad of doer, receiver, and the act itself</note> essentially and naturally. 
¶ **Conjugation** is implied in the second species of Rule C, in the essence and its correlates: such as in "goodness" and its correlates. For **goodness** is the principle and cause of its correlates descending from it, which differ from one another according to their diverse properties; just as in conjugation there is a certain principle <note>the root word</note> from which many words are derived, differing from each other by person, tense, mood, and so on. 
¶ **Declension** is implied in the second species of Rule C; for the act of bonifying and the "bonified" descend from the "bonifier" by generation, just as one case declines from another. 
¶ **Gender** is implied in the correlates of the second species of Rule C. For in them, every gender is implied. For the "bonifier" signifies the masculine gender by reason of action; the "bonified" signifies the feminine by reason of passion [being acted upon]; and "to bonify" [the act] signifies the neuter by reason of its neutrality. 
¶ **Governance** [Regimen] is implied in the greater power and virtue with respect to the "governor," and also in the lesser power and virtue with respect to the "governed" or "governable."

For it is fitting for one having greater power and virtue to govern and not be governed. But for one having lesser power and virtue, it is fitting to be governed and not to govern. Indeed, it is fitting for a Count to govern his simple soldier, and not the other way around. 
¶ **Construction** is implied in the triangle of beginning, middle, and end, by reason of proper order. For the beginning is prior to the middle and the end according to the way of nature; and this is clear through its definition. And also the middle is prior to the end itself, as is also clear through its definition. And the end is last, as is clear by the same reasoning. For the principle rests in the end; and this happens through a right and proper order. Thus, also in construction, the **subject** [suppositum] is placed first, and the **predicate** [appositum] is placed after, as when it is said: "Peter runs." For he does not order well who wishes to place the roof before the building of the house. But the foundation and the wall [come] after the building: for that is impossible. 
¶ **Orthography** [spelling] is implied in the Rule of Modality. For that rule teaches how a part is a part, and how one part is in another part, or joins with another part. 
¶ Also, how parts are in the whole, and the whole in its parts; and afterwards how the whole transmits its likeness outside of itself; so it is in orthography, in which it is taught how a letter is what it is, and how one letter is joined with another letter, and one phrase with another phrase, and one accent with another accent, etc. 
¶ **Figure** <note>In this context, a "figure of speech" or a grammatical license</note> is implied in the definition of **contrariety** and of **concordance**. It is applied to the definition of contrariety insofar as a figure is a fault made against correct grammar; it is contrary to grammar. But because that figure can exist within grammar through some reason it contains within itself, it is therefore applied to the definition of concordance. For by that reason which the figure possesses, it concords with grammar and is placed within grammar; otherwise, it would not be placed there.

<margin>89.</margin>
<margin>The form of morality.</margin>

**M**orality is a habit for doing good or evil. ¶ We treated **morals** in the Ninth Subject; and therefore, if a question arises about any morality that is explicitly stated in that subject, let one return to the Ninth Subject. But if it is implied, let one return to those things that are explained in that same subject; just as if a question is asked about injury, let one return to justice. And if it is asked about generosity, let one return to greed. For one contrary [is known through the other]...

# Tenth Part

<margin>Instructions for avoiding vice</margin>
...recognizes through the rest. He who makes one virtue the subject, and predicates the principles of this art of it, that same virtue is indeed multiplied and strengthened—not in its essence, but in its act. This occurs when it is said: "Charity is good; charity is great; charity is enduring," etc. In this way, he disposes **charity** <note>original: "Charitas"</note> so that it becomes a habit with which a person may act charitably in a good, masterly, and enduring manner. Conversely, whoever wishes to destroy **vice** <note>original: "vitium"</note>, let him make it the subject and predicate the principles of this art of it, saying: "Cruelty is bad; as much as cruelty is great, so much is it bad; as much as it is enduring, so much is it bad and dangerous," etc.

¶ Whoever wishes to use a virtue in a truly masterly way should run it through the "evacuation" <note>An analytical process in Llull’s logic to test all possibilities</note> of the **third figure**: for instance, when one says "Charity is good and great." Then let him ask what "good and great charity" is, and so on for the others contained in "Cell B. C." <note>A reference to the combinatory tables of Llull’s "General Art"</note> Afterward, let him descend to "Cell B. D." and so with the others, asking: "From what does the goodness of charity endure?" Then let him answer in the manner that questions in that cell are answered, in such a way that no contradiction follows between what is said in that cell and what is said regarding charity. This same method can be applied to **cruelty** <note>original: "crudelitate"</note>. Thus, by this method, charity will receive nourishment, but cruelty will not. For the good is lovable in itself when it is recognized along with greatness and duration through what was stated above.

¶ In the multiplication of the **fourth figure**, the moralist can use virtues against vices by running the virtue or vice through the table, inquiring for the "middle" <term>middle: a logical link or bridge between two concepts</term> artificially, just as a logician does according to his art. By this method, the moralist can habituate himself toward virtue and strip himself of vice—such as with charity and goodness, which are in harmony with a moral nature, because charity cannot exist without goodness. It is like a man who cannot exist without "animality" <note>the biological nature of being an animal</note>. The intellect greatly rejoices in such artifice and teaching.

¶ Every vice and every virtue can be found through the species of the **Rules**. Vice or virtue is discoverable by one method according to one species, and by another method according to another. Just as the senses find color in an apple in one way, flavor in another way, and weight in yet another. Similarly, charity, when run through the four species of Rule C, is discovered in different ways. The same can be said and discovered regarding cruelty.

¶ Whoever wishes to possess virtues and avoid vices, or wishes to multiply virtue and diminish vice, let him recur to the **fourth subject**, which is **Man**. According to how he finds "Man" run through the principles and rules, let him help himself to acquire virtues and avoid vices. If he is hindered in this, let him recur to the subject of **Imagination**, and then to the subject of **Senses**; then he will be better disposed to acquire virtues and avoid vices. If all these do not suffice, let him recur to the **first subject** <note>God</note> by praying; then let him see in what way **God** is run through the principles and rules, habituating himself in hope. This is the ultimate remedy. If he reaches the end, it is well indeed; if he does not reach it, he fails, because he does not know how to act skillfully using this art.

## On politics.

<margin>Form of politics</margin>
->**P**olitics is the art with which citizens procure the public utility of the city.<- It derives, in fact, from morality. Therefore, politics is manageable through our subject by acquiring virtues against vices—virtues through which the public utility is established—by running politics through the principles and rules of this art in its own way. Just as virtues and vices are run through the ninth subject, politics itself is known through its definition and through its "correlatives" <term>correlatives: pairs of terms that define each other, like "governor" and "governed"</term> designated by the second species of Rule C. Through the third species, it is the **habit of nations**. Through the fourth species, nations possess the **political habit**. Thus, politics can be run through the other species of the rules in its own way.

¶ Politics is the order placed in the **senses** by virtues: as in a city where a marketplace is established for things which a person uses by reason of necessity, such as victuals <note>food supplies</note> and other things similar to them.

¶ Furthermore, politics is the order regarding **well-being**: such as the beautiful layout of streets, squares, and high places, and the adornment of clothing and the like.

¶ Additionally, politics requires in a city walls, moats, and armaments, etc., with all of which the city can defend itself from its enemies.

¶ Between a city and its **lordship** <note>the ruling authority or "dominion"</note>, there ought to be **privileges** existing by way of a "middle"; just as a logician places a middle between a subject and a predicate with the definition of **concordance** and the **end** <note>the purpose or goal</note>. These privileges should be guarded by the **consuls** <note>city magistrates</note> and **citizens** <note>original: "burgenses", refers to the free residents or burgesses of a town</note>, so that between the lord and the city there may be a balance and determined law.

¶ Politics in a city is the **general form** with respect to the city. In any individual house of the city, however, there is a **special form**; and this is joined with a "middle" in which the general and special forms are united. This is done through the definition of concordance and through the mixing of principles; yet that middle is [freed] from every...

...with contrariety removed. ¶ **Politics** <note>original: "Politica"</note> is metaphysically healthy through the healthy mind of counselors who are habituated in the virtues: but it is weakened and deformed through counselors habituated in vices. ¶ Politics lives by substantial and necessary principles: but it is in danger of death when it relies on accidental and contingent principles. And since politics is not a difficult subject, let these things we have said about it suffice.

# On Law

<margin>
The matter and form of law.
</margin>

**L**aw <note>original: "Ius"; can also be translated as "Right"</note> is a regulated act in a person habituated in justice through the first species of **rule C** <note>Rule C in Llull’s system refers to the question "From what?" or the origin of a thing</note>. ¶ There are four primitive principles of law: namely, **divine law**, **law of nations**, **natural law**, and **positive law**. ¶ Divine law consists of the definition of the majority, minority, and concordance existing between God and man. ¶ The law of nations consists of the definition and the concordance and equity existing between man and man. ¶ Natural law consists of the necessary definition of reason, goodness, greatness, etc. ¶ But positive law consists of the voluntary reason of man—finding the law and applying the definitions of goodness, greatness, etc. And within these terms or principles, every kind of law is contained through the second species of rule C. ¶ Through the third species of rule C, law exists in another. And through the fourth species of the same, it has its action in the person being judged. ¶ Furthermore, law has form and matter in the second species of **D** and the first of **E** <note>References to the Llullian figures or alphabet where D often represents "Principles" and E represents "Subjects"</note> from which it is composed. In the second species of E, **justice** <note>original: "iusticia"</note> is the subject of law in judgment: it follows that justice is the subject of which the principles of this art are predicated along with their definitions; as when it is said: "Justice is good; justice is great," etc. ¶ From this it follows that justice is the "good and great reason" of the judge, so that he himself may perform a good and great judgment, etc. And through this it is clear that the principles of this art are the forms of justice itself, without which perfect justice cannot exist. ¶ Indeed, justice is the subject of those things which are sustained within it. Nevertheless, justice itself is the "form" in respect to a judge who is habituated in it. ¶ Again, it is the form by reason of the action which the judge has with it upon the person judged: and consequently it is clear that the **person judged** <note>original: "iudicatus"</note> is its matter, when considered in this way. For the judgment is performed upon them by the one judging, just as an act is performed upon the object of action by the agent. And this is clearly evident through the third species of rule C. ¶ In a right and perfect judgment, it follows that the judge should run justice through the principles and rules of this art, just as a discourse is run through a good subject. And if he does this, justice—combined with the act of judging the person judged—is a perfect and necessary form: and the judge can use it in his judgment without any doubting conscience. ¶ If, however, the judge does not run it through the aforementioned principles (as was said above), he uses the aforementioned justice poorly, contingently, and even with a **doubting conscience** <note>original: "conicientia... dubitatiua"</note>: which is a great and terrible danger to his soul. He who gives a great judgment without prudence and discretion is worthy of a painful judgment. ¶ Written law is true if the principles and rules of this art can be found within it. But if they cannot be in it, such law is indeed fantastic, feigned, and deformed. For the principles and rules of this art are true and necessary without any defect. For everything is true and necessary if it is such that it cannot be otherwise. Just as a crystal placed over various colors becomes colored itself, so the laws or canons, when they are placed or applied to these principles and rules of this art, are "colored"—that is, they are fortified by various necessary reasons. And quickly, through this method, a judge sees the truth of each side; which he cannot do without the aforementioned method; rather, he must look to see the truth only with a great length of time and laborious study, and even then doubt remains. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that **law is not an art** <note>original: "ius non est ars"; Llull argues that Law as practiced is often a collection of facts/codes rather than a structured science, and needs his "Art" to become systematic</note>; and that it cannot be reduced to an art except by reducing it through the aforementioned principles and rules. Since law is not an art, it is no wonder if it is confused and long-winded, and the intellect is hindered by it. The subject of law resides mostly in the soul, as much through memory as through intellect: which is contrary to the proper order of the powers of the soul. For the intellect is primary for investigating and finding laws, and the will follows it in choosing, and finally the memory in preserving the types. And because the universal is more than the particular, and because memory is the particular subject of particulars (from which there is no science), for many people law is not well-disposed or well-ordered in the soul. And from this it is clear that when principles fail, the art fails.

<margin>
Conclusion on why law is not an art.
</margin>

¶ The form of law cannot act outside its own proper matter designated by **rule G**, nor vice versa. And therefore it is necessary for the jurist to know what constitutes the matter and form of law. Form, in respect to the principles of this art, is the aggregation of your aforementioned principles: namely, the <term>justificative</term> <note>original: "iustificatiuu"; the power to make a thing just</note>, the <term>bonificative</term> <note>original: "bonifactiuū"; the power to make a thing good</note>, the <term>magnificative</term> <note>original: "magnificatiuu"; the power to make a thing great</note>, etc., which meet in one form by reason of concordance.

Instruction for jurists.

Furthermore, the **justifiable** <note>original: "Justificabile"; in this system, it refers to the capacity of a thing to be made just</note>, the **make-able good**, the **make-able great**, and so on, are the "matter" of law. Its "form," however, and the matter of its discourse, proceed along the straight line of the rules, together with the definitions of the principles. ¶ And in this paragraph, everything that can be said concerning law has been applied. ¶ In the science of law, the intellect is stronger when paired with the imagination than with the senses, because the imaginative power is higher than the senses; and since the intellect is a higher power than the imagination, it is therefore stronger both in itself and within the imagination. ¶ So that the jurist may know how to act concerning every power according to whether it is higher or lower, I advise the jurist to have knowledge of the subjects designated by **e, f, and g** <note>These letters refer to specific charts or "Figures" in the author's logical system representing different levels of reality or logic</note>. ¶ I advise that the jurist should discourse through the species of the rules before rendering a judgment. For a certain judgment is appropriate for one species which is not appropriate for another, as appears in the second species of **Rule C**. For in that second species, laws arise from **necessity**; but in the third species of the same rule, they proceed from **contingency**. This is made manifest through the definitions of **majority** and **minority**.

For by the method through which they are mixed, the physician will habituate himself to possessing the skill with which he knows how to make a mixture of medicines—in making decoctions, ointments, plasters, and syrups, and in

<margin>

According to how he can apply them within these rules, let judgment be made, expounding and declaring their authorities. ¶ For just as a money-changer has true knowledge and experience of good or false gold by rubbing it upon a certain black stone <note>A touchstone</note>, so the physician has true knowledge and experience through writings by applying them to the principles and rules of this Art, observing what "color" (speaking metaphorically) the aforementioned writings receive from them. ¶ And at this step the intellect greatly rejoices, by reason of the knowledge of the positive mode, because it can be reduced to the Art through the necessary conclusions of this Art.

If, however, the prince says that these things are difficult for him, let it be answered to him that he should do what he can according to his power; and beyond his own power, he should have his wise men <note>original: "sapientes"; the prince's council of scholars or sages</note> who know how to do this and give him counsel. This should be done in such a way that the principles and rules remain without injury, and the prince may be in harmony with the **Highest Subject** <note>God, or the ultimate source of order</note> and removed from all contradiction. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes through what movement the rule of a prince can be reduced to an **Art** <note>A systematic, teachable science</note> and how to produce knowledge of it. And would that a prince be found who reduces his governance to an Art, to which he might dispose his son and teach it to him, or cause him to be taught. And consequently, I grant to all princes on behalf of their sons that they should learn it.

## On Knighthood.

<margin>93rd Form: On Knighthood.</margin>

**K**nighthood <term>Militia: The profession and moral state of being a knight, involving both military skill and ethical duty</term> is a **habit** <note>A "habit" here refers to a settled disposition or trained capacity of the soul</note> with which a knight assists the prince so that he may maintain justice. For the knight was devised so that justice might be sustained through him. And therefore, the knight ought to habituate himself to justice through that manner by which justice is discussed through the principles and rules of this Art in the Ninth Subject, so that the knight may have perfect knowledge of it. ¶ Since the knight requires **prudence** in war, he ought therefore to have it as a habit, so that with it he may be stronger against his enemy; the knight must therefore know it according to how it is discussed in the Ninth Subject, so that with it he may defend himself skillfully against his enemies. For the Art is an unassailable habit. Indeed, the knight who possesses it has victory against the one who does not know how to use the Art.

<margin>What fortitude is.</margin>
¶ **Fortitude** is the virtue strengthening the heart of man, especially when he possesses knowledge of it; and therefore, the more it is known, the more it causes **audacity** <note>original: "audaciam"; here meaning courageous boldness rather than modern "audacity" as insolence</note>. ¶ Whence it follows that if a knight wishes to know fortitude perfectly, let him return to the Ninth Subject in which it is perfectly treated. ¶ A knight without **faith, hope, and charity** is not fortified in war; and therefore, let the knight clothe himself in the aforesaid virtues, with God’s help, through the manner in which they are discussed in the Ninth Subject. ¶ Through **goodness**, the knight wishes to be good; and through **greatness**, he wishes to have great victory, honors, and the like. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which knighthood can be reduced to an Art. And it also recognizes that the greater armors are in the soul rather than the armors of the body with which one is protected. For the Art does not consist in the body, but in the soul alone. ¶ It is fitting for a knight that he be noble by birth; **nobility** is indeed a great habit in the heart, from which arises a great audacity of the face and of the right hand, which cause victory when the audacity of the heart exists with them. ¶ In war, a great imagination and a great sense are necessary. ¶ The magnitude of the aforesaid things is known through the discourse of the virtues of the Ninth Subject. For just as one sword with a stronger arm overcomes another sword in a weaker arm, so one knight with greater sense and imagination overcomes another knight in war. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that sometimes a few knights overcome many.

**C**ommerce <term>Mercantia: The art of trading, buying, and selling</term> is a habit devised by which a merchant knows how to buy and sell so that he may multiply his money, as is known in the treatise of principles and rules: namely, by what manner one principle relates to another. Just as in trade, the buyer relates to the seller with his principles and rules, and the seller similarly relates to the buyer with his, so that each might be able to have that which is greater through that which is greater. ¶ Whence it follows that the merchant who knows how to discourse with his intellect, imagination, and sense through the principles and rules of this Art has a superiority...
