# Tenth Part.

The knowledge of buying and selling <note>This refers to the "Art of Commerce," viewed here as a moral and intellectual discipline</note>, whereas another merchant might not know the aforementioned discourse. ¶ A merchant, in what he does in buying or selling, acts with his intellect, will, and memory; and therefore he ought to use these very powers according to the natural order of the soul: namely, that the intellect should be the primary part in understanding, the will follows in choosing, and consequently the memory in preserving the mental images. With these, buying and selling are conducted in the marketplace. Therefore, so that a merchant may know how to act skillfully, let him place his imagination and his senses upon the trade, without which buying and selling do not happen. And he will know how to do this if he knows how to familiarize himself with the subjects designated by the letters **e, f, and g** <note>In the author's symbolic system, E usually represents the Body or Power, F represents the Soul or Wisdom, and G represents the Senses or Will</note>. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which one merchant multiplies money more than another. ¶ In the subject designated by **e**, it treats of man, and consequently of his body, for the body is a part of him. And because buying and selling are done out of the necessity of the body, therefore a good merchant should direct his intellect through subject **e** so that he may have knowledge of the things necessary for the body.

¶ The third species and fourth rule of **e** are great subjects for the merchant by means of rules **h** and **i**. For the same merchandise or thing is small in one context and great in another, according to the diversity of place and time. For things or merchandise have more value at one time than another, and more in one place than in another. And also more for one man because of necessity and utility, while for another man it is for the sake of what is good and honorable. ¶ Furthermore, the second species of rule **e**, by means of rule **g**, causes profit in buying and selling. For what is "proper" <note>A term from logic meaning a characteristic that belongs naturally and exclusively to a species</note> is directed toward a higher end than what is merely "appropriated." Therefore, a thing that is specifically necessary for a human being is further removed from being a mere "contingency" than a thing that is necessary only by accident. ¶ Trade in a faithful and virtuous man is a perfect habit; but in a man who is a deceiver and a sinner, it is an imperfect habit. Therefore, he who wishes to be a good merchant should habituate himself in the virtues through the manner in which they are treated in the **Ninth Subject** <note>The section of the Art dealing with Virtues and Vices</note>. For in trade, a well-formed habit establishes community and the society of man; a deformed habit, however, causes the loss of community and society. ¶ Many other things could be said about trade, but let those things which have been said suffice for the sake of brevity.

## On Navigation.

<margin>96. The form of navigation.</margin>
**N**avigation is the art by which sailors know how to travel across the sea. ¶ Navigation indeed descends and arises from geometry, and from motion, time, and place; these intermediate things relate to their own "correlatives" <note>A technical term in this system for related concepts that act upon one another</note> designated by the second species of rule **e**, which are: the mover, the movable, and the act of moving, mediated by time and place. ¶ A ship in one time is in one place, and at another time in another place. ¶ Since geometry and arithmetic descend from this Art—as was proved above in their respective places—it follows as a consequence that the art of navigation is permitted to descend from this Art, secondarily from geometry and arithmetic, as is clear from what has been said. ¶ And to declare this, I have made here this figure divided into four triangles, as is clear within it, and composed of right, acute, and obtuse angles.

## The figure of navigation follows.

->[Geometric diagram depicting a triangle within a circular frame, subdivided by lines to illustrate the "Toleta de Marteloio" or traverse table, used to calculate how much a ship deviates from its course.]<-

¶ And I suppose that in that place in which there are four acute angles, there is the **tramontana** <note>original: "trāsmōtana"; the North star or the North wind</note> and the port of the ship. Suppose that a ship is there wishing to go toward the **East**, but it instead travels by the **exaloch** <note>original: "exaloch"; the Southeast wind or the Scirocco</note>. When it has traveled four miles, those four miles along the Southeast path are worth only three miles toward the East. The reason for this is: because in the duration of motion, first a single unit or "point" is generated; and when the ship has traveled eight miles toward the Southeast, these are worth only six miles toward the East. The reason for this is: because a second unit is caused, which with the first causes a line composed of two units or points. And when the ship travels four more miles, a third unit is caused; and thus it is caused...

# On the Application. <note>This heading refers to the application of the author's "General Art" to the specific science of navigation.</note>

A triangle is formed through twelve miles; three times four, a square is caused; four times three. And in this way it is shown by what method a triangle and a square are composed in the movement of a ship. By the method we have given concerning the ship’s movement through twelve miles, a sailor can know that by traveling through the **Sirocco** <note>original: "exaloch"; the Southeast wind</note>, for every hundred miles the ship deviates from the East by 25 miles; with the ship admitting in four miles a <term>penca<gloss>a unit of navigational deviation or "offset" used to calculate distance lost when sailing off-course</gloss></term> of the **Sirocco**, one mile toward the East; the ship's movement existing first through a point, then through a line, and afterwards through a triangle, and finally through a square. If a ship departs from a port and wishes to go toward the East, but instead travels toward the South, it deviates twice as much from the East compared to the deviation it makes when it goes by the **Sirocco**. The reason for this is because the **Sirocco** sits in the middle between the East and the South. ¶ And if the ship travels by the **Libeccio** <note>original: "lebeich"; the Southwest wind</note>, but still wishes to go toward the East, a triple deviation is caused. And if it travels toward the West, a quadruple deviation is caused. ¶ We have shown the method by which sailors can judge the deviation from the place to which they intend to go; and the movement we have given to that art for recognizing deviation, by showing the general principles without which a ship cannot be in motion. These principles are as follows: namely, the point, the line, the triangle, and the square. And the reduction of one mile for every four miles of the **Sirocco** deviation, and two miles for every eight miles toward the South, and so on for the others. ¶ Now we intend to give the doctrine and art by which sailors may know how to recognize in what place of the sea the ship is; and we intend to exemplify this by showing how far one mountain is from another.

¶ I suppose that there is one mountain near the East, far from the port where the ship stays by 4 miles, which shall be called **l**; and that there is another mountain at the **Sirocco**, distant from the port by 4 miles, and that mountain shall be called **m**. And let there be another mountain toward the South, distant from the port by 4 miles, and let it be called **n**. ¶ Further, I suppose that there is another mountain near the South, distant from the port by 8 miles, and let it be called **o**. Now it is asked how far **l** is from **m** and from **n**. And how far **o** is from **l** and from **m**. ¶ To the first and second questions we respond thus:

¶ The figure has four triangles, as is evident by itself: 1, 4, 7, 3; they compose seven, so that the triangle and the square may have a composition. 1 and 7 are divided into two equal parts, each having 3 and a half miles. ¶ From which it follows that from **l** to **n** there are 3 and a half miles, with **m** being in the middle of **l** and **n**. By reason of which, **l** is distant from **m** by half of 3 and a half miles <note>which is 1.75 miles</note>. ¶ To the third question we respond thus: from the port to **o** there are 8 miles, and from **l** to **n** there are 3 and a half, as was proven above; and thus they multiply to 11 and a half. Wherefore it appears that **l** is distant from **o** by 6 miles minus a quarter <note>5.75 miles</note>; and thus the third question is solved. ¶ To the fourth question we respond thus: from the port to **o** there are eight miles, and from **n** to **o** there are two miles minus a quarter; and thus it follows that **m** is distant from **o** by half of ten miles minus a quarter, which is 5 miles minus an eighth <note>4.875 miles</note>; and thus the fourth question is solved. ¶ Just as an art was given for recognizing the distances existing between the mountains **l, m, n, and o** through the miles mentioned above, so you can recognize the distances of other mountains through miles by means of triangles and squares.

¶ For just as an arithmetician multiplies a number, counting three times three and four times four, so the sailor can act in a similar way. ¶ It has therefore been declared by what method sailors can recognize in what place of the sea the ship is, by judging the distances according to the **North Star** <note>original: "transmontana"</note> toward the East, the South, and the West, and the **Sirocco**, **Libeccio**, **Mistral** <note>original: "maistre"</note>, and **Grecale** <note>original: "grech"</note>, with respect to the place in the sea where the ship stays. And this doctrine is easy, brief, and very useful, and general, and applicable to particular cases. ¶ Through rule **g** and through the "elemental subject," it is recognized that if the movement arises from the East, it has a greater inclination toward the **Sirocco** than toward the **Grecale**. ¶ For the **Sirocco** is moist and hot. ¶ The **Grecale**, however, is cold and moist, which is caused by the **North Star**. ¶ Likewise, if the wind depends on the **Sirocco**, it has a clearer manifestation toward the East than toward the South: because the South is hot and dry; and it can be said of the others in their own way. ¶ Furthermore, the sailor ought to consider the qualities of the air. For if the air is thick and cold, it is already signified that the wind arises from the **North Star**. If, however, the air is thin and moist, it is signified that the wind goes out from the East; but if the air is moist and subtle, it is signified that the wind exits from the South. If indeed the air is dry and cold, it is signified that the wind proceeds from the West. ¶ Clouds, according to the colors they have, signify the winds: just as a red cloud signifies an Eastern wind; and if it has a golden color, it signifies a Southern wind; and if it has a white color, it signifies a Northern wind; and if it has...

...if it has a black color, it signifies the West wind. ¶ A cloud is sometimes composed of several colors; in that case, it signifies a mixture of winds. Just as there is more of one color than another, it signifies one wind more than another. ¶ Indeed, as for rain, the part from which the water emerges signifies the wind of that direction. And the same can be said for flashes of lightning and thunder in their own way. ¶ **Favonius** <note>The West wind, often associated with spring</note> signifies a circular movement of the sea winds, the wind having such a disposition as a sea snail or a tortoise has. This wind is indeed disposed circularly so that the sea water rises, just as fine dust does upon the earth. ¶ Furthermore, a <unclear>fibulo-nus</unclear> <note>Likely a specific type of cloud formation or localized wind</note>, according to how it is colored, signifies its own wind, just as was said regarding the clouds. ¶ Concerning the **Tramontana** <note>The North Star, or the North wind; here referring to the nautical compass</note> and iron, it is not necessary to speak; for we have experience of those things, nor is the cause to be sought here as to why it attracts iron. ## On Conscience.

<margin>Ninety-seventh form: On Conscience.</margin>

**C**onscience is the form with which the intellect afflicts the soul concerning things committed, according to what is marked in the **fourth subject** <note>In Llull’s system, the Fourth Subject usually refers to the "Soul" (Anima)</note>. Since knowledge is an active form through the intellect—which, as far as the will is concerned, is elective, and as far as memory is concerned, is preservative—therefore, he who wishes to use conscience well should lead it through the **ninth subject** <note>The Ninth Subject in the Lullian Art is "Instruments" or "Application"</note>. ¶ A "great" conscience is caused by the definition of **Majority**; a "small" one from the definition of **Minority**; but a temperate and virtuous one from the definition of **Equality** and **Virtue**. ¶ Conscience arises from the **Possible** and from **Understanding**, but not from the **Impossible** and **Ignorance**. And therefore, it is manageable with the definition of **Power** and **Intellect**. ¶ Conscience guided by **Principles** and **Rules** is well-known, especially if it is guided by the mixing of the Principles. For any Principle declares the cause in relation to itself and in relation to other Principles, by reason of which conscience causes clarity. And it gives as counsel that there be **contrition**, **confession**, and **satisfaction** for things committed. ¶ Conscience arises from the correlatives of the Principles along with **Love**, and it is in the third species along with **Fear** and **Sadness**. In the fourth species, however, the subject in which it exists has a "passion" <note>In medieval philosophy, a "passion" is an undergoing or an effect received by the soul</note> along with it, by means of the second species of **Rule E** <note>Rule E in Lullian logic typically asks "Why?" (Quare), dealing with causes</note>. Conscience, before a sin is committed, disposes one toward **Justice**, **Prudence**, and **Fortitude**; but after a sin, toward **Sadness** and **Languor**. And therefore, it is to be traced back to the definition of the **Beginning** and **Rule H** <note>Rule H typically asks "How?" (Quomodo), dealing with the manner of action</note>. ¶ Conscience lives with **Goodness**, **Greatness**, and **Perseverance**. But it dies with **Malice**, **Smallness**, and **Inconstancy**. For this reason, it is to be traced back to the definition of **Goodness**, **Greatness**, and **Duration**. ¶ Conscience is strengthened with the **first subject** <note>The First Subject is God</note>, by making it an object according to the discourse through Principles and Rules. And thus it increases its action, from which arise contrition, confession, and satisfaction. ¶ Furthermore, through conscience itself, sighs arise from the heart, tears from the eyes, and many prayers from the mouth; and this is signified through **Rule I** <note>Rule I typically asks "With what?" (Cum quo), dealing with instruments or means</note>. ¶ Conscience, together with **Divine Justice**, performs acts of mercy; and with **Greatness** and **Eternity**, it multiplies them. But through **Goodness**, **Greatness**, and **Divine Mercy**, mediating with **Hope** and **Penitence**, it gives consolation to men. ¶ Conscience does not sleep, nor does it allow a man to sleep, by reason of the loss of time and the need for penitence. And therefore, wakefulness, prayer, and diligence with fear are its kinsfolk or neighbors. ¶ The intellect, considering in this way, recognizes conscience thus discoursed; because a conscience that has been discoursed through Principles and Rules is unassailable and infallible, in the knowledge of which the intellect greatly rejoices.

## On Preaching.

<margin>Ninety-eighth form: On Preaching.</margin>

**P**reaching is the form with which the preacher informs the people to follow good morals and avoid bad ones, especially if that mode of discourse is through the **Principles and Rules** of this Art, and also through the **Nine Subjects**. Thus, the intellect of both the preacher and the listeners may abound in great material; such preaching is very useful and very easy, just as it is very skillfully crafted and built and situated upon a great subject. ¶ Just as the preacher skillfully crafts his understanding for the purpose of guiding others, so he ought to skillfully craft his will to love the will of the listeners, so that the sermon may be as valuable in its **actual existence** as it is in its **appearance**. And this is through the definition of **Equality** of the intellect and the will, so that in the sermon, the intellect and will may rest equally; for sometimes a sermonizer is habituated toward **vainglory** in his sermon. ¶ The preacher ought to skillfully craft the memory of the listeners with the artifice of his own skillful sermon. If he preaches from the subject being preached, things joined in nature through the subject—such as "The Justice of God is Great"—then the Mercy of God is...

# On Application.

...great: and one of these is as great as the other; by reason of which the preacher ought to exist in joy and fear, mediated by justice, prudence, and hope. And such a state of fear and love in the listeners is entirely rational and lovable, just as it is entirely intelligible. ¶ The preacher ought to act in preaching just as the intellect does in discovering the things of which science is composed: for the intellect creates science from sensible things in the **imagination** <note>The mental faculty that forms images of external objects</note> outside of the senses. ¶ Furthermore, it creates science from intelligible things within itself, outside of the imagination. Thus the preacher ought to descend to the sense, by giving it sensible experiences; and afterward he ought to ascend to the imagination, by giving it imaginable experiences. ¶ Then, in turn, he ought to ascend to the intellect, by giving it experiences of intelligible things. And the same can be said of the **will** and **memory** in their own way. If he does not do this, he surely obscures and confuses his sermon, because such a preacher or sermon is fleeting in the memory of the listeners, unknown in their intellect, and neglected in their will. ¶ In the **evacuation of the Third Figure** <note>A Lullian logical process where one systematically exhausts all possible combinations of terms in a diagram to find truth</note>, give the example of clearing out rooms; and therefore the preacher ought to clear out, in a similar way, the words or propositions placed in the **theme** <note>The scriptural text or topic serving as the basis for the sermon</note>. And he also ought to seek the means of making conclusions through that method which is given in the **multiplication of the Fourth Figure** <note>The Fourth Figure in Lull’s system consists of three rotating concentric circles used to generate complex logical propositions</note>; for through such things the intellect of the listeners is made firmer through understanding than through believing the **authorities** <note>The accepted writings of Church Fathers or Saints</note> of the saints; because in believing, the intellect acts outside of its own natural act, which is to understand. For each thing is more rejoicing and content when it can use its own proper act: and just as it was said regarding the intellect, so it can be said regarding the will and memory in their own way. ¶ In **geometry** it is said by what method one makes demonstrations. Similarly, in **arithmetic** he gives the example of the method by which the arithmetician counts units. ¶ Furthermore, in **rhetoric** it is said by what method the rhetorician ornaments his words; and therefore the preacher in his sermon ought to have the habit of geometry, arithmetic, and rhetoric, so that he may be practiced and illuminated by them, and with them he may practice and illuminate the intellect of his listeners. ¶ The preacher ought to be a **theologian**, so that he knows how to speak of God, and also a **philosopher**, so that he knows how to apply the effect to the **First Cause** <note>God, as the ultimate origin of all things</note> by moving through the subjects marked **c. d. e. f. g. i. k.** <note>In Llull’s Art, these letters represent Divine Principles: C=Greatness, D=Duration, E=Power, F=Wisdom, G=Will, I=Virtue, K=Truth</note>. And if the preacher knows how to do this, he will have great and broad material for preaching. ¶ The preacher in his sermon ought to define the members or parts of his theme and his sermon. For through a definition, the people come to know the thing defined. ¶ Furthermore, he ought to consider by what method it is moved through the principles and rules, just as the example was given in the **hundred forms** <note>Likely referring to Llull's work "The Book of the Hundred Forms"</note>. And by such a method, the intellect of the preacher and the listeners will have great rest. Since God is intelligible, lovable, and recallable with greatness, the preacher therefore ought to give great knowledge of God, so that He may be greatly understood, loved, and remembered; and this he can do with a mixture of principles and rules, and also with the **First Subject** <note>God</note>. If he does not do this, his sermon will surely be imperfect and fleeting. There are three places, one of which is perfect in every way without any imperfection: and this is eternal and infinite glory. Another is totally imperfect: and this is **hell**, in which there is everlasting punishment. The third, however, is partly perfect and partly imperfect: and such a place is this world. Therefore, the preacher must recite and declare these three places, to say what they are, what they contain within themselves, for what purpose they exist, and what utility they have in themselves. For a place that is perfect in every way is totally lovable; one that is imperfect is inwardly hateful. That which is partly perfect and partly imperfect is indeed lovable in part by reason of its perfection, and hateful in part by reason of its imperfection. ¶ While the intellect considers in this way, it knows by what method the preacher can reduce his sermon to the **Art of Preaching**, so that he may know how to make sermons more scientifically and easily; just as we have made one part of preaching in which there are one hundred and eight sermons composed or made scientifically.

## On Prayer.

<margin>Ninety-ninth form: On Prayer.</margin>

**P**rayer is the form with which the one in prayer speaks of God in a holy manner. ¶ Whoever wishes to pray well, let him dispose himself toward the good according to the **Ninth Subject** <note>In the Lullian system, the Ninth Subject usually refers to the Soul or the practitioner themselves</note>. For God is worthy to be honored with virtues, and not with vices. ¶ The speaker or contemplator prays or contemplates God according to the likeness of the **evacuation of the Third Figure**; thus the prayer itself is marked in that figure for evacuation by saying thus: "O Lord God, good and magnificent: since in You, Your highest goodness and greatness have the highest concord, by distinguishing and according naturally; and Your goodness and greatness are reasons in You: so that..."

# Tenth Part.

...you produce a great good naturally: so from your highest goodness and greatness, may you produce in the world, morally or effectively, many good and great things, through which your people may be good and great, by blessing and magnifying you, and having harmony with you. Because you, Lord, are essence and substance, in which your goodness and greatness have relative, good, and infinite correlatives <note>In Lullian philosophy, these are the active, passive, and verbal forms of a principle—for example: Greatening, Greatened, and Greatening-itself</note> distinct from each other, as appears in you. Since you, Lord, are the good and great creator: therefore may it please you that your people may be in you a good and great praiser and servant: so that you may have your people good and great in differing and harmonizing habits.

¶ Let the orator or contemplator, after he has emptied the **chamber b.c.** <note>A "chamber" refers to the combination of two principles from Llull's logical alphabet; here, B (Goodness) and C (Greatness)</note>, empty the **chamber b.d.** <note>Goodness and Duration</note>, and so on. ¶ O sweetest Goodness, existing in an eternal subject with distinct diffusion, and removed from all contrariety: you are of yourself primitive and eternal without any subjection: so from your kindness and eternity, defend your people from everlasting punishments. ¶ Let the contemplator or orator, after he has emptied the entire **Third Figure** <note>A grid-like diagram used to combine concepts to find necessary truths</note> from one day to another successively, then pass to the multiplication of the **Fourth Figure** <note>A series of revolving circles used to generate complex propositions</note>, contemplating and praying according to the mode of that figure: namely, through the **column b.c.d.** <note>A vertical sequence of three-letter combinations in the Lullian system</note> and so on with others, considering the natural medium existing between the subject and the predicate: and let him speak thus. O venerable Goodness, since you are naturally good with a great and eternal good in yourself, and from yourself without any other thing lying before you: therefore, do you not have your people in forgetfulness? It seems so. For in the world there is more of the evil-ones' influence than of the good. ¶ Indeed, the greatness of malice lasts longer than the greatness of goodness—far be it from you, Lord: because from your most kind goodness and greatness, it pleased you to lead out your people in time, when they did not exist, so that they might forever praise, bless, and magnify you. ¶ Let the orator empty the **chamber b.c.f.b.** <note>A specific path through the logical circles combining Goodness, Greatness, and Wisdom</note> saying: Lord God most high, your goodness is your great reason, and a good and great reason, distinguishing so that you produce a great good distinct from yourself correlatively: yet not as to the essence of goodness and greatness, because your essence is one. And because this is so: therefore let your highest production descend to us kindly and magnificently, by declaring and showing to us the good and the evil: and lead us into a great good, and defend us from a great evil. ¶ The orator praying thus could now present one object; just as the intellect, which cannot understand other species while it understands those which it finds. ¶ And in this step the intellect recognizes the mode by which the orator can compel his soul and bind it to the highest object **artificially** <note>Meaning "by the use of the Art," Llull's logical system</note> and continually while he prays. And the intellect has remembered the **Art of the Philosophy of Love** <note>original: "arte philosophie amoris" — likely a reference to Llull's work "The Art of Loving the Good"</note> which we made: and that it would be good if he associated the aforementioned prayer with it, or joined it with it. ¶ Furthermore, let the orator implore and bless God through that mode by which God is the discourse in the first subject. For God does not hear sinners against his reasons, nor even against their relations, which would do injury to himself, which is impossible. ¶ And in this step the intellect recognizes that since the sinner praying without foresight and contrition gains nothing good by his prayer, his soul mocks and blasphemes him. ¶ Again, the contemplator or orator asks God according to the fact that He is the First Cause, using the subjects designated by **c.d.e.f.g.i.h.** and also by **k.** <note>These letters represent Greatness, Duration, Power, Wisdom, Will, Virtue, Truth, and Glory</note> regarding the virtues. For through the knowledge of the cause, the effect is known, and vice versa. ¶ And in this step the intellect recognizes that the subject of prayer is very great and widespread. ¶ O orator, in your prayer love God more than yourself and also more than other things; and if you do this, you are just and prudent, and habituated in charity and holiness. This habit is your friend in prayer, so much so that through it your prayer reaches perfection. But if you do not do this, you have no friend; indeed, God is your enemy, because you do them injury. ¶ O orator, when you pray for sins committed, hold the justice of God with you by loving it, not by hating it; for if so, the mercy of God could not be your friend, because you would be unjust; and your habit would be cruel, and far removed from hope and charity: and even your loving would be perverted into hating, in which hating you would be habituated forever. ¶ O contemplator or orator, if you cannot understand and reach the height of divine reasons and their acts: pray by believing. For beyond one's power, nothing is blameworthy. Nevertheless, such understanding is possible. Such believing in your prayer will be your friend, and especially your understanding, if you can have it. ¶ O orator, in your prayer stir up your conscience and run it through the principles and rules; and if you do this, you will obtain your petition with it. And if you run the petition through the principles and rules, you will obtain a movement from the heart from which groans and sighs will go forth; and from the heart to the eyes water will ascend, moistening your face and your hands and clothes: and you will feel that water to be warm, which arises from a warm and fervent fountain: and that holy water will purify your **confession**. And if you run the confession through the principles and rules, it will lead you to satisfaction and **penitence**, which indeed will join you with God in eternal glory. ¶ O orator, in your prayer consider adversities and prosperities...

...which he gave to you through his love: adversities, so that you may have patience under his justice; and prosperities, so that you may have charity under his grace. And since both prosperities and adversities are given to you through one and the same love, bless, praise, and love the divine love, and return the greatest thanks to him. For with a real love, God loves that very love within you; and if you love those things in God, your love will indeed provide for an eternal loving in everlasting glory. ¶ O **orator** <note>In this context, the "orator" is the person practicing this method of contemplative prayer.</note>, if your intellect is hindered by your senses and imagination, ascend to the **first subject** <note>The "first subject" refers to God or the highest level of being in Llull's hierarchy.</note> by praying: run yourself beyond sense and imagination. Or, if you wish to descend, pray by means of sense and imagination, running your prayer through the subjects designated by **g** <note>In Llull's "Art," the letter 'g' often represents specific concepts like Wisdom or Virtue, used as a mnemonic and logical tool.</note>. And at that time you will see that lower forms can do nothing against higher forms in prayer; and the intellect greatly rejoices in this doctrine. ¶ O orator, run your prayer through a new subject by understanding, loving, recollecting, fearing, hoping, and returning thanks; and do not rest until sighs break forth from your heart and tears flow. If, however, you rest without these aforementioned things, you are already a good and great orator. ¶ O orator, help yourself with what has been said in the **hundred forms** <note>Refers to Llull's "Book of the Hundred Forms," a foundational text for his logical system.</note>, running through one form and then another; and run through any form by the **principles and rules** <note>The "Principles" are the absolute qualities of God (Goodness, Greatness, etc.), and the "Rules" are the logical questions (What? Why? etc.) used to investigate them.</note>. In this way, you will have a great subject for finding many new prayers. ¶ O orator, pray for the people. For universal prayer is very pleasing to God; then pray for yourself, for your friend, and for the dead. And do this **artificially** <note>term: artificially <gloss>meaning "with technical skill" or "according to the rules of the Art," rather than "fake."</gloss></note>, as was said above, so that your soul may be habituated to good and great prayer, and with such a habit, it may be bound and chained fast with God.

### On memory deduced through principles.

<margin>The hundredth form: on memory deduced through principles.</margin>

**S**ince memory is a power just as perfect as the **intellect** and the **will** (which we have treated perfectly in the mixing of the principles), we wish to treat it here perfectly by running it through the principles and rules. We do this so that we may know it perfectly, and also to provide a doctrine: namely, that just as we run memory through the principles and rules, so every form of the **hundred forms** can be run through the principles and rules. ¶ Just as memory is naturally good through **Goodness**, so morally its goodness is the reason why it may recollect the "good-to-be-recollected" objectively. ¶ Memory through **Greatness** is great; by reason of which its greatness is the reason why it performs a great act of recollecting, with which it may recollect a great "recollectible" or object (which is the same thing). Just as a hooded man has one **habit** <note>term: habit <gloss>A play on words; "habit" means both a physical garment (like a monk's robe) and a stable internal disposition of the mind.</gloss></note> through his hood, and another through his tunic with which he is clothed, so memory through **Duration** has one condition, and through **Power** another. For through Duration it makes its recollecting last, and it treats of what is past; and through Power it has another condition, and treats of what is possible. ¶ Memory has one condition with the intellect, and another with the will. For through the intellect it receives the species <note>term: species <gloss>Mental images or concepts of things perceived by the senses.</gloss></note> that are desired or hated; and in the same way it receives species from the will, it returns them to it. ¶ Memory is a virtuous habit naturally, because it naturally recollects an object virtuously; morally it has a virtuous habit. When, however, it recollects a vicious habit, it has a vicious habit by accident. ¶ Memory through **Truth** is true, and through it, it truly reaches the object by recollecting. When it reaches it in respect to the **End**, it is a just and true habit; but when it reaches an object against the ultimate end, it is an unjust and false habit. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes in what way virtues and vices are caused. ¶ Memory with **Glory** <note>In Lullian terms, "Glory" often signifies the joy or delight found in a perfected state.</note> has delight in recollecting, and with **Pain** it has sadness. Likewise, when it appetites <note>term: appetites <gloss>Strongly desires or seeks after.</gloss></note> to recollect and cannot, it has pain, with which it is a passive and privative habit. ¶ Memory with **Difference** recollects objects in diverse ways; for just as the intellect recognizes the differences of objects, so memory recollects them. The reason for this is that Difference is just as general a principle or instrument for the memory as it is for the intellect. ¶ Memory by reason of **Concordance** accords in its object with the intellect and the will, by recollecting an object that is understood and loved (or hated), so that the object is acted upon by these powers at the same time. ¶ Memory with **Contrariety** sometimes contradicts the intellect and the will, by not returning to them the species which they appetite to recover—either because it is not disposed to return the species, or the intellect and will do not appetite to recover them, or because the memory does not return them to them in the same way the intellect and will handed them over. Or perhaps the intellect is joyful and the will too ready, and vice versa; or the intellect appetites one species and the will another. ¶ Now, in the **Beginning**, it acts by recollecting: and memory is its form or instrument with which it recollects the object; and the object itself is the subject or matter; while the one recollecting is its end. And when that recollecting is hindered, the memory indeed suffers, and consequently the agent does as well. ¶ In memory, "to remember" is the medium between the rememberer and the rememberable, with which...

# Part Ten.

<meta>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from a previous discussion on how the soul's powers relate to their objects.</meta>

...and they join together memorable things. This assumes that measurement occurs via a straight line equally bounded between the one who remembers and the thing remembered. ¶ There are three "terms" <note>In medieval logic, "terms" refer to the fundamental components or boundaries of a concept.</note> of memory: namely, the power, the object, and the act. Memory has no capability outside of these. In terms of the "end of privation," <note>This refers to the state where a faculty exists but cannot function because its necessary components are missing.</note> memory is a "deprived habit," just as when the act and object are missing from it; it is like eyes lacking light and color. However, the ultimate "end" or goal of memory is to recollect what is recollectible. ¶ In terms of its greatness, one memory is "greater" than another either by its essence or by its quantity; for one memory possesses a greater act than another. ¶ Furthermore, when memory has a greater act, it is indeed a greater habit. I do not mean that its essence grows or shrinks—since it is a spiritual power, it is neither divisible nor corruptible—but rather that a person acts with their memory as they please. And thus, sometimes one recollects much, and sometimes little. ¶ Memory naturally and equally exists between the intellect and the will, so that it may equally receive and return the "species" <note>The term <term>species</term> refers to the mental images or "likenesses" of things that the mind processes.</note> that are understood and loved. Nevertheless, it sometimes receives loved species that are not understood. This happens when a person believes and does not understand by reason of their own pleasure; they desire to believe more than they desire to understand. ¶ Memory, when diminished, is focused on nothing; thus it follows that when memory forgets, it is a "privative habit" by reason of this diminution.

## On Memory Deduced Through the Rules.

<margin>
The fifteenth principal part, regarding memory deduced through the rules.
</margin>

It is asked: does memory receive species from the intellect more quickly than from the will? The answer is yes. The reason for this is that the intellect creates knowledge <note>original: "scientiam"</note>, while the will possesses deliberation by reason of its freedom. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule C** <note>In Ramon Llull's "Art," Rule C asks "What is it?" (Quid est?). The "species" are specific ways of applying the question.</note>, it is asked: what is memory? It must be said that it is a power whose proper function is to recollect. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does memory possess within itself co-essentially? To this, it must be said that it has its "correlatives": <note>A central Lullian concept where every power has an active, passive, and verbal form.</note> namely, the **rememberer**, the **memorable**, and **remembering** <note>original: "memorativum, memorabile et memorare"</note>. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is memory in another? It must be said that it is "good" in a good object, assuming that the intellect and will rest in that object. It is "evil" in malice, assuming the will loves that evil. Furthermore, memory is a "habit" in a subject, with which it guards knowledge. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does memory have in another? It must be answered that it has goodness in a good object, and magnitude in a great one, etc., since it has its act both in the subject <note>The person remembering.</note> and in the object <note>The thing remembered.</note>. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule D** <note>Rule D asks "From what?" (De quo?).</note>, it is asked: from what is memory? It must be answered that it is from itself, for it was created. It was certainly not "begotten," nor was it made from any pre-existing material. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: from what is memory? To this it must be said that it is from its specific matter and form, with which it acts through its species. ¶ Through the third species of the same rule, it is asked: whose is the memory? It must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it exists, just as a part naturally or morally belongs to its whole—like a "cloak belongs to the cloaked man." <note>A standard philosophical example of how an attribute relates to the person who possesses it.</note> ¶ Through the first species of **Rule E** <note>Rule E asks "Why?" (Quare?).</note>, it is asked: why is there memory? To this it must be answered that it is constituted from its own form and matter. ¶ Through the second species of the same rule, it is asked: why is there memory? It must be said that it exists so that beings may be recollected. Furthermore, it is so that humans may have knowledge of things past. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule F** <note>Rule F asks "How much?" (Quantum?), referring to quantity.</note>, it is asked: whether memory has "continuous quantity," since it is not linear? It must be answered that it does. Because it is a spiritual power, it is both finite and indivisible. Every finite being is "continuous." And if any spiritual being is finite, it is certainly continuous; therefore it is clear that memory has continuous quantity. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: whether memory has "discrete quantity"? <note>Discrete quantity refers to things that can be counted as separate units.</note> The answer is yes, so that it can possess its aforementioned correlatives through differentiation. For through the **rememberer** it has one correlative, through the **memorable** another, and through **remembering** another. Anyone who says memory does not have these correlatives is essentially saying it is empty and lacks its own nature, which is impossible; therefore it is clear that memory has discrete quantity by reason of its correlatives. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule G** <note>Rule G asks "What kind?" (Quale?), referring to quality.</note>, it is asked: what is the "proper quality" of memory? It must be answered that it is "recollectibility," just as "risibility" <note>The capacity to laugh—the classic example used by medieval logicians to define a quality unique to humans.</note> is the proper quality of a human. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the "appropriated quality" of memory? To this it must be answered that it is a moral habit—namely justice, hope, etc.; or injury, etc.; or grammar, etc.; or soldiery, etc.; or agriculture, etc. ¶ Through **Rule H** <note>Rule H asks "When?" (Quando?) and "Where?" (Ubi?).</note>, it is asked: is memory in time? It must be answered yes, because it is "new" <note>Created in time, rather than eternal.</note> through the motion of the subject in which it exists, like the soul moving within a mobile body. And thus it can be said of the other species of Rule H in their own way, which are designated by C, D, and R. We leave their explanation to the observant student for the sake of brevity. Since memory does not have a physical surface, it is asked: is it in a place? It must be answered yes: like a part in its whole without physical contact, just as in the elemental body...

It establishes memory's role in storing knowledge and its relationship to the intellect and will.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the mechanics of memory to the eleventh major part of the work, which focuses on "Questions"—a dialectical method of inquiry using Ramon Llull's symbolic logic. It concludes the discussion on how memory functions through "likenesses" and begins the systematic application of the "Art" to theological and philosophical problems.</meta>

<page-num>97</page-num>
->On Questions<-

...in which elements are composed without contact. Contact indeed hinders composition, as is clear in a heap <note>original: "monte"</note> of coins or stones, which is not truly a "composition" but merely an "aggregation." <note>In medieval philosophy, a true "composition" results in a new unified thing, whereas an "aggregation" is just a pile of separate objects.</note> ¶ It is asked through the first species of the Rule R: how can a person dispose their memory to recollect what they wish to recall but cannot? The answer is that the method consists in "B": namely, that a person should apply the definitions of the principles and the species of the rules to the "likenesses" <note>Similitudines: mental images or representations that resemble the thing remembered.</note> they wish to recall. For just as the intellect reaches the thing represented through a likeness, so the memory recollects the desired object through a likeness. For if someone sees a man similar to their own son, they immediately recall their son through that likeness. ¶ Through the second species of Rule R, it is asked: by what means does the memory forget? To this it must be answered: by a "minority" <note>A state of being diminished or lacking intensity.</note> of discourse through all the principles and species of the rules. For just as "majority" <note>A state of greatness or fullness.</note> causes a positive habit, so "minority" causes a "privative" <note>A habit of lack or absence.</note> one in its own way. ¶ This concludes the discussion of the "Hundred Forms"; a teaching has been given by which the artist <note>The "artist" refers to the practitioner of Llull's logical Art.</note> may know how to discourse upon any form through the principles and rules of this Art. And at the end of the forms, it was shown in what way the liberal arts <note>The traditional curriculum of grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note> can be easily learned through this Art.

<margin>
Other foreign questions that can be solved according to the method by which we will solve the other questions.
</margin>
The reason why we will refer some questions to their proper places is to avoid prolixity, and because those who know this Art will be able to solve them through those places in which their solutions are implied. ¶ Likewise, we say that through the questions we shall pose, we will provide the teachings for formulating questions by abstracting them from the meanings of the rules.

**I**n the table there are 93 columns; and because we avoid prolixity, we do not wish to formulate questions about all the columns, but only about seven columns. Through these, we will provide the teaching for making and solving questions through all the columns of the table.

# The eleventh main part.

## Concerning the eleventh main part, which is about questions.

# Concerning the questions of the first column: B. C. D. T.

<margin>
Rubric of the eleventh main part.

**T**his part is divided into six parts or sections. ¶ The first part concerns the questions we will formulate using the table. ¶ The second part is that which we will formulate regarding questions through the "evacuation" <note>The process of exhausting all possible logical combinations.</note> of the third figure. ¶ The third part is that which we will formulate regarding questions through the multiplication of the fourth figure. ¶ The fourth concerns questions we formulate by the mixing of principles. ¶ The fifth concerns questions we formulate through the nine subjects. ¶ The sixth concerns questions of the "hundred forms." Nevertheless, some questions we shall solve here, and others we shall refer to different places in this book where their solutions are implied and indicated. In those we solve, we will teach the practice of this Art and give the instruction for solving...

The first section of the eleventh main part regarding questions of the first column: B. C. D. T.

But so that it may be seen that the column is general, we wish to repeat it, abstracting some questions from it. And just as this column is general, so the other columns are general. ¶ Through the "chamber" <note>In the Lullian system, a "chamber" is a specific combination of letters—here B, C, and D—representing different principles like Goodness, Greatness, and Duration.</note> B. C. D., it is asked: is there any infinite goodness, immense through "bonification" <note>The act of making or being good; an internal activity of the divine essence.</note> just as eternity is through duration? The answer is "yes"; otherwise, eternity would not be entirely good, nor entirely great, which is impossible. ¶ It is asked: what is infinite and immense goodness? The answer is that it is an essence having in itself many—indeed, infinite and immense—<term>correlatives</term> <note>Correlatives are Llull's unique way of explaining attributes: every attribute (like Goodness) has an active part (the Good-maker), a passive part (the Good-able), and a connecting action (the Act of Good-making).</note> signified through the second species of "C." ¶ It is asked: of what does infinite and immense duration consist? The answer is found through the first and second species of rule "D" and the second of rule "C." And to this, rule "B" testifies: that it consists of the eternal correlatives of goodness and greatness, without which eternity cannot be infinite and immense (B. C. T. B.). ¶ Can goodness be great without distinction? The answer is "no," because there would be no natural reason for the good to act as good, since in every action there must be distinction. It is asked: what is the "great distinction" of goodness? The answer is that it is that which is found in its correlatives in which it is sustained, with which it shares its nature, and is a perfect essence (B. C. T. C.). ¶ Can goodness be great without concordance? And...

# Eleventh part.

It must be answered that no. For just as contrariety relates to non-being, so concordance relates to being. ¶ What is the great greatness of goodness? And it must be answered that it is so that it may have its natural correlatives <note>Llull uses "correlatives" to describe the internal relations of a principle, such as the power to do something, the thing being done, and the act of doing (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving).</note> b. c.t.d. <note>These letters refer to Llull's symbolic alphabet where B often stands for Goodness and C for Greatness.</note> ¶ It is asked: whether an angel is greater than the heavens? And it must be answered that yes. The reason for this is: because an angel has correlatives by which it makes God its object; the heavens, however, do not. ¶ It is asked: what is the great contrariety of the heavens? And it must be answered that it is the immobility which it has, assuming that it could not move itself. Just as fire would have a great contrariety if, through its own lightness <note>In medieval physics, fire was thought to move upward naturally because of its "lightness."</note>, it could not move itself. ¶ It is asked: from what does the great motion of the heavens come? And it must be answered that it comes from its correlatives, designated by the second species of Rule C: b.d.t.b. ¶ Whether there is difference in eternity? And it must be answered that yes: so that it may have its correlatives, without which it would have neither a nature nor infinite goodness. ¶ It is asked: from what does the goodness of the motion of the heavens come? And it must be answered that it comes from itself, as is signified through its correlatives: b.d.t.c. ¶ Whether divine goodness and divine greatness agree? And it must be answered that yes: for without concordance, divine goodness would not have infinite magnifying <note>The process of making or being great.</note>, nor would divine greatness have infinite bonifying <note>The process of making or being good.</note>. ¶ It is asked: what is the great concordance of divine eternity and divine goodness? And to this it must be said that it is the essence of their correlatives: namely, the "bonifier" <note>original: "bonificativi"</note> and "eternifier" <note>original: "eternificativi"</note> which coincide in the first number; and the "bonifiable" and "eternable" in the second; and "to bonify" and "to eternize" in the third. And these three coincide essentially in the one essence of goodness and eternity: b.d.t.d. <note>This triad reflects Llull’s view of the Trinity reflected in every divine attribute.</note> ¶ Whether there is contrariety between divine goodness and eternity? And it must be answered that yes, assuming that eternity were to hinder goodness from its act, and vice-versa—which is impossible. ¶ Supposing that there were contrariety between divine goodness and eternity: it is asked, from what would that contrariety come? And it must be answered that it would come from privative principles <note>Principles defined by what they lack rather than what they are, such as "non-goodness."</note> existing against the positive correlatives of goodness and eternity; which is impossible and a manifest contradiction: b.t.b.c. ¶ Whether difference and concordance can exist in the simple essence of goodness? And it must be answered that yes, assuming that goodness itself has its correlatives signified through the second species of Rule C, which are indeed many through difference, but are the same through essence by concordance. ¶ It is asked: what are difference and concordance in the essence of goodness? And it must be answered through the third species of Rule C that they are what they are: they are still goodness itself: b.t.b.d. ¶ Supposing that the world were eternal: whether difference and contrariety could exist together in its goodness? And it must be answered that no: for no good difference could stand in the presence of eternal contrariety. It is asked: from what does "good difference" come? And it must be answered that it comes from the correlatives designated through the second species of B: b.t.c.b. ¶ Supposing that the world were eternal: whether concordance and contrariety could exist together in its eternal goodness? And it must be answered that no: for otherwise concordance would have a "good act" of both agreeing and opposing from eternity and in eternity—and likewise for contrariety—which is impossible. ¶ It is asked: what is the great contrariety of goodness? And it must be answered that it is when goodness is in a natural subject that has been habituated with moral malice, as in a sinful man: c.d.t.b. ¶ It is asked: what is the great difference of eternity? And it must be answered that it is that which eternity has through its correlatives. ¶ It is asked: from what does the great difference of eternity come? And it must be answered through the first species of Rule D that it comes from itself. For no cause can be prior to eternity: c.d.t.c. ¶ It is asked: what is the great concordance of the heavens? And it must be answered that it is its own correlatives, through which it is what it is and moves itself. ¶ It is asked: from what does the great concordance of the heavens come? And it must be answered that it comes from its correlatives, with which it has motion and nature, and it moves and "natures" <note>To "nature" (naturat) means to impart a specific nature or essence to something.</note> all lower bodies: c.b.t.d. ¶ It is asked: what is the great contrariety of prudence and lust? And it must be answered that it is a moral contrariety. ¶ It is asked: upon what does moral contrariety endure? And it must be answered that it endures through positive and privative habits <note>A "habit" (habitus) is a stable quality or disposition of the soul, like a virtue or vice.</note> resisting one another in a subject where they cannot coexist: c.t.b.c. ¶ Whether justice and prudence have great difference and concordance? And it must be answered that yes, because they cause great acts through great merits. ¶ It is asked: what is the great difference and concordance of justice and prudence? And it must be answered that they are the great relatives <note>Terms or entities that exist only in relation to each other.</note> through which they differ and agree: c.t.b.d. ¶ Whether difference and contrariety can exist in a great essence? And it must be answered that yes, assuming the essence is composite, like the essence of man and of the elements. But in a simple essence, by no means: c.t.c.d. ¶ Supposing that concordance and contrariety were in a simple greatness: it is asked, what would that greatness be? And it must be answered that it would be an impossible essence.

# On questions

¶ It is asked: from what do great concordance and contrariety come? And for this it must be said, through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D in Llull’s Art asks "De quo?" (From what?), investigating the origin or composition of a thing.</note>, which is "concerning itself": For according to greatness, no being lies before d.t.b.c. <note>These letter combinations (d.t.b.c.) are part of Llull's symbolic logic, where letters represent specific principles like Greatness, Duration, or Power.</note> ¶ Whether in eternity there are difference and concordance? And it must be answered that yes: for otherwise in eternity goodness would not be the reason why it itself performs good. For eternity without concordance would have something by which it would stand apart from contrariety [and] idleness <note>original: "ociositate." In Lullian thought, an attribute like "Goodness" cannot be "idle"; it must always be actively "bonifying" or it would not be perfect.</note>, which is impossible. It is asked: from what are the differences of concordance existing in eternity? and it must be answered that they are from their own correlatives <note>Correlatives are the internal relations of a principle—the one acting, the thing acted upon, and the act itself (e.g., the Lover, the Beloved, and Loving).</note> through the first and second species of Rule D. ¶ It is asked: what are difference and concordance in eternity? And it must be answered that they are eternity itself d.t.b.d. ¶ Whether difference and contrariety can exist together in eternity? And it must be answered that no: because if it were so, eternity would be composed of several contrary and corruptible essences, as is evident in the elements. ¶ Assuming that the heavens were made of several contrary essences: it is asked, from what would its duration come? To which it must be said that it would be from positive and privative states, which is impossible d.t.c.d. ¶ Assuming that in the essence of an angel there were concordance and contrariety: it is asked, from what would the angelic duration come? And it must be answered that it would be from its contraries, which is impossible. It is asked: what is the duration of an angel? And it must be answered that it is concordance removed from all contrariety t.b.c.d. ¶ It is asked: whether difference can be the subject of concordance and contrariety? and it must be answered that no: because concordance relates to being, while contrariety relates to non-being in the subject in which they exist. It is asked: what is difference in concordance and contrariety? And it must be answered that difference in concordance is a positive principle, and in contrariety a privative [one]. ¶ It is asked: from what does difference endure? and it must be answered that it endures from its concordant correlatives through an essence removed from all contrarieties.

**I**t is asked: what is the great power of eternity? and it must be answered: that it is infinite and eternal power, as has been signified through its correlatives. It is asked: from what is the great power of eternity? And it must be answered that it is from eternal correlatives. Why is there great power of eternity? and it must be answered that it is because eternity can have infinite and eternal correlatives c.d.t.c. ¶ It is asked: what is the infinite concordance of eternity? and it must be answered that it is an infinite and eternal essence. It is asked: from what is the infinite and eternal essence? And it must be answered that it is from infinite and eternal correlatives, without which it could not be infinite and eternal c.d.t.d. ¶ Supposing that in eternity there were contrariety: it is asked, what would that contrariety be? and it must be answered that it would be an infinite and immense essence, composed of infinite and eternal contraries. It is asked: from what is the greatness of eternity? And it must be answered that it is from its correlatives, without which its great greatness would be finite and idle c.d.t.e. It is asked: what is the great principle of eternity? and it must be answered that it is an eternal and infinite essence. It is asked: from what is the great principle of eternity? And it must be answered that it is from its infinite and eternal correlatives. It is asked: why is there an infinite and eternal principle? And it must be answered that it is because eternity has infinite correlatives separated from all idleness c.e.t.c. ¶ It is asked: what is infinite power? and it must be answered that it is infinite concordance. ¶ It is asked: why is there infinite power? And it must be answered that it is because it has infinite correlatives c.e.t.d. It is asked: from what is infinite power? And it must be answered that it is from its correlatives removed from all contrariety. It is asked: why is there power without contrariety? And it must be answered that it is an infinite essence separated from all contrariety c.e.t.e. ¶ It is asked: why is there an infinite principle? and it must be answered that it is because in itself it has its infinite correlatives in which it rests. It is asked: why is there infinite power? and to this it must be said that it is because it cannot [exist] without a finite subject c.t.c.d. <note>This suggests that for infinite power to be perceived or categorized in this system, it must relate to the finite world.</note> It is asked: what is great concordance? And it must be answered that it is a great essence removed from all contrariety. It is asked: from what is great concordance? and it must be answered that it is from its great correlatives, such as the united, etc. It is asked: what is a great principle? And it must be answered that it is a great concordance removed from all contrariety. It is asked: why is it a great principle? and it must be answered that it is because it has great correlatives c.d.t.e. It is asked: what is the great contrariety of a principle? And it must be answered that it is an essence emptying the principle of its correlatives. It is asked: from what is the great principle? And it must be answered that it is from its correlatives removed from contrariety. Or it is from its correlatives which contrariety can in no way contradict or resist.

d.e.t.e. <note>These letter combinations (d.e.t.e., d.t.c.d., etc.) are symbolic codes used in the Lullian Art. Each letter corresponds to a principle: for example, D often stands for Greatness, E for Duration, and T for the triangle of principles like Concordance and Contrariety.</note> ¶ It is asked: why do eternity and power accord? And it must be answered that they accord so that they may be able to exist and act from eternity and in eternity. ¶ The concordance of eternity and power—it is asked, what is it? And it must be answered that it is the eternally powerful essence. ¶ It is asked: of what is the concordance of eternity and power composed? ¶ To which it must be said that it is composed of the eternizing and the possifying <note>original: "possificatiuo." A Lullian neologism referring to the active power of making things possible.</note>, the eternizable and the possificable, and the acts of eternizing and possifying. d.e.t.d. ¶ It is asked: why can contrary ends not exist from eternity? And it must be answered that it is because in eternity there is rest <note>original: "quies." In medieval scholasticism, eternity is characterized by perfect stillness and a lack of the "becoming" or change found in time.</note>. ¶ It is asked: of what is the rest of eternity composed? And it must be answered that it is composed of its own correlatives <note>Correlatives are the internal parts of any Lullian principle: the agent, the patient, and the action (e.g., the Lover, the Beloved, and Loving).</note> when all contraries are removed. d.e.t.e. ¶ Why can eternal power act from eternity and in eternity? And it must be answered that it is itself eternal primitivity <note>original: "primitiuitas." The state of being a first or primary principle.</note>. ¶ Why is eternal power an eternal principle? And it must be answered: because it can act from eternity and in eternity. d.t.c.d. ¶ Suppose the heaven is eternal: it is asked, what are its eternal concordance and contrariety? And it must be answered that its concordance is one active and passive eternity; and its contrariety would be another eternity that is active and passive: which is impossible. For eternity cannot be made of contraries, since it is infinite. ¶ Of what is eternal contrariety composed? And it must be answered that it is composed of a natural subject and a moral habit: just as if a cloaked man were wearing a cloak of fire <note>original: "cappa ignitiua." A metaphor for how a subject (the person) is affected by an external or added quality (the habit of fire).</note>. d.t.c.e. ¶ It is asked: what is the principle of eternity? To which it must be answered: namely, that it is the concordance of its correlatives. ¶ It is asked: of what is the concordance of eternity composed? And it must be answered that it is from the correlatives of eternity. e.t.c.d. ¶ It is asked: why can concordance and contrariety not be a single power? And from this it must be said: because concordance tends toward being, but contrariety tends toward non-being. ¶ It is asked: what is the contrariety of body and soul in man? And it must be answered that it is from contrary ends or contrary correlatives. e.t.c.e. ¶ It is asked: what is the power of prudence and the power of pride? And it must be answered that the power of pride is a privative habit; but the power of prudence is a positive one. ¶ It is asked: why are the power of pride and the power of prudence not a single power? To which it must be said: because the definition of concordance cannot bring them into accord in a single end, since they are contrary principles. e.t.d.e. ¶ It is asked: why can power not be made of contrary principles? And to this it must be said: For power has its principles as relatives and segregated from contrariety and concordance. ¶ It is asked: of what are contrary principles composed? And it must be answered that they are from contrary ends. t.c.d.e. ¶ It is asked: why is concordance a primary principle, but contrariety a consecutive one? And it must be answered that concordance is a positive principle, but contrariety is a privative one. ¶ It is asked: what is the primitivity of concordance and the posteriority of contrariety? And it must be answered that the primitivity of concordance is when many things relate to one; the posteriority of contrariety is, namely, when many things do not relate to one. ¶ It is asked: whether concordance and contrariety come from one and the same principle? And it must be answered: no, because they do not relate to one end.

And it must be answered: as great as its correlatives are. ¶ It is asked: why is the heaven mobile? And it must be answered that they are as many as are the correlatives of the divine intellect; otherwise, the divine eternity would be hindered by eternal contrariety, which is impossible. ¶ It is asked...

# On questions

¶ It is asked: from what are the **correlatives** <note>Lullian "correlatives" are the internal active, passive, and verbal components of a principle—for example, the power of eternizing, that which is eternized, and the act of eternity itself.</note> of eternity derived? And it must be answered that they are from themselves; and eternal **contrariety** cannot hinder this because it is not d.f.t.e. ¶ It is asked: why does **eternity** not have **quantity**? And it must be answered that it is because it consists of infinite correlatives. It is asked: how great is the act of eternizing of eternity? And it must be answered that it is as great as the divine intellect. ¶ It is asked: from what is the act of eternizing derived? And it must be answered that it is from the eternizer and the eternized, just as the divine understanding is from the one who understands and that which is understood. d.t.d.e. ¶ It is asked: why, in eternity, is **contrariety** not a principle? And it must be answered that it is because eternity is neither corruptible nor sinful. ¶ Suppose that there were contrariety in eternity: it is asked, of what would it consist? And it must be answered that it would consist of the contrary-making and the eternizing, the "contrariable" and the eternizable, and the acts of being contrary and being eternal—which is impossible. d.t.d.f. ¶ It is asked: from what is the **medium** existing between **fortitude** and **faith** derived? And it must be answered that it is from quantities, just as a genus is derived from its species. It is asked: how much contrariety is there between faith and unbelief? And it must be answered that there is as much as they differ from each other; yet that contrariety is not in a subject outside the soul, for in such a subject unbelief and faith cannot stand together. d.t.e.f. ¶ It is asked: why is eternity the first principle? And it must be answered that the act of eternizing is the first "middle" <note>In Lullian logic, the "middle" (medium) is the connecting link or the operational process between a beginning and an end.</note> within it. It is asked: how great is the medium in the eternal principle? And it must be answered that it is as great as that which is measured by eternity and the eternized. ¶ It is asked: from what does the eternal act of originating derive? And it must be answered that it is from the eternizing originator and the eternized originated. e.f.t.d. ¶ Assuming that the **intellect** were not joined with the body of a man: it is asked, why is there a man? And it must be answered that a man exists because the second species <note>Refers to a specific category in Llull's "Rule D" regarding the nature of substances.</note> does not fail him. d.r.e. It is asked: of what is a man composed? And it must be answered, through the second species of Rule D, that he is composed of body and a rational soul. ¶ It is asked: how great is the contrariety of a man? And it must be answered that it is as great as his parts are contrary to one another. e.f.t.e. ¶ It is asked: is the **power of God** as great as His **intellect**? And it must be answered that it is so, because they are the same principle. It is asked: why is there no **matter** in the divine power? And it must be answered that it is because there is infinity, in which matter cannot exist. e.f.t.f. It is asked: why must there be a **medium** in the divine power? And it must be answered that in the divine understanding, the act of understanding is the medium; and this is proved by Rule E. It is asked: how great is the "power-ing" <note>original: "posse." Here used as a noun to denote the active capacity or magnitude of the divine power.</note> of the divine power? And it must be answered that it is as great as its infinite **possifier** <note>original: "possificatiuus." A term for the active power that makes things possible.</note> and its **possificable**. e.t.d.e. ¶ It is asked: of what are the principles of man composed? Go to the "Ladder of the Angel" <note>A specific diagram or hierarchy in the Lullian system representing the ascent of the mind through various levels of being.</note> in Rule D of the second figure, and go to the second species of Rule D. It is asked: why does man have **free will**? And it must be answered through the first species of Rule E: because he is composed of contrary principles; furthermore, through the second species, it is indicated that he has free will so that he may acquire **merit**. e.t.d.f. ¶ It is asked: why is the power of the **imagination** not composed of contraries? And it must be answered that it is because its "middle" is simple. It is asked: of what is the medium of the imagination composed? Go to the second species of Rule D. It is asked: how great is the medium of the imagination? And it must be answered that it is as great as that which is measured by the imagining and the imaginable. e.t.e.f. ¶ It is asked: why does man have the power of existing and acting? And it must be answered because his principles are naturally disposed to this. It is asked: how much can a man exist and act? And it must be answered that he can do so as much as his principles are disposed to it. f.t.d.e. ¶ It is asked: of what are the principles of the intellect composed? Go to the first and second species of D. It is asked: why do the principles of the intellect exist? Go to Rule E. ¶ It is asked: how many principles of the intellect are there? Go to the correlatives of the intellect. f.t.d.f. It is asked: from what is the **instinct of the heavens** <note>original: "instinctus celi." This refers to the celestial influence or the natural "drive" exerted by the stars and spheres on the earthly world.</note> derived? Go to the first and second species of Rule D. It is asked: how great is the instinct of the imagination? Go to the chapter on the imagination, through the intellect and through the indicated medium. f.t.e.f. It is asked: why is there a medium of the intellect? And it must be answered that it is because without a medium, the intellect would not be a principle of understanding. ¶ It is asked: how great is the act of understanding between the one who understands and the thing understood? Go to the chapter on the intellect, and to the paragraphs indicated by the "beginning" and "middle," etc., and to the paragraph on quantity. t.d.e.f. It is asked: from what is the **influence** flowing into man derived? Go to the paragraphs on contrariety, the principle, and the medium, which concern the subject of man within the subject of the heavens. It is asked: why do the heavens act upon man? Go to Rule E as it exists in the subject of the heavens and in the subject of man. It is asked: how much are the heavens imaginable? Go to the quantity existing in the subject of the heavens, and in the subject of man, and in the subject of the imagination through its power.
