**I**t is asked: why can God do as much as he can through his wisdom and will? And it must be answered through rule *e* <note>In Lull's logic, "Rule E" usually refers to the question "Why?" (Quare), seeking the formal or final cause.</note> and through the first species of rule *g*. For God is as infinite through his infinite power as through his infinite intellect and will. It is asked: how great is divine power? And it must be answered that it is as great as is knowable through an infinite intellect and an infinite will. It is asked: of what kind is divine power? And it must be answered that it is of such a kind as is the will itself. (e. f. t. e.) It is asked: why is divine power an infinite principle? And it must be answered that because through his intellect, infinite things are spoken <note>original: "fata," perhaps meaning "expressed" or "decreed" in this context</note>. It is asked: how much is divine power knowable? It must be answered that it is as much as his intellect is infinite. (e. f. t. f.) It is asked: why is "to be able" <note>Lull uses the infinitive *posse* as a noun to describe the active capacity of God.</note> the **middle** in divine power? And it must be answered because in the divine intellect, "to understand" is the middle. ¶ It is asked: how great is the "to be able" of divine power? And it must be answered that it is as great as is divine understanding. (e. f. t. g.) It is asked: why does the **end** consist as much through divine power as through divine intellect? And it must be answered by this: that God is infinite as much through his "to be able" as through his "to understand." It is asked: how great is the end of divine power? And it must be answered that it is as great as the end of the intellect. It is asked: of what kind is the end of divine power? And it must be answered that it is such as is fitting for infinite **powering-action** <term>possificare: a technical Lullian term for the active exercise of power by the Powerer upon the Powered</term>. (e. g. t. e.) ¶ It is asked: why is divine power an infinite principle? And it must be answered that its "to be able" is loved through the divine will. It is asked: what kind of power is infinitely loved? And it must be answered that it is that which has infinite correlatives. (e. g. t. f.) It is asked: why can the divine will love one man more than all? **Go to** the definition of will, and of power, and of the **middle**, and also to the scale of the middle of the **second figure**. ¶ It is asked: what kind of man is more lovable by the divine will? And it must be answered that it is he whom the divine will can love more. It is asked: why is some man <note>Likely referring to Christ in Lull's theological framework.</note> more lovable than all [others]? And it must be answered because the divine will is absolute in loving. It is asked: by what middle can God love a man more? **Go to** the definition of will, power, and the middle, and also to the scale of the middle. (e. g. t. g.) It is asked: why is the end of divine power as lovable as the end of divine will? And it must be said that divine power is as much powerful as the divine will is willing. ¶ It is asked: what kind of end can the divine will love more? And it must be answered that it is that which the divine intellect can understand more. ¶ And in this step, the intellect knows which **law** <note>Lull often uses "lex" (law) to refer to different religions, such as Christianity, Islam, or Judaism.</note> is more lovable. (e. t. e. f.) ¶ It is asked: why could God begin a new world? **Go to** rule *e* and to the definition of the middle. It is asked: how great is the **novelty of the world**? And it must be answered that it is as great as the divine power can measure it. ¶ And in this step, the intellect knows it is **impossible for the world to be from eternity**. (e. t. e. g.) <note>Lull argues against the Aristotelian concept of an eternal universe, insisting that the world must have a beginning in time.</note> ¶ It is asked: why can God begin a greater beginning? And it must be answered because he can begin a greater end. It is asked: in what beginning does God have greater power? **Go to** rule *g* and to the definition of power and the end. (e. t. f. g.) ¶ It is asked: why can God cause a greater middle and a greater end? And it must be answered because he has infinite power. ¶ It is asked: what kind of thing is the **greater created middle**? And it must be answered that it is that in which divine power has greater "to be able," and in which that power itself can more greatly rest. ¶ It is asked: how great is the greater created middle? And it must be answered that it is as great as God can cause it. (f. g. t. e.) It is asked: why does God love some beginning as much as divine wisdom can understand it? And it must be answered because the divine will can do as much through loving as the divine intellect through understanding. ¶ A beginning that is greater, how lovable is it? And it must be answered that it is as lovable as it is intelligible. What kind of beginning is more lovable? And it must be answered that it is that which is more intelligible. (f. g. t. f.) It is asked: what kind of middle is intelligible and lovable? To which it must be said that it is that which God can more understand and love. ¶ The greater middle, how much is it intelligible and lovable? And it must be answered that it is as much as God can understand and love. (f. g. t. g.) It is asked: what kind of end is more intelligible and lovable? And it must be answered that it is that which God can more understand and love. ¶ It is asked: how great is the greater end? And it must be answered that it is as great as God can understand and love. ¶ And in this step, the intellect knows which **law is true** through the scale of difference and concordance. (f. t. e. f.) It is asked: why does the divine intellect understand a greater created principle than [our] intellect can understand? **Go to** the definition of intellect and principle and majority, and to rule *e*. ¶ It is asked: how great is the greater...

the intellect. And it must be answered that it was then when the greater end was begun.

# On Questions
## concerning the evacuation of the third figure.

<margin>The second part of the eleventh principal [part] which is about the questions of the evacuation of the third figure.</margin>

**I**N the **evacuation** <term>evacuation (evacuatio) — the process of systematically working through and "emptying out" all possible logical combinations in a table</term> of the third figure, many general questions and their solutions have already been made; and thus particular questions and solutions can be made, by holding to the same method which we held in the universal ones. For the particular mode arises and is derived from the universal mode, just as an effect is derived from its cause.

¶ It is said in **Cell B. C.** <note>Llull uses a "Great Alphabet" where letters represent concepts. Cell B.C. is where the qualities of B and C overlap.</note> that **Goodness** is great; and afterwards [it is asked] whether Goodness is great. And because **B** signifies: **God, Goodness, Difference, Justice, and Avarice**; and **C** signifies: **Angel, Magnitude, Concordance, Prudence, and Gluttony**, as has already been stated in the alphabet:

¶ Therefore many particular questions can be drawn from Cell B. C. For instance, when it is asked: whether **Divine Goodness** is great? Whether in Divine Goodness there are distinct correlatives? Whether in Divine Goodness there is **Concordance**? Afterward it can be asked: What is "Great Goodness" in God? What are the correlatives in Divine Goodness? And what is its Concordance in Divine Goodness? And then it can be asked through the second species of Rule C: What does Divine Great Goodness have in itself that is coessential to it? And the same can be said regarding Difference and Concordance. And afterward it can be asked through the third species of Rule C, seeking thus: What is Divine Great Goodness in another? And what is Divine Difference in another? And what is Divine Concordance in another? Then, in what manner does Divine Great Goodness have something in another? What does Divine Difference have in another? And what does Divine Concordance have in another? And once all these are done, any question can be solved by holding the same method we held in solving general questions: descending from the universal solution to the particular, agreeing [with principles], and avoiding inconsistency. For no universal is contrary to its own particular, and vice versa. But to provide examples of this would be too long. Therefore, we leave the solutions to the practitioner of this Art for the sake of brevity. For if a question is made in any way concerning Divine Goodness and Magnitude, let the solution be extracted from the definition of God, and from the definition of Goodness and Magnitude.

## On the questions of the multiplication of the fourth figure.

<margin>The third part of the tenth principal part on questions.</margin>
**M**ultiplication of the **fourth figure** <term>fourth figure — the most famous Lullian tool, consisting of three concentric circles that rotate to create triplets of concepts</term> is done in five ways, as has been said. And just as the multiplication occurs in five ways, so the questions can be formed in five ways. And thus we shall say something about the first way and the others. ¶ The first way is divided into three parts. ¶ The first is when one proves that the world is **new** <note>original: "mundus est nouus"; in medieval philosophy, "new" means the world had a beginning in time and is not eternal</note> through twenty reasons. And this is done through column b.c.d. And just as it is said of the world, so it can be said of those things which are designated by b.c.e. in the **alphabet** <term>alphabet — Lull's system of assigning letters to concepts (e.g., B = Goodness, C = Greatness, D = Eternity)</term>, by making solutions for each designated thing in its own way. Such as **b**, which signifies God, goodness, difference, justice, or avarice; and so for **c**, which signifies an angel, greatness, etc.; and **d**, which signifies heaven, eternity, and so forth. And thus every particular question contains its own involved solution. This solution can indeed be reduced to the **Art** <note>The "Art" refers to Lull’s overall system of logic and demonstration</note> by following the method of this Art. And just as we have spoken regarding the first way, so it can be said of the others in their own way. ¶ And let this suffice regarding the multiplication of the fourth figure for the sake of brevity.

## On the questions of the mixture of principles and rules.

<margin>The fourth part of the tenth principal part on questions.</margin>
**I**n the mixture of principles and rules, it is shown when any principle runs through other principles and rules, making a **predicate** <term>predicate — the part of a sentence or logic statement that says something about the subject</term> out of a subject, and vice-versa: such as "great goodness," "eternal goodness," "powerful goodness," and so on. Also "good greatness," "eternal greatness," "powerful greatness," and so on. Therefore, if a question is made concerning goodness and greatness, or concerning goodness and eternity, etc., let one return to the chapter on goodness and the paragraph on goodness and greatness. And if the question is about goodness and eternity, let one return to the paragraph on goodness and eternity; and so for the others. And let the solutions be extracted from those places in which the solutions are marked, and in this way: ¶ It is said in the first paragraph in the chapter on goodness that goodness is in itself the reason for a "good" that it should act or produce what is good. But because it is a "great" reason doubled for a "good" through greatness so that it might produce a **great good**, therefore, if it is asked whether goodness is the reason in God for Him to produce a great good, let it be granted through those things which were said above. ¶ Furthermore, it is said in the second paragraph in the chapter on goodness that goodness through **duration** <note>original: "durationem"; refers to the principle of Eternity/Consistency</note> is durable; and thus through duration there is a triple reason so that the "good" might act as good, great, and durable, as is clear. ¶ If a question is made as to whether divine goodness is the reason for God that He Himself produces an eternal or durable good, let one return to the chapter on goodness in the third paragraph. And let the solution be drawn from the text by reason of the mixture, the definition, of goodness and duration; and so for the others. ¶ Furthermore: what is that great good which God produces? Let one return to the chapter on goodness and the rules through which goodness is led down; such as when it is asked, "What is goodness?" And then let one answer the question through that text according to the definition of goodness. If it is asked, "From what does God produce good?" Let one return to the chapter on goodness and to the paragraph of **rule d** <note>Rule D usually refers to the question "Whence?" or "Of what?" (De quo)</note> in which it is asked of what goodness is made; and from that text let the solution be extracted; and so for the others. ¶ Just as we gave the example of the goodness of God, so it can be said of the goodness of an angel in its own way, and of the goodness of justice, and of the goodness of prudence, and of the malice of avarice and gluttony; and so of others in their own specific way. ¶ And let these things suffice concerning the questions of mixture for the sake of brevity. And this is because the Art is sufficient for making and solving other questions. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that the mixture of principles is a very general subject for making many questions. And since in the text the solutions are involved and marked.
¶ And this is the end of the fourth part of the tenth principal part.

Solution in the same rule. ¶ We have made these questions about God through principles and rules; wherefore if a foreign question <note>A "foreign" question is one not explicitly listed in the text but which the student should now be able to solve using the system.</note> regarding God arises, let it be applied to the text or the place appropriate to it, and let it be solved through that place by holding to the affirmation or negation in such a way that the text is not destroyed. ¶ Further, if many questions are made about God, let the method of the third figure and the seven columns mentioned before be maintained, in which we have made questions; and let solutions be given to them through the figures themselves. And the chapter on application teaches this. ¶ Furthermore, if an artist <term>artist — a practitioner of the Lullian "Art," a system of logic used to organize all knowledge</term> wants to have many middle terms <note>Logical links used to connect a subject and a predicate in a syllogism.</note> to prove something about God, let him return to the chapter on the multiplication of the figure of the Art, which teaches how to find many middle terms and teaches how to prove through the "prior" and the "posterior." <note>original: "per prius et posterius" — referring to a priori (from cause to effect) and a posteriori (from effect to cause) reasoning.</note> ¶ Since one cannot prove anything about God through a prior cause <note>Because God has no cause preceding Him.</note>, if a question requires proof through "equivalence" <note>original: "per equiparantiam" — a Lullian method of arguing from one attribute to another of equal status.</note>: such as if someone wanted to prove whether there is some infinite power, let it be proven through infinite eternity. ¶ Further, regarding what he wants to prove through equivalence, such as when it is asked: why in the soul are the intellect, memory, and will equal? To which it should be responded: because God is equally intelligible, lovable, and recallable. ¶ Further, if it is asked: why do three "correlatives" <term>correlatives — Lull's theory that every essence consists of an active, a passive, and the act itself (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and loving).</term> suffice in any power of the soul, as designated through the second species of c? It must be answered that in any divine reason, three correlatives are sufficient. ¶ If it is asked: why did God create one world and not many? It is proven thus: namely, that God is one; therefore he created one world. ¶ If it is asked: why does God love one creature more than another? It should be answered: because when he created the world, he understands the greatest end of creation that he could understand. ¶ Furthermore, if it is asked: whether it is more fitting for God to create greater things than lesser things? It should be answered that it is so. For greater things agree more with his "dignities" <note>Lull's term for the divine attributes like Goodness and Greatness.</note> than do lesser things; and so it is with others.

**W**hy did the angel sin after God created him entirely good? And it should be answered through the definition of "majority" and "minority." <note>These are Lullian "Principles of Relation." # Concerning Questions

<margin>On questions about angels according to the rules.</margin>

**Q**uestion is asked: by what means is it proved that angels exist? The solution is in the first rule <note>In the Lullian system, the "First Rule" usually asks "Whether" (Utrum) a thing exists.</note>. Question is asked: by what is an angel defined? The solution is in the second rule. ¶ Question is asked: what is the nature of an angel? Question is asked concerning the actions and passions <note>In medieval philosophy, "passions" refer to things experienced or acted upon a subject, the opposite of "actions."</note> of angels. ¶ Since an angel does not have imagination <note>Angels were thought to be pure intellects without physical sense organs or the "internal" sense of imagination used by humans.</note>, by what means does it understand imaginable things? ¶ All these questions are solved through the second rule mentioned above. ¶ Question is asked: what are the innate principles of an angel? Question is asked: what is the form of an angel, and what is its matter? Question is asked: to whom does an evil angel belong? The solution is in the third rule. ¶ Question is asked: in what way does an angel have causes? Question is asked: whether an angel rests with one end <term>end (finis): the goal or purpose for which a thing exists</term> or with many? The solutions are in the fourth rule. ¶ Question is asked concerning the continuous and discrete quantity of angels: assuming that an angel does not have matter, can it receive passions? The solutions are in the fifth rule. Question is asked concerning the specific qualities of an angel, with which it acts specifically; and likewise concerning the appropriated qualities with which it acts morally. The solutions are in the sixth rule. ¶ Question is asked concerning the succession and continuation of angels: since an angel is not corporeal, does it have measures of time? The solutions are in the seventh rule. ¶ Whether an angel is located in a place? ¶ Whether an angel passes through a medium? The solutions are in the eighth rule. Question is asked: by what means does an angel exist in itself and act outside of itself? ¶ Question is asked: by what means does an angel suffer? The solutions are in the ninth rule. Question is asked: with what does one angel understand another? ¶ Question is asked: with what does an angel tempt men? Question is asked: with what does an angel move stones? The solutions are in the tenth rule, marked by the letter K. ¶ Whether an angel suffers through fire? We say that it does: as is evident through the prior argument and through the first species of *e*, and through the second of *g*, and through the definition of divine power. For if God wills that an angel can move stones without a body, likewise by divine power it can suffer by fire. Question is asked: whether angels are our messengers and helpers? And it must be answered that they are. ¶ Because just as the heaven with its innate principles is a co-helper to the principles of elemental things effectively and naturally—so that they may have their own acts—so angels help: not so that we might have moral virtues <note>Meaning angels assist natural processes, but moral virtue requires human will and grace.</note>, and this can be proved through rules *b* and *c*.

### Concerning questions of the third subject, which is about heaven, through principles.

<margin>Concerning questions of the third subject, which is about heaven, through principles.</margin>

**W**hether the goodness of heaven causes inferior goodnesses? Question is asked: why do monstrosities <note>original: "monstruositates." The solution is in the second. ¶ Whether heaven moves itself? The solution is in the third. ¶ Whether heaven with its power can move lower things? The solution is in the fourth. ¶ Since heaven does not have an intellect, how does it ordain itself to move lower things? The solution is in the fifth. ¶ Since heaven does not have a will, what is the cause that it moves lower things to have an appetite? The solution is in the sixth. ¶ Whether heaven with its power moves lower powers beyond the capacity of elemental, vegetative, or sensitive beings—just as charity <note>Divine Love or Grace.</note> moves the will beyond its own powers to love the highest object and its neighbor? And it must be answered that it does: heaven, however, does so naturally, while charity does so morally; go to the seventh. ¶ Question is asked: whether heaven has innate truth with which it causes lower truths? The solution is in the eighth. ¶ Since heaven does not have a will, it is asked whether it has delight? The solution is in the ninth. ¶ Whether heaven has innate differences to dispose the differences of lower elemental things? The solution is in the tenth. ¶ Whether the concordance of heaven is an innate principle for it, with which it disposes lower concordances and aptitudes? The solution is in the eleventh. ¶ Whether heaven has innate contrariety? The solution is in the twelfth. ¶ Whether heaven has an innate principle with which it originates lower aptitudes? And it must be answered that it does. For just as a craftsman with his soul brings forth the shape of a chest <note>original: "arche"</note> from potentiality into act, so heaven brings forth sensible and vegetative forms; go to the thirteenth. ¶ Whether heaven has an innate medium <term>medium: a middle term or connecting link in a process</term> with which it moves and disposes lower media? The solution is in the fourteenth. ¶ Question is asked: what is the greater end of heaven naturally, without which it cannot rest? The solution is in the fifteenth. ¶ Whether heaven has "majority" <note>The principle of being "greater" or "superior."</note> with which it disposes and habituates lower aptitudes? The solution is in the sixteenth. ¶ Whether heaven has innate equality with which it equals and proportions lower equalities? The solution is in the seventeenth. ¶ Question is asked: what is the "minority" of heaven? The solution is in the eighteenth.

<vocab>heaven, corruptible, mobile, correlative, species, miracle, motion, will, soul, fire, quality, time, human, principles, intellect, virtues, sin, embryo</vocab>

# Eleventh part.

<margin>On questions of the heavens through the rules.</margin>
**Q**uestion is asked: why is heaven not from eternity since it is not itself corruptible? <note>original: "corruptibile"; in medieval science, the heavens were made of a "fifth element" (quintessence) that did not decay like earthly matter.</note> Go to the rule B of the third subject.
¶ Assuming that heaven does not move itself: the question is asked whether it would be the "first mobile" <term>first mobile (primum mobile): in the Ptolemaic system, the outermost sphere that gives motion to all others</term> by nature? The solution is in rule C. ¶ Question is asked: does heaven have innate correlatives formally and naturally, without which it could not cause lower correlatives? The solution is in the second species of C. ¶ Question is asked: does heaven receive "the more" and "the less"? <note>In Aristotelian logic, things that admit "more or less" (like heat) are qualities, whereas substances usually do not.</note> The solution is in the third species of C. ¶ Question is asked: what does heaven have in lower things? The solution is in the fourth species of C. ¶ Question is asked: why is heaven incorruptible? The solution is in the first species of D. ¶ Whether heaven has specified principles with which it acts specifically? The solution is in the second species of D. ¶ Question is asked: can the motion of heaven resist miracles? The solution is in the third species of D. ¶ Question is asked: is heaven necessary? The solution is in the first species of E. ¶ Whether without the motion of heaven there could be lower natural mobilities? And the answer is no. For just as the will without charity could not have the power to love God above itself, nor to love its enemy, so fire, etc., could not move toward water naturally without the motion of the heaven. For the heaven is prior, and the fire is posterior. And go to the second species of E. ¶ Question is asked: why does heaven act with oblique quantity <note>original: "quātitate obliqua"; referring to the circular/angled movement of the planets and stars</note> in itself, but with straight quantity outside itself? ¶ Question is asked: does heaven have discrete quantities since it is in continuous motion? Solutions are in rule F. ¶ Question is asked: why does heaven act through a specific species? ¶ Question is asked: are heat and dryness qualities appropriated to the sun? Solutions are in rule G. ¶ Question is asked: in what way does the time of heaven have the logic of cause and caused, with heaven being subject to it? Solution is in rule H. ¶ Whether heaven is in a place? Solution is in rule I. ¶ Question is asked: in what way does heaven act on lower things? And it must be answered that it acts through its own mode in a lower mode: just as the prior acts in the posteriority through its own mode. ¶ Question is asked: with what does heaven act in lower things? And it must be answered that it acts with its innate principles: just as a cause which, with its causes, causes causes.

And the sense causes the appropriated quality: go to the fifth [section]. ¶ It is asked: what is the sensibility of a stone, and from what does it arise? <note>original: "sensibilitas lapidis"; in Lullian thought, this explores whether a non-living thing has a capacity to be perceived.</note> And the answer must be that it arises from the disposition <term>habit <gloss>a stable quality or state of being</gloss></term> of the senses. And the answer is that it does not; just as the second vision of the eyes does not remain when the eyes are closed. And go to rule H. ¶ It is asked: where does the sense perceive the sensed object? Solution in rule I. ¶ Whether the sense reaches the substance? And it must be said that it does: for it is joined with it; however, not insofar as it is separated from it. Just as sight does not reach the substance of a stone because it is not joined with it. ¶ It is asked: by what manner does the sensitive faculty <term>sensitiva <gloss>the power of the soul that perceives through the five senses</gloss></term> perceive the sensed object? Solution in the species of rule K. ¶ It is asked whether the sensitive faculty perceives the sensed object with the likeness that it perceives: which likeness is the disposition of the sensed thing: like a cloak to a cloaked person; and go to the second rule K. <note>original: "cappa cappati"; a standard medieval analogy for how an accidental property (like a color or a feeling) is "worn" by a substance without being part of its essential nature.</note> ¶ Whether the sensitive faculties are joined with their own proper subject: To which it must be said that they are, as is evident through the first definition of concordance and the mean: and so that the principle may have a mean through which it can pass to its end. ¶ Whether the sense is joined with the sensed object: for example, with a stone or an audible thing, etc. And the answer is no: because the disposition is appropriated and new: just like a cloak on a cloaked person: for the cloak is not joined [fused] with the cloaked person, but is applied to him through contact.

# On the questions of the ninth subject, which is on virtues and vices.

<margin>On the questions of the ninth subject which is on virtues and vices.</margin>
**J**ust as the common sense <note>original: "sensus cōis"; the faculty in medieval psychology that integrates data from the five individual senses</note> perceives sensible things through its particular senses, so the soul, through its powers, gives virtue to things capable of virtue <gloss>virtuitificabilia</gloss> and gives vice to things capable of vice. And it does this by means of the principles of this Art—using the virtues and vices systematically <gloss>artificialiter</gloss>, just as a logician uses syllogisms <gloss>logical arguments</gloss> along with the principles of logic. For this reason, we intend to pose questions according to the aforementioned method, and the solutions are indicated through that same method. And first, we shall speak of justice.

# On the questions of justice through the principles.

<margin>On the questions of justice through principles.</margin>
**I**t is asked: whether justice, along with its "goodness," causes good and just things? Solution: go to the first paragraph of "Justice" in the ninth subject. ¶ Whether justice, along with its "greatness," magnifies great justifiable things? The solution is in the second paragraph. ¶ It is asked: in what manner does justice endure? The solution is in the third. ¶ Whether the soul accustoms itself <gloss>habitues se</gloss> by the power of justice, and how do they cause just things? The solution is in the fourth. ¶ It is asked: in what manner does justice exist in potential? The solution is in the fifth. ¶ It is asked: in what manner is justice lovable? The solution is in the sixth. ¶ It is asked: how does justice arise and how is it applied to laws <note>original: "iura"</note>? The solution is in the seventh. ¶ Whether the soul, without virtue, can cause justice, and whether justice can cause justifiable things? The solution is in the eighth. ¶ It is further asked: in what manner can a jurist easily learn natural laws? The solution is in the same [paragraph]. ¶ Whether justice causes rest along with justifiable things? The solution is in the tenth. ¶ It is asked: in what manner is justice known? The solution is in the eleventh. ¶ It is asked: by what means is injury <gloss>injustice</gloss> recognized? The solution is in the twelfth. ¶ It is asked: in what manner do justice and law differ? The solution is in the thirteenth. ¶ Likewise, it is asked: in what manner does justice relate to natural principles? The solution is in the same [paragraph]. ¶ Whether justice has a specific "middle"? The solution is in the fourteenth. ¶ It is asked: what is the end <gloss>purpose</gloss> of justice? The solution is in the fifteenth. ¶ It is asked: what are the causes of the greatness of justice? The solution is in the sixteenth. ¶ It is asked: with which principle of this Art does justice have the greatest agreement? The solution is in the seventeenth. ¶ It is asked: by what means is "lesser justice" recognized? The solution is in the eighteenth.

# Eleventh part

Why does justice exist? The solution is in the second species of E. It is asked whether justice has **continuous quantity?** <note>In scholastic thought, "continuous quantity" refers to things that are unbroken, like a line or time, rather than "discrete quantity" like individual numbers.</note> The solution is in the first species of F. ¶ Whether justice in the subject in which it exists is "in the making" <note>original: "in fieri"</note> or in a "completed state" <note>original: "in facto esse"</note>? The solution is in the second species of F. ¶ **It is asked** what is the **quality proper to justice?** The solution is in the first species of G. It is asked which qualities are appropriate to justice? The solution is in the second species of G. ¶ **It is asked** in what manner does justice exist locally and successively? The solution is in rule H. ¶ **Since justice is neither made of points nor lines**, in what manner does it exist in a place and overcome things capable of being justified? The solution is in rule I. It is asked in what manner justice consists in theory and practice? The solution is in the first rule of K. ¶ **It is asked**, with what things is justice that which it is? The solution is in the second rule of K. It is asked, with what is justice generated and corrupted <gloss>born and destroyed</gloss>? And it must be answered that it is generated with its positive principles and corrupted with the privation <gloss>the absence or loss</gloss> of its accidents. ¶ **It is asked**, how does natural law <term>ius naturale: a system of law based on a close observation of human nature and based on values intrinsic to human nature</term> exist? Go to the paragraph on modality mentioned above. ¶ **It is asked**, with what does positive law <term>ius positiuũ: man-made laws of a particular society, as opposed to natural law</term> exist? And it must be answered that it exists with believing and supposing, and with the contingencies targeted by the will and memory outside of the understanding.

## On questions of prudence through principles.

<margin>On questions of prudence through principles.</margin>

**W**hether the soul causes things capable of prudence through prudence in the same way that the common sense <term>sensus cõmũis: the internal faculty that integrates data from the five individual senses</term> perceives with its particular sensible things? And it must be answered that it is so; otherwise, prudence would not be a specific virtue, nor would the soul have that by which it could foresee and choose the good and avoid the evil. It is asked in what manner a person habituates <gloss>trains or conditions</gloss> themselves in prudence? The solution is in the first paragraph of prudence in the ninth subject. ¶ **It is asked** whether magnifying goodness is part of the nature of prudence? The solution is in the second. It is asked in what manner one instance of prudence prevails over another? The solution is in the third. ¶ **Whether prudence without providence <note>original: "prouidentia," here meaning foresight</note> is equally powerful?** The solution is in the fourth. It is asked: of what is prudence a habit <gloss>a stable disposition of the mind</gloss>? The solution is in the fifth. It is asked what kind of prudence is primary <note>original: "primitiua"</note> and what kind is derivative? The solution is in the sixth. It is asked in what manner is prudence directed: by a straight line or an oblique one? The solution is in the seventh. ¶ **Whether all things that can be foreseen are useful?** The solution is in the eighth. It is asked why prudence chooses labor? The solution is in the ninth. It is asked in what manner prudence and imprudence differ? The solution is in the tenth. ¶ **Whether prudence can exist without any other virtue?** The solution is in the eleventh. The solution is in the fourteenth. ¶ **It is asked** in what manner the prudent and the imprudent person relate to their end <gloss>their ultimate goal</gloss>? The solution is in the fifteenth. It is asked in what manner prudence and imprudence are opposed in superiority? The solution is in the sixteenth. It is asked whether prudence and imprudence struggle against each other in equality? The solution is in the seventeenth. ¶ **Whether prudence can exist in a subject in a state of inferiority <note>original: "minoritate"</note>?** And it must be answered that it cannot. For it is in the nature of prudence to choose superiority <gloss>the greater good</gloss>; and go to the eighteenth.

# On Questions

...whether quality can belong to prudence. And it must be answered that it can: just as an instrument can be bad when a bad agent <note>The "agent" is the person performing the action.</note> acts poorly with it; and go to the second species of G. ¶ It is asked whether prudence stands more upon **foreseeing the future** or upon **choosing in the present**. To which it must be said that it is the former: the reason for this is that future things are more numerous through contingencies <note>Events that might or might not happen.</note> while present things are known through experience; and go to rule H. ¶ It is asked in which principles prudence mostly consists. And it must be answered that it is in **goodness, intellect, virtue, difference, purpose, and majority**; and go to rule I. It is asked in what manner a person uses prudence: the solution is in the first rule of K. It is asked with which principles prudence is strong: the solution is in the second rule of L. ¶ It is asked whether the **essence of prudence** rests, increases, or decreases in the subject in which it exists. And it must be answered that it does not, because a <term>habit: a stable disposition or character trait</term> is indivisible; it is neither made of points nor of lines. But the intellect wonders at this: why does the **act of prudence** grow? It is because it considers the discrete quantities <note>Individual, countable parts rather than a continuous whole.</note> which it possesses.

# ## On questions of fortitude:
# ## and first through principles.

<margin>On questions of fortitude and first through principles.</margin>

**I**t is asked whether, once **fortitude** <note>In this context, fortitude refers to the virtue of courage and inner strength.</note> is established, "fortifiable" things <gloss>things capable of being strengthened</gloss> are also established? Just as when the power of sight is established, visible things are also established. And it must be answered that yes: for if not, then fortitude could not have <term>phantasms: mental images or representations used by the mind to process information</term>; just as the power of sight could not have visible things. ¶ It is asked with what things fortitude is nourished and governed: the solution is in the first paragraph of fortitude in the ninth subject. It is asked with what things fortitude is assailable <gloss>vulnerable to attack</gloss>: the solution is in the second. It is asked in what manner fortitude is conquering and dominating: the solution is in the third. ¶ It is asked what is the cause of why fortitude is strong: the solution is in the fourth. It is asked with what is fortitude more strong: the solution is in the fifth. ¶ Whether fortitude is stronger with **fear** or with **love**? To which it must be said that it is with love, for love is the cause of fear <note>We only fear losing what we love.</note>. And go to the sixth paragraph. ¶ It is asked whether any virtue can be strong without fortitude? And it must be answered that it cannot. For otherwise, there would be two different types of fortitude. And go to the seventh. ¶ It is asked in what manner a person is **bold**: the solution is in the eighth. It is asked why a person is **magnanimous** <gloss>great-souled or courageous</gloss>: the solution is in the ninth. It is asked in what manner fortitude and prudence agree with one another: the solution is in the tenth. It is asked with whom fortitude is greater: the solution is in the eleventh. It is asked how fortitude is corrupted <gloss>destroyed or decayed</gloss>: the solution is in the twelfth. ¶ Whether fortitude can be a specific virtue without phantasms: the solution is in the thirteenth. ¶ Whether fortitude exists as a **mean** <note>The "mean" is the virtuous middle ground between two extremes, a core concept in Aristotelian ethics.</note> between justice and prudence, and between justice and temperance, and between prudence and temperance? And it must be answered that yes: so that the virtues are greater in the middle than in the extremities; and go to the fourteenth. ¶ Why does fortitude cause victory? The solution is in the fifteenth. ¶ How did fortitude conquer accident? The solution is in the sixteenth. It is asked why fortitude is stronger with equality than with inequality? And it must be answered that it is because its correlates <note>The related parts or terms that define the virtue.</note> are equal; and go to rule B and the seventeenth. ¶ It is asked by what is fortitude defeated? The solution is in the eighteenth.

# ## On questions of fortitude
# ## through rules.

<margin>On questions of fortitude through rules.</margin>

**W**hy is **charity** <note>Original: "charitas," referring to divine or selfless love.</note> stronger in times of prosperity than in times of adversity? The solution is in rule B of the ninth subject. ¶ It is asked, **what is fortitude?** The solution is in the first species of rule C. It is asked whether fortitude has things capable of being strengthened in its potential through an innate "fortifiable" quality? The solution is in the sixteenth. ¶ It is asked in what manner sloth is strong? The solution is in the seventeenth. ¶ It is asked to what a lesser sloth is related? The solution is in the second rule, K. ¶ It is asked by what is sloth caused more: by the intellect or by the will? And it must be answered by making a distinction: namely, that it is caused by the intellect through laziness, and by the will more through distracting anxiety. The reason for this is because the intellect labors in acquiring "species," <note>In medieval psychology, "species" are the mental images or forms through which we understand the world.</note> while the will does so poorly. ¶ Why are idleness and distracting anxiety species of sloth? And the answer is because the intellect has no adherence to the truth because of laziness, and therefore it causes idleness; the will, however, because of the adherence it has to evil, causes distracting anxiety.

# On the questions regarding envy through principles.

# On the questions of wrath through the rules.

## On the questions of inconstancy through the principles.

<margin>On the questions of inconstancy through the principles.</margin>

**W**hether inconstancy has species <note>In this logical system, "species" refers to the specific sub-types or categories belonging to a general concept.</note> just as constancy does? # Part Eleven.

We leave this to the keen mind.
¶ Furthermore, we shall pose many questions regarding any chapter; and every solution will be embedded in every paragraph according to what the text requires: namely, the first question to the first paragraph, the second to the second, and so on. To be brief, we shall not name or assign the specific paragraph, but at the end of the chapter or rubric, we will refer the questions and solutions back to it. However, we propose to solve other questions immediately.

## On questions through the explicit and the implicit.

<margin>On questions through the explicit and the implicit.</margin>
**I**t is asked: in what way are applications made through the explicit <note>original: "explicitum"</note> and the implicit? ¶ How are these terms applied to the question: *Whether God exists?* ¶ How do they apply to the question: *Whether God is eternal?* ¶ How does it apply to this question: *Whether it is good that God is as infinite through His greatness as He is through His eternity?* ¶ How is it applied to the proposition: *Whether God is more active through His intellect than through His eternity?* ¶ How are these principles applied to the proposition: *Whether God is just?* Go to the tenth part of this book, to the rubric "through the explicit and implicit," in which the solutions to these questions are embedded.

## On questions through the abstract and the concrete.

<margin>On questions through the abstract and the concrete.</margin>
**I**t is asked: how is the application of principles made through the abstract and the concrete? And it must be answered that it is through the four modes noted in the tenth part of this book and in the aforementioned rubric. ¶ Through the first mode: as if it is asked: *Do fire and "fire-ness" <note>original: "igneitas"; the abstract essence of fire</note> differ?* Let them be applied to goodness and greatness, etc., along with their correlatives <note>technical term in Lullian logic referring to the active, passive, and verbal forms of a principle, such as "Bonificativum, Bonificabile, Bonificare"</note>, and the difference between the abstract and the concrete will appear. ¶ Through the second: *Whether there is a difference between entity and being <note>original: "entitatem et entum"</note>?* Let accidental goodness be applied through the abstract, and moral good as the concrete, just as "being" is. ¶ Through the third: *Whether there is a difference between heat <note>original: "caliditatem"</note> and a hot thing <note>original: "calidum"</note>?* To this, let substantial goodness be applied to the hot thing, and let accidental good be applied. ¶ Through the fourth: *Whether there is a difference between whiteness and a white thing?* Let accidental goodness be applied to whiteness, and substantial good to the white thing—just as to a white man, who is a substance. And go to the tenth part, to the rubric marked above.

## On questions of the application of the First Figure.

<margin>On questions of the application of the First Figure.</margin>
**W**hether a proof can be made concerning God that is separate from a "proof of the cause" <note>original: "pbatio propter quid"; a proof based on the reason why something is as it is</note> through equivalence? And as when one asks: *Are goodness and greatness interchangeable in God?* To this question, let eternity, power, etc., be applied with their definitions and their correlatives through the rule signaled by "C," so that a circulation of the subject and predicate is made; and go to the application of the First Figure <note>The First Figure in Llull’s system (Figure A) represents the divine attributes or "Dignities."</note>.

## On questions of the application of the Second Figure.

<margin>On questions of the application of the Second Figure.</margin>
**I**t is asked: how is the application to the Second Figure made? For example, if it is asked: *Is there a difference between one goodness and another?* Let the terms of the question be applied to the "ladder of difference" <note>A conceptual hierarchy used in the Second Figure to distinguish between types of difference: sensual, intellectual, etc.</note>. ¶ Further, if it is asked: *What are the most general, the intermediate, and the most specific principles?* ¶ Likewise, if it is asked: *In what way is the Second Figure applicable to or serving the First Figure?* Go to the application of the Second Figure.

## On questions of the application of the Third Figure.

<margin>On questions of the application of the Third Figure.</margin>
**I**f it is asked: *Whether goodness can be great without concord?* Or: *Whether goodness can have concord without difference?* Or: *What are the correlatives of goodness?* Let these be applied to "chambers" B and C <note>The Third Figure consists of "chambers" or "cells" where two principles from the First Figure are combined to find relationships.</note>, and let that which is signified by the signs of the chamber be held. Go to the application of the Third Figure.

## On questions of the application of the Fourth Figure.

<margin>On questions of the application of the Fourth Figure.</margin>
**I**f it is asked: *Whether divine goodness is as great as divine eternity?* And: *Whether God is as powerful through His power as through His intellect and His will?* Let the terms of the present question be applied...

...to chamber <note>Llull uses "chambers" to refer to cells in his combinatorial tables where different concepts intersect.</note> b.c.d. And the terms of the second question to chamber e.f.g. And let it be held that the letters of the chambers signify this: and go to the application of the fourth figure.

And "concordance" is another term: and so with others: let the question be applied to chamber b.c. and let that chamber be exhausted <note>original: "euacuet," meaning to systematically work through every logical combination within a cell until all possibilities are explored.</note> according to the mode of exhaustion of the third figure: and let those things which are drawn from that chamber be applied to the proposition: and go to the application of the exhaustion of the third figure.

# On questions regarding the application of definitions.

<margin>On questions of the application of definitions.</margin>
**I**f something is asked about a subject: let that which is being asked about be applied to its definition: namely, to define it: and to conclude concerning it through its own definition: as if it were asked: *Whether God has an infinite act?* God is an <term>infinite being</term> <note>original: "ens infinitum"</note>; therefore, God is not infinite without an infinite act. And so it is with others. And go to the application of definitions.

# On questions regarding the application through rules.

<margin>On questions of the application through rules.</margin>
**I**f any doubt is asked: let that doubt be applied to the <term>rules</term> <note>In this system, the "rules" are a set of fundamental questions: Whether? What? From what? Why? How much? What kind? When? Where? How? and With what?</note> along with its definition: and let it run through all the rules: and then such a doubt shall be made clear through the rules and their species: and its declaration will cause such a doubt to pass into either an affirmation or a negation. And this rule is infallible: just as a sign which truly and infallibly signifies that of which it is a sign. The same example is given in the nine subjects: and go to the application of the rules.

# On questions regarding the application of the table.

<margin>On questions of the application of the table.</margin>
**I**f it is asked: *Whether there is an act that is infinite and eternal?* let it be applied to the first column: and let it be asked through Rule C <note>Rule C usually corresponds to the question "What?"</note>: What is an infinite act? and what is it in <term>Goodness</term> through the definition of goodness: and what is it in <term>Greatness</term> through the definition of greatness: and what is it in <term>Eternity</term> through the definition of eternity. And this is signified through the third species of Rule C: afterwards, it is concluded according to what the letters signify. And so with others. And go to the application of the table.

# On questions regarding the application and exhaustion of the third figure.

<margin>On questions of the application and exhaustion of the third figure.</margin>
**T**he application of the exhaustion of the third figure is done in this way: namely, that if in a question <term>Goodness</term> is one term: and <term>Greatness</term> is another term: or if Goodness is one term...

# On questions regarding the application and multiplication of the fourth figure.

<margin>On questions of the application and multiplication of the fourth figure.</margin>
**I**t is asked by what mode a man can find twenty reasons for one and the same conclusion. ¶ It is asked how a <term>middle term</term> <note>The "middle term" is the connecting concept in a syllogism that allows one to link the subject and the predicate.</note> is found between the subject and the predicate to form a <term>syllogism</term>. How the major and minor propositions of a syllogism are proven. How <term>fallacies</term> <note>logical errors or deceptive arguments</note> are solved through this art. How other sciences can be easily learned through this art. And go to the application of the fourth figure.

# On questions regarding the application and mixing of principles and rules.

<margin>On questions of the application and mixing of principles and rules.</margin>
**I**t is asked how principle is mixed with principle to solve questions. How principles and rules are mixed to solve questions. It is asked by what mode <term>implicit principles</term> are applied to <term>explicit principles</term>: such as the "hundred forms" or other foreign forms: go to the application of the mixing of principles and rules.

# On questions regarding the application of the nine subjects.

<margin>On questions of the application of the nine subjects.</margin>
**I**t is asked if a question concerns God / or an angel / or the heavens / or man / or the imaginative power / or the sensitive power / or the vegetative power / or the elemental power / or moral matters / to which places one should specifically recur: and find the solution: go to the application of the nine subjects <note>The Nine Subjects represent Llull's hierarchy of being, from the divine down to the physical elements.</note>.

# On questions regarding the application of the hundred forms: and first concerning entity.

<margin>On questions of the application of the hundred forms: and first concerning entity.</margin>
**I**t is asked what <term>Entity</term> <note>the quality of being or existence</note> is. It is asked what the concrete form of entity is. What is the difference between entity and a being <note>original: "entitate et ens"</note>. And it must be answered through the second species of the rule...

On questions of essence.

# On questions of essence.

**W**hether entity and essence are convertible? <note>In logic, "convertible" means the terms are interchangeable in their extension—that everything that is an "entity" is also an "essence."</note> And it must be answered that they are: otherwise being and a being <note>original: "eē t ens" (esse et ens)</note> would not be convertible. ¶ **W**hether there is a difference between essence and being? go to the *Hundred Forms*: and to the chapter on essence.

<margin>
On questions of goodness.
</margin>
# On questions of goodness.

**I**t is asked, what is unity? Why is this goodness one? Why is this magnitude one? Whether in created things goodness, magnitude, etc., differ? And if they differ, it is asked why they differ: to which it must be answered so that unity may be joined with many unities, just as difference [is joined] with many things differing in number. ¶ **W**hat is the <term>concrete form</term> <note>original: "concretum." In Llull’s system, the "abstract" is the quality itself (Goodness), while the "concrete" is the thing possessing that quality (the Good).</note> of unity? and if it is said to be "one": I ask why it is its own concrete. I answer: so that unity may have a subject in which it is sustained, and so that difference may be able to enter between unity and "one" just as it does between essence and being; and go to the third chapter, which is on unity.

<margin>
On questions of plurality.
</margin>
# On questions of plurality.

**I**t is asked, what is plurality? ¶ **W**hat is the source of plurality? what is the cause of the difference of goodness and magnitude, etc.? ¶ **W**hat is the concrete form of plurality: go to the fourth chapter, which is on plurality.

<margin>
On questions of nature.
</margin>
# On questions of nature.

**I**t is asked, what is nature? ¶ **W**hether other substantial principles are natural? And it must be answered that they are, as is clear through the second species of rule C. What is the concrete form of nature? ¶ **N**ature, with what things is it mixed: go to the fifth chapter, which is on nature.

<margin>
On questions of genus.
</margin>
# On questions of genus.

**I**t is asked, what is a genus? <note>In traditional logic, a "genus" is a broad category, like "Animal," which contains narrower "species," like "Human."</note> To which principles is "genus" applicable? **W**hether absolute good is a genus? and so with greatness, etc. **W**hether goodness is more general substantially and accidentally? and it must be answered that it is. For goodness is prior by substance, but posterior by accident. ¶ **W**hether genus is a real being <term>outside the soul</term> <note>original: "extra aiam" (extra animam). This refers to the "Problem of Universals": do categories like "genus" exist in the real world or only as concepts in the mind?</note>? And it must be answered that it is: for otherwise the soul would create the difference between one species and another, which is impossible. ¶ **W**hether a brute animal can imagine a genus? it must be answered that it cannot: for otherwise it would possess science <note>original: "sciam" (scientiam), meaning systematic or certain knowledge.</note>. ¶ Furthermore, because the imagination does not reach an abstract object with line, figure, or color—and so with other imaginings—but it reaches the concrete; yet it reaches the concrete itself along with these [qualities]; and go to the sixth chapter, which is on genus.

<margin>
On questions of species.
</margin>
# On questions of species.

**I**t is asked, what is a species? **S**pecies, to which places in this Art is it applicable? In what way form acts through its own species. ¶ **W**hether species is a real being outside the soul? ¶ **W**hether genus without species can participate with the individual? **W**hat is the concrete form of species? what is the difference between natural and moral species? what are the species of virtues and vices <note>original: "itutū et vitioū," likely errors for "virtutum et vitiorum."</note>? go to the seventh chapter, which is on species.

<margin>
On questions of individuality.
</margin>
# On questions of individuality.

**I**t is asked, what is individuality? how is individuality definable? ¶ **W**hat are the <term>correlatives</term> <note>Llull's unique "theory of correlatives" suggests every quality has an active, passive, and verbal component (e.g., in Individuality: the "individualizer," the "individualized," and "individualizing").</note> of individuality? why is the individual indivisible? ¶ **W**hether the individual would exist outside the soul, assuming that species were not outside the soul? why the correlatives of individuality are not sensible <note>Meaning "perceivable by the senses."</note>. what is the concrete form of individuality: from the fact that individuality has concrete indivisibles; go to the eighth chapter, which is on individuality.

<margin>
On questions of property.
</margin>
# On questions of property.

**I**t is asked, what is property? ¶ **P**roperty, in what way is it an implicit principle in this Art? ¶ **T**he definition of property, to which rule is it applicable? Why is property the reason for the "proper," since it produces the proper thing itself? ¶ **W**hether property is the cause of appropriating, just as difference is the cause of differing. The concrete form of property, from what things is it [composed]? ¶ **P**roperty, how it behaves in natural and moral things. ¶ **P**roperty, in what way is it the cause of the sciences? And so with the mechanical [arts]: go to the ninth chapter, which is on property.

<meta>This page continues the instructional sequence for Ramon Llull's combinatorial logic. Having previously discussed Essence and Goodness, the author now provides a curriculum of "Questions" for the next set of metaphysical categories: Simplicity, Composition, Form, Matter, Substance, Accident, Quantity, and Quality. Each section directs the student to a specific chapter for deeper study.</meta>

<header>On questions.</header>
<sig>t3</sig>

# On questions.

<margin>On questions of simplicity.</margin>
## On questions of simplicity.
**I**t is asked: what is simplicity? ¶ Simplicity is the cause of what? To what is simplicity applicable? ¶ What are the <term>correlatives</term> <note>In Llull's philosophy, correlatives are the internal components of a principle: the active (e.g., the simplifier), the passive (the simplified), and the act itself (simplifying).</note> of simplicity? Go to the 10th chapter, which is about simplicity.

<margin>On questions of composition.</margin>
## On questions of composition.
**I**t is asked: what is composition? ¶ To what extent is composition applicable? It is asked: from where does composition arise? What are the composite correlatives? Whether composition can exist in a composite thing, assuming that its simple principles are not essentially in the subject? And it must be answered that it cannot; for the composite would have nothing from which it would be made, and the correlatives of composition—as well as the second species of Rule D and the first of Rule E <note>These "Rules" refer to the structural letters used in Llull's "Art" to categorize logical operations.</note>—would not exist in the world. And go to the 11th chapter, which is about composition.

<margin>On questions of form.</margin>
## On questions of form.
**I**t is asked: what is form? ¶ To which principles is form applicable? ¶ What is the difference between created and uncreated form? <note>"Uncreated form" refers to the divine essence of God, while "created form" refers to the organizing principles of the natural world.</note> Whether form has correlatives? Why is action part of the nature of form? Whether form can act outside of its correlatives? Why is form beyond the reach of the senses? ¶ What is the <term>concrete form</term> <note>original: "concretum." In this system, the "abstract" is the quality itself (like Form), while the "concrete" is the object that possesses that quality (the Formed thing).</note> of form? Which sensible things are signs of form? Go to the 12th chapter, which is about form.

<margin>On questions of matter.</margin>
## On questions of matter.
**I**t is asked: what is matter? ¶ To which principles of this Art is matter applicable? ¶ Whether matter has correlatives? To which it must be said: No; for if it did, it would already belong to the category of action. <note>For Llull, matter is purely passive; it receives form but does not possess the active "power" found in other principles.</note> From what is the concrete form of matter made? ¶ What is the universal source of matter? Go to the 13th chapter, which is about matter.

<margin>On questions of substance.</margin>
## On questions of substance.
**I**t is asked: what is substance? ¶ To which principles is substance applicable? Whether substance has correlatives? Whether every created substance is composed of form and matter? What is the concrete form of substance? Why is substance self-existing? And it must be answered: because through form it is an agent [active], and through matter it is a patient [passive], and through the conjunction of these it is a composite. Why does substance "stand under" <note>This is a literal translation of the Latin "substare," from which "substance" is derived—the thing that "stands under" or supports other qualities.</note> accidents? Because it cannot exist or act without them. Whether substance is perceptible by the senses? And we say: No; for the senses cannot perceive as much through accidents as substance truly is. And go to the 14th chapter on questions of substance.

## On questions of accidents.
<margin>On questions of accidents.</margin>
**I**t is asked: what is an <term>accident</term>? <note>In scholastic logic, an "accident" is a property (like color, weight, or location) that can change without the thing itself ceasing to be what it is.</note> ¶ Where is an accident applicable? Whether an accident relates primarily to its own purpose or to another? From what does an accident arise? ¶ What is the concrete form of an accident? It is asked whether there are two types of accident: namely, one intrinsic and another extrinsic? Whether the senses can reach the intrinsic accident? Whether the imagination can imagine an intrinsic accident without an extrinsic or sensible accident? Whether the intellect can produce knowledge without intrinsic and extrinsic accidents? And go to the 15th chapter, which is about accidents.

## On questions of quantity.
<margin>On questions of quantity.</margin>
**I**t is asked: what is quantity? Go to the definition of goodness, and define quantity according to the manner of the definition of goodness, saying thus: "Quantity is the being by reason of which the quantified thing quantifies the quantity." <note>Llull uses these recursive definitions to show how a principle operates through its own internal logic.</note> From what does quantity arise? Whether the cause of quantity is "consequence"? What are the primary measures of quantity? What is the concrete form of quantity? Go to the 16th chapter, which is about quantity.

## On questions of quality.
<margin>On questions of quality.</margin>
**D**efinition of quality: in what way can it be found? Go to the definition of goodness, and define it according to the manner of goodness, saying thus: "Quality is the being by reason of which the qualified thing acts upon the quality." Of what is quality an applied habit? Within what things is quality situated? What is the concrete form of quality? From what does quality arise? And why is it an accident? Go to the 17th chapter, which is about quality.

<meta>This page continues the curriculum of the "Eleventh Part," specifically focusing on the "Questions" that a student must apply to the various categories of being. Following the previous page's discussion on simplicity and form, it now addresses the final ten categories: Relation, Action, Passion, Habit, Position, Time, Place, Motion, Immobility, and Instinct.</meta>

<header>Eleventh part.</header>

# On the questions of relation.

<margin>Questions of relation.</margin>
**I**t is asked: to which terms is <term>relation</term> <note>Relation describes how one thing is compared or connected to another.</note> applicable, so that a person may know how to define it? What is a related thing? Whether <term>contraction</term> <note>In Llull’s logic, "contraction" refers to the narrowing of a general principle to a specific instance.</note> is the principle of relation? Whether a principle can exist without <term>correlatives</term> <note>Correlatives are the necessary internal components of any Lullian principle: the doer, the receiver, and the act itself.</note>? Go to the 18th chapter, which is about relation.

# On the questions of action.

<margin>Questions of action.</margin>
**I**s <term>action</term> <note>The process by which an agent produces an effect.</note> applicable to these things so that it may be an explained term? Whether action is the reason by which an agent acts upon what is "actable"? Whether the <term>concrete</term> <note>Llull uses "concrete" to mean the person or thing that embodies a quality; for example, a "lover" is the concrete of "love."</note> of action is the "acted-upon"? With what things is the concrete of action designated and declared? Go to the 19th chapter, which is about action.

# On the questions of passion.

<margin>On the questions of passion.</margin>
**T**o which principles is <term>passion</term> <note>In this context, "passion" does not mean emotion, but the state of being acted upon by an external force—the opposite of action.</note> applicable so that it may be defined? Whether "generability" <note>The capacity for something to be created or produced.</note> is the source of passion? Whether passion is the being from which the "sufferer" <note>The "passus," or the entity receiving the action.</note> arises? Whether the sufferer is the concrete of passion? In what way is passion an <term>accident</term> <note>A non-essential quality that can change without destroying the essence of the thing.</note>? Go to the 20th chapter, which is about passion.

# On the questions of habit.

<margin>Questions of habit.</margin>
**I**n what way is <term>habit</term> <note>"Habit" (habitus) refers to a persistent state, condition, or disposition of a person or thing.</note> applicable to the principles of this Art, so that it may be defined with them? In what way do natural and moral habits differ? What is the concrete of habit, and what provides its "habit-ness"? From what does habit arise? Whether there is such a thing as an internal and external habit? Go to the 21st chapter, which is about habit.

# On the questions of position.

<margin>And on the questions of position.</margin>
**T**o which principles of this Art is <term>position</term> <note>Situs, or the arrangement of parts in a specific place.</note> applicable? With what can it be defined? Whether position is an accident? In what way are the correlatives of beings situated? What is the concrete of position? From what does position arise, and where is it? Go to the 22nd chapter, which is about position.

# On the questions of time.

<margin>On the questions of time.</margin>
**W**hat is <term>time</term>? It is asked: to which principles is time applicable? With what is time multiplied? Whether <term>motion</term> is the sign of time? What is the concrete of time? Go to the 23rd chapter, which is about time.

# On the questions of place.

<margin>On the questions of place.</margin>
**W**hat is <term>place</term>? To which explained principles is place applicable? Whether place is movable? From what does place arise? What is the concrete of place? Whether the "placeable" and the "movable" are signs of place? And it must be answered that they are. Go to the 24th chapter, which is about place.

# On the questions of motion.

<margin>On the questions of motion.</margin>
**T**o which principles is <term>motion</term> applicable? From which correlatives do the correlatives of motion arise? Whether motion is born from the correlatives of nature? Whether "absolute motion" is innate? Whether innate motion is perceptible to the senses? Whether the "movable" is the disposition of motion? Whether in the course of motion there is a mover and a moved? Whether <term>appetite</term> <note>The natural inclination or "desire" of an object to move toward its natural state or place.</note> is the cause of motion? Whether the <term>heavens</term> <note>The celestial spheres or stars.</note> possess correlatives by means of motion? What is the concrete of motion? Whether the heavens end in motion or in the movable thing? Go to the 25th chapter, which is about motion.

# On the questions of immobility.

<margin>On the questions of immobility.</margin>
**W**hat is <term>immobility</term>? To which principles is immobility applicable? What is the "non-concrete" <note>The abstract form of the principle.</note> of immobility? What are the correlatives of immobility? Why is the immobile thing immobile? It is asked: in what way is something that is movable actually immobile? Go to the 26th chapter, which is about immobility.

# On the questions of natural instinct.

<margin>On the questions of natural instinct.</margin>
**W**hat is <term>natural instinct</term>? To which principles is natural instinct applicable? What is the concrete of natural instinct? It is asked: what is the general source through which every <term>form</term> <note>The essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing.</note> acts according to its own species? Go to the 27th chapter, which is about natural instinct.

# On the questions of natural appetite.

<meta>This page continues the curriculum of the "Eleventh Part" of the treatise, specifically focusing on the systematic "Questions" that a student must apply to the final set of principles and biological/psychological functions. It follows the previous page's discussion on the categories of Relation, Action, and Passion.</meta>

On the questions. Folio 117.

<margin>On the questions of natural appetite.</margin>
**I**n what way can <term>natural appetite</term> <note>original: "appetitus naturalis"; in this context, it refers to the innate, unconscious drive of all things—even inanimate objects—to reach their natural perfection or "home."</note> be defined? To which principles can natural appetite be applied? Why do general principles precede appetite? What are the causes of the <term>concrete</term> <note>The "concrete" is the specific thing that embodies a quality; for example, a "desirer" is the concrete form of the abstract "desire."</note> appetite? Whether appetite rests outside of the thing that is desirable? From what does appetite endure? From what does appetite grow? Whether appetite is both a mover and something moved? Go to the 28th chapter, which is about natural appetite.

---

<margin>On the questions of attraction.</margin>
## On the questions of attraction.
**H**ow can the definition of <term>attraction</term> <note>The power of a thing to draw another toward itself, often used here in a biological or physical sense.</note> be made? To which principles is attraction applicable? Whether attraction is in some way of the genus of <term>passion</term> <note>In medieval logic, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note>? Whether the attractor attracts the attractable outside its own essence? From what does the attractor attract the attractable? What is the concrete of attraction? Whether the attractable is the subject of attraction, and attraction itself is the <term>habit</term> <note>A "habit" (habitus) is a stable quality or disposition possessed by a subject.</note> of the attractable? Why is there attraction? Whether the attractor attracts through its own <term>species</term> <note>In Lullian logic, a "species" is a specific form or mental representation.</note>? From which attractions are moral attractions derived? Go to the 29th chapter, which is about attractions.

---

<margin>On the questions of reception.</margin>
## On the questions of reception.
**W**hat is <term>reception</term>? To which principles is reception applicable? Whether reception, in respect to its <term>correlatives</term> <note>Llull’s "correlatives" are the internal components of any action: the doer (e.g., the Receiver), the receiver (e.g., the Receivable), and the act itself (e.g., Receiving).</note>, is of the genus of action or passion? It is asked: where does reception receive the receivable? From what does it receive it? Why does it receive it? Whether the receiver is of the genus of potentiality, and the <term>corruptible</term> <note>That which is subject to decay or change.</note> of the genus of the object? Whether the potentiality moves itself with the object, or the object moves the potentiality? What is the concrete of reception? Whether it is a most general genus, and the receivable a subordinate genus? And whether the receivable has species? Go to the 30th chapter, which is about reception.

---

<margin>On the questions of the phantasm.</margin>
## On the questions of the phantasm.
**W**hat is a <term>phantasm</term> <note>original: "fantasma"; not a ghost, but a mental image or sensory impression stored in the imagination.</note>? To which principles is the phantasm applicable so that it can be defined? Whether phantasms are in the subject in potentiality through the "possible," or in the object through matter? Where does the potentiality receive phantasms? Whether phantasms can be generated without a potential passion? Whether phantasms are "in the becoming" <note>original: "in fieri"; the process of being formed.</note> through sense, or "actualized" <note>original: "in facto esse"; the state of being already completed.</note> through imagination without the intellect? In what way is knowledge or character generated? In what way is the same phantasm received in a different manner in the soul? Why is the phantasm more general in humans than in beasts? Whether the phantasm is the subject or the concrete of the fantasy? Whether the phantasm is constituted from the similarities of the principles? Whether the phantasm is in the sense? Go to the 31st chapter, which is about the phantasm.

---

<margin>On the questions of fullness.</margin>
## On the questions of fullness.
**W**hat is fullness? To which principles is the definition of fullness applicable? Whether a potentiality can be full without its correlatives? Whether a <term>compound thing</term> <note>original: "elementatum"; a physical body composed of the four elements (fire, air, water, earth).</note> is full without the essences of the elements? Whether idleness is a vacuum of potentiality, which is the concrete of fullness? Whether the full can be filled with things that are not full? Whether the correlatives of the principles are genera of fullness? Whether "full" signifies "to be" and "not full" signifies "not to be"? Whether a positive habit is of the genus of fullness, and a <term>privative habit</term> <note>A habit defined by the absence of a quality, such as blindness being the privation of sight.</note> of the genus of emptiness? Whether generation tends toward the full, and corruption toward the non-full? Go to the 32nd chapter, which is about fullness.

---

<margin>On the questions of diffusion.</margin>
## On the questions of diffusion.
**W**hat is <term>diffusion</term> <note>The act of spreading or pouring out a quality, such as how the sun diffuses light.</note>? And to which principles is its definition applicable? How many are the correlatives of diffusion? Whether goodness can spread itself outside another essence without its own innate diffusion? Whether the diffused is the subject of diffusion, and whether it itself is the habit of the diffused? Whether diffusion signifies essence? Whether "diffused" signifies a genus and "restriction" a species? Whether diffusion is the cause of generosity, and restriction the cause of greed? Go to the 33rd chapter, which is about diffusion.

---

<margin>On the questions of digestion.</margin>
## On the questions of digestion.
**W**hat is digestion? And to which principles is its definition applicable? To which correlatives are the correlatives of digestion applicable? What is the concrete or the subject of digestion? Whether the species of potentialities digest and are digested?
