## On the questions of expulsion.

<margin>On the questions of expulsion.</margin>
**W**hat is <term>expulsion</term> <note>original: "expulsio"; the act of driving something out or removing it.</note>? And to which principles is its definition applicable? What are the signs of expulsion, and in which subjects do these signs consist? Whether one <term>phantasm</term> <note>original: "fantasma"; in medieval psychology, this is a mental image or "sensory ghost" stored in the imagination.</note> expels another phantasm, just as in the vegetative life a new leaf expels an old leaf? Whether the act of one <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; a stable disposition or learned quality of the soul, like a skill or a virtue.</note> expels the act of another habit? What is the <term>concrete</term> <note>original: "concretus"; the actual thing that embodies the quality (e.g., a "remover" is the concrete form of "removal").</note> of expulsion? Whether sin is expelled by divine grace? And it must be answered that it is not, because sin was never in grace itself; rather, sin is expelled from the sinner by means of grace. Go to the 35th chapter, which is about expulsion.

## On the questions of signification.

<margin>On the questions of signification.</margin>
**W**hat is <term>signification</term> <note>original: "significatio"; the process by which one thing (a sign) represents or points to another thing.</note>? And to which principles is its definition applicable? Whether a good man is a sign of goodness, and vice versa? What is concealment <note>original: "occultatio".</note>, and to which principles is its definition applicable? Whether a hidden thing is a sign of concealment, and vice versa? Whether being is a sign of essence, and vice versa? Whether an <term>accident</term> <note>original: "accidens"; a non-essential property (like color) that exists within a substance.</note> is a sign of a <term>substance</term> <note>original: "substantia"; the underlying reality or essence of a thing.</note>, and vice versa? Whether the magnitude of goodness is a sign of goodness, and vice versa? Whether one contrary is a sign of its opposite, and vice versa? Whether the imagination can imagine without a sign, and whether the intellect can understand without a sign? Whether an act is a sign of a <term>potency</term> <note>original: "potentia"; a power or capacity to do something.</note>? Whether speech <note>original: "affatus"; the act of speaking or outward expression.</note> is a sign of the mind? Whether a sensible thing is a sign of a sense? Whether a subject is a sign of a predicate, and vice versa? Go to the 36th chapter, which is about signification.

## On the questions of beauty.

<margin>On the questions of beauty.</margin>
**W**hat is beauty? And to which principles is its definition applicable? Whether magnitude is the beauty of goodness? Whether <term>correlatives</term> <note>Things that exist in a necessary relationship, like father and son.</note> are the beauties of goodness? Whether moral virtues are beauties? Whether "greaterness" <note>original: "maioritas"; superiority or excellence.</note> is the beauty of virtue? Whether vices are the beauties of men? <note>This likely asks if vices can masquerade as beauty or if they serve as a dark contrast that highlights beauty.</note> Whether a greater faith is the beauty of a greater law? Whether disposition and proportion are beauties? Whether the ultimate end is beauty? Go to the 37th chapter, which is about beauty.

## On the questions of novelty.

<margin>On the questions of novelty.</margin>

Whether time and place can exist without novelty, and vice versa? Why a second novelty makes a first novelty old? Whether infinity and eternity are of the genus of novelty? Why nobility consists more in antiquity than in novelty? Why new things please men? (Is it because of the smoke on the road?) <note>original: "ex eo quia fumus in via"; this may be a metaphorical reference to the fleeting or hazy nature of new experiences.</note> Whether motion can exist without novelty? ## On the questions of the idea.

<margin>On the questions of the idea.</margin>

Whether the effect of an idea hinders the idea itself? Whether the finite and the new hinder the infinite and the eternal, and vice versa? ## On the questions of mathematics.

<margin>On the questions of mathematice.</margin>
**W**hat is mathematics? Whether mathematics is the cause of all sciences? Whether mathematics is a sign of ideas? Whether mathematics is like a "habit" of the intellect regarding infinite things that can be understood, just as faith is for infinite things that must be believed? Go to the 40th chapter, which is about mathematics.

<margin>On the questions of general rectitudes.</margin>
**W**hy are there six <term>rectitudes</term> <note>original: "rectitudines"; in medieval physics, these refer to the six primary directions or dimensions of space: up, down, before, behind, right, and left.</note>: and why are there six and no more, nor fewer? ## On the questions of monstrosity.

<margin>On the questions of monstrosity.</margin>
**W**hat is <term>monstrosity</term> <note>original: "monstruositas"; referring to biological "monsters" or birth defects—anything that deviates from the natural "blueprint" of a species.</note>? Whether monstrosity is a divination of motion in natural things? Whether monstrosity consists in the middle of a positive and a privative <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; a state of being or a quality that someone possesses. A "privative" habit refers to the lack or absence of a quality that should naturally be there.</note>? Whether a general monstrosity can be given from which particular monstrosities descend? ## On the questions of derivation.

<margin>On the questions of derivation.</margin>

## On the questions of shadow.

<margin>On the questions of shadow.</margin>

Whether ignorance is the shadow of the intellect? Whether sin is the shadow of virtue? Go to the 52nd chapter, which is about shadow.

## On the questions of the mirror.

<margin>On the questions of the mirror.</margin>
**W**hat is a mirror? Why does a mirror receive figures, and simple glass does not? From what does the <term>shadow of the mirror</term> come? What are the principles of the mirror's shadow? Why does a whole mirror cause one shadow, and when it is divided, it causes many of the same kind? And the answer is through this: that its quantity is both continuous and divided. Go to the 53rd chapter, which is about the mirror.

Whether one color can be given under which there are many colored things? Whether color colors the air through its <term>species</term> <note>original: "speciem"; in medieval optics, this refers to the "likeness" or "image" of an object that travels through a medium to the eye.</note>? In what way is <term>color</term> a proper and appropriated passion? Why can sight not reach color without figure? By what mode is one habit above another? Why are there not many different kinds of whiteness? And the answer is because color is a "most general genus": and go to the 54th chapter, which is about color.

# On the questions of disposition and the disposed.

<margin>On the questions of disposition and the disposed.</margin>

**W**hat is <term>disposition</term> <note>original: "dispositio"; in scholastic philosophy, this refers to the state of being prepared or arranged to receive a certain form or to perform a certain action.</note>? Which is a substantial disposition, and which is accidental? Whether a stone is so disposed that it might be endowed with sense? Whether the sense is disposed toward sensing? Whether the sense is so disposed that it might be imagined? Whether the imagination is disposed toward imagining? Whether the imagination is so disposed that it might be understood? Whether the intellect is disposed toward understanding? Whether God is more disposed that He be understood than the human intellect is toward understanding? And the answer is yes, though by means of faith. Whether God is more disposed to be remembered in the memory than the memory is to remember Him? And the answer is yes; otherwise, hope would be in vain. Whether God is more disposed to be loved than the human will is toward loving Him? And the answer is yes; otherwise, charity would be in vain. 

Whether God is more disposed toward creating the world than the world is toward being created? And the answer is no. For the effect is not as capable through its <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passionem"; here meaning the state of being acted upon or receiving an action, rather than an emotion.</note> as the cause is through its action. Otherwise, the heavens would be as capable of being extensively and infinitely large as they were of being created from eternity, which is impossible. Because of this, the intellect recognizes that it is impossible for the heavens to have existed from eternity, and the will greatly rejoices in this knowledge. Go to the 56th chapter, which is about disposition. 

Furthermore, it is asked: whether God is as disposed to act infinitely through His infinity and eternity as He is toward understanding and willing through His intellect and will? And the answer is no; for in God there is no "before" nor "after." Whether God is more disposed toward creating a larger creature than a smaller one? To this, it must be said yes, just as a greater agent is more disposed toward making a greater thing than a lesser one. When all these things are thus considered, the intellect and the will are greatly disposed toward rejoicing.

Go to the 57th chapter, which is about creation and the created.

Given that predestination might destroy free will, would the world be capable of being created, and could the justice of God have its own act within it? ## On the questions of fortune and the fortunate.

<margin>On the questions of fortune and the fortunate.</margin>
**F**ortune, what is it? Where is the subject of fortune? What are the principles of fortune? Whether fortune has more of "being" through its effect than through itself? Whether fortune "fortunes" the fortunate person, or does the fortunate person "fortune" himself with fortune—just as a knower makes himself knowing with the intellect? And the answer is no, because a knower makes himself knowing through understanding, but a fortunate person makes himself fortunate through ignorance. Regarding how fortune is, go to the 61st chapter, which is on fortune.

## On the questions of order and the ordered.

<margin>On the questions of order and the ordered.</margin>
**O**rder <note>original: "ordinatio"; the structural arrangement or "ordering" of the universe.</note>, what is it? Where does order begin? Where does it end? What are the primary principles of ordering? Whether predestination and the heavens can destroy the order of humans, plants, animals, and elements? Go to the 62nd chapter, which is on order.

## On the questions of counsel and the consulted.

<margin>On the questions of counsel and the consulted.</margin>
**C**ounsel <note>original: "consilium"; the process of deliberation or seeking advice before an action.</note>, what is it? To which principles is counsel applicable? Whether counsel has general principles with which it might be general? Whether the discourse of counsel is formed through principles and rules, and not deformed by a lack of discourse through them? Whether the discourse of counsel through principles and rules is reliable, and whether discourse without them is doubtful and dangerous? Whether counsel concerning <term>contingents</term> <note>original: "contingentibus"; events that may or may not happen, as opposed to necessary truths.</note> is dangerous? Why does counsel consist more of what comes before than what follows? Whether ignorance and sin are enemies of counsel? Go to the 63rd chapter.

## On the questions of grace and the graced.

<margin>On the questions of grace and the graced.</margin>
**G**race, what is it? With which principles is grace known? Whether grace can exist in an "undisposed" subject <note>one not spiritually prepared to receive it</note>? Whether grace can exist without charity? Whether hope is "formed" with grace? Whether faith without grace is in vain? Which virtues <unclear>provide</unclear> a greater disposition for receiving grace: the cardinal <note>prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance</note> or the theological <note>faith, hope, and charity</note>? Why is there grace? From whom does it come? How great is it? And whether it is a "proper passion" <note>a unique characteristic or property of a soul</note>. How is grace, where is it, and with what is it? And go to the 64th chapter.

## On the questions of perfection and the perfected.

<margin>On the questions of perfection and the perfected.</margin>
**P**erfection, what is it? From what is perfection derived? With what things does perfection rest, and in what does it fail? Whether the highest perfection can perfect the "perfected" from the "perfect." Whether the perfected can perfect the "perfected" from the "imperfect"? Whether power without action is perfect? Whether the ultimate end <note>the final purpose of a thing</note> belongs to the category of perfection? Whether moral perfection is a sign of natural perfection? Go to the 65th chapter.

## On the questions of declaration and the declared.

<margin>On the questions of declaration and the declared.</margin>
**D**eclaration <note>original: "declaratio"; the act of clarifying or revealing a hidden truth.</note>, what is it? Where does the intellect declare a doubt? In what way does declaration arise as a "habit" <note>a stable disposition of the mind</note>? What is the matter of declaration in this Art? Go to the 66th chapter.

## On the questions of transubstantiation and the transubstantiated.

<margin>On the questions of transubstantiation and the transubstantiated.</margin>
**T**ransubstantiation <note>the conversion of one substance into another, most famously in the Eucharist</note>, what is it? Whether transubstantiation is "in the becoming" or "in the state of having been done" <note>original: "in fieri aut in facto esse"; a common scholastic distinction between a process and a completed act.</note>? Why is there transubstantiation? How is transubstantiation made? With what is transubstantiation made? From what does transubstantiation come? How does transubstantiation persist in time and place? Go to the 67th chapter.

## On the questions of alteration.

<margin>On the questions of alteration.</margin>
**A**lteration, what is it? In what way do natural alteration and moral alteration differ? Whether natural alteration consists of an innate power, and moral alteration through a "born" <note>perhaps "acquired" or "naturalized"</note> power? From what is alteration? Why is it? How is it, where is it, and with what is it? Go to the 68th chapter.

</margin>

**W**hat is infinity? Does infinity have correlates <note>original: "correlativos"; in Lullian philosophy, these are the related aspects of a principle, such as the power to act, the object acted upon, and the action itself.</note> that are co-essential and natural to it? Under what conditions is infinity established? Can infinity be hindered? Whether it is more appropriate for an infinite being to <term>infinite</term> <note>original: "infinire"; a Lullian verb meaning "to act infinitely" or "to make infinite."</note> than for a finite being to limit? Whether the power that fire has to burn an infinite amount of wood—if it were to have it—is a sign of divine infinity and the divine "to infinite"? Whether the power that the human intellect has, enduring for eternity, to increase the number of things it understands to infinity—and in being devotedly wide in its loving—is a sign of infinity and its own "to infinite"? Given that the heavens have an innate memory, and if they were to count and recall infinite days in an eternal motion, it is asked: would both of those memories be a sign of infinity and eternity and their actions, namely <term>to infinite</term> and <term>to eternalize</term>? And the answer is yes: as is evident through the "argument from the lesser" <note>original: "per locum a minori"; a logical rule stating that if something is true in a smaller case, it is even truer in a greater case.</note>; and Rule B <note>A specific reference to the Lullian "Art," where letters represent philosophical principles.</note> cannot deny this; and go to the 69th chapter.

## On the questions of deception and the deceived.

<margin>
On the questions of deception and the deceived.
</margin>

**W**hat is deception? In what way do positive and <term>privative habits</term> <note>original: "habit9 positiu9 & priuatiui"; a "positive habit" is a learned quality like knowledge, while a "privative" one is the lack of a quality, like ignorance.</note> differ within deception? Whether the deceiver deceives himself, and likewise for the deceived? From what does deception arise, how is it made, and how may it be known? With what is it made, and with what is it recognized? And go to the 70th chapter.

## On the questions of honor and the honored.

<margin>
On the questions of honor and the honored.
</margin>

**W**hat is honor? Why is the one who honors <term>prior</term>, and the one who is honored <term>posterior</term>? <note>The author is asking why the act of giving honor is more fundamental than the state of being honored.</note> Why is the one who slanders more slandered than the one to whom the slander is directed? Why can the one who seeks honor for himself never be satisfied by it? And the answer is: because honor is owed to God alone by everyone. It is asked: whether one who seeks honor more for himself than for God sins more than another who sins through greed or through some other sin. Does God require anything else from humans except honor for Himself? What is a greater sign of God's honor: the honor that is "honored," or the honor that "honors"? Go to the 71st chapter.

## On the questions of capacity and incapacity.

<margin>
On the questions of capacity and incapacity.
</margin>

**W**hat is capacity? In what do capacity and incapacity differ? What is the cause of intellectual <term>dullness</term> <note>original: "ruditatis"; literally "rudeness" or "roughness," referring to a lack of mental refinement or slow understanding.</note>? Why is the intellect more capable of counting infinite units in number—assuming it had enough objects—than fire is capable of burning all bodies, even if it had a sufficient supply of wood? Whether the intellect is by its nature more capable of understanding than of being ignorant? Go to the 72nd chapter.

## On the questions of existence and agency.

<margin>
On the questions of existence and agency.
</margin>

**W**hat is existence? What is <term>agency</term>? <note>original: "agentia"; the power or state of being an "agent" that performs an action.</note> Whether any existence can contain as much agency within itself as it has existence? Whether the principles of the "First Figure" <note>A diagram in Llull's "Art" representing the divine attributes (Goodness, Greatness, Eternity, etc.).</note> can exist in any essence without agency? Whether a <term>separated intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus separatus"; a mind existing without a physical body, such as an angel or a soul after death.</note> can understand as much as it exists? Whether the principles can be in a subject without the "power of potential"? Go to the 73rd chapter, which is on existence.

## On the questions of comprehension and apprehension.

<margin>
On the questions of comprehension and apprehension.
</margin>

**W**hat is comprehension? And what is apprehension? In what way is the intellect both "comprehending" and "apprehending"? Why can the senses not comprehend a sensible thing through "sensing" as much as the intellect can through "understanding"? Whether the intellect can comprehend <term>intelligible things</term> more than fire can "ignitable things"? Why are the powers hindered by apprehension and not by comprehension? Whether the heavens moving eternally would comprehend more days than fire would comprehend wood for burning? To which it must be said: yes, because the heavens would cause the days within their own essence; fire, however, would not cause wood within itself nor in another. Whether through the comprehension and apprehension of the intellect, the heavens and fire are similar signs of the infinity of God’s creation of the world? Go to chapter 74.

## On questions regarding discovery and the discovered.

<margin>On questions regarding discovery and the discovered.</margin>

Is discovery an innate <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; in medieval philosophy, a stable disposition or quality of the mind.</note>? Can the intellect find a discovered thing outside of its own essence? How and with what does the intellect find the discovered? Is the discovered the subject of science? Does the imagination find the imagined outside of its own essence? And does a sense find the sensible thing outside of its own essence? Go to chapter 75.

<margin>On questions regarding similarity and the made-similar.</margin>

Why can similarity not exist without concordance? What are the "higher" and "lower" similarities? In what ways are the "prior" and the "posterior" similar? Does God have anything similar to Himself? ## On questions regarding the antecedent and the consequent.

<margin>On questions regarding the antecedent and the consequent.</margin>
**W**hat is an <term>antecedent</term> <note>In logic, the "if" part of a statement that leads to a conclusion.</note>? And what is a <term>consequent</term> <note>The "then" part or the logical result.</note>? Is there a necessary middle ground between the antecedent and the consequent? Can the antecedent and the consequent exist without the <term>correlatives</term> <note>original: "correlatiuis"; the Lullian concept that every principle has an active, passive, and connective component.</note> of the principles? Does the mobility of the object come through the prior or the posterior? Is there an object intrinsic and extrinsic to the act, and is that object prior—either as intrinsic or extrinsic? Go to chapter 78.

What is <term>privation</term> <note>The absence or lack of a quality that should normally be present.</note>? Are generation, corruption, and privation in a subject at the same time and all at once? Is generation active and corruption passive? Is the same agent both the one who begets and the one who destroys? Is privation of the same kind as generation and corruption? Does privation imply an essence? Do the senses reach generation, corruption, and privation? Are generation, corruption, and privation natural principles? Does corruption exist between generation and privation? Does corruption exist between "being" and "not-being"? Go to chapter 79.

Is it possible to know that God does not exist? <note>This question is repeated from earlier in the paragraph.</note> Is imperfection in God knowable? Is the perfection of God knowable? Does the human intellect acquire greater merit by understanding God than by believing in Him? Is God only "understandable" by us, and also "lovable"? Does faith elevate the intellect to understand the Lord as much as charity elevates the will to love Him? In the act of perceiving the Lord, does hope stand between understanding and loving? By what means is it known which law is true? By what means can many truths be spoken in...

## On the questions of philosophy.

<margin>On the questions of philosophy.</margin>
**P**hilosophy: what is it? In what way is there a greater subject for the philosophizing intellect? The intellect: in what way is it very general? In what way is the intellect very skillfully <term>crafted</term> <note>original: "artificiatus"; referring to the intellect being trained or structured by the "Art" (the Lullian system of logic).</note> to reach its objects? Whether philosophy is an image of theology? Whether the intellect, without great disposition and proportion, can be lofty? Whether the intellect fails when proportion and disposition are lacking? Whether the intellect can use its own nature without philosophy? Whether the intellect can be lofty without art? Whether the intellect with art is distant from ignorance? Go to chapter 81.

## On the questions of geometry.

<margin>On the questions of geometry.</margin>
**G**eometry: what is it? What is the subject of geometry? With what does geometry measure the measurable? Whether a theologian can measure the principles of the <term>first figure</term> <note>A technical reference to the "Figure A" in the Lullian Art, which represents the divine attributes.</note> in the same way geometry measures acute and right angles? From which principles do measurements arise? What are the subjects of measurement? Whether quantity is a <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; here meaning a stable quality or condition of these things.</note> of these things? Through which explicit principle is geometry explained in this Art? Whether the nine subjects are the subjects of geometry? Whether geometry can measure the nine subjects according to their own mode? With which principle and through which mode is geometry discussed through this Art? It is asked where the places applicable to geometry are found? And it must be answered: there where quantity is discussed. ¶ In what way does the intellect find geometry and use it? Through what mode does geometry abstract mathematical measurements from sensible things and multiply them? Through what mode does geometry, with sensible angles, multiply angles beyond the senses? Whether geometry produces knowledge of sensed quantity or of quantity beyond the senses? Whether geometry is a subject, or a sign, or an instrument for the theologian to measure nature, and for the moralist to measure morality? In geometry, which measurements are prior and which are posterior? By what mode can geometry measure an extended circular line and <term>square the circle</term> <note>original: "quadrare circulum"; the classic ancient mathematical challenge of constructing a square with the same area as a given circle.</note>? Through what mode can the circle be squared—that is, to measure a circular line with a quadrangular line, and vice versa? Go to chapter 82.

## On the questions of astronomy.

<margin>On the questions of astronomy.</margin>
**A**stronomy: what is it? Whether astronomy depends on geometry? Whether there is another <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>In the medieval geocentric model, the shell of the heavens containing the fixed stars.</note>, or another world, or another starry heaven? ¶ Since the sun is not inherently hot <note>A common medieval scientific paradox: the sun was thought to be made of "ether" (which is neither hot nor cold), but it generates heat through motion or rays.</note>, why does it heat the air? ¶ Many other questions could be asked about astronomy, the solutions for which are involved in the third subject, which concerns the heavens. As if it were asked: granted that there were another sphere, would there be distances and proximities between them in actuality or in potentiality? Go to chapter 83.

## On the questions of arithmetic.

<margin>On the questions of arithmetic.</margin>

What are the correlatives of number? ¶ It is asked in what way the first unity is the principle of number, and the first and second of the third unity? Why is number perfected in three unities? Whether the third unity is as close to the first unity as it is to the second? What is the first multiplication of number? In what way are geometry and arithmetic similar? Go to chapter 84.

## On the questions of music.

<margin>On the questions of music.</margin>

Why are there five vowels, and no more, nor fewer? From what does the voice arise? From what do the consonants arise? Why is this letter 'e' more capable of being composed with other letters in the alphabet than 'a'? And 'a' more than 'v'? And why do 'i' and 'o' not cause consonants as 'a' and 'v' do? In what way are vowels applied to the various elements? It is asked: why is the 'o' in the voice attributed to the heaven? Whether music descends from geometry? Go to chapter 85.

# Eleventh part.

### On the questions of rhetoric.

<margin>
On the questions of rhetoric.
</margin>

**R**hetoric: what is it? Why does rhetoric exist? ¶ What are the principles of rhetoric? ¶ How does the rhetorician <term>color</term> <note>original: "colorat"; a rhetorical term for using stylistic ornaments or "figures of speech" to make an argument more persuasive.</note> and ornament one thing with another principle? ¶ How is the subject ornamented with the predicate? How is the subject ornamented with its <term>correlatives</term>? <note>In this system, "correlatives" refer to the internal structure of a thing, such as the power to act, the object of the action, and the act itself.</note> ¶ How is one relative ornamented with another? ¶ By what method are subjects ornamented with definitions? ¶ How does the rhetorician ornament proportion with a natural <term>middle term</term> <note>original: "medio"; in logic, the term that connects the subject and predicate in a syllogism.</note> of the subject and predicate? ¶ How does the rhetorician ornament a proposition with an accidental middle term? ¶ With which significant words does he color his speech? ¶ Why is a word signifying something shameful not part of the essence of rhetoric? ¶ Why are old age, death, October, November, and such things, signs of shameful meanings? <note>Medieval rhetoric often associated the "dying" months or states of decay with the "shameful" or "ugly," contrasting them with the "beauty" of virtue.</note> ¶ How does the rhetorician praise a friend and disparage an enemy with beautiful words? ¶ How does the rhetorician ornament his words according to his office? ¶ With how many degrees does the rhetorician ornament his words? ¶ How does the rhetorician ornament the substantive with the adjective? ¶ How does the rhetorician ornament and color form with matter, and vice versa? ¶ With what middle term does the rhetorician color the beginning and the end? ¶ Why does the rhetorician ornament his words more with substantial principles than with accidental ones? ¶ How does the rhetorician color his words with the possible and the impossible? ¶ How does the rhetorician color his words with proverbs or examples? Go to chapter 86.

### On the questions of logic.

<margin>
On the questions of logic.
</margin>

**L**ogic: what is it? ¶ With what does the logician conclude by necessity? ¶ How does the logician investigate and inquire into the middle term between the subject and the predicate? ¶ How does the logician treat the <term>five predicables</term> <note>These are genus, species, difference, property, and accident—the ways a predicate can relate to a subject.</note> and the <term>ten categories</term>? <note>Aristotle's ten ways of classifying everything that exists (substance, quantity, quality, relation, etc.).</note> ¶ To which principles of this Art is logic applicable? ¶ Why can the logician not stand against the <term>naturalist</term>? <note>original: "naturalem"; likely referring to a student of natural philosophy or physics.</note> ¶ By what method is it known that this Art is general while logic is particular? Why is logic prone to error and never satisfied, but this Art is never so? Why is logic not sufficient for finding the true law, whereas this Art is? How do this Art and logic differ? Since this science contains logic within itself, why is it easier to learn and more permanent than logic? Go to chapter 87.

On the questions of grammar.

Where is construction to be applied? ¶ Where is orthography to be applied? ¶ Where is the <term>figure</term> <note>original: "figura"; likely referring to the form or structure of words.</note> to be implied? ¶ It is asked, where is the source of grammar in this Art? On the questions of morality.

## The twelfth principal part of this work, which is on habituation.

<margin>
The twelfth principal part of this work, which is on habituation.
</margin>
**T**his part concerns the <term>habituation</term><note>Original: *habituatio*. The process of turning a learned skill into a "habit" or second nature through practice.</note> of this Art, and it is divided into three sections. The first of these is about the thirteen parts into which this Art is divided. The practitioner of this Art ought to habituate himself to these, so that he knows how to apply a question to that place (or those places) disposed for the question according to the condition of the subject matter. ¶ The second part is that he should habituate himself to the mode and process of this Art by holding to the style of the text for proving and solving "foreign" questions in the same way they are explained in the text—just as one example is clarified by another. ¶ The third part is that he himself should have a way of multiplying questions and solutions toward one and the same conclusion, as is signified through the third and fourth <term>figures</term><note>Llull’s "figures" are geometric diagrams used to combine concepts logically.</note>. And let these remarks on habituation suffice for the sake of brevity.

## The thirteenth principal part of this work, which is on teaching.

<margin>
The thirteenth principal part of this work, which is on teaching.
</margin>
**T**his part is about teaching, and it is divided into four sections. The first of these is that the practitioner should know the <term>alphabet</term><note>The "alphabet" in this Art refers to a set of letters (usually A through K) that represent fundamental principles like Goodness, Greatness, and Power.</note> well through the figures, definitions, rules, and the layout of the table by heart. ¶ The second part is that he should explain the text well to the students in a reasonable manner, and he should not bind himself to the authorities of others; and the students should read the text in the schools. If the students doubt anything, let them ask the master about it. ¶ The third part is that the master should formulate questions in front of the students and solve them reasonably according to the process of the Art. For without reason, the practitioner cannot use this Art well. Indeed, it should be known that this Art has three friends: namely, subtlety of intellect, reason, and good intention. Without these, no one can learn this Art. ¶ The fourth part is that the master should pose questions to the students so that they may respond to him. And he should tell them to multiply the reasons for one and the same conclusion, so that they may find the "places" by whose reasoning they know how to respond and multiply their arguments. If, however, the students do not know how to respond, nor how to multiply reasons, nor how to find the places, then the master should teach the students concerning the aforementioned things.

It should be known that there are three degrees of comparison: namely, good, better, and best. And thus this science has three degrees for learning according to itself. Now a person having...

<header>On teaching.</header>

...[a man with] an excellent intellect, grounded in logic and natural philosophy <note>The study of the physical world and nature, a core part of the medieval university curriculum.</note>, and diligence: he will be able to know this art in two months: one month for theory, and another month for practice.

¶ A man having a better intellect grounded in logic and natural philosophy, and diligence: he will be able to know it in four months: two for theory and two for practice.

¶ A man having a subtle and good intellect grounded in logic and natural philosophy, and good diligence, will be able to know it in half a year: namely, three months for theory and three for practice. And if he cannot learn it in this time, it is a sign that he has a crude intellect, and that he does not have good diligence, or he is occupied with other things. And such a man will never be able to learn it. However, to learn this art more quickly, I advise that he first learn the <term>Short Art</term><note>Original: *Ars brevis*. For through that science, by a subtle and grounded intellect, he himself can know the General Art.
